Overall Vibe:
====================
This felt like the Darkest Dungeons version of Civilization- where you have to make the best of a bad situation- that situation being the *Ages System* and the lack of continuity between Ages. Every time you advance from one age to the next you change from one Civilization to another- so from Rome to the Normans to the Americans for example. This feels a little strange at first- especially since I liked playing as the ancient Romans and beating the Russians in the Space Race in Civ 2 through Civ 6- you used to get to define for YOURSELF what it means to be Romans in the Space Age.

The Ages System
=======================
Likes:
-You get to adapt from one strategy to another strategy from Age to Age (new bonuses, penalties etc.) Neat. Not amazing.

-Constant new unique units and structures (we'll talk about structures later).

-It was... different... I guess?... I dunno, comedy comes in threes! Moving on!
--------------------------------
Dislikes
-ARBITRARY. I played multiple runs and *still* don't feel like I understand WHEN exactly an Age is going to end. Forgive me for not reading endless tutorials- I'm a PRO at CIvilization games! I was chosen to LEAD not to READ! (The irony of the length of this review is NOT lost on me, nor my constant capitalization of random words- just imagine I am shouting those words and you get the idea). Anyway, the "randomness" of the ending of Ages really robs you of the full experience of the game. Period.
For example- I ended up finishing the Modern Age (the final stage of the game) without even researching Electricity. This SUCKS, because no matter how quickly I tried to farm culture, gold, production and science- the Ages kept ending before I was good and ready for it to end! (And I was playing on Marathon with max Age time limits- whatever that means).

-Forcing you to play as additional civilizations.
Listen- I love experimenting and trying out other Civs- but MAKING me play as Mexico just because I didn't unlock certain random objectives (that you have to remember ahead of time going into an Age) is RIDICULOUS. Sometimes I would get the notification for "You've unlocked this civilization!" and I was like "I don't freaking care about the Ming Dynasty or whatever- I am stomping Confucius into the ground right now with my Roman Legions!

-Resetting the Map between Ages.
This is probably the single most insane choice they made. Look- I understand, you want to try and keep the game balanced and prevent someone (like me) from DOMINATING THE WORLD in the Stone Age. But come on- scattering my forces to the winds, arbitrarily placing them in cities (you have no control on any of this) whenever an Age begins is MADDENING. I was about to CRUSH CONFUCIUS AGAIN but the arbitrary Age percentage calculator suddenly says "Time's up! Your opponent survives another THOUSAND YEARS" is ridiculous.

And don't even get me STARTED on how Cities DEVOLVE into settlements between ages- which COMPLETELY ruins the incentive for making cities at all. You just max out gold production and BUY whatever you need and use your Capital to try and build wonders. I kept thinking "surely this time the cities will stay" and then after playing 200 turns of an Age, I find out I should have just not made any settlements into cities in the first place. ENRAGING!

Then there is the Progress Meter itself for the Age System. I was dominating the map, outproducing in gold, science, culture and influence

User Interface/Buildings
=======================
I ran into a ton of problems that you will see others talking about (not renaming cities, buttons not working or requiring weird workarounds- accidentally skipping turns if you click too quickly despite having units awaiting orders etc.)
I can forgive some of that as it feels like every game is being shipped half-baked and they use the customers as  Beta Testers (this is just the reality we live in now, I hate it too), but it really felt like this game was not made by someone who plays a lot of Civilization games. It just felt... empty.

The buildings are a problem. Like I said- I like to try and min-max my civilization and reach space as fast as possible- I also try and hog as many Wonders as I can (MY Great Wall, China! Get your own!). I LOVED the idea that I could build every single World Wonder (within reason) inside of a single city like some mad scientist ransoming the world or some hyper-advanced civilization juxtaposed to a bunch of drooling cavemen poking each other with sticks.

This time- I felt like I could hardly construct any Wonders AT ALL- because the Civics and Science research was always lagging behind the Age System Progress Meter. I'm pumping 500+ Culture a turn and I BARELY got through the first two tiers of Civics on MARATHON WITH EXTENDED AGE TIME LIMITS. I had the production and the gold etc- and I frequently found myself being like "Meh, build another Cannon to crush good old 'Whatever-his/her-name-is...'" because my Capital wasn't able to build anything else. (Again, see lack of ability to progress). I understand that this could happen in previous Civ games, but this felt forced- like someone holding your head below water and calmly telling you to not struggle.

Bottom Line....s.....
====================
As I am writing this an interview with either Sid Meier or some game dev is droning on about all the amazing things they did and all I can think is 

"SHUT UP Sid! Stop trying to justify this hand-holding struggle session you dare to call a game to me! Let me crush the skulls of my enemies and nuke people as the Mayans in October of 2012 or whenever that calendar ended!"

This game tries really hard to make you "appreciate" other cultures/civilizations in the one way you should never have to: By Force. The beauty of older Civ games is that YOU got to write the full story of your OWN civilization and defined what it meant to be Romans in SPACE. This game leans too hard into the "reality" that certain civilizations are "gone" and "Others took their place". I get it- not everyone can be a winner like me! Some of us have to LOSE like Confucius, I KNOW! Just let me PLAY THE GAME without INTERRUPTING MY CONQUEST and setting me back and making me wear different faces like some weird Texas Chainsaw Massacre collaboration with the Civilization franchise!

What if I LIKED defying the odds and making Confucius lick DIRT while I built space stations on the Moon or whatever? What THEN SID? HUH?!

And now... a sober moment
==============================
I frequently notice that the games that survive the longest are the ones that do the least handholding and offer the most "write your own story" attitude (think Minecraft, Skyrim, Civ 2-6 and many others). This game has the *potential* like every other entry in the series to do just that, but instead we get a barebones, clearly "monetizable" through upcoming DLCs and "Expansions" version of the game. This entry in the Civilization series feels the MOST corporate and the LEAST loved by the designers, at times I felt myself wondering whether or not ANYTHING was different from Civ 6 to 7, and others CURSING the changes it DID make.

I've played every iteration of Civ and have been waiting for this to come and combine the lessons learned from Civ VI and perhaps shake up the format a little.  After nearly 30 years the way you play Civ hasn't really changed much so I was eager to see what innovations had come in.

And they have shaken it up.  But I'm not sure it's for the better, certainly not at the moment.

There are things I like, the era switches and legacy lines make for a much better quest system that the eurekas from earlier versions.  They let you keep a theme running without sending you off to randomly build 3 iron mines and then a theatre to unlock something, they thematically make sense.  The changes to Barbarians and city states also work well and make the world feel slightly more cohesive. But, if you're already fighting unhappiness because of your conquesting (which makes no sense as citizens historically like the fact that their empire is expanding and that they're masters of the world...) and then randomly, for no apparent reason that unhappiness ramps up as penalty after penalty is applied to further bring you down to widespread revolt, then it's not quite as ignorable anymore.

Anyway, lesson learned as I lost a bunch of cities as they revolted and switched, era changes over and I start afresh with a  militaristic expansionist empire, (who apparently get sad if you expand their empire...because...reasons).

The cities that had flipped now need to be reclaimed as they were fairly key to my infrastructure, so I spend a few centuries fighting for my own stuff back, and in doing so, invite more unhappiness.  Like, what?  I'm liberating our own cities and you guys are mad about it?  Ok....but what really gets me is that the AI Civs that got them have instantly post era change caught up with me in Tech which cuts my comfortable lead off at the knees. I'm playing a domination game here, and domination has gone back to a full elimination of all of the cities/settlements needing conquering, but apparently not keeping without an absurd amount of happiness management. So I restart and consider it lesson learned and will ensure that's better taken care of.  Here's the thing.  I now know that the crisis is going to come in and when, I know that it's likely to make expansion difficult so I start to plan around this.  Yes I@m planning on building a civ that needs to conquer everything in the world, but can't keep any of it without spending forever making sure people aren't too sad.

Then it hits me, I'm not playing against the other civs here, I'm playing against the game mechanics themselves.  My plan has nothing to do with who I'm fighting, it's about structuring a procedure to do what I want without global mechanics getting in the way.  Not reacting to what other civs do as the first play through demonstrated that the AI hasn't improved greatly so you can kinda work around it.

So here I am, not building my massive sprawling empire because it will make my people who literally have conquest in their DNA sad, and playing against what is essentially a giant digital boot that will come down, predictably.

That's not building a civilisation that will stand the test of time, it's conforming to restrictive game design.

I will keep playing and have faith that these things will improve over time.  But more for the fact that I love Civ rather than Civ VII which feels like it's picked up some cheap tricks which to me, guy the experience quite unnecessarily and at a very thematic level.

You know what's going to happen, you know when it's going to happen, and you build to make that function.  It's something I expect from a platform game, not the worlds leading 4x game...it's worth playing, but honestly, feels kinda souless at the moment.

If you're not already a Civ fan, I'd wait for an expansion and come back, if you are, then it's playable and enjoyable, but there's certainly a need for improvement.

I also think that the meta progression added helps increase long-term enjoyment, too.  As I'm deciding between leaders for run #2, I'm looking into their XP trees to see what cool policies + bonuses I can unlock + how to combine them for better future runs.  Admittedly, though, it can be frustrating to "miss" an achievement b/c you didn't know it was there - I ended up replaying the last 10 turns of my first file to capture a few extra cities before blasting off into space to compete an extra legacy path for a "Flawless" achievement I didn't know existed until after the run.

And again, the game isn't flawless:

-The UI has certainly had a ton of deserved scrutiny around it.  I feel that some of that outrage might be a bit over the top, but it has miles of room for improvement for sure.  
-The Civilopedia/Tooltips could be greatly improved.  There were a number of items I tried to look up but couldn't find answers for during my first game.
-AI needs work; I did my first run on Sovereign and other than being at war with half of the world for the first two eras, it didn't feel too terribly challenging.  Even being at war wasn't awful, because as usual a general + a handful of units could defend a town against a much greater force.  I might regret it, but I'm planning on cranking to Deity for the next run.
-Even though the era mechanic is supposed to reduce snowballing, by the time I was a few turns into the modern era I felt like I had pulled very hard ahead of the rest of the world, and it still ended up feeling like I was just clicking through my turns while waiting for my spaceship to blast off.


All that being said - there are a TON more positives for the game that I could list off, and plenty of criticisms as well.  If nothing else, I think that fact should show how good the game is, as it's the games that you really enjoy that you bother writing a review for + become passionate about its successes as well as (constructively) critical of its misses.  If this was an empty shell of a game I wouldn't bother playing more or taking the time to write this review, but I am very happy with Civ 7 in its release version + thrilled to see where it ends up.

So if you're on the fence, consider this review one point in favor of "not a disaster".  Totally reasonable to wait for sales, additional content, etc., if you're more of the patient gamer type, but if you really want to dive in now but are scared to due to some of the negativity, don't let that noise deter you.  And if you just really hate some of the changes to core systems in this game from the franchises history, then sitting this one out for now is totally reasonable, too.  No matter what you do, I hope you are happy with your choice + have a great day!  Happy gaming!

As a long-time fan of the Civilization series, I was eagerly anticipating the release of Sid Meier's Civilization VII. After spending several hours with the game, I have mixed feelings.

The Good:

Innovative Features: The new Era Shifts system adds depth, allowing civilizations to evolve in response to technological and cultural advancements. The dynamic Diplomacy System offers more complex interactions with other leaders, making alliances and negotiations feel more meaningful.

Visuals and Sound: The game looks visually decent, and the sound design and music feel nostalgic and well done. Each civilization feels distinct, from lush jungles to sprawling deserts, and everything in between. The improved art style feels like a perfect balance between realism and the series’ trademark charm.

The Not-So-Good:

User Interface (UI): The UI is extremely poorly implemented on PC and is weirdly slightly blurry. Resources on the map are hard to spot, and the icons for pretty much everything look bad. Notifications are both annoying to click through and simultaneously disappear without any reason. Tactility and telegraphing normally communicated through sounds, camera adjustments, and musical cues are either missing or have regressed into some sort of minimalist alternative. In general, I have to agree with most criticisms on this game, that it feels console-first and hardly geared towards the PC user-base. 


Missing Features: Crucial, basic things are completely missing. You can't automate explorers. A lot of key commands either don't exist anymore or are completely hidden to the player, and you just have to try old combinations that you remember from other games. You can't queue your tech tree at all. There's no quick movement/combat. All advanced options to customize the map, start parameters, and overall game rules are just completely gone. 


Performance:

On the Steam Deck, the game is mostly fine. The touchscreen functionality simplifies control inputs, though some functions were occasionally unresponsive and could be confused with bugs or misinterpretation of actions by the game's UI. The small screen sometimes led to losing track of units, which could be problematic during critical moments. While loading times were longer than desired, overall performance was steady, and graphics were visually pleasing, including the new fog of war system. 


Final Thoughts:

Sid Meier's Civilization VII introduces some exciting new features and maintains the series' charm. However, the UI issues and missing features are significant drawbacks. I'm hopeful that Firaxis will address these concerns in future updates. For now, I recommend waiting for patches before diving in.

Pros:

Innovative features like Era Shifts and dynamic diplomacy.

Visually appealing with a nostalgic soundtrack.

Cons:

Poorly implemented UI on PC.

Missing key features from previous installments.

Performance issues on certain platforms.

Undoubtedly a visual and mechanical high point for the franchise. Civ VII's myriad new systems represent a dramatic refinement of Civ VI's many half-baked design elements (e.g., a bloated and unintuitive civic/policy system, overdependence on pre-planning around tile-yields and high-commitment districts, and a stale diplomacy system, among others). Along with a *very* heavy dose of inspiration from Amplitude Interactive's civ-like game Humankind, Civ VII has achieved the absolute most important thing for any (but especially a Firaxis) strategy game: it's incredibly fun and full of interesting decisions while remaining very intuitive and accessible for all kinds of players. As a die-hard Civ V'er who was pretty disappointed with Civ VI, I'm already prepared to call Civ VII the best entry in the franchise--which it will no doubt become with a few updates and an expansion or two.

Despite this, the flood of negative reviews here is not entirely unwarranted. The UI is very mediocre, there are some strangely missing features from past games, and clearly 2K is continuing to push the needle on how much they can charge for these games with the giant DLC catalog this game will quickly amass.

For those reasons, if you're not absolutely compelled to jump in now, you may very well want to wait on this game and come back once some updates and DLC are out and get your haul of content during a sale. 

BUT, to reiterate, this game does, in fact, kick ass. I think the gameplay design here far outshines its shortcomings on launch or its hefty pricetag. Lord knows we've dealt with these things in past Civ releases, and I think Civ VII will certainly overcome these things in time to become a real highlight of the 4X genre.

HOT TAKE:  THE AGES SYSTEM IS AWESOME

I love how each game is broken down into ages where the focus is completely different in each age.  My favorite is Exploration where everyone rushes to the other continent to find new resources that spawn Treasure Fleets that you have to protect and sail back home.  Each Age is completely different and keeps long games feeling fresh.

HOT TAKE:  DIFFERENT LEADERS IN DIFFERENT CIVS IS FUN

This isn't World History Simulator.  Seeing people complain about "X Leader would never lead X country" irritates me because THIS IS A GAME and in another multiverse, things would be drastically different.  People think the MCU is genius with a zillion different timelines, but THIS has them pressed???

HOT TAKE:  NO BUILDERS IS FINE

Yeah, I do miss the early rush of using Builders to upgrade tiles to get that +2 Production bonus or that Strategic Resource, but the new system does streamline things and makes more sense.  When your city grows population, you decide which tile to focus development and if it's empty, it will be a tile improvement (culture bombing neighboring tiles).  When your city creates a building, it can go in any tile inside borders, also culture bombing if on the edge.

COLD TAKE:  THE GAME HAS LOTS OF ROOM FOR GROWTH/IMPROVEMENT

First and foremost: this is a mobile game, so its interface and the pacing is build as one. It is also cheaper on iOS (4 euros).

A stylistic tower-defence game that lacks a lot of room for the player to explore, leading to a lot of trial-and-error. Each level consists of a street or more with adjacent buildings. You've to figure out which store will be active in the preset buildings so that every customer eventually emptied its wallet by the end of the street. There are no differences between the pedestrians. If they walk on the same side of the street, they'll all have the same amount of money and they'll walk at the same speed. They'll go into the store if there's room.

The differences between the stores are the capacity, speed and income. How do you know what kind of store you'll need? Just choose one and see if it did great or not... Or just click the '?' and click the lightbulb for the hint...

Without any notification of how many pedestrians are coming, and without any info about their expendable money, this is just a guessing game. You'll clear the level if you hit the minimum amount of profit you've accumulated over several days. You'll inevitably fail, as you had no idea what combination of stores you would have needed.

With the preset store placements, the lack of information, lack of freedom and the small success window, Rip Them Off quickly becomes a tedious little game.

This game bills itself as a puzzley tower defense game, but is
none of the above. The way to solve each "puzzle" is to guess
correctly at what kind of shop should go where, and when to
upgrade them. There is no strategy or clue decoding. There is a
help button that tells you the correct answer, and that's
basically it.

Tower defense games give players choices and tradeoffs. Puzzle
games give players the tools they need to solve the puzzle. This
game gives players a bunch of things to try.

Pros: The music is nice. The flavor text is sometimes amusing.
Cons: It's not fun. I have trouble imagining anyone finding it fun.

A hard recommendation here but still one that I'm willing to make. You can see by my play time that I quickly realized what this game was and where it was going and decided it was not for me. However, I believe in encouraging artists and this recommendation comes in that spirit.

Going with the good things first, it's a *very* interesting concept and the aesthetics are beautiful. I love exploration in games but most games make it so hand-holdy that it detracts from the "exploration" feeling, Adriatic Pizza fully commits to it in a very interesting way which I would say is one of it strong suits. The map, traversal and exploration are beautiful and would love to see more done with them. It also has a lot of "mini-games" which mix up gameplay and their execution is good: quick, short and simple mini-games that engage you without overstaying their welcome.

That being said, there were three key areas where the game lost me: readability, story and writing.

To get the most mechanical and shallow out of the way first, like I said, the art direction here is great - that's not up for debate - however, the high-contrast look mixed with the pixelated-filter make readability an issue at times. It made my eyes feel tired very quickly which was made worse by the fact that white is often used as a primary color and a highlight color. This made reading some key aspects of the game hard (items you're highlighting, things you're interacting with, white things in front of other white things...).

Then there's the story which I'll combine with the writing. This feels like a game that was supposed to have a sort of Stardew Valley-ish or Papers, Please-ish kind of narrative. A story that is simple, personal and delivered in a ludo-narrative kind of way. However, from the first impressions it feels like it chooses to go for a sort of traditional ham-fisted exposition-first narrative that detracts from the minimalistic journey you'd expect. Which brings me to the writing.

Leaving aside typos/grammatical errors - which are understandable and to be expected from a non-english solo dev - it feels like the lack of familiarity with the language might have detracted from the script. Character dialogue lacks a humanity and personality making every NPC feel the same, which makes it hard to connect with any of them. In a game in which it seems like "people" would be a driving force, this is an issue.

In conclusion, Adriatic Pizza is an interesting game that's worth a shot and might be best suited to people that look for mechanical experimentation over narrative. It's a fun time and fairly priced so go give it a try if that sound good to you.

You play as a child who's exploring this world of unique biomes. Each biome has different enemies, with different variant attack patterns, as well as an increase in difficulty. You can craft unique weapons, armor, collect unique rings, purchase weapons, upgrades, and “relics” of sorts that can help you with make the best out of your playing style. There are challenges in this game, that honest took me far more attempts to beat than any of the bosses in the game. I believe there are no Iframes and there are times you may get hit more than once in any given second. 

Just like in a game called “tiny rogues” one may say some weapons and builds are easier than others. And there is a tier of best weapons versus the worse or most difficult to utilize weapons. I played on the normal difficulty / middle difficulty. You can explorer different biomes, jump around to a easier place or harder place depending on how you want to play the game. 

I like how you obtain the achievements, while achievement 100% of the achievements is no great tasks, it felt good to actually 100% a game simply by playing it and yes honestly I beat the game with 4 achievements still left.  I returned to my same game and obtained the last 4 achievements in less than 30 minutes. In otherwords there isn't this “rare” RNGness to getting these achievements and at the end of the day I enjoy that. 

The game overall is fun, I was a little bit frustrated by the tracking system of the enemies attacks. But to compensate for this the game does give you nice amount of terrain to try to use to your advantage. While facing the final boss this is not the case, but it took 3 attempts to beat the final boss. Bosses and challenges don't have the exact same pattern of how the fights go, they'll have the same attacks but the order of these attacks are randomized. The location of the enemy is never really the same, or atleast it never felt that way. 

Over all if you like “Tiny Rogues” get this game play it have fun. There's a nice short story, and some light reading, there are some moments that may give you a giggle and others that may frustrate you. But I never felt stuck, I never felt that I couldn't in some way progress.

Must get for any action roguelike enthusiast, who enjoys the bullet heaven/hell elements.

TLDR: Balancing is bad and there isn't enough variation.

I really wanted to like this game. As a big fan of Peggle and the roguelike/lite genre, I had quite high hopes for this game. Unfortunately it did not deliver.

The biggest issue I have is just how luck based it is. With other games such as Enter the Gungeon and Balatro, if you're a good player you can work with what you're given and win very consistently. That is not the case with Peglin. A good majority of perks and balls are just so trash and very hard to make viable, meanwhile there are some that more or less guarantee a win. All in all, the balancing is just terrible. On easier Cruciballs it's fine, but as you get further it becomes really apparent.

The second issue I have is with the amount of variation. Runs are way too similar and just blend together, resulting in the game feeling quite dull and boring after a couple hours. The amount of enemies and board types are far too limited for a game like this. 

Other than that, most of the other issues I have are fairly minor. This game has an incredible amount of potential to be so much fun, but it falls flat in too many areas. I can't in good faith recommend this game in its current state, especially for the $20 price.

If this game ends up getting updated in the future to address these issues, I will update my review. For now though, this game is quite the letdown.

Peglin is a run-based game that mixes Peggle-style pachinko with turn-based combat in the vein of Slay the Spire. You aim and shoot balls that drop down and bounce around different types of pegs, removing or changing each peg as it bounces. Each bounce strengthens your attack, and each attack is executed after the projectile falls into the abyss at the bottom of the screen.

The balls you shoot, as well as the pegs you hit, all have different properties, and you can also collect various artifacts on your run (and different types of projectile). The art is deliberately crude and fun, and some of the music is kinda catchy. The enemy art and attacks in particular are very imaginative.

Anyhow, that's Peglin. Like classic Peggle, there are elements of both skill and chance. This is clearly a small developer, and they seem committed to patching and reworking the game based on feedback, so it's easy to recommend this game.

I do have a couple of complaints:

1. You can toggle the game speed to 1.5x or 2x, but this option feels like a band-aid on an overall rhythm that doesn't work well by default. I'd much prefer if the map movement segments, as well as the character and enemy attacks, were automatically faster (1.5x or 2x), and the gameplay stayed at 1x. Or at least provided as an option. I shouldn't have to keep reaching for the speedup key whenever I'm on the map or when attacks are happening. Map movement and attack animations are just too slow, and 2x gameplay is just too fast.

* After you finish a battle against a group of enemies, sometimes you often find yourself on a "fork" in the map. When this happens, you have to shoot your projectile one last time on the playfield you just completed, but with no enemies to attack. This means you watch your projectile bounce around pegs that no longer give you anything but the occasional piece of gold before it finally drops into fire (damaging your health and forcing a retry) or sends you to your next battle or shop. These segments feel a little drawn-out and pointless and really slow down the rhythm of the game. I think just letting the player choose their route, a la Slay the Spire, would improve the feeling of momentum.

Other than these two issues, this is a fine concept and an addictive little run-based game that has the extra bonus of working very well on Steam Deck. If the concept sounds fun to you, it's definitely worth your time.

Peglin ascends to the zenith of indie game development ingenuity, a veritable paragon of design that masterfully intertwines the visceral gratification of pachinko-style physics with the labyrinthine strategic tapestry of a deck-building roguelike. This serendipitous confluence culminates in an experience that is simultaneously intuitive and profoundly nuanced, engendering a compelling gameplay loop that insidiously ensnares the player in its delightful web, perpetually prompting "just one more run."  It's a siren song of bouncing orbs and shattered expectations, a testament to the power of simple mechanics elevated by ingenious design.

The quintessential mechanic, evocative of the venerated Peggle, entails propelling an assemblage of orbs, each imbued with idiosyncratic properties, into a tumultuous maelstrom of pegs.  These orbs, however, are not mere projectiles; they are instruments of arcane power, imbued with elemental affinities and potent effects.  The "Bomber" orb, for instance, detonates with explosive force, obliterating clusters of pegs in a fiery conflagration, leaving behind a satisfying trail of smoke and cinders. The "Refresh" orb, on the other hand, replenishes the player's dwindling supply of re-rolls, offering a second chance at achieving pachinko perfection, a beacon of hope in the face of impending doom.  Each successful collision triggers a cacophonous symphony of sounds, a delightful chorus of pings, plinks, and booms that reverberate through the digital ether.  This auditory feast is accompanied by a dazzling kaleidoscope of visual effects, culminating in the exhilarating annihilation of the designated targets, often accompanied by a shower of glittering gold and precious gems that cascade down the screen like a digital waterfall.

Yet, Peglin transcends this familiar paradigm by introducing a roguelike progression system wherein players meticulously curate a deck of these potent orbs, each possessing esoteric abilities and synergistic effects. This ingenious amalgamation compels players to judiciously strategize their shots, optimizing their deck to unleash cataclysmic combos and surmount progressively formidable obstacles with aplomb.  Do you prioritize raw power with a deck brimming with "Critical" orbs, hoping to trigger devastating chain reactions that ripple through the peg-filled battlefield? Or do you favor a more nuanced approach, employing "Jinx" orbs to manipulate the very fabric of the game, turning misfortune into opportunity, transforming near misses into resounding victories?  Perhaps you'll embrace the chaos of the "Multicast" orb, duplicating your projectiles and creating a mesmerizing ballet of destruction.  The strategic possibilities are as boundless as the procedurally generated levels themselves, each playthrough a unique and unpredictable adventure.

Further augmenting this intricate gameplay are the panoply of relics unearthed throughout each odyssey. These potent artifacts, ranging from the mundane to the mythical, bestow passive boons and game-altering effects, profoundly influencing strategic decision-making and facilitating a diverse spectrum of esoteric playstyles. The "Lucky Horseshoe," for instance, enhances the player's fortune, increasing the likelihood of favorable bounces, turning near misses into lucky strikes.  The enigmatic "Hourglass of Chronos," on the other hand, grants the ability to manipulate the flow of time itself, allowing for the strategic undoing of ill-fated shots, a rewind button for the pachinko enthusiast.  These relics, combined with the ever-evolving deck of orbs, ensure that no two runs are ever truly alike, each journey a unique tapestry woven from skill, strategy, and a healthy dose of serendipity.

But Peglin's brilliance lies not only in its intricate mechanics and strategic depth, but also in its remarkable accessibility.  The game's difficulty curve is expertly calibrated, offering a gentle learning experience for newcomers while providing a formidable challenge for seasoned veterans.  For those seeking a more relaxed experience, Peglin offers a variety of difficulty modifiers, allowing players to tailor the challenge to their liking.  Whether you're a seasoned roguelike aficionado or a casual gamer seeking a delightful diversion, Peglin welcomes you with open arms.

This accessibility, combined with the game's inherent replayability, ensures that Peglin remains engaging and captivating for countless hours.  The allure of unlocking new orbs and relics, discovering hidden secrets, and achieving ever-higher scores provides an irresistible incentive to embark on just one more run, to delve deeper into the enchanting world of Peglin and uncover its myriad mysteries.

And what a world it is!  The vibrant and variegated color palette, reminiscent of a psychedelic dreamscape, assaults the senses with a joyous explosion of hues.  Whimsical character designs, imbued with personality and charm, populate this vibrant world, from the stoic owl presiding over the game board to the mischievous gremlins that gleefully obstruct your path.  Fluid animations breathe life into every element, from the bouncing orbs to the crumbling pegs, creating a mesmerizing spectacle that is as captivating as it is chaotic.  This whimsical presentation impeccably complements the game's lighthearted tone and contributes to an overarching ambiance of joyous, albeit strategic, destruction.

In summation, Peglin is an exemplar of innovative game design, a captivating amalgamation of familiar mechanics and novel concepts that enthralls and delights in equal measure.  With its addictive gameplay loop, profound strategic depth, enchanting presentation, and commendable accessibility, Peglin unequivocally deserves a place in the library of any discerning gamer, a veritable gem that shines brightly in the often-crowded landscape of indie games.  It's a game that will steal your time, challenge your mind, and leave you with a smile on your face, a testament to the enduring power of creativity and innovation in the world of video games.

I get that it's a rogue lite and the entire idea of a pachinko adjacent game is that it's kind of random but, even with these things in mind, I feel like it's a little too random. You get to pick 1 of 3 random relics at the start, and there's quite a bit of variance in relic power levels. Enemies don't show their intents (in terms of damage dealt and how far they'll move) so, even if they aren't random, they may as well be. Board layouts (like where the critical hit blocks are) are random. The order you get your balls is random. Which balls you can buy are random. I feel like there isn't a single area of the game where you get to have a meaningful impact on what's going on. 

Outside of this, there are some design choices that I think just make the game frustrating. 

Winning fights doesn't guarantee any prize. You are given the choice to buy balls, pay to upgrade balls, or pay to heal. This means that fighting, the core mechanic of the game, feels worse than chests or even events. 

Unless you have specific balls (which you must first randomly be offered, then happen to draw at the right time), you can only hit the front enemy in the row. This leaves little room for strategizing about where to focus your efforts and means enemies with ranged attacks can repeatedly pelt you from afar. 

Your starting balls are just basic damage dealers with no special effects and even the very first fight can be a swarm of a ton of enemies. Because of this, acquiring new balls to open up new options is essential. But balls cost money and you're only offered a limited selection of them after each fight. This means you're obligated to buy early just to have a ball that isn't garbage, but you might be spending your very limited money on something you don't really like, which feels bad. Given the number of other things to spend money on (ball upgrades, healing, removing balls, buying artifacts, interacting with certain random events), I feel you should get at least 1 free ball per fight victory. 

I really enjoyed Peggle when I played it years ago, but Peglin always just leaves me feeling frustrated. I don't think the highly random gameplay suits a rogue lite well, where some bad rolls can end your run and send you back to the beginning. And beyond that, I don't think the rogue lite elements added were particularly well handled.

[h1]SUMMARY[/h1]
Zombies Ate My Neighbors but bad....

So I was looking forward to playing this game based on the trailer, but actually getting to play it is another thing entirely. It has a somewhat enticing pixel art-style, but that's where the positives begin to end. First we see our first red flag on the intro cutscene, which is nothing but a wide open barren space, where the people who you need to rescue get kidnapped, for no other reason than Santa "hates metal!".

Getting to actually play the game, it controls fine, the shooting mechanics are...alright...But one thing that immediately stood out to me was the underperformance of the voice actor for the main character. He sounds very amateurish and does not quite match the portrayal in the game. From there, things only deteriorate. The levels are huge wide open spaces, when they should be tighter and more claustrophobic, or at least have more things going on in the environment. Everything just feels so empty. On top of that, there are discs you have to collect to buy upgrades, buy ammo and upgrades with, which involves freeing people, killing elves, and destroying the environment. That's right, so expect to spend minutes at a time making sure you destroy everything in a level for all those little discs so you can afford your upgrades and ammo. Tedium. That is what we call tedium.

Now it would be okay if that's where it ended but the gunplay is not very satisfying either. The elves apparently all die the same way, no matter if you shoot them, burn them, explode them, or "glory kill" them (yes, you heard me right, there are glory kills in here), so the responsiveness to your actions doesn't feel that interesting or fun.

Furthermore, the game just does not get very much more interesting. While in the game this was inspired by, Zombies Ate My Neighbors, you used unique AI and mechanics to create themes for levels, none of that is present here. Virtually all the enemies are identical to one another with the only standouts being the bosses. In ZAMN, you had chainsaw psycho's, killer dolls, zombies, aliens, the giant baby, giant worms, and a dozen others. Here you have elves, and gremlin looking things. That's it. The AI and abilities between them is not that particularly different, nor do they look drastically different from one another, making them blend in with each other very easily.

What really kills this game for me is the progression system. There's a little over a dozen levels, and then it ends. The reason for this being that you expected to die, a lot, akin to an arcadey experience rather than a more home entertainment experience, and it only takes 4 hits for you to die. In ZAMN, you have around 40 or so levels, and it gradually progressed with you needing to use your arsenal to defeat certain enemies and explore the environment, cutting down over-growth, blowing up hedge-maze walls, and so on. Nothing like that is here. You have a melee button and you just bust down doors and make your way forward.

There is very little to like about this game, really only grabbing your attention if you enjoy shooting up elves, with very generic, low-effort metal music playing in the background.

[h1]OVERALL SCORE[/h1]
Highly Not Recommended

[h1]REPLAY VALUE[/h1]
Above Average

**Also wanna add, the music is killer. Fits the game so well!**

There aren't as many weapons to choose from, but personally I felt that there were too many in ZAMN and a lot of them basically did the same thing or were useless.  In this case, you get four main weapons and a handful of super weapons, as well as traps you can deploy to either distract or destroy your enemies.  You also have a melee weapon which comes in handy as you will run out of ammo often.  Thankfully, it's easy to get money in the game to buy more ammo, so it's really not a major issue.

The game is set up as a roguelite, so after each run you are able to upgrade different things, like your weapons or health, and try again.  My only issue is that since there are so many levels, you obviously end up repeating the first few levels a lot.  Maybe that's just me, but it would be kind of nice to have a level select or skip once you reach a certain checkpoint in the game.  I wouldn't say it's the worst game I've ever played for lacking this feature, though.

I only have two gripes with the game - first, the lack of health powerups.  You are able to upgrade your health to six hits, but good luck getting back to six without literally scouring every inch of every level, and even then, unless you do a glory kill on every enemy, it's nearly impossible to get the health powerup more than maybe once or twice a level.  So you're sort of forced to pick off your enemies from a distance to avoid getting hit too much.  Again, not a deal breaker, just sort of ehh.

My second gripe is the voices.  I thought the little comments from the elves calling you naughty were cute at first, and the main character's growly quips were cool, but it gets extremely repetitive after several levels.  The elves basically say one of two things each time you kill them, and the main character says maybe five things just at random.  I can usually tune it out, especially with the music up louder, but it's still a little annoying.  Either have more variety in the things they say, or lessen the amount of times they say them.

Overall, considering the huge pile of garbage that is most Steam holiday games, this one is much more polished, much more fun, and worth the price.  If you're not into the metal scene or are offended by others making fun of Christmas stuff, then clearly this game isn't for you.  But you can't act surprised - it's a loud, silly game that shows you exactly what it is on the package.

I paused for a while before writing this review because Enter Digiton is a real mixed bag.

Absolutely gorgeous visuals - unique, striking, clean as hell, and memorable. The visual design of the entire game is phenomenal.

Instant deaths are common, particularly when falling into the numerous death pits. At one point I got stuck in a little alcove because I needed to perform an upwards dash to get out but couldn't because there was an NPC standing directly where I needed to jump and hitting up would just interact with it ad nauseam. The issues go on. Many of these things could probably be remedied without overhauling the entire game, but in its current state, it's a bit rough.

I'm going to recommend Enter Digiton due to its inspired visuals and overall presentation, but go in understanding that you'll need to be a huge metroidvania fanatic to overlook its many faults.

I got this game on sale for less than 1€ and I'm not sure if it's even worth that much. I wanted to get at least halfway through before posting a review despite noticing many of the issues I'm about to point out almost immediately, but after half a dozen deaths on the very first boss, I can't be bothered.

The first and biggest problem is the total lack of control customization (or any kind of options menu at all, really). If you have a QWERTZ keyboard setup, the game is unplayable, as the block button (Z) is miles away from the rest of your controls. If you press and hold 3 keys at the same time, your controls will lock up, so if you want to jump and dash diagonally, if you hold the spacebar for too long, the dash just won't activate. The up arrow is used for interacting with NPCs as well as advancing the dialogue, so if you try to skip through, you end up opening the dialogue box again. The range of the interaction is massive, so if you try to dash or attack up anywhere near them, you'll open up the dialogue when you didn't want to.

Regular enemies follow very basic movement patterns and seemingly serve no other purpose than to be a minor inconvenience on your way. They also have no hit confirmation, making whether you hit them or not a total guessing game. Enemy projectiles track to an insane degree, which makes the aforementioned inaccessible block a requirement to get through certain areas. The environment is drab and the only major difference in locations besides the enemies is the single color used per area. Every single platform in the game has a curved end so you can jump onto the edge of a platform only to inexplicably slide off.

The last update by the dev was about a year ago and he doesn't seem active on social media, so I highly doubt any of these issues will be fixed anytime soon.

It depends which area you take first. By accident I tackled the most difficult one first it seems, "marshall rabbit" without any upgrades is probably the most difficult boss in the game. There are bonus bosses after you beat each main boss, the game warns you to gain all 3 main abilities first, but to be honest the extra bosses didn't really felt like an "hardcore post game" challenge, they were all stationary and had pretty clear telegraphed patterns throughout, but either way they were fun to fight at least, there was enough freedom with the stage layout that you could optimize them pretty well. Would have like an boss rush mode or something like that.

The last boss was also pretty fun although it was more an autoscroller plattformer, still a welcome change of pace I suppose people who struggle with plattforming will have more problems there than me.

Still I was a bit disappointed by the last area, this one you can only access when you beat the 3 other main areas. I expected that the game now demands mastery over the 4 traversial skills with finnicky plattforming sections that bring out most of the potential of the games movement, but it didn't happen. Variety is the biggest problem here the level designs feels most of the time rather uninspired. It's okay for the short time, but I didn't encounter anything interesting. The level which is totally dark is probably still the most unorthodox one, when you have to push invulnerable enemies into spikes. (which was repeated in the last level again)

So yeah like I said not really a metroidvania, more like 3 open levels you can do in any order for accessing the 4th open one, all of them are interconnected by a short streamlined tunnel, since you already have a map of any area which shows you completely it's layout (no automapping) there is not really a sense of discovery. 

I couldn't bother getting 100% either, but still I obtained the achievment I suppose since the extra bosses came with an update it's now possible to achieve above 100% dunno if that was intentional, well it helped me obtaining all achievements without having to care about backtracking for every nook and cranny. Wasn't really motivated for this to be honest. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

So if you don't expect an metroidvania and rather a fun short little midcore plattformer, you're good to go.

Genre:
-Metroidvania 

Fit for me:
-Top 3 fav genre, so great!

Pros:
-I love the monochromatic, minimalist aesthetic.  It looks awesome.  Each biome has a distinct color and each one fits the Digiton World really well.  The art design really reminds me of Kunai or Gato Roboto, but I think Enter Digiton's art design may be more unique.
-Really well designed cohesive interconnected world that all fits really well.  This game gave me some Ato vibes, but I thought that the world building was much better here, and the biomes made more sense.  Each biome has a distinct theme, color palette, and unique enemies.  No one biome felt too difficult.
-Solid sense of progression w/ plenty of upgrades available to be unlocked.  You will gain 4 major abilities that you can use at any time, and you can wear one mask at a time.  Each mask has a strength and weakness attached to it, so there's some strategy to selection which I really liked.
-Good amount of collectibles make exploring really rewarding.  After unlocking a new ability, I always was excited to go back and try to find collectibles that I may missed in one of the areas I had already completed.
-The multipurpose shield was a smart choice.  It can be used to block, thrown like a sword, or can be thrown under you, giving you such extra air to try and find some secrets.


Cons:
-Not as responsive as the best metroidvanias out there.  It feels like there is a very slight delay.  You can't spam the block button or the dash, but it's possible that the dev thought the game would be better w/ a more methodical approach.
-You can't mark anything on the map and it doesn't tell you where you've already found items on the map.  Even w/ a guide, you'll probably struggle to find everything b/c you won't remember which items you found, and which you missed (I'm at 99.5% completion, lol).
-There's too much backtracking and it feels a bit too linear.  You will likely go through every biome a couple of times, but ultimately, you are forced to go the exact way that the dev wants you to go.  You must get every key in a specific order or you won't be able to progress.
-You can't rebind the controls and I'm not a fan of using z,x,c.  As a whole, this game is a bit rough around the edges.  It could use some modern quality of life updates.

Thoughts:
-I had a good time for most of my 7+ hours.  This is a creative metroidvania that should please most fans of the genre.  This isn't the most creative game out there, but it checks all the boxes for a well designed and interesting metroidvania.  It has a really nice difficulty curve that won't bore you, but also won't make you want to break your keyboard.  This is an easy recommendation when on sale.

Consensus:
-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  If you have already played the big guns of metroidvanias like Hollow Knight, Ori, and the Messenger, then this may be a good choice for you.  Support this solo dev and add Enter Digiton to your library.

Forgotten fields has a nice soundtrack mind you, but game sound effects were zero budget.

[h3]Minor issues[/h3]
As game mechanics go, it's very simple, not un-intuitive, but it never does anything with the game mechanics beyond the simple WASD and Q to jump.  The character often gets stuck trying to navigate past furniture, sometimes placed un-necessarily.  Some accomodations for this do exist, but I had to save and restart the game 3 times when the mouse just stopped responding at various points.

There are many cool areas in the game and fun parts, at least one of them which had me asking, [i]that's cool but what was the purpose of adding that to the game[/i]?  Which is the reason I say the game feels unfinished, some really nice parts to the game, and some parts that feel they got rushed.  The game lacks story arc, it tries to create one by having this underlying story inside the story, but since their arcs do not mirror at all, it merely confuses the player.  3 hours of clicking through dialog that would take 4 hours to read, basically destroyed all immersion the game could have had.

The most boring puzzle platformer I've ever forced myself to play.

This game has huge potential. The character controller is mostly smooth, I only got stuck a couple times and had to reload the last checkpoint. The character's movement direction is based off where your HMD is facing, I'd appreciate being able to turn that off. Sometimes you're sitting in the middle of the level and have to reset your seated position multiple times to face the right direction.

The crafting works nicely, but there's only 1 useful item currently. The first time this item is used in the story is absolutely useless, I just crouched and got by undetected.... 

The environment seems OK, but could use way more polish. The trailers look way nicer than the actual game (I have a 2080ti), but the game does run smoothly and pretty solid around 120fps but there were lots frames dropping.

The story seems pretty lack luster. The level design is tedious and the pacing is very slow. You'll find yourself taking 5 minutes to run to one end of the map just to flip a switch then run all the way back to where you came from just to climb a ladder or flip another switch. Or go down a ladder, for absolutely nothing to happen, so you go back up and finally an event is triggered. To which you then run to the other side of the map, solve a puzzle, then have to run all the way back and down the same ladder you already went down and back up.... 

The puzzles to open doors or turn on / repair machines are probably the most interesting aspect to this game... However I feel they lack imagination and are very generic. Tilt the platform to put the ball in the hole. Pull some levers to reflect light off some mirrors... Kinda meh.

These games do "Third-Person VR Puzzle Platformer" well, because they break the monotony of traveling through a level with combat... Something Rinlo has none of?

[h1]Simplicity and Artistry Make Good Games [/h1]

I hate story-focused games, and I'm a gamer who prefers gameplay over graphics. I like games with interesting mechanics and reasons to replay for hours and hours. I'm talking about games like [i]Monster Hunter, Elden Ring,[/i] and [i]Dead Cells[/i]. And then there’s this game—a story-focused game where the gameplay consists of clicking and admiring the artwork. A game I beat in less than an hour. Surely, I would hate this, but surprisingly, I think this game is a true hidden gem.
The simplicity of the story, combined with some strong themes, is this game's greatest strength—anyone can relate. Naturally, some people will be turned away; it is a love story, after all. But I would urge anyone who’s even remotely interested to give it a try. It’s a nice breather from the gaming landscape. Sometimes, these big AAA games have long, boring stories with some cartoonish villain named something like [i]Gilgamesh, Lord of Chaos[/i], and I often get lost in the absurdity of it all. That’s not to say that good, complex stories like Baldur’s Gate can’t exist and flourish, but I think a lot of games could look at this and take notes.
There are no tedious monologues or lengthy tutorials. You don’t have to look at some poorly rendered 3D model and ask them generic questions such as “[i]Do you have any jobs for me?[/i]” or “[i]What can you tell me about {insert quest-relevant thing here}?[/i]” All you need to play this game is a warm blanket on a cold night and some tissues. That’s all you need to know. It’s a simple game that looks good and has a heartwarming story. It took me less than an hour to beat but had more of an impact on me than some of these AAA games could ever dream of.

I think I paid less than a dollar for this game and I think that I've been given a memorable experience for quite almost nothing. There's a lot of love put into this small project, I was even more impressed when I learned that the creator also made the 3D assets for the game, with great attention to the creatures. 

There are genuinely unnerving moments in the game for people who read the other reviews and think of this as a just a lovecraft beach walking simulator. This is helped by the chilling score and phenomenal use of scale. Yes, there's a beach with lovecraftian idols and shipwrecks on it, but what they build up to makes these points trivial. There were many unexpected gameplay moments that had me more engaged with the game than I thought, such as the use of the Artifact in later levels. 

You can die but the game doesn't punish you too much and makes use of frequent save points. There are some sections where you might not realize that you need to run from an enemy, but these parts are relatively short. Puzzles just require a bit of observation and fiddling, but if you're paying attention it's not hard. Also as someone who loves to find hidden details and explore, I was very satisfied. 

I'll be brief with things I didn't care for, and that's the weak narrative, but I can see why the game needs it. It also makes sense for some things to feel aimless or confusing, considering the protagonist cannot comprehend most of what's occurring between ancient scheming gods. The voice acting quality varied from scene to scene, but it's fine for a small indie project. Notes collected throughout the game had spelling errors and sometimes didn't line up with the narration.

Last thing, I will give a platinum star to visual design and modeling, pick any review and it will praise the same things, just needed to put the obligatory "AMAZING GRAPHICS" part of the review.

I always try to give games the benefit of doubt but this one just doesn't have what it takes - not as a released game.

Open world - nope.  The actual area is very small and limited to only a couple of notable places.  I actually tried running to the edge of the world and once you leave the small initial area there is nothing.  I ran into the invisible wall that marks the end of the world so I know I got to the end. You can't survive out there nor even build structures (not unless you want to ferry the materials out) because the necessary resources are not out there.  Building a big house substantially outside the initial play area is probably the only way to make this game last more than one day.

Crafting - nope.  I go into these games looking for to build up on the technology tree.  But there is no tree.  There is an axe, a pickaxe and a hammer.  No way to upgrade those.  No better versions.  No swords, no bows, nothing else that is a weapon. Also no armor.  It is necessary to build some crafting tools but only so when one dies one doesn't have to run across the entire map again.  The basic tools are all that is needed to build all of the buildings.

Buildings - yes.  You can build buildings.  Wood and stone.  This would be the most "complete" part of this.  However that doesn't mean there are a lot of options.  Definitely less than 20. And there doesn't see to be much point in doing that.  I did seem to be able to escape the druids in them but I was concerned that it seemed more like because they couldn't figure out how to get through the door.  There is no weather to be protected from, the buildings do not allow one to heal (even though there is a bed), there does not even seem to be a requirement to use them for crafting.  I put a bed and chest in one but not sure that was even required.

Gameplay - not really.  Not really my thing but it seems like the only effective way to proceed through the game is to die.  Repeatedly.  Retrieving the goods to keep one alive, due to no technology means that getting the necessary materials will likely cost you more health than what it is worth.  I didn't solve the plot mystery because I had run out of the technology tree and seen all of the locations mostly before I even thought to look at it.  I am not really a great fan of the druids respawning in the same spot over and over.  At one point I had to kill about 10 of them and I knew the only way that was going to work was if I deliberately planned for my death and respawn to finish them off. For the vast majority of people I suspect they will find the actual play easy but irritating because there is no real way not to just expect to die. And the actual effective game area is very small.

I really wish I could have given this game a thumbs up, but I am too disappointed with my experience and a lack of response to do so. My story is as follows:

Having played the original ChronoBreach, I was incredibly excited to find out this game had managed to sneak out. I purchased it and started playing, but after a while thought something was off and looked at the Steam FPS counter down in the corner and saw an FPS count in the low 40s. "Huh," I thought, "that's weird. I've got a pretty sweet computer and am having no issues on any other application, yet I'm only getting about 40 frames per second." The game didn't feel very tight, unlike I had remembered, and after not too long I closed it down.

I loaded back up the original game on a whim and was immediately impressed again. The action felt quick, exciting, and smooth. I looked down into the corner, and saw that I was getting 60 fps. Even though I had a 120Hz monitor, it wasn't a big deal that it was capping at 60, since everything felt great regardless. I completed the game in a short amount of time, and after that, decided to give this game another shot.

I was immediately disappointed. The gameplay felt lethargic, slow, unresponsive, and somewhat inactive, and the game became more of a strategy game than an action shooter (normally, I like strategy games, but not like this). I look down at the FPS counter -- 38.

Eventually I decided I wanted to get all the weapons, so I decided to start using the arena to get circuits. And things started to go horribly wrong -- at one point, my FPS dropped down to 18, and it felt like I was in constant slow-mo. I would guess this game uses a frame-step tool, which works well with the timer, but it can cause things like this to be major issues.

My FPS never recovered. I was entirely unable to get above 30 fps after this, and I'm still disappointed that these issues are occurring on a computer with an 8-core 2.2GhZ CPU, 16G RAM, and a RTX 3050 Ti.

To the developer: I decided to do some more digging and found out the game was made in Node.js. While this is certainly a creative way to make a game, if it cannot have consistent framerates on overpowered builds that struggle nowhere else, I'm going to have to recommend you discontinue use of the framework.

[i]A beautiful Sci-fi puzzle game with a relaxing pace and a deep story.[/i]


Boinihi is the fifth opus in the Black Cube series but the first one to be played at the 3rd person. It has an hybrid gameplay where we control the main character movements with the keyboard while the exploration of the screen is done with the mouse as in  traditional adventure games (left-click to interact with an item, right-click to open/close the inventory). 
Pressing the F key also highlights any clickable items on the screen.

We start the game without knowing anything, only to understand that we play as a lone astronaut who just landed onto an unknown moon, and that he will have to explore it to uncover and understand its secrets.
The astronaut movements feel a bit clunky at first and the interface needs a bit of time to understand it, but after some getting used to, we are free to roam through 4 beautiful worlds that clearly have some Asian inspiration in their design.

Paying attention to details, reading everything carefully and taking notes on paper is mandatory to solve puzzles and progress in the game.
Helped by the mysterious moon inhabitants and the ship AI, we will find a mysterious codex whose design was inspired by the Voynich manuscript, but proved itself to be much easier to translate.
After a thorough exploration of the moon flora, we will also learn how to brew herbal teas and make essential oils while meditating. 

Great care was taken in the design of the different worlds as well as the different books and documents in the game. I was very impressed to see how similar-looking the codex content was to its famous model.
The game is a pleasure to the eyes and I enjoyed taking the time to observe every little details the dev has ingeniously embedded in its design.

Several videos are progressively available during the game and reveal more about the game lore as well as its making-of.
Do not hesitate to also check the bonus folder in the install folder to find more videos, the beautiful game soundtrack and a preview to a comics giving more insights into the game story.

I definitely recommend this game as any other games in the series to anyone who enjoys deep Sci-fi stories and puzzle games.

The game is so fascinating with really good story and quite good mechanism. I really enjoy playing it. I recommend the game to anyone that likes mystery and entertaining game. The puzzles are sometimes quite hard to beat, but if you concentrate and play the game, listen, read notes etc. the story revolves easier and puzzles are solved easier. Nice work!

Boïnihi is a marvelous journey.

A discovery. An initiation. Boïnihi is without a doubt the most accessible of the games in the Black Cubes saga. And like every previous opus, it can be played without having played the other opuses. The Black Cubes is the most opened and interactive game's series ever, which can be done in the order you want: over the finished games, the player gradually reconstructs the backdrop that serves as the universe, and can then return to the titles previously played with the newly acquired knowledge of this world if he wants to understand more details.

No matter which opus you start or end, therefore, the canvas ends up revealing all its riches. Boïnihi is, of course, the last game created in the saga, but it is still probably the best to start the adventure, while offering to the previous players the last piece of puzzle that leads the Black Cubes in a pure apotheosis. Boïnihi is a cult game that has become essential to the series since it was released.

Boïnihi is above all an adventure game. Suddenly, many of the gamers afraid of this category will flee, giving way to reckless players who appreciate various intellectual challenges. But this game offers more : here, exploration, dialogues, meticulous observations lead the player to decipher a mysterious codex, and learn about the spectral host who attracted him to this place. Displaying impressive graphics, this game is made with the Visionnaire games engine which has repeatedly proven its effectiveness. The atmosphere is relaxing, conducive to meditation, enhanced by pleasant music and successful visual effects.

In Boïnihi, the independent French developer Simon Mesnard has planned everything so that the adventure is less off-putting as possible: the puzzles are less complex than in the previous opuses, integrated help allows to reveal the interactive places in the decorations, an AI gives many clues when the player blocks, the manipulations to be performed are clear and intuitive, the gameplay is more dynamic using the keyboard in addition to the mouse, ... This is the most technically successful opus in its variety interactions.

In this last opus, Simon Mesnard also offers a wide variety of sets, places, puzzles, dialogues, interactive objects, and gameplay, to offer a title extremely well balanced in difficulty and interest. Very difficult not to appreciate this game which has become one of the favorites of fans of the saga. It is hard to imagine that such a game was the result of the work of one person.

Exciting, rich, accessible but offering many challenges, captivating, original, Boïnihi is one of the best games released this year. Magnificent ! If you were hesitating to get into BlackCubes, with Boïnihi you have no more reason : go for it, you'll love it !

- Maybe a little hint saying "the supervisor could see me taking it" or something. I am not sure how I found the random rock, if there was a hint for it I totally missed it.

Death Has a Million Stomping Boots is quite jokey, with lots of colorful characters, situation humor, and nods and references to other games, as well as films and television series.  The humor is light and upbeat without ever feeling too forced.  There is a scene with a talking pizza that is especially funny.  The title character is a likable sort of dude as well; as is the supporting cast.  Overall, the game is a joy to play.

The puzzles tend to punch above their weight class, as well.  The second act has three really satisfying puzzle chains back-to-back-to-back, very well designed.  

The developer of this game is also really active in supporting indie game development and really just seems like a stand-up sort of dude.  There’s really no reason not to grab this game up right this minute.

Captain Disaster is a very intriguing and charming sci-fi comedy title, that's definitely recommended if you like point and clicks, especially of retro aesthetics and absurd humour variety! I mean, what other game features great writing, intuitive interface, talking space pizza, nose people, bumbling captains, literal million stomping boots and sarcastic navigational computers? This game has it all, I tell you!

Captain Disaster in blah blah blah stomping boots is a wonderful little graphic adventure game. It's low budget, there aren't many locations, the interface is janky, the developers are also the voice actors, but it's thoroughly entertaining.

The protagonist is the typical useless, unlikable slob that classic adventure games feature so often. And everything else about this is classic too. Timed puzzles. Wacky characters. The pop culture references come fast and furious. But - unlike a lot of other games which go heavy on the references - this one doesn't come across as trying too hard. I think it's because it has legitimately good puzzles in its own right. Of course they are utterly absurd, but they're very deftly hinted, so if you listen closely to the dialog and pay attention to the descriptions of all the items, it's possible to figure out the solution based only on what they give you. The downside is that you still need to pixel hunt. In a modern adventure game, this frustration would be solved by having a reveal hotspots button, but I suspect the engine the devs used is too old to have that feature. Maybe something for the next one, eh?

Anyway, if you like funny oldskool adventure games, this should be right up your alley.

"Captain Disaster in: Death Has A Million Stomping Boots" is a humorous old-school Point & Click game telling a silly story about a sloppy spaceship captain who gets himself into all kind of unusual situations.

Progress in the game is done through trials and errors and a thorough exploration of the environment:
- Click on everything you see (left-click to interact with/pick up an object, right-click on a object to get some funny comment or hint)
- Talk to everyone and explore all dialogues choices
- Try to combine any items in your inventory with any other inventory items or objects in your environment.
- Try different solutions of a puzzle to see how it affects it until you get things right.

Fun little adventure game in the style of Lucas Arts classics.

The puzzles are mostly fair and solvable. There isn't much pixel hunting (the game even has a joke in one area where you can click on a single weird pixel, and your character comments "This isn't that kind of adventure game."), most of the puzzles feel logical. As an adventure game veteran I would rate them more towards the easy side, but they still require a bit of thinking.

The only puzzles I found a little annoying were the ones that require you to wait around for an NPC to leave his spot, or listen to conversations that happen in the background to get a hint for one puzzle. My favorite puzzle was the one in your spaceship, when the hand scanner doesn't recognize your hand because it's too clean and you have to add all kinds of dirt to your fingers.

The humor is pretty decent throughout, although a little over-reliant on references. You'll see a lot of Star Trek, Star Wars, Doctor Who, 2001 A Space Odyssey, Space Quest, and other popular sci-fi and adventure game franchises referenced in this game. While the game's jokes are pretty good when it puts some effort into them, I don't find references that funny on their own. For example, you get to explore a junk heap and there's the Voyager from Star Trek and the Millennium Falcon from Star Wars, just because. Is it cute? I guess. Is it funny? Not really. Does it break the fourth wall? Absolutely. The game has a lot of creative alien races of its own, so it's not like all these references were necessary. I'm just not a fan of shoving in references to other sci-fi franchises for no reason.

The story is pretty fun, your main character is an even more bumbling idiot than Roger Wilco, and the NPCs are various flavors of goofballs. Just what you'd expect from a classic humorous point & click. The humor is very close to Space Quest, but the gameplay is of the Lucas Arts school: no dead ends, no deaths.

If you like classic Lucas Arts style adventure games, this will be right up your alley. Recommended.

It's a decent shooter, I bought it because I liked the Dev's previous game. 
But the grinding necessary to unlock the weapons and upgrades needed to survive the game's later stages is way too long. 
The time spent repeating the same levels over and over seems to be a "feature" or 'extending gameplay' but that's not the case with this modern system. 
Instead of learning the enemies and being able to clear late levels with skill, the game has armor levels for you and the enemies that make it a joke if you're not powered up to the level that the dev's intended foe that level. 

Imagine skillfully weaving around enemy fire and scoring hit after hit, only to realize that the same enemies you've been encountering since level one now has advanced armor and with your pea shooter you'll need to be doing that for another 5min to make a dent. ; P

Now compare that to say Raiden, even with a low power gun your skill can get  you through the levels without 30 min boss fights.

Works for me (though I admit I waited for a sale), wanting something to fill a few minutes at a time for my work-from-home "coffee-breaks." The fixed pace of each level ensures I won't feel compelled to play longer than I intended. The reviewers who pointed out that this game can be a bit "grindy" aren't wrong, but that's okay for me, as I'm not playing it for long enough at a time to get bored. A former music major, I recognize the value of practice and getting closer to the next weapon upgrade is a nice reward for putting in the time repeating previous levels. The alleged story is pretty silly, but I don't imagine the devs spent enough time on it for it to have taken anything away from the rest of the game which feels pretty well polished.

This game is running on the Unity Engine. You have full locomotion and snap turning. The game was running at a steady 90 frames per second on my 1060 GTX.
