Great artistic design and graphics, has fun gameplay and it's really cool that there's animated interactions with furnishings (like washing your hands at the sink or laying in the bathtub), but suffers from balance and progression issues as well as a very poorly designed world.

Some progression issues would be things like the order in which you learn new crafting recipes. For instance, learning to craft iron bars and equipment at level 12, but you can't make iron bars until you get the Reinforced Furnace at level 14, which you can't make until you learn the Reinforced Workbench at level 15. By the time you have enough iron to do anything you'll be nearly level 30 and already have everything you need to make steel gear.

Poor balance issues include the fact that there's very few enemy types and most enemies just have one move. They punch forward or hit the ground in front of them. No enemies provide any challenge, not even the bosses. Attack whilst airborn and you'll almost never get hit. Jump, unload your skills and a combo, land, repeat. This allows you to easily defeat enemies 9 levels above you regardless of your equipment. Enemies 10 levels above always seem to only take 1 damage. Gain a single level and suddenly they take hundreds of points of damage.

Some armor sets are not worth making due to lack of enemies to drop necessary materials and also because the stat difference is so low (+2 defence per item per tier). Carapace seems to have a low drop rate and few enemies drop it at all. You need carapace for almost all armor sets, so it's best to save it for later. Make a set of wood and/or leather gear and skip copper and iron armor sets so you'll have enough carapace to get decked out in steel or silver steel armor.

Another balance issue is healing items. They're so incredibly plentiful and powerful that I've never bought or crafted any consumables, I just rely on daisies, which you get from the very beginning and still provide adequate healing at level 35+. (A single daisy heals 305 HP.)

Now for the world... It's just awful in every way. It has nothing interesting anywhere. Open spaces are few and far between, meaning you're constantly digging to get anywhere, and everywhere looks almost exactly the same, just different colors for each biome and reskinned enemies. Horizontally the map is very limited, you can only go a couple hundred meters before reaching the edge of the map, so almost all of your travelling will be done vertically, which is not particularly fun. There's also no change in biomes going left or right - only up and down. All the dungeons are very much the same regardless of where you find them.

All of this aside, the game is still fun overall and I hope that some of the issues get ironed out since the game is still in early access.

P.S. Please do away with the combat and building-specific toolbars. It's clunky and annoying. Give us two bars that we can swap out and place anything on either bar.

- The game is beautiful. To add onto the point above, I love simply...looking at the background/scenery. Trying to discern functionality, what people did there, etc. 
- Did I mention how much I love the spear throwing?


Negatives:
- Story is almost too "loose" for me. Won't elaborate too much, as this is highly subjective and you either feel it or you don't. Although I suppose saying that says something. :|
- Quick-travel is a pain in the butt. I will admit it was my fault for awhile in not making full use of the Circe stations, (I feel like this wasn't possible in the demo?) but even with that knowledge it felt like too much. As said in the video, I absolutely love that sort of thing in MMOs (and other multiplayer games,) but in metroidvanias with lots of backtracking, it'd feel like a punishment if not for the game being beautiful. 
- Being attacked from off-screen sucks. I don't want to spoil where this happens if anyone is reading this without playing.
- Upgrade parts...out of nowhere, you suddenly need them in a certain order. This is crazy to me and I think any upgrade item you find should go to the tier you're on. I got screwed over by this and it didn't feel great.
- Currency shards don't have much value at all. I was never even close to being short for an upgrade, but I also didn't find a few despite looking over the entire (perceivable) map.

That's a long list of negatives, but they don't ruin the game. Do I regret paying $34 CAD for a 10 hour game? Nope. Why? Because games like Ender Lilies and Somber Echoes are more of an experience than a game to me (although they are obviously both.) I uninstalled Ender Lilies twice, and it is now one of my favorite games of all time. Anyways....

Despite all the brain-farts I had and the frustrations encountered, my primary criticism? It's too short. T_T

Guys, find a girl who loves you as much as this game loves projectile enemies.

That's all I have to say for now.

Alright. [i]The Fabled Woods[/i] is done and dusted. This is a walking simulator with a fairly unique "remember" mechanic that I'll talk about later. I think my quick synopsis is that it was an interesting game and is pretty good as a walking sim. The story itself was good enough to keep the game moving forward but wasn't particularly noteworthy. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3430186694

Right. So, the story is told through the eyes of three different characters. Sort of. Or maybe what you thought you were seeing throughout the game was more the way in which one person was interpreting everything and justifying why things happened the way they did by more or less guessing as to how the other characters thought and what brought them to this point in time. You'd have to be the judge of that. However, it's also a bit heavy-handed from a writing perspective and as a result, you really never have any sort of connection with the characters, whether it's love and appreciation or disgust and disdain. The story never develops things to the point where a player is going to really care. It's all just stuff you're witnessing, and when it's over, you'll probably forget all about it fairly quickly.

Which is a shame because handled a bit different, this could have been a memorable and horrific story that stays with you, but it just never gets there. And the voice acting, while also okay, does nothing to enhance the story at all. You never really get the sense that the voice actors felt any sort of connection with their characters either. It's not wooden voice acting, but it's just not compelling. Todd's VA was probably the most invested, but even still, it's just okay. Not bad. Completely serviceable. But meh.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3430186583

Now the graphics on the other hand were pretty nice. Much of it is standard walking sim fare, but there are moments in the game where the graphics just hit right and can be truly stunning. And I would say the graphics more than anything else in the game, carry this experience. Especially when you compare the real-world visuals with the "remember" world visuals. The contrast is pretty compelling. Similarly, while you are in Remember mode, there are also interesting and creepy sounds playing. Kind of like people speaking in an almost inaudible whisper that sounds like a chant of some sort a cacophony of lost souls trying to reach out to the living. And that seems to rise in intensity as you look around. 

As you explore, you will find points of interest and at certain points, you will be prompted to trigger "remember" mode, which is like a horror version of an investigation mode. Where all the colors in the world withdraw except deep red hues where blood pooled or splattered, and some general red haziness. Along with highlighted words and glyphs that offer some sort of message. The whole thing almost looks like the world is on fire. Which was kinda awesome. Following the bloodstains will unlock parts of the story in some areas and advance the story in others. One thing the game doesn't tell you to do is use this mode in every area whether prompted to or not. Do that.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3430186638

And I'd say that's really the game in its entirety. Outside of the "remember" mode stuff, you just walk around examining objects and unlocking the story until you reach a crossroads at the end, which offer two endings. Really just one, since one of the endings forces you back to the other anyway.

I saw where this game originally released for $20. That's crazy. The retail price dropped to $9.99, and that's still too much. It's on sale at the time of this review going live for 99 cents. That is the proper price in my opinion. This game is okay, and it has some special moments, but it's only an hour long and isn't really a memorable experience. It's okay, but one you'll quickly move on from. So, worth a look, but only when it's heavily discounted.

This game is a semi-interesting, janky, and familiar walking simulator. While I have endless respect for anyone who attempts to make games, this one felt so unrelatable and similar to dozens of other projects. The soundtrack was nice, and the unity-laden scenery was quite beautiful at times, but other than that, I seem to have no good comments. The dialogue was decent, I can respect the self-loathing, psyche-breaking moments of characters. But the voice actors were so abysmal at their job, all emotion and sincerity was missing. Each performance felt like a different breed of problems. The first narrator sounded like a Shakespearean actor trying to sound off his lines for those at the back of a playhouse, the second sounded as if she was reading the warning label of drug facts on television and the last narrator had zero fear in his voice to indicate any connection to his actions.

The story was meh, nothing too extraordinary, and if anything felt forced and uninteresting. I did like the snippets of lore placed around the game with letters, newspapers, and notes for the player to get interested. The "remember" mechanic could have been very interesting but had little going for it. It initially felt scary like something was happening, but then it became redundant and annoying.

Kovox Pitch is a weird game, and honestly it's hard for me to think of who this game is actually made for. I probably put 10+ hours into the demo of this game when it was playable before the games release and I loved every minute of it. Now that the game is out I'm finding myself less interested than I was before release, as if I feel like something is missing. The design is all over the place with mechanics clashing a little bit in the later game, and a simple concept being complicated to the point where it's honestly made less fun over time. The game clearly isn't made for rhythm game beginners because it gets tough fast, and stays tough (up until the final 3 songs which are the easiest in the game for some reason). Yet it's also seemingly not for rhythm game veterans because it doesn't put up a meaty challenge in comparison to any of the more hardcore games in the genre. Not to mention little things, such as the song list resetting to the top in between every played song, make it really hard to want to grind out high scores in the different tracks...

With all that being said you can really tell this game was made with love. The story is pretty bad, but the ending did pull on my heart strings just enough to make me think it was a good story overall.Meanwhile the music might be close to my favorite soundtrack in any rhythm game I've ever played, this foreign (russian?) alt rock really vibed with me all throughout, and will definitly be a list of songs I will track down and listen to even outside of playing the game, which is rare for me when it comes to rhythm games soundtracks.

I still come away from this game not really sure who should play this, but if the soundtrack seems interesting to you, and you like the prospect of a medium challenge in comparison to other rhythm games, than this is the game for you. With some issues ironed out, the game polished up a little more, and the soundtrack expanded a bit, I'd consider it a must play for rhythm game fans.

As someone who loves to pick up rhythm games from time to time, I really liked the first half of this game. The main mechanic was pretty simple, but satisfying and its simplicity combined with easily readable (after a couple of tries) rhythm patterns of baseballs made for a really enjoyable experience. 

Unfortunately this experience was kinda ruined by the red-blue mechanics. I think what ruins many rhythm games are when developers start feeling like their main core loop is not enough and start to design some weird patterns that only they can really understand. That's what red-blue balls felt like for me.

It's worth mentioning that Kovox Pitch has very indie difficulty progression where one song you can surf through on your first try pretty easily and right on the next song you're gonna restart like 20 times. And then the next song you are gonna return back to like a couple tries. This makes for a very annoying difficulty spikes that really break the flow of a campagin. The one that I'm probably not gonna break through is track 5.2, where the very high tempo is combined with truly unreadable patterns and (unfortunately) irritating song. After like 10 tries the fatigue kicks in and you basically just shut the game off, cause you won't keep up with the tempo anyway. For some reason I'm sure that if I manage to beat this level, I'm not gonna have such difficulty later on, but if I'm wrong, then I guess it's a skill issue.

So I'm kinda torn apart since the game is really great for a half of it, but becomes just unnecessarily complicated after that. I guess I wouldn't recommend it if you're not ready to give some levels a lot of time and if you're not familiar with rhythm games in general. But the absolute highlight of a level+song combination on 3.2 is one of the best rhythm levels I've ever played and is definetely worth some frustrating moments!

ENDLIGHT is an example of how a developer can pour all of their love, hard work, and dedication into a game that still isn't good. 

Don't get me wrong -- there [i]is[/i] a good game in here. It's genuinely funny. It's genuinely innovative. And it's genuinely fun.

The problem is, the game gets in its own way a little bit too much. It's the sort of game that I have no doubt was playtested extensively, and yet didn't see the kinds of significant changes that would have been required in order to really elevate the good parts together into a great game. Instead, we have moments of good game punctuated and obscured (sometimes literally) by interruptions to the flow of the experience. I won't spend too much time getting into everything, since frankly I could probably write a 10-page paper about everything this game does right and wrong, but let's just say that this game has been incredibly eye-opening to me about how effort, technical skill, and love on the part of the designer don't necessarily translate into a cohesive, quality experience.

Anyways, despite all that, I still recommend this game. Why? Because not everything worth playing is perfect, or even, well, good. My experience with ENDLIGHT has been positive despite the faults, because I've enjoyed the experience and I've been able to appreciate the parts of it that do work. Unfortunately, I don't think this will ever become a successful game to the average player, because while I can see a world in which an ENDLIGHT-like does break through and become a hit, it would require a lot of extensive tweaks to the formula that might end up making it a completely different game by the end. That being said, if you've ever considered yourself a [url=https://news.mit.edu/2015/harbinger-failure-consumers-unpopular-products-1223]harbinger of failure[/url], or perhaps just an optimist more willing to overlook faults than the average person, then you'll probably consider playing ENDLIGHT to be a positive experience, like I have. Just make sure you choose a comfortable setting for the visuals.

[b]sunset shapes[/b] is a tetromino-based 3d puzzler inspired by the excellent [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/759000].projekt[/url], but with pleasant colors of the fall. or the sunset, I guess, but there are multiple trees and such in the game, so it works either way.

you get a bunch of tetris-like shapes and have to position them so they reproduce the shadow on the wall (shoutout to mike oldfield) and the floor. first gripe already: [b]I wish there was a 'skip drop animation' setting[/b], waiting for pieces to land, bump around and finally settle is annoying. and they should be more scattered when the level starts, separating everything to see what's what just adds to the busywork, and once they fell in a way that I couldn't separate them, had to restart the level. shapes often get in the way of each other anyway, you often have to make them connect or fill each other's holes (not as dirty as it sounds), but [b]controls are too clunky and frustrating[/b].

left click or tab to select a piece, wasd or arrows to move it around horizontally (arrorws aren't mentioned anywhere), e/q to move up/down, 'r' to rotate, holding right click moves the camera and mouse wheel zooms in/out. [b]movement by default is based on the viewpoint[/b], so after rotating the camera, left will move the same piece in a different direction than before. [b]a toggle got patched in[/b], and while it makes a certain amount of sense to consider directions while facing the wall, for me it's more logical to look at the shadow, as the wall has nothing to do with the puzzle, and based on that I found fixed controls useless. they kinda work from an angled perspective, but rebindable controls would still be necessary and might fix the issue.

the alternate keyboard option means w/s is used to move pieces up/down and a/d for left/right, and if you want to move them in the other two directions, you have to rotate the camera first, so it's even worse than the other one. gamepad works too, might be better, can't be much worse, haven't tried it.

[b]50 levels[/b], one unlocked at a time, level numbers and names had to be patched in for level selection. mechanics include heavy blocks that fall down without anything to support them. neat idea but really annoying, even more so because they don't just fall into place if unselected, but bounce off other shapes, land and bounce around a bit more before they can be interacted with again.

then there are [b]constantly moving or rotating pieces[/b] unless they're currently selected, have to make them stop by blocking their movement with another piece, or time things so they line up properly for the solution. horrible idea, made only worse when both block types are present on a level, or when they're bugged and go through each other (which isn't a bug, apparently, but an intended mechanic somehow).

the music is fine, piano-based, calming, the graphics are very basic, but walking along the wall of solved levels is pretty cool, tells a story of a long journey. there are separate volume settings and a windowed mode toggle that produces a resizable window, better than nothing. and you can choose from multiple languages as well.

out of curiosity, I unlocked all the levels by editing the save to see every mechanic, but didn't solve everything because [b]controls, physics, some questionable mechanics and bugs soured the experience, it's simply not fun to play[/b].

An alright Cuphead clone that focuses on platforming over boss rush. It tries to capture the magic and appeal of that fan favorite, but it just ends up flat to the point of a free flash game. Even how the game feels cheapened.

In this game you need to clear all enemies in the rooms leading up to the boss fight. The problem is you restart when you get hit once. This is the difficulty and, unlike the aforementioned obvious inspiration, the foes don't move on a pattern and the first set alone with multiple fast moving floating eyes can crowd you or sneak in on you at a moments notice. There's also no check points, adding to the artificial difficultu scale.

Also, the store page says it is fully compatable with a controller. Unfortunately at this time, it is not. I used an Xbox 360 controller and most worked, but the calibration has pause as the up arrow on the d-pad, and not a single button is assigned to attack. Thankfully this is simple enough that using a keyboard (WASD, space to jump, j to attack) won't be that much of a hassle.

That said, combat is a bit exhaustive. While you only get one hit, the enemies require multiple hits to formed into a ball, then you hit said ball to get it to roll off screen at the bottom. It can push you, so inadvertantly coming into contact with an enemy is pretty easy.

Overall, it IS a fun game for what it is, but it definitely lacks everything that made the Cuphead such a memorable experience. This is the main reason I lost interest after just under an hour of playing. It is worth grabbing, but $20 US ($18 on sale at the time of writing this review) just feels way too much for a hollow shell of it's inspiration. Yes, it's kind of enjoyable, but you're better off playing the originator and waiting on a far better sale.

[u] It isn't terrible [/u] 
There are parts of Beyond Mankind which are unique and made the experience interesting; such as the character creation, the world-building and some of the survival mechanics. The bad graphics don't really bother me, I actually enjoyed the atmosphere of the levels. The characters are well voice-acted, the dialogue options are funny and relatable. 

[u] But this is where it goes down hill... [/u] 
The issues start with the combat and controls. The overall state of the combat is incredibly bad and it's a major part of the game. Combat and AI isn't like graphics, it can't be ignored or nostalgic. It takes a lot of fun out of the game when the AI is this under-developed, to a point where it's 'stand in one place, shoot' or 'run in a line and attack'. 

The story isn't great. It's very basic and the pacing is off. There isn't enough time to learn the characters in the introduction; you're thrown into a situation and they feel like generic NPCs. Fallout 3 came to mind in the sense that you see yourself grow up with the characters, it's a much softer introduction and you get familiar with their personalities. For Beyond Mankind, you can instantly tell the pacing is off, even when not comparing it to a AAA title.

[u] Conclusion [/u] 
The final straw is hiding somewhere in the game's design; it just feels unengaging. I'm coming to this conclusion from how I feel and asking myself 'Do I want to boot up Beyond Mankind?'. The answer is naturally no and I find another game to play. I really really wish I was engaged, I believe the devs have tried hard. It's just in a state which I can't enjoy. I hope the studio see the feedback and work on it, it has room to grow.

Others have gone into detail re the multiple bugs, clipping issues, hard cut scene edits, poor outdoor environmental textures, janky movement controls, and even jankier combat controls.
Most examples are not exaggerations, and many reported @ release have yet to be addressed.

Some we did not see mentioned:
Enemy attacks connect through locked doors or walls
Enemy corpses block doorways requiring jump>> crouch>> crawl gymnastics to pass through.
Melee combat: attacks will often not connect with targets shorter than you unless you crouch or go prone, even with swords

The inventory/crafting system does not pause while open: a very poor decision considering you often have to navigate through different full screens (INVENTORY VIEW on open for some [food, water bottles, weapon] items, CHANGE VIEW/Zoom View(?) for other [first aid, bandages, water [b]again[/b] ] items, and CRAFTING VIEW to actually create something) to access or use items.

The only reason we continued playing was the belief it HAD to get better... Viking Conquest right?
The voice acting's passable to good so far, even if the voice editing makes the computer talk like a single run on sentence.
Also, how can they get such good facial textures and animations on some characters, while also making others look like stick figure beggars? See Vishpala @ tutorial vs training room characters
The same with some interior areas looking so fantastic vs shockingly bad foliage, cave interiors, and building facades.

The story itself does get more interesting as you proceed, especially the faction interplay; but the cut-scene jumps and hard edits are jarring.

I've gifted multiple copies of Viking Conquest to friends, and would still do so gladly.

A nice party game, good for showing vr to starters.

You are a street traffic regulator and only need 2 commands to make the traffic flow the way you would like. You point out a vehicle or person with one hand, and either raise your hand palm to them to make them stop or wave your palm towards you to make them move (faster). There are some fun situations that make your job more interesting, like mini games whille regulating traffic. Your aim is to get the highest score. You can also make hand gestures to characters, and they respond back, but that is only a gimmic that doesn't influence the overal game flow.

As it is now you get like 5 intersections, each in a different city. Each of these 5 can be played in day, night setting. Making for different difficulties. You will burn through these very very fast. I hope they will add many many more.

The party play in this game, is fun'ish. And it actually is coop and not versus. The non vr players must help to achieve the vr players objectives as fast as possibe by spawning cars, people, and items. The objectives not only wants you to be a good traffic regulator, but aso a bad one by giving you objectives to let crash and run over people. The non vr players do not need to install any app, They go to a website that lets them put in the game code the vr players gets, and play. This is for now, really nothing more than tapping icons to spawn things, so that gets boring pretty fast.

The graphics are nice, cartoon like. So no blood or body parts go flying. Making this good for children. And with the simplicity it has now in single player and party play this game is more for the younger players, or a vr showcase.

Overall it is not bad, the concept is fun, the controls are good, audio is fine, everything about this game is good. But as it is now, only fun for a few hours. As many vr titles, traffic jams seems like a proven to work concept with limited content.

Hello fans,
having completed Vampirem yesterday I have to say I’m impressed. The game was developed by one person only but seems totally fleshed-out and bug free, and it is really funny to play. The story is not the longest, but for only 13€ more than OK. I highly recommend giving this game try, and the developer is really responsive and caring for constructive critics concerning this game.

Gameplay is astonishingly fluid, it’s really funny guiding Raven trough the dungeons, warping around and slaying enemies. The warp skill reminded me of the good old Jedi Knight/Jedi Academy where you could use Force Jump to get to locations you would normally not and find great extras there. 

The only thing that felt odd and slowed the game play for me is the health/mana system here. Health is called blood, mana is called essence. Both does not regenerate naturally (there are items to regenerate your health up to a certain percentage of your max health, but we’ll get to this). Blood comes from finding and using blood stones and blood potions found from smashing urns and barrels. From the very same and after killing some enemies you find essence crystals which recharge your mana bar. You cannot use the blood stones directly, but you have to burn essence to convert blood into health using a special healing skill. The blood stones get emptied while doing so and need to be replaced or, in rare cases, refilled.  Not bad in the first level, but gets worse as the game continues.

After the first few dungeons, I found myself constantly low on essence AND blood. The fights in the game aren’t easy and even trash mobs can pack a hefty punch. Even if you have a filled blood stone but are low on essence, you cannot heal yourself. If you have full essence and plenty to spare in your inventory but have no blood stones, you cannot heal yourself. If you’re low on both, that’s where the fun starts. Using any of your skills takes essence, too. This leads (for me) to not using most of your (well-designed and useful) skills most of the times because you need every ounce of essence to keep your health up. 

While healing through blood stones and recharging your essence via crystals works well in the beginning, it does not in later levels… it seems to be based on raw numbers: while a certain amount in the beginning is enough for two complete refills, it will get you only 25% later as your max health and mana increase. I went to to a boss fight with 250 essence spare in my inventory and two epic blood stones and thought I was well-prepared, only to find out that the essence was enough for about one healing and left me without essence thereafter. For me it would feel better if a percentage would be refilled, not a raw number of points. During nearly every boss fight, I got completely depleted of both blood and essence, so no healing and no using skills at all, leaving single melee as the only option. While it its possible to regain essence (especially because after dying every urn/barrel has re-spawned) replacing blood stones is very difficult, so chances are high you go into round two against the boss with some or full essence but still no chance to heal. And during the story line, boss fights came in relatively quick succession, so I hadn’t recovered from the fight yet and had to fight another boss, with about 1/3 health and essence. Regeneration items are not that helpful… I had several of those equipped and reached 16% health regeneration, which gave me about 70 health. Not bad, kept me going vs. trash mobs, but was excactly one hit from most boss attacks. Combined with chronically empty essence bar, this leads to: rush in, melee once or twice, hope you’ll not get hit, repeat until either the boss or you are destroyed. A magelike playthrough with more casting and less melee seems to be impossible… there is no way you’d find and regain enough essence.

I don’t know how to solve this, but the developer should think to get rid of blood stones completely. Healing skill should still take essence but no stones anymore. This way you still had to balance between healing or attacking, but at least you CAN heal if you got essence. Also, there should be better ways to regain essence. Loot from urns/barrels is totally random, so you can either find many crystals or not enough to keep you alive. Maybe essence should regenerate, at least until a certain amount (maybe depending on an unlockable skill in the skill tree? Raven is regaining his power during this journey, this could reflect this.). Or maybe items with regeneration should regenerate  both health and essence, or there should be items with blood/essence steal on strike, not on kill. There is life-steal on some items but with +2 PER KILL it’s next to useless. 

Also, loot of anything not a ring or amulet could be more common. I found exactly one boot and one armor in the whole story. Weapons drops are bit better, but could also be more common. And please please please: town down the snakes! One single snake seems to hit harder than a boss, and a trap with three snakes often mean certain death if you're not with full health.

These are just a few suggestions that the developer could think about to flesh out the game experience.

To conclude: I had much fun playing Vampirem and can recommend it. It sometimes feels brutal and a bit rough at the edges, but it’s more than worth its cost.

This game is linear, meaning that you can only play the game one way. You cannot store healing stones, if you drop them to be recharged, it will only charge one stone and you lose the rest. Recharge stations are rare. There is no map to the dungeons, so you are required to remember every where you have been. There is no save feature, unless you exit the game, and then you have to restart that dungeon over again. Once you pass a check point, you cannot go back, so if you miss something important you are just screwed.

You meet your first human in the library about 5 hours in. Though the game will not allow you to drain her, turn her, or even seduce her. 

Overall the controls work great. The graphics are not too bad, but could be better. The biggest problem though is that you cannot save your game and that it is linear.

It's a wonderful game. I find it very nice for unwinding after a frustrating day of work or classes. One can get their fill of the game in about a 15 minute game session, though it's definitely a little longer than that, and feel refreshed and ready to reengage in the day's activities, enthusiastically.
The mental health portion of the game deals with negative thoughts that one might have on a particularly frustrating day. I find collecting the Mantras calming, almost serene, even with swarms of enemies closing in in waves.
Even players that aren't dealing with mental struggles during work or school will enjoy this twin-stick shooter style, geometry wars influenced game. I just find it particularly helpful as one who does get frustrated often and who turns to video games to unwind and relax. Even if you have all the Mantras and aren't searching for more good feels, there is an endless mode, with infinite lives and infinite enemies, where one can blast baddies to their heart's content. On the other hand, if the reminder of good feeling is what you need, there is a journal where one can review all the Mantras they have collected thus far, even flip to the specific Mantra they are looking for, to feel better about a specific situation they were put in or encountered.

The co-op mode is particularly a fun and interesting challenge, where one can have their friends join them on the journey through the darkness of their own mind. Each additional player will play a smaller ship almost just like the ones that follow you while collecting Mantras. If the lead player should die during this cooperative adventure, the next player in line will take control of the group, becoming "promoted" into the bigger lead ship until their own death. All allies who aren't controlling the group can also sync their button clicks and break off from the main ship, helping alleviate some pressure with temporarily improved guns.

The controls are simple and easy on either controller or keyboard-mouse, though I find it feels more natural with controller.
Overall I'd give the game a 5/5 for it's genre. What's more impressive is that a single developer made such a gem.

An interesting game that you should be able to complete in under 2 hours. You play as a detective who reviews CCTV footage for the police in order to answer questions about events/crimes.  At its heart, CCTV Detective is like a hidden object game. For each scene, you find clues and cameras. Then, you watch CCTV footage searching for details. At times, you are asked to find a car in footage from a highway camera. Overall, it is a game that tests your ability to observe and report.

Pros - does a good job of simulating the process of investigating a crime using video footage - at times, it feels very real.
Cons - most scenes have 5 cameras with around 2 - 6 minutes of footage each. This means you are sitting for quite a bit. For me, this felt very passive and I grew restless and started jumping the tapes forward to shorten the time I needed to watch. 

I'd recommend this game to those who enjoy using their powers of observation and don't mind watching more than 'doing.' The game auto-saves and provides you multiple chances to recover if you get an answer wrong.

"The Adventures of Fatman: Intergalactic Indigestion" is an absolute travesty of a game, a sequel that should have never seen the light of day. As a follow-up to the mediocre original, this title manages to stoop even lower.

Gone is any semblance of charm or effort that the first game may have possessed. The switch from Sierra-style pixel art to a hideous cartoonish aesthetic is a visual assault on the senses. It's as if the developers opted for the cheapest, most amateurish art style possible.

The gameplay is a pitiful excuse for a point-and-click adventure. Puzzles are insultingly simple, making you wonder if they were designed for toddlers. The lack of a save option is a sin in modern gaming, instead replaced by a primitive checkpoint system that feels archaic and lazy.

The controls are a disaster. Basic commands like "use," "talk," and "look" are reduced to mindless drag-and-drop actions, stripping away any semblance of immersion that might have existed. It's as if the developers couldn't be bothered to implement a functional interface.

At a mere 30 minutes in length, "Intergalactic Indigestion" is a slap in the face to anyone who spent their hard-earned money on it. There's no depth, no voice acting, and no meaningful interactions with characters. It feels like a rushed, unfinished mess that should have never been released.

In conclusion, this sequel is an abomination that tarnishes whatever goodwill the first game may have garnered. "The Adventures of Fatman: Intergalactic Indigestion" is an embarrassment to the genre and a disgrace to anyone who dares to call themselves a gamer. Steer clear of this disaster at all costs—it's an experience you'll regret from start to finish.

I will preface this review by saying I do not normally play games like this, and I have never played Super Smash TV before, the game that this is supposedly influenced by.  That said, I have had a good deal of fun trying out this game and have a few things to say about it.  WIthout further ado, let's begin.

Some small issues I encountered when playing:

- When booting up the game, the resolution defaults to 320x200 60hz. I was unable to see any of the menu items clearly.  It was not without some assistance before I could select the appropriate menu options to adjust to my desired resolution (1920x1080 60hz).  As a consequence, I was not able to read the opening sequence without having to change the resolution, which can affect one's initial impressions of the game.  Of course, this issue could vary depending on what system the game is installed on.

- No option to stop autoplay text.  During the scenes that describe the story before getting into the gameplay, you are given two options: Press [A] for Next, and Start for Skip.  There should be an option to toggle autoplay text, for simply user convenience.

I do not think I have played much twin-stick shooters in the past, if at all.  To keep this review brief, I will list my pros, cons, and thoughts when it came to my experience in playing this game.

Pros:
- Game plays smoothly and controls are intuitive enough.
- Art style is quite appealing for this type of game, background art and character design are serviceable.
- Music is pretty good throughout and adds to the atmosphere of the game, especially during the final boss.
- Bosses are well designed and fun to play against, especially the final boss.

Cons:
-  Low amount of content,  I feel there is definitely room to add more content especially in terms of progression. Starting off, the game, at least on the first level, can be a bit overwhelming with all the new spells.  I can see the appeal of figuring out the spells on your own though. Perhaps more smaller levels in between the boss-centric ones that only spawn a few certain types of spells at a time (aside from the spells you learn later on) before ultimately adding them as an option to randomly appear once the player becomes more accustomed to the types of spells there are and how they work.  Mini-bosses can be created as more content.  There's a lot more that can be added, but I think it does not necessarily have to be too complex.  There's definitely a roguelite element too that can possibly lend itself to this game.
- Lighting can be a bit of a detriment.  The low lighting could just be by design choice, but I think for instances where the Spellbearer is facing upwards, it becomes harder to discern where they are because of the black cape that does not glow.
- Screen Spam.  This might actually be tied to the lighting, but it becomes hard to register where things are when a lot of things are going off.  Of course, one could always not fire their magic and focus on dodging.  Maybe change the lighting of similar enemy attacks and one's own magic?  This could just be a design choice.  The lighting in some parts I think can be adjusted.

Notable Thoughts:
- I found it interesting that the points do not reset when dying (losing all your lives.)
- Also, dying at the boss level does not reset you back to the beginning of the entire level, which I see as a good thing
- There are moments during the final boss where if you die and not have enough speed boosts, there will be places where death becomes inevitable (such as after the lasers stop firing and the body moves a lot quicker.  Could be simply game design choice, so I don't necessarily consider it a con, just means that dying once can snowball into dying many more times until one can pick up enough power-ups.
- (Possible bug?) There are times where it feels I don't die or lose a life, even though I am at 0 lives.  Perhaps there is a mechanic I am not aware of or it is simply a bug.

All in all, I think this game has a lot of potential and can definitely be polished further to create a truly magical experience.

I had discovered this game through undorthodox channels - it was posted to a torrent tracker and from the title I thought it was a joke by the uploader, so came to steam to see if it was for sale. I'd purchased it not expecting anything close to the standard of what I just enjoyed.

In short you play through a story that reminded me of 'Ozzy & Drix'; playing as a dormant Antibody Agent who's reawakened inside NotTomHanks' gut after being swallowed,  in a last ditch effort to fight the 'baddies' and prevent another celebrity death.

The game doesn't provide a compass, HUD navigation way-points, nor provide a torch any more illuminating than a damp paper match. I was disorientated across all 3 axis at times, felt lost and occasionally saw no obvious route of progression. The lack of security or comfort your dollar store flashlight, handwritten map created as you venture through the alien levels was reminiscent of the 'Amnesia' series and with this brought genuine moments of fright followed by dread as my gun locked up through uncontrolled panic firing leaving me to be engorged by humanities most famous snot villain. 

Despite it's length and lack of complexity, CoC: MW has this delightful 'Homemade' charm throughout it's well executed 'less-is-more' approach to game play mechanics. 
The humour throughout is delightfully quirky, in places bending the usual video game 'rules' or 4th walls to achieve something uniquely silly. The delivery of the humour feels natural, unlike for example - Borderlands' corny one-liners, references and jokes that feel like they've been forced into the script with some help from the hydraulic press youtube channel.

The game has left me surprised in that it's made me experience such a broad range of emotions in such a short time that I start to wonder how so many titles produced by larger game developers frequently miss the mark. My expectations were low, however, were they higher - they'd have still been pleasantly surpassed. The finale was so much more rewarding thanks to the acting. If this is the first game from this studio, I eagerly await another.

I'll write a full review once i get further in the game and have a more firm grasp on the mechanical intricacies , but here's a little something in the meantime in case you're on the fence about this one:

This is not a fetish game, at least not in the way people generally use that term. There is no titillation involved with the piss mechanic(s). Urine is abundant, but its inclusion is all body-horror focused, with a truly wild narrative reason backing it up. I find fetish content generally repulsive, and despite going into the game feeling as though i'd be grossed out, I was pleasantly surprised to find the game grotesque without it being especially vulgar or off-putting. 

About the gameplay: The game is difficult and unforgiving. Some of the items necessary to follow the story are extremely well hidden, and will require eagle-eye focus related to context clues and environmental detail. The crafting system is quite robust, and i find it very well organized and easy to contend with. Combat is simple, the selection of weapons I've managed to find have a really unique style to them, and it is a lot of fun to engage enemies -- that is, when you're able to without getting overwhelmed or risking an increase in the hazardous fog. Speaking of the fog, that's the game's on-the-fly difficulty modifier, and it can take your experience from a relatively easy time to a god-awful, overwhelming hellride. When the difficulty suddenly spikes because you forgot to manage your character's actions, the world changes. Greater amounts of enemies spawn, with new variants depending upon your fog level. There's more to it than that, but I don't want to spoil the fun. It's a real "Fuck around and find out" philosophy, and each incident that makes your world spiral out of control is an opportunity to learn your limitations and weigh the risks in future encounters.

Ace of space is a game of the Shoot ’em up genre, the theme of the game is space flights, cleaning up sectors of the cosmos from hostile space inhabitants.
The basic mechanics of the gameplay is to destroy the enemy, the game has three variable parameters: health, the amount of charge for the special ability of the ship and the number of bonus points given for the destruction of one combat unit of the enemy, for the automatic activation of amplifiers on the example of restoring health, energy shield and slowdown time, the level is given a certain number of explosive rockets, which are very helpful in places of large concentrations of the enemy.
The game has four paths to planets that need to be cleaned, and for each of these tasks, we are assigned different spaceships.
Each ship has its own unique gameplay due to various special skills:
the second ship, by virtue of its strength and slowness, has the ability to regenerate health, which makes it possible to go to ram (the ram mechanics work in a certain way, when your ship comes into contact with an enemy ship, the ship is destroyed, and damage is caused to you)
And in comparison, the third ship, a high-speed but slightly armored ship, has the ability to accelerate engines, and you can easily fly around opponents and burn them with flame from the engine nozzle.
The gameplay ships are very closely and competently intertwined with the gameplay, for example, the second ship called the pain train is designed to transport goods and people, or a supporting role in a combat operation, and due to its arsenal and armor it has less mobility.
Each level in ace of space is unique and delight with different opponents both gameplay and stylistically.
Ace of Space also offers a global ship’s pumping system, which directly affects your gameplay improving the ship, with each pumping of the ship’s aspen, it changes its appearance and adds new weapons to the arsenal, the fourth level of the ship’s pumping gives you an extra weapon, unique on each ship, emphasizing the peculiarity of each ship.
The player welcomes the original stylistic sound track, which perfectly conveys the atmosphere of space adventures.
The fourth level, conceptually different from the others, in it you are given a ready-pumped fleet and one life without points of conservation and special ability, we are presented with unique opponents, with a truly magnificent design that really conveys the culture of an alien race and is accompanied by its unique original soundtrack.
It is pleasant to play in Ace of space, the author’s ideological presentation that the combat spaceship must have sufficient combat power to withstand the enemy is warmly received by the player, Ace of space does not torment the player with his helplessness, but rather gives him the opportunity to play for the soul.

Super Cable Boy manages to keep your interest by giving you access to additional abilities every once in a while. You can switch between unlocked abilities at any time in any level, and chain them together. Completely optional collectibles either require precise execution or using your abilities in creative ways (or both).

I'd say the main route is just difficult enough for most people, but there's a lot of secret bonus levels for those who want a more extreme experience, and it gets really, really tough. But even when you struggle to complete a level, much like Celeste or other gems, it's (almost) never frustrating, and it's always a blast when you succeed.

The very first maps are far too easy and don't seem promising, but the game does evolve quickly to meet the bar for gamers that are looking for a challenging platform game involving precision, fast-paced small/quick levels. The cable mechanic allows you to perform what other games offer as “double jumps”, but requiring some level of mastery which increases the difficult.

The level design is good and definitely helps to showcase the game mechanics. Most of the levels also offer collectable items that require mastery of the game mechanics to reach them. Casual gamers can complete the game ignoring these items, but they're there for pro gamers who would find the game too easy w/o hard challenges otherwise.

There's not only quality level design, but also quantity. So there's plenty of time to master each mechanic. However new mechanics are introduced when your character find “cartridges” (the game term for permanent power-ups). Once power-ups are acquired, new maps become accessible. The power-ups change the mechanics and the levels to make the game feel fresh even in the face of so many levels to play. Old powerups are still useful (and required) for many levels ahead just showing how the developers are very skilled at level design in platforming games. Not only quality, but also quantity. Quantity, but in a way that doesn't getting boring (new mechanics help to keep the game somewhat fresh even with too many levels).

Some levels also feature multiple exits allowing access to secret areas that offer even more challenges.

I do suggest a gamepad with good analogs to play. Most 2D platforming games only make real use of a D-pad, but this one is different. For aiming the cable at the walls (or aiming flight for one of the power-ups that you unlock), good analogs help. There's some sort of auto-aiming, but good analogs will only help.

If you're a really casual game you can change the game speed in the settings to make the game easier (you can choose a speed between 20 to 100% in steps of 10).

[h1]Poor controls[/h1]

Firstly, there is no realistic way to switch quickly between the 4 different movesets (cartridges). In the final world, it seems like the original design was to have players switch between different cartridges, but I assume that when playtesting this most players couldn't perform the switches in flight, thus leading to the introduction of giant blobs that automatically switch you to the correct cartridge. The implied promise of the game--that you would be able to use the different moves fluidly--is never realized in a meaningful way; instead the game is designed so that a single cartridge is used per level (and mostly, per world). One way to address this may have been to allow different controller buttons to control the different moves instead of having each cartridge use two buttons, but this would remove the feeling of swapping cartridges, which is unfortunately part of the visual design of the game.

Secondly, a lot of the controls are oversensitive and inconsistent. Jumps are fixed height no matter the duration of the jump press unless you press down when jumping. The voltage/rocket cartridge has really sensitive controls and makes the precision required in its world (and especially its boss) very frustrating. The triple jump cartridge's dash doesn't go in a single direction and can be changed in midflight, which led to some unexpected deaths.

[h1]Confusing Visuals[/h1]

The readability of stages is often quite tough. Because the camera is zoomed into Cable Boy at all times and the stages are rather large in comparison, you must memorize the stages to react with the sort of speed that is necessary to complete them. There is a built-in camera scroll/zoomout on the right joystick, but it's unusable unless you're stationary, and in later stages you'll be moving and airborne for basically the entirety of the stage (unless you're using the cable cartridge to attach yourself to something).

Even worse for memorization is the color change cartridge. In my opinion, this should not even be a mechanic in the game--it is not fun to try to keep in mind where invisible platforms and killzones are so that when you change colors in midjump you don't die. I do not understand why the choice was made to make platforms invisible when you're in the wrong color instead of making them "transparent" in some way. As it is, this was by far the most frustrating thing in the game for me and I really feel like the levels that depend on the color change mechanic are much less interesting because the design of the power is not great.

Finally, I just really did not appreciate the visual design of the game once the "glitching" really got underway. In both Firewall and Core worlds (the final two in the main story), the number of incidental sprites that are meaningless is a real drain on my attention. The fire effects in Firewall on the safe platforms makes it feel difficult to remember on a moment to moment basis what is safe. The glitch effects in Core are all weird and unique. This culminates in the final battle, where some of the tentacle sprites and blips that come off the final boss can kill you and some cannot--after spending a whole game trying to learn to ignore all the little sprites everywhere, in the final battle I actually couldn't tell what was killing me for the first several attempts because I was visually filtering out the boss' attacks.

- Early experience so far has been that the game seems to have a fair difficulty until it suddenly murders you out of nowhere after several joyous challenging experiences - and unless you want to use the good ol' Engine to attempt to make this less likely, you're out of options - which is a shame, because the difficulty seems fair until it really and truly does turn on a dime and murder you for the crime of not already knowing what was about to happen. Very good enemy communication and warnings, otherwise - so the zero warning deaths being the only way that I die have been so frustrating in my very very brief time with this game that they're actually the only thing that I really remember other than beating the challenge room with the Runes effect for a flamethrower so that I could get to try ANYTHING new because the game gives you no ingame currency to work with.

I'm sure that the game is great - but having played Nuclear Throne back when it came out and enjoying it quite a lot, this isn't hitting the mark for me, which is a shame - I'd expect a difficult game, but as a veteran of the genre, having been murdered in the same "wait I'm dead?" fashion every single time? That's just too bitter a pill to swallow. The game either has to be punishing but fast or have checkpoints - this is far too punishing for the amount of time that it feels like you're investing per run - unless the run ends after the first boss is defeated, which I'd hope isn't the case.

I'm new to the game, but not the genre or difficulty, I just find that this has been "death as a surprise mechanic" IN SPITE of how well tuned the rest of the game has been - narrowly avoiding harm the whole way through feels incredible - the problem is genuinely that when I HAVE died, it's because there was NO warning - it was a "see that? That happens. Learn from dying and remember to anticipate that" which, no. That's not what I enjoy. That isn't fun for me. And I shouldn't have to enable god mode to experience a game that's 99% great because that 1% is what keeps killing me.

The rest of the game is so good that I wish I'd had OBS running because I'm actively trying to gaslight myself into believing that I'm wrong, but I've literally seen the bugs that killed me in my first run and they do just shoot bullets outta nowhere, so I'm going to believe that the other two things are correct as well - namely, one boss just burrows and murdered me with nearly no time to even realize it had burrowed before it popped up under me and killed me with one shot to kill it, and the random surprise aoe or contact damage or something that happened with one of the golden mask wearing enemies right as it was about to die - it might have been reflecting out of nowhere, I really can't say for sure, but it wasn't a fun surprise.

If enemies have to be designed this way, at least give me some cheesy "know your enemy" zoom in and show me what they're capable of doing or something - I'd seen the mask wearing enemies and had been jumping on them before killing them to deal with them - that's why I'm very confused - I was doing that just fine until randomly I took enough damage to trigger the damage shield, then the boss re-entered the room, I got it low, then it burrowed and killed me because I was already very low.

Sour grapes, but I've also legitimately not had this experience with a game before where I just went "wow that was ruthless and unnecessary" - and I'm sure that I'd do better the next run - but it feels artificially designed to make me feel that way - this is no Dead Cells in those moments - there's no real warning - just death. Feels very bad.

Fixing the controller aiming would help immensely - as it stands, while at my PC I simply don't want to keep playing this game. While laying down and winding down I can stomach wasting time as that's by definition what I'm there to do, but I don't want to be frustrated and feel cheated just before bed - like a loser? :P Sure! But like the game just went "hah.. no" ? NO! :O

And maybe I'm objectively wrong. Maybe if I were to give it just one more go I'd see that I'm just getting old. But I haven't had any reason to try to gaslight myself until this game so.. I highly doubt it.

For example, during the fights, you have to wait quite a while for the NPCs after your own turn. It would be more fun and interactive if you could control your allies as well. This way, you'd also understand which cards they can use. Of course, this would make the game easier, but the developers could come up with a solution for that.

A second point of criticism is that it would be more enjoyable to be able to choose more cards, which could be done at night while dreaming. Just give an extra skill point every day. That's more fun than occasionally being allowed to do this and having most cards randomly placed in your deck.

A great game with a surprising amount of depth despite its quirks. The murder mystery itself has the same structure every run, with minor variations, but there's a lot of variety in perks, cards, and quest variants. Don't expect high logic. If your ingame journal tells you a clue is correct, do yourself a favor and just roll with it.

At low difficulties, the fun is in seeing how the murder mystery plays out. Combat isn't a challenge, so just play through the mystery and enjoy experiencing all the wacky systems like tactical diplomacy and deduction mode. All the systems have a breezy simplicity and whimsy that keeps the game from being a slog. Why does deduction mode involve shooting at words over ghosts? Because I'm a genius imperial era Judge Dredd, probably.

At the highest difficulty, the fun is in overcoming the weird curveballs the game throws at you. Try to cram in as many quests you can each day to meet the Magister-General's strict deadline for solving the mystery. Sweet talk the bandits to save your health, bluff to save your time and money. Push your luck and explore to the bottom of a dangerous ancient crypt. Get rich and bribe the church for intel on a character's motives, or get knocked out and lose a whole day recovering. Don't blame me when the Magister-General shows up expecting results and fires you for your incompetence.

Well I guess I have the job of posting the first english review on this game. I bought Hani because Im obsessed with roguelike games and this one seemed relatively polished for its early state. And I have to say, I was quite impressed. Hani is still very much in "alpha" as the UI is very basic, there's no real story, structure, or "tone" set yet. However, that which is present is surprisingly fun. The graphics are clean and easy to read (mostly), the combat is pretty fun and can get frantic, and all of the moves are quite varied. Thats all one can ask for at this stage in development. If youve seen this game pop up and avoided it due to the lack of reviews, I would say give it a go, especially if youre a roguelike nerd too. I would really like to see this game get some popularity so the devs can flesh it out more thoroughly.

And message to the devs: Keep it up. Theres some serious potential here to make a popular game.

UPDATE AFTER MORE HOURS: I have to hand it to Hani, this game is really really great. I've played about 20-something hours now and that was over a good number of sessions. The central combat mechanics of Hani allow for some really wild combinations and synergies of skills, and some runs end up looking absolutely insane by the end. There's tons of ways to pair up your abilities and these abilities come in an impressive variety considering this is made by a lone developer. Combat itself is frantic and fun and runs smoothly on my shitty computer. There's a very personal feeling to the entire game and the silent protagonist adds to a constant dream-like atmosphere. Even though I have no clue what the story of the game is I really liked the ending, its short and sweet and oddly heartwarming. 

Of course there are plenty of areas where Hani could use improvement. Its nowhere near finished and the entire experience has an "early-access" vibe to it. The graphics and especially the animations need refinement. Content is an obvious issue and although there's enough now to keep it interesting for a bit, its not a game you can play for hours in a single sitting. The "basic" abilities need more variety since you use them through most of the run and there are only 3 or 4 to choose from. I'm not quite sure where to find info on the game and therefore not sure how to do things like unlock costumes or interact with "secret faces." A compendium or something with this information would be an awesome addition. 

If the Starmyth does read this updated review, theres one thing that I hope they take away. Please fix the slot machine chances. I have literally spent thousands of coins on a machine without a single win just to see how long it would take. I have won before, and sometimes I win multiple times. Just a small boost in win-chance would make the risk much more worthwhile because as of now, its not worth the gold to use. 

Alright, rant over. As you can see I have spent a good amount of time with the game and thats because at the end of the day its just fun. The Outlast Trials is a co-op survival horror where you are thrown into gloomy Cold War laboratories, forced to undergo brutal tests for freedom. Unlike previous parts, here you can (and should!) play with friends: the single player mode is more difficult, and the enemies are sometimes annoying - their attacks are sometimes easy to avoid, sometimes impossible to predict. 
The atmosphere is oppressive: an alarming soundtrack, flickering light and bloody locations plunge you into paranoia. Survival depends on stealth and luck - one mistake at the end of the mission crosses out 40 minutes of progress. The graphics are not revolutionary, but the detail pleases. 
Ideal for fans of the series and lovers of co-op, but it quickly becomes boring. It is worth playing for the adrenaline and an evening with friends, but it is unlikely to hook you for more than 100 hours.

[h1]The Outlast Trials: Where Therapy Means Running for Your Life[/h1]  

[i]Welcome to [b]The Outlast Trials[/b], the game where you and your friends get to experience the joys of psychological torture, courtesy of the fine folks at Murkoff Corporation. It’s like a team-building exercise, but with more screaming and significantly less trust.[/i]  

[h2]The Good[/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b]Terrifying Atmosphere:[/b] The game oozes dread and paranoia. Every shadow could be a lurking psychopath, and every distant scream is a reminder that you’re next. It’s like a haunted house, except the exit is just an illusion.  
[*][b]Co-op Chaos:[/b] Teamwork makes the dream work—unless that dream is a nightmarish death trap. Whether you’re heroically saving your squad or shamelessly using them as bait, the multiplayer experience is peak horror-comedy.  
[*][b]Unique Gameplay:[/b] The game constantly throws new horrors at you. Just when you start feeling competent, Murkoff pulls the rug out from under you and laughs.  
[*][b]Replayability:[/b] With randomized elements and multiple trials, every playthrough is a fresh opportunity to make the same dumb mistakes in slightly different ways.  
[/list]  

[h2]The Bad[/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b]Stress Levels:[/b] If you weren’t anxious before, congratulations, you are now. Your fight-or-flight response will get a full workout.  
[*][b]Learning Curve:[/b] The game doesn’t explain much. You will suffer, you will fail, and then you will finally understand… right before failing again.  
[*][b]Toxicity:[/b] The player base ranges from supportive teammates to players who would sell your soul for a flashlight battery. Proceed with caution.  
[*][b]Time Commitment:[/b] Once a trial starts, there’s no turning back. Hope you don’t have real-life responsibilities, because Murkoff doesn’t care.  
[/list]  

[h2]The Ugly[/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b]Your Team:[/b] No matter how prepared you are, you’re only as good as the one guy who insists on sprinting into danger like it’s a speedrun.  
[*][b]Your Ego:[/b] Think you’re good at horror games? The Outlast Trials will personally see to it that you are not.  
[/list]  

[h2]Overall[/h2]  
[b]The Outlast Trials[/b] is an intense and chaotic horror experience that’s as fun as it is traumatizing. It’s not for the faint of heart, nor for those with weak Wi-Fi. The steep learning curve and unpredictable teammates can be frustrating, but if you thrive on fear and teamwork (or betrayal), this game is for you.  

Just don’t be surprised if you start double-checking dark corners in your own house after playing.  

[quote=My Fractured Sanity]  
“Final Rating: 8.5/10 – Would recommend, but only if you enjoy being stalked and psychologically dismantled.”  
[/quote]

-THINGS THAT REALLY HOOKED ME-
-Visually horrifying: My friends and I are horror fanatics, and first playing the game and evolving with it as they released more maps it was always an 'Ooo' or an 'ah gross'. -The community is really nice: In my entirety of playing, I haven't come across any players that have given me a hard time, especially during events, everyone is super welcoming and helpful. Even outside of events, if I have a task or a certain map I have a low score on, most people I play with will help me get a better score. The community is also why I really press this game. At first I was really insecure about playing with others because I didn't have a mic, and I just didn't like mic call-outs, but I even had played in a group that was nothing but in-game pings and call-outs. After dedicating 41.1 hours to The Outlast Trials and securing 59% of the achievements, I've experienced the game both with friends and solo, occasionally teaming up with random players. Here's my detailed review, highlighting the pros, cons, and mixed aspects, with a special focus on the Escalation Therapy mode.

🟢 Pros:

1. Intense Cooperative Horror Experience 🧟‍♂️The game delivers a chilling atmosphere that is amplified when played with friends. Coordinating with teammates enhances the immersion and makes each trial a heart-pounding experience.

2. Escalation Therapy Mode 🕹️This roguelite mode introduces a series of randomized trials with escalating difficulty. Starting with minimal equipment, players build their loadouts as they progress, facing increasingly challenging scenarios. The mode offers high replayability and tests both strategy and endurance.

3. Varied Gameplay Modes 🎮Beyond the main trials, modes like Escalation Therapy provide diverse challenges, ensuring the gameplay remains fresh and engaging.

4. Atmospheric Design and Soundtrack 🎵The game's environments are meticulously crafted, and the haunting soundtrack intensifies the sense of dread, keeping players on edge throughout their sessions.

🔴 Cons:

1. Steep Learning Curve for Solo Players 🧗‍♂️While cooperative play is exhilarating, tackling trials alone can be daunting. The difficulty spikes significantly in solo mode, which might deter some players.

2. Limited Progression Persistence in Escalation Therapy 🔄In Escalation Therapy, if all players die, the session ends, and progression resets. This can be frustrating for those who invest significant time only to start over.

⚖️ Mixed Points:

1. Randomized Loadouts in Escalation Therapy 🎲The random nature of loadout selections adds unpredictability, which can be both thrilling and challenging. While it encourages adaptability, it may also lead to situations where players feel underprepared for certain trials.

2. Community Engagement 👥Playing with random players can be hit or miss. While some sessions are cooperative and enjoyable, others may suffer from a lack of coordination or communication, affecting the overall experience.

💲 Value for Money:

Priced at $39.99, The Outlast Trials offers substantial content, especially for those who enjoy cooperative horror experiences. The addition of modes like Escalation Therapy enhances replayability, making it a worthy investment for fans of the genre.

🏁 Conclusion:

The Outlast Trials successfully blends horror with cooperative gameplay, delivering a terrifying yet thrilling experience. The Escalation Therapy mode stands out as a highlight, offering a challenging roguelite experience that tests players' endurance and adaptability. While solo play presents significant challenges, the game truly shines when experienced with friends.

🌟 Final Verdict: A must-play for horror fans who love a challenge—whether alone, with friends, or with complete strangers.

I am very confused by all the positive reviews, since my experience has been the complete opposite. 

I do agree that it's a very simple sidescrolling 2D platformer with appealing graphics that doesn't take much thought or effort, but this is where my review skews off in a different direction.

Because it's very simplistic in design, it's imperative that what's there should work perfectly, and when it comes to the control scheme, that's just not the case. Firstly, the controls cannot be rebound, and in any game that uses the B button for jump, that's always my first instinct. That mild aggravation aside, the controls just aren't consistently responsive or accurate. The side to side movement often results in the character aiming his weapon up, as if he's shooting something above him. This makes everything else more difficult. You can't jump or duck, or even avoid projectiles accurately because the controls don't work properly.

I would definitely give this game another try when the control issues are resolved. There are some things that I appreciate, such as the checkpoints, that can't be fully enjoyed because I have not found the game to be consistently playable. There are definitely times when I want to reach for a simple shooter, but right now, Rusty Gun is simply not that shooter. 

I've requested a refund and cannot recommend it at this time.

A fun variant of the match three genre.
The story is that you are collecting items for some ritual, but it is really only a conceit to give the game a theme. It does that well enough though.
The art is nice much of the time, though the quality varies. I find the music quite pleasant, but you can turn it off if it bugs you.
There are a variety of levels of difficulty to suit your taste. You can give yourself a time deadline or a move deadline depending on your style.
There are a variety of odd things you have to do to move ahead, some common, like 'match the piece that is locked in place' or 'match next to a piece to cause an effect.' There re also squares you need to match multiple times to finally get it to count as clear.
One thing I do like is often you only get the result if the match is the result of your action rather than the random result of falling colors. Not always, but enough to make things feel less accidental. 
Every once in awhile a different kind of puzzle pops up. I get the impression you can skip these, but so far I have simply done them. The three types are a simple jigsaw, one where you have to connect the pipes (which is fun enough, but seems well out of character to the theme of the game) and a sliding puzzle to remove one of the pieces which is usually in the form of cars and trucks in a parking lot, but here they are just slats of bamboo. 
Nice to mix things up.
The only thing I notice missing is the chance to re-try a level if you want to get a better ending. (You earn one to three stars based on something, your score I think) and I have yet to see a screen showing all of your levels so you can go back. The stars don't seem to add up to anything yet, so it doesn't seem like a big deal.
All in all a fun game, an easy thumbs up.
ADDENDUM: 9.3 hours of play start to finish. Not too shabby, and I feel like it has some replayability. Only found one totally broken level, but it was skippable, and one partially broken level that I found a work around for. 
EDIT: I've put a lot of hours in to this now, and am most of the way through my third time, lots of replayability.
ADDENDUM: Closing in on one hundred hours, and I really find this game keeps me coming back. I think the best part about it for me is the fact that many things you do only work if it was the result of an intentional switch by you. Too many match-3 games, random-ish chance creates power ups and such and do too much of the work. This is a nice mix of helpful drops and requiring thought and effort. Plus I can skip over the filler levels. I enjoyed playing them the first time thru, but now all I want is the match-3. I wish there was a random level maker or something, but I still enjoy going thru the same eighty or so levels levels over and over.
ADDENDUM: Not for completionists, not all of the achievements seem to work.

I am 27.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ing minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.
