For starters, consider this more of a "side vote" than an outright downvote. If the review score was very low, it would be a thumbs up. As it stands, however, the quality level needs to improve for me to justify a thumbs up at the current rating.

A quick summary of the positives: The combat is mostly good, there are a number of challenging encounters. The boss fights are kind of good. There is some gimmickry at work, but for the most part they are the good kind of boss fight - big scary thing, loads of health, dangerous attacks which can be avoided with skill and cover. I enjoyed them. The weapons are mostly fun to use, too, with some creativity in their design.

The overall theme of the game is fairly unusual as well, another positive; you get to play as a sort of gender-swapped Sarah Kerrigan (Zerg Queen of Blades), mixed with an insect vampire from that one Darkest Dungeon expansion. So, you run and jump and flap around looking for blood to accumulate focus points and upgrade your arsenal. Also you use upgrade points to revive if killed, assuming you've gotten to the level's first checkpoint before dying. You an even get some of them back by making it back to where you died, which is a nice touch. Bit soulsy. Like it!

Now for the stuff I'm a bit more ambivalent about.

The damage system is strange - your health is extremely vulnerable unless covered with armor, and you may never have more armor than health. Thus, if you take a bad hit while low on armor, most of your health is gone and in the absence of healing pickups (which are thankfully usually plentiful) you might be staggering around mostly dead for half of the level. Health pickups convert to armor if your health is full, but armor pickups can only be used for armor. This makes it a bit tactical how you use the pickups, but at the end of the day, the smart way is this: Get the armor-restoring upgrade for your armor-cracking hitscan rifle (or the chaingun, which also seems to have the same armor-heal upgrade for some reason) and just use a few bits of the ever-plentiful bio ammo to fix your armor after a moderate or heavy hit. Fast, effective, and it means you can save all health pickups for healing any lost health.

On the topic of anti-armor hitscan rifles, some of the enemies have them too. This can be a major problem, as they can remove most of your armor from across the map and then have one of their cheeky friends take all your health in one hit. Adds to the sense of tension and urgency in combat, true, but it can feel a tiny bit annoying to frantically look around trying to find the jackoff who's nuking your health from a mile away, while also dodging all the regular, avoidable projectiles. It walks the tightrope between fun and frustration, as it were, and it's wobbling a bit.

There is a lot of platforming, with a slightly annoying amount of precision required for some of it. If you want to go secret-hunting for upgrade resources and other goodies, you can expect a lot of careful jumping, long falls and tedious climbs to restore your previous progress. Still, if you enjoy platforming in first person (and who doesn't love that, slightly sarcastic tone!) then you will find some fun here.

The story is... okay. Sometimes it kind of feels like it's pulling in different directions. The protagonist has a duality about him; ostensibly a guardian of life, but also an undeniably effective mass slaughterer. The enemy faction is interesting enough, and (without wanting to spoil too much) it feels alarmingly plausible. It could be worse, but it suffers a bit from some UI issues; for instance, advancing through dialogue is done by pressing the E key, TWICE per text window. Except when it just sort of skips one without a single press. And also, the in-game text says "hold E to skip", and says nothing about how to proceed. It feels clunky, interface-wise, which brings the experience down a bit.

This neatly moves us on to the purely negative - the aforementioned interface issue is not confined to the story events, but also appears in-game. Reloading frequently takes two or more presses of the reload key. Throwing a grenade may or may not. Switching weapons or using a "quick" melee attack, again, might take several presses. Cancelling a shot or even a reload to swap weapons rather than stand there reloading slowly while being shot to pieces? Nope, if you fired the last shot, you have to wait for the reload to finish. Except that sometimes your weapon doesn't even start reloading until you hammer the reload key a couple of times. Try to heal with an empty hitscan rifle? No heal, no reload. And it still takes a few presses to swap to another weapon, or start reloading the thing. This is all a lot more trouble than it should be, and greatly diminishes the feel and flow of the game.

Melee is odd and messy and doesn't work very well. Your sword produces mostly vertical slashes, but without much actual vertical sweep, so odds are you won't hit anything that's not standing still right in front of you. You also have a charged up power attack which, again, will probably miss. Which isn't great for an attack that takes a second or two for each attempt. It also managed to stop working almost entirely when I tried to use it to finish off a late-game boss for the fun of it; charge-up, release, lack of actual power slash, perpetual charge-up pose, weapon swap, try again, same result. Not great.

Elevators, which appear in some of the later levels, do not work some of the time. In the final level, there is an elevator whose recall button breaks the elevator and forces you to restart the level. There's also an issue where you resume from a checkpoint partway through a level (several of the levels are quite large, to the game's credit) and you inexplicably start with no weapons at all - not even the sword. And this game is not designed for "pistol-starts", i.e. Doom having many or all of the weapons obtainable within each level. You need your sword and weapons to get through breakable walls and such. There is a workaround, thankfully - you can restart the entire level, which in some cases means a significant amount of progress robbery, and play through the whole thing in one sitting, which should be doable for most people - but it's an inconvenience and it shows a definite lack of polish and bug-squashing.

At the end of the day, this is a game that's being sold for money, and there's an embarrassing amount of janky code and interface trouble for a finished product.

If it sounds like your cup of tea, there are still worse games to spend one's money on. But there are also a fair number of better games, albeit none with quite this mix of styles and themes at play. Ambivalently semi-recommended.

I've been playing Tetris for decades and only now do I find out that adding a third dimension to Tetris is the actual and only way to play.

A great Tetris variant where the play space is two rows deep and instead of falling pieces, you just grab the next piece and place it anywhere you want (even floating above the others). There is no rush other than trying to get on the leaderboard, so it can be a nice relaxing game or it can be a hectic race to do better before your time runs out.  You can conveniently adjust the height and placement of the play space and serving deck to accommodate your play style (tall or short.  Left handed or right handed).  Coins and hearts appear at the top of the play space and fall only as you clear lines.  You have to fill in around these obstacles but they give extra points (coins) and extra time (hearts) when you clear that row.  There is also one new piece that forces you to play across both rows, which can be handy or infuriating, depending upon what you need.

The local leaderboard is tied to the account, so you don't get to identify who got what score, so in a house of Tetris nuts (like mine) you have to keep track of who has high score manually to ensure bragging rights.

Highly recommended if you like Tetris and VR.

This would've worked better if the developer just made traditional Tetris in VR instead of trying to reinvent the wheel. In order to clear lines, you have to complete the line in 3D space, both in front and back of the playing field. This not only slows down the game but makes placing the new block, a T block with one side rotated inward (making it 3D), especially frustrating. The developer seems to have realized this by including another new block, a single square to plug holes, but it's so rare that they're almost never useful. Other problems over vanilla Tetris include a lack of upcoming block preview, no increase in speed because of no falling blocks, and broken balance because you can place blocks anywhere. There's also no fail state outside of running out of time in Score Mode... You're expected to just realize the game is over when you can't place more blocks and hit the quit button.

I feel bad for putting a red thumb on what was probably someone's first solo project but they're still charging money for this. With how many variations and spin-offs of Tetris that have been released over the years, there's no reason to buy this. It's not even fun to play seated because of the range of motion required to place pieces. You're better off just playing vanilla Tetris for free on countless websites in your browser.

What does boring mean anyway, tiresome? Uninteresting? Repetitive maybe? No one ever says efficient. How could boring mean efficient you will most likely be asking. Imagine a hurdler and a free runner, the hurdler will just run and jump over the hurdles when they need to, quick precise jumps over the hurdles, but the free runner will run, slider under the hurdle, front flip, cat pass over the hurdle. The hurdler will likely win, but the audiences eyes will be on the frankly flamboyant parkour artist as its more interesting than the strictly boring hurdler. This is a perfect metaphor for the protagonist in this game.

There are many different types of contract killers out there, some people love close combat with knives, or other blades, others like to be stealthy and use the famous garrotte wire. Heck some even somehow get others to do their bidding like the famous Chester Wheeler Campbell a fairly dangerous contract killer during the 80s, some use guns up close and personal, maybe even a suppressed weapon for the slightly more silent ballistics kill. Then of course there are the killers that leave no trace, people that make it look like a suicide, or an act of god, perhaps a choking or a heart attack. Then likely the most boring of them all. 

The marksman. Someone that sits on the building opposite and waits for the perfect kill shot, takes out the target and leaves. Imagine how the John Wick Franchise would be if someone just shot Mr Wick from five hundred metres away with a high powered rifle, I tell you what it would be like, terrible, it would be a short film and rather boring. 

Unfortunately for Hollywood, this is the most efficient way of killing someone quickly and in the smallest amount of time possible, no fannying around bribing guards to put Ricin or Aconite into someone food or drink, no messing about with knives or guns close to the victim. No trace. 

One letter. B. What does this mean to you, the common man. If you have never played this game, likely nothing. It could be a name, it could be an insect or animal. Or it could be a trained killer. 

B short for Boring or Bodhi (no one is really sure) is the name of our protagonist in this game, although he is an emotionless killer with no empathy, sympathy or remorse, he is a legend in his field. 

He has never failed a contract, never missed a shot and somehow is not only the cheapest contract killer, but is also the easiest to contact. Yet no one has ever heard his real voice, seen him or had any conversation with him. He will either seek out open contracts or you send him some basic details on your desired victim.

Bodhi is a codename, nobody wants to call him boring as, he doesn’t deserve that treatment, he is one of the most reputable killers in the business, so we call him Bodhi. 

Bodhi has no family, no friends, no colleagues and no acquaintances, he works alone. Some say he was raised by wolves, others say he just spawned and people even say he doesn’t exist. But we all know that’s not true, Bodhi has successfully killed 1000s of people without being caught.

How does he complete such feats you may be asking, well I will tell you.

First we’ll start with appearance, Agent 47, is a bald, 5 ft 10 man with a barcode on the back of his head who often wears a two-piece suit, not very conspicuous if you ask me. Bodhi however is trained in blending in. He wears normal, casual civilian clothing, often looking like a tourist or a resident of whatever country the hit is taking place in. Whatever he is wearing, wherever he is, he will always carry a bag, a rucksack maybe with a hidden compartment, where he stores his weapon of choice

This takes me nicely on to the rifle he uses during every contract. The Remington Defense CSR (Concealable Sniper Rifle), a lightweight and compact 7.62mm bolt action takedown suppressed sniper carbine with a 14 inch barrel. It is small enough to collapse into a normal sized laptop case and powerful enough to take out a human being at up to 1500 metres, this is something that Bodhi takes advantage of. 

Legend has it Bodhi only brings one bullet to his jobs, his rifle may be suppressed, but any gun shot noise is bound to give people a fright, one job that caught the attention of other contractors was the triple threat trio, they were 3 dangerous men, who ran a very large drug cartel together, an open contract came out to take out all three men for the low, low price of $50 million. The information put out about them was that they were at a friends wedding, putting family first. Other contractors that were there said they heard one rifle round being fired, somehow taking out all three of them in one shot, the bullet went cleanly through all of their heads killing all of them instantly. The police arrived instantly, eager to get some dirt on these 3 high class criminals, but they found nothing, except one little thing, the letter B engraved into the bullet lodged into the third man’s head.

The police and eventually the other contracted killers that were at this venue waiting to kill all three found that the place that B shot from would have been directly in the open, but no one saw anything out of the ordinary, he went unnoticed. 

It was at this point, which was fairly early in his career (as far as we know) that others became aware of this living legend, someone so efficient, could even live. Somehow this guy is still one of the cheapest killers in the business and can often kill someone within 48 hours, wherever they are. 

They say the only thing holding him back from being quicker is the lack of quicker travel options, think of that, a killer so efficient, that the only thing holding him back is the fact planes don’t fly fast enough, its completely crazy. 

For all anyone knows, Bodhi could be a semi normal guy or girl, a family man perhaps, maybe a someone that can get away with travelling a lot. But I guess we will never know. This game unfortunately doesn’t give anything much more personal, we don’t ever see the character we play, nor even hear his voice. I am really hoping the second iteration of this gives us a little more information about this illusive creature. Well that’s unlike me, I never ramble on about back-stories. 

What’s the gameplay like then. Yeah its not good.

Its spectacular, somehow its taken all the best parts of all the favourite adventure and action games, mixed them together into one game, it pretty easily takes elements from tomb raider and hitman not to the point that its just stealing assets from the other games, no, of course not, like most of the games I play, this game is very immersive, on a few of the contracts I took, after playing them to their fullest I started feeling like a psychopath, I mean seriously the brutality of these kills is insane, it can take tolls on your very being. Which is why there certainly should be an age warning on this game.

The graphics are simple, but still easily manage to suck you into the game and live it likes its real, it was never designed to be like the real world, no, few people actually have the need to take people out for cash in real life, although the extra dough would be nice. 

So coming to a conclusion, is this game worth it. Yes of course it is, this game (in the UK) is 79p, seventy-nine pence, are you kidding me, buy this game now if you don’t own it already, if you like the hitman series or hell, even the tomb raider series put your decaff, almond milk, caramel syrup macchiato down and buy this damn game. Next time you go to Starbucks don’t pick up the extra marshmallows in your hot chocolate, buy this game.

The more I played this game, the more I got annoyed by it shortcomings. Halfway through my 150 hours played I had to install mods to make it bearable again.

If, like me, you got interested in the building in automation part and possibly played modded Minecraft before, I am going to say straight away - modded Minecraft is a much better experience.

The game loop is as follows:
Get stronger > Collect materials > Advance Age > Go to next zone

Sprinkled in between are caves, which there are 4-5 variants, followed by treasure rooms, which use the same 2 rooms but with a different puzzle or boss.
Another thing in between are the instances, which also use the 3-4 layouts with a different coloring, mobs and bosses.

It brings up that strange feeling of "same same, different, but still the same". It starts being obvious after first 2 zones. This also includes enemies, which in 95% are different flavor of goblin (insert goblinslayer.jpg).

The things that is the most jarring is the concept of building, automation and inventory. You can automate every single resource in this game if not every item in this game. But doing so will end up with user developing a possible brain aneurysm /s 
Automation is just good enough for a user to be able to make every item, but nothing beyond that. The more automation you place and the longer they run, the more the game performance takes a hit, since there is no automatic off switch, nor a way to dispose of overflow of resources, which will cause items on your conveyor belts to stack at the very edge of your container's entrance, waiting for an open slot in order to fall in. Over a long period of time and throughout multiple areas where your place your automations, it grinds the game to a halt.

Building is another thing - wall/floors/roofs are modular and are available in different themes. But not all themes have the same amount of options. When used according to templates (which user can craft and place anywhere in the world, but can only dismantle them piece by piece... annoying as hell) the buildings can look really nice, but at some point you have to choose between practicality and looks - and that is disappointing.
In addition to above, there is placement - there are 3 placement types most of the time - free, grid and "action". I won't go into detail for each one, I'll just say that the building aspect would benefit immensely with a toggleable snap function, since IMO "action" type does not cut it, unless you start building in a spot dictated by world chunks, and that can get really annoying for 'some scenic spots'.

And lastly - inventory. I would risk statement that inventory management is the most important aspect of such games. Or maybe I've been spoiled by "Applied Energistics 2" too much.
A simple "Craft from containers" feature would go a loooong way in alleviating most of the issues. Instead, we have to manage well over 200 different types of items, from which most stack to four stacks of 100 in one slot, but can stack less if some of these stacks are enchanted (and you can only strip enchantments from items manually), while mid-game containers are up to 40 slots large, which forces you to craft dozens of them. Now good luck finding that specific part you need to craft something that will be used to craft something else. Over and over again.
I don't get it why it must be that hard. There is no pride in braving through an annoying inventory system, honest.

Yet despite all that, you can encounter specific parts of the game (puzzles, areas, descriptions etc) that really show developers love and creativity, which IMO makes this game an interesting case study for other game developers.

The sad thing is there is way too many things to do in order to improve the overall experience, while it definitely won't be profitable enough to ever do so. I just hope that the devs of Craftopia learned from this experience and will make sure their next game will be better (at the time of writing this, Palworld is the next game, but I didn't play it and unfortunately cannot afford it right now)

I thought Toem was cute! It gives me major Scribblenauts vibes. While their gameplay differs (photography vs. creating objects with a magical notepad), both games have you help people by collecting stars in thematically-distinct regions and seem primarily aimed at younger audiences. They also have a similar art style.

Now, apologies for what will be a spoiler-heavy review, but humor me, as Toem has left me ruminating on its color palette.

[spoiler]For almost the entire game I wished there was a bit of color. I found that the lack of color hurt the game's visual appeal and wondered if the devs just made that choice to lighten their artists' workloads a bit. However, after finally seeing toem at the end, I realized I couldn't have been more wrong. I didn't even realize right away why toem was so darned beautiful and impactful, but suddenly it dawned on me that the beautiful aurora was the first time that the player ever sees color.

This could be reading into things too much, but I took "seeing toem" as a metaphor for having a change in perspective on life. Our character travels far and wide to realize that the world we once found gray and lifeless was actually full of color. The preceding hours of seeing wholesome and beautiful things in monochrome really set up that point, so I think the color scheme choice was critical in letting the ending have the impact it did.

You start the game sitting on your bed in your room in a totally gray world looking at flowers through a TV screen. When you walk into the next room, the first thing Nana says to you is "Look who made it out of their room", as if you had been spending a lot of time in there lately, and venturing out at all was a big step for you. That's what allows for the "the day you've dreamed about", of seeing toem, to finally come; it's a return to life, or at least the start of one, brought about by literally seeing the world from a different perspective through your camera, which stands in for a shift in emotional perspective. There's a reason that Nana doesn't want you to try to experience it through her photo album; it's a lesson that is best learned yourself, and she realizes the day has come that you're ready for it.

I was curious about the meaning of toem, and an online dictionary informed me that töm (i.e. toem) means "to empty" in the devs' native Swedish. You could therefore interpret "experiencing toem" as "experiencing nothingness", or leaving behind the self and having an encounter with the sublime at the top of the (likely metaphorical) mountain. This would point to having a profound and transformative emotional experience while viewing yourself from an outside perspective.[/spoiler]

Other pros:
* Lovely music. A couple of the tracks were downright special.
* Cute and wholesome. [spoiler]I love the guitar wizard :)[/spoiler]
* Decently fun gameplay loop. The photo compendium might be the closest I've been to the trick book from SSX Tricky since I was a kid.
* The game isn't voice acted, but the dialogue still gives the impression of being in Swedish, which I found interesting and fit with the setting and developers. Always fun when games unintentionally leave me thinking about linguistics.
* Some nice attention to detail, like [spoiler]setting a trend with your hat in the fashion show and encountering people around town wearing your hat afterwards.[/spoiler]
* Some cool and unexpected moments [spoiler], like the moose DJ area and the cosmic deer.[/spoiler]
* You can pet most of the animals.

Cons:
* Nearby objects looked blurry through the camera even without zooming.
* I found the menus to be a bit clunky to navigate. For example, if you access the quick select menu via the X button, you have to be holding the d-pad arrow when you let go of X to get the selected item to actually to open. It should open the second you hit the d-pad. Also, the pause menu and backpack buttons are flipped from how 99% of games set them.
* This is almost certainly a me problem, but I didn't realize until Basto that you can change the zoom level with LT and RT. For the entire base game I just tolerated the suboptimal zoom levels that would sometimes carry over from cutscenes and smaller rooms until the game would reset them on its own.

Found a demo of this game a while back while looking for an RTS to scratch this little itch I’ve been having and I gave it a go, and thought it was okay. Something that would be perfect for the app store if it wasn't filled with crap and ads. And after playing the full game, I was surprised how much I was enjoying myself.

Lets get the story and presentation out since there’s not much to talk about. Plot is just some guys get shipwrecked and end up on a quest to deal with a necromancer and ends on a meh cliffhanger. The art looks fine. Bit generic but everything was laid out in a professional manner. Although the human characters are clearly using  the same with different bits for the different units, I wouldn’t be surprised if the other races did that too. But hey, if you're going to be cheap, best be cheap in the places no one will notice.

Now for the gameplay. Starting with the size of the maps. I was a bit disappointed that there were only 8 levels and 3 of them were already in the demo. But when I got to level 4, I was actually impressed with the scale of the map since the first 2 levels didn’t need scrolling and the third just went up and down. The fourth level actually felt like a proper RTS map and it had landmarks like the stairs leading to the castle area. Some scaffolding near you starting point. There’s a blocked area where a fire elemental is prowling around. Color me impressed. And the rest of them levels weren’t bad either.

To be fair, I can easily see this as a port of a mobile game with its controls. You just click on an intractable item and the game picks the required unit. Need to collect an item? A worker would be sent to pick it up. Need to deal with an enemy? The game sends the required unit to deal with it. Want to build something? You can only build on designated building sites.

That isn’t to say it’s completely automated. There is a bit of linearity to the levels as you need upgrades certain units, and enough houses for those units to proceed and some side quests are done through naturally progression so thats easy rewards. You also have an inventory that you carry throughout the game that can carry things like level ups for you fighters, items to make gathering resources easier and potions and spells to make combat easier, and if you going for 0 losses, they are a must have. Also you can buy and sell resources to get more money for upgrades, gather ingredients for potions for healing or dealing with hazards or just buy items from the Witch’s Hut

While at first, 8 levels might seem disappointing, it’s probably a good thing cause they seemed to be out of ideas by the end and level 7 seemed like a proper final level compared to the actually final level with it’s tricky combat encounters and having to cancel commands when hazardous floors started to act up. Though if they want to do a sequel, I hope they do more with the cleric cause he really feels like a glorified key whose features could easily be done by the wizard.

So yeah. This game was a pleasant surprise.

GRID Legends – A Fun Ride with Some Frustrating Pit Stops
GRID Legends is a game that delivers high-speed thrills, but only if you're the kind of racer who doesn't mind a track-focused experience without open-world exploration. It's packed with intense races, but the lack of scenic variety might leave some players wanting more. If you're expecting the freedom of Forza Horizon, this ain't it—it's all about structured track racing.

The Good Stuff:
✅ Fast, Fun, and Accessible – If you just want to hop in and race without worrying about deep sim mechanics, GRID Legends keeps things exciting.
✅ Great Dual-Clutch Support – If you're using paddles, the shifting is smooth and responsive, giving you that race-day adrenaline rush.
✅ Plenty of Cars and Tracks – While it lacks open-world freedom, there's a solid variety of tracks and vehicles to keep you busy.

The Annoying Stuff:
❌ Aggressive AI That Feels Unfair – The further you climb in the race, the more the AI goes into Terminator mode. Expect to get rammed, blocked, and squeezed off the track like you're in a demolition derby.
❌ Broken H-Pattern Shifting – This is where things get really frustrating. If you're using an H-pattern shifter, downshifting can be a nightmare. Even when following the correct sequence, the game will sometimes throw your car into neutral, refusing to recognize the gear change. Fixing it mid-race? Good luck—you’ll have to press the clutch, move the shifter back to neutral, and then into the correct gear at least three times before the game finally decides to cooperate.
❌ Repetitive Track Design – If you're looking for beautiful landscapes or dynamic racing environments, GRID Legends might feel a little dull. It’s track after track after track—no breathtaking scenery or open roads.

Final Verdict:
GRID Legends is a fun game if you're into structured, no-nonsense track racing. But if you’re looking for an open-world experience or a flawless manual transmission system, you might end up more frustrated than entertained. It's got solid speed and exciting races, but the AI and H-pattern shifter issues can make it a bumpy ride.

Upgrades are a whole separate issue. Think upgrading your car gives you an edge over your opponents? No, absolutely not. Instead, AI cars get faster to match your upgrades. What's even the point of this system?

Taking heavy inspiration from it’s tongue in cheek name, Dark Sales is a 2D Souls-like game with charmingly simple visuals and strikingly challenging gameplay. Taking place in an office setting with most enemies being other employees the game is satisfyingly solid. We spent a few hours with the game and here are our spoiler-free first impressions.

How does it look?:
The game is highly stylized with simplistic but very effective visuals. We initially had some difficulty discerning what we could and couldn’t interact with in the relatively open world but the game’s consistency and informative tutorial set us up for success in the long run. Whether you’re resting at water coolers, fighting pencil pushers, or exploring a sewer you’ll be pleasantly surprised by the look of Dark Sales.


How does it feel?
Dark Sales has very solid controls. We tried the game with both a keyboard and a controller, we found the latter much more enjoyable while the game was still perfectly playable using the fairly intuitive keyboard controls. The game proves itself challenging and worthy of its name early on with punishing combat and satisfyingly rewarding kills that you’ll feel you worked for. Once we found ourselves acclimated with the controls and finished the tutorial there really wasn’t anything to complain about as far as playability, another solid win for Dark Sales.


How does it sound?
In a word the game sounds fantastic. From the main menu music to the auditory feedback of landing hits on enemies the game feels lovingly put together. We found the boss music intense and the water cooler (Dark Sales version of bonfires) resting music perfectly serene just as it should be. We think the sound design is a huge win for Dark Sales and something that can’t be compromised on for a souls-like game.


Final Verdict:
Dark Sales is definitely worth a buy, currently listed on Steam at $14.99 with the developer working on console releases in the near future Dark Sales is more than up to the task of delivering a quality, highly stylized, and endlessly charming experience to fans of both the office aesthetic and the souls-like game genre. We were optimistic going into this review because the idea of Dark Souls meets Suits: A Business RPG is an exciting prospect. You can move around the AI creatures, you can rotate the sky around to get a better view, or you can plant plants that will change the rotation of the planet. You'll get different results.

While I did manage to get most of them to survive on my next playthrough, there wasn't enough variety to hold my interest. Rather than being curious about all the different possibilities, I was numbed by all the sameness. I kept trying, but eventually had enough after about 45 minutes, mostly filled with lackluster & forgettable moments. 

This is running on the Unity Engine. On my 1060 GTX, I was getting mostly 90 frames per second, although I would get dips to 45 frames per second at times. The interactions are all simple, mostly point and click, and then grab type interactions. I did experience an issue where the game kept taking me in and out of the view of the planet for no apparent reason.

I normally like experimental VR type games, but this one just didn't do it for me personally. I think others may enjoy it more, but the AI was more like AD (artificially dumb). Just too simple overall. Didn't make me ask bigger questions like are we ourselves in a simulation or care at all about the story (was there a story?).

Worthy addition to the 'Escape the House' genre. Game is lovingly crafted by a small development team with pleasing art and sound effects. Environments focus on a Victorian style house, with a past. The game is divided into separate rooms, each with stand alone puzzles to solve in order to exit to the next. There is no backtracking.
There is a high level  back-story that is told through notes found throughout the house. You stumble upon several corpses but, for the most part, there are few horror elements.
The mechanics are a hybrid point and click. You click to move in a designated direction but then can pan, full circle, from your new view point. The environment is very detailed in each room and it is unusually dark until you start using your torch to light lanterns and candles. There are no timed sequences so you can play at your leisure.

There are a fairly limited number of hot spots in each area so you can quickly assess what information you have as possible clues to solve current puzzles.  This makes the game fairly easy for experienced puzzle solvers. My only sticking point was towards the end where I misinterpreted the environment and thought I had solved a puzzle (which I had not).

I'd recommend this game to those who enjoy the escape genre  and like casual puzzles. Although I enjoyed my time spent playing Possession 1881, I prefer to have clues implied rather than given (conceptual rather than outright). For me, this makes a game more challenging and engages my mind in a different way.

I've gotta be real. I love this game. It's like someone made the game of my dreams. I'd completely recommend it if it wasn't for one caveat: [b]the version I love is still in open beta.[/b] 

There's no denying that the game launched in a very weird state - It wasn't what the trailers showed game-play-wise. What was shown was a structured, level based rhythm shooter. What we got was an arena-based rhythm shooter with auto-beat-mapped levels, meaning the beat maps we made from an algorithm. Because of that, the game can sometimes feel off as some notes don't seem to fit too well. I would say it's an enjoyable yet flawed experience, but I wouldn't be able to recommend anyone get it off of the vanilla game. 

That's where the beta comes in.

I don't know what happened behind the scenes, but it seems like the game was forced to launch in a state that wasn't fully what the developers wanted. Was it due to the publisher needing more funding, an over ambitious release date, or pressure/obligations from Epic to release the game due to the grant? I honestly can't say.  But what I can say is that the Beta made me excited for the future of this game. Yes, there are still some bugs and kinks to work out, and yes, some of the charting feels off still, but they've put the structured levels back in and have tweaked some of the charts, and man am I having fun. I thought I would play maybe 10 minutes when I heard the beta was available, but I ended up playing for an hour without realizing it. The gameplay feels fast and chaotic yet never overwhelming, and it has a satisfying difficulty to it. It's extremely satisfying to blast enemies away and jump and dodge in perfect time to the music while trying to beat the song to the next checkpoint. It feels like I'm starting to see what the developers wanted all along, and it's got me excited for what's to come.

Even with all its issues I can't lie about how much fun I'm having while playing the beta, which is why I still recommend it. 

Is it fair to recommend a game that doesn't even have it's most optimized version out yet? Probably not. Should this have been delayed for release or put into early access? Probably so. Even so, the engagement I've seen from the developers on their discord tells me we're going to see the best form of this as soon as realistically possible, and that my purchase wasn't for nothing. They've stated the next update coming will be the public release of the beta and we should expect it soon with more updates following shortly after. 

The TL;DR is this: [b]Something happened behind the scenes and the game released in a disappointing state, but the beta proves the developer's commitment. You can rightfully wait until the game has its next update for what's been shown in the trailers, or you can get it now and support the developers as they work to make good on what they've shown us. I do love me some Rhythm games, but I’m not the best at FPS’s, so any time I can combine the two together and use my love for rhythm to help combat my slowly deteriorating hand-eye coordination, I’m all for it.  Rhythm FPS’s have been cropping up at a higher rate in recent years with the likes of BPM and Metal: Hellsinger gracing PCs so seeing studios’ iterations of the genre is just more music to my ears.  After seeing Gun Jam put out solid ideas and presentation through its demo, its 1.0 release has come and gone and, well, fans are not pleased.  Gun Jam is currently Mixed on Steam, which always piques my interest, so I dive in and see what kind of flavor this Gun Jam is.

Gun Jam plops itself in the, “what if Audiosurf but with Guns” seat at the Rhythm FPS table.  Gun Jam slots in 10 original tracks to blast to in 3 arenas and a checkpoint-based stage.  Each character has 4 weapons that are beat-specific: the harder the beat, the bigger the weapon.  The OST ranges from Metal to EDM and sticks within those goalposts throughout, which is where the custom OSTs come in to butter the bread, but we’ll talk about those later.  Your goal in each Arena is to hit the highest score you can before time runs out, which is marked by the end of the song.

Controls are pretty simple and easy to pick up.  Your normal Attack/Dash/Melee are available with each character having an Overdrive activation, think like your Ultimate.  Attacks are done differently than other titles within the genre, as instead of being on each downbeat they are done based on specific instruments and pieces of each song.  These pieces and instruments also dictate which weapons you’ll use throughout the song: smaller beats and cymbal hits will use the purple machine gun, normal selected downbeats will use the yellow shotgun, quicker selected half-beats will use the blue railgun, and big booming bass notes or selected finishing four-beats will use the red grenade launcher.  Your dash is also attached to these weapons, as bigger weapons provide a bigger dash with the trade-off of losing your power on that beat.

I say “selected” a lot back there, this is because Gun Jam picks which beats you can actually do things on.  This makes positioning absolutely key, as big dashes needed to escape remove your big damage needed to kill enemies and damage is the only way the enemies will leave you alone.  Proper positioning is double needed because some songs will have pockets where no actions can be done so you’re left walking and/or jumping with limited movement which will have you getting hit and your heart meter down quickly.

I can respect the duality of having to choose between movement and damage because it makes smart play a key factor in maintaining a high combo, but not being able to dash/attack on every downbeat really slows the tempo of Gun Jam to a crawl sometimes, and it’s a real mood killer.  If you’re given 3 blue half-beats followed by a triplet or two of purple machinegun hits, your dashing is limited, and if you’re in a newly populated area (enemies will spawn in waves pretty much right on top of you when it’s time for them to spawn), having no movement is a guaranteed hit against you and you just have to deal with it.  Getting hit in games like these without the manual feel of human error makes taking damage deflating and off-putting: two emotions you never want in your up-beat, high intensity title.

These two adjectives run parallel with the game’s soundtrack.  Gun Jam comes pre-loaded with 10 tracks and they’re…okay.  Genres ranging from EDM to Trap Hop and Metal fill out the selections, and…look.  I understand licensed tracks are expensive and it can feel more in-house and special when a game provides its own jams to run its own courses.  But most of these tracks just aren’t good.  There’s one Metal track talking about one’s blood sugar that is more hysterical than riveting, and not because I’m diabetic.  There’s where the previously mentioned Custom OST comes to do what it can to help.

There’s no limitations to which songs you can add to your game, so long as they’re .mp3’s.  Since stages go as long as the song plays, most custom songs will be shorter experiences than the provided songs, but playing whatever song you want is pretty dope.  But we can’t have nice things as the beatmaps are automatically made and most songs do not have coherent beatmaps to coordinate a fruitful campaign against your enemies.  So while we are out here playing whatever songs sound dope, be ready for a coin flip of whether they actually work.  (Custom Beatmaps are currently in development but were not available during play.)

But if we’re really going to address the issue in the room here: this needed more time and funds.  With a fleshed out and promising demo, Gun Jam 1.0’d to what feels like a skeleton of what it wanted to accomplish.  Desperate to stand out against a stout lineup of Rhythm FPS’ of the past few years, Gun Jam attempts to shake the genre’s foundations and misfires in almost every aspect.  There’s a chance this game could show its true colors months down the road, but the entire band needs a tuneup before you buy a ticket.

 The demo that came out several months before release was amazing! The music was somehow curated to line up perfectly with the timing of shooting enemies, as well as the traversal of the levels. You were able to feel yourself get faster and better as you improved and got further each time. The high beats when you were swarmed with enemies, the small lulls that allowed you to dash to the next area, it felt like it all made sense. Like when you first start out, you get slapped around a bit, you dont reach the time gates fast enough, and you need to learn. And as you learn, you started to feel how the timing of each area lined up perfectly with the songs, the amount of enemies in a given space, and how far you needed to traverse at any given time; when you practiced and improved, the flow just clicked in your mind and felt so good, even if it could be too challenging sometimes. All of that seems to be gone now.

So what happened with the full release? Why does it feel so bad?? 
To start, lets just get this out of the way; the music is phenomenal. Truly the crown achievement is the soundtrack. Unfortunately thats where it ends though. The graphics are not impressive, but we already knew thats not why we're here, so we can ignore that. The level design from the demo seems to have gone out the window. No more corridors or mazes to navigate, now its just 1 big room. This creates a new problem where you don't know where enemies are coming from anymore. Previously as long as you kept marching onward, you knew that enemies would come face you head-on. But now that you're just playing in a big room, you can get swarmed from all directions. This simply does not work for Gun Jam. There's no radar. There's no minimap. There isnt actually anything to allow you to gather info to fight back. Hell for a game all about audio, the 3D sound design is atrocious. You can't hear enemies around you at all, they barely make a sound, which is why changing the game from gauntlet-style corridors to just 1 big arena is so frustrating to me.

The other major issue I have with this game is the auto-mapping of the song beats; basically those colorful cues for when youre allowed to fire your gun. Yes "allowed to" because you literally cant deal damage off the beat of the song. And the flow of the beat? Completely random. No idea how the hell it ended up SO different than in the demo, but the timing of when youre allowed to shoot feels so wrong. For a few seconds you'll be firing to the beat of the backing drums, then maybe it will switch tempo to like the bass or lead vocals or something and just completely throws you off. Like come on, I'm still clicking to the beat of the drums back there, they didn't go anywhere, so why did you have to change it up on me? Why is it that in the demo it was able to seamlessly flow from slow to quick and back to slow shooting and it all made sense with the phrases of each song, but now it feels so random?? It just feels so bad when you are swarmed on all sides by enemies, but the game said you need to wait 2 seconds until the next note where we will allow you to shoot gun. bro i am not jamming.

Besides that, the weapons themselves are kinda bland. No visuals or sounds or effects that really stand out. Kinda sucks not having any control over your arsenal at all, apparently only the song may decided for you which gun youre allowed to shoot when. Oh are you surrounded by a hoard of small guys? shotgun or aoe blast sure would be nice, but we're just gonna give you this zapper you can tap once every second. Maybe this doesnt even matter at all since there is hardly any enemy variety. nothing but 'big guy who walks at you for melee' or 'small guy that walks at you for melee'. I remember the demo also had a couple flying guys and a large robo boss type but thats about it.

man it doesnt feel good at all to crap all over this game that i was so excited to play. i seriously considered refunding this, but because i love the music so much i just cant do that. this game showed so much potential in the demo that seems to be all  gone now. no more levels, no progression, no story even. its literally just 'insert coin to play arcade game for a few minutes'. if they were to just manually adjust the firing of the weapons to the specific beats of each song, and then make those flow into actual maps, this game would be amazing. it would make it feel like an actual curated, tight, lovingly crafted experience. but as it stands now, cannot recommend this game. I've deleted my old review as I needed space for this updated review. This is my second edit of this review.

I've tried the update and, unfortunately, my opinions on the game are generally the same as before. I have a few things to clarify and add, but, it's still a game I wouldn't recommend anyone purchase. Not even on sale. If you want a rhythm shooter, play Robobeat for the easiest custom music options available and speed, Metal Hellsinger for the best progression and hardest music, and BPM for the highest challenge in the form of randomness. 

Compared to the demo, the current state of the game is still a major disappointment. Now, developers, I'm not whining about how the game isn't like the demo because I refused to give the game a fair shot. I'm whining about how the game isn't fun, and it isn't fair to assume the problems I, and others, have are because of our inability to adjust to the new system, as you have discussed on the official discord. The game has major problems from the ground up that are only exaggerated by it's current implementation. I will go through these problems, and discuss how and why the demo handled them so much better. 

In short, absolutely nothing is curated and that is felt. This is the biggest problem in the game. Every point will only server to expand on this. I will be comparing this to the demo at times because the demo was actually fun.

1. The beat mapping is terrible, and the reason why is that it went from manual beat mapping to automatic beat mapping, and every single problem in the game is only made worse by this. 

If you happened to be playing the levels with actual traversal, which I'll be ripping apart in a moment, it's entirely unfulfilling. Why is it unfulfilling? It's because the automatic beat mapping has no sense of progression. It doesn't actually follow the notes your ear hears and wants to play to, it follows whatever it automatically wants you to play to. You can be early in a stage, launching rockets everywhere, only to be stuck in a tiny room with a slow firing beat and no way to continue. This isn't an issue in difficulty, this is an issue in sense of progression. It's a rhythm game, don't make me feel like standing still is the best option. When you took the time to plan where the player will be, and when, LIKE THE DEMO, you curate the most amount of fun out of every given environment. Having easy to follow beats when you quickly travel from one arena to the next, fantastic. Having crazy combinations of beats to follow in a huge room full of enemies, an absolute blast. Ignoring both of those means you have no way to put fun in the players lap, only frustration and disappointment.

Why is this a problem in the first place? Because they thought allowing players to import their own songs meant that they could also just do the same process for their own songs, and on the off chance that players uploaded short or slow songs, that they'd need to compensate for stage sizes, which I will also talk about later. Now, the songs in the game aren't fun to play. Why would I even try to put my own music in the game when the game isn't fun on it's own? Why did the devs think that adding custom songs took precedent over the game itself being fun? I don't know. 

2. The levels are too small, and the progression is bad. They are either one arena which doesn't highlight the games strengths or have poorly put together levels you can traverse until you reach an arena you are stuck on for the rest of the song.

The levels being so small hurt it so much. The songs being poorly mapped is bad, but this makes that issue significantly worse. Of the stages, you have a few that are just one arena and a few that are a few hallways with an extra arena(s) before reaching the final arena. All of the songs that come stock in the game are too long for every single one of these arenas. There's not one song that plays well with any level, I've tried. Why is this the case? Because they were worried that the levels were gonna be too long and custom music wouldn't allow people to complete the stages. News flash, you can have single arena maps solely for custom tracks AND curated tracks specific to levels. 

These small levels force the player into an unfun gameplay loop. You pick a song, load up a level, try to get to the arena for the fun part, several levels lock off the arena until you kill enough enemies in the hallway, you kill enough, get to the arena, and just have to kill more enemies. It's not a new system to gaming, but the strengths of the game aren't with killing enemies. The strength is in speed. Let's talk about the gameplay loop for the demo. Run to the nearest arena as soon as you can because you are on a short timer that only gets extended with checkpoints, then when you make it to the arena you are in "objective survive" mode, once completed repeat until you reach a boss who is also focused on "objective survive". Killing enemies helps you survive, but you aren't locked from continuing with kills. This worked fundamentally better as well, due to the fact that the songs were level locked, had a sense of progression with the stage, and timing out was a real reason to always keep moving forward.

3. The game is designed around speed and nothing in the current game encourages speed like the Demo. 

How is the game is built around speed? The only two options of things you can do on an action indicator are attacking or dashing, that would imply that they are equally important. How does the game currently encourage speed? It doesn't. The songs are so long for such short stages that it feels like you could do nothing on half of the beats and complete handily. The stages being only one room, for a majority or the entirety of the level, means speed is useless outside of dodging a handful of boss attacks. And why would you try to move fast? Every locked point in a stage is locked behind kills, so dashing is a genuine waste of time unless necessary. So every room feels sluggish and boring.

How did the demo fair differently? As previously stated, the demo was focused on speed. It encouraged you to go fast because missing a beat counting as a "miss" meant you were supposed to do something with it. When you have no enemies, that means dash. You have a timer, and a real chance to run out of time if you play slow, so that means I should go faster. No checkpoints or arenas are locked behind kills? So that means I can focus on dodging. Soul Elegy is a turn-based dungeon crawler to be exact. I didn't find the roguelike part yet and probably won't in the near future. 

I had the game on my wishlist for a long time now but it was released with Chinese text only. Now, I saw the English text is available so I decided to try it out.

[h1]Dungeon Crawler?[/h1]
Even though the game's description doesn't say anything about being a dungeon crawler it basically is one. You go on a mission in an area and have a goal (Beat enemy X, finish 5 battles, find X, etc.). The area is divided into several rooms you can see on a mini-map. Every room has several cards you need to reveal first. It's either a chest, an event, a battle, or whatever else the game has to offer. As a side note, it certainly doesn't lack any content as of now. One card will reveal the way into the next room. After archiving your goal, you can back to your base. 

[h1]Base[/h1]
Your base consists of several buildings. One of these is called base (Yes, it's called the exact same. Probably because of a bad translation). This building lets you permanently upgrade attributes of units (for example more health) or give bonuses for future explorations (recover 5 mana after entering a blank tile in a dungeon, etc.) in exchange for some resources or currencies. Most things can be upgraded multiple times. 
Then there is a time rift. It lets you rewind the game to the previous day which feels a bit like cheating TBH and isn't really the meaning of a roguelike. 
In the undead habitat, you can recruit new units, and the cursed temple lets you cure negative effects in exchange for gold and time. 
Then there is the warehouse. Everything you collect during your exploration will get in there. Well, not everything to be exact. After every exploration, you can salvage some stuff... And the game tells you that everything you don't salvage will be salvaged automatically but some of these things land in the warehouse... I don't really understand it myself. There is some system behind this mechanic but It is explained pretty bad so I can't explain it either. 

[h1]English translation[/h1]
Like you probably know by now, the English translation isn't good. I'm not a native English speaker but I'm sure even native English speakers will have problems understanding everything the game wants to explain to you. The warehouse is just one of several examples. 

[h1]Battles[/h1]
Battles are turn-based but don't seem like the core of the game as a battle usually doesn't last longer than a few seconds. There are dozens of different units in the game with dozens of abilities in total but still, a battle won't last long enough to warrant being called strategic. This seems to be the result of a bad balance. 

[h1]Balance and difficulty[/h1]
The balance is all over the place. Some Units do crazy damage and can kill an enemy with one hit, others do not even half as much damage (With everyone being on the same level of course). This results in some battles ending in the very first turn before enemies can even move while others take a bit longer (I didn't have a fight lasting over a minute yet). Even some fights with a note saying "Hard" ended after my first attack and I'm already playing on the highest difficulty the game has to offer. On the other hand, some events can kill you instantly if you have bad luck but let me explain it in detail.
Most events are based on luck. There are 2 to 4 cards that will get mixed. You need to choose one of them and this decides if you pass or not. Some basic events will let all your heroes die instantly, meaning the exploration is lost, your units get a negative effect (skipping the first turn in future battles) and you need to restart.

[h1]Roguelike?[/h1]
The game's description says Soul Elegy is a roguelike but if you die in an exploration, you can retry it again. You can even rewind time (a whole day, one turn within a battle or the whole battle if you lost, etc.). I don't know how that's a roguelike. 
There is a timer in your base, telling you the knights will "penetrate" you after x days. Maybe if you die then, the game will end and you need to restart everything but since you can rewind time this doesn't sound plausible. 

[h1]Units[/h1]
You can upgrade units with stones and artifacts giving them better attributes. Aside from that, they gain exp after every fight. For every level up, they gain a new slot for stones and one skill point. With skill points, you can upgrade an ability or learn a new one. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
[*]There is a lot of content (Items, units, enemies, etc.). It doesn't feel like an early access game content-wise. 
[*]Many ways to make your units stronger with artifacts, stones, and leveling them up. 
[*]Randomly generated dungeons with many different events and happenings. 
[*]The base offers a lot of upgrades. [/list]

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
[list]
[*]The translation is so bad, you won't understand some mechanics at first (maybe after playing some more and trying it out). 
[*]Turn-based fights are a joke with them being over after a few seconds even on the highest difficulty. 
[*]The balance is all over the place. 
[*]The music doesn't fit the theme of the game IMO. [/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Soul Elegy has a lot to offer but certainly not fun. I just did not enjoy my time with it. Aside from the bad translation and not understanding some mechanics (I'm sure I would understand them after trying it out more), the battles are so underwhelming It feels like a clicker game. Yeah, I've just played an hour but there is no point in playing more if fights, on the highest difficulty, after the tutorial and with a note saying "Dangerous" or whatever, end after my first attack. I don't think this is the core of the game or if, it's just outright bad. There is no initiative for me to play more.
Maybe it's due to the fact this is still in early access or the targeted audience aren't strategy fans but I just can't stand to play more of it and I can't understand why it has so many positive reviews. 

I certainly can't recommend this game right now. Maybe I'll try it again in the future, but for now, I will refund it.

One increase SO much faster than the others and stuns your characters at the beginning of every fight.  SUPER FRUSTRATING.  Meanwhile, the game cuts you off from leveling until you beat the first "boss" level.  BUT, you can't level up past level 2 until you do, and it's HARD.  Not only that, you have to do it fast because your city gets attacked in 5 days (each day is a dive into a random dungeon) by several waves of enemies.  It backs you into a corner at every step and creates a constant feeling of annoyance.

Resources are really hard to come by, which is fine, but honestly even on the easiest mode I felt the difficulty eventually just spiked to a point where I can't progress past the second dungeon.  Maybe I'm just bad at it, but the game has a rewind feature both in base and in battle that I shamelessly scummed so that everything went well, and I am STILL getting crushed.  I have good items all my characters and am leveled up as high as it lets me.  

Basically the game takes some of the challenge of strategy out of it with this feature, yet blocks you from grinding, fully customizing, taking it slow, buying items (no place to buy potions that cure the 3 ailments listed above), etc.  I just don't understand the design choices and I feel lie there's nothing I can do differently to make my team stronger.  This makes for a wholly unfulfilled feeling when succeeding and a hopeless feeling overall.

There is so much potential here.  This should still be in early access until the balance is fixed and the translation is finished.  I can't understand half of what the game is telling me either.

This Game is criminally underrated!  

It's a beautiful blend of Strategy, Adventure, and even minor dungeon crawling!

Lets start with the Positives about the game.

Music?  Atmospheric, unique to each district and definitely carries the tone of each faction and their respective beliefs. 
Music is fantastic.

Graphics?  At first one might not be used to the more obtuse (unusual compared to other games) graphics and renditions, but once you look past that, it really sells itself well. Additionally, if you're familiar with Teslagrad [/spoiler TeslaDAD amirite?]  and World to the West, The character design is a return to form and stays true to the world-building that Rain Games has done.

Gameplay Loop. 
Bear with me as I'm not the most articulate.   You run around the various districts of Mesmer fulfilling favors, missions, negotiating, breaking in, blackmailing, riding hogs, grapple hooking thru the areas, or sneaking thru the night (more on that)

Each of these tasks is self-explanatory. The Game gives you DISTINCT locations where to find what you're looking for or WHAT area you're needing to be in.  Clues are within the text of the mission given.  Breaking in is a treat in itself.  You have a lock-picking mini-game which, once you figure out the trick, is no trouble at all.  The fact that each house that you CAN break into has it's own thematic approach is beautiful.
Blackmailing / Favors are a way of ensuring that your needs are met albeit with some additional steps or with a little bit of loose lips. 
Each of these elements leads to the "revolution" sim as it's been dubbed. 

The Grapple hook mechanic is also very nifty and is VERY WELL outlined by the blue boarders on the mini map.
I think the one thing that gets me is the sneaking around at night.  It is VERY EASY to avoid the guards, (and avoid being caught while chased) but sometimes their light source radius isn't telegraphed enough or it seems as if they see me when I'm several stories down (looking at you canaries area / Aesthetica stairs) Additionally, if I don't have the hog OR a grappling hook,   I don't think you can escape unless you make it to the under-city which can be difficult in itself.


Camera - Good
The camera is fantastic and does well to follow you above head or over the shoulder.  there ARE some minor camera snafus like when on steps, but this is mitigated if there are no bluecaps on the steps to cheese you. Otherwise great work is done to showcase the richness of the City of Mesmer.

UI - Mixed
If I'm being honest, I have some misgivings about the UI.  At first I felt it was rich and vibrant, useful and easy to use but when I started acquiring more and more goods, It became overbearing on my actual screen.  I like that it's nice and organized for the type of goods I have.  Blackmail, Foods, Drinks, Money, Art,  but after awhile it just takes too much real estate.  If they could be decreased in size, I would have WAY more fun sneaking around at night. 
Additionally,  It would help with the mission details (if you choose to get all of them at once, don't. You'll fail more that way) also tend to take up real-estate on your UI and they could benefit from taking a tone-down in size.

I would like to say though,  The Stacking of same items (The passes / Coercion) Is a great idea and should be applied to all of the items so they take up less room on the UI.

Now.  Lots to enjoy!  Game-play elements!  Lets talk about what I didn't like.

Tutorial. 
There is none. You're fresh off the boat making revolutions now and chances are, from this lack of info, you're going to fail several times in your initial runs.  While this is immensely frustrating at first, once you get the hang of it, you are REWARDED QUITE WELL. 
I would say that if there was A LITTLE BIT of hand holding, it would benefit from it greatly and people wouldn't be turned off almost immediately. 

Glossary. 
I would LOVE for there to be a glossary so I can keep track of all the cool stuff I've broken in to, seen, heard, about people. 
Not only would it add some nuance to it (such as showing characters preferred tastes and their characteristics) But it would nudge people more so into successful revolutions.

Load Time / Transition Screen
At the initial Game state,  there is an almost 5-6 minute load time (I timed it,  it was 5 minutes 54 seconds)  Now, in the world of 2020-2021,  This isnt okay.  HOWEVER.  I realize that this loading time, loads THE ENTIRE GAME.  There are virtually NO load times within the entire game whatsoever and after playing thru several runs, realize that this is probably for the better.
I think, if there was a disclaimer about this specific load time, or whats happening in the background, it might add to the play experience for people.

Bugs.
There was a bug that I encountered,  I was carrying a cake to the house of teri (This should be marked on your map btw at all times, please add it)  and interacted with a cat.   I was stuck in the animation until I instructed Teri to try and open a chest / door in which she automatically dropped it and I was free to move.  I can see this being a problem through if it was at night and Blue-Caps were chasing me.
There was also a 1 time occurrence where after getting caught by the police and enjoying their free social housing, The music was playing in the background but the game wouldn't move forward until about 3-4 minutes later.

For me this is minor but for others, they may not have the patience and assume the game crashed.

An delightful unique little experience, basically its an adventure with an very open ended nature. It's not procedually generated, everything has its place and as such the time managing aspect stays motivating even if you fail to spark the revolution during your first runs. The city has a lot to offer and while the quests might be very fetchy, they tell interesting stories and are not trivial in a sense that everything is tied to time as a ressource, so even trivial quests might be not that trivial if you know that you have a lot of time to spend for them.

Unfortunelately the game is very buggy, merely by opening the menu in different cutscenes. I had to restart it several times during my almost 7 hours of playtime.
I'm also not that fond of the sneaking at night, simply because there are no ways to distract guards, you are at the mercy of their random route, which can become very annoying if you have to carry a crate or lockpick at night.

But asides from these complaints the game felt very unique, basically it's a large sandbox and I was really curious to get accustomed with the city, sometimes in buildings the game even turns into a text adventures.
Also I truly value that the game saves automatically for every passing hour, if that wouldn't be the case and it would rather feature manual quicksaves it pretty much would have ruined the game, but with the automatic saves the game is much more tense it would be boring being able to reload after every failed roll it would've been way too tempting, Rain Games definitely made the right decision, not every game benefits from manual quicksaves.


So it's an experience I can recommend, simply because its so fresh and unlike anything else. I feel not that much of an urge to return to it once I managed to win the game and overthrow the king, but I remember the time getting accustomed to the game very fondly it feels like one of these old games as a kid when you really had to find out a lot of things on your own, when not everything makes sense from the get go, this game basically accomplished to invoke that sentiment, where so many more polished games rather failed.

Magic spells and skills are of what I seen all SGB free stuff also.

Absolutely no custom sounds used at all, again.. a great shame, I wish the devs spent more time looking into custom music. Some of the Music tracks are okay, the ones that's pre-packaged with SGB.. i'm not knocking that at all but i'm just disappointed.

GAMEPLAY: 6/20
This game is labelled as Rougue0like / Rogue-lite.. my ass it is, this game is just a simple plain Dungeon crawler with a menu used to build your characters, Equipment, and item bag up, that's all this game is. I really wanted to like this game and was hoping for it to be a lot more than what it is.. and that's EXTREMELY BORING!

You wonder around a dungeon floor, killing stuff for Gold and looking for 1 or 2 chests. get to the end of the floor, kill the boss, and repeat the same thing on the next floor. When you die it's NOT game over, you get sent to a black screen that's menu driven where you upgrade things such as your characters levels, armor, weapons, stats, another one that sees new classes become available. Whilst it all may sound fun.. it's REALLY NOT!

SYSTEMS: 8/20
Menu driven upgrade system, a 3D (Doom-like) exploration of dungeon floors that DO NOT change every time you enter, a class system that has you recruit different classes. I think that's all I care to mention. OH! the ONLY good thing is the custom battle UI/HUD,, that's totally original cos stuff like that ain't easily done in Smile Game Builder, it's quite a process to set that type of thing up. (Later learned that's the standard look of the HUD/UI when using 2D in SGB)

OVER ALL: 41/100
I wanted to like it but it's just disappointing, it's boring as hell! I slowly felt my brain melt as a slid down further and further into my chair. Do I recommend? absolutely not, not in this state.

MESSAGE TO DEVS:
You've probably moved on from this project by now but there's a LOT of things you could do to improve things for this game. Have a little group chat after defeating the bosses on each floor bringing the story together in little ways. Use background pictures in the menus, such as when choosing things to upgrade, a simple picture of a guild hall in the background would make it much better. Custom graphics and even music would make the whole experience better.

[b]Sweet House Love[/b] is a lewd match-three game about a man moving in with three ladies.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[b]Sweet House Love[/b] is nine-parts match-three, and one-part visual novel. Each game of connect-three nets gold pieces, which can be used to purchase "gifts" from the shop. Gifts can be given to your choice (of three) ladies, increasing their affection. As new "levels" of affection are attained, you will unlock short visual-novel portions in addition to sex scenes (provided the DLC is installed). 

[h1]Story[/h1]
Arata's new in town, and he needs a place to stay. He finds three roomies to pad with, a pack of promiscuous women. He showers them with expensive gifts, and in return they provide him with sexual favors.

If you ask me, I think Arata [i]dogone-done[/i] hit the jackpot!

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The titlescreen is basic but otherwise presentable. You may adjust your language preference from the "flag" icon on the upper-right screen. Audio can be muted via a "mute/unmute" button in-game. The user-interface is acceptable, but it seems a little rough around the edges. The English and writing were [b]awful.[/b] I appreciate having reading material, but whoever translated this game failed miserably. Although, even if the writing received the basic spellcheck it needs, I doubt it would make each conversation less stiff. Reading the visual novel sections of this game was [i]dreary.[/i]

[b]- The Goods-[/b]
There are fifteen animated, mildly interactive sex-scenes to unlock. The animations leave something to be desired, but they are definitely [i]serviceable.[/i] Each scene can be progressed by rapidly spamming the mouse buttons. The number of clicks it takes to reach orgasm requires some ridiculous concentration. I was disappointed by the lack of [i]moneyshots.[/i] I think the elephant in the room is going to the models themselves — [b]they[/b] [i]leave something to be desired.[/i] None of the characters are exactly top-notch, and the animations are repetitive and prone to clipping.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
I recommend this title. If you're willing to look past the writing and visuals, [b]Sweet House Love[/b] is actually a competent match-three game with tons of sex-scenes. I was impressed by the amount of the content this title offers for such a low price point. While it's [i]definitely[/i] rough around the edges, it wouldn't take much to turn this game from a [i]good-buy[/i] to a [i]great-buy.[/i]

TLDR: Sadly unplayable. The game unexplainably doesn't allow saving except at the end of in-game days that can last up to 20 minutes (this is by design). Several game breaking bugs, crashes, general inconsistency and lack of information make it a complete chore to make it through these time units, leading to very high frustration and waste of time. Apart from that the game is generally poorly designed and unfinished.

Long version:
Stone of madness is a tactical stealth game like commandos or shadow tactics. The first big difference vs those  games is that you cannot issue orders simultaneously to different characters, since you are always controlling just one of them. This creates friction and dumb situations (e.g. one of the characters can taunt enemies to start a chase, but your other units cannot move or act during the chase). Control scheme is completely horrid especially on controller, requiring several random button presses for actions. This shouldn't be the case when every character has something like 3 actions. The upcoming keybind update (yes, no rebind at release) will not fix this because it's not a matter of which button does what, but the whole control scheme. 

As mentioned at the headline the biggest problem is the lack of saving. There are a lot of ways things can go wrong, without counting the numerous bugs, and you will lose progress often due to things that are out of your control, such as enemies that spot you while being obscured by the foreground, or my favorite, which is that when a cutscene pops up, your character will lose his disguise, often in the midst of enemies. Mistakes are punished with high resource costs, and also there is a price for every day that passes. This makes for a tremedously infuriating experience, and heavily punishes the player for exploring and trying stuff, which is where the fun is. 

On the technical side, bugs are very common, from crashes to broken quest progression, to graphical glitches. Quality of life is extremely low and the different UIs are just not well thought out.

On the artistic side, graphics are simple but quite nice,  but the story is lackluster. The beginning has some mystery but it quickly devolves into doing chores in the same areas. Characters are interesting but their stories and relationships are never explored.

I'm conflicted about this game. It's not something I expected, and I personally don't like the gameplay. But that's because I expected it to be something other than what it is. I bought it looking for a game like Shadow Tactics, Desperados or Commandos. Instead, I got an Invisible Inc. where you basically have to be stealthy 24/7 and any combat is absolutely devastating to your characters (sanity loss, finite resources). It's not a bad game by any means, but you should have a clear understanding of its genre before buying it.
