[h1]Either the bugs or the gameplay will drive you mad[/h1]
[b]This review contains no story spoilers[/b]

[h3]Intro[/h3]
[i]The Stone of Madness[/i] is a stealth game from the creators of [i]Blasphemous[/i]. Set in the 18th century, you guide a group of inmates in a monastery in the Pyrenees through an investigation into the dark and macabre goings on. Led by Father Alfredo, you must uncover the mystery behind a series of disappearances and escape.

[h3]Visuals and Art Style[/h3]
No review of [i]The Stone of Madness[/i] could start anywhere else but with the visuals. Taking from the Goya painting "The Bewitched Man", the hand-drawn artwork gives the game a classic animation look. The character animations run smooth and the models are nicely detailed. Much like [i]Blasphemous[/i], the art drips with religious overtones that colour every aspect of the game.

The levels are richly detailed too. The monastery is a labyrinth with a network of corridors, tunnels and stairways that run through it like a warren. Each section is dreary and lush in equal measure and while the stone rooms started blurring together in my mind making it harder to remember locations and routes (the game has no map), each area has enough to distinguish itself from the rest.

[h3]Sound and Music[/h3]
If it's not Artwork that The Game Kitchen get right, then it's the music. The music is perfect. Neat period tracks plays in the background, helping to immerse the player into the setting. From nice piano pieces to lovely string arrangements, the whole soundtrack is expertly tied to the setting on screen.

The sound design is a bit more basic but it does just as good a job as the music, the soundscape is quite muted which gives each major action an impact due to the sound ramping up; the slamming of a cell door, the whack of a baton, the sound of a gunshot, each carries a real impact due to how the sound makes the action stand out as something exceptional.

[h3]Storyline[/h3]
So the Art, Music and Sound teams did their jobs well, how'd the writers do? Well…not good it has to be said. The premise is basic: you are all imprisoned unjustly, now complete the tasks and get everyone out. There are two scenarios to play which offer two contrasting ways the story can go. The story is delivered through admittedly excellent animated cutscenes or dialogue that's incredibly stilted because the characters are speaking for the benefit of the player, not to each other.

Speaking of the characters, there should be some sort of crime to waste potential this plentiful. Each of them has such a compelling description that isn't fleshed out in the slightest. I'm not asking for hours of flashbacks on each of them but if you're going to create characters this quirky and likeable then you've got to give some backstory. The longer scenario has you seek out a series of engravings which detail the building of the monastery and the mental decay of its engineers but there's no meat to the story to get invested in.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The main gameplay loop is days split into day and night sections, each altering how you progress through the levels. General exploration and interactions are easier during the day, whereas accessing the forbidden areas is usually easier at night when there are fewer people around but then you've got the ghostly animas to contend with too. At the end of every day cycle, you can either do some recon or return to your cell to rest up, recharge, craft and prepare for the next day.

Each of your characters has a different set of skills and figuring out which you need at any given time is essential to progressing. Alfredo can use his background as a priest to deliver guard-distracting sermons, conduct exorcisms, heal and even impersonate a priest allowing him to walk through restricted areas without worry. Leonora serves as the character who can directly knock out or kill guards and carry their bodies. She's also the lockpick and can be upgraded with the ability to throw ropes and even use guns. Eduardo is the muscle who also can knock people out with huge chain swings. He's the resident giant who can move huge boxes and planks to create new paths. Agnes is the witch who can cast spells putting out and starting fires, foreseeing the contents of containers, up to casting hexes on guards and summoning swarms of flies that can eat dead bodies. The group is rounded out by Amelia who functions as the scout. She can crawl through small tunnels, and plant traps to distract or incapacitate guards.

But it's not only your characters' strengths you'll have to manage, you'll also have to manage their fears and maintain their sanity levels. Alfredo can't be near a  body, Eduardo is afraid of the dark, Agnes has a thing about mirrors, Leonora is afraid of fire and Amelia is terrified of the stone gargoyles. Their sanity also takes a hit at the end of each day as the stress of incarceration takes its toll. Ensuring they are all recovered before each day is a never-ending task you'll have to stay on top of. Should any of your characters' sanity bottom out, they'll be bedridden until the next day when they'll awake with a new issue for you to contend with such as arthritis meaning no running, or a complex where they'll harm themselves.

It's through these barriers and others that the game adds variety to the gameplay, some of the characters can't read so they're useless for any task involving reading and Eduardo is mute so he can't complete any tasks that need talking. While these seem restrictive, they force the player to think creatively and come up with novel ideas for completing objectives. The game gives you little to no guidance on how to do this and is wide open to allowing the player to come up with any solution to solve them.

Sometimes the barriers can seem contrived though, Eduardo will lose his mind standing in the shade, outside on a sunny day but can be left in a cupboard for hours on end without breaking a sweat, Alfredo is afraid of bodies but only ones that are not plot-specific. Then there are the Soldiers, mother superior and Inquisitor NPC's that serve as the games elite mooks. They're somehow immune to a wide variety of your abilities, including getting shot.

However, the main issue is that the game seems unfinished with a large amount of bugs present. These ranged from minor ones like screen transitions leaving all the previous scenes' characters onscreen to game-breaking ones like objectives not triggering or the particularly annoying one where Alfredo will remove his disguise at the start of every cutscene meaning triggering a cutscene in a room surrounded by guards meant getting caught the instant it ended.

The gameplay also suffers from a lack of Quality-of-life features that are common to the genre. The devs borrowed the stealth mechanics from [i]Commandos[/i] and [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] but ignored their innovations such as a tactical pause or AI commands. The lack of an ability to queue up actions is an inane one, as so many of the game puzzles depend on multiple actions being performed one after another by different characters, you have to switch to each character manually, reset the screen and hope you can complete the next action in time.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Featuring a Goya-inspired art style, [i]The Stone of Madness[/i] will both enthrall and drive you mad. It has as many bugs as it does ideas and playing the game is like walking a tightrope. When it works, it's brilliant, when it doesn't, it's an unplayable mess. Once again the Game Kitchen has managed to perfect the elements surrounding the core of their game but are let down by faults in that core. The controls are jerky and often don't respond in time, the storyline is non-existent, the characters aren't memorable and the gameplay loop gets old FAST. I still really liked what worked though, enough to recommend people keep their eyes on the patch list for this.

I wrote too much so here's the tl;dr on top...and the review will have to continue in the comments >.> (this is much more of a description of what the game is rather than a personal critique of the game)

Overall[list]
[*]The game is fairly well-made from a technical standpoint. There are bugs, but I’ve only crashed once in 30+ hours, and the bugs I’ve spotted aren’t the most consequential thing in the world tbh.
 [*]From a design standpoint, the “gamepad first and only” mentality is holding it back quite significantly, but if you play with a gamepad anyway, then it shouldn’t matter too much to you.
[*]From a creative/visual standpoint, the game is quite good. The pre-rendered cutscenes look great (I rather like how they often left in or added pencil marks to add to that hand-drawn feeling). The writing is, for the most part, immersive enough (“big ask” notwithstanding), the stories are interesting, the fact that NPCs will react differently depending on who you’re talking to them with is great.
[*]I think this is a very important game for the genre. The free roam/open world aspect is definitely something I want more studios to pick up and expand on. The fears and limitations of the character is something that’s a bit off-putting at first, but after playing around with it for dozens of hours, I kind of want more of that in future games.
[/list]

Gameplay[list]
[*]Free roam/Open world game rather than level-based game (rather unique in the stealth genre).
[*]Gameplay loop is 10 to 20-ish minutes of daytime (25 at most, if you’re a delinquent) where you actually play, followed by a night phase where you can (among other things) heal, craft and choose which 3 people you’ll be going out with during the next day.
[*]Can’t take out enemies in any permanent way (you can kill them, but they’ll come back (be replaced) a few days later). Only 3 of the 5 characters you have can even knock out or kill enemies, so you’ll rely more on distraction than elimination.
[*]You can however permanently open up shortcuts and spawn points throughout the maps to make your incremental progress faster.
[*]1 prologue + 2 lengthy campaigns. The campaigns are mutually exclusive, so you’ll need a separate save file for both, but you can skip the prologue so you don’t have to play it twice.
[*]Campaigns are split up in chapters made up of quests you have to complete to advance. These quests nearly always have multiple solutions or workarounds, so you can be blind to one of the solutions and still make it through (and then find out 7 hours later that you were meant to do THIS thing to get through normally, not that other thing…not that I would know anything about that >.>)
[*](that being said some of the missions can be a bit obtuse in where you’re supposed to go, like the game telling you to go to the library while not telling you at all where that would be, or telling you that something is in a changing room, but the changing room kind of looks like every other room, so it barely even registers as something that might be a changing room)
[*]During the different chapters of the campaigns, the enemy placement will be different and the maps will change a bit in order to keep things fresh and reflect story progression.
[*](small commendable QoL thing: switching between characters if they are spread across different maps is surprisingly smooth)
[*]Active skills are a bit underwhelming and unbalanced, tbh. Alfredo is quite overpowered as every single one of his skill is useful, be it his lamp that allows him to investigate and take care of Eduardo, his robes that allows him to (mostly) freely walk anywhere in the map, his sermons that are long-term distraction or his blessings that make prowling around in the evening much less of a hassle. Meanwhile, Leonora’s 3 skills either kill, knock out, or kill at a distance (which can double as “push button from a distance, however). Eduardo only has a short-term distract (and he can easily be spotted and apprehended when he uses it) and an AoE knock-out (yes, just 2 skills). Agnes starts with 3 active skills, but learns more as she levels up (at which point you’ll still be limited to 3 skills, but choosing them from among 6). Amelia is probably the most underwhelming of all. She technically has 3 skills, but the only one I ever used was pickpockted, as her other skills and just more cumbersome versions of Alfredo’s sermons (as is Eduardo’s distract skill, for that matter).
[*]This is imbalance is counter balanced by the passive skills, where alfredo has quite few and Leonora and Eduardo are the most versatile in that department. Leonora can deal with locks and climb some walls, Eduardo can deal with locks, barred doors/barrels and make bridges from planks. Agnes, being stronger than them on the active skills front, has almost nothing on the passive skills front (gather herbs being her only one, iirc), and Amelia, being small, is able to fit in narrow passages no one else can and is less penalized when caught.
[*](commendable QoL thing related to lockpicking, pickpocketing and the like: Item containers, be they boxes or NPCs, have an outline indicating if you have emptied them (green), if you haven’t emptied them or haven’t looked at them yet (yellow) or if they’re locked (red). This makes is SO much nicer/easier to hunt down that last dagger you need for the dragon chests)
[*]Overall, all the characters end up having situation where you’d want them, but it also means you will have obvious favorites for the daytime phase. (ie., Eduardo will always want to be with either Alfredo or Agnes, because of their ability of manipulate light (see next point))
[*]Every character has a fear that you have to manage and that can get worse if you don’t manage you sanity properly (being in contact with that fear will lower sanity, get to 0 and your fear gets worse). Alfredo is afraid of violence and corpses. Leonora is afraid of fire (big ones, not, like, candles…unless that’s something I haven’t come across that happen if you lose enough sanity >.>). Eduardo is afraid of the dark. Amelia is scared of gargoyles (and, with enough sanity damage, even pictures of them). Agnes doesn’t technically have a fear, but she’s a witch and using spells drains her sanity. Moreover, mirrors drain her sanity for counter-magic reasons that I didn’t pay attention to :V Managing all these fears takes quite a few hours to get used to, but eventually it becomes kind of second nature (and you get good enough at healing sanity overnight that you kind of stop caring at some point anyway tbh). That being said, the radius at which you can be affected by a fear can be pretty wonky. A gargoyle that scares Amelia despite being 3/4s of the screen away? Check. A corpse being next to a spawn point so Alfredo immediate loses sanity without you being able to do anything about it? Check. Eduardo being in full light but still being scared because the circle around him brushes up against some shadows? Check.
(similar to the aforementioned “corpse near a spawn point”, some places that should be safe zones, like map transitions points, simply aren’t. If you park your character there, an anima will end up spotting you, or the transition point lands you in a prohibited zone and it’s possible for a guard to be looking straight at it when you come in with absolutely no way of knowing ahead of time if you have to start running out of the guard’s vision)
[*]The camera is locked to the character you’re currently controlling. I wouldn’t really mind normally, but compounded with the multiple layers a single map can have and how it peels back the layers only as your character approaches doors and other types of layer/room transitions, it can make it quite impossible to even know if guards are there and looking at where you’re about to enter (which can be quite a problem if you’re trying to enter a prohibited area…looking at you, library upper balcony >.>)
[/list]

An interesting take on stealth games, ruined by poor execution.

THE GOOD

The environment and character design is pretty good and does invoke the atmosphere of a secluded asylum that hides a lot of mysteries behind its many locked doors and secret passages.

Characters have unique sets of abilities that can be expanded through "research" to acquire new/improved abilities or opportunities for the night phase of the game.

Managing squad between missions can provide a much-needed change of pace.

Characters having personal phobias that affect their gameplay (they lose sanity when in range of the source of their fears) is interesting. Characters can also acquire more mental disorders if their sanity drops to zero which takes this mechanic a step further.

THE BAD

Characters having personal phobias that affect their gameplay is interesting... on paper. In reality, the way levels are designed you constantly run into your characters' phobias and it becomes a drag. And if you get the "upgraded" versions of those phobias like I did with Amelia's fear of gargoyles where the range of the phobia increases and she starts seeing them in tapestries too, it stops being an exciting mechanic and becomes a constant annoyance. Also, Alfredo can't look at unconscious bodies because he detests violence? How does that make any sense?

And that takes us to the next pain point which is the writing. It's lackluster at best. While characters have interesting designs, there is nothing interesting in their dialogues and interactions. They just don't click together. Jokes are often out-of-place and the storyline itself is... well, it is present and that's all I can say. It's nowhere near as exciting as the promises of the setting.

Lack of voice overs makes characters much less relatable, especially against their well-crafted appearances. Probably a budget limitation but still.

There isn't a lot of variation in beating rooms or getting into certain locked areas. A lot of times you would have to perform a specific sequence of actions with specific characters. A bit more open-ness to how you approach each room wouldn't hurt.

Camera is locked to the character you're controlling, which greatly reduces your ability to plan stealthy routes and execute any kind of a long con.

VISION CONES. Anyone who can mathematically explain how they work when you are on a different elevation than a guard should get a Fields medal. Terribly inconsistent, and this is one of the cornerstones of stealth games.

Switching between characters and between their abilities feels very clunky control-wise. You waste a lot of time selecting the character you need, selecting abilities, selecting contextual actions when there is more than one available. There is no way to sync anything or plan like you'd do in Mimimi games, so it never feels like your characters are actually a TEAM and not a group of individuals who happen to be in one place. There is a way to make other characters follow your currently-controlled character, but due to the phobia mechanics, it becomes a really annoying adventure.

Managing the squad may become a chore at some point, but so do a lot of things in this game.

While separation into day/evening/night and the changes that come with each shift are cool in theory, in reality the time pressure makes every day a rushed routine. Longer timers (at least for the day phase) would give you much more room for exploration and screwing around.

And that last sentence touches upon probably the biggest flaw of the game. Due to things mentioned above like weird vision cones, time pressure, unexpected cut scenes, lack of camera panning and other factors, it feels like the game punishes one of the most exciting aspects of being imprisoned inside a mysterious monastery - EXPLORATION. It never felt for me like I'm exploring the asylum, it felt like I was going through the motions because the objective and the game timer told me so.

THE UGLY

Technically the game is not in a good state. In my 5-ish hours, I already had cut-scenes break, triggers not being handled properly (for instance, after I got Amelia in my squad, I could still on following days investigate the barrel where she was hiding and the investigating character would actually say she was still in the barrel while she was literally standing next to him), guards getting stuck in one place, input lag on my PS5 controller in the pickpocketing mini-game, and just last night got soft locked in the quest progression about 25% into the "middle-length" campaign. Not sure if the game was rushed or the devs burned through the budget and had to roll out something, but this is NOT release quality.

THE HOPE?

I really want to like this game but can't recommend it in its current state. It feels rushed, and while its core is intriguing, the execution is sub par. Maybe future patches can fix and rebalance things, so we can have the great setting and interesting mechanics click with the actual gameplay?

General Summary: Definitely an improving gem in the tactical strategy genre in the vein of Mimimi games.  But that's a unfair comparison.  Because while the Mimimi games updated the old Desperados and Commandos style game, Stone of Madness does something completely different.  And for that I want to give them an A+ for creativity.  I haven't seen this much attempt at doing something NEW in a game in a long while. Yes, certain beats and mechanisms can be found elsewhere.  But the combinations of mechanisms with an AMAZING story premise is what gets me to give them a thumbs up.

Now let's start with the Pros and Cons:

- Pros: great non-cliched story.  Set in a very unique period/location.  They don't give in to boring cliche's of "the whole church is bad" or "the whole church is perfect" they create a fair balanced take on a unique time of history.  Plus, without giving to much away the premise of the villain is fascinating.  He's rather horrible, but if he is right about his idea on how to help the mentally ill...then is he wrong for wanting to do it? (Yes,he is....but again, I don't want to give too much away)
- The characters are compelling.  I love how they are a rag-tag group of people with their own baggage and weaknesses.
- I like how they do their best to make everyone useful.  And once you can start upgrading their skill they all do.  And planning you actions becomes essential to maximize your day.
- I like how they dropped a merchant in the game.  Good balance to keep the flow going.  Did you forget to craft an extra lockpick in your cell last night?  No worries, you can go buy one from the merchant.  His stock is limited, but it was a brilliant move to keep you from having to go through another cycle to crack a chest or door.
- The instructions were mostly good.  Good be streamlined a little, but overall fine.

Cons (which are all theoretically fixable...which is more than I can say for Starfield):
- Bugs.  I'll be real I never hit a game stopping one, but there are bugs.  That said, the devs are actively patching so this should quickly become a thing of the past.
- A couple of level design issues: this a minor, but near the end, there is a weird situation where you need the priest to open the tunnel for the girl so you can get around the gate...but the priest can just...open the gate.  So that made zero sense.  And since it was at the tail end I suspect that's why it didn't get caught.  Also, certain areas are intuitive to find.  So better cues on that would be nice.  But all this (like the bugs) is fixable.
- Saving: The biggest legit complaint is the inability to save during a mission.  I understand this is to build tension.  But even an auto save halfway through the day would be nice.  That said, the length of the missions are fixed to the day.....which is 20ish minutes, I think?  So it isn't the end of the world.  

Overall, a really good game that would be made great if the devs keep smashing those bugs and find a way to make peace with players on the who save thing.  Great job devs!

This might just be my platonic ideal indie game. Simple controls meet high-concept gameplay, with outstanding art direction reminiscent of movies like Mandy (2018). More of a score-attack puzzle game than a shooter, the campaign tasks you with efficiently clearing out cultist filled environments using only a single, telekinetically-controled rifle bullet. Pacing is tight, with a steady drip of new gameplay wrinkles to keep things interesting, and an ending that arrives well before things start to get stale. Plus there is a new hoard mode for anyone worried that the story might be too short.

If I were to nitpick, there are some problems with the UI. I accidentally reset all my progress at one point, but it didn't take long to catch back up. Otherwise, if the gameplay footage looks even remotely up your alley, Children of the Sun is a must play.

The gameplay's core concept is rather basic, but well-executed: you have one bullet to kill a bunch of enemies, but as long as you manage to take down an enemy, you get to fire another shot from the bullet's last position. As you keep advancing, both extra abilities and complications are introduced, keeping things sufficiently varied.

The total number of levels isn't all that high, which is both a blessing and a curse: the game doesn't last long, but I fear it'd be extremely likely to overstay its welcome if it had more content to offer, because I feel there's only so much you can extract from the game's concept.

The difficulty is largely on point. It gradually rises over time, but never becomes overbearing; the final level might be an exception here, with its two phases being a touch obnoxious to deal with, but it's a minor misstep at worst.

Overall, Children of the Sun is a perfectly fine distraction for an evening or two. I would love to experience more of the same in terms of art style and the setting (it's painted in broad strokes, but the gist alone is potent enough), but as for the gameplay, I've had my fill.

Children of the Sun, while being slightly too short for my tastes, is an exceptionally well conceived and designed video game. It challenges you to consider 3D space as a puzzle as you zip from one point to the other in the avatar of a bullet, manically causing fatality after fatality of the heretics who oppose you.

The visuals and audio serve to set the tone beautifully and induced me into this strange fever dream-like trance where the only objective is clearing a level and moving forward. The story is effectively told in flashes and it does just enough to give you an idea of why you've decided that being the second coming of John Wick is your only recourse in life.

The level design is absolutely outstanding. In conjunction with the abilities, you're given a fair bit of freedom in how to approach levels. With your character being a sniper, the distance that is involved in this sort of assassination gameplay is also well respected by the game design. This makes strange things like shooting someone from a hundred meters away and then immediately turning your bullet around 180 degrees and sniping someone on the other side of the map feel completely natural. There are some fun challenges as well, one per level. 

I wish this game was a bit longer just so I could see a little more of that story and see where else this gameplay model could have been taken. It's really not a gripe or anything, and mostly comes off to me as a testament to how good the game is. But yeah, maybe another ability and 5 more levels would have really hit the spot for me.

Notes: Great little metroidvania. The swinging mechanic takes a while to get used to because the way momentum works is very different from how most other games with grapples work, you will get used to it eventually though and it gets a lot more smooth once you get a couple upgrades.

The only downside I would say to the game is that it is short, my first playthrough was 1 hour and 18 minutes. I got it on sale for 4$ and I don't regret my purchase at all, was an enjoyable hour, and there is some replayability with the achievements if you want more of a challenge.

Quick Description:
-A cute little flower saves the day in a grappling hook adventure!  A few abrupt difficulty spikes aside, this is a fun and creative mini metroidvania that is well worth the asking price for fans of the genre.

What's Good:
-Checks most of the boxes for what is expected from a metroidvania.  The entire world is interconnected, there are several unlockable upgrades that allow you to explore once unreachable areas, and there are fun collectibles to be found.  
-Really adorable art design and color scheme.  Each biome has it's own theme and color, along w/ new enemies and environmental hazards.
-The soundtrack fits well with the theme of the game.  It's very soothing, uplifting, and helps push you forward on your adventure.
-The grappling hook is the main mechanic, and although not perfect, is really rewarding as you figure out how to use momentum to help you reach hard to reach areas.
-Although the story is limited, it is really sweet and heart warming.  
-Cheap as balls, under $8 and on sale frequently for under $4.

Could Use a Few Changes:
-Most of the game will involve you using the grappling hook to fling from one screen to the next, but it can feel very abrupt due to the speed at which the grappling hook attaches to almost all surfaces.  This lead to a lot of frustrating, accidental deaths.
-Very little in the way of a tutorial or guidance in the more challenging areas of the game.  The hardest parts are figuring out how to use momentum with the grappling hook to reach the next area of the level.  There's quite a bit of trial and error, but nothing really prepares you for a couple of these spots.
-A couple major difficulty spikes may turn off causal players.

Thoughts:
-I had a good time playing Lorera.  I think it is able to compete w/ other fun mini metroidvanias like Gato Roboto, Ato, or Enter Digiton.  You don't see a ton of pure platformer metroidvania's, so this one has been on my radar for a while.  No, it isn't perfect but as long as you moderate your expectations, I think most fans of the genre will have a good experience.

Consensus:
-Middle of the Road Game (Tier 4 and makes up 25% of my reviews).  I think a few accessibility features would be a nice addition in a future update, but outside of that, I don't have too many gripes about my time w/ Lorera.  If you are looking for a compact and fun metroidvania, look no further, this is a solid choice.  This is such an easy recommendation when on sale.  Seriously, who doens't love grappling hooks?

The original Alone in the Dark is considered the granddaddy of survival horror, inspiring Resident Evil that later became the flagship game series of the genre. This new Alone in the Dark is the remake of the original and interestingly, it adopts many mechanics from Resident Evil and things really come to a full circle.

What sets it apart from Resident Evil and other survival horror games, is that the game is a lot more cinematic. It has David Harbour and Jodie Comer playing two leading roles, both of whom are very talented and charming actors. Sadly, I think they are underused as the script doesn’t have a lot for them to work with. I would much rather the budget was spent polishing the game instead of hiring two famous but expensive actors because this game has issues I believe more development budget can fix.

Firstly, optimization is far from satisfaction – frame rates don’t show abnormality, but when you turn the camera relatively fast, the game always has micro-stutter that causes small screen tearing. It happened to my friends as well and I used G-sync and tried several adjustments, but the issue still persists. Though I don’t feel sick about it, it is uncomfortable and I would advise those who have severe motion sickness not to play the game. 

Secondly, the quality of experience is inconsistent. In each chapter, you explore the mansion and another realm. The time in the mansion is mostly enjoyable, but when in another realm, some levels are great but some are so underwhelming that I just don’t want to experience again. The dimension shifts can also feel kind of abrupt sometimes, breaking the flow and making the experience feel cut-off and fragmented, since cutscenes might be triggered unexpectedly, interrupting current exploration and advancing the progress to where you can't go back.

Playing at hard difficulty really feels the stress from resource management, which is done better than recent Resident Evil. Therefore, it necessitates the need for melee. However, shooting is already kind of wonky and inaccurate because of the micro-stutter, but melee is where it really drops the ball. It feels unresponsive and clumsy and particularly frustrating when fighting monsters crawling on the ground. Because of the low hitbox, your swings often completely miss the enemies when they were supposed to land. This goes to show where the budget is really needed – not fancy actors but improving fundamental aspects like the bad coding. 

As you can choose from two characters, technically you need two playthroughs to finish the game since each character has one or two levels of their own, exclusive collectibles, cutscenes and endings. But I only did Emily playthrough not just because I don’t think the difference is substantial enough, more importantly, I don’t want to experience the micro-stutter, poorly designed levels and irritating melee again in a short amount of time.

Survival horror games are typically known for replayability, but beating the game only unlocks a harder difficulty where you can use all guns from the beginning. There is no weapon upgrade, and I went through most of the game with melee just fine at hard difficulty, so I don’t believe unlocking all guns brings any substantial gameplay difference, nor does it have any new weapons or outfits to unlock, adding more reasons for me not to play another playthrough.

Aside from the shortcoming with shooting and melee, the combat flow is great and fluid. It really gives you that bada*s feeling when you're picking up environmental objects as throwing weapons, dodging with precision, and seamlessly mixing gunplay with melee to take down enemies. But it is quite a missed opportunity to not add different types of melee weapons with their own unique features. That would definitely add more depth and enhance the combat experience.

In terms of the story, it is a bit abrupt and incoherent that there isn’t a strong connection between the antagonist you deal with for the majority of the game and the final boss, who needs a bit more build-up. But I might be wrong, as I didn’t do the Edward playthrough.

The music is also nice. Overall, though this review may sound mostly negative, nothing is unbearably bad about this game but nothing particularly stands out, either. As a 7-hour short game, it is a decent pastime.

Fantastic blend of post-RE4 survival horror from the "over-the-shoulder" era and third person adventure segments. 

It felt like the kind of more classic survival horror experience we haven't had in a very long time with the focus on atmosphere and storytelling over jump scares and I wouldn't have a problem recommending this to someone that likes less intense horror in the vein of classic Resident Evil.   

It's a weird comparison because it's an obscure game now, but the segments in the mansion where you're just exploring and solving puzzles with little combat outside of a couple scripted lapses into the nightmare world reminded me a lot of Murdered: Soul Suspect. 

The only complaint I have is that both characters have the same exact levels with different cut-scenes outside of a brief section of the second-to-last chapter that's based on their personal memories and unique for each of them.

Pros:
-Two optional protagonists that play different roles in the story.
-The dark world has so many unique aesthetics that are simultaneously beautiful and terrifying.
-The game constantly drops you between the real world and the dark world without warning, which can occasionally be irritating, but also creates this constant uneasiness that is perfect for horror.
-A story that hits a lot of horror cliches, but is still really unique overall.  

Cons: 
-Game stuttered quite a few times while playing. My gaming laptop isn't crazy good by any means but usually doesn't struggle to run these types of games.
-Combat isn't fluid at all, potentially by design to create tension in the game, but mostly just creates tension in my body.
-The scares for the first half of the game are ENTIRELY made up of jump scares. The game has the option to use stealth but that's almost entirely impossible when every battle is unplanned.

Overall though I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves a good story and a bit of a scare.

Finding a wholly unique game in today's market can often present several challenges across many fields. From story - to animation - to gameplay - even the 'big boys', those triple A companies many of us have grown fond of over the years, begin to fall into the category of an entirely underwhelming experience.

What you find here, however, is a carefully considered game that merges old ideas with a new, innovative, young, and exciting mind from which this games developer has arrived with a newfound sense of vigour that reaffirms their clear investment in one thing...

...PRECISION.

There is no shame to be cast on the man who tries; and while the afore mentioned 'big boys' take on each new project with a war chest large enough to invade a small country - we find in 'The Forsaken Ruins' an approach that cannot be mastered at the command of daddy warbucks, but instead one that comes from the heart. From the soul.

While, as is the nature of 'indie' games, the occasional bug may be found, what you also find - if you approach this game with an open mind, and the same sense of spirit in which it was likely created - you will discover a horror game that has you looking over your shoulder; both in the virtual, and real world.

With thoughtful sound design that brings with it the same eerie presence of the 1980 movie; 'The Shinning', you cannot help but pause the game to regroup your senses - and make sure your lights are still on.

The dark hallways are not your friends, for they already have their own...

Ever-Bleed Keep attracts you beyond the limits of the light. Where a firefly finds its calling in the blaze, 'The Forsaken Ruins' makes the void its sweet, sweet honey. And you the bug. The Unity Engine only enhances this sensation. Wits must be kept, and an eager ear to the ground would serve you well should you wish to survive this nightmare.

Although desperately trying to maintain an anti-social distance to the creatures that dwell in the shadows that keep them - I made it my mission on one play through to approach them as intimately as possible before my life was taken. What I found were monster designs well beyond what one might expect from a one-man-band project such as this. Colours pierce into the darkening voids and highlight the many grotesque details that stain these creatures' flesh. Their shadows and forms haunt you as you scurry silently through the maze that they call home.

Beyond the gameplay you find a narrative that leaves you eager to find all of the hidden notes and journals left behind by your predecessors. The stories and tales that linger in Ever-Bleed Keep only enrich your nightmare and showcase the effort that went into creating this game's wonderful world of lore.

In summary, this title sets the standard for any and all solo game devs to follow. A brilliantly crafted multi-layered puzzle game that has you searching for clues and a means of escape. That wonderfully disgusting sensation that many horror games fail to capture is most definitely present in the deep depths of 'The Forsaken Ruins'.

Your purchase would not be a waste - your time could not be better spent - the experiences you find in this scintillating game will stick with you for many moons. Higher regard for an indie game, especially one that comes from pouches such as these, I could not possibly give.

A masterpiece in many aspects. But most importantly this is a masterpiece of singular achievement that I hope only brings as much joy to its creators heart, as it does to mine.

Before going into detail: the game runs great on the Steam Deck. 
I specifically picked it up to play it on the Deck and the only thing I noticed was that I had to use the touchscreen to start the very first game, everything beyond that was done with the normal Steam Deck Gamepad Controls.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
The gameplay of "Somber" reminded me a lot of other Metroidvanias like Ori and Hollow Knight - abilities are unlocked as you play the game like double jump, dash, etc.
Navigating the game world works fluidly and while there is an in-game map I only had to use it occasionally.
Dying is a non-issue since checkpoints are plenty and it is rare that I had to travel more than a few seconds from the checkpoint to the place where I died which I loved.
This helps a lot in the more challenging sections near the end. The game has some tricky bits but overall it is very accessible even for new players of this style of game.
The play time is around 1 hour, more if you want to complete everything (Steam seems to report the wrong playtime since I played it mostly on my train communte to and from work without an internet connection).

[b]Graphics:[/b]
"Somber" has a distinct style that appears to be inspired by Limbo but not as bleak. Contrasting white elements often indicate danger and are to be avoided.
On the Steam Deck the game ran at a solid 60FPS throughout which is excellent.

[b]Sounds:[/b]
The game features very fitting atmospheric background music and sounds, as well as a Voiceover to guide the player through the story. 

[b]Verdict:[/b]
I picked up "Somber" during the Steam Autumn Sale for around 5 bucks which is great value for around 1 hour of gameplay and even some replayability to collect all in game upgrades and items.
The Austrian radio station FM4 had a feature review about the game a couple weeks back and I am happy they did because that's when I found out about it.

Game played entirely on the Steam Deck. Excellent loading times, no stuttering/crashes, no issues whatsoever. :)

The game IS actually very interesting, but I am refunding it because it's not quite ready for prime time AND it hasn't been updated since mid February so I'm afraid it's abandoned. If it's not abandoned, and continues to be worked on, I do plan to re-purchase it because I think it will be a fun and reliable little time-waster.

Play is turn based in the way that a game like Civ is turn-based. You start a turn by choosing what to do to your various tiles--your tiles are the ones that are showing, the top tiles on the cube. You can work the tiles, meaning you extract resources from them, or scout them for enemies, or improve them so that each turn will reap more resources. Resources at the beginning of the game seem to be food, gold, wood, and iron. If there are more resources later, I don't know. Could be? 

You can also choose to build your army, build your population, or train someone, in addition to working and/or improving your tiles. 

Additionally, you have a god or goddess that you have to keep happy--a little like in the old Pharaoh/Cleopatra game, in that if the god feels too neglected it will grow angry and do mean things to you. Here though, you can simply appease it with gold. I did not play long enough to find out what the other options were.

Finally, before you end your turn, you spin either the top, bottom, left, or right, section of the cube, which will give you a somewhat different batch of tiles to work with on your next round, and end your turn.

There are seasons and in winter you depend on water tiles for food--I guess everyone goes ice fishing?

So, with some additions and smoothing out of issues, it could be a fun little strategy game.

What I didn't like/Issues

Not an issue but the tutorial (hey, at least it had one!) required me to "press enter" a lot. I'm annoyed by games that make me use both keyboard and mouse. That's just me though: I realize that many people prefer to play kb+m even when they could use a controller. Not me. I'm a controller girl, all the way. Anyway, this tiny issue could be solved by changing "press enter" to "click here or press enter." Poof. 

There was nothing in the tutorial to prepare me for whatever happened with my center square, the castle, but something was going wrong. I think it said "Improve relations," but it didn't tell me how to improve relations, nor with whom I should improve them. I clicked on it and it said something about prestige and after a couple of rounds of this the problem seemed to go away.

I did not have enough gold to keep my god happy, which, I think that just starting out a person should have enough, or access to enough, to get going at least. If they mismanage their funds later and their god gets mad, that's on them, but give them a fighting chance in the early game. 

There were a few too many events and honestly my entire reign lasted like 3 years, if that. It could have been because the god was mad, I don't know, but... yeah. That was harsh. Also I got messages that my land was.... I forget the word; I don't think it was "contaminated," but it meant about the same thing, but it didn't give me any clue whether there was anything I could do about it, if it was permanent, etc. 

When my reign ended, and I chose to exit the game, it did not exit gracefully, but instead apparently crashed with a new window with something about an error and I had to click "abort" to make it go away. So that needs fixing, obvs. 

Again, this feels like it could become an interesting little game with some work. It would also, however, be easy to not add enough variety to it and wind up with a very repetitive game, and there's no way to know which way this one will go. But if it looks like it's going to be interesting, I definitely will re-purchase it, because I love little time-waster games like that, and wind up with hundreds of hours in them because I play them while I think about things, mull things over in my mind... and while I'm waiting for things like the dryer to finish or the oven timer to go off.

If the game had been updated recently I would not be seeking a refund for mine, so check to see if it's getting regular updates and if it is, then yes, I recommend it. If it's still stuck at last update in mid February, then no, I do not recommend it.

Cannonship is a side scrolling horizontal shoot em up of the gradius variety.  The pixel art and enemy diversity offers a lot.  However, the ship is woefully underpowered and slow, there are few hp power ups on each stage and no weapon power ups.  You can upgrade your ship in between stages, but you may not have much gold as this game requires a lot of dodging and surviving and replenishing health means not being able to better any of the other stats which becomes a major problem in later stages.  Your health does not reup after completing a stage nor after a continue, and there is only one continue.  

All of this matters because a game that starts out gently quickly becomes one filled with bullets and some enemies that take multiple shots.  Getting to the menu and even knowing when your game is over is challenged by how fast the game moves in and out of menus if you are holding the shoot button during a stage at which you die.  All that said, I know that this is a first offering from this developer, who has made quite a beautiful game.  You could probably complete it with a lot of level memorization and exactly the right upgrades.  

More continues (true continues), a shield option, replenishing life at the completion of a stage instead of requiring 30 gold at the end, and a slightly faster and more powerful ship would make this game a must buy.  Until then, if you like an old school arcade game that is pretty unforgiving and very beautifully crafted, then this is your game.

I really like the upgrades and skill trees in this game too. They actually add something noticeable and meaningful with each upgrade, and most upgrades really feel like they're worth it. I feel like a lot of games nowadays have skill trees with such minuscule upgrades and buffs that it's hardly even noticable.

Regarding the combat, this game does have really fun combat. It's got lots of spells (Or curses as the game refers to them) and weapons, giving the game a vast array of possible abilities, not even mentioning relics. If you're just looking for combat, I can assure you, the combat is really good.

The art style is also really unique and quite frankly, just amazing. It's a pleasure to the eyes, and it really is some of the most unique graphics/art I've ever seen in a game.

In summary: if you don't mind a management game, give this a go. It's got a lot of management, which is absolutely still fun, but the combat is great.

1. Managing the cult became a chore for me pretty quickly. Constructing everything the people need, and managing it was a distraction from crusades, rather than something that felt enhanced by it. Animations are long, and the payoffs were small.

2. Game was trivially easy, until it wasn't, and it didn't feel like progression was doing all that much to lighten the load. Beat the first two zones without a single death, and it didn't feel close. Third zone was also a breeze until you get to the boss. I wouldn't say it was TOO hard, just that it was much harder, and the progression didn't actually alleviate that very much. Your weapons deal more damage, but for the most part you actually just need to not get hit. Higher damage weapons help, but instead you just need to learn attack patterns and...not get hit.  

3. The combat just isn't actually that interesting. Weapons aren't interestingly different, enemies aren't that interesting, and spells (curses) are pretty limited in use. Crusade runs are crazy short, and just weren't very interesting.  

Altogether, it summed to an experience that was wonderful to look at, but after 10 hours, I don't think it was really that fun to play, and I'm pretty sure I won't finish it.

As always, I want to preface this by saying I'm generally more critical on horror games than most, but all criticisms are to lend a perspective for what I enjoy in horror and hope to see different in future games. 
FM is an indie horror game that is more or less a walking sim, which is cool with me, however, the story elements are very dry, incoherent at times, very slow paced, and the interactive parts aren't compelling. 

- The gameplay mechanic the game uses to keep you engaged or to at least have an interactive element to it is that you are to listen to audio cues and hold RMB to look at a corresponding object. It's a bit bland and repetitive. It just leads to you walking around and zooming in on objects. There's one other element where the game has you collect several items in a relatively small area. It's tedious and incredibly slow paced to an already slow paced game. Which leads me to..
- The walk speed in this game is dreadfully slow. I don't know if the thought was to draw out dread or tension, but the game doesn't really do this particularly well. There's long hallways (yes looping hallways too) and it takes forever to walk down them with nothing happening in between. 
- If there's a looping hallway mechanic, I'd like to see more things change between loops. Even more on pacing, each loop the game feeds you one or two lines of the story and the slow walking pace leaves a lot of silence until you reach the next loop where you learn a little bit more of the story. It's nickel and diming and I feel like it could be tightened up to make the game more cohesive. 
- FM takes a lot of inspiration from PT. All things are pretty derivative, but this game almost takes a little too much and it makes it pretty predictable. 
- The horror elements are almost non-existent. There's not a lot of atmosphere and for whatever reason there's a lot of furniture being upside down and red lights are thought to be scary. 
- The story wasn't engaging enough for me to follow it properly. That's probably just me being dumb, but I was a bit confused between who died when and it didn't make sense to me chronologically. So instead of a moment of a plot twist or reveal, I was just confused and unsure if I just misunderstood something before. 

Look, this game is more than I could ever accomplish on making a game, but there's a lot of elements that could be tweaked for what I would see as a more enjoyable experience. The game is inexpensive and it's about an hour long so it could still be worth a try for you.

Any "horror" to the game relies on predictable jumpscares.

There are two methods of solving "puzzles", which is a larger number than there needed to be. One is just simply interacting with things, one is having to zoom in on specific objects. The zooming in mechanic was pointless. It didn't enhance the game in any way. Functionally, it was the same as just interacting with objects except being more finicky as I frequently found that even though I was zoomed in on the right object, I needed to adjust where I was standing because it didn't count.

The concept for the "puzzles" is that you listen to the radio telling you about the "story" and you're supposed to find a relevant object, but one of the first couple zooming puzzles didn't even make sense. You're in what I assume is a morgue and the radio tells you about how a neighbour heard gunshots, called the police, then went to go knock on the door (instead of, you know, waiting for the police). Logical options for things to zoom in on might be the door or a telephone, but [spoiler]it was a scale.[/spoiler] Not sure how that was remotely relevant to what I was being told.

The story itself was bland and the "plot twist" was as predictable as it was stupid. I got pulled out of any care for anything in the story when it went on to talk about [spoiler]the grandparents. The children told them frequently about how the dad beat them and how they only felt safe in the dark where he couldn't find them, he's a known alcoholic, and the grandparents "feared for the safety of the family" but... never once thought to get literally any authorities involved? And nothing happened after he beat the mom so bad she had to go to the hospital?[/spoiler]

The "twist" was so predictable specifically because the game [spoiler]constantly went on and on about how terrible of a person the father was and how he was an alcoholic, valued his gun more than his family, and regularly beat them. When you shovel tons of "Look how terrible he is" into the player's face, then he obviously could not have been the one to kill them or else there's literally zero development in anything. Making him the killer in the end would've just been an hour of "This person was terrible, did terrible thing to the surprise of literally nobody in-universe."[/spoiler]

As for the voice acting, I unfortunately can't tell if the lines were just delivered poorly by the voice actor himself or if the stilted manner of speaking was done intentionally (possibly not by the speaker himself) as an attempt to get across a sort of distortion or something, but in the end it didn't matter.

It's a good game giving an alternate story of Achilles' fight in Troy, it fuses souls-like with hack'n'slash and it does it pretty well, Achilles: Legends Untold reminds me a lot of God Of War (the old ones, the good ones) I just wish it was a bit more polished, it has great scenery, excellent sound and audio design, great soundtrack (I only wish there were more tracks) good atmosphere and graphics, good variety of weapons and special abilities, good level design as well as boss and overall enemy design. With a lot of areas to explore and loot, the maps never feel empty. wherever you go there's gonna be either a bunch of enemies or some chests or gold etc. The game is easily 100% achievable within 20 hours, so for those who want a game that doesn't drag too long yet they like to explore and complete all the objectives of entire maps, this is for you. The combat is satisfying, combos vary based on the weapon you carry, you either dual weilding axes, swords, spears or you can blend in different weapons together, 2 handed swords, or one handed weapons and a shield. There are also special abilities tied to certain weapons, all in all the combat variety is very good, especially in late game where you can slaughter everything with ease. Last but not least, I want to talk about difficulty, I was surprised when I saw that such game didn't take the lazy route of simply buffing enemies' hp and dmg. Don't get me wrong, enemies indeed need more hits to be killed, and they also shred your bar, but they are challenging because they act smarter, faster and a lot of times they have new abilities.
On the other side of hand, the game suffers from low budget voice acting and cutscenes (which is understandable) enemies have the same voice lines and voices. You'll hear the same guy saying the same thing whether he is a soldier or a creature of darkness. Some dungeons are almost indentical, bosses are extremely easy on normal difficulty but some outright impossible on hard difficulty, some normal enemies will literally one hit kill you on hard difficulty, I mean.. why? To give a clearer view, in the last map of the game the enemy numbers massively increase, which means every 5 meters there will be a group of enemies, that leads to face multiple groups at the same time, now imagine that 2 of them can stagger you and 2 others can one hit kill you. It's a good challenge but if that's the case on hard diff, what happens on expert? They kill you with eye contact?
Anyway I think I cherry picked a bit with this one, it's not a big deal at the end of the day, it happened to me 2-3 times so I think it's alright.

All in all, for a game of this caliber, Achilles: Legends Untold definitely delivers what it promises and while not being a mind blowing game, it's a good experience and an easy game to add to your collection of perfect games. I would recommend even on full price if you are heading for 100%.

I have to appreciate the fact that such a game exists, it is quite detailed and it is clear that they have put a lot of work in it, in spite of the fact that the player base (I mean us, the gamers) is clearly smaller than for football.

But... there are many things that left to be desired. For example, my main complaint is about the tactics. Most matches I just sit and watch, since the tactical options are very limited, not much to change that would have a big impact on changing the course of the match. While I don't know much about rugby IRL, I highly doubt that those are the only tactics managers have at their disposal. 
----------------------------------------
EDIT: I've searched closer and THERE ARE ways of affecting the tactics. Selecting "Ad Lib" instead of "Structured" for attacking and/or defending tactics, you are presented with a screen where you can choose from 5 forwards moves and 4 backs moves. They are coded A...E (A...D respectively) and you can see what they mean by holding the right click on their squares.

This improves my opinion on the game, although I still find the approach to tactics quite limited and cumbersome.
----------------------------------------
Then: there's no interaction with the press and with the players individually, other than sending them to individual training session. You can't actually see the chemistry in the locker room and on the pitch, you can't see if and why you are liked or despised. There's some reputation indicator and some emails from the GM adjusting their support to your results, but not more than that.

Also, during a match, I hardly see any kicks from my team or the opposition and the lineouts... well... let's just quote Nigel Owens here: he's straighter than 90% of the throws and still there are no penalties.

Overall, it's a great *start* of a game development, but there is not very much to do so that you actually feel engaged or make any difference for your team. Many things are just automatic, outside of your control. But again, it feels like there is a will and there's definitely a way to make the game better. I'm rooting for it.

Feylin is more like a kids homework assignment or a home demo/project rather than a serious game.  It's an incredibly shallow 3D rendered 2D top down wave survival brawler, as simple voxel (not pixel, as the "developer" tries to describe) assets come walking at you or shooting you, so you whack them with your sword thing and see how long you can last before uninstalling the game, because it's garbage. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features lazy low-polygon voxel "Minecraft"-like "art", making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  A lot of amateur developers see Minecraft's success and assume it's because it looks bad, not because it had unique and appealing game mechanics, and they try to emulate the success without understanding it.  It also happens to be easy, and doesn't need any proper talent in terms of game development/graphic artists etc.  That's why reviewers are faced with so many of these terrible games with confrontingly bad graphics.  Developers must learn that Minecraft succeeded despite the bad graphics, not because of them.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected in the general public reception.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  That's right, only 4.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in the game is to be expected.  Gamers just didn't take this low quality game seriously, and for good reason.

I went in with a totally open mind. I don't mind that the graphics are limited, that's not why I play games. I play games for fun gameplay and good underlying mechanics.

Rare is it to find a game made by a one-person studio where they explain the basic control scheme right off the bat. There's a few characters "in town" and they have some witty dialogue that actually made me laugh, and then a guy holding a sign who gives you a little tutorial. I was actually impressed with this aspect. It got me up and playing in under a minute, and I got a laugh out of the good humor.

Sadly my enthusiasm quickly dissipated as I entered the cave and started the main game. First, there is no apparent goal to the game, just keep proceeding through level after level of the cave. A glaring problem occurred immediately: I reached the "end" of the first level and walked through the exit. But I found myself right back at the start of the same level! So I proceeded through it again, and exited the cave. I found myself back at the start of the same level... AGAIN. WTF? I wasn't sure if there was a bug or something, so I carried on. That's when I realized that there are perhaps 5 or maybe 10 levels in total (can't say for sure) and they are selected at random. So in my playthrough I went through 20 levels, and I saw the same maps over and over and over and over again. Same monsters, same items, same placement of gems, everything identical.

I don't mind map recycling, it is a common practice. But the EXACT same layout 3 or more times in a row? Or you might have the same map twice, then a new layout, then RIGHT BACK to the map you just played two times. It sticks out like a sore thumb and makes you question if there's any actual content here.

The worst part of it all, is that there is no challenge whatsoever that I can see. All of the foes I encountered were the equivalent of Mario Goombas... just jump on them or walk past. Way too easy. Also, no incentive to gather resources in the maps, because as I said, they are all the same, no challenge, and it doesn't seem like anything changes one way or the other even if you do collect the gems and unlock items. Why even bother gathering items when you can literally walk from the start of a map to the end, with absolutely NOTHING presenting any kind of challenge or threat.

To the positive, I did find some cool items which I think were creatively done. A belt which saves you from falling, and when you do it send you flying back up! Portable springboards, heavy rocks you can throw which propel your character the other direction with inertia. Definitely some interesting concepts are in place to make navigating the levels a bit of a creative exercise. But again, since there is no apparent risk/reward/point to any of it, you can just walk/jump from the start right to the exit, and not bother with any of it. There is no REASON to use anything or explore the levels.

Really this game needs a TON of work. About a hundred additional maps would be a good start. More than two or three Goomba-type monsters. Some kind of reason to want to explore the maps. Lots of gameplay hasn't been put into place. Why have all kinds of cool items with powers when there's no compelling reason to even use them?

I'm sorry to say to the dev, who clearly put his heart and soul into it, that it needs A TON of work. This barely qualifies as a game as it stands, even though many of the items and powers are pretty cool. The core game hasn't been made yet though. What is my goal? What is the risk/reward for doing anything? None of that is in place yet.

I refunded after 17 minutes. I will keep watching this game and I hope the dev keeps working on it. I don't mind supporting smaller devs with cool ideas. But I need the gameplay to be worthwhile. Keep at it dev, you've done pretty good so far but keep going. This game isn't ready for the public, it is AT BEST a pre-alpha.

I thoroughly enjoyed this little game, in the same way as I enjoyed surfing in CS:S. Similar vibe. The game revolves entirely around a very grounded grappling mechanic. You don't have any air strafing, you don't have any rope length manipulation. You just have a rope, a thing it's stuck to, and your existing momentum. It feels unintuitive, but rewarding to master. It wasn't until I was over halfway through the game that I really, truly grasped how the movement works. Until that point, I thought I had figured it out several times, but every time the next level would throw me for a loop by requiring me to think about the momentum from a different angle.  

It's a very direct, simple game. In a good way, in my opinion. It doesn't have any fluff, it just gives you a mechanic that you probably haven't dealt with in exactly this way before, and then gives you a series of tests so you can hone your skills with that mechanic.   

As for the criticisms: There's very little art/visual [i]design[/i], it's a utilitarian pile of assets which is often ugly. The music is also distracting and unpleasant most of the time. The game is short, and could probably do with either "themed" sets of levels which would have more coherent art styles and gameplay themes. I'm imagining something like a "cave" set of levels where you're dealing with lots of claustrophobic, mazey, quick gameplay, as opposed to another set of levels which might revolve around massive jumps and big open levels, etc.  

But for what it is (especially on sale for $2 as it was when I bought it), I enjoyed it!

Magicdweedoo is one of the most unique developers around. His games are deep, challenging, and full of detail. Mealmates is no exception. If you like minigame games like Warioware, you'll love this. In Mealmates, you (and your friends if you have them) play minigames to earn money to feed your meal mate, which is some kind of anthropomorphic food creature that you eventually must eat. The better your meal mate tastes, the better your score.

Mealmates is hard in a good way. In the spirit of Warioware, you're only told enough to not be completely lost, so you won't understand at least half of the minigames your first time through. This is good. Similarly, the meta-game doesn't hold your hand, but let's you discover how the game is meant to be played.

The music deserves special mention. Composed by magicdweedoo himself, the music is weird and diverse and yet somehow consistent, and it sets an incredibly unique tone. When I streamed the game people kept commenting how great the music was, and I'm glad I bought the full version that came bundled with the soundtrack.

Anyway, look, if you're bored of games that all feel the same, play Mealmates. And while you're at it, play Ticket, which came our a few years ago from the same developer. He makes good games. Play them.

Having played a little over an hour, I can already see that there's still a bunch of minigames I haven't encountered and a ton of content that I haven't yet seen based on the exploring the world and checking the menus. There's a bunch of stuff I still haven't figured out and I don't know how deep this rabbit hole goes.

It's difficult to explain this game beyond "exploratory minigame collection". It's easier to just take the plunge and take a gander for yourself.

Recommended if you like minigame collections, extra recommendation if you like experimental games.

Do you want to play a party game without breaking friendships? Then mealmates is for you. This sequel is a direct upgrade from the first game, where you can do more than just spoil your mealmate, play minigames and give him away to be eaten. You can customize your mealmate with clothes you can find in the "neighbourhood", cook recipes which can later be bought in the shops and unlock things by completing achievements.
The replayability is GOLD, the music is GOLD, the game itself is just GOLD.

Worth the money. Some day I will invite my friends to give this a try.

These minigames can be played either solo in story mode, or multiplayer in party mode. Additionally, when you complete story mode once, you can play infinite mode, to level up a mealmate as little or as much as you want, and farm for cash and items.

The minigames themselves range from a simple luck check, to fairly engaging and tense, especially in mulitplayer. Some minigames use surprisingly clever mechanics too.  While there's no online multiplayer, remote play works fairly well, and can support up to 4 players.

Anyways, while it might look like a confusing fever dream when you start, once you explore the city and its unlocks, the various buildings, and the minigames, overtime, it'll start to make sense. Maybe too much sense.

This is an unashamedly happy game with it’s cute cartoon graphics, it immediately brought a smile to my face.  This continued as it is a fun unique game. Some puzzle games manage to be technically good but are somehow lacking in the fun factor, this manages to do both.

It’s a mix of Sokoban on some levels, and/or ‘move one and you move all icons at the same time’ (ie like woodways). The objective on most* levels is to find soil squares and bring together all the same colours on them so they ‘bloom’ on the squares.  New game mechanics are introduced making it more interesting as you progress.  The cherries although clever once you ‘get’ it, might be the least intuitive of them.  There is a tutorial level introducing the main aspect of the new game mechanics and mostly this is enough.

The one slightly negative thing for me was that on latter* levels I didn’t always understand what the level objectives were.  I usually like to know what objectives are, not to work them out -having the time spent on HOW to accomplish the objective rather than try a few things to figure out what the objective is. On a few levels, I accidentally finished rather than purposefully work them out.  This was the case in the latter stages when it is impossible to do everything (keep everything alive).  But once I figured that out, I mostly got it.  I’d have preferred that you had to keep everything alive in every level, that would have been more intuitive and logical (for me anyhow).

I really liked that there was an option to turn off the moving screen (it was making me sick), there was an undo button – z key (recent update says it is now unlimited).  There is also a hint button which is always a great idea. Here it’s a well thought out, different amount of moves for each level. It’s only ever the starting moves but it is supposed to be a hint button, not ‘a keep clicking this and you’ll get the solution button.’  I didn’t need it, but maybe if there was a 2-3 moves hint from where you were that would be good although maybe programming that would be hard.

It has 73 levels in total, with hints in most levels but not in the last set of bonus levels. In-game options are - screen resolution (2560 x 1440 the highest), windowed/full screen, moving background on/off, separate sliders for music and sound. I don’t like hard games, and here it was a perfect level of hardness for me – a few tries and I got it. I’m really bad at Sokoban (I keep practicing at it but still don’t get better!) but don’t be put off if you don’t like Sokoban, the Sokoban side isn’t hard. 

I appreciate that I could 100% a game with zero timing elements in it, you could take as many moves as you want in a level. There was an undo button, that alone deserves a good review. Thankfully there are enough other good fun unique things going on to make me recommend this fun, casual game.

I guess my expectations were too high for this game. Maybe because it was released in 2020, I thought it would support wide screen monitors, and have pretty good graphics, sound, user interface. It has none of those. It has graphics. It has sounds. It has a user interface. Those are the best things I can say about them.

The first thing I noticed was the game started in 1024x768 resolution. On my 4K monitor. So as soon as I could get to the options I went to change it to my native resolution (3840x2160). It turns out that's not an option. In fact, there are only three resolution options. The aforementioned default, 1600x1200, and another one in between that I can't remember now. No 1080p. No 4K. Is this 1995?

Speaking of 1995, the graphics have about the right quality for that. When I turned up all the graphics settings to the highest (which gave me a warning that I need to have at least 1 GB of memory!), it was still quite bad. Low resolution textures, blocky models, etc.

Setting up the game in the first place took quite a bit of dealing with the crappy UX, but eventually I figured out how to get actually into the game. Meanwhile, the menu is overlayed on a scene which is perpetually rotating around, making me dizzy.

There were some sounds playing the roughly corresponded to what was happening in the game. But the garbage truck only seems to have two engine sounds: running and not running. No matter what speed it's moving, it makes the same sound.

Operating the employees and truck is very clunky. Basically, you hit the spacebar to make something happen, Enter to switch between the workers, and arrow keys (?!?!?!) to move them around or drive the truck. They don't move smoothly or exactly like you might expect, but eventually you can get them to do what you want.

The actual process of picking up garbage is extremely repetitive, which I guess is to be expected. It's quite a pain to have to keep switching between workers (one driving and one picking up) and commanding one to do what you want by moving the arrow keys then hitting the spacebar over and over. And when the garbage is actually dumped into the truck, the garbage bin clips into the truck. For some reason the truck doesn't have an opening on the back for the garbage to go into?

On the plus side, traffic seems to react to your presence in the roadway and doesn't run you over.
