This is one of the most unique, visually pleasing, and heartwarming games I've played in a long time. Though it doesn't delve to deeply into lore or philosophy, it manages to tell a compelling story that asks surprisingly profound questions about the nature of identity, hope, and friendship---all while centering on a feline protagonist who can't communicate except by meowing and clawing things. It's made me reflect on my own friendships, including with my cats, who don't seem to understand what exactly made me so emotional when the game's credits rolled but were right there to comfort me anyway.

I would recommend this game to just about anyone, not just people with a softspot for cats or an interest in sci-fi dystopias. It's a brilliant work of art that provides a meaningful experience, and it's well worth the cost despite its short length. Even after just finishing it I'm eager to dive back in and find more sheet music for Morusque to play on his jerry can guitar and to curl up among the cushions in Clementine's loft for a little longer. It's these small moments that really make it special, the moments of rest and meditation that are an essential complement to the game's story elements and action sequences. 

As I finished the game I was reminded of a quote from John Gray's book Feline Philosophy: "Humans cannot become cats. Yet if they set aside any notion of being superior beings, they may come to understand how cats can thrive without anxiously inquiring how to live." This game, which puts the player in control of a small feline amidst the ruins of a man-made world still rife with humanity's troubles even in the absence of human beings, offers an opportunity to seek the understanding Gray suggests.

There is a lot we can learn from cats that is easy for us to lose sight of, has hectic and stressful as human life can be. The quiet hours spent in relaxation, play, and curiosity are just as important as the time we spend working towards a paycheck or some other goal. Can you imagine a cat "on the grind?" Of course not. Because cats understand innately that you don't need wealth or achievement to get what matters out of life. Sometimes all you need is an inquisitive mind, a friend to play with, or just a soft pillow to curl up on for a nice, long nap.

[h1] Darker Version of Sword Art Online? [/h1] 

Disclaimer: the game has psychological themes including horror elements and insects. Player discretion is advised. This is a short point and click adventure with unique art by a Russian dev team known as Topchangames. They have not released any new game yet but I surely adored the 8 hour experience I got with this game. Also note that there is no working English guide for the game. 

[b] Story: Interesting and Dark [/b] 
The story revolves around two characters who are supposed to be a couple but met in an online game. They meet in real life but they are of different statuses so there are a lot of challenges which they must face. There is also a side story of a rock dude and another woman which flashes from time to time. The story makes you curious and it gives an artistic representation of one's mind. The whole story progresses alternating through two locations the gloom and the real life. The gloom is like a limbo. You question whether you are actually dead or alive at this point. So dive in and explore various character stories, their psychological perspectives and at least two endings (the game says 4 but read on for the bugs!) with a handful of interesting puzzles and mini HOG scenarios. The game also is pretty LGBTQ friendly and shares some hardships they go through. 

[b] Characters: Variety and Psychological Personas [/b] 
I thought the characters were very nicely developed they have their own backstories. Kiel is a rich money bag who is obsessed with video games. Ophelia is the same but not rich and works as a maid. Ophelia's sister works at a mansion and is a hard worker. Kiel's snobby parents are also introduced who does not understand their son at all nor the pressure they put on him. The waitress is a sweet and shy character and the rock dude seems carefree and persistent. There are also the workers at the mansion and the unnamed characters of the limbo version on which they are personifications of one's negative thoughts. Each character goes through their own development which is interesting to see. 

[b] Gameplay: HOG [/b]
Gameplay has mini HOG scenarios and collecting items to solve puzzles. You explore several locations. The characters cannot run and you cannot use keyboard keys to move around, you use the mouse. I feel like it would have been better if the keyboard keys can be used than the mouse. There are run away from enemies scenes which needs you to click and go away but the walking is at a steady quick pace still it needs to be more faster. 

[b] Art and Music: Amazing OST and Cute art [/b] 
The music is amazing as hell and the art is super cute. The animation they have when they walk is super adorable. It is a very unique art style which you don't see much. The music is very catchy. If you want to enable the voice option for the characters you can download a Russian voice pack from the in game menu settings. Did not use it since I am used to pixel games but I expect it's fine voice acting. 

[b] Achievements: Broken, No guides available [/b] 
Here is the single con in the game: broken achievements. I have searched far and wide for achievement guide but did not find any. Two or three achievements I think are broken, where I did replay the game again and it does not amount to it. There has been a discussion on it on the community hub. This is disappointing and the devs does not seem to respond and there is no patch for it. they last seemed to be active on 2021. There are 4 endings imo: 3 bad and 1 good. I got 2 of  them and the achievement counter says I only got 1/4. If anyone knows any way to get the other two please let me know. 

[b] Overall [/b] 
A very nice short point and click adventure game with memorable characters. Bugged achievements and no new developer response, also no english guide for the game anywhere to be found.

I started playing this and before I get wrapped up thought I would write a review. I always love the books where you can decide the ending. Fun in an unusual, quiet, interesting way.

Now, I don't think it's a bad game, even if you take the price into consideration, but there are a lot of small balancing issues that I didn't expect in a Streets of Rage 2 tribute, and honestly, I don't see a reason why the dev can't solve them, it just needs a few adjustments with the I-frames, numbers, and the timing as well - they don't feel like huge design problems, just small oversights (fixable if the dev wants it). It plays almost exactly like SOR2, pretty much the same move set and combat depth, maybe with a few missing moves - unless they changed the controls for reverse hit and toss recovery.

I personally didn't have any issues with the hit detection, but I think there are other issues that may create that feeling like something is wrong. I suspect the real problem with the game is the lack of I-frames on some of the moves that traditionally would be safer. You can take damage during special attacks and throws, I think they should either have I-frames, or instantly give you a big damage reduction, it does not feel good when you lose half of your health while doing an animation. I mean, if you worry about balancing, maybe the cost of the move could be a little higher, but put in those I-frames so you can actually do it safely. Not everything has to be exactly the same, but you want your moves to be practical.

The combat really isn't all that bad, I actually like that impact feel overall, it just could use a bit of work with timing and numbers. The throws in this game just do a very low amount of damage compared to SOR, you can probably double it from what it is right now, especially the one where you jump over the character, traditionally I think it was the strongest regular move, but here it deals the damage of like a few regular attacks, you want to reward the player for doing it. Another problem I have is that you can't cancel out into the forward+forward+X attack out of hit animation, the command is not recognized unless you do it cleanly, so you pretty much can't chain it properly (like you could in SOR2). The distance on the knuckle dash attack is a little too unsafe, and the way it registers make it unsafe as well, it needs to be more practical like the dash kick. 

For the content, you know, it's a 60-minute game which is fine for the arcade style, 3 characters, some skins and all. I kinda wish you encourage the player to replay the game for some concrete rewards, not just optional difficulty, maybe a different ending, some difficulty-specific skins, or a new mode after beating the game. Also, why no intro, I don't need a story in this game, but it could use a small intro you know.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I think the actual gameplay and the impact feel on the attacks is good, I don't think the game plays badly at all. Again, the problem is with the lack of I-frames on some of the traditional I-frame moves, some numbers are off, and the distance on the attacks could be adjusted. It's not a bad SOR2 tribute, just a few issues that I think you could solve.

(+) I mean it looks decent for $5, I personally don't have problems with it, there are 3 characters, you can unlock several skins, and it mostly follows the SOR2 themes.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Balancing [/u] - you could use I-frames on special attacks AND throw animations too. Now, maybe you would want to balance how much it costs to use them in return, but it would feel better if you didn't drop half of your health doing the animation. The damage on throws is WAY too low compared to SOR, they are not even worth using. I would say increase the basic and back toss by 50%, and the jump over throw by 100%.
I would like to see the dash attack for the girl to be a bit safer, maybe slightly better distance and faster trigger on the impact. You know I never found the dash all that useful, maybe entering and exiting it could give a small damage reduction for a few seconds, just a thought. 

Now, SOR2 never really had a proper juggle system with no mods, but you could still do some basic chains, I think you should still look into adding some combinations. Right now you can chain 2 flying kicks, it would be cool if the special attack or dash attack would extend the chain, and at some point, the body would drop no matter what. I am sure it's complicated, but it would make it feel a bit better, like the SOR4 right.

[u] Content [/u] - I mean it's fine for what it is, I just think you could encourage the player to replay the game with some rewards. Maybe if you beat the game once you can unlock a new mode with more enemies and a different ending, or difficulty-specific skins instead of just getting them. You don't want to rely on the player to just increase the difficulty for replay value, give some type of progress, something that changes and justifies replaying the game to get it.

[u] Nitpicks [/u] - why no small intro, you know, SOR is known for that build-up, you could have given a reason to be hyped to find the boss.
The OST was a little weak, I get it but, it's not a great fit for the game.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

I didn't hate the game, I enjoyed it for what it was, just needs a little work with the balance. Even if you manage to fix those things, I think you should consider adding better reasons to replay the game, give some unique rewards like a modified difficulty with a special ending, even if the second run was a little different, I think it would feel more wholesome, otherwise, the game is okay but I am moving on right away. I like that you added a lot of skins, but you should have attached them to challenges, not just easy giveaways, I would have preferred the SOR remake store unlocks. I really don't think it's a bad game, but you kind of neglected it a little, mostly a lot of silly mistakes.

Ok, so... where to start? I guess I should start with the good.
 - Game has a satisfying grind loop.
 - Controls are fine.
 - Environments and layouts are fine.
 - The game is a fun time sink.
 - Cool tech and devices.
 - Simple but nice lore you can put together in the background. It isn't very deep, but its more than the first game had.
 - There is a cat and you can pet it.
The bad, and this list is going to be a lot longer:
 - Tutorials are.... busted. Plain and simple. I've had tutorials for mechanics come up for the first time on like my thirtieth time doing something.
 - Time is WAY too fast, like, an hour in game lasts like six minutes, which, sure, a fair amount of time, but when routines only last an hour or two, it makes it really hard to get in anywhere and then get back out while grabbing things. If you have to pick a lock to get in, half your time is gone already.
 - Minor glitches here and there.
 - No discovering tips yourself for later - what I mean is, in the first game each location had tips you could either learn yourself or you could buy info of. Either way you did it, the info was saved for your future use. Now its either you buy it or you have to memorize everything yourself.
 - Much of the game feels undone. Like some have said, almost like a beta build or something.
 - They finally added a save mechanic in the menu, but you can't actually use it when you'd want to... say like when you're hiding and have to find an escape route? You can save only in open areas you aren't trespassing on. Which means, if you go to one of the "big" heists, you better hope you can get it all in one go, because you can't save during it.
 - Heists are a cool idea... bad execution though. The heists are just unique locations you have to explore. Personally I feel calling them heists is just a misnomer. Because you aren't actually stealing much of anything, at least not compared to what you steal everywhere else.
 - The drones... it's kind of clear the drones took inspiration from games like more recent Assassin's Creed and the Watch Dogs games (at least Watch Dogs 2, I never played any past that one honestly) - which is fine, you know, letting you scout an area and plan routes and all of that... except you can't change the camera view. You are locked at like a 40 degree angle the entire time. If you want to select something with it, you have to move the drone backwards, up, or down. Which, if you're in a tighter location.... well sorry, that's a no-go.

While I personally enjoy the game, I can't in good conscience recommend it to anyone. It feels incomplete. Its buggy. Its unintuitive in a lot of ways. Its less interesting than the first game mechanically. And just... I don't think it's worth 20$. If you do want to get it, just wait for it to go on sale.

Ok, so after playing a bit more.... yeah I can't in good conscience even recommend this game unless you can get it for like $5 or less. I've finished the story since posting this original review, and its not good. Like, I didn't expect a masterful narrative or anything, but christ.... it's just bad. Heists are even worse than I originally thought - the final heist in the game has like a total of 5 different items you can steal. It's ridiculously easy if you take some time to think about it, and it's not satisfying at all. Some of the other heists are jsut absolute garbage. For instance, the heist "Do Not Disturb the Devil" in which you are stealing from a haunted place while a rejected resident evil boss walks slowly around the area... oh, did I say slowly? I mean, slowly, until you take a single step and it rushes at you at mach 3. And again, YOU CAN'T SAVE DURING THE HEIST. So if you want to get everything there, you either have to make multiple trips between it and your base, or you have to get everything perfect. The enemy has a set path, sure, but it also seems to just leave that path randomly for no apparent reason. It only goes through like 3 rooms, but the second it hears even the slightest step, BOOM, it's in whichever of those rooms is closest to you. I have mixed feelings on this game. I enjoy ARPGs/looters and 2D space games, and this game somehow scratches neither itch. Most of the game is relegated to navigating tight corridors in what are essentially dungeons, which makes playing the larger ships much more difficult and ends up being more of a detriment unlike most space games where the goal is usually to get larger, more powerful ships. This would be okay if the "dungeons" had at least some space to move around for larger ships, but this is only true for the final acts of the game. It's especially jarring when you enter NG+ mode (similar to how difficulty works in Diablo II) and play through the early game dungeons where the enemies are tiny and you have no room to dodge anything in a larger ship, forcing you to have to switch to a smaller ship. At least the game doesn't make you reroll anything other than a new ship to equip to do this, as your equipment carries over between ships (other than equipped turret weapons, which have to be manually swapped over to the new ship).

Normally, one of the best things about ARPGs is the freedom to develop different builds and figure out how to minmax them, and then spending resources/time to try to minmax your equipment. All that the game offers is a tedious equipment combine system to try to reroll new gear, and a very expensive "gambling" store that will take hours worth of money and turn it into a handful of likely useless items. The game doesn't really even attempt to streamline drops to equipment that you can even use. It would be akin to playing Diablo III or IV and mostly getting drops for other classes than yours. The final nail in the ARPG coffin is that there isn't really much of a power fantasy at play here. Sure, you can get marginally better gear and become stronger, but you never really reach a point where you're mowing down hordes of enemies to sift through loot drops. Finally, it really sucks that there's no way to spend money to improve the gear you already have. The game drops you rare artifacts that can do these things, but they are quite rare and too numerous to consistently get the ones that you want. It would be nice if you could spend money to reroll the gear you already have like most other modern ARPGs.

It also doesn't scratch that 2D space itch since again, you are mostly just exploring cramped dungeons rather than doing space game staples like doing jobs, improving reputation, making money, etc. Some faction's ships are also terrible in pretty much every metric for a bullet hell game like this. The best example are the Founders large ships. They are all very wide making it impossible to dodge bullets, and the fixed weapon hardpoints on the ships are light years apart making it so you have to constantly spin your ship back and forth to hit enemies with your 2 weapons. Every other faction has thinner ship profiles with weapon hardpoints that are much closer together, making them far more useable for this style of gameplay.

Overall I don't hate the idea altogether, and I did have moments where I had fun. I just don't really enjoy the execution. It would be nice if the dungeons had more space and more enemies, and if NG+ was more friendly. It would also be great if more of the story actually took place in open space. But, it could just be that maybe this game isn't for me, and that's okay. If I could rate this halfway with like a "Maybe" or (3/5) I would've done that.

This game has light rpg elements to it: There's combat, but there's no exp. You get stronger at the end of each dungeon, but there's no weapons, no armor, no inventory to worry about, and you heal at the end of each battle.

I am, however, giving this a thumbs down for a few reasons.

I like the design of the dungeons, the use of a set of core assets to bring a sense of identity to them but also foreboding along the way. I don't like how wide and large the dungeons are. The main character walks slowly which is understandable considering the atmosphere. A button to run would be great for this, making the walk speed faster, or making the dungeons not as wide and as long as they are.

Combat is why I am not recommending this game. Your primary attack is a slider where you have to time the button push (think Undertale/Deltarune). A successful attack gives you one energy (max 4) to your magic gauge.

The wrong magic spell hits for 5-10, the right one hits for 20. On all enemies. The weakness is [spoiler]usually lighting, and almost never shard[/spoiler]. Sometimes a full magic bar with the right spell hits for 80. Sometimes it doesn't.

So, combat works like this: Punch -> cast, punch -> cast, punch -> cast. The music doesn't make up for the tedium. The only variety in enemies combat-wise is how much they hit you for and what lines are written when they hit you. When the final dungeon came around, I grabbed a debugger so I could two-shot every enemy because I was just **done**.

This game has multiple endings, but when you get to the end (I got 1), you do NOT get the option to start over. Oh no no no, if you want to start over, YOU have to manually delete your save or uninstall/reinstall the game. Seriously?

I really like the music, the ambiance, but I despite how slow this game feels (slow walk speed in overlarge dungeons), and I loathe the combat.

Summary: Dungeons of Clay contains all the rogue-lite goodness that you would expect from the genre. It is fun and action-packed with its fair share of unlockable and modern twists. But what truly separates Dungeons of Clay from others is its atmosphere, theme and soundtrack that when combined together, bring you on a funky journey of complete sensory overload. 7/10

Gameplay:
As a whole the gameplay of Dungeons of Clay is at a point I could call it good, but not anything more than that. The generation of levels is well done. There are lots of varied items. Plenty of unique and gameplay changing characters. Lots of interesting elements and a fair share of unlockable to add new content to the game as you progress.

It plays well and offers everything that a rogue-lite fan would ever want, all the while being exhilarating when things go right. But it isn’t without its frustrations. Due to massive difficulty spikes and the rather counter-intuitive design of the gem shop, a lot of deaths feels like it was down to the games design and bad luck as opposed to the fault of the player.

Atmosphere:
The atmosphere of Dungeons of Clay is an absolute delight. There is no mistaking the post-apocalyptic theme of the game between the monsters and the journey, but it is so much more than just that. There is a real retro vibe throughout the game that is brought in by neon designed displays and a primarily jazz-themed soundtrack that gives it a really funky nature.
Each stage and boss of the game has its own unique track, that while jazz-themed, has a number of other genres and out of place notes that tend to suddenly pop in and out, sometimes completely changing the music track altogether, occasionally to the point of distortion.
When you mix this no rules soundtrack, the game's theme and enemies with its funky nature and retro vibes, it brings you on this journey of complete and utter sensory overload. This overload then gives a sense that makes you feel like you’re tripping out after eating something you probably shouldn’t have or you were given an extra dosage of morphine. It’s pure magic.

The atmosphere is what separates Dungeons of Clay from any other roguelike out there. It is whacky, it’s funky and it is completely bonkers. But it is that weirdness and those shocks to the sensory that bring you on one of the wildest adventures you will ever encounter in a game.

Conclusion:
Dungeons of Clay is one of those games that no matter how many times it pisses you off, you can’t help but love it and keep going back for more. Between its retro and funky design and art style and the completely crackers atmosphere and generally enjoyable gameplay, it is a game that brings you on one hell of an adventure.

It has its annoyances along with designs and mechanics that could have been done better. There are times you will find yourself waving your hands around and cursing at the screen after dying for the 5th time in a row to a homicidal duck in a barrel or acid-spitting plants.

But when things go right and in your favor, it is one of the most fun, action-packed, mindboggling and colorfully demented roguelikes you will ever play. And with that, I give Dungeons of Clay a 8 out of 10.

Cons:

Full disclosure, I'm recommending this more because I think it's interesting than because I think it's good.

Basically, you have 2-5 players, each of which is a color. Each color has its own deck theme (blue floods the board, green grows stuff in the ground, etc). The goal is to chain gems of your color together, bump them up against gems of an enemy color and infest them like some sort of zombie plague, until you eventually infest their core and destroy them. Hopefully you destroy everyone before someone gets stronger than you and destroys you. I don't really understand why in particular the dev decided that space rocks fit this theme at all but, que sera sera.

The main issue is that you don't really start the game with anything unlocked, so you have to grind vs AI to unlock cards if you want to make your own deck, else the game is just going to give you random cards for your deck. The game with just random cards is not very good. I lost one game just from drawing the same card 10 times in a row. Progression based unlocks are ok when the game is at least interesting early but this game definitely isn't. Also just from what I saw of the cards, I'm not terribly convinced even if I could make a deck the game would feel consistent or balanced at all, although it's a card game played on a randomly generated board so it probably isn't meant to be.

I think the fun I did get out of it is just the fact that it's a very unique idea and its a very open problem space to reason about (5 different colors, lots of different board sizes, 4 different possible player counts). It's a very unique game and I enjoy unique things just because they're unique, so I'm recommending it on that basis. I think as a fully fleshed out game, it leaves a lot to be desired.

The brilliance of Elden Ring is in how the game makes you feel while playing it. This game makes you feel a certain way that so few games offer. In the beginning you will feel restricted and daft for not knowing what to do. About level 6 you will realize what is actually going on.

The feeling of restriction wears off once you realize that you actually have TONS of options for overcoming the challenging levels. The game tells you so little (less than The Witness) that every little bit of progress makes you feel super clever, and that's often justified. There's secrets, hidden paths, speeding running opportunities, and so much more.

I cannot say enough good things about the game. But it would be unfair to not mention it is very difficult at first. (my time with the app is way larger then whats show on steam)

TLDR: came for one thing and stayed for features that arent even listed.
The storepage doesnt make the app any justice.

For starters its like Legend Keeper, World Anvil and similars but whitout subscriptions fees. that alone means a resounding YES, RECOMENDED.

But i was surprised to find it already goes beyond that and aims to be much more- theres already all the foundation to actually run games with Mythic Archive, going into the role of a Roll 20 and similars, and a extremely interesting system for automating rolls that ive never seen before; Its like the kinds of scripts/mods programers do for specific rulesets in Foundry (a virtual tabletop app) but completely adjustable in the app itself- to the point ive been able to 'program' so to speak 2 weird self-authored rulesets. All the stats, skill rolls and so on, even the more complex or multi-step.

I could be already runing games with it if the maps/images were working online (right now multiplayer isnt loading the maps for players yet if they run on the web, but would work if everyone had the app).

The most awesome thing for me so far was a wizard chargen builder- it allows to create a extremely user friendly step by step process of character creation for the players; At every step explanations and lore/pictures are possible, and all the busywork of assiging points, writing down skills or whatever a system uses can be automated wich is freaking amazing for non-veteran players (and even for veterans for speed).
Feels like how digital adaptations of famous ttrpgs (like dnd) handle character creation. Even rolling stats can be automated.

In brief the features:
-maps with markers and drawing, markers and areas(shapes) can be linked/show to articles, sheets, etc.
-The pages/articles are like a wiki, with easy hyperlinking (start typing and it matches existing pages)
--Amazing layout options and editor for the pages. Very clean, intuitive, includes columns layouts, pictures with text, tables, etc
--secrets and sharing options (ways of showing and hiding what the gm want from the players)
-Tabs for any pages(and character sheets)
-online chat, dicerolling, initiative tracker
--advanced automation/triggers that can be used in the chat but also inside the pages
-character generator step by step, fully customizable
+a very interesting way of making projects and modules- it allows to create details for a ruleset for example as 1 project, and then any number of other projects that can call information and functions from the ruleset; So it allows to make a basis like the rules and not needing to repeat or import into different campaigns


Now for the cons:
-the web version (very handy for players joining) cant show images and maps yet, only users with the app can see those.
-no line of sight, fog of war or strict grid for battlemaps yet
-no fancy extras like corkboard or relationship maps like some similars do, but similars are aparently planed
-some roughness around the edges (but surprisingly polished for me, i was expecting way less from early acess)

And the biggest one imo, to the point its almost a cardinal sin: No Documentation, nor tutorials nor any tips.
For the most part they're uneeded, the whole writing and map handling is extremely well polished, clean, responsive and intuitive...
...but the character generator and creating the events(automated rolls to advanced scripts) is up to the user to figure out. Theres examples built in and builders for most things that help the process, but even figuring those out is tricky as of yet

While the game features some creative designs, several critical issues make it exceptionally frustrating, including:

[b]1.Movement Speed is Too Fast[/b]
The pacing is overly rapid, leaving no room for a relaxed experience.

[b]2.Excessive Difficulty[/b]
The game is too challenging, and a bit of bad luck can lead to sudden and unexpected failure.

[b]3.Unreasonable Randomness Logic[/b]
Often, when repeatedly interacting with a single tile, the same outcome is drawn multiple times in a row. This makes players feel their efforts are futile, leading to extremely high levels of frustration. Shouldn't each draw at least yield a different result?

[b]4.Inconsistent Tile Rotation Mechanism[/b]
When the hero steps on the 6th tile and moves to the right, the 6th tile cannot rotate. Only when the hero reaches the 7th tile does the 6th tile become rotatable. However, after just 3 seconds, the hero steps on the 6th tile again.In this short 3-second window, players hardly have time to perform effective actions, making the state almost entirely random.
Similarly, when the hero steps on the 2nd tile and moves left, the same problem occurs.

In other words, the game's 7 tiles each have different difficulty levels:[list]
[*]Hardest: Tiles 2 and 6 (reaction time: 3 seconds)
[*]Moderately Hard: Tiles 3 and 5 (reaction time: 9 seconds)
[*]Moderate: Tile 4 (reaction time: 15 seconds)
[*]Easiest: Tiles 1 and 7 (reaction time: 33 seconds)
[/list]
[b]Additional Frustrations[/b]
On top of the aforementioned issues, the boss randomly rotates tiles and changes their functions, which only worsens the situation. Players end up feeling impatient and as if the developers are toying with them, rather than genuinely providing an enjoyable gaming experience.

I would not recommend this game to anyone. While the Steam review community generally maintains a mild tone, I feel compelled to speak the truth: the game developers do not treat players with respect and show no regard for the player experience.

This is not a learning tool. You need a basic understanding and knowledge of Kana in order to play this game.
There are no lessons, study cards, nothing in the game that would actually teach you what each Kana are. Not even a JPEG of the Hiragana and Katakana alphabets for you to learn from. 

Even when you get the answer wrong, the game says out loud which answer you pressed, but does not show you the kana which would have been the correct answer. So for an example, if the game wants you to pick "Mi", and you pick "Hi", the game will say out loud "Hi", and you take damage. Then the game moves on. There is no opportunity here to learn other than trial and error, which is not very effective or fun.

There is no bonus reward for choosing the answer quickly, nor does there seem to be a penalty for taking your time, as the zombies only seem to damage you when you choose the wrong answer. 
No time trial mode, survival mode, anything of the sort. You choose a difficulty, but going for a harder difficulty at the beginning is nearly impossible, no matter how good your Kana knowledge is, since for some reason the difficulty raises the hit points of the zombies and due to the weapon system, you will not be able to do much damage. I understand the "idea" behind this mechanic, but I don't understand how it is supposed to be fun or educational in any way.

Pro mode, which mixes both Hiragana and Katakana choices gives no additional rewards to the players, but it is the most fun mode of the three to play. 

This game might be fun if you're at a very specific period in your studies, where you have already studied and learned most of the Kana and want a quick way to test your memory, but even for that, there are better alternatives.

1. Actually good music
2. Nice art.
3. You will have to take time to understand the game, overall it is not that difficult - and it has some Cultist Simulator vibes of "learn while you play", but, honestly, in certain cases hints would be extremely helpful. It took me a lot of googling to find out what exactly "pure essence" is, for example. Nearly every info you need is in the tooltips, but you do not always know which images on the screen actually give you tooltips.
4. The gameplay itself is actually rather good and engaging. The game doesn't take too long to complete - but as it is a mixture of Mafia and a card game it seems like it can be fun in multiplayer too.

Just beat Dread Templar on Hard mode, what a great game. If you enjoy retro style FPS games, this is basically a must play. The gunplay feels great, the dash function adds some nice movement options and the rune system used to upgrade your weapons adds some needed depth. The level design is cool and there are plenty of enemy types. Almost all of the weapons feel useful in their own right, although there were 3 weapons that became my primaries (dual hurricane pistols, wave shotgun and black bow with explosive arrows). The trap gun has very limited use, there were only a few sections where I felt like laying down traps really helped me survive, in part because the effect of the traps is very short - it stuns the enemies for maybe 5 seconds - if the stun time was doubled the trap gun would be much more useful. The rocket launcher felt weak but maybe that's because I didn't focus on upgrading it. The biggest issue with Dread Templar is the enemy AI - the enemies cannot jump up or down ledges so unless they are a flying enemy, you can simply jump up or down a ledge and the enemy will keep trying to run toward you without attacking making for an easy kill. Also if you slowly sneak around corners, you can generally alert just 1 or 2 enemies at a time while the others sit in their spawn points waiting to be triggered. Overall though Dread Templar was very fun to play and it had a good amount of content especially for the price I paid for it on sale (4 dollars). If you're a fan of Quake and similar retro styled FPS games, Dread Templar is a must play. Very solid 8 out of 10.

[b]Firstly to address some of the negative reviews;[/b]

- Keyboard works 100% fine, for me at least (although controller does feel better especially with the mixing mechanic, I find keyboard slightly annoying for it, but it does work).

- Personally I found the tutorial to be good enough, wasn't bugged - tested with both controller and keyboard. Though I could see where some people maybe thought so where it does not let you interact with anything other than the exact object you need to interact with (quite few games do this in tutorials). Could maybe be bit more visible and clear, but in my opinion I thought the tutorial was pretty cool.

- Style of game play is maybe comparable to Overcooked in a sense that you don't have set customers you need to attend to but rather a time limit and you try to get as many customers served as possible, I was able to get 2-3(max) stars pretty easily all the levels I have played so far on medium difficulty. This is essentially same principal as in Overcooked where you have more orders than you can do, as they constantly keep coming and you just want to try get as many in time limit for max money/stars/score. This can feel overwhelming at times but so far I'm mostly finding it fun and challenging.

[b]Positives:[/b]

- Interesting concept and fun, new game play in the time management genre where you can control each arm separately or together for speed boost
- Art: charismatic, cute, and interesting characters + overall lovely level design
- I'm really enjoying the story so far, even though I often tend to skip story stuff in games + bonus codex entries which offer extra info on different customers, the bath ingredients etc.
- Controller controls are really fun but do take some getting used to (you can rebind everything except mixing I think, for both input methods)
- Nice audio
- Remote play together works really well, and co-op is awesome
- It's and onsen managment with yokai xD

[b]Negatives:[/b]

- Keyboard ingredient mixing mechanic controls don't feel great to me and can't be rebound as far as I can see (could be wrong, also controller on other hand is really fun for mixing, can see why controller is recommend by dev)
- Minor bug where my mouse cursor stays on screen, even when playing with controller nonstop, bit annoying but fine when I move it to side or other monitor
- Potentially other bugs others have mentioned? I tried both input methods and have multiple monitors and all has worked fine for me, so it is either on their end or not extremely common bug that might affect some users but not all (I would say chances are its going to work and to test for yourself and if it does not work for you, you can always easily refund)

If you are struggling with game play mechanics even after tutorial or want to see more how the game works before buying, I recommend briefly watching game play videos on youtube (that's what I did before buying).

Overall I would definitely recommend trying out this game for yourself, especially if you like games like Overcooked and are interested in onsen/yokai/japanese culture, it's a really cute and awesome game. Don't let the negative reviews (especially ones with less than 5min game play time xD) discourage you like they did to me initially, I regret not getting this game sooner. Only thing I hope they improve is minor bugs and quality of life improvements. I really love the game so far.

I hope this game gets more love, as it really deserves it in my opinion. :)

Played around with the dock now for a bit.

The main selling point of the dock to me is the aesthetic and its general simplicity. You just buy the dock, start the software like a steam game and then there it is. It appears right away and is fairly intuitive to use, although I would like to see some explanation as to what exactly can be done how (maybe add a documentation on your website/steam page).

For its relatively young age, I didn't expect the dock to feel so solid. The animations and graphics make it feel really solid, although a bit chunky at times. I now use it to store my game icons I would previously have on my desktop. If configured, the bar folds away quite nicely on the desktop so it's barely noticeable but always there when you want it.

I also really like the container feature. In addition to the dock where I now keep all my games, I use these containers to group together programs I use for different projects. Idk if that was a bug, but I sadly couldn't add any folders my containers.

What I thought was a bit annoying was the fact that you had to manually add the individual .exe-files to the dock/container. When I tried to drag my already exising link files I had on my desktop to the bar, it showed this ugly "link arrow" on the icon windows uses to indicate that the file is a link. Also, when I then removed the link file from my desktop, the program would not open.

Also, weirdly, you have to be in the non-minimalist mode in order to resize your desktop containers. This, however, is not explained anywhere, so it took me some trial and error to discover that.

It seems like the project is worked on actively at the moment, so I hope my feedback will somehow find its way into the dock. Really looking forward to futher improvement and especially the different skins that will be available with the next update.

Oh and a little thing I'd like to see in a future version is the ability to let the bar minimize itself even when you are not using the minimalist mode.

Now to conclude, really solid dock. Personally, I don't mind spending the extra couple of bucks compared to free dock alternatives, but that (obviously) depends on your circumstances. I really like the aesthetic the dock comes with and ease of using it. So even though it has its slightly rough edges here and there, I can soundly recommend it.

While I like the cell shaded artistic style of this game, I almost have to wonder if too much time was spent on the superficial than the core game mechanics. First, and I know it's stated to be in a "future plans", but I'll say it anyway. This is 2020, don't release a bow game with only one hand supported, not even to EA.. Just don't do it. Second, if you are going to make a bow game in such a packed space, at least get the bow mechanics down first. I love bow titles, and have probably played all of them to date. This one, however, is the first where I felt that the bow action was completely lifeless. It looks decent, but it feels terrible, from the odd pixie dust emitting bolt physics to the draw, drop, and sadly, impact. In the theme of feeling lifeless there is absolutely nothing satisfying about actually hitting your target. If it didn't flash red or fall over dead, you might not even notice that you had hit it at all in fact. The arrows just fly off as if they are in their own anti-gravity field. Fire an arrow up into the sky? Well, unless you lightly strum it, you will never see it fall. Now I am left handed, so admittedly I was annoyed by having to play right handed.. it just sucks in bow games - but given that it was acknowledged as a to-come feature I wanted to give it an honest go. Frankly I struggled to play it long enough to even be able to leave a review as, using my bad hand aside, it was simply not fun. My suggestion to the dev team - you have a decent looking engine and art style, but I would highly suggest taking a few steps back and taking a much closer look at your game mechanics and physics. If you had spent enough time on the core engine, the left handed thing would not be an issue - because you would have proper mounting points, draw variance, offset, and the like. These things are necessary if you really intend to make a fun bow game. Making the bow shoot like a limp pistol with no recoil and a pixie dust tracer is not making it more accessible to the casual player.

The net? I'm sorry to say for the price I expected a lot more of a solid core to be there, and at least a little bit of fun. $15 is a hefty tag for any EA title.. I sincerely hope I am proven wrong and that there are some serious engine improvements to come - but sadly, my instincts are telling me that this is DOA title, and possibly a quick cash grab for an abandoned WIP (Work In Progress).

Oh yeah, and DO NOT release bow games without ambi-support... ever. Or did I say that already? :p

This is a wave based VR Archery game where you have to defend your village from enemy minions along with your own life. You only have your bow to defend with. You do get to pick a upgrade/spell after a few waves which you can use if you hold an arrow pulled at max strength for a few seconds, but besides that you don't get anything else. The village has it's own HP along with you having separate HP as well. The game ends once you get hit enough, or enough minions reach the villagers.

Controls:
Pressing the A button on your right controller switches which hand is holding the bow, while you use the other hand to pull an arrow back with the other hand via the trigger button. You only stand in one spot, so there's no movement or teleportation, and you also can't rotate in-game.

Pros:
- Variety of different enemies to kill, with some running straight at the entrance to your village, some summoning more minions and others that will attack you directly via projectiles or flying into you.
- Some upgrades do make it easier to deal with groups of enemies or aims arrows for you
- It's cheap at only $3 AU.

Neutral:
- Nothing really stood out either in sound or music
- Some upgrades aren't that good, like the multi-shot upgrade.
- You only stand in one spot, so it can be hard to hit some enemies

Cons:
- Aiming the bow is weird/bad because it mainly follows the hand holding the bow, and it would regularly lose track from time to time or aim in a slightly or completely different direction. I've haven't had this issue in other archery games.
- Once shot, the arrow is pretty quick at the beginning of the shot, then loses alot of it's speed near the end. It wasn't fun to shoot the bow.
- There are no in-game options to change, nor is there any menu. I can't even quit the game unless I access the Oculus menu. (Oculus platforms can't access the steam VR menu in games when the bottom left button is disabled, like this one)
- You can't re-centre where you are in-game, and there are no ways to rotate the camera so you have to rotate IRL.
- It was quite common for the enemy remaining counter to display an extra 1 or 2 minions even though I couldn't find any others.
- If you die and then start again, you'll get this afternoon like glow that doesn't go away.
- The game did bug out on me and fully crash on me, with me having to take my headset off to close the game via desktop.

Summary:
Even though the game is sold for a very cheap price, the amount of issues annoys me too much, even if it was for free I wouldn't recommend it. It's a simple wave based VR Archery game held back by it's aiming issues, bugs and lack of any options.

Unfortunately just a poor experience. I could only sit through ten minutes before too many issues had piled up and I decided to get a refund. In my short experience, here are the issues I noticed:
 - No options settings on title screen start up. Being able to configure things like graphics and audio settings before starting a game is important to a lot of people.
 - No options for camera controls. Once again, being able to configure camera sensitivity and inversions is standard. None of these options are present in this game at all.
 - Awkward, and sometimes outright broken dialogue system. The way to talk with someone to walk within a certain proximity to them; this will immediately put the dialogue box on the screen. It is hard to tell how close you must be for this to happen, so sometimes if you accidentally press the button to continue the dialogue when text comes up that you weren't expecting, you will just miss whatever the dialogue box had to say. In my ten minutes this happened several times. The final straw of this was when I tried speaking to a fox in a shack, and trying to progress the dialogue just didn't work at all. It would make a sound as if the fox was speaking, and I could catch a few frames of it trying to scroll the dialogue, but it just was not working. There is no reason for a dialogue system to behave this way in a finished product.
 - The pause menu screens are similarly problematic. Sometimes it just doesn't save your preferences when you exit the menu. Opening the pause menu back up will appear as if you're on the main pause menu, but in reality it keeps the previous position of the last menu screen you had been in before closing the window, and just shows you the incorrect screen. This makes entering, exiting, and maneuvering the pause menu incredibly frustrating.
 - The ambient audio and music does not seem like it was designed to actually loop, and often cuts into itself in distracting and jarring ways.

Objectively speaking, these are the concrete problems I had faced in ten minutes alone. I faced many more subjective ones concerning the quality of the writing and visual appearance that I won't detail here since it may not bother some people. However, this game does not feel finished in any way. It makes me so sad to write this, I'm always in indie devs' corners any time I can be, but this is really rough. Can't recommend picking this up unless there are significant overhauls.

The main issue with the game is it's a collection of various mechanics, without enough setup to understand them until you fail and try them again.

The second issue is there's no character depth, development, or engagement of any kind. You are one of two generic but inclusive avatars without any other characteristics to provide interest as to why you might want to be them.

The third issue is there's no reason to care terribly much about the threat. Future cyber-network going down sounds like a good thing, to be honest. The villains are generic, flat, and wholly unengaging, and you will not care about their motivations or about preserving whatever it is they're trying to destroy.

But the second two issues would be forgivable except for how bad the main issue is. You cannot build an assortment of half-baked mechanics which only add intensity through time pressure, novelty, or visual noise. You cannot have mechanics which require immediate understanding without setup or introduction. You cannot require a user to find danger by first blindly encountering it without visual cues to understand what might be dangerous. You cannot build mechanics which require experimentation to understand, but which cause immediate failure if done imperfectly the first time you ever see them.

For many different systems to work, you have to teach the player how they work in the world you've built. Just like every platformer has easier intro levels so you can get used to the movement, just like every shooter has simple levels to get familiar with the weapons before needing them for intense moments, Operation Tango needed a concise, tightly developed set of mechanics which are introduced well in simpler or lower-consequence ways before building on them and adding pressure. Operation Tango completely fails at this, so you have to fail your way through many of the mechanics, most of which you won't see twice. And the ones you do see repeatedly are frustrating.

As a $5 game it would be fine. At $20 it's a hard pass. I regret not playing it sooner after purchase and finishing it faster, so it could be refunded.

The game has a similar philosophy as "Settlers" or "Banished". You start with workers from different species that excel in various tasks. The target is to complete the game's objective while keeping the food and resolve (morale) in check. 

I completed the hardest difficulty (Adamantine Seal) - which takes quite some take to reach it. As such, I would like to think  I experienced a good part of the available game & mechanics. 

Positives: 
- It's quite easy to learn the game. The UI / mechanics are intuitive. 
- Difficulty scales gradually. The pace feels about right. 
- The game is well made. I only encountered a few minor bugs in hundreds of hours. 
- I like the general system and playstyle. I enjoy colony-type games so I am probably biased. 
- There is reasonable diversity between runs (different species, different cornerstone, different starting buildings ...etc). 
- I like the seal system (every mission has their individual objective but it contributes to the overall main quest line). 

Neutral: 
- I like the city and upgrade approach but I would have liked to have more options there. Like exchanging starting benefits options before a new settlement or seal specific challenges. 
- Seal missions have predetermined completion quests. I would have preferred the quest to have some randomness. It would be more difficult but I think it would be more interactive. 

Negatives: 
- My biggest complaint would be the end-game design decision. In order to be effective, your target is to complete a settlement as soon as possible ( faster completion = more years =  more missions = more rewards). This creates a scenario where most of the settlements are aimed to be a "speed run". From a player perspective, it is more interesting/interactive to have a massive settlement with 80+ workers with multiple supply lines and brutal nights. But if you reach that point, you are working against the game goal (to finish the settlement as fast as possible). This also results in some imbalances: cornestones that aim for fast wins are the best; those who aim for bigger settlements are among the weakest; some species are better than others, some starting locations are far better than others ...etc. I would have liked to see some rewards that are given provided one can successfully sustain a bigger base (e.g. 1 seal for every forbidden glade, 1-time seal for surviving a night with 100 workers, 1 seal for every x completed dangerous events ...etc). This way the player would have the option to either go for a quick and fast settlement or decide for a bigger one. 
- There is a bit of micromanagement that  - in my opinion - doesn't add much to the positive player experience. For example, exchanging between builders -haulers - and farmers all the time. I think there should be a default "work". If the current task (.e.g farming) is completed, then a default assignment (e.g. hauling) is assigned. I agree with changing assignments when there are pros and cons to consider. But there is no positive in letting the farmers do nothing each 1/3 of a season. Either one is efficient or not. And that should be automated. 

Overall rating:  88 / 100.

I genuinely started off liking Against the Storm, but the further you get into the difficulties the more tedious it gets, with additional negative modifiers and additional hoops to jump through to complete the session. Each seal completion really incentivizes you to play the next difficulty to get enough shards to complete the next seal to follow the metaplot, and lower difficulties may not get you the number of seals you need in time - additionally, the further out you go, the higher the minimum difficulty of the embarkment is, pushing the player to embark on those higher difficulty options. Why progress the seals other than metaplot? So you get more resources for the Citadel metaprogression. Which does things like add resources to your starting caravan so you can actually build some production buildings at the start, or adding a production building that let you make many key items - poorly, at high cost, but beneficial for the build chains so you are not fully reliant on RNG to get a building to complete the chain, or even adding bonuses to each race in your settlement like showing you where the first set of fields is where you can build a farm the first time you recruit a Human, so you don't have to spend half the session opening the wrong glades and never getting the constant food production that would provide. 

Except like many modern roguelite hybrids, this metaprogression is poorly balanced, and time consuming, which makes it feel like busywork rather than enjoyable on its own. It makes the higher difficulties less tedious to tackle (especially with some of the more helpful bonuses), but it just feels like an absolute chore to get through. Speaking of chores, they just add more chores without opening meaningful doors and mechanics past Veteran in terms of the difficulty options. The first three difficulties add mechanics each jump - after Veteran comes Viceroy, which is the same thing as Veteran with new forbidden and dangerous glade events to threaten your settlement and that the forest is more hostile by a multiplier of x3 instead of x2, but they don't do anything "new" really, they are just more of what you have seen before on earlier difficulties, and they just cost a ton of resources that you may not have been able to produce unless you have enough bonuses from the metaprogression tree and otherwise they apply so many negative benefits your game may actually end, such as the Stormbird which as far as I can tell by searching across the internet, people have been complaining is poorly balanced even with a good settlement for years. I don't just mean negatively either - the Stormbird applies an infinite storm effect, locking you to a year until you finish it (which you could delay), which is abusable in its own right if you were lucky enough to find it early. The Stormbird is just absurdly out of band in both directions and I cannot understand the intent of including it compared to every other event. I suppose that its very existence changes the logic pattern of whether you should open forbidden glades at all, but the higher difficulties disincentivize the opening of small glades due to hostility modifiers, so that just leaves dangerous glades if you do not want to starve but want to ensure a manageable event. What a forcible winnowing of the meta - it creates a very rote playstyle even though the apparent point of RNG building choice to create more unstable, dynamic push-and-pull gameplay. 

By the way, the tree also has a level attached - as you go through various sessions you get XP, when you level up you unlock new buildings and cornerstones (buffs) to show up in the game. THIS metaprogression mechanic is where the actual doors are opened for new build orders. Except its just as slow as the tree since its a blocker on the tree - without those later buildings and cornerstones, the game is not necessarily giving you the tools to win on higher difficulties. The amount of XP seems really low as well no matter the difficulty and even with completing various achievement challenges, which just exacerbates the issue.

I assume the decision not to bind those buildings and cornerstones to the higher difficulties and instead to a metaprogression level was so that you can use them on the lower difficulties and practice various build chains, but without overwhelming people when they start to play, and because of the complexity of creating a system that could both leave them default on the higher difficulties and then unlock them for use on the lower one once you cleared the higher one. Though perhaps they could have used their training missions for this. In all honesty the buildings beyond the first few levels matter less than the cornerstones, but they both add to how obnoxious the metaprogression system is - even if it is justified ludonarratively. 

In positives, I genuinely like the give and take between blight and production starting with the Veteran difficulty. I enjoy the season model and how each session naturally pushes you to modify your build chain on the fly or attempt to produce enough of your current resources to trade for the things you need to complete the Orders. I enjoy the fact that a session can take no more than one hour or maybe two at the higher speeds and therefore allows a bite-sized city building experience. I genuinely did get 30 hours out of it so I would say I got my money's worth, and I may play some more now and again, but anything that sufficiently annoys me more than it captivates me gets a negative review especially when the causes will not be immediately apparent to the player.

This is an odd game, it claims to be a city builder and on the face of it you are building (repeatedly) a small village, but it does not tap into the core motivations of the genre, and while it has an innovative core engine, the rest of the package is poor. 

The core engine of the game is the economic model, where it asks you to mix and match whatever you have to hand to accumulate sufficient blocks of more complex resources to complete objectives. After a certain number of objectives are met you 'win', there is also a timer to end a game early if you fail to badly. Periodically you have to expand into an adjacent area to get new resources, and often need to complete an objective there or suffer a penalty. This works well.

The problem is... everything around it. I would argue that one of the core draws of a city builder is making something personal to you. But you can't do that here, the game engine pushes the player to optimise out any flair. This is not helped by the fact that the theme is paper thin, the art assets are very generic and what you are doing minute-to-minute often makes no narrative sense. Indeed, there are various perks you unlock in the game, which have significant effects, but none of it follows any logic. Wonder why your flour making facility now periodically outputs oil? Don't think about it, Playing with the engine can be fun, but there is no immersion in the gameplay.  Moreover, as a rogue-like, there is also a meta-progression system, which mechanically works fine, but there is no flavour or narrative to it. I was also left wondering if the depth-to-complexity trade-off is set right here. The game has lots of 'stuff' in the form of perks, buildings, events, etc, but I felt like I was just doing the same motions with different labels attached to the resources - I think a player should form 'builds' in this type of game, but the design directs the player to just do a bit of everything, and so each village feels the same.

In short, this is an interesting curiosity. The developers might be onto something with the core engine, but they are going to need to find a better vehicle to put it in.

This game is really, really good.  I'd argue it's either genre-defining or genre-creating, depending on whether you see it as a city builder or something else.  Quite innovative with its mechanics.  I would say it's almost ideally suited for me.  I like city builders, but I generally don't like sandbox games.  I need concrete, externally-supplied goals or I lose interest.

This game sure has that.  Honestly, it looks like a city building game, but it's really more of a mix of resource management and puzzle-solving.  I love that.   I love that there's basically no focus on playing Pretty Princess Dress-Up.  Aesthetics play no role in how well your town actually functions.  

And it can be hard.  Not until you hit the higher Prestige difficulties, in my experience, but once you're at or near the top, it isn't easy.  You very much cannot screw around; you're on a clock and you have to be adaptable.

There are some cons, I suppose.  The blueprint system is a key source of that need to adapt, but in the end, you have to do four things to win: Make/keep your people sufficiently happy (well above simply not leaving), complete orders, solve Glade events, and spend tools to send caches.  It's entirely possible to, say, never get offered a means to make tools, which means sending caches en masse is not going to be possible, especially at high enough prestige where trade becomes much more unfavorable.  Or you might simply not find sufficient sources of food in the glades you open.  I lost a run yesterday to that (Ashen Thicket).  

But if you make your peace with that, the game is incredible.  There's a lot of room for player skill without the need to train muscle memory or memorize vast amounts.

This is a city builder game, but it's not trying to be an endless sandbox for creative expression. The game is focused on doing the fun, early part of city building--before your cities become a self-sufficient machine that spits out money. This game hands you a handful of tools, a random setup, and tells you to sort things out before you run out of resources or time. Along the way, it drip feeding you more tools and encourages you to expand your territory to fulfill your growing needs. The more you expand, the more problems you have, but the more tools and resources you have to solve those problems. As soon as your settlement becomes self-sufficient and starts printing points, the game ends the scenario, hands you a bucket of resources for meta progression and says, "Great job, try it again with a different set up". If your settlement instead starts bleeding villagers and running dry on resources, you will quickly enter a death spiral that ends your run.

This game does not want you to get bored or lost. It wants you to be in a sweet between "I have some inefficiencies I need to optimize" and "Oh god, I have so many problems I need to solve". If you start winning too hard: congrats, you have won. Here's your reward. Try it again with a harder setup. If you have lost control: yikes, looks like that's not going well. It's ok. You'll get 'em next time.

Meta progression in Against the Storm is not revolutionary. You unlock more starting resources, more random buildings to play with, more races whose preferences you need to consider, upgrades to your buildings and villagers, etc.. But the overall puzzle is addicting and the over-world is full of map modifiers, on-off challenges, and choices that offer enough variation to fill up hundreds of hours of playtime.

There's no insane late game shake up. Once you reach the end of the upgrade tree and have seen the harder difficulties, it's mostly more of the same. But at that point, the game has more than earned its price tag, and I'm happy to put it down for a while until I feel the urge to go back in. Updates have also been generous with new content and improvements. Huge recommend. Easily one of my favorite games of the past couple years.

A few weeks ago I bought Against the Storm to play on my Steam Deck for a flight, and now I have over 120 hours in it! Surprisingly this runs really well on the Deck. There are a few minor inconveniences with the keyboard, trading, etc as the UI is a little small, but it manages to fit all of its features. I think I've played more than I would have on PC just being able to chill out on the sofa.

I won't say a lot about the core gameplay loop as plenty of other people have covered it, but it does a pretty good job of introducing things a bit at a time and letting you discover mechanics and strategies while unlocking things.

There's interesting variety between settlements and cycles, and the game is nicely designed to encourage you to keep trying harder difficulties to get a little more without forcing it on you.

There are a few flaws that are mostly inconveniences rather than gameplay issues. It's a bit micro-heavy when you're trying to get the most out of your villagers. You can set some detailed parameters around production but can't reconfigure a whole recipe or ingredient, or can't say "use whatever we have the most of". It would be nice to have seasonal profiles e.g. avoid glade during storm, make a woodcutter go and work in the rain collector. I also wouldn't mind seasonal autosaves and being able to reload them slightly easier, or just auto-pause - there are a number of times I've had to recover from not pausing in time when the season changes to manage hostility which could have been avoided easily! But that's an ADHD problem, not specifically this game :D

It also feels like the meta progression is very staggered. You typically earn about one upgrade per settlement, which doesn't feel bad, but I've played 100 hours and completed the gold seal (first credits play) and I feel like I've still got most of the upgrade tree to go! I don't massively mind this, but it does mean there are a decent number of features I probably won't reach in the time I play it.

It's very hard to reinforce battles that are already happening because usually your soldiers will not reach it in time, and as soon as you lose, the enemy will have it's units restored in their castle, so all that effort will be for nothing. You can't maneuver your armies all that well either because each second they stay on the field, they lose resources and have to go back to resupply, so unless you have planned every single step of your attack, you will not even be able to take advantage of attacking from multiple angles.

The game gives you access to small groups of soldiers which you can hire as mercenaries to help you out and annex them eventually, but sometimes when they lose a battle, you have to pay them again to reinforce you next time, which can be pretty annoying on the early game economy, which requires at least 1000 bucks to do any action such as hiring the mercenaries, sabotaging the enemy castles, etc. Eventually you can outgain all of those costs and all that will matter will be the time to take those actions but i find that pretty unbalanced.

The game has a manual battle option which doesn't work unless you have at least two allies on the field and other requirements which i still don't know to happen, but you can count that most of the battles you will not be able to manually fight. The battles are very simple and all you can do is order your units to walk to specific spots on the map and try to use your other units to do a pincer maneuver and kill everybody. Fighting manually is much better than waiting for the battles to finish on the campaign map, so you want to play every battle, but they end up ultimately being the exact same fight since there's only one good strategy.

Diplomacy requires you to send an officer to the clan you wish to gain trust with and that takes quite a while to get done, usually by the time you can finally have an alliance, you will already be at war with someone else, but having an alliance doesn't even mean you can count on your ally, it just means you won't be attacked by them. To have them reinforce you, you have to build even more trust and it is a resource that gets used whenever you ask them to do anything, so you need to keep sending officers if you wish to get anything done diplomacy wise. Just like with the economy, it's very annoying to deal with early game, but you might find yourself having a lot of officers to spare later on to do this for you. 

You can become a stronger clan's vassal if you wish to not get immediately destroyed, but that costs you the entirety of the diplomacy system, which will be completely locked off for you with the exception of the clan you surrendered to, but that doesn't even guarantee they will help you out, that just guarantees they won't attack you.

After about 5 hours of gameplay i was still stuck on my 2 castles outgaining any costs i have while trying to wage war on the same enemy while they get reinforced every single time and whenever i'm close to getting their castle, either resources or lack of soldiers take it away from me. Any action i use to damage their castle or take their soldiers away to battle them out of the castle ends up being a waste of time and money since they get reinforcements from a much bigger ally and restore their units extremely fast at the same time.

In the end, i really like the idea of the game and it's simple yet complex enough to keep you hooked, but it's very annoying to play since the game keeps pushing you back to deal with X, Y or Z situation so the game ends up being reaaaally slow and unrewarding.

If you fancy some spelunking to go along with your spatial organization puzzles, you can't go wrong with [i]Blockicker[/i]. When an inquisitive young fellow inadvertently finds himself trapped in a mysterious subterranean complex, he's forced to correctly align scores of curiously shaped blocks in order to open locked doors so that he can once again relish the wonder of natural light. This burly boy doesn't believe in getting his hands dirty and he's certainly not afraid of stubbing the toes on his right foot, for with a series of swift kicks, he's able to send the heavy blocks careening towards their proper destinations. Certain puzzles must be solved in order to proceed down the pathway to freedom, but many of them can be tackled at a later time. Players will need to be methodical, but none of the puzzles are too rigorous. The music loops quickly, but it's still very pleasant and nicely compliments the SNES-esque visuals.

Perhaps I'm mean-spirited, but I wouldn't mind seeing this kid accidentally descend into the depths once again; [i]Sokoban[/i] fans would be all the richer for it.

First let's keep in mind how little money you actually spend on this game.
The idea of it is great, and I definitely think with a little more time put into planning it out this game could have shined. As it is right now, it's still looking a bit dull and I want to go into why that is.

PROS:

[list]
    [*]Great idea - I've never encountered a dating sim that focuses on personality before.
    [*]Asking the colours questions was great and having them interact at times over each other's answers was also great.
    [*] The sprites of the revealed love interests are also really good (I admit I have no idea if these were free assets like I know some of the backgrounds were).
[/list]

CONS:

[list]
    [*] [b] Barely touch on the colours' personalities. [/b] For a game - even a short one - about judging personalities over looks, I was looking for some more meaningful interactions. The questions were a good start but I felt like there could have been a few more - or another more creative way (a Round 2 so to speak) that uncovered more of their personality. After the questions when I saw 'Life Story' pop up on screen I thought that meant we'd learn about their past and how it shaped them as a person; not their literal life story after dating you.
    [*] [b] Some choices might as well not even be there and don't match the personalities we have come to know. [/b] My example of this is when the option to marry your chosen colour arrives. You get the illusion of 2 choices 'Propose' or 'Wait for them to propose'. I chose to wait for every partner, and every time it would say 'They don't propose because they were waiting for you to be as assertive as you were when you...'. For the more shy personalities this makes 100% sense. But there were at least 3 colours I would argue could have asserted themselves. [spoiler] Yellow is flirty and confident - and yet they don't propose at all when you wait for them? It just didn't strike me as making sense and since this is a game focusing on personalities it isn't something I can just look past. [/spoiler]
    [*] [b] No interactions with the colours actually feel meaningful. [/b] I know people have commented on the length of the game and said it's too short. I don't have a problem with that because long doesn't mean good or even better. What this dating sim about personality lacks is... personality. You get to know the colours on a surface level, but not enough that it even makes you want to know more. The questions was a good call - there was a nice mix of light-hearted and more serious questions. Then there was the date stage which was... alright. Then you had to buy them a gift and hope it was the right one (you get a hint during the questions stage), and then... you get an epilogue of your life with them? Asides from the questions stage, the characters barely speak at all. The epilogues for all colours are more or less exactly the same
[/list]

Overall, it was an interesting experience. I am curious as to why the developer decided to charge money to play it. If this were free I would say go ahead - it's an interesting enough idea to give it a go, regardless of the lacklustre content. However, I can't recommend paying for this (even for as low a price as it is) because it just is not worth the money.

I was intrigued at first, but the range of options is so small, and it turns out pretty much exactly the same no matter who you choose, i.e. "Blue was happy you chose ___. Green trusted you because you ___ instead of ___. You had a great relationship." There were a handful of interesting outcomes, but all in all they aren't much different (if you get to the end), and a lot of the text is recycled and repetitive.

Plus, considering the minimal amount of text, I'd have expected better proofreading. And the cinematic text during the--I suppose you could call it the epilogue?-- of each story crawls so abysmally slowly I became very irritated. There was no option to make it go faster that I could see, either.

The personalities seemed fun, and the relationships between them were interesting and I believe exploring those would also be very engaging.
