At first glance Potion permit looks like your basic "Oh its Stardew but i make potion, cool" kind of game. For the few firsts hour of gameplay you'd be right but the more you play the more you realize that this game is so boring and repetetive. 

First problem :The grind.
This game is so unnecessary grindy. The amount of ressources and money you need to collect to achieve an upgrade or doing quest is downright ridiculous. Sometimes a single upgrade can put you in this position where all you do is cut wood and break stone for the next 1 to 2 IRL hours and praying that someones gets sick in your clinic so you get that little cash. Makes me wonder if the devs played their game to feel the system they've put in place. My advice : reduce the cost for the upgrades, drasticly.

Second problem: The minigames.

At first, I loved those minigames when you'd have to play around ingredients to make a potion. The diagnostics system too. But after a while it becomes really old and feels repetitive. My advice: Make it more difficult over time or just remove the system after "mastering" the diagnostic of certain diseases.   


Third problem: Gathering ressources.

Unlike Stardew valley, Potion permit has a specific zone where you collect wood/stone and your ingredients. The problem here is that everything is pregenerated to give a certain amount each day. Exemple, lets say for a quest you need to give x 10 daisies. You go fetch daisies but Uh-oh it only spawns 3 daisies per day and you dont have any cause you used you lasts ones to make a potion. So for the next 3 days you will have to come back to the same spot and gather the same daisies. Once again it is grindy and becomes old real fast to see the same layout eachtime. Same goes for wood and stone. My advice : Change the layout,  spice it up a bit. Randomise some places and add some unexepected things. Make it less dull and repetitive.

Fourth problem: The characters.

Honnestly, I normally dont get too hung up on this normally. But the caracters are bit predictable in their respective story line. I think cracaters just need a bit more love and more complex stories. Its not a big issue as mentioned above but it does makes the game seems more "meh". My advice, flesh out a bit more your caracters.

Conclusion: I haven't really played all those hours in the game (I AFK a lot) but i can safely say that I cannot recommend this game not even as a relaxing slow paced game. It lacks alot of things and It feels unifinished. But I think with the right amount of work and passion, this game could eventualy reach a status worthy to be compared to a Stardew Valley like.

Potion Permit's spin on the farming sim genre sees you as a budding alchemist/chemist moving to a small-town to help heal decades-old mistrust of chemists. While there is no farm to tend to, there are sick patients who need medicine, and you can craft them healing potions through a tetris-like brewing game using foraged items around the island. The graphics are adorable and there's a whole cast full of quirky characters to get to know and romance (plus you have a pet dog!).

However, this game does come with quite a few drawbacks:
-Because this game is rather story-driven it doesn't quite feel like there's the same replayability to it as other similar games
-The music is a bit lackluster (or at least too quiet)
-The fishing mini-game is a bit too simple (at least for my personal tastes) 
-It is QUITE a grind to gather all the materials needed for all the upgrades you'll want for your home, your clinic, and your tools, which can make the game a bit of a slog
-While the visual change in time of day is cool, there isn't really a way to track the weeks, or a change in season, or any way to celebrate villager's birthday (aka no calendar)
-Some of the simple mini-games associated with researching potions, or diagnosing patients get really boring after you've done them a few times

But all that said, I have really enjoyed playing this game and figuring out its quirks. I would recommend it to anyone wanting to expand their collection of farming sim games or anyone who doesn't mind a bit of a grind for achievement hunting.

Potion Permit is one of those games that I kept on my wishlist for a long time, because I couldn't decide if I wanted to buy it or not. When I finally got it, though, I was quite excited - I like the way it looks, I like the story that is different than, "one of your relatives left you a farm to care for", I like the idea that there's a puzzle game to create a potion. Plenty of positives for a good start of the game.

However, the more time I played, the more tired I was getting. I read the reviews that said the grind was off-putting, but I honestly thought that it wouldn't be that bad. Well. It was.

I was working on restoring my reputation by helping people, I got myself a cute girlfriend (Martha stole my heart), and I helped the townsfolk with their requests. And, of course, I was caring for my loyal companion, Pancake the dog. Still, everything was overshadowed by the grind. I had to plan my days wisely, because I'd spend lots of time collecting resources to brew potions that I would later sell to earn some money. Plus, every single quest that I got from the townsfolk was, "Collect 50 roses", "Collect 30 Honey", or whatnot. Saying it was tedious would be an understatement. 

Even though my head hurt and I felt physically tired from playing the game, I'd go back every day and try to reach 100% completion. I was so close! Then I stopped at 97% and that was it. I could not for the life of me move further. Eventually, I was so frustrated, I started looking for answers online - there were a couple things I was missing and I could not figure out how to unlock them.

Meh. It is common that the game stops before reaching 100%. If you don't romance one of the townsfolk, who gives you a recipe as a "thanks for dating me" gift, you'll be missing 1 important thing which prevents you from reaching 100%. I appreciate that you can date only one person at a time, but why would you make something so crucial to perfect the game difficult to obtain? I mean, some players will get the recipe, of course. But there are other recipes that are impossible to find or the game doesn't trigger relevant cut scenes. 

It was exciting in the beginning and I was really looking forward to playing the game. I was even recommending it to my friends when I first started! But as the story progressed, I grew more exhausted. Playing the game eventually felt like a chore, and a chore that didn't bring any results, because I wasn't even able to reach 100%. It seems this is something that the devs are aware of, because it has been reported multiple times, but they refuse to acknowledge it.

Shame. This could have been a great game, but it needs some more work - especially to make it more interesting and less tedious. The story is nice; the rest... not so much.

I cannot recommend buying this game.  It looks like a good one on the surface; cute pixel graphics, a town in need, and a unique job description to save the day.  

But then you click "play."  

Does anyone remember the intro to the GBA game Golden Sun?  The endless emote boxes, the long-winded dialogue, the button mashing just trying to skip it all and get past it?

This is worse.  Because it isn't just the intro.  EVERY SINGLE CUTSCENE is like that.

You say, who cares about that part, I'll just go cure patients.  For every patient, there is 1-3 minigames to play.

There are a lot of mini-games in Potion Permit.  None of them are fun.  But you can cut out about half of them if you gather ingredients to make serums that let you skip particular mini-games.

So you go off into the wilderness to gather.  You figure this part should be fun; after all, if you like craft sim games, chances are you'll like the gathering process.

Not in this game.  It's okay for the first couple game days.  But your tools can only be upgraded by advancing the story, and even then, they only get slightly more powerful.  So, you are still hacking away at early level plants, when you have a max level sickle.  

You stamina never levels up.

In order to advance the story you will need more wood and stone than you can fathom.  EVERY SINGLE QUESTLINE in this game requires an absurd amount of resources.  (And this, coming from someone who stockpiles like a hoarder in the My Time games)

You can't upgrade your clinic until the last area of the game is unlocked (end of storyline, basically), and let me tell you, that clinic is UGLY.  If I was sick, I would just go home, and not sleep in the cruddy beds.

So, you think, at least I will get the Steam Achievements, and then never play the game again.  Only, lo and behold, even the Steam Achievements are all about the grind.  Nothing about making your house/clinic/town awesome.  It's all about how many times you've smashed rocks or trees (they're mistranslated besides, it isn't gather 1,000 stone, it is smash that many stones INDIVIDUALLY)

You try to take a break from the achievements by befriending townsfolk, only to be reminded about how bad the cutscenes are.  Either there is a sharp culture divide between wherever this was made, and the US, or it was translated very poorly.  The dialogue is either vague and confusing like a game from the '90s, or so stupid, I can hardly make myself keep reading it.

You keep asking yourself, why am I playing this game?  You may have a little time to kill, or want to rest for a little bit, but the whole time you're playing this tedious, annoying, GRIND, you realize you'd rather be cleaning the bathroom.  Seriously.  Or at least eating a cookie and having a cup of tea.  Actually,  just staring out the window would be better than the last few game days I grit my teeth though.  And it's dark out; there's nothing to see.

Yes, the current view out my window is more intriguing than Potion Permit.

Super Glitter Rush is a cute and amusing little Boss Rush shoot'em up. Shots cost energy which you can earn by collecting coins you get from shooting into enemy bullets and flinging them back and by picking up special enemy bullets that are safe. The amount of bullets that hit the boss with your shot is your chain. Chains are not cumulative, however you can increase the chain value of your shot if it's deflected back. There are no leaderboards, which is a shame, but there are a couple fun achievements that could keep you entertained for a (short) while. It's not too hard to get them all. The last boss can be difficult but all you have to do is grow the chain value of your shot.

Disclaimer: This is a mature game that has an old school vibe of early rare games with it mature yet childish jokes. This may be a great game for people who grew up in the 90s but may seem stupid or boring to others.   

Teratopia has a strange cast of characters from the main characters you play and the bosses taking on a more mature aspect but not enough that your parents wouldn't mind you playing it as a kid, well maybe one boss does pass that line.  All 11 bosses are part of the same family from the aunts, mom, and dad and the grandparents. Each with their own unique fighting style and way you should go about attacking them. Their character design and the mature themes they have to them, truly give me 1990s Rare games vibes, almost like a kid's game art style of Banjo Kazooie with the adult humor of Conkers Bad Fur Day. 

The way you defeat the bosses is up to you depending on who of the 3 you choose to fight them with. You can change out any character at any time when you are inspecting the map to return to the levels. 

You can play as Tucho the melee variant with his up close and personal punches and with a high damage but somewhat low health he is more of a hard hitter and end the fight soon type of player. 

Benito the Ranged character fast with a descent range to fire upon enemies but the damage is low and large groups of enemies can take a while to dwindle down. 

And lastly Horacio the wizard with a decent poison attack that damages over time and can be stacked up to 6 times. The only issue I had with him was his moment and doge it just feels clunky and a little uncontrollable.   

All can summon minions to help them in battles. There are 5 minion variants melee, ranged, berserker and mage are exactly what you think they are, the last one is the engineer that can use turrets around the map to help you and like to eat carrots. Every main character has the same minions but they play different roles like the berserker for Tucho is a tank that deals good damage and for Benito his berserker has high health and doesn't fight only taking the agro to give the other summons time to finish them off. The minions are alright I tend to forget I had them for most of the game but they can help you out when you are in a tight boss fight and some boss fights need the help of the summons to distract the boss or disarm traps, they may have set. 

So that’s really all you need to know of the game and really my opinion of it. I think it’s good fun, teratopia is one of those turn your brain off and just punch things type of games. Nothing that will really push you to the max. I loved the visuals with its gross looking characters and absurd boss fights. The level design is decent but with the controls feeling a little floaty especially when you jump can be a recipe for disaster. I died more from falling off the map then I did from standard enemies. If the controls were tightened up and possible a little more work on the level design this would be a great game, but im not disappointed that I played it I enjoyed the 4 in a half to 5 hours I played the game. There are some achievements that I missed when it came to collecting things and I think I will make run another playthrough to get them. I think the game is fun enough for another playthrough.

I bought Forsaken Portals cheap on sale. During the first few hours of playing, I liked this game. I appreciate Indie games trying to do something different, and this looked like a casual version of the X series. But the further I got in the game, the more apparent it became that this store page is riddled with deceptions. For that reason, I do not recommend the game. It should have been honest about what it is - a battle card game with the theme of a space simulator. Instead, it hypes up game play elements that do not exist:

1) The universe is not "huge." There are a few, sequentially unlocked space sectors with a clear, one-way direction through.

2) You don't "build your own space stations", you buy 1 of 2 prefab options and decide where to plop it down.

3) Upgrading your ship is not how you defeat "the strongest enemies in the galaxy." For that you have to upgrade your card deck, which is not specific to your ships.

4) You will not "build a trading empire.' Prices do not fluctuate, there is no supply/demand dynamic, and your small cargo hold is the same size even as you progress through the ship choices.

5) There are no "huge hand designed worlds" to explore. The same station types repeat in numeric sequence, like Power Plant I, II, III, and offer the same basic services and goods.

6) You're not going to need your station for "exploring places that could not be reached otherwise." The map is revealed and you already know your destination - you just need a gas station to reach it. Otherwise, the station is superfluous. The interior of your station is 4 rooms with interactive terminals, connected by long hallways. There is absolutely no reason these terminals could not be combined into one and accessed from space, and that would have been much more efficient.

7) It's not "sometimes necessary to defend oneself." The combat card game is the core mechanic. You cannot advance without card combat.

8) And god, if only the card combat animations went as fast as they do in the edited video, but they don't. I am not asking for explosions and whirling lights to be entertained. I just want the option to turn the animations off to get through the card battles faster.

Ultimately, the veneer of mining, trading, crafting, and missions has just one purpose - manufacture more and more cards for your deck so you can defeat enemies who have progressively better decks than yours. That's the game play loop. When you aren't card battling, you're making/getting more cards. So if that's your thing, here's the game for you. I'm telling you this because whoever created this store page didn't and should have.

There really is nothing at all wrong with this game for what it is. The developer's should be forthright and proud of what they accomplished. What's wrong is what the store page represents the game to be and the inflated price that goes with it.

Tyrannis is a turn-based wargame that pits rebels using guerilla warfare vs. an overwhelming mercenary army. It has interesting mechanics that allow for a lot of tactical flexibility. The fact that you don't know where the enemy is creates a sense of paranoia and urgency that feels unique. Multiplayer is also a blast if you have some friends.

An absolutely kickass game with a lot of potential. Not only is the gameplay great, but the story and all of the intel reports are top class. Since this was made by a TNO dev, it has a distinct TNO-type vibe to it that I absolutely love.

Tyrannis is the best video game adaptation I have seen of tabletop COIN games like those designed by Brian Train or Volko Ruhnke. The lack of proper polish and some confusing features do not ruin what is the DEFCON of counter-insurgency. Simple moves give rise to great complexity in this simulation of upto two government players (the game says they are "mercenaries" but any counter-insurgency player will recognize them as the state or security forces) and upto five insurgent factions.

This game is lacking some basic features I would expect in commercial software these days. Specifically, there is no way to turn the music off! Neither is there any audio slider. The soundtrack is kinda generic but very satisfying to listen to and successfully captures the complex emotions which are present in any insurgent situation. However it saddens me that I cannot listen to my own music while playing this game. Of course I could route the audio through different speakers and reach the desired effect, and for me this did work, but for the average consumer it may be awkward.

Another thing that really makes the gameplay worse is the lack of ability to re-map the hotkeys. I have a mouse with five buttons on it but I can only use like one or two of them (the main ones). I would love to hotkey those remaining buttons to different views and unit actions. Hopefully you grognards play the game I do, with a good drink in one hand and my mouse in the other. Maybe add in some hotkeys for manipulating the state, media, cells, and units therein?

This brings me to the map. The graphics are quite good, very smooth, consistent, and have the dot matrix effect you would expect from WarGames(1983). My only nitpick is a carry over from the previous paragraph; there is no way to easily switch between the different map filters. You can either left click on the icon several times (repetitive and annoying) or you can use the hotkeys (which cannot be rebound). The hotkeys are not bad, but it bothers me to no end that I cannot have them on my mouse.

Fortunately those two small nitpicks are where the game stops being frustrating and starts being fun. This game truly innovates by allowing players to craft their own factions with unique combinations of abilities. This is a feature that is undersold and in my opinion should be expanded upon. There are a couple of faction abilities that are not really clear, some of them seem like archaic runes or algebra than an actual ability. It would have been nice for those abilities to have a tooltip clarifying on what they actually do. Instead we have to guess what this does: ".1 + infr / .2 * inf cost" or something like that. It does not tell me why I would want to pick it.

For the most part the abilities are clear cut; +10 Mil to income, reduce the cost of your troops, increase media propaganda effect in regions, etc. Each faction has two points unless it commits to non-violence in which it gets four points. These points will be spent on faction abilities, with each weak ability costing 1 point and each strong ability costing 2 points. Strong abilities are usually just stronger versions of weak abilities. You can mix and match these abilities to achieve some interesting results.

For example, in my most recent game I was able to pitch two government players against three rebels. One of the government players was focused on having a strong military to physically destroy rebel units, but the other government player was designed to conduct media propaganda campaigns and fight rebel influence in the cities by reducing the effectiveness of rebel cells. I don't think that many people will appreciate the nuance of this design. Counter-insurgency is a politico-military phenomenon, that is to say that you must win hearts at the same time as you must remove heads from bodies. This is true for the insurgents as well, since they will need the support of the population to counter the strong initial position of the government players.

This is a COIN game, so government players start with all territories. Rebels move their units freely around the map. Each side only has a vague guess of where the other side's units are. Thus the rebels will most usually have the element of surprise, knowing where the enemy fixed positions are and where to strike. This is another place where the politico- side of the equation shines through - if rebels get enough sympathizers in a region then they get to see what enemy troops are in that region. How do rebels do that? They establish cells in states either through paying for it, or by stationing military units inside states. Each turn the rebel units will construct cells in their place of occupation (the state they are in).

My rebels comprised three factions; one oriented towards military combat, one oriented towards generating political support (this one is non-violent), and one which is a mix of both. Playing in any of these roles is satisfying. Each turn you have to carefully consider whether you want to move your troops, and how. The government player comes closer to discovering you location every turn, will you stay mobile to make their efforts useless? Especially in the early game, the rebel player is typically avoiding combat and using their few units to build support and only hit where the government players are weak. This is something of gamble sometimes since the rebel players also do not know where government units are with 100% certainty. The combat is simple; you can have as many units attack are as eligible. When units attack they attack all at once. When combat happens, the side with the most units win and winner takes all (after political modifiers and faction abilities are applied). So the losing side loses all their units. If it is a draw (the units are equal in number) then no one dies and nothing happens aside from infrastructure damage and civilian deaths. It sounds simple, but what it leads to is you gambling with your units. If you think a state is undefended then you can just send in one unit to attack and capture it. But you don't know, it could have two units. If it has two units and you send one unit, that one unit will die. So maybe send 3 units? But what if they have 4? See, that's the dilemma. One game the rebels attacked a major stronghold controlled by the government. They had 16 units go into combat and found out that there were 15 government units there! In that single battle the government lost so many units that the rebels were able to overrun government states and take over enough to win the game. If the government would have had at least one more unit, then they would have been able to force a draw, in which case they would have had another turn to reinforce their position and possibly put down the rebellion. This is also a good lesson in the concentration of force.

For either player, the way to win battles is to mass your forces into a single large army and roll through the map. So is that a winning strategy? I am not sure yet, since I don't consider myself as having mastered the game yet. Most games begin with the rebel player having only four units and the government player having many. Additionally the government controls all the land and thus all the income. By mid game the insurgent players should be earning enough to where they can replace their losses (although ideally they are moving their units around to prevent them from being cornered and destroyed) and build up the political support they need to win the game. In the end game I usually end up with at least a couple of death stacks of 4-8 units.

What stands out is the unique physics-based size morphing mechanics. I've never seen a game character control quite like this. The three different sizes modify the cat's size, weight, and the way it reacts to surfaces. The controls make it fun - if a bit challenging - to discover and master the manoeuvres needed to navigate the varied levels and obstacles. 

Learning to navigate is needed to gather the items necessary to progress through the game or, for those who are up to the challenge, complete the game with all items collected. Not only will you be reward with a collectable upon reaching an item, you can often earn a bonus collectable for reaching that same item under a specified time (restarting the level is instantaneous which is very much appreciated for trial and error purposes when attempting the harder time trial objectives).

I recommend this game to people who like to bounce and roll around.

I would highly recommend this game for those seeking an interesting platforming experience. There is a sense of progression as you go about the game, unlocking new levels and hats, which motivates you to complete the game further. The yarn ball hidden in each level serves as another challenge which motivates the player to explore the level further. The different areas create a sense of diversity which helps keep the game from becoming stale, and the concept, while simple in design, is thoroughly explored throughout the game.

If you like platformers with deep movement mechanics, I recommend. It's a neat little game. That's the TL;DR.

This game's biggest strength is that it makes the act of simply moving your character from place to place, regardless of the environment, something to be mastered. It's simple and intuitive - you bounce - but there are a couple of very significant ways you can modify it. First is the relationship between the three states your cat can be in, I'll call them bounce mode, control mode and speed/weight mode. Bounce mode is self-explanatory, you will bounce as you touch any surface. Control mode is the normal state, and it's where you're able to adjust the most while switching between the two other states. If there was a slight miscalculation, using this mode allows you to correct it before it's too late. Then there's speed mode, which I think is the crux for the great learning curve. It makes you small, makes you go very quickly (especially down slopes), but it also makes you plummet from the air very quickly. It effectively turns you into a ball-shaped anchor, which means that it can be quite volatile. This is the hardest thing in the game to master by my estimation (outside of maybe consecutive wall-bounces), it's essential to playing quickly but can be a very risky maneuver. Learning the intricacies of how to weave the speed mode into many of your bounces can be tough and frustrating, but it's rewarding to do so. One of the most fun parts of the game for me has been the tried and true act of simply jumping across some platforms that are placed out sparsely. There's a lot to consider in the moment-to-moment even for such a fundamental platforming concept, as if you want to go fast, then plummeting down onto platforms with speed mode just before you bounce off of them is essential, but quite risky, since you may just miss them entirely. One really needs to learn the trajectories of the modes.

Secondly, the environments will inevitably shift the way you approach the movement.

Some levels make you utilize speed mode to gain momentum to launch yourself somewhere far, others force you to be wary of environmental hazards, and others yet will make you have to learn the skill of wall-bouncing, which is another very high-skill ceiling action. Many of the levels are pretty rudimentary platforming concepts, but paired with the movement system they present new challenges. The extremely common trope of moving platforms is one of the hardest levels in this game. They only show up about 70% of the way through the game, whereas in most platformers you'll likely see them within the first few levels. The game also has environmental modifiers like ice and water which shift the way your modes function a bit. Ice makes you go extremely fast in speed mode but with less control, and water retains the normal functions of the modes but you're obviously floatier; it's water. They don't show up super often but it's a nice change of pace now and then. 

These two things together make for a remarkably deep movement system. You'll have to frequently adjust based on the level and your knowledge of the systems. 

For criticisms, it can be unpolished at times. At a few points you might tumble out of the level and fall into the endless void. It does not happen often, and even if it does, the restart is instant so at most you're losing like, 30 seconds. Collision boxes for enemies/some obstacles can be unclear and typically a bit too big (seems to just be a big rectangle usually, which can lead to the models being a little bit off naturally), which is understandable for a game made by 1 person. The same goes for the lack of visual effects that could help with clarity. There are some weaker levels. They're presumably there for the sake of exploring the concept thoroughly, and I'd say the game as a whole does a good job of that, but that ambition tends to leave some levels with the short straw.

All-in-all, a unique platformer with a lot of mechanical depth. Quite liked it by the time I finished it.

so what's it like? well, this is the kind of game you play when you just want to spend an hour or two a day wandering around a fun little island, spotting weird creatures and digging up treasures. (unless you're a lunatic like me, and you play it for 9 hours over a couple days to get a 100% clear.) that's really all there is to it! there's no combat, no puzzles, it's just a fun and easy little luck-based game where you collect eggs and nuts, buy items to help you find all the xenos, and talk to the great characters living on this wild island.

some people in the reviews here think that gets dull quickly, and i don't blame you if you're the kind of person who needs a little more. but for me, it's more than enough just uncovering all the bits of weird and hilarious writing that Willy is always putting out. this game is absolutely jam-packed with it, with 240(!!!) xenos of various types to find, each with their own funny description, plus coins, merit badges, journals, eggs, claw machine prizes, fossils, gems, weird video games, and even emails from your friends and little decorations for your camp which change based on which character you're playing. 

if you're like me and you love games where you scan or collect stuff just to read the fun descriptions, a la Katamari's amazing collection all narrated by the King, this might just be the game for you. i found it to be a great and cheerful diversion from the harshness of our current time, and i really did adore every second of it and fall in love with all the weird creatures and fun characters all over the island.

plus, here's the thing: it's only 6 bucks! if you end up getting bored before maxing out your collection, that's fine, isn't it? it's cheap, so you can just play it for as long as it's fun and then put it down until you feel like it again. that's the kind of laidback game it is. don't let yourself get frustrated just because it takes some time to track down every last little thing-- just relax, explore and enjoy the island with its great music, fun graphics and awesome writing.

willy elektrix has never disappointed me thus far and this is no exception. for something with a little more game to it, why not try ALIEN SQUATTER or even the totally-free VOID PYRAMID or RAMBLE PLANET? give it a chance! there's so much life and character and sheer uniqueness in these games, i don't know how you could resist its charms.

If you have a Steam Deck, you're gonna love cozying up with XOO: XENO XAFARI. This sweet, offbeat, 2D collectothon was BORN to be played on a Deck!

I got XOO: XENO XAFARI because I am a big fan of A. Hagen's previous RPG-with-combat game VOID PYRAMID (which I described as: If the DOS game "PHAROAH'S TOMB" had a baby with the French indie RPG "OFF!" and then made game developer Porpentine the godmother and sent it off to be raised with her,) and RAMBLE PLANET, a sort of puzzle-exploration game where you were hunting for pieces of your ship.

Both games had phenomenally evocative writing that brought their simple, stylized sprites and alien worlds to life. XOO is no different! Gameplaywise, it more closely resembles RAMBLE PLANET (which I never finished but enjoyed my time with) in that there's no combat and a colorful map to explore. But where RAMBLE PLANET had a pretty severe aesthetic that was hard to "read", XOO has vibrant color-coded zones, flora, and fauna that strangely put me in the mind of Pokemon; very cheerful...but a little twisted at times (lots of vampiric creatures and creatures described as being able to kill you or overtly hostile...but only in their descriptions).

The gameplay loop is simple: wake up, go rambling, pick up eggs, look at xenos, talk to robots, and explore the map. These activities fill up your different notebooks. When you run out of energy, you wake up again at the last campsite you built. Little surprises have been sprinkled in but so far, I haven't detected any sort of a hidden mechanic. 

You get a little bit of story from letters from home (which I guess vary depending on your starting character) and notes sprinkled throughout. But otherwise, it's just a really relaxing, fun play. The descriptions of things are often chuckleworthy--I find myself reading them outloud to my spouse and getting a chuckle in response!--and build this fantastic world in the back of your head.

It's perfect for playing on the sofa. About the only thing I can't comment on is the music, since I'm usually playing it on mute while something else is on, but it's still fun and engaging. Well worth your money.

It's interesting to see that this and Elasto Mania (its sequel) only had a discount in mid-2023 the last time. But boy these are classics that are worth playing! Elasto Mania has a lot of new features (hence the Remastered name) but this one comes in its pure version with Dosbox emulator in the works.

Many of us played these two in secondary school that we began in 2001. We exchanged chat messages on floppy disks where we used an xls file to message one another. 2 years later we finally got to know the world wide web and joined the gaming community of this game via IRC and of course on their respective websites. Lots of opportunities to play various cups and also to meet foreigners and learn English by chatting with them.

The game is a Hungarian product but the biggest playerbase is found in Finland and if you check the official website (Moposite) the forums are still active. It's fun seeing someone actively posting using my old nick in English (that I ditched for a Finnish name for a couple of years). 

It's a shame that the Hungarian community went downhill (pun intended) in a couple of years: less activity from players, unnecessary competitive attitude between members within the same team and way too much interest in Counter Strike. We were part of clans and I had a classmate bragging about founding the very first (not only in our country but in the gaming scene) that we joined very soon after starting to play these games. Too bad the emphasis was on the concept of "the more the merrier" which meant that after a while people started quitting (we did have most members but without any real added value). The founder did not have much to say and went on to becoming a university dropout later and wasting a lot of time with Dota.

I kept on playing. We had something called OYC (One Year Cup) and that is where my career ended with Elasto Mania. I think I ended up 10th. This was without a team, without any help and without replays that went around between the best players. It felt good receiving a compliment from one of the top players at the time in my country who invested time into checking out who else ended up on the list.

But back to Action Supercross. The original one released in 1997. You launch it, you collect the apples and you touch the flower to complete the level. And you do this 42 times. Then you come back and redo everything faster, better. Physics are interesting especially when you keep holding the directional key in the air. Pressing both keys used for rotation gave us the supervolt. This meant that the bike rotated faster and while it was a bug this was actually used to make completion of a level easier (faster). If you managed to press both keys at the same time exactly the amount of times you needed to (without holding them) you did an alovolt. 

You can play around in the level editor if you want and download some external files to play on. Do try this one and if you like it you can move on to Elasto Mania but a word of warning: the game can get you hooked easily!

In short, veteran players will likely greatly enjoy the challenges of the platforming in Lumione.

Edit for clarity: This game is nothing like Ori or Hollow Knight besides the aesthetic. It is not a metroidvania. It is completely linear. The challenges are completely platforming-based. The gameplay is much more akin to Celeste, but the level design is very unique and more difficult than most of Celeste, C-Sides included.

In-depth review below:

Lumione is a very challenging puzzle-focused platforming game. You play as Glimmer, a Fairy of the deep sea. Quickly you are introduced to your main mechanic: A short flight, recovering whenever you touch ground or a bubble. The controls are somewhat floaty, and momentum felt very weird to me at first, but as the difficulty ramped up I started finding that the floaty controls and momentum allowed for very interesting design and challenges in each screen. 

What do I mean when I say challenging?
Lumione will introduce a new mechanic, give you a screen or two to make sure you understand what it's doing, then it throws down the gauntlet. Screens quickly turn into daunting series of jumps with no breaks or safety until you reach the next screen, and it's all-or-nothing. There are only a few individually precise jumps, but it's stringing them together with consistency that provides the difficulty in this game.

What do I mean when I say puzzle-focused?
At first, the levels are very straight forward. You fly from the start of the screen to the end of the screen by hopping on a few platforms. Towards the end of Chapter 1 you will likely trial a few different paths before you get the correct route to the end, and as you get deeper, levels become just as difficult to "solve" the path as it is to execute the platforming--and there have been many screens that I am certain I solved the hard way because I couldn't figure out a better path. There is a lot of room for multiple unique solutions in each room, and it's up to the player to find--and execute--these solutions.

This all said, there are certainly some flaws. The controls took a bit of time to feel intuitive, and sometimes I'm still not sure about the momentum. Overall, I feel the game could have had a balancing pass of forgiveness for the player--dying while clinging to the wall because the spikes on top of the platform stuck out too much, or a laser just barely clipping my cute little horn when I feel like it shouldn't count.

If you're a bit new to platforming games, this might be a bit daunting, but with enough patience anyone can chase the light. For experienced players, this game won't wait before putting you into some tough spots, and the level design really starts to shine by Chapter 2 and on. I highly recommend this to anyone that can be patient with the fact that they will probably die a lot on the same screens.

Firstly, there are lot of comparisons to games like Ori and Celeste in these review. This game has a hand painted artstyle and is a 2-D platformer, but it isn't a copy. It explores unique themes and had some pretty neat movement that is distinct from them.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game, though it was frustrating at times. For those who have played other precision platformers, you will likely also enjoy this game. For those that saw the graphics and music, this is game is very difficult. I would put it bordering the "almost unfair" difficult category, which is the root cause of frustration. According to steam achievements, the game has a 7% completion rate at time of review. For what its worth. I think this is because of the difficulty.

The soundtrack is phenomenal, and the graphics are beautiful. Each of the zones is distinct in their appearance. In terms of "art", this game is 10/10.

Gameplay wise, the central movement mechanic is the ability to "fly". This is an omnidirection controlled dash, whereas a game like Celeste as a single directional dash that has no in air control, Lumione leverages the ability to move without gravity for a short time. I really enjoyed this play and thought it was unique from other platformers I've played. Additionally, every chapter has a set of unique platforming mechanics, introduced one at a time then combined together towards the end. However, there are usually 1 or 2 simpler screens before the game absolutely lays down the gauntlet with challenging screen one after another. I'd say it could use a more gradual increase in difficulty. I also found the first chapter to be much more difficult.

Often times, the same screen is used once the next ability is achieved and it leaves you marvel at the level design put in, especially noticable in chapter 3. I thought every one of these mechanics was used in pretty cool ways, most of which are pretty unique to the game with exception of the last one which clearly takes inspiration from Celeste. The level design alone makes many screen a puzzle to be solved in addition to requiring precision movements, which added to my enjoyment.

In terms of the afforementioned frustrations: Due to the nature of the fly ability and hand painted graphics (instead of hard pixelated), much of the controls feel extremely floaty. This is fine, but it can sometimes be difficult to tell where certain hazards begin and end. The devs put an insance effort into making the hitboxes actually align with the painted geometry and its actually detrimental in some cases. Spikes stick out ever so slightly and it will make some jumps that seen very doable nearly impossible. 

There is a point in chapter 3 that requires timing movement to particles that are shot at you. This was really well handled by having them only starting shooting once you start moving. A similar strategy was NOT implemented for some moving bits early in the game, and it absolutely should have been.
The hitboxes were my main concern, and it was easy to push past them, but for new players to this genre it might ruin your experience.

The dialogue is good, but you can tell that much of it was translated. It seemed way to formal for the English I am used to in most games. Not a big deal, barely noticable, but it made some of the quotes interesting.

One final note was some weirdness with momentum and in-air speed. It seemed that on my DualShock4 that you moved faster in the air with the D-Pad as oppose to analogue stick. I'm not sure if its a weird bug or my controller, but it made some jumps WAY more precise than they should have been. Just an fyi.

For those with potential disabilities or even just poor reaction times, there is no assist mode in this game (as there is with Celeste). I think this could be a very good addition to the game, especially considering the topics in the story. Everyone has their own mountain to climb, difficulty is going to different for everyone.

Final thoughts: Lumione is a great platformer with great art style, music, and level design. There were some hitbox issues, but those could be easily solved and didn't prevent me from finishing the game. Would recommend to fans of this genre, but would warn new players that this game is quite difficult, probably on par with Celeste B and C sides and Farewell.

I'll be speedrunning this game for SGDQ 2022, and after over 120 hours with it I feel like it deserves a thumbs up.   But with a little asterisk.*

* is because the criticisms that I'm reading in the negative reviews are largely valid.  For a precision platformer, this game has made some odd choices.  In particular players will likely find frustration in the lovingly handcrafted, artisanal hitboxes.  What does that mean in practical terms?  It means that the cool organic-looking wall that has a 92 degree incline probably has a matching 92 degree hitbox.  It means that the little divot in the ledge that makes it look worn and natural is also a spot where Glimmer will slide off that ledge and die in a pit of spikes.  It has the same energy of the old 2D Worms games where a bunch of explosions generates bizarre terrain, and you have to deal with there being 3 pixels that you just can't stand on but they are nonetheless still there interacting with the physics engine.  See that tiny gap between hand-drawn spikes? Yep you can probably stand there.

On your first playthrough this property of the game won't be anywhere near as big of a deal as the *intentional* difficulty that the game has, particularly in the later chapters.

On subsequent playthroughs, chasing after speedrun achievements and whatnot, you might get agitated as you realize that sometimes you just slide off walls and die in a way that seems completely random and inconsistent.  A lot of people rightly call this out as a crappy or unfair feeling experience.

But way beyond that, with even more experience and replay, this game really starts to shine again.  You start understanding what specific sets of pixels should be avoided, you get enough mastery over Glimmer to make extremely precise movements, and you really unlock potential for some high-skill-ceiling gameplay.  This game is chocked full of tricks that are only achievable through extremely precise movement and attention to detail.  A lot of the rooms seem like they have been designed to have incredibly fluid routes through them, but only if you can execute near-perfectly.  I can't say if this level of depth is intentional or not, but I can say for certain that it is there, and incredibly rewarding to discover.

There are also plenty of things about this game that nearly everyone praises.  The art and music really are beautifully done.  But don't let the Ori aesthetic fool you, this game plays a lot more like (and intentionally borrows heavily from) Celeste.  Many sections of this game are probably harder than the C-sides, so don't pick this title up expecting to breeze through it.

I am certainly not saying that you have to push the game to world record tier competitiveness to get enjoyment out of it, but I do want to put it out there that *if* you choose to do so, you'll find that the depth and challenge only increase as the frustration and sense of unfairness decrease.

This game is labeled as "Precision Platformer", yet the precisions in the game are quite lacking. First of all, please standardize the hitbox of platforms and spikes. I know the aesthetic of round edges looks epic but there is a reason why platforms in platformers are blocky. For example in the first chapter, there are serveral corners where you cannot ledge yourself onto for a wall jump despite the wall appears straight.

Secondly there are uneven walls in many precision sections. I don't know if this is intended or for aesthetic as the surfaces of the wall that is indented will mess with your wall jump and grab, especially in a timed section.

The decision of making the character floaty with HUGE inertia, and jump that last longer if you press the button longer isn't exactly my taste. The floatiness makes it harder to anticipate your landing location especially with moving platforms - and they are already hard to latch on because they are typically small with round corners and uneven surface. 

There is a very significant boost when you release the dash button when you are dashing upward, but only upward, and combining with the floaty character feels kind of counter precision. You can get used to it but it'll definitely take some time.

Despite that it is challenging and each rooms isn't as straight forward. I never feel boring playing it. For the price I would still recommend this.

This is a precision platforming game, without the precision. 

1. The wall graphics often have tiny imperfections and bumps.  The developers thought it would be cool to model this into the game's physics, and as a result, your character will unpredictably stutter and slip when trying to execute precise jumps, making you fail to jump when you pressed the button.
2. Spike hitboxes are inconsistent. Sometimes they kill you because your toenail scraped against the side of them, and other times you can stand on the very edge of a spiky platform with the spikes sticking through you. I've even seen cases where I landed directly on the spikes, but was somehow able to jump straight off of them without dying.
3. You can fly into walls, glitch through them, get stuck inside, and die.
4. There will be laser beams that will be blocked by terrain, but the top of the terrain has no hitbox, so the laser beam passes right through what seems to be solid terrain.
5. There will often be walls and floors that are ever so slightly sloped, while the moving platforms will travel perfectly straight.  As a result, you'll be riding the platform, and get clipped by the tiniest tip of the spikes, and die, without having a clear frame of reference for where you're supposed to stand to avoid this. 

The music and graphics are absolutely beautiful, but hand-drawn art like this just does not work with precision platforming. It's too difficult to judge where the hitboxes are.

I played Celeste, both Ori´s and now Lumione on 100%, and I'm disappointed to report that Lumione falls short of expectations. Despite my dedication to mastering its challenges, the game presents significant hurdles that detract from the overall experience.

One of the most frustrating aspects of Lumione is the lack of control over the character, especially during crucial gameplay elements like being launched along pathways or executing dashes. Far too often, I found myself at the mercy of the game's mechanics, unable to steer my character effectively or regain control in time to avoid obstacles.

Adding to the frustration is the uneven design of the game's map. Rather than providing a consistent and predictable environment, Lumione's surfaces seem almost deliberately irregular. This inconsistency means that even when I executed what should have been a perfect jump or maneuver, I often found myself careening off in unintended directions due to the unpredictable terrain.

However, perhaps the most egregious issue plaguing Lumione is its hitbox design. The hitboxes, especially those of the spikes lining the walls, seem disproportionately large or small. This design flaw leads to countless unfair deaths, as I frequently found myself succumbing to spikes that I swear I should have narrowly avoided.

In conclusion, despite my initial enthusiasm and dedication to mastering Lumione, I cannot in good conscience recommend it to fellow gamers. The frustrating lack of control, combined with the uneven map design and unfair hitboxes, detracts significantly from the overall enjoyment of the game, making it an experience best avoided.

Grabbing the side of a platform with spikes on top would kill me or would kill me once the platform moved, even though visually I'm not touching the spikes. The distance traveled when jumping off of walls or using the dash often feel inconsistent.

All in all, the game is beautiful, I love the gameplay that it's trying to implement, and I probably will end up finishing the game. However, for a genre that demands precision from its players, I feel there's not enough precision in the game's execution. I can tell that the developers put a lot of love and care into this game and hope they will continue that love and care to improve upon a great foundation. A few patches to provide some extra polish would definitely flip my review to a "recommend".

2. The dash ability carries way more momentum when Glimmer finishes it going upward.  Because of this, certain dashes are pretty difficult to time.  I felt like I was fighting with this mechanic more than having fun with it.
3. Earlier in the game, it isn't obvious that certain paths lead to stars (the bonus collectibles in this game) and there is no way to go back for these if you pick the path that progresses you in the story.  As a completionist, this physically hurt me (not really, but I was pretty sad when I missed a couple of the stars because of this).

If Ori and Celeste are 10/10, then I'd rate Lumione 8/10.  It's a very solid and fun game with great level design, but unfortunately certain screens/puzzles/levels (whatever you want to call them) felt like chores due to my first two complaints. First thing to make clear: This game is nothing like Ori or Hollow Knight. If you're expecting a fish themed metroidvania, this isn't it.
Also at the time of this review, I have only played the first chapter. This will be based on my first impressions of the game. 

Lumione is a beautifully drawn side scrolling platformer that is painfully difficult. The game requires very precise movements and any misstep puts you back at the start of the room. Every movement matters and the game is unforgiving if you even so much as hesitate with your jumps. The type of platforming you'll be doing right off the bat feels like stuff you'd expect to see mid or late game. 

Spike hitboxes feel cheap sometimes and I found it incredibly frustrating that when I stumbled upon a split path, I couldn't go backwards to check the other room once I progressed onto the 'correct' path. 

You will die numerous times in each room and those who get frustrated easily should avoid this game. But those who enjoy brutal platforming challenges will probably really enjoy this one. It is a game that you should try the demo first, to see if this level of platforming is your cup of tea.

So would I recommend this game to the average gamer? No, I wouldn't. But to hardcore platforming fans? yes.

This game is difficult to the point of annoyance, which is saying something because I've played, beaten, and enjoyed difficult games before, like every single Dark Souls game. Those games have a sense of satisfaction when completing a challenge. This game does not - your reward for completing an intense challenge (at the very start of the game no less) is another equally difficult challenge, over and over again.
Spend your money elsewhere. This game is so incredibly slow. Graphics are pretty, storyline is ok, but gameplay is pretty bad. I really wanted to like it, but alas.

Precision platforming needs precision movement and collision detection. I really wanted to like Lumione. It's very pretty. The sound effects are good. The story would be fine but it seems a bit like it targets a younger audience - an audience that could not handle the platforming in this game. Granted, I didn't play past Chapter 1.

The last segment of Chapter 1 is what made me put down the game. In this room I experienced:
- Touching a downward-pointed spike and not dying
- Touching an upward-pointed spike and not dying
- Touching that same upward-pointed spike from the same angle and dying this time, only because the spike was part of an in-motion platform
- Not touching any spikes on the thin platform that falls and dying

The floaty controls can be forgiven being that it's underwater. But "fly" underwater is a bit odd, and is but a brief glimpse of precise control.

The ability to look ahead in some rooms is basically useless, since half the time you can't predict where the triggers are for falling platforms OR when a random laser beam will start slowly rotating into the level.

If you like replaying the same segment over and over, give it a shot. Otherwise, seek games like Celeste where the precision movement and collision are polished more than Lumione.

I love these +1/-1 solitaire games, and I'd never played one developed by DigiMight, so I wanted to get their take on the formula.

Overall, I think that they did a pretty good job. Although the abilities were simple and straightforward, they certainly aided in the completion of some of the more challenging levels. I also liked the tension created by the time pressure cards present on the tableau. If you remove too many other cards without removing the time pressure obstacles, a card will either be subtracted from your deck or added to the board, depending on the obstacle color. Blue obstacles remove a card from your deck, while orange ones add an additional one to the tableau. 

As always, there is room for improvement. Although the player can have up to two uses for each ability, the in-game display does not indicate how many uses you have remaining. Therefore, you'll sometimes be caught off guard (having only one use of an ability when you thought you had two), and may not be able to finish levels that you thought you had "in the bag."

There are also level obstacles that cannot be removed unless the player achieves a streak of perhaps four card removals. This isn't a bad idea in theory, but since the layouts are randomized, there are times when you just can't achieve the streak necessary with the cards available. You'll remove all the cards above the obstacles and then be forced to restart the level in hopes of a more favorable draw. This never feels good.

If you also enjoy this style of game and have played most of the more popular iterations on Steam, DigiMight isn't the worst developer you could check out next.

There's really something so important about the way a game makes you feel. In a week, I might look back at this game and poke a hole in one thing, and be disappointed in some other. But right now, having just finished the game, I truly feel like this was something uniquely special. It took just a little bit of time to really hook me in, but once it did, it didn't let me go. 

Games based around player choice or creativity sometimes end up feeling listless or shallow to me, sometimes sacrificing depth of character or an actual sense of agency to accomplish what they set out to do. But somehow for a game that stayed relatively linear, I always felt like my choices mattered and like my options weren't especially limited. Maybe that has something to do with expectations, I don't know exactly how to say where my head was at going in. But despite letting me make my own choices and mistakes, and doing my best to navigate a complicated socially-driven narrative, I pretty much always felt like I was making the right decision. In those occasional moments where I really wasn't sure if I was making the right decision, my mind was never in a place of trying to choose the right path to "win the game" like you might in other branching narratives. Instead it was reminiscent of making a hard decision in real life, something where you kind of know what might happen, but the difficulty is in living with what you choose. 

I would recommend this game to almost anyone. Even if it is a game with a number of different endings and thus a reasonable amount of replayability, I think it's also probably one where it's best to play once and put down, if just for a while, to let the story live inside you for a bit, to let yourself feel its full effect before diving back in to experience it again at its fullest.

This is a mixed review, but I'll recommend to boost the current rating a bit. I'll start with the positives...

+ Performance and fidelity seem a bit improved over DW9, though still far from ideal on my system. On the other hand, seems like they may have removed some things to achieve that.  Removed or reduced weather effects, smaller battles, something like that. It's hard to tell exactly.

+ Compared to 8E, I don't notice soldiers blinking in and out of existence nearly as much, so that's nice. Non-officer units also feel a little more active during the battles.

+ The castle sieges are pretty fun. Much more refined than the siege challenge from DW9. Fights with officers feel more difficult, too. The maps are surprisingly replayable. 

- I said surprisingly above because there is little variety in actual map layout. 9 doesn't really have 'level design'. You have a fort with four walls and a big field around it. That's what a castle looks like, and that's what pretty much every map feels like. Capture point layouts add variety, but the route between any two points is mostly a straight line. This wouldn't be a huge problem to me, except that...

- ...the castle sieges are the ONLY actual battle type, as far as I can tell. A kingdom invades another territory, fights a single battle at a castle, and either captures the territory immediately or doesn't, and that's the whole game. No invasion timers, no raids or quests, like in DW8E. This point seems unforgivable to me because DW9, the game this is based on, had outposts and random quests all over the place, and an entire world already made. They surely could've put some side quests in the open world, and used parts of the map as raid battles just by plopping down some capture points. 

- 9's open world is still there, but it's almost entirely unused. The game is mostly interacted with through menus, like the previous Empires game. You can still enter the world by going on a 'stroll', but the only thing to do there is talk to and recruit officers, which you can do much more efficiently from the map screen. Technically, you can ride your horse for five minutes to go have a five second conversation with that officer you want to talk to, but even someone who enjoys the open world like me isn't going to do that when there's nothing else to find out there except some random bandits and animals. And I don't mean the boss bandits from 9, I mean trash mobs. Just endless hordes of trash mobs as far as the eye can see [or as far as the game can render them, which isn't that far]. No moving armies, no merchants, nothing. Crossing the map to a new city, you'll find its doors closed and its streets empty of interaction, unless you count a few random dialogue NPCs left over from 9. 

- This one may be partially personal taste, but I still think 8 looks better. 9 can do large landscapes pretty well, but character models and interiors consistently look worse, imo. That's a much bigger problem in Empires, where you spend a lot of time in the menu staring at a single room and its characters with some very bland lighting and textures.

DW9 was an ambitious game that didn't do everything it was attempting well. 9 Empires seems like they either felt they needed to scale back a lot to make something functional (understandable, given the game's reception), or they just ignored 9 entirely and made a typical Empires game. But the game feels like less than its predecessor in either case. A lot less Empires content than 8E, and far less open world content than 9. The only time I can really recommend this game to myself is when I want some faster, more free-form battles than 9's sprawling, scripted quest chains. 

The frustrating thing is that it's not hard to see how they could add more variety. I assume they must've spent all of their dev time on the castle battles. Hell, I would pay money for a DLC that just added raids and some random go-here-and-kill-some-tigers quests. It'd be lazy content, but lazy content is fine in an Empires game, imo.

Touhou DollDraft is a Strategy and Resource Management game that pits you against three other players in a battle of dollified Touhou characters. DollDraft features a short Single Player mode, a Multiplayer room system, and a Doll gallery.

The game play is split into three parts: a doll buying phase, a placement phase, and an auto-chess phase. During the first two phases, you must use your currency wisely to buy a team and swipe other players’ dolls. In the auto-chess phase, your dolls duke it out in a battle of Power to ultimately inflict damage on the other players.

This game play loop is satisfying when all the information is available to the player. That being said, that is the beginning of Touhou DollDraft’s design issues. First and foremost, the tutorial is dramatically bare. It is too fast-paced, not presenting what the information means during game play. Notably, it neglects to explain terms that are present in many skills, such as mentioning “S Points” and “B Points,” but not explaining what these points are. What really exemplifies this issue is that you can sell your dolls, but the game never mentions this.

While it is normal for a Multiplayer game to have a bare Single Player mode, the Multiplayer requires four players to use the same room code, as opposed to random matching. This significantly hurts the viability of its multiplayer aspects, since it is quite a hassle finding three players of a niche fan game.

For what it is worth, the art is quite cute and the game play itself allows for creativity when creating your doll dream team. But the incredibly brief Single Player story and lacking Multiplayer options make Touhou DollDraft difficult to play when you want to.

It's an odd piece of gaming history that's worth playing if you like retro FPS games. The overall plot to the game is very interesting, as it's about an artifact from space that transforms an Area 51-type government base into a labyrinth infested with aliens. The goal is simple: kill all the aliens and move onto the next floor. And yet, oddly, without a guide onhand this game is virtually unplayable. The Bradygames guide is in black and white and very hard to read but basically necessary to finish the game because many of the secrets aren't optional.

At the higher levels this game is hard, unforgiving and requires serious patience. Fortunately, the lower levels of play let anyone jump in. "Corporal" difficulty is basically casual mode. Just kill a few aliens and move to the next floor. "Lietenant" is probably the best difficulty for most players. You have to kill 75% of the aliens on each floor to progress. "Captain" difficulty is much harder, as now you have to kill 100% of the aliens and there are a lot more of them. Plus, you have to find the map to see where all of the aliens are and it's quite often hidden far off in a random area of the level. "Major" difficulty is just insane. Now there are way more enemies and they take more damage and you still have to kill 100% of them with limited ammo. 

What makes this game worth playing is the quirky weirdness to it. It runs on the Wolfenstein 3D engine and looks pretty good for its time. The only issue with the combat is the fact that you can't strafe. You can drop mines to blow up enemies but they don't always follow you in a straight line so this can be really frustrating. You'll mostly be using guns against the various quirky creatures this game throws at you. You'll start out just fighting little eye drones but as the game progresses you'll encounter enemies that morph into furniture to disguise themselves and invisible enemies that require using an infrared visor to see them. There are also terminals that allow access to blue and red doors. What makes the game fun is not the run-and-gun FPS type of gameplay you find in games like Doom, but in the "what order should I proceed" sort of difficulty that's usually saved for adventure games. When you shoot your gun the enemies are alerted. This can help or hinder you, as they will now be chasing after you but you can now see them moving whereas they were invisible before. 

Unfortunately you REALLY need the Bradygames guide to finish this game- there are just so many hidden passages that unless you are willing to search the entire map clicking everywhere you will never beat this. Also once you reach stage 21 the game stops giving out regular ammo and you are forced to use the alien weapons which have very little ammo and constantly run out. If you don't find the secret ammo cache on level 21, the game more than likely cannot be finished. 

The Steam version is based on the CD version of the game, so once you reach level 30 (Which is Corridor 7) you face the "final" boss, Solrac. You weirdly fight him earlier in the game but the Bradygames guide claims he is the one guarding the portal to the alien world. He's basically a creepy skull with tentacles with his brains sticking out. Once you kill him you have the option to destroy the eye or go into the portal. No matter what you do the ending is the same, but there are ten extra levels and another final boss inside the portal. These levels are WAY easier since you don't have to kill all the enemies and can simply run to the exit on each stage.

[h1]The game doesn't escape the shortcomings of the genre[/h1]

Prostitution sims tend to be pretty uninspired and same-y, and this is no exception.

Same issue with having a female protagonist that you deliberately walk into moral hazards in order to corrupt her - which breaks ludonarrative synergy.

Same issue with the character having spontaneous amnesia the second an event ends - walking around as if they hadn't just been sexually assaulted.

Same issue with boring clichéd scenes - just a tickbox effort of content inclusion.

Same issue with reusing assets constantly - instantly destroying any narrative significance to what the player is doing.

[h1]The game is quite happy to race you through the JRPG combat[/h1]

JRPG combat is almost always a rubbish element of eroge - fantasy combat has nothing to do with sex, and when you've played one RPGMaker JRPG you've played them all.
Fortunately this game abstracts out the combat - so while you're roaming through the thoroughly boring and barren dungeons, you can defeat enemies just by walking into them (at the cost of some HP).

Boss-fights do actually trigger typical JRPG combat where you've got the usual attack, guard, spells, items menu driven bunkum.
They're pretty brief, a couple of them have a few gimmicks to keep it fresh.  They're fine, if boring and totally redundant.  They still feel like padding, but fortunately it's not padding that is too cumbersome.

[h1]The metagame is mainly resource management[/h1]

The game has a fundamental ticking-clock element (5 days until game over), which forces you to make trade-offs between your limited time; the gold you earn from doing quests and jobs; and your HP which depletes while doing various jobs as well as fighting monsters.

You can regain HP by resting - at the expense of time; or using potions - at the expense of gold.

So your playtime is spent rotating these resources trying to make net gains, whilst gaining the 50 victory points (towns people who will perform a ritual with you) needed not to lose automatically on the fifth day.

It's a tolerable game design, but not one I found particularly interesting.

[h1]The game has lots of varied minigames[/h1]

There's a Pac-Man style maze game; there's two quirky dungeon-crawl events; there's a bemani minigame; there's a quick-draw game; there's a puzzle or two.

They break the game up a bit, and add a degree of polish, but they're not particularly fun or worthwhile on their own, and don't really make the game seem any less superficial.
Worse still, there's a couple of movement based puzzles which - as always - suck because RPGMaker's movement and hit-detection is fundamentally weak and ill-suited to these things.

All of them are fair, they all work fine, aren't too taxing, but they didn't really do anything to tackle the game's core deficiencies.

[h1]The sex scenes are boring, unoriginal, repetitive, skippable, and disposable[/h1]

Don't get me wrong, the art's good, the main character's attractive enough, etc, etc.  But as is typical for the genre; the publisher; and to a lesser extent, the medium - it's all rather weak and bland stuff.

Probably the biggest problem is how it constantly reuses art-assets non-stop, making about two thirds of its content entirely redundant.  You can go to the recollection room at the end and see in the thumbnails "oh, it's identical pose with X random faceless NPC; now it's exactly the same scene even though it's happening with a completely different random faceless NPC".

Lazy, low-effort, low-value.

[u]For a game with such a fundamental focus on slavery, and constant sexual assault, it's very tame and low-stakes.  It leans into the "cutesy-oopsie" side of non-con tropes, which leads to some tonal issues.[/u]

It totally fails to make any meaningful use of the standard corruption tropes, so in that respect is very much inferior to competitors such as [i]Tina: Swordswoman of the Scarlet Prison[/i]

The closest thing it has to narrative routes is that you can advance various prostitution jobs through increasing levels of kinkiness as you progress - but as there's typically only 4 events per job, and they're all open-ended, it falls completely flat.
So you get an unsatisfying combination of "ground hog day" repetition of events while you're waiting to progress; and then spontaneous amnesia of what has happened the second you leave the job and move on to something else.

[h1]The game isn't substantially better than the alternatives[/h1]

The presentation is, as I said, slightly better than prostitution sims like [i]President Yukino[/i]; [i]Fallen ~Makina and the City of Ruins~[/i]; etc, etc  It's roughly comparable to [i]Treasure Hunter Claire[/i] - maybe a little tighter and more interesting.

But it isn't good enough to overcome the defects of the genre; it's not very good value for money; the content isn't particularly engaging; the sex scenes are bland.

If you love Prostitution Sims, then sure - this is another typical example, and it's way lighter in its non-con sensibility than most of the others (maybe with the exception of [i]THClaire[/i]).

But I'd recommend skipping it for most people.  [i]Tina[/i] establishes a tolerable minimum standard for the genre, and if you've played that, you don't really need to play any others.

So - let's get this out of the way, the game is damn near perfect. For an H-game it's long (roughly 22-26 hours), it has a good story with great characters. To my surprise (and great delight) none of the characters are trope-y and all five main girls are very distinct - both visually and from a personality standpoint. Your MC also has good development, and despite being a male H-game MC isn't really scummy to any degree. The UI is incredibly simple and doesn't require any work or exploration to understand or comfortably use. The leveling system is great, in that it actually requires a decent bit of strategy to build a decent character (at least until you're very high level). Speaking of level - don't be disappointed when you realize there is NO WAY you'll have everything you wanted at or before level 100, as you can buy skill points at the endgame for surprisingly cheap, AND the level cap is not 100. (I /think/ it's 999, but my highest character is 158, so I can't definitively say what the cap is.) The world is fully integrated - there is no overworld, so the maps are pretty and have had a lot of work put into them; the only downside is that you'll actually need to commit various routes to memory, but even if you can't the various warp points make travel pretty easy, overall. The BGM & SFX are truly excellent, and the CGs are among the best I've seen in an H-game; even on par with some of the top tier HVN CGs.

Which brings me to my first of three (albeit minor) complaints - with the amazing quality of the CGs and the fact that the characters are all distinct and quite likable; I wanted more. There are disappointingly few CGs of the 5 main girls (4-5 each, and not all are H), some also had some questionable cropping (ie - there was one of penetration, but the girl was only shown from the waist up); all were also pretty vanilla - there was a grand total of 1 anal scene. A little more variety would've been nice, but given the superb quality of the CGs I can forgive the shortcomings.

My second complaint is that you can't really expect to gear up every time you get to a new town as the gold comes in at a disappointing trickle. You can farm for the gold you'll need, but it is a slog to get through. Nevertheless, your stats increase at a generous enough pace that it isn't critical.

My third, and final, complaint is that obvious time was taken to develop the interpersonal relationships, with all of the main girls eventually falling for the MC - which is great, but barely gets addressed at the end. A scene or some text before the epilogue, of what happened to those characters and relations would have been greatly appreciated (though, to be fair, the info was strongly hinted at - I just prefer something a little more concrete).

Overall, (aside from those 3 minor drawbacks) this game is phenomenal; and I won't hesitate for a second to give it my hearty recommendation. The dev indicated that he/she has already begun work on another project - if it turns out half as good as this, I cannot wait.

Samurai Shodown is a rather unusual fighting game in several respects. Here we have a completely different fighting technique, which involves waiting for the right moment to strike.
