Strike Team Gladius is essentially Strike Team Hydra V2.0, or even V1.5 with some improvements. You gain allied units that are a bit more powerful, but also bigger and badder enemies that are even harder to kill. Some gaming mechanic changes and UI changes were added. All in all, STG presents a more coherent game that represents a minor evolution of the game engine and design that adds onto STH, but little else. 

STG is clearly derived from Strike Team Hydra, its predecessor, in that most of the menu screens are the same, or at least have recognizable counterparts in the game. However, there are many notable differences. 

STG is a hex-based turn-based tactical combat game where you can take a dozen different classes of soldiers (6 at a time) through a campaign (chained missions) against the invading Sethari. There is no elevation on the map, but fog of war is in full effect with weapons reaching most of visual distance. 

The ST series has a counter-fire mechanic where the unit being attacked can retaliate (counterfire) but is often limited in the number of counterfire available per turn. Otherwise, the game is similar to XCOM where you can take half-cover or full cover behind objects, you shoot, you shot some more, hit end turn when you used up all the action points on all assets you control. Then enemies does the same, repeat until one side has achieved victory condition. 

STG now has armored units on the map joining your fight, and AI units fighting by itself. Unfortunately, sometimes, the AI units behave like kamikazes even on mission where your objective is to make sure they don't die. For example, there was a mission where you are to protect \a downed pilot. Instead of sitting still waiting for rescue, the pilot is charging enemies... with just a pistol or carbine. ARGH! 

On the other hand, it is actually quite cool to see tanks, APCs, and even rocket artillery pummel enemies alongside your soldiers. Unfortunate, these AI doesn't understand "overrun" (physically run enemies over). 

Somehow, after playing a bit of of STH, the changes in the play mechanics and UI felt somewhat backwards. Basically, in STH, the larger UI has the elements larger and easier to read, like how many action points left. It's much harder to read with STG, where the UI elements are somehow much smaller even when both games are set to 1080p. 

Also, STH and STG have different AP mechanics. In STH, movement and actions use the same pool of action points. You can move a lot, or you can shoot a lot, or you can mix shooting and moving, but the more you shoot the less you move. But then, the whole game was about fighting onboard a cruiser boarded by the enemy with tight corridors and rooms. In STG, movement and actions are separate. You can move to the maximum distance, but still perform all the actions available to you. This requires a bit of tactical adjustment from STH, but necessary because in STG the maps are also more open with enemies may be coming from multiple directions. You  are planetside dodging burned out ruins, rocks, destroyed vehicles, and so on. Often, the mission ends when you've destroyed the enemy teleporter beaming in reinforcements. 

The skill tree is a little different and a lot of skills unlocked early, so you don't have to grind through initial missions with an extremely limited arsenal. Almost everyone have the first few skills unlocked, and some have up to 10. However, the color palette is a bit weird, and I have no idea why the swordsman is holding his two-handed sword like a bat at a baseball game... 

The game also made cover very effective. Units hiding behind full cover is 85% covered. Add some natural bonus and to hit drops to under 10%, which is extremely low. However, liberal use of grenades and other explosive ordnance will even the odds, at least at easier levels where grenades can kill instantly. 

Unfortunately, the AI pretty much relies on rush, and occasionally use a grenade. So it is up to you to don't get near enemies or terrain features that will go kaboom. 

The graphics are quite good, and character models are improved from STH. However, as mentioned before, UI seems to have taken a step or two backwards. Some UI scaling would have been nice. And a lot of character animation is way exaggerated. And the death animations are all pre-packaged instead of ragdoll. 

The economy is also a bit stingy on the easier levels, and doesn't improve much on the toughest levels... same as in STH. On easy, a typical mission is worth a few hundred credits, only enough for a lousy item. On the tougheest missions, you're looking at a few thousand credits, but some of the very best items are over 25000 credits. Also keep in mind you are outfitting at least 6 soliders, each of which has a DOZEN OR MORE pieces you can upgrade, with some strict class restrictions. At least when you trade the item back in you don't lose anything. 

All in all, when it comes to turn-based tactical combat, IMHO Silent Storm and XCOM (the Firaxis one) are still the best. Strike Team Gladius does somewhat scratch the itch with its own mechanics, but a tactical combat game with a somewhat clunky UI, brain dead AI, and no dynamic campaign in 2022 is aiming a bit low. Recommended, but with reservations.

Original Review:
Strike Team Gladius is a solid squad based strategy game by WaveLight games.  Your 6 squad members will fight aliens in a variety of outdoor environments, with a large variety of allies and enemies.  It is currently in early access and has some rough edges, but progress has been fast on sanding them down.  Definitely worth a buy if you are a squad based strategy fan!

Pros:
Lots of characters choices - there are 22 different characters (11 roles with male and female variants) to make your party of 6 from .  The skills of the male and female are very different, as are the base stats.
Fun inventory system - lots of inventory slots, and lots of loot provides a satisfying gearing up process.
Large variety of enemies - from alien dogs to infantry to huge monsters with poison breath, your squad will fight many different types of aliens.
Lot of allies - A variety of armored vehicles, turrets and infantry types will aid you in various missions.  You often take direct control of them in addition to your squad.
Solid core rules - The basic rules system is fun, though a bit under explained at the moment
Wide variety of skills - From smoke grenades to explosive ammo, there are lots and lots of skills with a big diversity of effects.

Cons:
Rough around the edges - this is an early access game, so somewhat to be expected.  The updates are regular, and have already smoothed a lot of problems, so hopefully by release the whole thing will be a polished experience
Really needs a tutorial - this is in the works according to the developer, but as noted above, the rules aren't obvious unless you go digging around in the help.  The rules aren't hard to follow, but they aren't explained enough yet, especially some of the subtleties
Uneven difficulty curve - again, this is something that has seen big improvements since launch, but certain levels are still extremely difficult unless you go back and replay some earlier missions to improve your levels and gear.  
Limited strategic layer - The strategic layer basically allows you to change your team and buy new equipment.  Not a problem for me since the tactical layer is so much fun, but if that is what makes these games fun to you, it might be for you.

So overall, I like the game a lot.  Definitely recommended, as long as you can stomach the typical issues of early access!

Overall, a very good tactics RPG.  It plays more like a tabletop game in some ways as it uses a counter attack system and a fixed number for movement and attacks rather than an action point system.  Once you get used to it, it makes for really fast gameplay.

Graphics: Decent enough and seem well optimized. Nothing ground breaking but not bad at all. Lots of nice particle effects, reflections and so on. Nice atmosphere in the desert levels. I haven’t seen any of the other areas yet.

Audio: Decent audio with nice music and ambient sounds (at least in desert levels). Sound effects have good punch while voices are okay, a few are a bit cheesy but not too off putting.

Gameplay: There’s surprising depth here and I haven’t explored it all yet. The game’s focus seems to be throwing a lot of different enemies at you from lots of directions and having you come up with ways to kill as many as possible. Catching a whole bunch of aliens in the radius of frag grenade or rocket launcher is really satisfying. I love that the alien corpses hang around for you as a visual reminder of the carnage at the end of a battle.  I’m still wrapping my head around a lot of the rules. Action points seem to change for no real reason during a units turn sometimes and I’m not sure if that’s intended or a bug.

If I could summarize, it feels like a mix between heroes of might and magic combat with loot and stats from a typical RPG and a bit of xcom thrown in. I’m looking forward to diving into this more and the developer seems really responsive on the community board.

This is a god game where you play as a Magical King that creates his own kingdom from the ground-up, starting from a small castle to an expansive empire. The map is procedurally generated and infinite, so the potential for conquest and expansion is the same. The meat of the game lies in its extensive management systems, with terrain, buildings and units all having their own unique capabilities that have to be synergized in such a way as to guarantee success and the happiness of your people. All of this can be altered by the King's magic to be optimized and there's an extensive in-game tutorial and hint system to properly explain the details. Once you get a handle on the economy, then it's time to start expansion via capturing enemy buildings, building outposts and castles. There's a handy system to coordinate your troops included that allows you to designate attack locations, patrol points or lead your men into battle. Otherwise AI is automated and will defend, gather and seek out new resources without the need for oversight. The game includes three difficulty levels, one for building, one for new players and the "Real" difficulty where you'll face deadly foes and can easily lose your King if you're not careful. For the price it's essentially robbery, so pick it up if you like complex management sims but don't necessarily care if they're graphically simple.

A number of reviewers have commented on the somewhat clunky graphics. I do agree with that (especially having played Talos Principle 2 immediately before playing this) but I can forgive that as this was created by a small team that can never compete with the larger developers, and game-play is way more important than any fancy graphics. And it's game-play that brings me on to the major failings of this game...

The game premise draws heavily from the likes of Talos and Portal, but these games start with gentle tutorial, usually starting with a cube and pressure-plate. This game however is straight in with at least 10 different game mechanisms, and little or no guidance; you just have to fathom it out for yourself. Also, some of the puzzles are really hard and repetitive. I was doing ok until I hit the time-portal mechanic. Then it got so hard that I got bored and just started auto-completing the puzzles.  

Looking at the percentage of players that gain each achievement, only around 25% actually complete the tutorial section. And only around 6% manage to get to the final set of puzzles. That's a terrible attrition rate, but I'm not surprised.

There was a bug in one of the early puzzles where a door wouldn't open. However, resetting and re-playing the puzzle opens the door. Not only was that frustrating, but it cast doubt in my mind about all the other puzzles I struggled with; did I get it wrong, or is it a bug? I encountered a few other bugs, but they didn't really affect game-play.

It's such a shame, because this is so nearly a decent game, but the learning curve needs shallowing-out, and some of the puzzles need to be made easier and/or less repetitive. I'd give this a score of 4/10 as I did actually enjoy a number of the puzzles.

The jist of the game is that you and 3 other sinners with dodgy haircuts are flung into various 20-25 minute missions where you must slog through waves of mutated degenerates like so much murderous fleshy sewage. You get guns and various sharp implements to help get the job done.

There are only a handful of mission types and tilesets which you play repeatedly to gain experience points to level up your gear, unlock perks, etc. Yes, it gets repetitive, however missions don't always play out the same way depending on your team composition, the tactics enemies decide to use, random elite enemy spawns, etc.

[h2][GAMEPLAY][/h2]
It's possible to enjoy the game entirely as a shooter or as a slasher by adjusting your character's build. Some of the 4 classes are more suited for certain things, but you can at least succeed in the "medium" and "hard" difficulties even with haphazard builds, with the hardest difficulty needing a more focused/optimized build.

I like how complex/nuanced the combat can be. Hitting enemies on exposed flesh does more damage than hitting armor; shooting tanks on their backs will make them explode; melee weapons have attack patterns you must learn to take advantage of, etc. Some melee attack animations are better for sweeping a mob with headshots while some are better for brutalizing a single target with a downward cleave, that kind of thing.

This game and the dev team take a lot of flak, and a lot of it is deserved, but for $40 it's a cool game. At this point it goes on sale regularly, so grab the deluxe bundle with bonus Aquilas (cosmetics currency) for around $20 when you can.

[h2][COSMETICS][/h2]
Speaking of cosmetics, this game has a lot of them, but a ton of them can only be bought in the cash shop. As a result most of the teams will look like the same 4 grungy misfits in rags, with an odd player here and there looking way cooler.

The cosmetics are decently priced, I can live with $4 helmets and $2 weapon charms. The problem is you have to buy Aquilas in bundles so you're dropping like $30 at a time (I think devs do this to cut down on transaction fees) and you usually have a small leftover balance you can't use unless you buy more Aquilas.

[h2][MODS][/h2]
The devs allow harmless client-side mods, and this is what kept me interested in the game. There are useful mods that do things like minimize the obnoxious parts of the game or improve readability, and some even allow you to customize your weapons and clothes to look like anything found in the game, including the cash shop items. Feel free to create the heretic-slaying waifu of your dreams.

Escape room games generally ask you to find some code, enter it into a device, and boom, a door opens or a cabinet unlocks through some hidden mechanism. The Room games are different in that, most of the time, the mechanism IS the puzzle. "If I turn this wheel it will make that ball push that cog upwards, which will connect to the moving cog and raise the mechanism. Then I can move this pin and lock the thing in place." And it works fantastically well, partly  because this is an 1800s world of carefully forged, lovingly crafted devices. Every single object in this game is a virtual work of art, and the textures feel real to the eye.
Room 1 focused on one large puzzle box, Room 2 jumped a bit between environments; both felt like practice and a warmup. In Room 3 the developers found their stride, with an expansive hub, multiple rooms and alternative endings. Room 4 just hits it out of the park! The environment is more focused, the various rooms are carefully interconnected; you can glimpse through well written journals and notes at a story of love and sacrifice that ties the thing together. You can make yourself tiny and go into toys, mechanisms, and dollhouse rooms, which feels a lot like being in the dioramas in the Chicago Art Institute (now THAT would be a neat theme for Room 5 or 6!!!)
One notable thing is that not a single puzzle felt unfair; every answer can be discovered with careful observation. I would strongly recommend to turn hints off at the beginning of the game (I think they should be off by default!) It is not a difficult game, but solving the puzzles always feels rewarding because the mechanisms are so cool!
It's a shorter game than Room 5 (it takes about 5 hours, maybe less), and the length feels just right, it doesn't try to stretch longer than needed; but I would recommend buying it as a bundle with the others when it's not at full price. One possible con is that the hardware requirements are higher than the previous; a desktop without a dedicated graphic card will probably lag and need to reduce the graphic quality. But it does look stunning and plays very smoothly. Highly recommended!

The game offers a wide range of tasks:
- Rod fishing
- Net fishing
- Trap fishing
- Line fishing
- Cooking
- Exploration
- Photo mode
- Cleaning up trash in the sea
- Tasks for the townfolk
- Providing townsfolk with their favourite dish
- Renovating the town
- Boss fights (more puzzles than fights, which I like)
Early on, the game gives you almost complete control over how you want to allot your time. Lots of tasks can be done in parallel, there's always something to do. - Farming
- Ranching
- Breeding
- Crafting
- Fighting
- Mining
- Decorating your house
- Romance
- Complex friendship

The game features unlimited inventory right off the bat, which is a blessing for a digital hoarder like me. Sadly, it lacks some QoL features on this front, but it's not egregious.

Time runs on a day / night cycle, but without seasonal mechanics. You can pass time faster by sitting on benches, reading in your nook, or sleeping. You can sleep anytime and wake up in the morning, in the afternoon, or at night. Sometimes, time is slowed to a crawl for story events. Cooking doesn't take up any time.

I experienced a couple of bugs, but I never lost any significant progress or had to use the emergency teleport. If your boat gets stuck, you can call an in-game tow service, and the save system is incredibly generous. You can save almost anywhere / anytime and the game autosaves after sleeping.

I can't say anything about mouse/keyboard, but playing with controller was perfectly fine.

You have a dog, and you can pet it.

The soundtrack is nice and never became grating or repetitive.

There is a co-op option, but I haven't tried it.

I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. It's definitely worth full price, I got ~40 hours out of it and haven't gotten 100% yet.

So, welcome back. If you're here you probably know about this game, if not, here's my attempt at being brief. cyberpunkdreams is a really neat and overwhelmingly fresh game that's flourished over the years of development.

I'm going to start this by saying I'm on the writing staff. So, yeah. I've been testing one version or another of this game off and on since 2016 through its alpha, beta, and now gamma. The testing I've done has been a lot longer than my working on things. So, understand. I know the flaws and where they are.

I've been able to get this much time (18623 as of the edit) out of the game: A) Because cyberpunkdreams is meant to be taken in over time, and B) Because there is a massive amount of content to dig through (and the game is continuing to grow). cyberpunkdreams is a text based game, so the quality of the gameplay is in its writing, the quantity of said writing, and the choices you can make throughout it. Be prepared to make choices. Lots of choices: about who you are, why you're here, and how you interact with the world. Who are you?

So, why are you here and what are you doing here? Well that's up to you, but most of us are here for a job. Whether that be an investigation or one last run in the core. You are for the most part a blank slate free to define yourself, having had your past scrubbed out of you to avoid being tracked and caught. There are always indications of who you once were, but that's a question for later. You're here to do a job and the path to doing that job is where the bulk of the content lies.

So, what do you do in Cinci? For awhile you'll be scrounging around, learning the city, and engaging in various schemes to establish yourself. Given time though you'll start to engage in more and more lucrative trades and businesses, get your hands on higher quality equipment, and find better sources of income to successfully establish yourself. Challenge gangs, bring war to the streets.

As the game is named, this is a cyberpunk game, and as the creator puts it: back to basics. cyberpunkdreams is a game about criminal activity, the punk aspect and how it relates to the cyber. The suffering and heights that come from that, living with the consequences of how you act and relating to your circumstance. You probably won't have much of that cyber stuff for awhile, but if you persist you can start getting your hands on the tech needed to start having an impact.

It's up to you how you establish yourself, and the choices you make along the way define who your character is as a person. There are easy ways to make quick cash, and there are hard ways to make alot. How do you treat other people and interact with them? Are you a nice guy, the bastard who goes around breaking limbs, or somewhere inbetween? Most of us are somewhere inbetween. Go straight vigilante some day. It's fun. He who makes a beast of himself gets rid of the pain of being a man.

Explore the world, learn about it, find stories within it. Meet its characters, build your resources, and develop an organisation of your own. Prepare for your mission, eventually you'll need to pick up the pieces and act on it. You need to make the right choices, and be ready at just the right time to make your impact.

And remember, there are characters. An important part of this game is the characters, their stories and how they react to your choices and behaviours. Build a crew but word to the wise, don't look to make all of them part of your crew, it will drive you crazy trying to cater to all of them in the long term.

Gameplay wise, well that's tough. This is a text based game built around choices, there are games resembling this but not of this level of complexity. Pick a storylet or branch, a card. Make a choice, see the impact and move forward. Fairly simple on the surface, but it's about building routines and growing as a character as you experience the writing.

World wise it's a well thought out depiction of the mid future, we're somewhere around the 2090s, and things feel like it. A combination of climate change, societal collapse, and wars have broken America. Without going into the state of the rest of the world. Corporations drove privatisation and have strode through what was once the territory of the government. Taking over where the local government has faltered. Corruption is rampant, and everything is for sale. Technology has advanced, the panopticon is nearing a reality, and hope is dim unless we start a fire.

So, about that cyber stuff. Technology is constantly moving forward, and the commodification of human advancement is a reality. Even basic knowledge and memory is mutable and implants are speeding this up with the development of spikes. This is particularly the subject of my content.

So, Implants Implants Implants. There are some and we've been promised more. The ability to upgrade the human body and the symbiotes you take in. More radical body mods and prosthesis. The ones that are there are worthwhile in my mind, though you'll need to be pretty established to start picking them up. Being bulletproof is always a worthwhile goal.

We're not at terminator levels yet, but that will happen for us if we want it and work for it. See you at the Harmont clinic.

Honestly, I think I will be chasing the TMS dragon the rest of my life. I long for the early days where I would wait outside the stall for a customer to leave so that I could flush for them. Sure, sometimes they'd clog it, but it added bits of variety throughout the routine. The climax of the game was when Jake (yeah, I named them) came in one day and I was trying to clean it up before he sat down, but I guess he didn't see me and came in anyway. It was an awkward moment, but apparently it bothered Jake so much that he froze in stasis for days just staring at the stall. The thing is... "Jake" was still coming in... but it was like he didn't see the other version... only I could. I devised a plan where I could "realign" the Jakes, and it worked! My life had purpose, and I was doing good things for people. I was managing a toilet, but I also felt like a bit of a spiritual leader for these people as well. 

At first, I thought upgrading the toilets would make my customers' experience better and my life easier, and while they are objectively better, it feels like something is missing. I feel like a pet who lost their owner, checking back in on the stalls hoping to flush or clean them, but that day never came. My days in TMS are unfulfilling now - I bought everything that the shop sells, and sure, I can eat beans and hire dancers to come over... but there is nothing on the line anymore. Yeah, I could downgrade it... but I end up just hiring a maid and plumber every day to take care of it. I don't even bother with the air freshener anymore, as the bathroom gets plenty of revenue from my EXTREMELY loyal customer base.

It just goes to show, that success does not equal happiness.

I was browsing the Steam store looking for my next game to play. Then there it was! A cat's head with an interesting blue tone to it. And me thinking cats are pretty cool bought it without hesitation. I actually didn't look too much into it, just a few screenshots and the words "murder, mystery, puzzles and cats". What followed was a fun little puzzle game with a "paw-some" story to back it up. 

[h1]Story[/h1] 
You play as Theo, a cute white cat, who is sleeping in the middle of the night dreaming. To then be suddenly awoken by a calamity in the house. Theo, being the curious cat he is, goes to investigate the noise only to find out that his owner has been murdered. Prompted by both the narrator and Theo's eagerness, the chase begins to track down the culprits but there is more to the plot than meets the eye.  

The plot is actually pretty interesting and I was not expecting to get this invested into the story. In my experience most of these types of games do not offer a coherent story. Usually they will just change up the visuals or areas to give the player a sense of movement or difference. Yet in Bright Paw each level transition makes sense and is justifiable in the world we are in, helping to piece together a story.  

[h1]Gameplay[/h1] 
Theo is tasked with traversing through various levels in a turn-based style system. Each level has a set grid layout and the player is given cards to guide Theo through the puzzle to reach the exit. These cards can range from a simple wait, to various movement patterns to more special cards and hovering over each card will give a preview of how it will play out.  

It sounds simple but it progressively gets more difficult as new mechanics are introduced that Theo has to avoid or utilise to make it to the end which can involve gaps, electricity, rogue robots, fire and lasers. This led to me constantly having to consider each action, as I didn't want to see the little cat get hurt. But the developers do not punish your failures, they have implemented a rewind button to quickly correct any mistake. 

Overall, I think the developers have done a good job at the difficulty curve. Sure, the early levels might have been a bit too easy but some of the later levels had me scratching my head for a while trying to figure it out. And these were the most fun! I would have loved to have seen more of these difficult levels throughout. Perhaps they could do some further updates with more levels or a "hard mode". 

I'll quickly note that there are also a lot of collectibles spread throughout each level which are occasionally highlighted. Clicking on these will give further explanation on the surrounding environment and character backgrounds while also unlocking different skins for Theo. 

[h1]Visuals/Sound Design[/h1] 
The visuals are done pretty well, there is plenty of variety to each level and a surprisingly high level of detail in each. The option to change the camera view is a nice touch, it was great to get a better idea of the level. 

The music done by Will Bedford is nice and definitely fitting for the game, it certainly helped to reinforce that investigative and puzzle solving mood. But I think he did an even better job in those more intense moments. Narrator, Sam Hughes, did a great job as well and explains what is happening through each level which helps to engage the player in the story and raise awareness to certain hazards. And, the emotions delivered throughout his performance was top notch.  

[h1]Conclusion[/h1] 
In conclusion, the team at Radical Forge have produced an enjoyable puzzle game with an engaging story. It will last you about 4-5 hours depending on if you rush, and there is little replayability unless you want to get all the collectibles. But I think for the price it is definitely worth it. I would recommend this to anyone who is wanting a casual puzzle game to occupy themselves over a few afternoons.

Having just started this game for the first time, I have to say I am incredibly impressed by everything I have experienced so far. 

The level of polish is incredible (Especially considering the size of the dev team), with amazing little animations and visual effects bringing characters and settings to life. The visuals are cohesive and immersive, with a great range of unique environments and assets being coupled with gorgeous lighting and colour which really pushes the individuality of each Act. Not to mention the music, which is mysterious and makes me want to keep pushing on. 

The core gameplay is simple, but I can see the complexity of the puzzles and mechanics increasing exponentially and I'm excited to see where it goes. Not to mention the use of a card system instead of a more traditional movement mechanic is inspired.
I also want to commend the inspection mechanic, which simply adds another layer that fleshes out each level.

I have to say though my favourite part of the game so far is the voice over. The writing is witty and the actors performance is great, not to mention how many lines have been written that many players may never hear. I already find myself standing still at the start of each level just to see if anything will be said (A moment near the start of the game had the voice over get increasingly agitated by the fact Theo wasn't moving, I loved that). This level of thought isn't necessary, they could have skimped and made life easier for themselves but they didn't, which is why it's inclusion elevates the game from "great for indie" to great full stop. 

Finally, I have to mention the extras. The clear effort that has gone into inclusion in Bright Paw is heart warming. A little addition that could mean a lot to a few is always worth it.  

I would love to say to say Bright Paw is greater than the sum of it's parts, but it's parts are all so great as is.

Bright Paw is so much more than what you initially expect. Lairchitect could be a really good 'dungeon master' game if the creature AI and balancing were better, but SokPop being SokPop only made a solid foundation and kicked it out the door before it was fully polished. It's not that I don't like it, I am just disappointed that a game with so many fun mechanics has so many silly problems, hence the replay value is not very high. The complexity is actually very good, there is a lot of synergy between different creatures and traps, not to mention that you can even redirect liquids, like pushing lava into the tunnels. Your creature AI can be a pain in the butt, your workers can get aggroed across a very long distance which constantly wastes time and resources. If they just reduced the worker's vision I think it would be a lot more tolerable. Same goes for a lot of soldiers, even though the 'rat' can attack anyone, it does not prioritize the closest enemy which would be common sense. 

On a positive note, I really like the way the game generates creatures by giving you a different unit based on the floor tile. For example, the ground gives you a rat, but if you have a wooden floor, it will give you a slime, or piranha if you had water over - also applies to higher creature tiers, giving even more choices. Each unit has its place, everything from a hard worker to a tough fighter and everything in between. The problems arise when you realize that gave is heavily biased toward playing traps, and in many cases, those can do some friendly fire, creating huge dead zones where you can't place creatures. The game does not do a good job explaining some of the mechanics and there is a lot of hidden information going on in the background. There are only 4 "story" missions which could be completed around 1 hour, but you can also play the endless mode which is more or less the same, not a lot of visual variety. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

+ interesting tile-based unit generation, different tiles give unique units
+ decent mechanical depth, lots of synergy and positioning play 
+ endless mode

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Creature AI problems[/u] - Workers get distracted too easily, their vision range needs to be reduced, or you can have some kind of command to switch the priority from mining to combat. I think that creatures like 'rats' should attack the closest target, even if they attack anyone. When prioritising which walls to mine, I wish the units would do them in order instead of RNG which is what it feels like right now, sometimes my workers leave the walls to go build a road that was placed later, or perhaps they should just finish whatever is closest to them. 

[u] Needs some custom challenges [/u] - even though I like the core gameplay, there is not enough variety in the random landscapes so I end up using the same strategy. If developers maybe made like 10 custom challenges, maybe a map covered mostly in water or lava, it could change how I play, or maybe force the player to play with some limitations, and give achievements for it. Additionally to the endless mode, you could have those preset maps by developers and player would have to adapt a new strategy to complete them. I already 100% completed the game, and I feel like I could drop more hours if only there was something else to grind.

[u] Balancing issues [/u] - you need a ton of traps to get far into the waves as the creatures do not scale that well, and having a ton of traps tends to create some negative synergy as most of the creatures also get hurt by traps (although there are a few exceptions). I wish the game had some kind of upgrade system for creatures just so you had a better progression and not just placing more traps. I know some monsters benefit from certain creatures and tiles, but it does not do anything when enemies have 20 times more health, so really you just placing like hundreds of traps that wipe everything in sight. I wish there were more immunities, I have to place electric traps near water to get far into the game, but then I don't get to play any water creatures. 

[u] Lack of information [/u] - I had to figure out a lot of things on my own as the game does not clearly explain stats and things that go on in the background. 

[b] Overall Thoughts: 6/10 [/b]

Functionally the game wants you to separate out a dungeon into "biomes"; here's the plant biome, here's the water biome, here's the lava biome, etc. It's kind of a neat concept and one seen in other games I quite like, like What Did I Do To Deserve This.

However, the strongest unit is a water biome unit, map generation makes three very straight paths directly to your crystal, and you can't really control where lava pops up until you can mine some obsidian, which requires lava and water interacting.

So the most viable strategy is actually to just flood the central chamber and fill it with frogs and crabs and let them obliterate every enemy that shows up, supplementing them with skeletons from the heroes you kill. Boring.

If you want a game in this vein, but with direct control over your units and a much more compelling way to design your dungeon, check out Wratch's Den.

I am very pleased with this game. It is really fun to play. [Edit:] In total I spent close to 6 hours with it. i did complete it with 100% of everything (except two achievements).

The controls of the car are near perfect (I am playing with controller). The controls are tight, fluid, intuitive and fair. I did never have to think about them, which is good. [Edit:] During all the 6 hours playing it there was never a problem with the controls. I would say one of the best I played in my 37 years of playing video games.

The animations of the car are surprisingly lively, it feels like a living thing. The graphics are nice, cute for a hardcore precision platformer. And the music does fit well. [Edit:] The graphics and music are good. Still, I personally would have used a more serious/ grunchy/ glitchy graphics style and maybe a bit "harder" music. That would have fit better the hard game, I personally think.

The length of each single track is perfect, not too long and not too short. Restarting close to the end does feel just a bit like a penalty, as it should be.

[All edited:] I played all 30 (I think) levels, and completed each with 100% (all 90 stars, all 93 bolts and 1865 nuts). Unfortunately the number of nuts collected is not shown on the overview map, so it is necessary to check a level again for remaining nuts. I did not collect the last two achievements, not sure if they are possible or what they actually mean.

[Complete edit:] In first plays I felt like the meta game was too light. But now after completing I must say it is absolutely ok for this type of game. Only thing I would add is showing number of nuts for each level on map.

I would compare this with Trials Rising, which I played very much. Rolling Adventure is overall easier, but much more relaxing. The controls feel better/ fairer than in Trials. Especially, Rolling Adventure allows to turn the car over without serious issues, which is nice.

[Edit:] It is hard. But I personally did not perceive it as super difficult. There were maybe three levels where I struggled. And one level which felt unfair, because the very tricky part was at end, and I had to repeat it multiple times. I think overall my car exploded/ felt down about 350 times (estimated based on time and 250 times killed achievement).

Even after completing it I can highly recommend the game if you like difficult, precision games. It is a very solid and very different precision platformer.

Had some fun with this game.  First off,  a lot of indie games out there are going for procedural generation, endless play, and for me that's not really appealing.  I don't have a lot of time to play games so I like to play a game, finish it, then move onto the next game.  In that respect, Guildmaster fits the bill.

This is a tactical strategy game.  The mechanics have some meat to them.  Characters have varying health, armor, evasion, energy, movement etcetera- and each weapon gives a different group of attacks which can have additional effects.  Effect like damage over time, energy drain, stun, forced movement etcetera.  You also have magical attacks, single target, AOE, or can give buffs or debuffs.  Some characters also have a special ability that only they have. You buy and sell gear in the guild.  You can't save in mission, there are checkpoints but they're lost if you close the program. But if you fail a mission, you can sell your unused gear for full price and outfit you heroes another way.  Items only decrease in gold value when used in a successful mission.  You also have leader-bought global spells and can get some general party buffs with enchantments. 

There are not a huge amount of missions. Didn't count them myself but I believe it's about 14 which I finished in about the same number of hours on hard difficulty. That doesn't sound like a lot, but for me it was fine.  The missions don't have a lot of scripting or special events until near the end, but each mission does feature a new enemy type.  Each hero also has post-mission dialogue that is unique to them and the mission. So it's a decent length game and there really isn't any padding.   

The dialogue and story is aimed at humour and a fair amount of the content is interacting with the characters and reading that dialogue. Similarly some re-playability would come from reading dialogue of other characters, though- tracking which ones you took to which missions would be hard in and of itself.  It's a fairly significant part of the content so, if it has no interest for you- that's a good chunk of content you're going to miss. 

Overall I had fun, it was challenging at times but not too stressful. The graphics are of another time, but it's a very small dev team so- that's up to personal preference.  The animation is fairly limited but there's a lot of it and each hero and enemy has their own artwork. 

I think for criticisms, I'd say the game could be more efficient with its content.  I'd prefer to see more dialogue in mission, like character barks, and less outside of it. Instead of unique dialogue to each mission, each character could have a dialogue tree that unlocks over time- so less conversations, but experiencing a greater percentage of the content.  The combat could be pushed a bit more, would have liked to see more support enemies (like ones that grant buffs), more special abilities, or enemies that required more specific approach. Also the game could use a little padding I think just to extend it a bit, not every mission needs a new enemy, but would also like to see a bit more scripting or special events in mission. AND would have also liked to have use more items, I found there were so many weapons I never bought because there's only four heroes and often I'm selling old gear to get new stuff so sometimes I would skip over entire tiers of weapons.

Overall, it's a bit of fun. Good length.  And also a decent foundation if the dev wants to add more content or build off the framework down the road.

I just completed Guildmaster: Gratuitous Subtitle on Normal after about nine hours of playtime.  I liked it, and I would recommend it if you want to scratch the turn-based tactics itch but can't abide grinding or don't have hundreds of hours to play through Disgaea or Agarest.

In this game, you are the head of a typical fantasy-RPG adventurer's guild.  People come to you with generic fantasy quests, and you hire out parties of your mercenaries in exchange for gold.  While you begin the game with a very small number of heroes, new people will join your ranks after almost every quest, and you will finish the game with over a dozen playable characters.  

Each character in your roster has slightly different stats and can accommodate different types of equipment loadouts.  There's melee fighters, alchemists, archers, and mages, and a few folks with hybrid builds.  About half of them have special abilities; one can throw poison knives, another can tank like a champ.  Since some characters are mandatory on certain quests, and since using a character will tire them out and knock them out of commission for the subsequent quest, you will have constantly rotating party as you play.

The game is about fourteen quests long or so, and each quest tends to take a little over a half hour to complete.  Combat is turn-based, and generally your objective is to navigate a corridor or a large open area to eliminate the enemies or reach a goal at the end of the stage.  In later stages, after a Big Bad is introduced, the objectives become more interesting.  The combat difficulty is balanced well, and there's a number of weapons, abilities, and status effects to play with.  There is no perma-death; a character who falls in combat is restored when the quest is completed.

In-between missions, you can wander your little guild, do a bit of shopping, and speak to your adventurers.  While the quests themselves are very RPG-standard, the guild hall is a madhouse that might well be located in the middle of Monty Python and the Holy Grail's Camelot.  Everyone has something new to say after every mission, and each dialogue reads like a vaudeville skit.  The humor is reminiscent of A Bard's Tale or West of Loathing, and is a lovely little thing to break up the game's questing.

The game's ending is great, as well.  The final mission is challenging yet very satisfying, and the closing sequence is worth the price of admission.  This is a solid title from a small developer worthy of your support, and you should totally buy it.

You'll quickly learn what the optimal strategies are to use to dispatch certain enemies. Picking the right characters/equipment becomes very important to completing each individual mission. The combat is a little more simplistic than something like X-Com, but still enjoyable and satisfying. If you are used to this type of game, you won't find it overly difficult. The missions are varied enough so you will still be challenged at times. Additional game modes added in a recent update also increase the playability of the game further. Overall, a bit thumbs up from me. If you are into turn-based, strategy combat games you will likely enjoy this. Incidentally, the developer of this game has a presence of Youtube/Twitch and is a worthwhile follow, pretty easy to find if you google jimmakesgames or jimplaysgames.

[b]Waterpark Simulator[/b] is a walking simulator that takes place in a waterpark.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Walk about and enjoy the scenery. There are a handful of waterslides to choose from. Once you reach the top of a slide, you have the option to ride them -- camera control is surrendered as a cutscene is played. The world is well populated by ladies (but they might as well be cardboard cut-outs!) They just lie around and [i]act creepy.[/i]

[h1]Story[/h1]
There is no story (and I'm not making one up!)

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The titlescreen is animated and thematic, but the low quality slide doesn't exactly advertise "quality". From "Settings", you may adjust audio, display and graphical preferences. The game is full of visible seams and floating models, no doubt an indication of the time spent on this title. The characters in this game are actually rather attractive. It's too bad the vast majority of them are copy/pasted into the world, locked into static poses (rendering them no better than fancy mannequins).

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Buy for the memes (actually, [b]don't buy this game[/b]). This game [b]isn't funny,[/b] and [b]it isn't fun.[/b] The interactivity this game provides is no better than watching POV movies -- actually, I'd say [i]it's worse.[/i] Niether allow you to control the camera, but at least YouTube wouldn't make you walk a virtual flight of stairs to click "replay". Unless you relish the prospect of watching statues and climbing stairs, save your dollar -- learn [i]origami[/i] or something. [b]Uninstalled.[/b]

Interesting little VN that falls horrifically short of it's mark.
It's trying very hard to be a short, sweet and to the point story with cute girls and a middle school kid's fantasy of being whisked away to a fantasy land, where life is carefree and girls are suddenly fighting over dibs on you. Why they're fighting over a dude who can't bother changing out of his T-shirt and jeans for a wedding with a princess, your guess is as good as mine.

I actually quite like this style of VN. Dumb protag ends up in a new world, girls all go after him, he goes on a few dates and picks who he liked the most. Dimension of Monster Girls is also on Steam and did that fairly well. Yeah, it was generic and silly compared to pretty much any serious novel, but it gave a barely passable story with some nice artwork that played to a niche.
Hanapon Princess tried and fell short. The characters look nice and I like their designs, they even have some basic animation for mouth movements and extremely limited voice acting. Nice little touches like that make all of the difference sometimes. The backgrounds are nicely drawn, evening injecting a self-serving promo for one of their other VNs as a poster in-game. 

After that it just seems as though they gave up with the rest of it and cut corners everywhere. From having the protag in the same outfit in all scenarios so they wouldn't have to draw another to having the room he's staying in the fantasy world be the exact same as the real world counterpart. Seriously, would it really be that much more effort to draw a minimalistic Japanese room or a simple formal outfit for the main character?
Even the length of time the game is set in seems so rushed; as though they were going to have a multiple-day or week long scenario and after writing the first day, called it quits. Apparently the marriage ceremony has to be tomorrow, but nobody mentioned anything about it until the day of. Not even a hint that it was happening from any of the characters. Not that it really matters, the whole thing reads like a rushed DeviantArt fanfic.
There's nothing wrong with a story taking place in only a day or an afternoon or an hour or a minute. But the shorter the story, the more every minute that passes in it has to count. Imagine rewriting the same story, however the deadline is revealed from the very beginning and each chapter of the story covers a couple hours. The less time you have to work with, the better you have to use it. As it is, this whole thing feels as though you've just finished the prologue as the end ceremony starts. You're thrust into a strange world with 4 beautiful girls and have to get hitched to one of them before you can even memorize their names.

I think the developer actually has a lot of potential. Effort was very clearly put into this, just in the wrong places. Before worrying about the tiny details, as nice as they are, make sure you have a working story. Even if it's generic and overdone, the tiny details will help carry that.

This was was slightly fun.  The game consists of the player getting 4 pre-made fighter heroes and is tasked to fight 1 battle on each level of the 100 floor tower.  The player can save the game after each battle with limited access to any gear upgrades.

At level 10 the player has to fight a boss monster and after that, the player is given the option to switch classes with no information about what each class can do.

At level 11, the player is given a access to NPCs that are selling new weapons and armors to choose from but the player cannot afford anything and the battles are getting longer and longer.  After each battle the player is forced to buy consumable items to heal because no class has any healing magic which is frustrating.

There is no way to grind or repeat any battle in order to get stronger for the next battle as the game is designed with 1 fight per floor, this feels bad.  I only got to about level 13 or so before I gave up.  The monsters you fight at each floor may be pre-determined, but the monsters randomly hit too hard, they can hit multiple times, and multiple heroes per attack while the player can only hit one enemy at a time and has very limited access to supplies.  Magic is not available enough and the one class that can cast spells runs out of MP after a couple spells, and is required to buy supplies to refill MP, and the player need to choose between healing items of MP items.

With the player having to sell what ever small loot that drops from the last level's monsters for a little gold just to turn around and spend that on healing items just to be able to fight the next level is very frustrating and begins to loose its charm very quickly.

The fights are not balanced, and there needs to be a way for the players to build up their characters to fight the next level in the dungeon.  In the current state the game is not fun to play after a certain point.

First of all, it is the first game I've played that features both realistic graphics and a good system for irregular buildings. At least the villagers' homes and the farm fields and roads you are allowed to shape them by yourself by setting out the four corners of the plot. Because the fences and borders align to roads and other buildings, this is the best game I've played in terms of giving you medieval villages that actually look fairly lifelike instead of some square grid suburb where the houses happen to have thatched roofs. The music is highly fitting and it definitely adds a new level of realism that you actually see the villagers using oxen to drag logs and carry planks over their shoulders when building something, and resources often have to be worked in several steps. (E.g most games would go grain -> bread in a single step, Manor Lords goes grain -> flour -> bread, and to make shoes it goes hides -> leather -> shoes, and so on). 

The game is still noticeably in early access, but is being actively worked on. It is always a difficult balancing act for devs to choose between launching new features to show what they have in store for players in the future, and fixing bugs and smoothing out existing systems. The game has been mostly solo developed by a guy named Greg for many years, but is getting more and more help to see this through from his publisher Hooded Horse, which has seen many of my favorite games through to the finishing line. The scope of the devs ambitions is huge though, and he may well have to scale them back in the future. 

It feels unfair to criticize a game in EA, but it does have some quirks you should be aware of. It is NOT an action-packed game focused around military conquest. It is more of a satisfying kind of organic development over time where you meet the needs of the village as it grows. As is, you only get a handful of development points to unlock new technologies, and each village has it's own technology tree with no shared knowledge between them. This is partially by design, as the goal is to have several cooperating villages in your barony rather than one totally self-sufficient megacity, and the resources on the map will totally change your strategy. However, it feels pretty silly that your tame sheep don't breed at all unless you unlock that technology (I am fairly certain the sheep know how to do that without having it explained to them), but the sheep aren't that expensive to buy so unlocking that technology would be a huge waste. I guess I'm stuck buying new asexual sheep when I need to expand the flock? 

My main contention so far is the trade system, but I expect it will be fixed. Trade prices are static and heavily slanted to your disadvantage. The export prices of pretty much everything is very low, and if you lack some crucial resource the import price is truly punishing and most of your total wealth will be spent importing that thing. Whereas in a real economy (both historic and current) it would be possible to earn money by importing a raw material and refining it into something more valuable, as Manor Lords currently works, this is impossible as even the most valuable exports sell for 6-12 gold while even the cheapest raw materials cost 10-12, e.g importing raw iron ore and exporting finished swords would land you at a considerable loss. (Protip: just reroll the map until you have one with good flax fertility because otherwise all you do is try to earn enough money to buy enough flax, of which you need loads, the harvests are very poor and the import prices are outrageous).

I played the game when it came out and decided to give it another go once it'd gained more subtance. Alas, a year later, that extra substance isn't quite there yet. 
There are many many things this game does well, from the graphics to the gridless urbanism, but at this stage, it still mostly feels like a demo, with too many things alluded to but still not there... Judging by the progress over the first year, it might take a while to get the kind of city described in the main illustration.
Gameplay-wise, It also takes forever to get anything done, so a lot of your time will be spent looking at your lone cow dragging a single log at a time out of the 8 needed from one side of the map to the other. Time acceleration ought to alleviate this but alas, doing so might get in the way of the mandatory micromanagement of every single of your individual working villagers. Get distracted and miss the critical window for harvest and sowing, and your settlement will be toast. I'm yet to find any trace of the "complex economic and social simulations" referred to in the synopsis, but I can still roleplay hide & seek with my villagers to find out where they are vs. where they ought to be.
Some current game decisions also seem odd, like farming in a medieval society being apparently a 3 months a year job for a minority of the population, with hunting-gathering almost more efficient, or churches devoid of any clergy...
Still, that game deserves to succeed, and I'll probably check it again in a year. In the meantime, if you're on the fence, there might be games more deserving of your time and money, like the excellent Urbek.

Granted, some people don't mind having to read everything to understand the complexities of the game, but others like me will find it unintuitive due to how many moving parts there are to keep track of. Often I found myself hunting down supplementary resources to understand the game, which I normally consider as a con -- this game being no exception. I feel like if I have to go to watch a video to understand how to get a certain resource because it is reliant on managing your oxen, there is a problem there. 

The game also feels unfinished although granted, it is. I am intrigued to see where the game will go, and make no mistake I did enjoy it. I just don't think it is recommendable at this stage of development and I think there are a few bits and bobs missing for me to consider it complete.

I tried my best to enjoy this game and just couldn't. There is so much missing from the game, it makes it nearly unplayable. It's not even worth it on discount, in my opinion because it's not early access, it's simply unfinished. The UI is horrible, skill-tree branches unfinished, a lacking trade system, a town expansion system that makes no sense (can't use population from your other towns), instructions are lacking, the gameplay mechanics are almost purposely unclear, and to top it off, there's absolutely information, graphs, or other essential information provided regarding what you're producing and how much you're consuming to determine if you're meeting the needs of your town. How is this missing in a production management game? 

It's almost as if they designed the game to be purposely confusing and lacking information so they can pad your game time of mostly spending it trying to figure out how the game works or why something isn't working like you thought it would. If it actually worked and there is information to be found and discovered this would be okay. But I kept find myself thinking I'd find it or figure it out eventually, only to be later realize the feature I was expecting just didn't exist at all. 

A house with a home garden makes food. Cool. How much? Who knows!? It doesn't tell you, it just makes food, okay? Low on food and need more? Build a farm or garden. How big or how small? It doesn't tell you. A bigger plot makes more food and little one makes less food. Will that be enough? You just have to wait and see. Yet, you have a specific number of food you need to keep track of and you're not supposed to let get too low. See the issue? You give the player a number of how much food they have, but your game lacks a tracking system to tell them how much food they're producing. 

There's absolutely no UI telling you how much food you're making, how many food processing buildings you have and how much they're producing, how much your town is consuming, etc. This makes it incredibly difficult to build your town and manage resources because it's literally all just guesswork. Information like this is essential for a production/city-building game, yet doesn't exist in this production/city-building game. 

Exactly how are materials transported and is it working properly? You don't know! Just trust the process bro. And when that process will guarantee to break at some point or be incredibly inefficient because there's no UI to assist you in this, you'll soon find out because you'll be out of that material or your building won't build efficiently and you'll have to guess why. 

This game is like an unopened brand-new PlayStation box on Christmas day. You open it up, the outside looks amazing and pretty you know it's going to be good. But as you dig deeper into the box, you discover that it's not actually a PlayStation in the box, but a Temu FunStation. You play it anyways, hoping, that just maybe, it will at least be half as decent. But the more you play it the more you realize it's just all for looks and can't actually perform on anything. 

If the dev could actually focus cleaning up the production-chain style part of the game and add the necessary UI that's required for a production-chain style game, finishing the tech tree, tweaking the trade system, and... you know what, I won't list it all. It's basically the whole game that's unfinished - not early access, but literally unfinished. it has the potential of being an amazing game. But in my opinion, it's not even close in it's state right now.

Neat game, ruined for me by "arbitrary limits," and "magical, eternal production" via points.)
The two biggest ways to remove dopamine rewards.
(The lazy way to increase difficulty.  The disappointing, cheat-mechanic instead of realism and reward for carefully-planned development.)

What do I mean by arbitrary limits?  Limits that are BS.  When devs can't figure out how to balance things.

Example: Dawn of Man - a game too easy, because flat, build-able land = winning easily.  
(So instead of balancing the game by introducing more calamities like early blizzards / crop failure; they just made 90% of land hilly un-buildable.)
That's all that restricts you.  Not your creativity, your skill - you run out of flat land.

Same with Manor Lords. Unfortunately.  You run out of points.

Don't get me wrong!  I was very enthusiastic to try it out. I love medieval times, loved medieval dynasty, loved similar games, I love city builders! I love total war!
I load up Manor Lords:  Slap in the face WTF time! 

"Winning = City Development Points."
Development points _should_ be powerful ways to specialize your towns. 

Reality:  Development points "unlock" basic, real-life stuff.  Yeah.
Reality: Stuff that happens normally, in real life, well, it's "disabled," and you must unlock it. 

Example: "The Sheep Point."
Does it _enhance_ sheep reproduction / survival? Is it like specializing in veterinary medicine and advanced, selective breeding?

Hell no, it just "enables sheep breeding." 
WHAT DO YOU MEAN IT ENABLES SHEEP TO BREED!?  They can't **** without it?

So - Manor Lords is the game where I need to invest precious points into teaching sheep on how to ****?

Really!?

Same with "orchards."  
Oh, you can't make orchards unless you "unlock" them.  
Yeah.  
All my peasants just can't figure out sticking apples in the ground to plant them from seeds, and picking fruit off trees later. Just toooooo advanced of a concept!  Nevermind that's been done since the Bronze Age. 
Better unlock it!

What about magic?  Oh yes, unlock "deep mining" and all of a sudden, mines can last forever.  Eternal ore production. Magic! 
For a game supposed to be specializing in realism.  What the heck? 
Deep mining tech was very limited in medieval times, and not even as good as in Roman times. 

What a cheap, cheaty, non-rewarding "win button."
Since this only applies to "rich" nodes, looks like all I must do for eternal production is conquer the lands next door that have "rich" deposits too, until I have eternal production of all goods.
(God I've fall asleep already.)   No challenge.  

Just follow the cookie-cutter "First make building A, then a bunch of building B, then a bunch of building C, until you have X population, then make buildings D...get enough money for soldiers, and take the next region. Doesn't matter how you design the town, really, just lather, rinse, repeat!)

What's pushing me to conqueror new lands?
The "non-rich" (aka non-eternal) nodes are going to deplete really fast.
Nevermind that some quarries used by ancient Romans are still in use today.   They truly can produce stone / iron for thousands of years. 
Oh, but - you'll run out of stone in 4 winters, and have to trade for more, or go get an eternal stone mine next door...

Arbitrary limits, and arbitrary abundance, that doesn't make sense.

Why does this not give me much hope for enjoying the gameplay in the future? Even if "bugs" are fixed?
These points - are just poor design.

It's just not a good sign when fake barriers to normal, real life things are put in place for "challenge."

If one thing is changed, I'll return to and probably enjoy the game very much:
So this is my feedback - 

Remove the arbitrary, fake barriers.  

City Dev points should enhance specialization, not gatekeep it.

Want challenge?  There's all sorts of things one can introduce, take your pick!
Introduce more interesting problems that can occur (specific to this era!)

Like:

Betrayal / crime.  Disloyal citizens bribed to open the gates for enemies.  You'll need a secret police to find traitors.
New natural disasters.  Crimes like arson, peasant revolts, riots.  Not just people "leaving."

Introduce the black death, cattle plague, (scramble to switch from oxen to draft horse plowing after 90% cattle loss in a single year!) blights and famines, religious zealots, cults, witch hunts, breakaway religions and crusades.  
(Wouldn't it be cool to invade your neighbor because they're still pagan? Or be the defender of the last pagan kingdom ala Lithuania? Could you build a kingdom that could withstand constant Teutonic Knight assaults?)
Now that's excitement!

Introduce different ethnicity like Jews, mass-migrations from other nations, ethnic / religious tensions and the like.
Ya know, the emergence of the Cathars.  The Inquisition.  Do you resist / support these trends / movements? What are your potential consequences / gains?
Crusaders need to march thru your land - they'll perhaps try to kill the Jews of your town, maybe they'll steal - but, if behaved, they'll also buy a lot of goods on the way to the Holy Land.  Do you take the risk and allow them in? 

This game pretends like only Christianity, and one branch of it, exists. 
In reality - places like Medieval Spain crammed Jews, Muslims, and Christians of all sorts of heretical faiths together - and they had to figure out how to get along.  True progressives like El Cid - worked with anybody. Others, utilized hatred / pograms.

As a leader - will you give into the calls for blood from the superstitious who blame the crop failure on witches?  Will you burn a few at the stake to appease a blood-thirsty crowd or will you spend influence points to talk them down, maybe open your own wallet to ease the famine / tension? Or will you  be forced to watch it happen when you were too foolish to store extra food, thus you have no recourse? Too many unhappy rioters, not enough soldiers to quell? Maybe you have to flee for a while in exile, and return, take back your land, but indebted to the lord or lady who helped you.

Muslims war refugees want to move into your town? That will cause some friction, but, their benefit - very fine, pure-blooded horses.  (Warhorse stable unique building?)
Your people tolerate a Muslim Quarter - but what happens when enough move in to want a mosque?  You can upgrade the stables, but risk ethnic violence.
The other towns around you - go Muslim.  They threaten you with war, unless you tear down your churches, or convert them to mosques.  What do you do?  
Stand for Tolerance of all faiths? 
Convert, or die? 
Evict your Muslims and stand for Christianity-only?  Hope Crusaders come help, or the Pope donates funds to you?  Deus Vult?

Path of Tolerance - could have the best rewards as it can be the most challenging. The most unique buildings, the most complications for keeping all happy.  Intolerance - easy, but limiting. 

Introduce - fear as a mechanic.  Public executions, Iron Maidens.  Right now approval / love is the only mechanic for order and growth.  What about peasant rights? A lord of old, could restrict people from moving away.  They'd still reproduce. Fear, can influence growth. 

These sorts of ideas  / true medieval challenges could be explored.  
For now, it's more like your people are robot workers, all of the same ethnicity, same religion, same personality - all happy with more access to goods, all unhappy if eating the same bland food per day. 

This over-simplification has no bearing in the tumultuous, exciting, politically-charged peak ethnic-tension world of medieval Europe.  
Automate farming already; (I really don't want to babysit every ox stable and "optimize" how fast fields gets plowed,) and get to the meat-and-potatoes of real conflicts, and conflicting agendas. 

( A world, by the way, in which sheep already know how to ****!)

At the time of this review I'm at 50 hours and I am impressed already. I haven't managed it yet but the game can already be completed from what I've seen. The gameplay for me has been pretty solid. I've only had 3 CTDs and since I started playing after update 4 I haven't encountered or already knew and avoided any bugs. The thing that stands out to me are the visuals. Everything is stunning. Greg has really put a lot of work into the attention to detail. The seasonal changes and weather effects are smooth. From snow cover to random small rain puddles. So far I have to say that fall is my favorite to just pause and look at up close. At one point I had zoomed in to a hunters camp to time something out and ended up just watching him work. I could see the deer running around through the forest in the background and leaves falling from the trees. The ability to go from full top down city builder to close enough to see the individual bees flying around the apiaries and even see the villagers moving around inside the buildings when the doors are opened. The clothing differs from person to person. The market stalls visually represent what is available at the time. I've played many full release games that don't even begin to go into this much depth.

I love the building system. To be able to turn off the snap to road feature and build a realistically meandering village and turn it on to create the transition into the orderly layout that would naturally evolve over time is a fantastic option. One of my favorite building features though is the plot layouts conforming to the alloted space. Even the orderly layouts look natural with their small deviations. You can get close with some effort and patience but there is no hard grid.

I do have two gripes though. The story takes place in old Germanic countryside but the people are all British. Not sure how that will be addressed but I do have faith that eventually we will see the dogs roaming around that I constantly hear barking in the background. Maybe occasionally chasing the chickens or following beside the hunters. Aside from that, this game is already great in it's current state and can only improve from here.

Altwaldheim is a simple menu-based city management game where you have to build up a town and defend it from invasions.  The game only has one screen, an image of your town which gets filled with new buildings as you construct them, similar to the town screens of the Heroes of Might and Magic games. Actions are performed by going into menus and choosing them from a list.

You can construct buildings, recruit soldiers, and assault dungeons. You can perform as many actions per turn as your resources allow you to, and when you end your turn you gain income based on your production. When a new turn begins, there's a chance to get an event where you have to make a decision.

The core gameplay is pretty simple, but it works very well. You have to balance your construction and recruitment budgets to make sure you have a solid economy, but also enough soldiers to survive the regular enemy assaults. Events often come with choices that improve your relations with one of the town's factions, while decreasing it with another. Tax income is tied to the happiness of the factions, so it's important to keep them all happy. Dungeons offer high rewards but can wipe out your army if you assault them with too low strength. Every decision matters, and surviving the final battle is extremely difficult.

While the gameplay is great, the writing is more of a hit-or-miss affair. It goes for a very silly brand of humor filled with absurd situations and silly characters. Moreover, it's very [i]German[/i]. As a native German speaker, I noticed some wordplay that is kinda cute in German but doesn't really work that well in English. There's one event where a guy with a speech impediment asks you a question, önd öll thö önswörs öre wröttön löke thös. A lot of the humor feels like it was intended to be written in German and then translated to English, and will probably feel a little weird to players who don't speak German.

Overall, it's a cool little indie game with good gameplay and [i]quirky[/i] writing that's worth checking out if you like simple but challenging city builders.

I love city builders and making units in general.  Game is very challenging I've played 17.5 hours a few days into purchasing and even though made it to final boss twice i still have not beat the game yet.  Addictive game play and replay value is high.

Key to starting is focus on 1. gold 2. food 3. wood.  i do not make any units until i'm attacked at the start.  when i am attacked I focus on making a few units ie 20 archers maybe 10 thugs 10 militia then attack the small camps ie peasant militia and archer camps.  make iron and stone mine and the remaining buidings.  pick one faction to focus on and maybe have a subfaction as 2nd ary.  for me i choose military and later capitalists.  but there are relion freethinkers and nature ie guardians.

Favoring one faction gives rewards ie more resources or more troops etc.  There are 2 super units ie darius and bertha who take some rng to get but are super super super good.  If you take specific dialogue options its possible to attack other dungeons ie like bandits other caves etc.  

For me the hard part is monk boss he is very challenging.  And will take several attempts to be able to defeat.  After that when you get access to faction headquarters you get access to each faction's 'elite" units which are very strong.  also get access to officers which have aura that increase damage 10 percent.  there are support units that specialize in killing monsters ie woodcutters/adventures.  archers that specialize in killing melee.  there is magic fire, light, anti mage, priests that heal.  there are regualar milita/sodiers and then special units like horsemen and mace/spear units berserker units.  and tons of other special units demons, skeletons, spiders, etc all that can join your party.  

do you take 1000g now and pay back 1200g later?  do you pay 1000g now and get 1500g later?  do you kill horses for food?  do you cut down the trees or replant them.  do you do a quick fix on mine or more of a permanent fix for a little more resources.  do you pay to get more economy more people into your town or hold onto those resouces to make more troops due to an immediate attack coming.

Game for me is well worth the 10 bucks and hope you guys give it a try.  there are idk 4 different ages i think each age has new dungeons new buildings and units to unlock.  getting to age 4 and getting the knights/mages/etc is where it really gets interesting for me.  so many different choices and options.

If you're a fan of the Friday the 13th movie franchise, like me, then you're probably looking at Emerald Lake and thinking about how similar it appears to be. The game is about an abandoned children's camp that's close to a lake, and it closed for mysterious, undisclosed reasons. You can see a guy wielding a machete in the screenshots, and the 'big bad' is a buff dude that wears a white mask. While it's true that the similarities are there, Emerald Lake is a far less enjoyable experience than what even the worst Friday the 13th movie ever had to offer. In fact, the game is a completely broken mess. You'd have more fun watching Jason Goes To Hell, you know, the WORST movie in the series (change my mind), than playing this disaster.

When checking out YouTube videos of the gameplay from July 2020, Emerald Lake appeared to be in a semi-playable state. Not the best, mind you, but progression was at least attainable. The player was able to pick up notes, keys, and go through the campaign until the constant crashing made them so mad they gave up. It seems as though the August 2020 update broke the game entirely, because none of that is possible now. It's impossible to get past the second level, as no matter what you do you cannot pick up a key to progress. Notes cannot be picked up, they just flap around and then fall back to where they were laying; so they're unreadable. Despite two attempts at "fixing" getting stuck on tables, in the five minutes I played I got stuck on a table twice; I did manage to wriggle free, though, so "fixed" it is I guess. The game also crashes when it tries to load the next level, but that's to be expected for an FPS Creator title.

Even if Emerald Lake does get lifted from its unplayable state, it's not a title worth wasting your time on. It's an excruciatingly typical no-budget Russian horror "game" that resorts to key-finding, puzzles that are solely door codes, and stealth sections with deaf and blind AI. It's truly disgusting that Valve keep allowing this kind of filth not only on to Steam, but let it stay despite reports and flags. Just another piece of kindle for the dumpster fire.
