[spoiler]This is my first proper review, I'd say, so I just picked this game to kinda practice the Steam review Formatting, if you know what I mean, so take this review as like a kid's essay on how they hate school or something [/spoiler]

Alright, let's dissect this one by one. 

[b][i]The game features:[/i][/b]
[list]
[*][b] Pixel art graphics [/b]
[/list] Yup, checks out so far

[list]
[*][b] 21 levels [/b]
[/list] Honestly couldn't keep tracking of how many levels were there because all them just looked the same but with a different colour palette and a few different blocks. Not that the amount of levels matters in the first place since you can't choose which ones to play.

[list]
[*][b] 14 Bosses [/b]
[/list]While technically not a lie, it's not entirely true either, you got your 7 normal bosses and then final mega-boss with 7 [b]PHASES[/b], but that doesn't make it into each individual boss, Mr. Developer, like, c'mon. Also, some of the bosses were so strange, I mean, the first boss you encounter, [spoiler]you literally do NOTHING, as in, you just don't shoot it? What kind of boss is that? Why would you finally give a player a gun and a "challenge", and then proceed to add a boss where you [i]don't[/i] shoot it to win, you only set the expectations low. [/spoiler]

[list]
[*][b] A few weapons [/b]
[/list]Okay, the weapons are actually quite cool and they all come with their pros and cons. Use a bazooka that deals a lot of damage, but you give up your movement, quite a nice idea and an alright execution. HOWEVER, and I'm so pissed about this, but you're NEVER told how you can access the weapons via Numbers (1, 2, 3 etc), not even a random scribble or text. So I literally went through hell of mundanely shooting small pellets with a default weapon, when I always had access to a freaking machine gun that does about 4 times more DPS.

[list]
[*][b] A lot of NPCs [/b]
[/list]There are, indeed, a lot of NPCs, but it's not like you're gonna care about any of them, not even a single one. They are hardly different from each other, which would've been fine if only they at least had names. So I was just reading random texts of dialogue, not knowing who everyone was, hell, I didn't even know who [i] [b] I [/b] [/i] was!!! The story was barely concise and you really had to piece everything by yourself without any hints at what exactly is going... I mean, you'd have to read the short bio of the game on Steam to even start understanding that it's about War World 1, why couldn't have this been explained in-game? Let alone that, you don't even know who are you playing as, is it supposed to be self-inserting?

[list]
[*][b] Unique rope mechanics [/b]
[/list]Unique they definitely are. Good? No, not really, but definitely unique. I don't even understand the purpose of the rope mechanic in the first place? Like, you don't get to secrets, even though there aren't any, you don't get to use it during bosses, not that it would be helpful. Then is it really important during the mundane story sequences? The parkour itself was abysmal enough, the rope just made it even worse.

[list]
[*][b] Meaningful music [/b]
[/list]Tell me in what fucking way is it meaningful. All I heard is literally two soundtracks during the game, one of which just felt like the sped version of the other. At some point it just became white noise, it is so empty and ear-piercing - YOU CAN'T EVEN TURN IT OFF BECAUSE THERE ARE NO SETTINGS! Unless I'm literally blind and the settings were only accessible with the fucking Number pad or something.


In addition, while the movement and jumping on and off ledges was a bit wonky, I could forgive it, but my god why would you add such atrocious recoil on the guns in boss sections where you have to actively move around. It would've been far better with no recoil or if the recoil actually served any purpose, like, using it to slightly propel yourself in the air, but you just get stuck in midair. 

So, uh, yeah, kind of a shit game, I honestly don't know what i expected from 79 cents that I wasted. Not just the money, but also the time. Though, a bit of a rant doesn't hurt every once in a while, right?

I think I like it. It's quite neat as a "sketchbook" to quickly check some ideas or just to have fun - without getting serious with a DAW. Couple of instruments and drum sets is good enough and whole operation quick and easy to set. As a lazy bassist, I do appreciate the guitar preview, which allows to transfer ideas faster. Nudge grid and scales options are also cool as a "randomizer" if you will. No Undo/Redo, but Save works and you can copy/paste notes if need be to recover. Some disappointment comes with an audio export however. No volume control makes drums typically too loud, thus sometimes clipped. Also bpm is not matching initial setting, checked in several software. So... export is probably usable to some degree - but with a lot of extra tinkering which lefts a question is it worth it. Drum machine alone is quite good. Would be neat to be able to add a second instrument (so set up a bass and drums and play midi with piano for example). Couple of extra options would really elevate this little app. Still - I don't think it aspire to be a DAW so I suppose for the money to possibilities/fun factor - I still quite like it. Good also for people starting in this area due to simplicity of use. Core purpose is yet to improve mainly on music theory principles, so keep that in mind. It's not really a "music making" software. I used it lately as a drum machine to jam on bass with it  - and I must say it is quite cool for that. Few drum styles and possibility to make it more complex (changing melody and beat pattern in time) is really handy for a solid jam session. What is it?  

I would describe Death: The Ascension as a card/puzzle life-choice simulator in which you aim to optimize your chances of a successful ascension by manipulating event probabilities.  It has a deck-building type of mechanic in which you add cards to your deck, but the deck is not a draw-deck.  Cards in your “deck” influence the chances of drawing cards into the player’s five card hand from an infinite pool.  In other words, if you have only one card in your "deck", you have a 100% chance of drawing five cards of that type.  You are playing cards against Death as your opponent.  Death has their own deck that has similar draw mechanics, but only draws one card per turn.  Each turn one card from each deck is played with four possible events dictated by the player’s card with varying probabilities for each event known ahead of time.  

Card Play Mechanics:

Unlike most deck builders, cards are not purchased with resources.  After each turn (contract), there is an outcome based on probabilities that the player can influence strategically.  The events are in two layers of hierarchy.  First probability is whether the outcome is a "success" or "fail".  "Success" outcomes then divide into "formidable" (best) or just "good" events.  "Fail" results divide into either "bad" or "terrible" events.  Therefore, each player card has four possible events that can be created from a single card.  How these probabilities are controlled is based on the quantity of the various resources accumulated at the time.  Each card's four possible results (events) are unique to that card and have thematic names that must be learned by the player because influencing these events is how the player controls his deck.  

After the contract with death is signed, the resulting outcome is shown as an event card on the table with its unique name.  Event cards are not added to your deck, but the player will be presented with three cards after the contract is burned from that event and must choose one to add to their deck.  These three cards are always the same whenever that particular event is created by any card.  Death's deck is also influenced by the events.  Death's deck mechanics must be observed and learned by the player as it is not shown to the player.  Death cards do have visible effects that are not based on the events which are shown on the face of the card.  These card effects can be countered only by finding the matching player cards that are color aligned to either cancel the effect for that turn only (blue) or to remove the card entirely from Death's deck (red).  This alignment information must be learned by observing how your hand and deck cards change color dynamically after a death card is played to the table.

Resources:

Souls are the key to the end game god gamble.  Souls are acquired by taking more of a chance at failure by incrementally lowering the baseline chances of success for each card play contract.  Choosing cards with the highest chance of success increase chances to successfully gamble for souls.

Gold, Love, Fame, Law, Hate, Time, and Souls can be used to 1.) Influence probabilities of player card events to bias them to your strategy 2.) Perform rituals to exchange card types from your deck directly to your hand, convert resources to other resource types, etc.  There is also a random quantity of resources unique to each game that must be used as final payment that Death demands as a prerequisite to an ascension attempt/gamble.

Blood is a unique resource gained by the ethical choices made every three turns when presented an encounter.  You can influence this even more by choosing from three different levels of corruption for your character.  More corruption will result in higher resource penalties, but more blood money and hate are the reward.  

Law is also a unique resource that is quantified in the game as a direct result from certain types of events.  Law represents the degree to which justice wants you behind bars.  You must make choices during an encounter with the law that can negatively impact your progress to accumulate resources.

Time is a resource that can be impacted positively or negatively by events by impacting the number of turns left in the game.

End Game:

The endgame is interesting and unique. I will not spoil too much, but it is designed to give replay value by having successively increasing win conditions and includes probability and gambling.  There is a mysterious puzzle aspect to the game where you may choose to answer questions posed by Death in order to take a “chance” at a higher level of ascension during the ultimate end game gamble.

Conclusion: 

First let me tell you why I like abstract card games with a theme.  They free up my brain’s limited bandwidth enough to allow my imagination to crunch on its own invented stories.  I can’t tell you how well the game play is balanced or fine-tuned from a skill vs. luck standpoint.  However, I found that each game length was just the right and challenged me to make careful choices and study the events necessary to manipulate them carefully.  This, in turn, led to a sense of my own story with ethical choices and corruption by my own hands.

I found the game very enjoyable from a thematic and creative card play perspective with interesting probability influencing ideas.  The artwork, color palette, and music are well done. The colors and art style are bold, moody, and eye-catching.  More polish would benefit the User Interface screens in a few areas, but I eventually learned how each worked. There is a lot of English translation issues throughout the game if that bothers you, but they reminded me that this game was developed by a single person’s efforts with a creative goal and vision for his game.

One question all TTD-Clones (and let's not pretend this is more than that) have to withstand is "does it offer more than the original?"
Here the answer is clearly no. Rockets don't add any gameplay- just a connection between different biomes.

What I would expect and what let me down:

- Updated graphics: It's a rather blunt copy of the original, but sprites, movements, tiles, buildings look wonky and out of place. No coherent artstyle. OpenTTD hasn't aged gracefully when it comes to it's graphics, but at least it's not a jarring mess.

-Quality of life and simple, intuitive UI: I gave up after a few minutes because I had to klick on the same buttons over and over again to perform simple tasks. Give me a key to close windows. The massive input lag doesn't help. 
Please check out Transport Fever 2. It's such a joy to set up routes, upgrade stations, exchange vehicles, move them to different routes etc.

-Economy and simulation: Yeah, what's up with that? 3 Houses generate enough passengers for a full blown train line? Seems like it took the already rudimentary economy simulation of TTD and made it worse.

In the end, IMHO it should not have entered EA in this state. Performance is weak and hinders gameplay, balancing is strange and artstyle is off. Having sprites with wrong perspective jank around is no fun to watch.

TL;DR: If you like the retro artstyle, play OpenTTD, if you enjoy Eye Candy, polished UI and a complex Economy, play Transport Fever 2. If you want to set up a bus line on the moon this is for you.

My suggestions to developers after my playthrough on version 1.01:
- Less aggressive popups in the tutorial please.  I was trying to build a train and the window popped up every minute or so after I closed it so I could focus on building, and the cycle repeated.
- The same tips appearing when I don't have capital to do research.  It seems every month I received a tip to do vehicle research, any time I wasn't researching.
- Keyboard shortcuts are a must IMO.  A key to cancel operations, switch to bulldoze mode, switch planets, etc.
- Early-game subsidises are sometimes impossible.  I won't have the money to subsidize helium 3 to earth, building the most basic rocket is 700k+ and you barely start the game with that much.
- With subsideys, please allow us to quick-view both the starting and ending locations; finding the ending location is a bit difficult between location A and location B.
- If you're going to stick to a moving-window mechanism, allow windows to "save state" and be minimized.  Opening and closing windows with the mouse became quickly tedious.  A better window-management system would be nice.
- Performance optimization when zoomed-out would be nice.  There is significant stutter when moving around with the WASD keys or right-click mouse.
- The "hill up" and "hill down" mechanism could be cleaner; it's difficult to tell what part is actually moving up or down.  Maybe a transparent overlay of the final product rather than arrows?  I many times accidentally raised or lowered the wrong thing since the arrow appears at the vertex, rather than the center.
- I wish I could, while they are in depots, share components, such as swapping out a train engine with the same cars.  If this can be done, I couldn't figure out how to do it.
- Not all windows update dynamically.  If I rename or recolor a line, I have to open and close the "Lines" window to find it updated, which is a hassle when trying to organize things.


Bugs I found in version 1.01:
- If you do "hill up" on an area and can't do it because of proximity to streets/rails, you are charged anyway and the "hill up" doesn't occur.
- Price mismatches on many items between the label price in the bottom bar and how much they cost when placed on the map.
- Sometimes my trains returned to the wrong depot; they would drive past the depot they were made on and went on to another line entirely.  I'm not sure why.
- I'm pretty sure if you *start* a rail or road on a spot already with the rail or road, it charges you the cost of that square that already has the rail and road on it.  If you start your rail/road one off, then it's cheaper by one square.
- It seems that some industries can be placed immensely far apart from their "home town".  For example, I couldn't find an "East Wylington Factory" for 10 minutes until I searched for it in the industries tab, and it was basically on the other side of the map.
- The drop-down for selecting a line will *sometimes* cut off the text of the line; I named my lines "Passenger Line X" and put them all the same color, so it wasn't possible to figure out which line I really meant and had to go through them all.
- If you name two lines exactly the same thing by mistake, then they strangely interact with each other; I sometimes saw buses assigned to the wrong one or to both of them, somehow.

Solar echoes is a game that was largely made by a single guy, and the end result is pretty impressive to say the least. 

Gameplay: Pretty standard for a visual novel. You read the story and at certain points you are presented with some choices to make, your choices actually do matter so you have to be careful with what you pick. Some choices will even result in a game over so choose wisely.

Story: The story is pretty straightforward. You are Trey Donovan a former military man who has been selected by the government to travel to various alien worlds with the goal of uniting all the alien races under one banner. In order to do this you have to bring back a delegate from each alien world to the peace conference and hopefully order will be restored in the galaxy. However whether or not you succeed is based on the choices that you make.

Characters: This where the game really shines. Watching the interactions between the characters and watching their relationships grow and develop over time is the most engaging part of the game. Of course how these relationships will develop will be based on the choices that you make. My favourite was Oasu by the way.

Graphics: The character sprites are really detailed and have a wider range of emotions to express how they are feeling. I will be honest some of the backgrounds did feel a little bland at times especially on the jungle planet, but it was pretty minor since it's the characters that are the most important part of the game. It would have also been nice to have some walking animations for the characters but due to the limitations of the game this is understandable and not a huge deal.

Music: I enjoyed the music of the game. It has that classic sci fi feel to it, the same that you get when watching some of those old sci fi shows on tv. So yeah it fits the game nicely.

All in all a pretty solid game overall and it's very impressive since it was mostly a one man show. As far as visual novels go, this one is pretty good and is definitely worth your time. I give it a solid

8/10.

Could this be the best visual novel of 2022? I think there's a strong possibility, even though it is only February!

There's really a lot to love here in terms of the story, characters, world-building, writing, and even animations. In fact, this is one of the most "animated" visual novels I've ever played! You can tell the developers put a lot of effort into the various cut-scenes, character movements, action scenes, and other elements that make the whole experience feel dynamic and alive. They didn't have to do it, but they did, and I commend them for that! ^_^

You can tell the writers know a lot about science and astronomy as some of the conversations and lore feel very well thought-out and researched. I feel like this is the kind of game you need to have a PhD for to properly appreciate all of the scientific details and lingo. Again, the devs didn't have to go this far, but they did and it shows just how much passion there was in this project. I am very impressed with that!

Overall, I will give this game a score of 8 out of 10, and you might be wondering how come it's not 10 out of 10? Well, there are two big downsides in the otherwise stellar experience, in my opinion:

[olist]
    [*]The game NEEDS more save slots. This game has many choices, big and small, that are fun to explore and try out, but having only 5 save slots makes that task virtually impossible and unwise.
    [*]I really wish the alien characters were romanceable, at least some of them should be, I believe. I think that would add more drama, storytelling possibilities, and will just let the player get to know them better. It just seems like a big missed opportunity not to do it in a story like this, you know?
[/olist]

In fact, if the devs add a Kitheya romance route, I will personally buy 10 extra copies of The Star Legation and gift them to all my friends and whomever comments on this review!
[b]YES, I AM VERY SERIOUS ABOUT THIS![/b]

Other than that, I have a list of small nitpicks that I think the devs could look at and perhaps address them better in the game's dialogue and world-building,

[list]
    [*]The Interstellar Union is not a mouthful of a name, so why do all the characters insist on shortening it to ISU all the time? It feels a bit unnatural to me.
    [*]I find it hard to believe that the space-faring humans would use Fahrenheit and the imperial system instead of the metric and Celsius. Maybe if there was a better explanation as to why that's the case, I would buy it, but the game acts as if humans just always use those, even though in our world only about 5% of the planet utilizes those measurement systems instead of metric and Celsius, which are objectively better.
    [*]How come Trey is only 27? I mean, he was in the military for years, then spent years managing a dangerous prison colony, and was even chosen to be the Humanity's representative for the Interstellar Union. I mean, sure, it could be just me feeling inadequate as I have turned 28 today and haven't accomplished even an iota of that, but I mean, he even LOOKS older! I assumed he was in his 30s just based on his appearance.
    [*]I think it's a bit of a shame we didn't get to see the Krissethi homeworld more aside from that throne room. I mean, yeah, we saw some other planet of theirs, but it wasn't their homeworld.
    [*]I like Akanutoka, but it feels like his addition was some kind of DLC of sorts as he doesn't appear on the game's title screen and there isn't really a way to get to know him or his people better. Was he perhaps a part of a plotline I missed? 
[/list]

[i]Flowstone Saga[/i] is a unique mashup of ideas: Storytelling, relationship building, and character progression (levels, skills, equipment, classes (kind of)) of traditional RPGs, Tetris-inspired battles with some interesting nuance, puzzle solving that can be thought provoking but also never requires a huge commitment, and even some limited town building / decorating are all present here. It’s an ambitious mix that largely succeeds, though some elements stumble due to design choices and technical issues.

[h3]What I Liked[/h3]

[b]Concept: [/b] This particular concoction of features isn’t something you see everyday, and it’s certainly not something I ever thought I would really care for. But I am glad it is a thing even if it can sometimes feel like it’s not fully realized.

There are many small but impactful additions to the traditional Tetris formula that make battles both engaging but also occasionally frustrating (more on that later). The option to flip from active to turn-based battles is also welcome, though the latter makes everything significantly easier. This, along with multiple difficulty settings, does however make [i]Flowstone Saga[/i] more approachable.

[b]Familiar Faces: [/b] As a huge fan of Impact’s previous work, Tangledeep, it’s nice to see Mirai and company make a return. I’m not entirely certain whether [i]Flowstone Saga[/i] is a direct sequel or a spinoff, but it feels kind of in between somewhere. Either way, you absolutely don’t have to play Tangledeep to enjoy this game, though some references will fly over your head. But seriously…go play Tangledeep, too.

[b]Presentation: [/b] Hearkening back to “good ‘ole times” with its SNES-era inspiration, [i]Flowstone Saga[/i] is both a visual and tonal delight. While I don’t find it as appealing as the studio’s previous work, it’s nonetheless solid across the board.

[b]Fishing: [/b] Any time a fishing mini-game is designed to not be brain-dead simple, you have both my heart and wallet. Timing and random button sequences have to be executed to ultimately snag a fish, but the rewards can be well worth it on top of just being a nice change of pace from the core gameplay. 

[h3]What I Disliked[/h3]

[b]Fit and Finish: [/b] Despite its strengths, [i]Flowstone Saga[/i] feels like it needed one last round of polish before release. Issues vary in severity, and fortunately most are but minor annoyances. There are a few spelling/grammatical mistakes through the script, fishing can occasionally have visual bugs, the main menu can become obscured by an overlay which requires a reboot to restore, and bluetooth audio seems to mess up when you try to connect after the game has been in suspension. 


More concerning are the hardlocks, of which happened several times and interestingly have always been during boss fights. Auto-saves and the ability to save anywhere help remedy this, but it’s nonetheless a bandaid to the actual problem. To be fair, these all were experienced on Steam Deck and may not apply to other platforms, but it’s still worth mentioning.

[b]Pacing and Balance: [/b] Storytelling comes in bursts, with long stretches of little plot development followed by dense info dumps. The ending also feels abrupt, making the overall pacing uneven.The story and characters have their moments, but it’s not an overly compelling tale and the odd pacing just doesn’t really do it any favors. It ultimately leaves you wishing that it was more spread out, or some bits even cut altogether…which isn’t ideal for a story-driven experience.

Similarly, there are pacing issues to combat, with some normal encounters feeling like endurance tests while boss fights can be surprisingly easy and short. This inconsistency in challenge and pacing may stem from how certain enemy mechanics are designed rather than player skill, such as the damage reduction ability that certain enemies have which requires additional setup (thus time) to properly counter.. As a result, there’s never a consistent “happy medium” feeling between challenge and the length of encounters.

[b]NPCs: [/b] While the core visuals are solid, NPCs mainly remain static, which makes towns feel lifeless. Most have really nice idle animations but that’s unfortunately about it - there’s really no pathing or movement by most NPCs, and that would have added much-needed vibrancy to the experience. 

[h3]Consider Buying This If…[/h3]

You’re looking for a genuine spin on the typical retro-inspired RPG formula, want to ease yourself into the RPG fray through genre-unique concepts, or you just like Tetris/Match-3/block-breaking games. If you enjoy RPGs with unique mechanics and don’t mind some rough edges - on Steam Deck anyway - [i]Flowstone Saga[/i] is certainly worth a look.

[h3]Overall Opinion: GOOD[/h3]

A couple things I've noticed that could be improved, right off of the bat:
1. The game has a tendency to freeze for 2-5 seconds pretty regularly (inputs still work, so you end up 10 yards away from where you were headed). Fixing that would be great!
2. There is a sneak mechanic and a backstab mechanic, but it's not very well developed. Enemies pick you up almost immediately, even at the edge of your field of view (which is pretty small). There's no way to speed up your "creep walk" so you're guy is very slowly walking towards enemies that turn around quickly and insta-aggro. And there's no "tall grass" mechanic, so successfully sneaking past or sneaking up to get a critical strike is pretty much non-existent, IMO.
3. I like the ability to parry, block, and dodge. I also like that phatrolling due to heavy equipment load does come with a benefit. Parry timing is difficult, but it should be, so that tracks. My only beef is that rolling has no detectable iframes, so you can be hit while rolling. I think that makes the dodge mechanic closer to POE than a soulsborne or soulslike.
4. While the game does have a decent amount of RNG during enchanting (which randomly upgrades a regular item to blue or purple with no way I can see to determine which one you get when you enchant) and item drops, it would be nice to see some way to increase your chances of getting the stats you want other than farming weapons and gemming/enchanting until you get the RNGGods to smile upon you. That or putting higher tier gems/enchants with stable stat increases (less of this +3-25 damage, depending on how lucky you are today). I'm not a fan of those mechanics, they don't really drive engagement and I'd rather grind out a good gem from a quest or boss drop or combine mats to increase an enchant that gives +10 dmg flat instead of collecting 25 items and rolling for luck on whether I get +3 or +25 (which usually ends with selling all 25 items cause you got bad rolls).
5. With the amount of items that drop in game, it would be cool if you could dismantle for some mats (leather, iron bars, etc) instead of just vendor trashing everything.
6. Item usage is a little clunky and I found it hard to use anything other than the quick item during a fight. Most games fix that by letting you "scroll" or equip 3 or more items that you can scroll through instead of a button-hold menu that requires you to re-slot the quick item w/o the benefit of slowing time. This forces you to select the item while the real world goes on in real time, slot it, and then use it; which in an action game where timing your rolls and parries is everything, means you're getting hit while trying to find your stamina potion.
7. On to the Potions and items that increase your stamina, focus, poise, etc. They're very short lived, and due to 6 above, I did not find it worth the effort to try to use any more than one item at a time via quickslot. So recovering your focus and then switching the quickslot to use a weapon oil became enough of a hassle that I just accepted a "one item rule" during gameplay.

It's early access, so nothing in the above is out of the range of a fix if the devs want to. The game is still fun and I enjoy the animation style, layout of the areas, and the feel of movement and combat.
Area resets are nice and the enemies seem to level up with you, so going back to an earlier area doesn't mean facerolling all of the enemies (although you can definitely tell you're much tougher in the beginning zone).
Attacks feel heavy and committed once you press the key, dodging at low and mid weight is responsive, and the stats will make sense immediately if you're accustomed to any game in the soulsborne genre.
Upgrades are nice, there's plenty of drops and chests, lots of resources and even daily and weekly quests for money and items.

I also enjoy the ability to upgrade slots via boss fights or weekly quests so you can unlock more storage space, additional main and off-hand weapon slots, ring slots, and tool slots (pickaxes, shovels, etc).

I like the story and the ability to upgrade vendors/do some rebuilding of the main hub. That's a fun mechanic with actual benefits and positive changes to the town that you can see.

JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: All-Star Battle R stands as a resplendent testament to the grandeur of Hirohiko Araki’s enduring legacy, transmuting the boundless eccentricity, flamboyance, and narrative ingenuity of the original work into a most exhilarating interactive experience.

At first glance, one is immediately enraptured by the sheer fidelity with which the game encapsulates Araki’s inimitable artistry. The cel-shaded visuals are nothing short of a triumph, rendering each character with meticulous precision, their every pose and motion imbued with the unmistakable dynamism of JoJo’s celebrated aesthetic. The animation, fluid and masterfully executed, captures the very essence of the source material, ensuring that every battle unfolds with the theatrical flourish befitting a saga as illustrious as this.

Yet, All-Star Battle R is not merely an exercise in visual fidelity; beneath its dazzling veneer lies a combat system of commendable depth and refinement. Striking a delicate equilibrium between accessibility and complexity, the mechanics accommodate both neophytes and seasoned combatants alike. Each character, plucked from the expansive pantheon of JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure, is rendered with remarkable authenticity, their abilities mirroring, with painstaking accuracy, the idiosyncratic powers that have long captivated audiences. Whether one commands the spectral might of a Stand, the mystic potency of Hamon, or the esoteric craft of the Spin, every skirmish brims with strategic nuance and exhilarating unpredictability.

The game’s reverence for its source material extends beyond its mechanics and aesthetics, for each confrontation evokes the indelible spirit of JoJo’s legendary battles. Signature techniques erupt onto the battlefield with cinematic grandeur, unleashing an unrelenting spectacle of bombast and bravado. The auditory design, too, is a triumph, with each resounding ORA ORA and MUDA MUDA reverberating with an intensity that only serves to heighten the immersive splendor of the experience.

If the title falters, it does so only in its online infrastructure, which, while functional, lacks the seamless polish that might elevate competitive encounters to their fullest potential. Yet even this shortcoming is rendered inconsequential by the sheer joy derived from executing a masterfully timed Stand Rush or a climactic Heart Heat Attack, each maneuver resonating with an electrifying satisfaction that transcends mere gameplay.

For both ardent disciples of JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure and connoisseurs of the fighting genre, All-Star Battle R is nothing less than an imperative acquisition. It is a reverent paean to Araki’s opus, a kaleidoscopic fusion of art and combat, and a title that demands to be experienced in all its ostentatious glory.

Final Appraisal: A Magnificent and Essential Experience for Any Devotee of JoJo’s Spectacular Mythos.

I'm someone who likes the idea of keeping lots of fish but does not like the idea in practice. This game perfectly scratches the itch for that. It's all the fun parts of fish keeping, and none of the bad parts--or at least, it's fairly easy to avoid the bad parts so long as you take care of your fish and plants (which is easy to do). It promotes good fish keeping practices and feels realistic but not so realistic that certain tasks feel like a chore. I really like where the game is at currently and am looking forward to the future planned features.

It's very satisfying to try to figure out how to organize plants and junk in a scene to optimize growth, but I found it was also lenient enough with how successful you have to be to finish a scene that you can afford deciding to do stuff that will look good over maximizing utility often enough that it feels you have agency over how the end result actually looks.

I pre-αlpha tested the original and for my work I was rewarded with a level editor (after suggestion they added it to the final build)  that enables me to make my own levels; unfortunately, the editor wasn't made public.

Anyway, I was really pleased to see the  remastered version of the game; thought I was expecting to see the same levels in an enhanced form.  Instead I was met with over 130+ levels  that were totally different to the original, which was a pleasant surprise.

The game mechanic is basically the same,  with the usual tasks such as flipping off spectators, kissing buildings,  crashing through score plates and landing on a pad using the parachute to break your fall.  The original level selector has gone, replaced by a linear level selector, with all levels apart from the first locked. 

Unlocking  levels relies on you  scoring a certain amount of points by falling and surviving  to the  landing pad.  You also score up to five stars depending on the score you achieved. This is slightly different from the original that awarded you teeth instead of stars.  

You can only earn a total of five stars per level; if you fail to get five stars on your first try, but, say for example you gain three, the next time you  attempt  it and win  even less, they will not count, you have to score more than your previous attempt for them to count.  This method may take those not as skilful, much longer to  unlock later levels as it seems you need to  score  five stars to be able to unlock the next  level.  Though  there is a little leeway once you pass later levels.   

I'm not sure if my previous experience of the game, both the original and my Steam versions; with hundreds of hours of game play between them, for both the original  and  it's sequel  For the Awesome and even the game Beat That Ugly Baby,  made me feel  the new version seemed 'at least so far' relatively easy to beat compared to the original.  I've managed to  win five stars  for the first 20 levels  easily with no issues, though level 21 is causing me some grief.

The movement  when falling seems  less sluggish than the originals, which sometimes felt like you were fighting against  the movement, whereas in the new version, movement is very fluid.


If you loved the first & second versions of this game,  the remastered version  is certainly worth buying at full price (IMO); however, if you've no real feeling for the game, then perhaps pick it up when it's on sale.  I'm not aware of any other game that's quite like  these gems.

p.s.  

I'm hoping  to contact the developers to see if they will give me a level editor for this one as I'd love to create more levels, but whether that will happen IDK; as  I'm talking at least 15 years have passed since I did the αlpha & βeta testing for  Dejobaan llc, so it's unlikely they will remember me.

This is a really nice basketball game for people who aren't very good at sports games. I also own NBA 2K Playgrounds, and this game is much easier to play.

TL/DR Version: This game is broken, unfinished, or both. Don't buy this game if you're expecting to be able to play, y'know, an *actual* game of basketball.  

[b][u]Big: issues:[/u][/b]
-There's hardly any AI to speak of, 4 of the  5 players stand around doing nothing. 
-The stealing function is just a matter of walking through other players to get the ball, and this includes your own teammates. 
-Passing is 50/50 at best, inbounding the ball is almost impossible-- when you try to inbound the ball, a player from the opposing team will teleport to your position and take possession. When the opponents try inbound, one of your players will teleport in taking possession, etc until eventually someone is able to pass the ball in. More often than not the 'AI' passes the ball to the other end of the court where it goes out of bounds and the situation repeats. 
-Switching players feels random and is unintuative. In defence I think you take over your nearest player to the ballhandler, but sometimes you don't. It's... weird. 


[b][u]Minor nitpicks:[/u][/b] 
-There's no rules really, other than a quarter timer and out of bounds. There's no in-game menu or way to pause the game I've seen so far. 
-There's no options to speak of. No ability to change the short quarter lengths, or sound, etc. 

[b][u]Sidenote:[/u][/b] I don't quite get how some of these other reviews are saying they are enjoying this because it functionally doesn't work at all. 

Like, it's nice looking, and I want to think it'll be patched and that it's maybe not some kind of asset flip, padding for a portfolio or abandoned project, but it was released in mid 2020, so... *shrugs** Ultimately, it's basketball game that almost delivers a basketball game.

The puzzles are primarily a combination of pattern matching and association -- figure out what applies to what, and decipher the pattern. The recurring domino theme is a nice cohesive touch to the puzzles. There were several tried and true mechanisms, while also having enough novelty and uniqueness to be appealing. I appreciate that the audio puzzle did not require and tone sensitivity.

Be aware there are no in-game hints, but most of the puzzles are easy. I got stuck, requiring outside help, in only one place. I perhaps did  a bit of wild clicking when looking for this bit. Otherwise I felt my activity was fairly directed, understanding what to do from the visuals.

The strict time limit adds a nice sense of urgency, and the addition of a "notepad" in the game hearkens back to the days of PC gaming where game booklets and manuals had pages of empty space for the player to write down learned knowledge. The $5.00 price tag is more than reasonable for this type of game (I'm reminded of "Frog Detective," in that sense). I'm looking forward to playing more.

One of the most fun games I've ever played with enough content to keep you playing for a while. Devs are awesome and actually seem to look at feedback. Eh. I was really hoping for something great here. At a $20 asking price you expect the game mechanics to be really solid, and it's just not there yet. 

The putting is what is most off to me. If you release right handed backhand flat and level (or nose down even) the disc will go up by at least 2 feet and hyzer left, every time. There's a moment it snaps upwards, almost like the physics are coded to do that. It's got to be the most frustrating aspect. I'll even put anheizer on the putter to compensate for this behavior, and still it will spin out to the left really hard, like I'm putting with a 14 speed driver. Now I like me an overstable approach putter, but this thing is ridiculous. I'd even compensate for the overstability, but with it going up by two feet I have to release really low, like waist level, and practicing that bad form can't be good for the real course. 

So now you know the putter is comically overstable, what about the midrange, that overstability sounds like what I would probably want for my driving disc (you start with a midrange and a putter). Well when you pull your disc right because the mechanics are a little screwy you can expect a very understable disc, comparable to a light weight prodigy F5. Trying to flick it forehand I always get an understable roller, or backhand you'll get a distinct understable fade to the right

I'm streaming to an oculus quest 2 via virtual desktop. I hope the developer takes the time to improve the physics, because there are a lot of fun game mechanics there, like there's a screen that tracks where your shot landed, and you can either walk to your throw, or teleport to it. It's just the physics is absolutely the most important aspect to someone like me who really enjoys the sport, and it's disappointing to pay 20 bucks and it to be this off.

Good luck.

I so wanted to play this game.  I am an avid disc golfer and it was one of the few things I could enjoy with friends until the weather got cold.  It's unplayable even after the "physics update".  The mechanics in no way match real disc golf.  The stupid Sports Champions game that came out with Playstation Move controllers over 10 years ago was more realistic and definitely more fun.  The developer has much work to do before this should even be listed as early release.  It is not even beta.  This is a non-functioning concept.

This is an excellent Disc Golf experience.  My friends and I play IRL about once a week, and while it takes some adjustment to throwing weightless VR discs; the physics of this game are consistent enough that you can apply your real-life disc golf skills into the game with just a bit of practice.  The environments look great, and the terrain of the courses feel diverse and realistic.  I was able to maintain a smooth wireless experience on my Oculus Quest (1) over Virtual Desktop on High settings.  The visuals aren't photo-realistic, but they are good enough I feel that I'm able to be immersed in the experience.

There is a sense of progression in the game with earning "chains"/currency for how well you do on each hole, these can be spent to unlock additional discs - each with their own flight characteristics.  Each disc really does feel and fly differently just like they would in real life with respects to the Speed/Glide/Turn/Fade ratings, which are all detailed in the disc unlock screen.

For new players, I'd suggest unlocking the purple putter as soon as possible.  The one you start off with is much too floaty, and I found it almost impossible to toss it in the basket without it bouncing off the top rim first and then just handing it in.  Overall I feel like the putting is a bit too floaty in general, and the putters could use a physics adjustment to give them a bit more weight - especially when thrown lightly.

Great game, looking forward to more!

Hi,
I have been playing this with a friend for many hours now. Since the early beta version, which had quite a few bugs, nowadays this is running stable and it brings quite fun to play this with friends. This has become one of my favourite multiplayer games for VR!

I have given it a fair shot, and maybe will even continue trying to play a bit in the future, but for now it just doesn't really feel like a great vr disk golf game.  If you are a left handed player, just forget it.  The flight physics are totally against the left handed throw, and nearly all the holes dogleg to the left, and/or have big trees to the left.  As a lefty disc golfer, i have gotten used to arcing the disc high on the throw to get it to go far to the left, but with this game, inevitably the disc corrects, levels out and grounds to the right, as it would for a right handed throw.... they need to work on their physics.

The scenes are ok, but could be better, with a little wind blowing some leaves around, or a wildlife here are there.  The hole setup, besides the above mentioned right handed-ness, is unimaginative, and lack the vistas that would make a truely great experience, and make me "feel" the course.  There are some spectacle holes that feel good to look down the hill from.

First of all, let me say that I haven't ever played disc golf in real life. So I cannot tell you if physics is matching exactly the real world experience or if it feel "like the real thing".

What I can say, however, that it is a nice and fun game that I am enjoying a lot. There is a helpful short tutorial for disc golf dummies like me and then you go and try your best on the first course. More courses become available once you finish the first one.

Graphics is certainly not exceptional but nice enough that you feel like being outside on a disc golf track. I am a graphics enthusiast and only kind of happy with the best of the best. So I'd love to have more detailed and more realistic graphics but at the same time it is certainly good enough that it serves the purpose and you feel fine on the track.

After a steep learning curve I slowly start to understand a bit what matters when throwing that disc and what influences the distance and flight behavior. Physics behavior seems to be consistent to me, i.e. when the shot is bad then I feel also that it was my fault and when I did the basics right, then the disc seems to consistently do what I would expect it to do from what I learned so far. So I have the motivation to play more, get better and to enjoy the tracks.

I have a lot of fun with this game so far and can absolutely recommend it. It offers an enjoyable performance at a reasonable price and when you like VR sports games like golf, tennis, table tennis, etc. then you're probably also going to enjoy this one.

Great vr disc golf game, physics are pretty realistic for the most part. Did notice the disc doesn't really slide or skip off the ground or ricochet off trees much. Takes some time to get used to throwing without a physical disc in hand but I feel that the throwing physics are solid, not perfect but that is too be expected when compared to IRL disc golf.

I was say this game is in an early stage where you're investing with hope for improvement. If you're young and want something playable and fun as you know disc golf, stick with Disc Golf Valley (DGV) for now. 

For me the physics needs a lot of work. If I throw a disc into a cliff it should at least hit and slide down or roll, not stick to the side of it. Also the first midrange they they start you with claims 4/6/-1/1.. if you throw it on an anhyzer it will flex out like an overstable disc. It currently lacks a lot of true flight qualities that DGV has obtained over a few years of work.

 I love that they want to achieve a solid multiplayer which is the one thing DGV (vr version) currently lacks and for that reason I'm hopeful that over time these features will improve.

My recommendation would be for the developers start or have some sort of discord or facebook group and organize some sort of league night similar in the way that Hops&Hyzer has been done through DGV. Would be a good start to develop a community and make up for the other issues the game currently has making the investment more enticing for others to get on board.

I saw the older reviews of this game and decided to take a risk with this one while it was on sale.

I've been playing disc golf off/on for a few years now (no where near that great at it, just a hobby!) and saw this as a cool way to play when I can't get out of the house.

The beginning tutorial drags on a bit for people who know how to play DG. I had to play the first course with only a putter, which was a little annoying. However, after unlocking the first mid, things got better.

The most awkward thing about the game is putting. I either drop the disc at my feet or sling the disc 100ft away. This results in needing to get a tap in on every hole.

Holding discs in VR feels odd at first but you eventually adjust to it. Somehow almost every throw I release tells me I'm hyzer, which I can't tell if that's my fault or if the game isn't tracking my hand correctly... (hyzer release is a IRL problem for me, thanks game) 

However, for 11 dollars on sale, this is a good replica of playing DG and I would recommend it! If some of the physics problems were worked out, and the putting problem was fixed, this would definitely be on its way to a huge hit.

Misc: The chain sound is a little annoying/very loud and unrealistic compared to real life. If it were turned down by about 25% and if there were a variety of different recordings of the chains being hit instead of the same sound each time, that would be a huge QOL for me personally. The nature sounds are great though!

Also it would be nice to have some details on the holes of each course - par and lengths. I ended up taking drivers into one course I just unlocked and never used as all 18 holes where under 70m.
Would even be better to be able to save/load preferred loadouts for each course, or even just manually naming them yourself would work.
Also for me the challenge is trying to break par or beat previous best. Would really like to be able to see my best score for each course. At the moment I am taking screenshots of final scorecard but seems steam vr has issues showing these in VR so have to check in flat screen.

This is a tactical puzzle game and it's very well done. You play separate levels with a set number of units with the objective to kill all of the opposing units within 3 rounds. If you don't kill all of them, you lose. Obviously, if the opposing side kills you first, you lose. 

The isometric view is simple with no frills, but it works. The units are little slimes that have rudimentary animations. The music is a chip tune melody that gets kinda repetitive but is not offensive. 

What shines about this game is that it uses all the best features of great SRPGs such as elevation, direction of attack, movement, speed, and different unit types to make some interesting and (at times) challenging matches. It's like playing a streamlined version of Final Fantasy Tactics that's meant for short bouts. In many ways, it's like a mobile game, but I don't mean that in a bad way. 

Another plus is that the developer could have stopped with just one unit and rely on the puzzle hook to keep players engaged, but you do have different types of units like rangers, archers and mages. These units make battles interesting and add to the strategic layer. 

Oh, and it comes with a level editor so you can make your own maps and scenarios. It would be nice if they set up the Steam Workshop for user created maps.

As a fan of the Playstation game series ([i]Devil Dice[/i] on PS1, it's sequel [i]Xi-Jumbo[/i], and [i]Bombastic[/i] for PS2), I bought this game thinking it would offer a similar experience on PC. It does not, and as such I'll be mainly comparing Cube Raiders to these games.
✅ In terms of gameplay mechanics it's essentially the same as the first game, but with the possibility to climb dice or jump off them at any time.
✅ Decent art style and music for a casual game... it does not justify the need for a dedicated graphic card, however.
✅ Similar to the PS2 release, Puzzle mode levels feature scenario obstacles and hazards that interact with dice too, which slightly increases the challenge...
🟡 But, that's the only new strategic element. Unlike the original games, dice do not have any inherent properties beside how the environment affects them.
🟡 A somewhat modern notebook should be able to run a game like this just fine. Ice Temple levels cause FPS drops, and the game does not offer video settings.
🟡 Overall, the game itself is somewhat easy, so I've decided to just complete every level and achievement.
❌ The game has some notable bugs, and [b]player movement is sluggish[/b]. Why are the characters so slow? Why do characters sometimes drop off the die you are trying to climb?
❌ There's [b]no way to swap key bindings[/b]. I had to connect an USB keyboard for co-op mode because my notebook does not have a right CTRL key. Is this why they recommend using a controller?
❌ Unlike the original games, there's no incentive to chain-connect dice, [b]which was the main appeal of the original game's Arcade mode[/b]; there's no additional points or time gain for chaining any additional dice to a group of connected dice in Endless mode, which makes chain-connect counterproductive.
❌ Unlike the PS1 games, dice can't be rolled over dice that are emerging from the ground, or the ones that are dissolving on the floor after clearing them, which becomes an annoyance given there's no way to predict dice generation that may block off your path.
❌ Steam Achievements are bugged too! I'm missing some achievements despite clearing every level available.
TLDR; I would not recommend this game, specially if you are expecting a PC Devil Dice.

The game also introduces platforming. While it's great to break up the combat with some platforming, it's not done well here. Rayne sometimes ignores ledges or just jumps in the wrong directions. It's manageable most of the time but still noticeable. 

You also have more enemy variety but not nearly enough to prevent the game from getting repetitive.

The graphics are better, with more interesting levels, sections in daylight and a better sense of place. It's still a early 2000's low budget game but it's an improvement from the previous one.

This is a pretty cool audio music visualizer for VR and Non-VR. WARNING: Only KBM is currently supported, so you cannot use motion controllers. In fact, there is no input during the VR experience. It comes with 5 pre-made scenes with included music tracks.

The editor is a little on the clunky side, but it is a robust, powerful tool that is easy to use, but will take time to master. I was able to make an experience using one of my mp3s that was half-way decent on my second attempt. 

App is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting 90 fps for the most part, but it definitely had some frame rate drops here and there. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs. 

I do recommend this app, but more for people who are interested in tinkering / creating their own audio/visual experiences using the editor. The 5 included experiences are nice though, but they probably aren't enough to justify the price. Some people have complained about the 3D, and it's true it's like a sphere with 3D layers effect. However, I enjoyed them and I especially enjoyed tinkering with the editor. The editor makes this a unique experience for VR.

Indika is a unique story-driven game set in an alternative Russia. It focuses on its titular character, an ostracised nun who is tasked with delivering an important letter and must traverse the game’s harsh and surreal environments.

Overall, it is an impressive and original game that blends genres and mechanics to create an unusual experience. It will take around 4-5 hours to complete and boasts diverse and satisfying gameplay, a strong and emotive narrative, stark, realistic visuals paired with intricate pixel art, and immersive and atmospheric sound design that creates an interesting juxtaposition between various elements of the game. Indika definitely offers something different and I thoroughly enjoyed this unique experience. I’d highly recommend it and believe it is a title that would be enjoyed by a wide range of players.

The sequences don't have much connective tissue, nor enough substance to really piece together what's happening: flashback sequences explain what happens in the past, and explain how Indika ended up where she was [i]at another point in the past,[/i] but have no bearing at all on the present in which the player meets her. They don't explain what's going on, only add more content.

This game contains fine examples of what people should be attempting with the medium, but the minimal interaction and needlessly disjointed segments left me with the nasty suspicion that [i]Indika[/i], like David Cage's work, is the output of someone who couldn't cut it making films, as saw video games as an easy Plan B. There was another section that had you running away from something but the main character was running and weaving through obstacles at what felt like a light jog which ruined the suspense. plus the motives behind that scene felt unrelated to the over-arching story

This is a very rare kind of game.

Set in a grim, washed-out 19th-century Russia, Indika meaningfully examines the difficulties of engaging with religion in the brutality of the modern world. Frequently raw and uncomfortable, at other times relatable and touching, it encapsulates both the warmth and cruelty inherent in our interactions with other people and the spiritual.

Instantly noticeable is the game's use of Orthodox Christianity as opposed to Catholicism like in other games, like Blasphemous. While certainly critical, Indika's depiction of the religion is in many ways skilful and poignant, and is particularly effective in communicating the game's themes to players who are already knowledgeable about Orthodox traditions and practices. The game's discussion of theological problems is fairly accessible through the characters' dialogues, but is also expressed tactfully through the story and environment; a particularly memorable example is the house of an iconographer who had not painted any of the icons' eyes, linking in to a later discussion of the nature of the soul. As an Orthodox Christian, I definitely appreciated the level of accuracy and detail in this regard, and the relevance of many of the critiques posed by the game. Our human tendency to weaponise religion against ourselves is a particularly powerful topic.

The setting of the game itself is another incredibly strong aspect. With beautiful visual and sound design, the game is somewhat akin to a modern fairytale, merging the surreal with the recognisable. Playing it felt like if an Eggers film had been made into a game (which is very high praise, haha). It commands excellent usage of scale and composition, communicating the character's powerlessness and the frustration of engaging with a confusing, nonsensical world presented as a caricature of common Russian motifs. Interspersed with puzzles and beautiful pixel art segments, Indika is a rare example of how games can be a highly effective artistic medium. 

Altogether, I was incredibly awed by how meaningful and skilfully presented Indika was. It felt less like a game, and more like a profound film or novel. Beyond being beautifully designed, all of its little details served a narrative or thematic purpose, contributing to its setting and theological examination. It's far more than a "nun adventure game" or a few cinematic hours. If you return to it the level of attention and detail it offers to you, you will come away with a very memorable and meaningful experience.

[h3]HIGHLY recommend Indika[/h3]

[b]Story:[/b]
The narrative is fantastic and compelling. Indika's "bond" with Satan and the characters around her felt very grounded and real. It was extremely satisfying to slowly unravel the doubt that she feels about the church and the lifestyle that comes with. 

[b]Puzzles:[/b]
Puzzles were thematically interesting and not too difficult. Most took me around 5-10 minutes to solve but having Satan yelling at you sometimes made it hard to focus. Loved finding all the easter eggs, books, and trinkets hidden away in strange corners of the different areas. Also really enjoyed how the game pivots back and forth to other gameplay modes as you progress the story.

[b]Audio:[/b]
Audio design is stellar and the music was incredible. All the voice actors did fantastic work but Satan and Indika really stand out. Some of the machines you operate in the game almost seem to sing their own song as you use them. The "dog" sounded especially terrifying...

[b]Graphics:[/b]
Much better graphics than I was expecting for the price I paid. Great motion capture as well, all the movements looked and felt very good. Level design was well thought out and the architecture was often surreal and breathtaking. Excellent attention to detail especially in the homes of the local peasantry.

[b]Notes:[/b]
Whatever you do, don't rush this one. It is a very slow burn and it really pays off to stop and sit on a bench for awhile to reflect on what you've seen, done, and heard. 

Please give Indika a shot if you're thinking of buying it. Indie sleeper hits like this definitely deserve it.

For this review, I'll compare The Majesti with Sydney's World (previous game made by the same developer).

[h2]Story[/h2]
Overall the story is great and fun to follow. There's a pacing problem in the beginning, but it gets better afterward. Few characters are also memorable, especially Chee Chee. I also find story revolving around 3 factions is a decent setup.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
While the combat is still better than many low-cost RPGMaker games out there, it's a downgrade from the previous game. I feel there's fewer tactic/strategy involved. In addition, if one or more characters in the party got defeated, those characters wouldn't get any exp to level up. That means later fights would be harder due to lower stats and not having access to some skills.

Aside from combat, you're just walking to a specific destination or talking to certain characters most of the time. If you don't pay much attention to the story, you wouldn't know where to go and there's no/little indicator of the destination. Even worse, some areas have unusual designs where it's not clear which path you can walk and you can hit "invisible wall" which is somewhat frustrating.

[h2]Visual[/h2]
I notice some improvement in its visual aspect, although overall I feel it's still mediocre. Some areas (such as Cheetah Kingdom) look great, while some others look somewhat ugly (such as the world area/map) or heavily use generic/stock-looking assets. The game CG is great though.

[h2]Audio[/h2]
The audio aspect has the biggest improvement here. There are fair amount of great background music. The sound effects/SFX also got a bit better. My only complaint is some background music in some areas is too quiet, where I initially thought the area has no background music.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
The Majesti is definitely better and more enjoyable than Sydney's World. Story-rich or RPGMaker enthusiasts might want to try playing this game.

KIRO is a short yet very fun horror text adventure that was only recently released. As the genre suggests, you need to type in commands in order to move, open doors, open chests, battle, etc. The game follows the adventure of a town hero, given the title of Kiro, on his quest to rid the crypt below the town of all evil. 

Exploration is key in this game as you are initially dropped off with nothing to defend yourself and nothing to navigate with. The game map operates on a 5x4 grid system and rewards exploration by placing a chest in every room. Each chest either contains a weapon, weapon ammo, or a map. The layout of the game is different every time you load it up, making for some great replayability. Fighting enemies is simple yet satisfying, although if you lack the necessary items for battle, running away into another room is always an option too. The main boss of the game makes for an exciting experience as you run from room to room avoiding it while searching for items. As far as audiovisuals go, this game is both aesthetically pleasing and also able to provide a nice atmosphere with it's great use of ambience. [spoiler]The ending song is also such a great song.[/spoiler]

Ultimately, if you're looking for a great, yet short, horror adventure experience this is the game for you. For the price I'd definitely recommend it. I'm looking forward to see what the developer has next in store for this game or it's potential sequels.

I'll admit that the main reason I decided to check out this game was because a cute mushroom Goadstool presented it to me. You could say I've been... [i]goaded[/i] into buying this game. I'm sorry, that was foul.

Anyway, I'm glad that I checked it out - because KOR is a well-crafted game. It sets out to capture this magical atmosphere of classic pokemon games - and by classic, I mean the ones that were on the Gameboy. And it succeeds at that task with flying colours. The setup, the level design, the flavour of the dialogue, and of course the aesthetic - all extract that goodness of what made classic pokemon great, and use it to create a brand new adventure.

The battle system is fun, but I have some complaints. It feels very much like pokemon, but without animal cruelty - in fact, with no cruelty whatsoever, the fighting is supposed to be virtual. You level up, you learn/set up your moves, choose your affinities, what have you. It's all great. That said, I found the time window to get an S rank ridiculously short, and could only pull it off with the simplest moves. This leads to another problem: what's the point of getting a different, stronger attack, if you won't be able to get an S rank due to longer combo, and will deal much lower damage?

Also, I found the difficulty a little high towards the end, and found the available moveset somewhat shallow. In the end, I won (Intended difficulty) with a relatively simple strategy, but what finally earned me that final boss kill was 100% perfect execution of all my moves. So it's a bit of a mixed bag. Don't get me wrong, this is an incredibly good idea and with some tweaking this could become the best thing since [strike]sliced[/strike] banana bread.

A thing of note is the fact that you can warp through walls. This is a very simple thing, but makes traversal and exploration  fun, making you feel like you're breaking the boundaries of the game. It also fits with the general theme of the game, which is... ah, yes. I'm not going to spoil things. Let's just say that the theme, and the overall plot, are very, hmm.. relevant to the real world. It's done adequately, too, when you notice what it actually is about.

To wrap things up, let me just quickly say that the music is incredibly good, and completes the excellent aesthetic of the game. There's variety and quality both. It really feels like pokemon while also being nothing like it. Quite amazing, actually. So, should you get this game? If nothing else, this is a very interesting attempt at pushing the turn-based RPG genre forward. It's also fun and well-paced - there is no annoying grind, unlike in pokemon. There also are no random encounters. So even if you haven't played the old pokemon games, this is quite nice. And if you have? Then it's almost a no-brainer, mainly because of how skillfully it manipulates the fabric of that nostalgic feel. Enjoy!

A note to the dev: Good hello to you! I'm hoping you will make more games, I will definitely be watching what you cook up next. KOR is quite fantastic work, especially considering this is your first game. Also, yes, I saw what you did there. Keep it up, my friend!

KOR is a cheap, polished, and mechanically interesting game developed almost entirely by one person! We need more developers like Goadstool in the game industry, and for that reason alone you should buy KOR.

As others have noted this is an enjoyable RPG that is very reminiscent of GameBoy era titles like Pokemon. The experience is far from simple nostalgia scratching, as Goadstool has built upon that influence in ways both big and small.  The combat mechanics are easy to pick up and challenging to master. The range of ability choices, skill point allocation, and the often tactical and dynamic nature of encounters make victories very rewarding. There is so much to explore in Kor, as almost every object can be inspected and every NPC interacted with. Goadstool has been actively engaged post-launch and I have seen bug fix patches come in. 9/10, this is the kind of product that I wish more indie devs were trying to produce.

KOR starts strong with a silly world, sinister happenings in the background, and questions needing to be answered. However the game then turns to hyper precise inputs and large empty spaces to navigate without much help. The point that really turned me away from the game is the first real ‘boss fight’. Up until this point on the intended difficulty every enemy executed combos at about the same level of the player; Es and Ds with the occasional B or F. The boss uses almost exclusively As and Bs, while also using moves that the player doesn’t have access to yet themselves. To call this fight a difficulty spike would be a bit of an understatement, as even after I switched to casual difficulty the boss still took 15-some attempts to defeat. The game also contains puzzles which require you to turn in one place. Normally in a Top-down RPG there’s a way to do this fairly easily, however KOR’s window to ‘lightly tap’ a directional button to turn feels like it may be a near frame perfect endeavor, and it's not one I can do on queue. I Played the game up to an abundantly large map where you need to locate 4 ‘clues’ to continue, and despite sinking an hour and a half of my life to just scouring for the last one, I could not find it. I feel this game needed better accessibility options, because I want to love this game, I really do, but I could not finish.

Kor popped up in a retweet from a gaming friend of mine, and I was hooked from the trailer's nostalgic visuals and catchy music. I impulse bought this game, guessing it would be something right up my alley.

I was right.

The game of Kor aims to simulate the feeling of playing an old Game Boy game, and it executes this perfectly.

The graphics and overworld feel ripped straight out of Pokemon (almost to a fault), and the music reminds me both of some older Game Boy titles (Pokemon Trading Card Game comes to mind) and newer titles (Undertale, Everhood). It must be noted that the music is composed by Lewmoth, and nearly every track had me humming along within 5 minutes of encountering it. It's so damn catchy.

The dialogue in this game is anywhere from typical RPG discussions about the world, to parodies of gaming tropes, to downright nonsense, in a good way. You always feel enticed to talk to every NPC and check every object, no matter how normal it seems. And there are a *lot* of objects to interact with.

I don't want to dig into the story too much, firstly as not to spoil the experience, but I also don't think the story is the reason to play this game. It's good, but not anything mind-blowing. There is a story here, though, and it serves as a nice accessory to the package. Some themes hit hard, but not hard enough that you question life as a whole.

The gameplay mainly consists of challenging NPCs to a handheld game (which is called Kor, funny enough) where you use typical moves in turn-based RPG combat. The strength of moves mostly depend on executing button combos shown on the screen, followed by combo-ing certain moves together either to debuff the opponent, take advantage of your Haste stat, or use attacks in an order to do massive damage at once.

There are several schools of attacks and you can choose to mix them, or prioritize one school. There are no wrong answers. Besides, most of the game's difficulty is based on how many battles you choose to face during the game, and how quickly and accurately you can execute button combos.

One more thing I want to say about this game: the developer, Goadstool, is someone that definitely plays games. I had the pleasure of talking with him while I was streaming this game, and while I won't divulge all of the insights, he confirmed some positives I had for the game.

For example, a big downer in most RPGs is random encounters. Gone. Feel like you have to use potions and Pokemon Centers to keep health and magic up? Gone. Feel like you messed up your build and need to either pay currency to change it or start the game all over? Gone. For a game that's supposed to resemble Game Boy games, the amount of quality of life additions that would turn others away from RPGs is gone, and I love that.

Please check this game out. If the trailer made you want to play it, the price of entry is more than fair, and you'll still be humming tunes in the shower after you're done with the game. Congrats, Goadstool, Lewmoth, and others involved in the game. I'm looking forward to what you do next!

Also there's a side game that's just awful, but it's optional.

Other than that, it's a pretty solid game with decent music. I wish there was a bit more to the story, but what's there works for what it is. I'd definitely recommend playing the easier mode if you have arthritis or have difficulty doing specific fast inputs.

It's well built but very tough. Maybe a bit TOO tightly regulated in the resource department, but at least that keeps you from snowballing out of control. Even if you have to save before you shop just in case you run out of money and can't win without a skill you're missing. C'est la vie. At least respeccing is free.

An excellent and well-polished game. Kor faithfully captures the magic of playing Gameboy games as a kid while also managing to be a creative and unique game in its own right. I loved exploring the world and interacting with everything; basically all of the items in homes and stores, for example, have their own unique descriptions. The story and world building were well thought-out as well, and I enjoyed learning about the world of Kor as I explored. Intentional difficulty was also harder than I expected, which was a pleasant surprise; I felt like I really had to think about how to allocate my stats and skills in order to win some of the harder fights.

A lot of love was put into this game and you can tell. Kor was great and I'm excited to see what Goadstool does next!

Really charming RPG that captures not just the look but also the feel of GameBoy JRPGs.  Explore the world, meet colorful characters and challenge them to fights.  

The combat system has a clever balance of simplicity and depth, alongside with an element of time-based technical execution.  You collect more moves to add to your arsenal as you go on, and the moves are interestingly designed, with various benefits and drawbacks.  I'm still fairly early in the game, but already there have been situations where I have to switch tactics and react to enemy moves (for example, in one combat the enemy used a shield move that would cause counter-damage to me if they took damage that turn, so I intentionally failed my combo input so that my attack wouldn't go off).  

Aesthetically the game nails that GameBoy look, in the environments and characters as well as in the UI.  The music is also excellent.  

While the game definitely wears its Pokemon influence on its sleeve, it is different enough to stand on its own, and captures a bit of that feeling of playing a new GameBoy JRPG for the first time.

Kor has this battle system where you execute a sequence of inputs that will make an attack or ability more effective depending on how quickly you pull them off. At first I didn't think I would like it, but it grew on me! With each new move comes a new sequence of inputs. 

I think there a lot of good elements to this game, especially if you're a fan of Game Boy like titles. For $10, I think Kor is well worth picking up. I will say, I almost wish I could somehow put this on an ez-flash to play on my GB.

While the main character and dialogue from characters can be pretty funny at times, there are a few drawbacks; The combat style, although super unique, took time to fully grasp. Also it's possible to rely heavily on basic attacks throughout the playthrough, potentially diminishing the depth of the experience (but this may have more to do with the difficulty I selected rather than mechanics, to be fair. I also found myself traversing long distances, leading to moments of monotony during gameplay.
Overall, Kor is a charming adventure game. Despite its minor flaws, it has a really catchy chiptune soundtrack, super unique combat system, and an endearing protagonist. Fun for an afternoon at home!
