[h3]Flavours of Fluff[/h3]
Cascade Cafe is a well-framed brain teaser. What you see is what you get - a relaxing puzzle with a warm atmosphere. It's all about combining tiles, matching values, creating paths, collecting usable items, setting traps, exploiting board gimmicks, and using auxiliary abilities that usually do something listed above. Sounds like a lot, but it's actually all there is. Think ahead, enjoy the well-animated cascade effects you cause, and don't sweat it. Despite never playing the Cascade board game, I breezed through this one with relative ease. Not prodded by hardships or a sense of achievement, but having the calm disposition and pristine autumn melancholy in my sails.

I dig the art style and the sound accompaniment, they're both deliberately lucid and comforting. I appreciate it when the intent and the end result are in agreement. The same goes for all the small talk and mild humor that fit the atmosphere. I found the characters cute, and for a change, these moderately anthropomorphic animals don't look abundantly sexy. Give this dev a medal for this. Everything is perceived in a better light when a polite cat in a soft sweater explains stuff to you so kindly over some soothing music purring in the background. You play as a geeky hare? A nerdy rabbit? Who cares? The story is all flavours of fluff.

[h3]The Chill Trap[/h3]
Yeah, it isn't a visual novel, abandon your hope. Try the demo if you're in doubt, it's representative - the game doesn't get better or worse than that. Cascade Cafe is but a neat distraction to play in short bursts. My playtime includes nothing but singleplayer content, a handful of Puzzles, Vs. CPU, and the main course of the Story Mode, consisting of 30 matches. Getting all gold medals was slightly tricky and involved some luck, but I didn't mind as long as it meant staying for a bit longer. If you're into multiplayer, more power to you... but not that much. They won't ever have enough of a player base to feature full-blown online PvP, so I hope you'll be content with friendly duels.

All in all, it's such a joy to learn something completely new to you and have that simple pleasure of laid-back, mildly mind-flexing fun. Would I prefer an interesting story? Eh, I guess. Would I love to play against a less braindead AI in Story Mode? Certainly so! You can raise its difficulty in Vs. CPU Mode... but nah, it's just as clueless even at its best. Anyway, teabagging these critters felt satisfying either way and was worth the price of admission, even without a discount. Some of my friends may call me a hypocrite since I always go around preaching "what's the point in a puzzle game if the puzzles are easy?", to which I'd say... nothing, you got me there! I fell for the chill trap.

[b]cascade cafe[/b] is a story-driven hashi/bridges-like (for lack of a better comparison) with excellent cartoony presentation. you're a bunny called nymo, who finds a group playing something in the local cafe. it turns out to be [i]cascade[/i], a neat competitive board game, and as they're a friendly bunch, they offer to teach nymo how to play, hoping he'll become good enough to win the tournament. there's an [b]in-game manual[/b] to bring up anytime, but I'll go through the basics quickly.

it's all [b]turn-based[/b] and the goal is to reach a certain amount of points before your opponent. it's [b]played with tiles that have a value and a number of bridges[/b], yours are a different color. it's important because the only time your tile can touch the opponent's is if it also touches one of your own. well, one of the only times, as rainbow tiles act as a joker in this sense. when holding a tile, valid placement options are highlighted.

bridges are crucial, as [b]you're aiming for connections between the same numbers, a sequence, or creating a loop, all only with your own tiles[/b]. 2 are already good enough, so 1-2 works, putting a 2 after in the next turn counts as 2-2, but ideally you'd put a 3 there, so 1-2 becomes 1-2-3. increasing and decreasing sequences are accepted, but [b]only bridges matter for loops[/b]. as long as the tiles form one, they can sport any number, but sequences and other stuff are still awarded. strategic placement can lead to nice combos, counting all newly-created paths. outgoing bridges are fine too, so a square with some extra lines outwards is still a loop, but if you utilize all of them, it's a 'complete' and bully for you.

[b]lucky paths[/b] are part of every level past the tutorial. you can place any tile there, but using the designated one (same value and/or bridges, ideally both) as part of a path gives extra points. items covering the markings is not ideal though. [b]gimmicks[/b] are shown before starting a level, stuff like score multiplier or penalty tiles.

[b]abilities[/b] manipulate already placed tiles, set traps, etc. they're not single-use, don't count as a move, but consume [b]energy[/b], which has to be collected by placing tiles over energy balls on the board. unlocked ones can be viewed from level select (it's a diary with a couple of tabs), you can have up to 3 activated.

[b]items[/b] are collected the same way, they're single-use but don't need energy. no section for them in the diary, and you'll run into them sooner than they actually unlock between levels, which is weird.

[b]story mode offers 30 levels[/b], no difficulty settings, but it's not a hard campaign. the reset button only puts the current piece back, level reset is in the pause menu. and there are some [b]standalone puzzles[/b] as a bonus. solving the 5 easy ones unlocks intermediate levels one by one, not sure how many there are altogether. the goal here is reaching a score within a certain amount of turns with a given set of tiles.

[b]no mid-level saving and levels can take a while[/b] with more mechanics and higher scores in play, so it's a problem. rating is based on the number of moves it takes to win and the opponent's stats can also be viewed after, which is neat. what's less neat is you also get a bronze/silver/gold rating if you lose, even though there's one for loss and it was the opponent who won in 8 moves, not you. it's meaningless, of course, and doesn't unlock the next level. no retry button if you win, so going for gold is more finicky than it should be.

[b]controls are mouse-based[/b] and are as easy as clicking and dragging a tile to place or move it around the board. [b]click a placed tile to rotate[/b], then the 'end turn' button when you're done. being the dumb shit I am, I forgot about rotation as soon as the tutorial message disappeared and was having an incredibly hard time simply scoring, let alone winning. a reminder got patched in, so it should be easier to remember.

[b]online multiplayer or against the computer[/b] on 10 levels of difficulty on boards unlocked in story mode are also possible. 'chillout mode' is just a potentially noisy screensaver, you can watch the computer play against itself while listening to the soundtrack. don't think it was worth however long it took to implement, especially when there's other areas in need of improvement.

settings include separate volume sliders for the pretty good audio, resolutions and windowed mode. they're available while playing as well. text display is fast enough (instant would be better), thankfully no gibberish or repeating text display sound and dialog can be outright skipped. I would've preferred no ellipses and there are some typos, missing apostrophes and punctuation (a lot less after pointing them out).

[b]it's really fun, looks and mostly works well[/b] and the price tag is more than reasonable after it got a bit fixed up based on feedback. there's [b]a demo to try if you're uncertain[/b], progress carries over to the full game.

Tile laying, number matching game.  Played on one of a number of different boards (square grids with varied out of play blocks on each), join up your tiles to form sequences or sets of numbers and form loops or close off your network.  Then gain extra abilities (eg increase a number, rotate a tile in play, eliminate a bridge, ...) to mix things up a bit.
I bought this about a year ago, played a couple of times and then kind of forgot about it.  Noticed it again yesterday, loaded it up and I've just finished the storyline mode.
It's fun, and there are some interesting strategy and tactical decisions to make.  The characters are cute - you're a bunny, there's a sloth, and a little bird and others - the music is fine for a chilled mood, and the different boards with various bonuses and gimmicks keep things entertaining.  The story is fine, if uninspired - you meet the characters and play them all multiple times leading up to the big tournament (which turns out to be a single game).
The biggest downside for me so far is that the computer doesn't seem to play particularly well, at least in the storyline.  The final boss is built up as a huge obstacle, with what you expect will be OP cards to play against you, but in the end doesn't offer a challenge (I beat them by I think about 500 points on a 700 point target).  Haven't tried the AI outside the story though - there are I think about 8 difficulty levels, so maybe they scale up better,  
There are a few spelling errors in the story dialogue, but not so many that it's annoying.  (And because your lines are pre-scripted, they sometimes don't make much sense, such as when you tell one of the characters how you took their advice in the game, when I really hadn't - but maybe I was just being nice to them because they played so poorly...)
Despite the snark there, the game is pretty good value for money.  I always aim for an hour of entertainment for every pound I spend on a game, and Cascade Cafe has delivered on that already, and I'll continue to play - certainly to try out the different AI levels and then to try against humans.  Young children will probably enjoy it as a not-too-difficult game to play against cartoon animals.

Guilty Gear Strive, Arc System Works’ latest brawler, is a masterclass in fighting game evolution, blending accessibility with depth. It’s a visual and auditory feast that keeps the series’ legacy alive while inviting new players into its wild world. The gameplay shines with a refined mix of high-speed combos and the new Heat system, encouraging aggressive playstyles. Rollback netcode ensures online matches feel seamless, a godsend for competitive fans. The roster, now bolstered by Season 4, blends returning icons with fresh faces, delivering chaos that’s as stylish as it is brutal.
The music is a standout—Daisuke Ishiwatari’s heavy metal soundtrack roars with tracks like “Smell of the Game,” fusing shredding guitars and operatic vocals into a pulse-pounding adrenaline shot. Each character’s theme, like Sol Badguy’s gritty riffs or Elphelt’s bubblegum-metal mashup, amplifies their personality. Art direction is equally stellar, with 2.5D cel-shaded graphics that mimic hand-drawn anime. Stages burst with detail—crumbling castles, neon-lit cities—while characters animate with fluid, exaggerated flair, making every fight a spectacle.
Elphelt Valentine’s redesign is a highlight. Returning in Season 3, her new look ditches the frilly wedding dress for a punk-rock edge—leather, spikes, and a rifle that screams attitude. Her bubblegum-pink aesthetic now packs a rebellious punch, perfectly matching her quirky, chaotic moveset. It’s a bold glow-up that respects her roots while feeling fresh. Then there’s Lucy from Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, Season 4’s final addition and the series’ first guest character, slated for summer 2025. Her sleek, monowire-wielding netrunner vibe fits Guilty Gear’s flamboyant future-punk ethos like a glove, bridging anime and gaming with a crossover that’s got fans buzzing.
Strive isn’t flawless—its story mode leans too cinematic, and some balance tweaks irk purists—but its music, art, and bold character designs like Elphelt’s and Lucy’s make it a knockout. This is guilty pleasure done right.

(rating is at 9/10 because I'm positive there's people like LTG in here somewhere, I just never interacted with them)

You can literally turn any character into anything, and all these mods are client-side and safe for online play too! Final Verdict: 100/100

Guilty Gear Strive is my favorite game, it has beautiful visuals with great music and sound design. It is a fighting game much easier to get into compared to others, while retaining plenty of interesting moments and its own complexities. It skips a lot of simple execution checks (an example would be having a dash macro instead of double tapping a direction), which gives you more focus on the bigger picture of the match. As a result, these simplifications allow the player to improve at quite a rapid rate and catch up to the more experienced opponents. (it also helps that the game hasn't been around for decades unlike the older titles)

Don't think you'll reach the top so quickly though, after all this time I only feel like half the player (at best) I could be, so you won't be running out of things to do anytime soon. 

  I highly recommend playing with friends or just find sparring partners. Learning new things and showing it off to your friends in a match is very exciting and it gives you something to work for; catching up/not falling behind/getting ahead. 

Anyway, the game's alright I guess

[b]- Disclaimer -[/b]
I have updated this review to reflect my current thoughts on this game, as of October 6th, 2020.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Wander a confined area and and play "dress up" with two ladies (or you can unlock more via DLC).  There isn't a goal to [b]Photo Studio[/b]; I'd consider this to be a sandbox game. You can dress and pose the NPCs, and take photos or videos using the in-game cameras. You can also adjust the strength and temperature of the preset lighting, or even change the on-screen projection behind your model. By adding Youtube links to the "YoutubeUrls.txt" file in [b]Photo Studio[/b]'s base directory, you can play any video in the background (or since there's sound playback, listen to some jams as you play the game.)

[table][tr][td]To read the full length "Gameplay", check this review out on Wombat Trap (dot-com).[/td][/tr][/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
There's Anya, Gabriel, Mei, and then there's uh, the photo guy. He's your everyday photo guy, busty tummy and plaid shirt, the whole artist get-up. Gabriel visits whenever photo guy needs to short a couple or porno flick. He's a pretty chad guy, always there when Anya and Mei need him.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
There is no titlescreen, it's [i]straight[/i] to the action. The user-interface is extremely poor, and navigating the game is absolute pain. Much of the game is operated by a panel with a limited number of (comically cartoony) buttons, instead of a traditional menu or interacting with objects directly. You are forced to cycle through options one-by-one, and your movement is restricted by a set of fancy animations (which will often seize and make you unable to leave the control panel.) You can adjust audio and graphical preferences from the ([i]unattractive[/i]) pause menu. The player animations don't usually work great; when he moves forward, he [i]drifts forward[/i] instead of walking.

[b]- The Goods-[/b]
The base game contains no goodies.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Wait for a sale or a few updates. However, if this is a game that looks interesting to you, definitely pick it up (even if it's a little rough around the edges.) The developer is surprisingly punctual: on release, I ripped her game a new one because it didn't have a functional camera. Come the next day, and there's not only a functional camera, but there's also a brand new (and functional) video camera! Grab the game, and put in your words for updates. Still, I think the game should have stayed behind closed doors before its (awful) release, and the price is well above what it should be given the current state of the game. Between the base game and one adult-DLC, it's thirty-five USD: that's more than what you'd have to pay for most adult, triple "A" games!

Imagine going to a beautiful lakeside cabin in the heart of Finland during the midsummer solstice, and before you actually set one step inside the cabin where you will be staying you already posted 6 photo's and 11 comments on social media.

I would've never guessed so, but this game really benefitted from a second playthrough. While my first one was pretty frustrating or confusing at times, having to guess where to go with that achingly slow walking speed, finding many of my "own" in-game posts unbelievable or stupid and getting annoyed by the fact that my followers wouldn't comment on the magpie with the key in its mouth even if it's very clearly sitting in the background of my photograph etc.; in my second one I had to get the achievement for oversharing anyway, so I went full toxic asshole mode, only liked and posted the most anti-stuff and finally understood, what this game really is and when it works best: As a smaller, cuter "The Beginner's Guide".

The writing can be underwhelming either way, I wish there was a little more attention to detail and reactions to the relevance or order of my posts, most of my followers seem to be on the lower end of brain activity and while I appreciated the general design, especially the one of the main mystery was a bit too childish or cutesy for my taste.
But with a low price like this, some pretty funny moments, an unexpectedly scary little moment that really got me good, convincing sound design (if badly mixed at times) and an unusual, interesting subject matter at hand in both levels of the script, I can still wholeheartedly recommend this unexpectedly thoughtful, realxing and cute yet genuinely mature little adventure. Unit 404 is a puzzle game in which you need to manipulate buttons, switches, and various other mechanics to get your robot across the room to its destination.  The difficulty is that the buttons/tiles can only attract each other; they cannot repel each other.  This requires you to think and plan your moves carefully.

The first 20-30 levels are fairly easy, but the difficulty definitely increases from there.  I'm currently on level 46 (out of about 75, I believe), and I've gotten stuck on several levels so far (after being stuck on level 39 for over 30 minutes, I finally resorted to looking at a walkthrough for a hint on that one).

I recommend this game to those who enjoy puzzles, but only if you don't mind getting stuck and really having to think about the solution and plan several steps in advance.

Imagine making a fantastic puzzle game, then ruining it with lack of undo and unskippable animations.

Unit 404 has a lovely aesthetic, including music and animations. Its earlier levels are doable and enjoyable despite the already annoying lack of undo, but in later levels (i.e. roughly around level 46, when the Rotator block is introduced), lack of undo becomes outright unacceptable.

That plus the long and unskippable animations makes the game unfinishable, because it turns the process of puzzle-solving, which should be enjoyable and quick and full of exploration, into a conservative experience where you're afraid of making any moves at all - because any mistake means you have to replay a bunch of the level. And heaven forbid if you misclick; then you still have to replay the lengthy levels.

It's a pity how much a single design decision can ruin what could otherwise have been an unambiguously great game.

I was hooked on this one right from the start- if you're intrigued enough about this game that you are reading the reviews, I can assure you it's worth a play through (or two, or three, or more)! 

PROS: I felt like I was able to develop my player character in many creative, meaningful ways. Many CYOA games have these set brackets your character can fall into and there's not much development beyond that. In this game, I felt like my character had personality that was developed throughout the adventure, and through my choices they were able to experience a world that changed and adapted around them. For something that is the draw of CYOA games, it's something that I don't see too often, but I felt that IIPTC excelled at it. 

As expected with Heart's Choice, the romance is well written and all three LIs were intriguing in their own way. I was determined that my character would be with Charlotte (I'm guilty of choosing before I even start the game lol) but darn it if Katharina didn't enchant as well- I was pleasantly surprised at how unique and special each of the options are. And I really appreciate that there's a friendship option for all of them (and plenty of non-LIs) too :)

CONS: The story flowed beautifully throughout the first half, but after the first confrontation with Apollon, things started to  feel very rushed. Passages that were once an entire page were suddenly just a few sentences or a line or two apiece. The plot that had been building up so intricately seemed to just... fall apart. There were still threads there, but it honestly felt like things were wrapping up only to be told that X amount of words were still needed. The random notes, one after another, about where support lies- from the people, the court, and foreign influences- was so abrupt and out of place (and one after the other) that it jerked me right out of the experience. Such a shame to have things so rushed!

That being said, these little things didn't ruin the game for me and I do highly recommend it. The author is very skilled with words and this is definitely a story to be swept up in! If you are searching for well-written LGBT+ interactive fiction, you should give this game a try.

The products that result from asset flips aren't "real" games.  They lack depth and content, because they're just simplistic copies of demos or tutorials.  In this case, "Clowns" is just a basic 2D retro pixel 1-screen platformer shooter with enemies that fall from the top of the screen, and doesn't have any merit as a proper, fully fledged PC game, so a copy+paste of it can't be recommended.

Asset flips don't involve any professional game development.  Sure, sometimes they may change a few cosmetic things, swap out different assets etc, but at heart it's functionally identical to the asset they're ripping off.  Asset flips are an insult to both PC gamers and to professional game developers who create genuine, high quality PC games.  Asset flips like this are harmful to the gaming industry and to Steam because they reduce the visibility that sincerely made indie games should have.  They make it harder for gamers to find genuine games made by honest developers.

To cement the position of this asset flip as nothing but a cash grab, it was dumped onto cheap DailyIndieGame shovelware bundles very shortly after launch.  Don't reward this morally bankrupt, unethical behaviour from Big Black Bear/Repa Games/ImperiumGame.

Pipe Mania is an ancient game from 2008.  It's a whopping 16 years old at the time of this review.  The game lacks support for the typical features of modern gaming PCs, hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on contemporary machines.  The game looks and feels dated.  Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an old game.  This seems to have be lingering on Steam with an inflated price to try profit from abandonware.

This is a re-hash of 1989's Amiga game, Pipe Dream/Pipe Mania, but it's not copyright infringement, it looks like Empire Interactive are a valid copyright holder for it, so that's something.  That doesn't mean this is a great game... Pipe Dream has been rehashed so many times (heck, it's the hacking minigame in Bioshock), and this teenaged rehash isn't a winner.  You get some different skins/game modes etc but is that really what was needed to make a smash hit out of something that would today be more fitting as a Flash game?  Nope.  And I'm never going to tell gamers on Steam to spend money on glorified Flash games.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio, due to the age of the game, it predates the 16:9 widescreen gaming standard established back in 2006.  It's possible they're marketing this towards people using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game is being specifically marketed towards people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.  It's obviously not going to look right on a modern 16:9 gaming display.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Pipe Mania is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $4 USD, and it's not worth it.  The game is just too old, hasn't been modernised.  And as the old saying goes, you can't go home again.  This is also competing with over 11,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

It was a rainy night when I decided to give Pipe Mania a spin. The city outside my window was a haze of neon and bad decisions, and I figured this old dame of a puzzle game might distract me from the weight of the world. But instead, it felt like she pulled me into her web—a slick, polished trap that looked promising, only to leave me wrestling with frustration and regret.

This wasn’t my first tango with the pipe puzzle genre. I’d seen her offspring in games like BioShock, where puzzles had more finesse and let you think your way out of a jam. But this? This was a relic of the past—rough around the edges and unforgiving as a double-cross.

[hr]

[h1][b]The Allure: A Dame with Style[/b][/h1]

She had looks, no doubt about that. The presentation was all class—animations that flowed like bourbon in a cheap glass, sound effects that clinked and clattered like poker chips in a smoky backroom. She even had the audacity to bring some personality to her act, with themed levels and quirky settings that felt like walking into a speakeasy full of colorful characters.

And for a moment, I was under her spell. I could see why she’d become a legend. Over 250 levels, a name that echoed through the annals of gaming history—this was the kind of dame you didn’t just forget. But the deeper I went, the more I realized she had a nasty streak.

[hr]

[h1][b]The Crime: A Rigged Game[/b][/h1]

She didn’t play fair. From the first level, I knew I was in for trouble. The pieces she handed me? Random, like pulling cards from a stacked deck. Couldn’t rotate ‘em either. Try building a network of pipes with tools like that, and you’re just begging to get burned.

And the penalties? Oh, she was cruel. Lay a piece you don’t use, and she’d dock your points. Try to fix a mistake? She’d dock you again. It didn’t matter what you did—she’d find a way to make you feel like a sap.

Then there was the Flooze. It surged through the pipes like a mob enforcer after a debt. You only had a few seconds to plan before it came barreling down the line, forcing you to slap pieces down and hope for the best. Strategy? Forget about it. You were playing her game, by her rules, and she didn’t leave much room for finesse.

[hr]

[h1][b]The Mystery: Why Bring Her Back?[/b][/h1]

There was something tragic about it all. Why bring this old dame back, dressed up in new clothes but still clinging to her outdated ways? She didn’t even have the decency to adapt to the times—no resolution scaling, no modern controls, no forgiveness for mistakes. She was a relic, and she didn’t even try to hide it.

I couldn’t help but think of all the imitators that had done her act better. BioShock’s hacking mini-game came to mind—cleaner, sharper, more rewarding. Even the cheap knockoffs I’d stumbled across on Steam had more sense than this.

[hr]

[h1][b]The Verdict: A Classic That’s Seen Better Days[/b][/h1]

She wasn’t all bad. She had charm, she had history, and she had content—more than enough to keep someone who could look past her flaws busy for a while. But me? I couldn’t shake the feeling that I’d been had.

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]

    Stunning visuals and sound design.
    Nostalgic appeal for those who remember her heyday.
    Plenty of levels for the masochists who stick around.

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]

    Random, non-rotatable pieces kill any chance of real strategy.
    Harsh penalties punish experimentation and mistakes.
    The Flooze’s relentless march makes planning impossible.
    Outdated features with no modern conveniences.

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b]

She was a dame with a past, and maybe that’s enough for some. But me? I need more than style and history to hold my interest. I need substance. And this game didn’t have it. So I put her back on the shelf, poured myself a drink, and wondered why I ever gave her a chance in the first place.

I wish there was a neutral review option because Across the Obelisk is a good and well made game, but it just isn't for me. The systems and gameplay is really crunchy and flow well, but my biggest problem with it is that there are too many options for making builds.

Now that sounds insane considering I'm talking about a roguelite, I completely understand-- how can so much replayability and so many options be a bad thing? For me, it just gets overwhelming quickly. I like to think that I'm good at balancing a lot of things in games. I've been playing PC games for over a decade at this point and can usually adapt to a game's systems, but this just feels so different.

The options are immense. First, you have more than a dozen different characters to pick from (with only a small portion unlocked at the beginning to ease you into it, luckily), each of which have different archetypes. Then, in singleplayer, you have to build a 4 character party. Then, after that, you have to assign any skill points you've gotten from playing characters in the past to multiple different trees in 4 different tabs. Then, once you do that for all 4 of your characters, you get into the game and are immediately greeted with a town where you can spend gold to buy from a selection of equipment for each of your individual heroes or magic shards to craft [i]nearly any card in the game for any one of your heroes[/i].

Then, of course, after you leave and start having encounters, each card is so unique and has so many different abilities tied to it that you're spending most of your time reading really dense and content-filled tooltips and trying to figure out what your wide selection of starting cards does... and of course, when you win that battle, each of your 4 heroes is given a selection of 3 random cards to pick from and add to their deck. I'm sure you can see how this gets complicated quickly, especially when you start finding cards with crazier and crazier abilities or trying to synergize with your gear and skill tree upgrades you picked at the beginning of the run.

I'm sure this would all be more manageable if you only had to worry about a single hero (if you were playing the co-op multiplayer mode for instance), but the fact that you have to balance the needs of an entire party in singleplayer makes it overwhelming to me. 

I'm surprised that I'm writing this as a fan of roguelike games and don't mind these elements in others-- but Across the Obelisk feels different to me. I suppose the difference is that in similar games like Slay the Spire, you're presented with a small selection of choices and need to make the most of what you can get. In Across the Obelisk, you're presented with an entire library of cards, multiple full skill trees, and shops filled to the brim with items and told to make the most overpowered build you can before even fighting your first encounter.

TLDR: Don't buy this game if you get overwhelmed easily or suffer from analysis paralysis in gaming, and do buy it if you love carefully crafting complicated and unique builds and don't mind spending a while getting to grips with the mechanics.

Out of all the games which follow a similar formula of blending in within a crowd of bots (such as Thief Town or Unspottable), this game is by far the most intense and addictive. I have actively searched for games which do a better job than this one, but I have not found anything yet.

Now you may be wondering, what makes this game so much better than the others?
Well, first of all, in other "hiding in plain sight" games (such as Thief Town and Unspottable, as I mentioned before), every player is hidden and is actively trying to battle each other. While this may sound like a positive, this actually removes a lot of the tense moments of having someone walk just by you as you blend in, since everyone is hidden just the same. Also, since every player is preoccupied with trying to discover the others, there isn't enough of a focus on actually trying to blend in and stealthily hide your every move.
"The Mutineer", on the other hand, pits exactly 2 players in an extremely close quarters scenario, with one Overseer attempting to find one Mutineer blending into the crowd. Due to this, both players will be wary of every move and the Mutineer will have to be extremely cautious with their actions, since the Overseer is placing all their attention on them. This also results in those phenomenal tense moments when the Overseer just passes over the Mutineer.

Here is a basic rundown of how the game is played.
The mutineer has to cause a total of 4 engines to be sabotaged at a single point in time, whereas the overseer has to stop the mutineer by providing a gigantic uppercut to the face. However, the overseer only has a small specific number of chances to punch and stop the mutineer (with the default number being 3, but this can be adjusted).

The mutineer's sabotage animation is identical to the regular engineers' "repair" (which is only an animation and does not impact the actual state of the engines) animations, meaning that they can use this to frame innocent engineers by sabotaging at the same time while they "repair" an engine. Since the overseer is only notified that a sabotage has happened, and not which engine was sabotaged, they can be tricked if the mutineer succeeds in doing this.

On the other hand, the overseer, along with having 3 "punches" to stop the mutineer, also has a specific small amount of "commands" which they can use to ask an engineer to actually fix a sabotaged engine. However, engineers don't always agree to actually fix it and can simply walk off. On top of that, there is a small chance that the overseer asked the mutineer, which results in an incredibly tense moment for the mutineer, giving them the option of either fixing the engine to play the role of an innocent engineer, or completely ignore the request despite accepting the command, which wastes one of the overseer's "commands" but risks them being caught.

The Light At The End Of The Ocean is a short visual novel that explores a light mystery about a shipwreck survivor. The surface story has enough depth to be entertaining and not obvious while still wearing its narrative themes like a neon pink shirt. As a short experience, this visual novel offers enough substance to be worth a look if you are seeking a quick easy story that is still sufficiently poignant to exist in-between the gap of deep introspection and turning your brain completely off.

Pros:
* A cute and surprisingly intricate art style that services and meshes well with the narrative. The artist/writer put time and thought into designing their characters art and it shows.  
* A simple standard and functional interface that should be familiar to anyone who has ever read a visual novel.
* A short, well-paced story that lasts long enough to tell its tale without overstaying its welcome.
* Good transitions between scenes. I was especially impressed with a specific fade transition between daytime and night, especially for a project of this scale.

Cons:
* Although the narrative is short by design, this visual novel would probably have benefited from an additional structural alternative ending that doesn't fork only at the conclusion. As designed, there is one "bad" ending, one "good" ending that requires a specific choice combination, and one fork from the "bad" ending that only requires a single choice variation and is not particularly influenced by the plot and still uses the same story path. An additional plot-based ending that forked from the current linear narrative somewhere before the end would have provided some needed depth to make the story not completely linear.

The Light At The End Of The Ocean fulfills its role as a short but enjoyable visual novel. This is not a work you would pickup to spend half of or a full day engrossed in exploring, however as an after work or after school experience to unwind to this VN is a good choice. I would also struggle to recommend this VN at its full price given its length, however at a discounted price the experience is well-worth the cost.   

Score: 7/10 -> Cute, quick, and straight-forward visual novel to enjoy

For what it is, the developer made a faithful retro platformer similar to what you would find in the SNES library. On a side note, the FishHead games started in 1998 so it's cool to see an indie developer going back 20+ years and still making progress, just looking at the games you can see him improving so much in terms of visuals and game logic (sorry I know I sound like an obsessive fan). The game has 4 worlds that are separated into multiple stages and one bonus world, or about 5 hours of content for 100% completion. It also has some traditional platforming progression in a form of unlockable power-ups such as double-jump, wall-jump and swimming power, although I am not sure why the Fish dude could not swim in the first place ;). Oh yea, you can also ride a goose sometimes, too bad you can't do that during regular stages like a certain dinosaur.

Visually, I thought the pixel art was very enjoyable, I like the whole 'Fishman vs Tomatoes' premise. Some would say that every great platformer starts with a very unlikely character - you know, plumbers, hedgehogs, 7-up mascots, or a worm in a power suit (at least you got the weirdness down). The game has good platforming controls, I am particularly happy that all the basic moves use the classic inputs like 'up' to grab or just bouncing off walls with no extra buttons - you would be surprised how many people ____ that up. All the compliments aside, I do feel like the game is missing that 'secret ingredient', every game that I love in this genre has something special about it, some gimmick like hitting blocks with your head, spinning into a ball or using your head like a whip. You made a decent game, but it just feels like a tribute instead of being FishHead experience. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

+ faithful retro aesthetic and soundtrack
+ decent length with some bonus content
+ cute characters, riding a goose :)
+ decent controls, some power-up progression

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] General Feedback [/u] - the big thing that I found kinda clunky was the lack of invincibility frames, you have 3 hitpoints but the enemies can get very lucky and hit you 3 times in 1 second (usually in the corner or on the belt). The game has some occasional problems with hidden death pits, there is no way to look down at the time of this review. Additionally, I would like to be able to perform a regular jump while on the ladder. Oh and the boss fights were too short, I know you just making a simple game, but you can beat some of them in 6 seconds, maybe they needed a second phase.

[u] Secret Ingredient [/u] - sometimes I find myself attached to a platforming game even without any story, something about the level design that makes it memorable. This game, it's kinda like getting over obstacles, you not taking full advantage of the player's desire to navigate the world, but there are moments where I feel like you had the right idea. So I would just say, double-down on exploration, more secrets, hidden characters, make the currency more relevant, maybe unlockable fish hats, I don't know, just more than just levels that feel like an obstacle. 

[b] Overall Thoughts: 7/10 [/b]

I think the developer and myself are holding on to the past, the developer makes a decent but predictable retro game, then I buy it because it reminds me of something that I played as a kid. So where do we go from here? Maybe next FishHead game could be a Metroidvania? Whatever it is, I just hope that you enjoy what you doing, even if only 3 people play it.

It’s a short, entertaining game built on idioms.

For some reasons, I expected a variety of English language-based puzzles, but “The Game Is On” is based almost exclusively on idioms. There will be a tiny speck of different puzzles here (a few math ones come to mind), as an extra incentive to find all the jigsaw pieces scattered across all the levels, but in general – it’s fairly straightforward.

I like the humor here – a bit silly, a bit wacky, probably not for everyone, but it can be discerned from screenshots and trailers almost immediately, so those who would go for it – most likely will “get” it.

 While the humor works, when it comes to actual idiom guessing – it can be a hit and miss. A good portion can be solved by using brain cells, but quite a few will eventually be solved by clicking every possible combination of available items until the result will be displayed. In about half of the cases I thought “Oh, man! I should’ve known that”, but in the other half it was “Oh, wow. This wasn’t what I was thinking AT ALL”. Keep in mind though, that Boris is from south-east Europe and his English “not very gud”, so maybe it’s that intriguing foreign logic applied to English idioms that made things slightly confusing. Fun, but confusing.

 There’s a hint system, by the way, but I didn’t find it to be immensely helpful – it just highlights everything you can click on, that’s about it. In a way, it did force me to sit and think longer than I probably would have otherwise, but it could have definitely been something more solid. Developer is responsive on forums, however, so that’s cool.

There’s pleasant looping BG music present – just enough to keep you going for yet another short level, and the graphics are “simple cartoon” style, but it totally works with the humor and the game itself.

Basically, if you know what you are walking into – a short game based on silly idiom guessing - it’ll be an entertaining brainteaser/confuser (yeah, I made up the last word – let’s hope Boris will pick it up, hehe). Won’t be for everyone, as this is as indie as it gets, but I enjoyed it, so no regrets.

Although the game is not what I would describe as a 'sandbox' mode, once you get some experience, it begins to feel this way. With a great selection of turrets to choose from, each one having a different effect on the enemies, it really does feel like you have unlimited ways of playing the level. Not only is this just fun from the get-go but it means that the game does not get boring. 

Every component part of the game is designed extremely well. Currently, there are 4 turrets to play with: one of them is a standard laser gun, another fires more powerful shots at a slower pace, another slows enemies down, and the final turret fires a laser that inflicts a constant stream of damage upon the enemies. Working out which turrets to use in each circumstance is particularly fun and, of course, depending on how you use them, how many you place, and where you place them, your success at levels will certainly vary. There really is an art to playing this game well and, when you do, it can be immensely satisfying. The actual models for the turrets perfectly suit the genre of the game and look really cool, particularly the slime beamer.

The colours of the game really pop out at you: the level tracks are a neon pink, the lasers fire bright neon green colours, the enemies are brightly coloured balls, and there are flashing explosions when enemies are destroyed. These are not easy to notice but, when you zoom in, you can really grasp the finer details of the game. On a purely visual level, the graphics are tremendous and work seamlessly with each other. 

The soundtrack of the game is equally as impressive. I have no clue whether this soundtrack was composed by the creator of the game, but it is certainly unique and I have never heard it anywhere else. It nevertheless perfectly suits the graphics of the game and its genre which, to me, seems to be a cross between tower defence and arcade games, with a disco theme. [To the publisher - could you please make this theme available to download, I'd like it as a ringtone!]

I noticed that the publisher and developer of the game, Ben Shattock, did all of this on his own. From what I gather, this is a one-man job which, given the tremendous detail and quality of the game, is a remarkable achievement. 

As you might be able to tell, I would highly recommend this game to anybody reading. Not only is it extremely fun to play, but there are a lot of levels, multiple difficulties, and numerous ways of playing the game, all of which ensure that boredom is unlikely to occur. I for one am pleased that I bought this game and I'm sure that you will be too!

[b] B67 is a short, rough game, and that's both good and (obviously) bad. Being torn between positives and negatives of the game, I've decided to label the review as "Reccomended" to support the developers. [/b]

[b] ON ONE HAND [/b] it is a quite refreshing top-down shooter. The enemy soldiers while being somewhat dumb are really deadly, melting health bar in an instant if given the chance in form of player's poorly timed reloading. Managing long reloading animations is a key to survival, as each weapon holds amount of bullets enough to dispose of 1 or 2 enemies before running dry. Guns feel satisfying and powerful to use against the enemy heavy armor, justifying high bullet cost gunplay.

The art style is another higlight of the game. The combination of voxelated 3D, pixelated hud and distoted audio gives B67 a great mashup of arcadey and horror feelings (the latter being criminnaly ignored by the game trailer). Surreal stuff happening around, established evil alignment of playable character and videogame take on office environments create an atmosphere of a playable horror B movie, and a good one at that.

[b] ON THE OTHER HAND [/b] it falls flat as a roguelite. Yes, there are randomly stitched floors, variety of guns and permanent upgrades, but there's no substance to all of theese. Floors are completly devoid of any reason to explore them (besides finding the last stuck enemy) while allowing player to easily cheese trigger disciplined AI by camping doorways or corners. Each weapon within one of four categories (pistols, shotguns, SMGs and assault rifles) feel the same, one is barely more powerful than another. On top of that the guns are easily accessable from just looting the bodies, so there's no enjoyment in loot hunting associated with the genre to be found here either. Upgrades are basically total ammo caps, again nothing interesting. Considering the above I've easily got to the game ending on the second try, and while I generally had fun during the run it was waay too generous with the "continues" and the difficulty.

[b] TLDR; For what it's worth I would recommend B67 as a fun top down shooter for one or two fun evenings, don't expect fleshed out roguelike elements [/b]

I know this game came out over a year ago and I'm not certain if the developers even remember that they made this game, but there are a couple of suggestions that I'd like to make that I think would take this game from great to perfect.
The AI isn't as bad as some people in negative reviews have made them out to be, but they do seem kind of inconsistent. Dodge rolling seems to be a great way to confuse your enemies for a second and it seems to reset the AI's aim time if they haven't already started shooting, but sometimes enemies will just stare at you for a solid second before you get to them and take them out which can kind of take you out of the experience. I think a great fix would be to slightly decrease the amount of time it takes for the AI to lock onto you as you get later into elevator levels, essentially adding another element to the increasing difficulty. 

A really simple but great addition would be to add some pickups around the levels, even something as simple as occasional hidden ammo or armor drops that you have to seek out around levels would make exploring levels a lot more fun.

A more complex addition that I wouldn't really expect to ever happen would be some kind of simple weapon modification system, being able to attach a suppressor to weapons to allow you to silently take out some guards before alerting the rest, or a laser pointer that gives you a more accurate judgement of where you're aiming, or jungle-taped magazines for increased reload speed. 

My last recommendation is a more personal one, some kind of system that allows you to add your own music to the game would be great. I really liked some of the music, and I particularly liked how each new level starts a different song, but there's not many songs so they start to get kind of old eventually (excluding the shop level theme because that shit is smooth). There's not really an easy way to emulate the way music works in this game when turning music on in a browser.

As someone who's played a bunch of rogue-likes (Binding of Isaac, FTL Faster Than Light, Wazhack etc.) I can safely say that I really enjoy this game.

Unlike other Rogue-lites, you've got a progression sequence that can carry on over multiple runs, so no playthrough, however small, is ever a waste. But this opens up other choices to consider - will you stock up at a shop floor or push on and risk death but save your money to help your chances in your next run?

Graphics are a nice '2.5D' pixel artstyle, and the game is played from an isometric viewpoint in a 3D environment.

Sound design is extremely satisfying, from the thuds and pings of your bullets against enemy armor to the ding of the elevator to let you know you've cleared a floor. 

The game gives you the controls but deliberately leaves out other mechanics for you to discover and learn on your own (example Protip - you can figure out what ammo will go in what gun).

There are a bunch of weapons in the game from silenced pistols to heavy machine guns. The gameplay shone the most for me in the later floors when I completely ran out of ammo and had to resort to killing each enemy with the previous one's gun. 

Should've stocked up.
Nearly got myself killed.
Felt like a badass.

There are 67 randomised floors to traverse in the main game and an endless mode I'm working towards the highscore on. 

As a last note, with the way this game works it's definitely open to speed-runs / challenge-runs, and has a great arcade-style feel that means it's viable to jump on and play even if you've only got a few minutes to spare.

While I have not gotten very far in this game, I can tell you that it has a good amount of polish and some very interesting new mechanics, most of which are connected to the language learning aspect of the game. 

The language learning mechanics actually bring a lot to Shujinkou. For example, early on you can pair your attacks with different elements represented by hiragana, and enemies have weaknesses tied to certain elements and the characters that make up their names. Additional language-related mechanics unlock over the course of the game, and each of them add some depth to the combat and how you interact with the game world (e.g. mini-games and non-combat activities). Also, because the mechanics are uniquely tied to language, they are unlike anything you would find in another DRPG; Cryptmaster might be an exception to this rule, but that game is a bit of a genre oddity.

This is also a full-fledged DRPG that seems to be offering quite a bit more than recent titles from devs that could be considered veterans of the genre. Maybe it is just me, but I feel like DRPG fans have been inundated with Wizardry clones that have copy-paste classes and abilities save for one or two character options; this is the first DRPG that I have played in a while that breaks that mold. I don't really know how to rate the maps, and I think that there is a chance that they are a bit simple/small, but I will take simple over needlessly convoluted or trap-laden any day. 

I think there are a few drawbacks with this game. First, there is a ton of dialogue for a DRPG, and I feel like it really takes me out of the action of the game even if it is entirely appropriate. Second, I really wish that transition screens and in-dungeon movement were smoother and faster. To make matters a bit worse, D-pad input is lagged, which the devs really ought to fix. Lastly, there is the price, which is very high compared to many DRPGs at release and will absolutely be a barrier for entry for many folks that are a part of the target audience. That being said, there seems to be a ton of content and side activities in the game,  and it is very clear that the devs put a lot of time and effort into every aspect of the game.

Anyway, for now the game will get a fairly strong recommend from me because I love DRPGs and this brings something new to the genre unlike most other titles. At this point, it seems a like a perfect game for genre fans (especially if they want to learn Japanese) so long as they can get over the price point. If my opinion changes drastically, I will update this review.

First things first, I think it's worth addressing the sort of elephant in the room for many people, which is the price. For me personally, whether or not this was 30 or 60 dollars would not change my own personal life significantly, and I'm happy to help indie teams, or in this case, lone developers, make ends meet. Your personal comfort level with that may differ based on your career and employment or financial situation, and that's fine, I'm just addressing this from my own POV.

Now, for the game review. I'm not very far in the game yet, so this is more of a preliminary review. For context, I'm a Japanese learner who is somewhere between N4 and N3, so that's going to color my review a bit. For those of you that aren't really JP learners, that's between 'pre-intermediate' and 'intermediate'.

I'll say flat out that if you're not really interested in learning the language, that this game may not be for you. It's something of an 'edutainment' game, in that it features learning quite heavily in the mechanics and systems of the game. For people who are already JP language learners, this game starts you off at the pre-N5 level, in other words, teaching the kana. If you haven't started learning Japanese, and you want to, I can recommend this game as a great way to get your foot in the door. If you want to, you can and will quickly learn the kana using this game, and I'd say you'll be able to read anything in hiragana (+ with furigana) pretty fast.

Regarding that, so far, most of the learning seems vocab based, with enemies using romaji names that you must (or really, should) match to their appropriate kana. So far I've only encountered hirigana, but I assume that katakana will appear, and I assume kanji will, at some point, start showing up as well. The rest of the instruction for language, so far, have been in boards spread across the labyrinth, which teaches (so far) the stroke order for the hirigana kana and their histories (which was interesting!) as well as some simple grammar. I'm not sure if grammatical concepts will ever play a role in the game itself, though I think there'll be some degree of deeper complexity in how it uses the language. Incidentally, the game does seem to not follow 'standard practice' in teaching the kana, which I found kind of interesting; you learn the ten ten forms of the k and s lines before you learn the m or n line, while normally you'd learn all the kana, and then all its variants. I don't really mind it, just curious what the reasoning there was.

As far as the gameplay and polish goes, so far, it's pretty good. Combat is a mixture of snappy and slow, but is adjustable. As far as other dungeon crawlers go, this is somewhere closer to Etrian Odyssey or Labyrinth of Yomi compared to the Refrain series. Unlike EO, there's no rows (yet, at least, they may be introduced later), and elements play something of a bigger role, at least early game. Like in EO, there's resource spots in the world that you can harvest from, and a lot of directional shortcuts that really did evoke EO3 or 4. So far, the combat hasn't been fleshed out, but given that there's additional greyed out options for me, I'm sure it'll develop much more and get more complicated, which is exciting for me. That said, at least so far, unlike most DRPGs, you don't pick from classes or create your own characters, which has its ups and downs. Personally, I don't really like the hyper minmax elements of a lot of DJRPGs, so I'm ok with that, but if your favorite part of EO3 is running around with the crazy broken builds, then I don't think that you're going to get what you want. In some ways, I think that speaks to the polish (so far), since a lot of the old EO game breaking builds were bugs or improperly balanced. YMMV there. A fun addition is a day/night cycle, but also a week cycle  where each day corresponds to a day of the week which is related to its element. 

Storywise, I'm enjoying it, though I don't have a lot of buy in just yet. It doesn't have the emotional weight for me that Gallaria had, yet, for instance, but it certainly is more story focused than any of the EOs or Labyrinth of Yomi. A big part of that is that the characters are predefined, and so there's quite a lot of dialogue of them talking. I like text heavy, story heavy games and VNs, so this doesn't bother me, but if your only goal is to run around a maze and hit things DJRPG style, know what you're getting into. I think the setting (so far) is kind of like Japan with the name filed off, but again, I'm in the very early game (cleared Dungeon 1, second town), so I expect it to open up considerably.

As far as complaints, I don't have many yet, though it's certainly not a perfect game, but I'm happy with what it is. I think my biggest nitpick is that I'm not really a fan of the kanji font, which isn't a real problem.

I've only played the bit, but I can echo what others have said: seems surprisingly polished for an indie game. The graphics look much better in motion than they do on some of the stills (I was a little wary after seeing the trailer, but at least on my graphics settings the 2D characters / movement on 3D background feels more reminiscent of Paper Mario than, say, Boomer Shooters or cheap Unity platformers).

What I do what to recommend to people is the language settings. I was pleasantly surprised at how well designed this was for learning! Usually when trying to learn Japanese with a game, you are relying on knowing a huge chunk of Japanese grammar / vocabulary going in, so that you can read about 80% of the text without help. This leaves a pretty large gap between people just starting or having studied a bit of Japanese, and people wanting to play games - After a year of studying and finishing an introductory textbook, you might still have another year ahead of you before something easy like Pokemon becomes accessible.

In this game, the story and combat text is all in English. The names and items are all in Japanese. This is great, because it solves that core "gap" issue - I can play the game comfortably, and bite that 20% of words I don't know without becoming overwhelmed. The ability to switch rapidly between Kanji, Kana, and Hepburn pronunciations is also nice, because it means I don't have to use a third party utility to pronounce words.

There is also to be said for "discovering" the enemy names, and then reinforcing that memory each time you attach. As a memory tool, It goes a long way to quickly digesting a big chunk of very useful Japanese. It is certainly much more fun than flashcards! Probably quicker too.

Some people might know GameGengo's review system, which ranks games roughly by inclusion of Furigana (Hiragana guides to Kanji pronunciation), Japanese Voices, Dialog Speed, Replayable Audio, and Replayable Scenes. In this game, there is no Furigana viewable with the Kanji present, though you can quickly toggle between the two, so I would give it full marks there. There are no voices for the main text, though all Japanese words do have Japanese audio to go with them in a study log, and all "found" words are reviewable at almost any time. I don't know that scenes are replayable, but I also haven't hit any cutscenes with Japanese in them (they may only be in English).

I'm pretty obsessed with learning Japanese so when I heard about this game a few years ago I've been waiting in excitement for its release. I've never played a dungeon crawler game before and was honestly worried I wouldn't be able to play due to motion sickness. Camera Bobbing (Labyrinth) can be disabled in the settings. When in the labyrinth I can have the map on full screen so when I'm doing a bunch of turns in the labyrinth my motion sickness doesn't get triggered as my eyes have something still to focus on. So yes this game is motion sickness friendly! 

When the demo came out I played the main story and did ALL the side missions which are on the 要求看板 Youkyuu Board. The missions you do on this board are requests from citizens within that town that are in need of help. 

要求 (ようきゅう)
看板 (かんばん)

Doing the side missions on the 要求看板 helps you gain money and EXP in the game which is especially helpful if you are struggling in a labyrinth and need help with leveling up and getting better combat items at the 木武器屋 (もくぶきや). If you are a sushi lover then beware as there is A LOT of sushi in this game which you can get at the 黒寿司 (くろずし). This game only strengthens my sushi cravings!!! Language settings can be changed at anytime and even though setting it in Japanese (kanji/furigana) doesn't turn the entire game into Japanese it still does effect change to when exploring areas like the towns, buying items, special abilities (which get unlocked later in the game), the menu screen, etc. The dialogue is still in english and the blue text for words is usually shown in english or romaji (you can press 3 on the keyboard to see the kanji/furigana of the blue text word. The game is dialogue heavy which is fine with me since a large percentage of games I play are 乙女ゲーム, so if you don't like text heavy games then this may not be a game you'll enjoy. 

The Labyrinths I feel are a good brain workout as when you enter the map only shows where you have gone in the labyrinth (what tiles you have walked through) so if it's your first time then the entire map is blank only showing the spot where you are at. You have to explore the labyrinth to reveal more on the map. In the labyrinth there are 悪魔 (あくま) akuma which are usually animals that have been corrupted and the dangerous 野獣 (やじゅう) Yajuu!!! In combat against for example the 悪魔 you can damage it 3 different ways. 1st way is using a kana character that is part of their name, 2nd way is using an elemental orb that matches with the day of the week, and 3rd is using the elemental orbs they are weak to. Speaking of elemental orbs I wasn't excited about them at first as that is how we learn the kana is through these orbs which take awhile to get through  and I already know the kana. I would say learning that the orbs can be used in 3 different ways as mentioned above during combat and also that we get introduced to a word that uses that kana when first getting the orbs I actually liked a lot as it often exposed me to words I didn't know at all.

I've been so busy with the main story and the 要求看板 side missions that I haven't even tried out the 風ロビー (ふうろびー) Fuu Lobby which has a bunch of different Japanese practice mini games such as a Japanese counter game, grammar games/sentence forming, verb conjugation, radicals game, vocabulary game, etc.

There is just so many activities and things to do in this game it's insane! (And looking through it looks like there are 3 minigames that haven't been unlocked yet so I don't even know what those will be until I get further through the story, and this is me at about 100 hours of game time/I have cleared 5 labyrinths.) And let me just say real quick that the music in this game is incredible especially when fighting in boss battles. (There was 1 boss battle where everything including the music that went along with it just made my jaw drop, it was すごい！)

For me personally the cons at the moment is the blue text words in game text box only in english/romaji (clicking on the number 3 does reveal kanji, furigana, romaji, and english all together of that word). I would prefer seeing the blue text words in kanji/kana form and then clicking on 3 on the keyboard to see the kanji/furigana/english all together no romaji. This is a trilogy game series so I hope for the 2nd game that is how the blue text is done. The other con to me is the inventory/storage limit for items such as 悪魔 drop and resource items. I'm okay with the inventory limit, but the storage limit needs to be expanded. My understanding is the developer is going to work on expanding the storage limit so there will be less stress on guessing which items to keep and which items to discard as it can suck when discarding items to make room for more items and then accepting a side mission from the 要求看板 requesting x items that were just discarded!

There are so many features/activities to do in this game that it feels impossible to list every single one in this review, so I hope people are willing to give this game a chance.

Aside from answering questions, the gameplay is mostly rhythm-based, pumping your heart in time to the beat of the music to stay alive just a few more minutes. After a while this intensifies and the meter starts draining faster, and if you hit 0%, it's game over and back to the beginning.

The Heartbeat is a good game to try different options and see what happens, and it helps that it has a nice cyberpunk aesthetic and the important text is fully translated into English as well. There are some mistakes in the spelling/grammar, but that's not a big deal. At only a dollar, I'd definitely recommend this game if you think you'd replay it.

You play a mayor of a cyberpunk metropolis who has overworked himself to the brink of death. Messing up the rhythm shortens the mayor's life even further, so you have to multitask: keep up the rhythm and read what your personal assistant has to report to be able to make a decision.

A whole playthrough only takes 5 minutes (and you will most likely not finish the game in your first run[s], at least I did not), but the multiple ways to either defeat the epidemic or to be defeated by it kept me entertained for about an hour. For the very low asking price, I think that's more than fair. The English translation is a bit shaky sometimes, but overall they are fine.

I'm not really sure if PANIC STATION is an asset flip.  Some elements of this game certainly make it seem like the developer put some effort into assembling some kind of original here.  On the other hand, a lot of the game assets don't seem like they were created by the developer, but they haven't credited any asset creators for supplying assets, which might be a case of plagiarism.  There's no evidence, so we need to give the benefit of the doubt... regardless, asset flip or not, the quality here is indistinguishable from many asset flip/cash grab scams, and that's a problem in itself.

There's also the contributing factor of the fake/paid review manipulation, which, if nothing else, will mean this game will be removed from Steam if Valve ever gets around to enforcing their own rules for developers.  Also, you know, who is arranging such admittedly nice looking assets for a trivial first person adventure where you walk around an empty space station and press "T" to turn off 8 monitors?  Because that's all this game is... yeah, if this isn't an asset flip, I'll eat my hat. 

Taking this shovelware seriously as if it was a genuine attempt to make a game, it doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 12 players, and the worst part is these weren't genuine players, these were the Russian fake review accounts that the developer paid to make the fake reviews.  Since the fake reviews are all done, now the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

The main objective is to complete 50 stages to escape the castle.   Each stage comprises of block puzzles which the player must interact by pushing them.  By pushing away the blocks it opens the path to switches.  By pressing these switches it opens the exit.  The player must quickly exit the level before time over.  In addition, there are ninja tools that the players earn as they progress through the game.  These tools introduces a new element into the puzzle solving which makes the game more complex as the player progresses.

As a bonus, this game has a level editor to create their own levels and publish them.  Levels from the community can be downloaded to play them.  

But is the game fun?  It all depends if you like block puzzles.  50 levels is fine and it didn't overstay its welcome.  With patience and persistence the player can finish this in one sitting. 

There are a few gripes such as the stage music not being able to loop seamlessly if you're in the same stage for too long.  Also, for players who are seeking variety, unfortunately, the majority of the game has a set pattern of go through each floor.  (push blocks, find switches then exit the room etc).  This is a block puzzle game at its core.  Players that do not like block puzzles should not play this game.

But for players that likes block puzzles try this game out.

[h1] Shallow Chinese Tank Arcade[/h1]

As it stands, right now, Armored Company of Heroes is an interesting proof of concept that is far from being complete enough to be worth the 15 dollar price tag. The only good thing I can really say about this game is that the graphics are pretty good for early access, but even the pretty tanks can hardly distract from the bare-bones gameplay. Each missions involves you doing the same point-and-click style of combat that begins to grate on your patience even before the first mission is over. Worse, the game requires you to drive through empty, desolate landscapes for up to five or ten minutes at a time until you reach your next "sit here and shoot" spot. The arcade-y mechanics of the game don't help in the variety department either (No bullet drop of any sort, restocking ammo is done by running over Mario Kart style pickups, hitting an enemy on the side does the same damage as hitting them from the front, etc.) 

So while I will be keeping my eye on this game to see if the developers eventually do anything with this foundational pre-alpha they've built, I can't recommend it to others to buy in its current state.

Having played Hero Armored Company for about 10 hours now, already some things can be said about this tank sim. Let me begin with the most important thing: I like it! This game has the potential to become a great tank simulator.
Does it have problems? Yes. Does it need improvement? Absolutely! But that doesn't wipe out the fact that this is the most fun tank sim I've played since World Of Tanks (and I've played a LOT of WoT!!!) - and for me at some points it even superseeds it!

THE GAME
For now only part of the single player content is available with a Story Mode (with at this moment 8 missions) - an aspect I definately miss in WoT! Single Player Mission Mode and Multiplayer Mode will become available at a later stage. So far I have been grinding myself though the Story Mode. 
The location is the fictious Republic ov EVIA, apparently bordering China. At your command is a modern line of Chinese tanks, starting with the ZTL-11 (which actually isn't a tank but an 8-wheeled IFV with a 105mm L7 tank gun - as comparative with the M1128 Stryker MGS), and working your way up to ZTQ-15 light tank, ZTZ-96 MBT and eventually the ZTZ-99 MBT. The missions in Story Mode are challenging, even on the easiest level. Each mission proves a tad more difficult, encountering ever better enemy tanks, up to the American M1A2 Abrams. As said, fortunately you also get better tanks along the way. Attack helo's and incoming artillery add to the mayhem wich makes a battlefield, but hey: you can put in some of your own. At your disposal are arty, helo support and even cruise missile strikes! Furthermore you have your own main gun to fight with, well equipped with APFSDS (sabot AT), HEAT and HE, as well as a 7.62mm coax MG, and on top of the TC's hatch a 12.7mm heavy MG.

THE TOPS
I very much like the fact that you can position yourself in most crew slots (where in WoT you have only outside and zoomed-in view). This reminds me of a fairly old tank sim called Spearhead (1998), which I occasionally still play. You have four slots: outside view, Tank Commander slot, Gunner slot and Top MG slot. The only one missing is the Driver slot.
Outside view is mainly used during movement from one point to another, having the best overall view. But I found myself mostly switching between the Tank Commander's and Gunner's slot, fighting the vehicle as it should be fought: the TC looking for targets, and the gunner disposing them. In TC slot you can also take the shot, but you have better zoom in Gunner's slot - then again you have a better overall view in TC slot. Like I said, as it should be. The Top MG is for taking out helicopters, but I found out it proves immensely easier to shoot those down with a single well-aimed HEAT or HE round from your main tube - hence the fact I rarely use the MG slot. 

THE TIPS
1. Looking through your battle sights you have different view modes - normal day view, IR and thermal, just like you would in your everyday modern battle tank. However, the latter should enable you to see through the fog of war (i.e. smoke from burning vehicles, explosions and smoke launchers) - and guess what: it doesn't. If anything, using IR or thermal restricts your view rather than enhancing it. I found myself using IR, then thermal, then switching back to day view and grittingly having to wait for the darn tank to appear out of the smoke before being able to have a clear shot at it. So there would be a major improvement to be made by the developer! 
2. I sometimes noticed my tank moving sideways when standing still, so that's a glitch to mend.
3. The Top MG and coax are for engaging dismounted infantry or soft vehicles (like trucks, jeeps and small recon vehicles), but so far I haven't encountered any of those in the game, which renders them pretty useless. It's pretty fun to shoot the coax at a T72 while your main tube is reloading, but it doesn't even scratch it. So it would be nice to add targets to the game that you can engage with your MGs. Perhaps they will be added in the final version - I sure do hope so, it would add to the realism. Really, please do!
4. I wonder if it wouldn't be better if the speed controls would be handled by, for instance, plus ( + ) and minus ( - ), instead of holding down the W key. Now your speed is either zero or max. With + and - you would be able to manage your speed - sometimes it simply is better to creep forward than to charge ahead at full speed.
5. I sure do hope that in the future we will also see tank lines from other countries! The M1A2 is already in the game (but at the wrong side, haha!), but I'm also thinking British Challenger 2, French Leclerc, German Leopard 2A7, Isreali Merkava IV, Korean K2 Black Panther, Japanese Type 10, Russian T80/90 and Armata, and so on.
6. For realism, I would add the Driver's slot.
7. In Story Mode, the missions have to be fought from tart to finish - no saves available. Perhaps it would be nice if at least one or two autosaves were implemented (quicksave would even be better!), because it can definately be an itsy-bitsy frustrating having to start the complete mission over again from scratch when you are destroyed by the very last enemy tank...
8. Sometimes the AI of friendly tanks is not just that. On two occasions I had my own tank flipped on the side by another tank of my platoon because apparently I was in its way, and on another the mission vehicle (a missile launcher which I was to protect during the drive to its deployment) was flipped over by an AA-gun vehicle engaging an incoming helicopter - making the mission impossible to execute. So that might need some work.

CONCLUSION
Hero Armored Company is a potent tank simulator, with realistic graphics and gameplay. Already it has given me hours of fun. With the improvements I recommended it can potentially be the game that pushes World Of Tanks from the leading position in the genre. 
Like I said at the beginning: I like it!!!

After waiting for a while for new updates, I looked into the developer's track record, to simply put it, they kind of have this a tendency to abandon project, and the discussion on Steam of this game seems like similar situation.
