Born Race is a game that we notice its simplicity and limitations in the first few seconds, which is not necessarily a bad thing, many games from the Flash era (which Born Race is very reminiscent of) were simple and limited, but excellent. It could be a game to put on the shelf of games that remember this era, which would be great for someone like me, who spent this entire era consuming countless games. But some points really harm the game. The mechanics are not very precise, which greatly harms a game where speed and the aforementioned precision are fundamental. This could be left aside, if there weren't the second and biggest problem: The bosses. There's no problem with them being difficult, and I don't think they're exactly difficult, the problem is the lack of clarity and problematic mechanics that make some bosses, like the robot, which is the second boss, beatable basically by luck. It could be an interesting game, but the boss fights hurt everything too much. A pity.

The theme of this game usually leads to meme games. Games that just want to be funny, without real mechanics and design. Born Race turns the "race of life" into a very interesting narrative, with characters, objectives, plot, development. And aside from the story, there's a great game to be played, with moments that require precision, others that require strategy or puzzle-solving.

Really recommended! Don't wait for a sale, it is really content-packed for the price

------------------

I would definitely liked a sequel. Maybe a longer one that could take this game to another level.

[b]enypnion[/b] is a short point & click adventure starring young jonathan, who's going on a fantastic journey in his sleep, so the title fits, as it roughly translates to [i]dream[/i].

can't say much about the story without spoiling stuff, but suffice it to say, the kid will visit spooky and colorful locations and meet friendly and not so friendly characters, while solving mostly trivial puzzles. basic chess knowledge might come in handy at one point and [b]there's some trial & error, as well as fail states if you do something stupid, but you get to try again almost immediately without losing progress[/b].

[b]the presentation is fantastic[/b], excellent artwork matching the fairytale-like setting, nice music, but no voiceovers. separate volume settings are available, plus saving and loading anytime over 8 slots. always appreciated, but it's not really necessary here, as the game [b]only takes a bit more than an hour[/b], but you might want to save here and there to get to the other ending faster.

dialog can be skipped line by line, but I wish cutscenes were clickable too, especially after a failure. nothing else to criticize, a few typos here and there, but nothing major. the price is more than friendly and [b]due to its low difficulty it can work well as someone's first point & click adventure[/b].

Again you should know what you're getting yourself into if you decide to purchase this game, it's a Game Jam Survival Horror Game with Fixed camera angles, embrace the Jank and enjoy the bits of humor in it and you'll get your $0.99 worth.

This is a really lovely game! A sweet, relaxing 2D plataformer that is challenging enough to be fun (specially if you, like me, are not really used to playing this type of game), but easy enough to make your experience something relaxing and entertaining, not stressful and tiring. I enjoy and look for relaxing, cozy, positive and cute games, and [i] Jumpy Paws [/i] checks all the boxes I look for in a game. :)

The levels are very cleverly designed to be just the right length and to hide surprises even from the start, so it's not absolutely obvious where to go or what to do, but it's logical enough for you to find the solution without having to wreck your brains out for it. 

I particularly love the graphic aspect, which makes the game have a happy feeling about it (helped along by the music). And our main character is a lovely little puppy, with cute interactions and reactions to the environment, which makes it very easy to connect with him, and makes me worry and care about him even if I'm spending only a short time helping him cross just one level in a small playing session. Also, the colorful scenarios, the nice little accessories that you can get as you move forward in the story, and the overall "feel" of the game are things that strongly appeal to me, and have made my time playing this game fun, relaxing and cozy, even when I'm facing certain challenging parts that don't go my way as easily as I'd like. That's one of the things I value the most in a game: how much fun I have playing it, without ending up stressed and even more neurotic than I was to begin with, and this game helps me enjoy myself, while challenging me at the same time.

The fact that you can reply each level to improve your score and earn more bones and jewels than you did in your first run is something that I've particularly enjoyed since, like I mentioned, I'm not very used to playing plataformer games and I needed some time to get used to the mechanics of this type of game. But it's all well explained, with a clear tutorial at the beginning, and, since the game supports my controller, it's all the more convenient to play and to do well even if you're not an experienced player, which is encouraging and, again, reinforces the feeling of accomplishment and fun you get when playing it.

Overall, I feel like this is a lovely game, with a cute little main character that you'll enjoy helping out and customizing to your taste. A game that's been done with care and that will provide you with many hours of really enjoyable fun, specially if you're looking for something relaxing and entertaining to do that won't take you all day long to finish, won't stress you out and that will, in general, give you a feeling of joy and optimism when you play it, which may be exactly what you need.

I'm looking forward to continuing my journey through the world of [i] Jumpy Paws [/i] and help him travel the world! And I definitely recommend anyone to try it and enjoy it too. The world needs more smiles, and a little curious and adventurous puppy on a mission is a little bit more of cuteness and fun in the world for us to enjoy and share. ;)

[h3]A true masterpiece.[/h3]

In of itself the game is art, which is hard to quantify in one's mind when you're wanting to know whether to play it. However, if you give this game the time and attention it deserves, and yes, that means eliminating all distractions for at least an hour, you may just find yourself in a magical, otherworldly experience that gives you the sort of vibes you won't find in many other places.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]Important:[/h3]
One thing to note however is that it doesn't necessarily conform to the traditional ideals of a video-game. What I mean by that is that navigation is limited, your dialogue choices don't have any immediate impact and there isn't a whole lot to interact with. Despite these points, if you think of it as somewhat of an interactive movie, or something akin to a reflective journey - rather than a game in the conventional sense - you’ll find meaning in its quiet moments. 

Let's take the train segment for example; your dialogue choices don't drastically change the course of events, [b]but that's not the point[/b], because after you've had your conversation you get to sit alone in a quiet carriage to dwell on the ideas you just explored. It's the practise of giving purpose to these topics and intentionally engaging with them through thought that brings this game to life. If you play it as any other video-game, merely attempting to tick the boxes or complete the objectives (though there are none), then you are doing yourself a disservice, as you're not playing the game with the spirit it was created for.
[hr][/hr]
I can say with certainty that this game is one of my favourites of all time, if not at the very top of the list. Though I can understand some of the other reviews that refer to this game as talking to their "16 year-old self", or to a "Philosophy 101 student", I don't believe it's entirely fair. The topics explored in this game— [spoiler]accessibility, the nature of art, personal growth, love and friendship, privacy, the existential weight (or lightness) of life [/spoiler] and more—are deeply real and worth reflecting on at any stage of life; dismissing these themes as juvenile or overly simple assumes that these questions should only be asked once, rather than revisited and reinterpreted as we grow.

I truly believe that if you can open your mind before you engage in this experience, and offer yourself to the in-game conversations in an intentional manner, you will come out of it a more thoughtful person in the very least. Be ready to put down that damn phone, challenge your presuppositions, and sink into the depths of this game.

I played this game because I quite like the first one, here comes the (first?) review:

[h1]Character[/h1]
3 characters, no hidden character or such.
Each has different style of punching combos.
I like the fact that you can spam a flykick-uppercut combo from early stage, but in later stage you can't because all the enemies start blocking.
Also make me think, how come they can block attacks but I can't, that could be useful.

Compare to the first one, no unlockable characters, which is a little disappointing.

Saul's special attack is a little broken, make him outright more OP than the other two in my playthrough.
Air combo is quite interesting in this game, because both you and your enemies can be hit mid air.
However, when it comes to you being in air, enemies can really spam that on you.

I remember in the final stage a big guy just spam a knock down punch to my death while I'm in air, which is less enjoyable.
It would be nice to have a break in-air stance too.

[h1]Enemies[/h1]
Enemy sprite design is a real gem of this game, you can still see new lesser enemies popping up even in the final stage.
You need to remember who can fly kick, who can break grab, those was quite fun in my playthrough.
It would be good to see some enemies that can grab you or dodge attack using backflip... those moves I remember seeing in my favourite old school beat'em up games.

[h1]Boss[/h1]
Bosses are quite interesting. I can see the developer actually put a lot more effort on the first boss to make him look bad ass.
Seeing a little of that after the first one though, even the final boss, doesn't have a 2nd stage like on the previous one.

Still quite enjoyable. I like the female boxer boss where she is super fast and try to approach you for a undercut constantly. Which really stands out on the rest of the playthrough because normally I'm the one chasing the enemies.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Not a bad game, what more do you expect for 2 dollar? And developer certainly put a lot of effort on the graphic design.
Consider it is a bit more pricey than the first one, you would expect a bit more, but this game certainly offers a lot less replayable values: no unlockable modes, no unlockable characters, which is a shame considering that's a lot cool sprite designed.

Still worth a try, keep on the hard work! Looking forward to the 3rd one as well! (Was that 1st of May or 5th of January? I can't get that date format right in the Easter egg :D )

Grunnd is a point and click adventure game with no adventure and poorly implemented pointing and clicking. I'll be up front and say I did not like this game. I enjoy surreal and interpretive works like Pathologic or Who's Lila?, but this was a slog to get through. It feels like half of a game. I can put aside the short length (3 hours), but the ending choices felt rushed. I didn't care about any of the "characters" and really had no reason to care. Most of them blatantly refuse to answer your questions and are so off-putting that I could care less what fate besets them. 

The jank of this game is unbelievable. The "Hero" (that's what he's called) will just walk in place randomly, walk back and forth desperately trying to figure out how to walk down some stairs and moves with all of the speed of a crippled sloth. The movement is agonizingly slow. You can fast travel almost anywhere any time and it makes for some unintentionally bizarre moments. Interacting with the wide open gate to the "farm" will cause the narrator to still comment on how it can be opened from the other side. When I grabbed the ticket from the outpost, went down the elevator, and came back up, it reappeared in the slot to be picked up again. Going down the one way elevators, upon fast traveling up the hill again, the elevator was reset. This game is a mess. Indie or not, there is a supreme lack of polish here. Almost every line of dialogue is voiced, but then dialogue will appear with no voice acting when everything else is voiced. Many lines of dialogue will not match the voiced lines and are often littered with grammatical and spelling errors. The controls are atrocious. Clicking to move is finnicky and interacting with prompts seems to work 50% of the time. In dialogue, lines will sometimes just flow on their own, but then randomly will require me to click "Continue" to get the next line of dialogue. Why? The keypad got stuck on screen at one point requiring a save reload. The game got stuck loading indefinitely requiring a full restart.

Even when the game is working, it's just not fun, compelling, scary, funny, just boring. It's a tedious experience overall. There are moments of tension that had me hooked, but it just never goes anywhere. It's always just a little eerie, but the moment fades before there can be any payoff. Details about the setting, characters, and story are drip fed so slowly and in such a fragmented manner that it's hard to stay invested when almost nothing is revealed. Entire plot points seem to just disappear from relevance all together. Why did the fortune teller say she'd help me later when that never happens? Why was there a dark cave in the side of the mountain that I can't enter? Why does everyone comment on how the outpost lacks any doors, but I still have the ability to enter it? How did "Hero" even get in? He mentions there aren't even any windows either. What were the trash collectors doing with their victims? It's like an assortment of secrets that just stay as secrets. No climax or resolution.

The biggest issue I have with "Hero" is that he's the gateway to this strange dreamlike/nightmarish little town, but I can't put myself in his shoes. He'll be just as confused as we are making it easy to connect with him, but then he'll just say and do weird shit for whatever reason I can't fathom. Why would he ask some guy he just met to join him at an inn? Why is talking to some woman holding a baby we've never met previously like he knows her? I don't know her. He's just as much of a weirdo as everyone else. Pathologic worked because the Bachelor was just as much of an outsider as we are. He's easy to connect with.

For the positives, the voice acting is mostly good, sometimes awful. The narrator is very good. He does his job well. The man at the disco was terrible. It's like he was switching inflections at random while talking. The boy, bless his heart, spoke like he's just reading words without understanding what they mean. The art style is very beautiful. It feeds into the bleak neo-noir atmosphere of the game. There's a lot of thick shading to everything and it reminds me of Disco Elysium a bit, but much darker. There are issues here as well with bugged animations and weird scaling. The bouncer at the disco looks massive when he's guarding the door, but then is normal size when he's outside. The soundtrack is incredibly atmospheric and tense. A lot of good ambient tracks that helped with the immersion. However, that metal track was just jarring and felt out of place.

Grunnd is just a little too vague for my taste and with all of the jank, it's a hard sell. Multiple endings to an unpleasant experience doesn't undo the tedium of playing the game just to get there. It's just not something I'd ever play again and I can't in good faith recommend something I didn't enjoy. (4/10)

I gave it an hour. Mainly because the noir-esque atmosphere and the music were promising me potential. But everything else is best described with the word "janky".

Movement is slow and imprecise, which together with confusing hotspot interactions (sometimes left-click instead of right-click is necessary, sometimes correct positioning of the character is necessary, sometimes there is no hotspot or it is not near the point you are ultimately interacting with -- in one word: janky) makes for a frustrating gameplay experience.

The dialogue, again, is janky. Voiceover often does not match the written text and sometimes the same character is voiced entirely differently (best example is the very first NPC you meet, which sometimes sounds as if speaking through a radio and sometimes as if standing beside you). The dialogue choices feel underdeveloped and pointless, as you have to click on all of them anyway and the replies do not necessarily match the questions. It's not as bad as Solasta's dialogue randomizer, but it feels disjointed too often not to be noticable and irritable.

Quest design is strange as well. Less than an hour in I got access to an island, where something happened that clearly communicated to the player that the way back was cut off. Except, it wasn't. Maybe there was a hidden trigger, but I just progressed normally on the island and surrounding places, when I realized that fast travel was still possible and moved me to the starting locations. Similarly, a large structure that "has no door" turned out to be accessible immediately (again: hidden trigger?) just by walking to its left and pressing the arrow, apparently teleporting me inside that "structure without a door" without any explanation. It's just so confusingly janky.

Once I felt that I was losing interest amidst all the gameplay confusion, I stopped playing and likely will not return. Not sure how many hours are left, but considering the game is actually quite pricy for its content, I feel that this was a buy that I will regret. A shame.

I'd recommend the game to very specific players who look at the screenshots with awe and are willing to endure countless technical issues. But I must admit, I wasn't able to stay immersed, and I really wanted to.

Down and Out is like the retro brawling games in an open VR world. This game gives me retro vibes of games like Streets of Rage and Back Street Brawler, but in wonder VR. The game is open world, a few city blocks and very detailed and interactive. You can grab and throw objects at people, ride a bike, spray paint a wall, even push a shopping cart around.

The game will have you fighting angary people, or just making people angry to fight, there is a brawl waiting to happen around every corner. The game is more then just a fighting game as well. You will have a bunch of mini games to play, like defend your spot, find the wallet, chase and beat down the pizza guy and many more. You will also earn cash, build rep and level up. You can also buy and sell items. Over all the game has lots to do and keep you playing.

The combat system feels good. It is easy to block, but the hitting is like old school Punch Out. Watch for an opening and attack when the enemies starts a punching motion. I was able to fight three people at once and come out on top. The combat is also a great workout and will have you out of breath and working up a sweat. that's where the mini games come in, and give you time to rest up for that next brawl.

This is a great game for a workout and fun brawling game with an interactive world to be immersed into. Will you rise to be King of the streets?

I like the concept of the game. The early game is great, but it gets really difficult to scale. There are behaviors that can be programmed into the bots, but you have to go to YouTube to figure out how anything actually works. I would have much preferred a programming scheme like Autonauts, where it's very clearly defined what your bots are doing in the world, and if a bot is stuck, you can see immediately where it is on the logic chain.

I really like to dig into production chains, but I spent more time micromanaging my resource collectors than anything else. Fewer resource nodes with higher resource counts for default settings would help immensely with this. It's also frustrating to know that there are hidden recipes for converting items and bots, but no information in-game on how to gather them. The research tree has nodes requiring resources that you haven't unlocked yet, but won't tell you what they are.

Overall, I think the biggest problem with this game for me is that I expected a production game with a side of exploration, but it really feels like an exploration game with a side of production.

Genuinely a horrible experience with developers that do not give two fucks about the game.

I'll start off with the good:

Now the bad:
[b]Punch Accuracy[/b]
This is the biggest one. Shots will constantly miss even if your opponent is stationary or in the middle of throwing. It doesn't matter who you are. You can either be Usyk or Robinson and they will constantly miss the same amount of shots. Even something as single as a jab is completely unaffective the majority of the time as it will either completely bounce off the guard or miss entirely. This is why people spam hooks to this day as it is seemingly the only shot that connects consistently. Crosses and uppercuts are completely pointless and you are actively putting yourself at a disadvantage by using them.

[b]Movement[/b]
Quick slips are allocated to one button and thus you have absolutely no control which direction the slip occurs. Then you have rotational slipping which is completely pointless as shots will not land anyway, and when they do they completely break your guard. 
You cannot move whilst throwing simutaneously, and so movement is extremely robotic and unintuiative. You have to throw, then move, then throw again, then move. This makes finishing nearly impossible. You can have your opponent dazed, they will have absolutely zero defence, but because you cannot move and throw, you cannot finish them off consistently - unless of course, you spam hooks. 
Weaving is completely useless as there is constantly a delay. I want to duck under hooks, however I have to perform the action at least 4 different times before the game actually registers the movement I want to make. It should be better than this. Give me the option to swap stick combat with stick dodging and this problem would be fixed immediately. Instead, I have to hold block and power toggle to weave, which makes no sense. 

[b]Stamina and Recovery[/b]
Stamina is the most inconsistent thing I have ever seen in a fighting game. Even UFC 3 and FNC does this better, which came out years ago in comparison. Every single shot will use up stamina, which is fine, however movement and blocking will not. So most matches are just either spamming the same shot over and over again, or standing in the pocket waiting for somebody to throw. 
In Career Mode, the AI stamina is straight up unfair. They will throw 12 punch combinations, all of which will miss or are taken on the glove, and will still have enough stamina left to throw one random power hook out of nowhere. Meanwhile you can throw, at most, 4 shot combinations before needing to stop and regenerate. It makes absolutely no sense at all and makes it feel like technical skill doesn't matter at all. 

[b]Power Shots[/b]
These are extremely overpowered and there is genuinely no reason to use any other shot except for powers, because these are the only shots that will land more consistently than standard or counter shots. Heavyweights specifically, it is even worse.

[b]Countering[/b]
A prominent counter puncher will always be at a disadvantage here, and punch accuracy is a primary factor to this, but it also makes every other stat of that fighter completely redundant as they will not have the tools to push pressure. You are guarenteed to always lose.

[b]Bugs[/b]
There are still day one bugs from early access that still have not been addressed. Fighters turning around in the middle of the ring, unlimited round timers, ghost punches, desyncs, fighters falling outside of the ring, models T-posing, KO randomness from jabs, fighters getting counted without a knockdown. The list goes on and I'll be here all day. Since the December update, I have noticed even MORE bugs crop up which they are not addressing. But hey, please buy the Jake Paul fighter pack. 

[b]Character Customisation[/b]
It is as bare bones as it gets. There about 12 hairstyle options, 6 tattoo options and 4 hair colours. There is a bit more modification on actual body structures but that is so redundant considering you cannot customise anything else. 
There literally only three different shorts designs, three shoe designs and 5 glove designs - 2 of which are product placement. 

[b]Anti-Cheat[/b]
There isn't one. Don't bother touching online. There is an unbelievable amount of hackers that can one hit KO you, have unlimited stamina and unlimited HP. 

[b]Online Play[/b]
Also terrible. Constant connection issues and horrendous desync where your opponent can hit you from across the ring.

I can sum up this game in one word: disappointing. While the voice acting and artwork are acceptable, it's more the plot that's the problem. For an otome game, I expected a certain level of romance, and the romance is basically non-existence in this game. After finishing up three routes in the game, I find myself bored and not caring about the characters. If you want to play a romance story about the Shinsengumi, I suggest playing Hakuouki.

The cover art lies; the actual art through the game is not the same quality..BUT the expressions are refreshing; similar to watching old school anime. If you have played Hakuoki this is gonna be a bit of a let down when it comes to the character styles and story (you would want to play this first probably.) I made it through 1 route and part of another; it tends to be more cute than romantic. Overall--i still plan on trying to finish but i feel it wasn't worth the price but i'm snooty like that. The voice acting is GREAT~

So, the first thing you need to know about the game is to wait until it is on sale for at least 50% off. It has a good amount of content, but that content is not worth 50 USD. 

The art? Great. They clearly worked harder on the CG's as opposed to the regular character models, but it's all okay. I have played otome games with way worse art, but know that this is an older game, so expect it to look older. Hakuoki looks better, and I like the character models better, but this is not without it's charm. 

Voice acting? Amazing. Can't praise it enough for that. 

Story? Well if you're familiar with the story at all, then you will know what's going on without looking at their glossary. It may be too much for people who are only looking for the fluff romance part. But that can be said of Hakuoki as well. So basically, if you like this period of time in history and are looking for a story that isn't just all sugary romance this is for you. Basically the thick plot without all the romance made me care more for the characters as people, rather than just eye candy to fawn over. Probably not the best visual novel for newbies to start with though. Be advised that bad things happen to some of the love interests in the game. 

I finished all routes except one, so here are the thoughts on the specific routes. I will be comparing some of them to Hakuoki, because how can you not?

Kondo- Okay! So you can date Kondo in this. But, be warned for newer players to this story: He is married and that might turn you off. It is completely possible to miss that he's married until you are well into his route, too. He's a flashy playboy type. I personally hate that type in these games and the already being married with a child made me at some point towards the end stop playing it. [spoiler] It was around the same time that you meet his wife and she is still very much in love with him, but spills that she knows he cheats on her and can tell that he actually loves MC. Poor woman actually pleads with MC to be with him and make him happy when she can't, because he'll always go back to her or something, IDK I was zoning out during this because I was cringing so much. This isn't romantic. It's not cute. It's not endearing. Sure as hell isn't romantic. It's double the awful because you can pinpoint the moment he fell in love with you to when he took you to the red light district to meet his other mistress and they both beg you to dance for them in the most awkward scene I've had to play through. Love this game- Hate Kondo.[/spoiler] 

Okita- Hakuoki Okita was awful to me. I guess he just played around too much? This one however, is great. Loved it. He was sweet. Even the ending, which is bittersweet. Soji has TB, it's terminal in the 1800's, so be warned this is not going to be an overly saccharine story. [Spoiler] Kondo's wife cameos in this story as well, after the war MC lives with her to raise a baby in the Dojo. Since Okita was to take over the Dojo from Kondo,  I suppose it is poetic that his child will take it over. As I said, bittersweet. [/spoiler]

Hijikata- This version of the demon is more tame to me than Hakuoki. I liked both of them though, this one to me just feels softer. This is another sad route but even so I felt closure and satisfaction after finishing it. The ending felt right.

Yamazaki- This one is by far the most departure from Hakuoki. It was downright jarring to me, because I love that sweet ninja bastard. Not that I don't love this one, too. Yamazaki at points in time in every story route I went through gave me some form of comfort, or a smile. He is a ray of sunshine in this game. Yes, he dresses like a woman and yes, he is prettier than you. That's fine. He's also a really fun person to be around.

Yamanami- Second biggest departure. This departure is plot related. He still fully reminds me of his Hakuoki counterpart [spoiler]at least before that one turned into a vampire[/spoiler]. This is the shortest route in the game. He is a smart ( if not clumsy ) inventor whose ideology is a more peaceful one. He starts a school. It's adorable. I cried during this route. 

Todo- Ugh. Okay. So, I like him. He's a brash, competitive little bastard. But I went back and played Hakuoki once while playing through this and it was his route. He is so much better in Hakuoki. This one seems more sure of himself and his ideals, but I much prefer his personality in Hakuoki. I think it's because of how cute he is. 

Sano Harada- This is the member that looks the least pleasing to the eye. He and Shinpachi are meant to look rough around the edges, but Sano to me looks downright ugly and a little scary. This plays into the enjoyment I got from his route though. He is super sweet and fun. He is a gentleman and this is a hill I will die on. One of his first events is [spoiler] him taking MC to a diner because he has a thing for the daughter of the owner. Pros:
- The MC can fight and take care of herself, unlike a lot of otome MCs
- The MC has goals other than just finding a man
- There are interesting historical events happening
- It is less depressing than Hakuoki and the endings [spoiler] are happy (except I believe Yamanami, Okita, Kondo and Hijikata's endings)[/spoiler]
-  There is gay, gender non-conforming, and polyamorous representation  (although I have some issues with the way the poly route went)

Cons:
- The romance is very "all of a sudden I guess they're in love now"
- The art is pretty dated looking, especially the sprites. It is hard not to compare these characters with the same people from Hakuoki, and these ones are (in my opinion) so much less attractive
- The main character looks so much like one of the love interests (Heisuke) that it's distracting 
- It's hard to figure out why the characters are attracted to each other
- The humor didn't really land for me
- The music is pretty unexciting
- The routes are pretty much the same except you change who you have short scenes with along the way, so it is very repetitive 

I would probably buy it when it's on sale if you do buy it.

[h1] Horror at its Peak [/h1]

I'll start with the things I didn't like, because there's a lot less of it
[list]
    [*]OST (Listening to the theme for 6 hours makes me want to drill a hole in my head)
    [*]Art style (I'm [b][i]FULLY[/i][/b] aware the kawaii aesthetic is necessary for the game, not a fan 🤷)
    [*]Repetition (there are 20+ endings to this game, I have to do 20+ playthroughs with same dialogue)
[/list]

And the rest of the game is an absolute master class in horror. If you want to make a good horror game or want to know what good horror looks like, you abso-fucking-lutely need to play this game.

[h2] Why so good? [/h2]

Something that I see so many games get wrong when they label themselves as horror is they become just another shitty startle simulator (walking simulator with [b]LOUD NOISES[/b] and scene transitions, usually to a "monster" 🙄). Many times games don't have a reason for their monsters, but rather [i]excuses[/i] for them so they can use them to "scare" the gamer.

Horror is taking ugly truths of the world and makes them tangible. [i]Metamorphosis[/i] by Franz Kafka is about a man, who may or may not have turned into a giant insect. It's how he's treated by his family before, during, and after this metamorphosis that's the real horror. The idea of a family turning on someone who once fed them because he's disabled is pure horror. (disclaimer: there are several interpretations of this story).

NEEDY STREAMER OVERLOAD takes the ugly truth of younger audiences still reaching emotional maturity and thrusts them into the adult world where they need to make money by validation (followers). The game explores this from a female streamer's point of view, and explores it very well, AFAIK. There are several pandering stream tactics only available to females that you can chose in your playthrough, [i]while[/i] also getting to see the real person behind the business say things like "maybe I should buy a vibrator with all the superchat money" or feeling the need to hide their SO for fear of losing followers (monetary loss).

[h2] It's just business ... unless ... [/h2]

The game isn't [i]preachy[/i] about the ugly truth it exposes. It doesn't say the gross, degenerate, creepy chat messages are bad, it recognizes they exist. It also shows how comments can be positive (yet inert), off topic ("I'm 7, who else is 7 and likes KAngel"), or demeaning ("ur ugly and ull never be famous"). All the while the protagonist is talking her own shit about her fans ... "fans". We really get to see the real version of our protagonist and her streaming persona in her tweets:

[table]
[tr]
  [th]Streamer Tweet[/th]
  [th]Personal Tweet[/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
  [th]Please ask for help from others especially when things get too unbearable.[/th]
  [th]but dont dm kangel with your problems coz dealing with them is a pain![/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
  [th]I would never trick you or turn my back on you😌[/th]
  [th]i will shit talk yall on my priv though lmao[/th]
[/tr]
[/table]

In this way we get to see a monster of this game; the relationship of the streaming persona (KAngel) and our protagonist. She doesn't feel like she can be herself with her audience. She's only doing the things she does to accumulate fame and wealth. And this comes at a heavy cost ...

[h2] 'Sanity.exe' not found [/h2]

The reason that compelled me to write this review was the INTERNET OVERDOSE ending. There are a lot of great endings. I'm only halfway through, but all of them seem like real endings to real people's streaming careers. However, INTERNET OVERDOSE is so sad, so macabre, and so genuine in it's delivery that I didn't know how to feel beyond accepting the reality that is the decline into madness, brought about by the system (to make money), the inexperience (of the individual), and the perfect shitstorm to get it started.

[h2] The bigger picture [/h2]

To reiterate, the game isn't just about needy female streamers. Yes, the protagonist is needy and needs more time to mature and yes the only source of income is through streaming, but moreover it's about [i]humans[/i] need for validation from society. To be wanted. To be loved. To be accepted. It's a game that shows the horrors of chasing the wrong things in society, will ultimately lead to your demise.

I spoke about how the real monster was the streaming persona relationship, but in a bigger picture one can ask [i]why[/i] does that monster exist, though? This is what good horror does. It makes us ask questions that don't have neat little answers wrapped in super kawaii ribbons. There are plenty of failures that existed to create the "evil", speculative or concrete. Our protagonist may be missing parents/guidance, she has a lack of schooling, the system that requires her to make money, the people she idolizes, etc., All of these allow her to justify her actions and the cycle repeats for the next generation. How can it be solved? ... Can it be solved ...? Maybe KAngel has the answers, we'll have to tune in and ask her 😉

In other words, there is not enough here to satisfy a certain sadist or edgelord demographic. I'd say it's maybe about half of where it needs to be for that to be the case. If you are purposefully trying to make bad things happen, there's going to be a boundary you cannot cross, and the game will just take over with a lackluster ending you've probably seen before. I had an idea of the type of "people" this game is catering towards just from the looks of it and didn't think it'd be for me but I liked the music I'd heard from it so I decided to pick it up anyways. Unfortunately both my notions were correct.

[h2] TRUTH [/h2]
NSO's popularity seems to mostly stem from it's presentation and subject matter rather than it's substance. A game about dating and bossing around a mentally ill, terminally online, co-dependant anime girl really just sells itself to both e-girls who can't wait to claim "she just like me" and fat discord mods who fantasise about having a relationship like this in real life.

[h2] AME/KANGEL [/h2]
At times Ame did somewhat remind me of certain people I've interacted with online over the years with some of her habits and actions but her character isn't very deep and she doesn't have much personality outside of what I previously mentioned (co-dependant, internet addicted, mentally ill). The people I've interacted with on the other hand are in fact human beings that suffer from mental health issues. Ame just comes off as a "cringe LARPer" for lack of better words.
When Ame is acting as KAngel, she acts like your average streamer perfectly, so good work to the dev for capturing the soulless boring online influencer personality so well. She also reminds me of V-Tubers at times which makes her even more insufferable. If this was not the devs intentions then whoops, I still think they did a good job.

I'm sure there are plenty of people who claim to relate to Ame but she is not relatable in the slightest and anyone who claims to relate to her is likely, again, a "cringe LARPer" themselves. I've seen a couple people state they do suffer from things like BPD and do not like the games portrayal of the condition and I am inclined to believe those people far more than the fans who I believe are mostly all self-diagnosed lol.
I only agreed with a couple points made by Ame throughout the whole game, being that people who say stuff like "If all you did today was just breathe, that's more than enough. It's okay to just exist." are stupid and that people who fawn over live streamers, especially female ones are massive losers.

[h2] GAME [/h2]
The gameplay is meh and after a first playthrough there is nothing to gain from not just using a guide to get every other ending, I know it's intended as a narrative experience but I wasn't expecting such a straightforward VN.
The gameplay is as follows: Ame has a stress meter, affection meter and mental illness meter, you pick what she will do 3 times per day, depending what you pick the meters will go up and down. Certain actions unlock new stream ideas and what streams you choose to do affect the meters substantially. Gameplay ends when you hit one of the premature ending caused by things like getting affection to 0 or doing a certain stream category 5 times, otherwise the game ends on day 30. Ame's goal is to convert as many Pokimane tier 3 subs into her own paypigs as possible.

Speaking of tier 3 subs, the viewers messages is one thing done really well, the fans are just as sad and pathetic as the chatters in a real woman's livestream and the haters say stuff that's par for the course in a real streamers chat too. The Twitter and 4chan users are also pretty realistic most of the time, the haters and horny people are portrayed very accurately.

One thing that is done not so well is the music, yes I said I liked the music even before I had played the game but in-game it is not utilised well at all. For 95% of your playtime you hear 1 of 3 tracks which are all fairly short loops, the song changes every 10 days and only during events does it change to anything outside of the 3 loops. I really like the first 10 day loop and how it speeds up from day 6 forward but the other 2 songs got very old very fast. I get this is probably some "it reflects the repetitiveness of her day-to-day life as a NEET" thing but it just had me muting the game and opening Spotify or having a YouTube video playing on my later playthroughs until I hit a new event or ending, the games themes are even less impactful while listening to some random playlist or Norm Macdonald clips.
There are so many songs that play once for 30 seconds and then you don't ever hear them again and I was shocked there were still new songs popping up after spending 9 hours and having finished all but 5 of the 27 endings, it is really disappointing that such good music was made and yet it was so poorly used throughout the game.

I've played through every ending (so I've played more of the game than 90% of it's fanbase :p) with the hopes of one actually being satisfying but as it turns out they were all very underwhelming, of the 27 endings almost all of them boil down to a combination of you getting cucked, some random cryptic shit, you getting dumped, Ame quitting streaming and Ame having a mental breakdown.
The quality also varies quite a lot, many endings are almost instantaneous and are just a couple text messages from her then a text box that appears on screen with a single line of writing before you're sent back to the main menu. The ending for ignoring her messages has a special place in my heart as one of the worst endings ever as I kept accidentally triggering it due to choosing what to do next before I even got the notification that she sent a message.
The finale to the game when you complete every other ending is also not very interesting in my opinion and for how long the "secret.txt" file is teased, being on the desktop from day 2 of your first playthrough, it didn't feel like a very big payoff when you can finally look at it, basically P-Chan (her boyfriend, the player) never existed and she is just schizo.
I'm not sure if it's only in the English localisation but when Ame talks about movies during one of the streams she clearly references Fight Club which has almost the exact same twist ending, I actually did really like that detail.

The localisation is just really well done in general. I honestly love that there is a lack of dumb "trendy" internet slang which is impressive since the game is all about the internet. Not even the translators of my favourite Japanese franchise, Yakuza, could refrain from adding dated Twitter buzzwords like "incel", "simp" and "boomer" to the recent titles so props to the translators for this game.

[h2] CONCLUSION [/h2]
Games that tackle the subject of mental health are a dime-a-dozen these days so if you're actually interested in the subject and not just playing this game to fit with your aesthetic of being a loser, you should try out Celeste or if you're up for something a bit more existential, play Everhood.
Both games actually have something to say and have great gameplay, neither are specifically about the internet but Celeste deals with themes of self doubt, identity, depression and anxiety which NSO is heavy on.
Everhood is more about identity, morality and mortality and is one of the most underrated indie games I've played.
Omori is another game about depression, anxiety and isolation but it's creator has their share of controversies and I never actually finished it but I enjoyed what I did play and have heard good things.

At the end of the day despite my negative feelings towards the game I don't HATE it, I think a game that criticises internet culture is a pretty unique idea even if I don't think it was done very well.
It's popularity also seems to have done good for Aiobahn who made a great soundtrack and the developer is probably set for life so good for them.
If nothing else at least it was 10 hours spent not playing League of Legends, so inadvertently it actually did help with my mental health.
Game is good if you are mature and don't play if you are looking for a happy game

I'll be honest; I bought "Sunset Drive" for its visuals, and as such I feel almost ashamed to complain about anything else in the game because, at least graphically, the game gives me exactly what I expected from it: a neon-drenched environment that looks like Van Art: The Game. Of course, I already own a game exactly like that (2018's "Outdrive"), so this may not have been the wisest purchase I've ever made.

"Sunset Drive's" graphics are undeniably sharper than "Outdrive's", of course, and the seeing the lights reflect off the hood of the car was surreal and beautiful. On the other hand, "Outdrive" boasted slightly more variety in its backgrounds and map design, so it's a wash as to which is better in this regard. They're both quite pretty though, so I'm not really complaining. "Outdrive's" soundtrack was by far superior; both feature a number of synth-wave music tracks, but "Outdrive" again had more options and variety in its selection.

"Sunset Drive's" gameplay is similarly limited, largely consisting of time trials as you race down the highway swerving around traffic. Fail to get far enough, or keep up your speed, or hit too many cars, and the trial ends. Keep going and you bank increasing numbers of virtual bucks that can be used to upgrade your car (to ludicrous levels; speeds of 1000kmh are possible!) and your garage. There are no opponents to race against, but you can modify the amount of traffic to increase or decrease the challenge.

Unfortunately, the rewards are so minuscule - especially in the beginning - that upgrading is more frustrating than anything else, and the races themselves aren't any more engaging. Swerving around traffic entertains for about ten minutes, and after that the only motivation to keep going is to see how much money you can earn for upgrades, and the pace at which your bank account grows is annoying slow. My solution was to set the game to "straight roads, no traffic", tape down the accelerate key, and then walk away for several hours, which earned me a hefty chunk of change, but I doubt that's the expected method of progression. 

Of course, "Sunset Drive" is still in Early Access to perhaps my complaints are unfounded; it is possible that more variety in terrain, music, and game modes are forthcoming. But at the moment, there's little the game has to offer except some nice graphics and a few minutes of gameplay, so unless you get this game on sale (as I did), it's not really worth the price.

Pros:
- beautiful art
- well-designed puzzles (images suited to puzzles)
- suitable, pleasant music
- several different sizes of puzzle
- different shaped pieces for variety
- full control of the background colour (or you can use a softened version of the image)
- you can zoom in and out of your workspace (mouse wheel or keyboard)
- various shuffle, restart, and other functions that can all be accessed during play

Cons:
- the music is good; however, just one piece plays for the entire duration of a puzzle (each new puzzle has new music)

[ADDED] - having a few set colour backgrounds would be helpful (otherwise it takes some experimentation every time
[ADDED] - a few puzzles are very dark in smaller sizes

[b]Overall:[/b] I'm very happy with my purchase. The price is right for the game play. The story provides a nice framework for the art and sequence of puzzles, but that's it.  Buy the game if you enjoy doing puzzles, and especially if you like dragons and high fantasy settings.

My Jigsaw Adventures - Forgotten Destiny is the...  Fourth installment of the series.  (You can play the games out of order as they each hold their own story and universe.)  Played through everything and 100%ed achievements in 10.3 hours using a mouse, though it can be longer or shorter depending on what puzzle size you choose.  Difficulty is easy.  

- This time the universe involves Dragons!  

- There are three puzzle categories, Story, Blitz, or Challenge.  You need to play X amount of Story in order to unlock the other two.  

- There are 20 puzzles in Story, 10 in Blitz, and 15 in Challenge. 

- Each puzzle in Story can be played with normal pieces, arrow pieces, or mosaic (square) pieces, and there is a variety on how big you want your puzzle.  In Challenge and Blitz the size varies, and on Challenge the puzzle piece type can vary even more.

- The art is awesome and you can use it as wallpaper or check it out in the game's Gallery after uncovering it during gameplay.  Some of the art was weirdly dark for me compared to previous MJA games.  Turning up the brightness on the monitor and changing the background image helped with this.

- The story is OK.  It strings you along for each story puzzle.  Sometimes if I beat a story puzzle it gave me the outro blurb starting at the bottom and I had to scroll up to read it all (this is a very minor quirk).  

- The music in this version is nice.  Some of it, like song 02, felt mercilessly repetitive when I was doing much larger puzzle sizes.  There's no way to change tracks mid puzzle.  

- Achievements are all easily attainable.   




In the end, you're getting My Jigsaw Adventures - Forgotten Destiny because you A. Really like puzzles, B. Really really like Dragons, or C. Are really really really stressed out and need to chill for a few hours.  All are good reasons for picking this little puzzle beauty up.  It's got dragons in your FACE, it's got heroic music, and most importantly it's got puzzles.  Lots of puzzles.  More puzzles than you can shake a stick at.

There's a lot here that makes Devastator a worthwhile twin-stick shooter. 

Enemies can mutate/reproduce if not dealt with in time. Pickups on the map are always worth chasing as they recharge your shield/power or your bomb, and that bomb recharge pickup also morphs the map into something different, giving reason to think about the risk/reward of grabbing it or not. The bombs also freeze most enemies even when they're out of reach, meaning even if you know your bomb won't connect with a troublesome enemy, maybe it's worth it anyway to give yourself some time to close the distance. It seems like grabbing the pink bomb pickup freezes certain enemies for a split second as well, giving you even more reason to plan when you should grab it. 

There are red variant enemies that can't be damaged by your shots. At first glance just an irritating feature, but upon figuring out you can destroy them with bombs or even by using the warp pads, they felt fair, and added to the constant decision-making and strategy-formation that was already present. 

It's honestly pretty impressive how many interesting mechanics are present in this game, and given that it's priced so low, I'd definitely give it a shot if you like games like Geometry Wars and other fast-paced twin-stick shooters. 

My ONE caveat is the problem with visual clarity. I had to tweak some settings, as the game was way too bright, had a jarring flickering effect for some things, and even still, the map can get very hard to read at a glance. My advice to the devs would be to lessen the time for the enemy destroyed animation/effect, lessen the visual flair slightly for when you make contact with an enemy without killing them, change the color of the enemy bullets since they're the same as the enemies, and give those bullets priority/foreground so they're always visible even when you destroy a bunch of enemies on top of some enemy bullets.

Tides of Time is a single player action adventure game with an unusual concept - after twelve minutes the game resets and you have to start all over again. After the initial confusion about how I was supposed to make any progress at all, I just started playing and now I think it’s actually quite a brilliant game concept. One might think, that it gets quite repetitive and boring, but that isn’t the case at all. With every game cycle you gather more information about the world, which leads to different paths and tasks for your next five minutes. You might spend your whole time on helping the old farmer gathering his pigs or solving a puzzle, just to get a clue and fight your way through hordes of pirates in the next game cycle. 
Besides the concept, the game is designed in a playful pixel art style, which I found to be quite gorgeous. Dialogues are kept short and amusing and helped giving every NPC his unique character (I actually started calling one of them my grandpa and visited him and his storyline as often as I could, just because I fell in love with the old bud). Most importantly the games soundtrack is chosen very nicely and plays a big part in creating a different atmosphere in every game section. 
Overall, I really enjoyed playing Tides of Time to the point that I couldn’t put my controller away (you can play with controller or mouse and keyboard). It’s not the most challenging game and as a rather experienced gamer, I would have liked some fights or puzzles to be a little bit harder, but that’s about all I can really criticize. Looking forward to more content like this.

After finishing the game a week ago, I can surely say that I really enjoyed it and that it is one of the best indie games that I have ever played. The game is heavily influenced by the Legend of Zelda games and especially by the top-down NES, SNES, and Game Boy titles (which are my favorite). In fact, while playing, it felt like a modern Game Boy Color game, which I loved since Game Boy Color is the handheld with which I grew up.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
In brief, you play as a young man named Charlie, who is trapped in a time loop and relives the same day, the Festival of the Red Sun, all over again. In particular, a dark shade that was trapped in the lighthouse of the main island causes the Red Sun to come close to the world and burn everything (An idea inspired by the Falling Moon in Majora's Mask). The player has 10 minutes until the Sun destroys the world and when this happens, the game is reset.

[h1]General Review[/h1]
The first thing that I really liked is the lack of narrative.  You wake up on an island, without any introduction, trying to figure out what is going on and what you need to do in the game. You just pick up a sword, because as we all know very well: "It is dangerous to go alone!".  You have to talk to everyone that you meet and explore a lot in order to steadily build the story. The overworld is a group of islands scattered around the ocean, most of them having a specific purpose in the story or a treasure to obtain. The exploration is hard as you don't even have a map showing where you are. This is something that I really liked. It has been a really long time since the last time that I had to grab pen and paper in order to sketch the map myself and keep notes of my findings. This made me feel like a real corsair! 

The hero learns some intuitive skills (e.g., teleportation) by leveraging "ancient technology" (Breath of the Wild reference), which allow you to reach previously unreachable places. Through your journey, you will need to free up the three guardians, who will give you important information on how to make your way to the final boss and defeat it.  The combat is not tough, with the exception of some locations in which it would be better to explore a little bit more and gain some "heart containers" before visiting those areas. There are also some interesting puzzles that leverage the unique skills that you learn through your journey. I really liked the music. In my opinion, the best music track is the soundtrack of the Old Kingdom, as it truly achieves to travel you to an imaginative world. 

[h1]Analysis of the time-loop mechanic[/h1]
The main element of the game is the time-loop mechanic. As mentioned in the summary, the game resets after 10 minutes of playtime. At first you may be annoyed, but if you give it a try you will quickly get used to this concept. In fact, you don't really need anything that you collect during a specific day for your journey. What you actually collect is information, which you add up in order to find your way to the final boss and learn how to defeat it. So the idea is that after each reset you just set the goal of the current day and you try to achieve it. For instance, you say: "I will pick up my sword. I will go to the next island to pick up a shield. I will travel to that island and I will do this and that". The next day, you set another goal and you mark another path. 

This mechanic has received bad criticism in other reviews. Personally, it didn't bother me that much. I really understand the concept of the time loop, as it adds a significant amount of difficulty to the game, since otherwise the game could be finished in a maximum of an hour of playtime. Don't forget that this game has been developed by a single (!) developer and this idea is brilliant. However, I need to admit that at some points I felt some pressure in order to reach the goal that I set for the day before the time ends, which was a bit stressful. I usually play this kind of action-adventure games in order to unwind and relax, not to rush. However, this happened very few times in the game, so it wasn't a big deal for me. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
To sum up, as I already mentioned, this is one of the best indie games that I have ever played. The fact that this game was made by a single developer is impressive. All the love that he put in this game and this detailed work with respect to the graphics to look so beautiful and to resemble the old Game Boy Color games is mind-blowing (at least for a Zelda fan like me). [i]In my opinion, this game is a tribute to the Legend of Zelda series.[/i]

I am hoping to see a sequel to this game. Probably, a similar approach to the Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask could be followed (but the other way around). The time-loop mechanic could be completely removed and in order to increase the difficulty of the game, several carefully designed dungeons could be distributed all over the overworld. This is a concept that I would definitely give it a try.

this game is an awful mess, as if it were published straight from a weekend game jam.

The controls are awful. You can't customize the keybindings, which is already annoying. The movement feels extremely floaty and your character will not stop moving until a second after you release the key, which is perplexing and is awful to control. It's so unreasonably difficult to move around, I thought at first it was tile-based given the delayed movement. This alone was immediately the biggest turn off for me to the game, I physically cringe at how garbage the controls are.

The game requires you to use left click to attack, although the movement of the mouse has no use as it neither controls your ranged attacks nor the camera. Yeah, the camera can't be moved and is at an extremely awkward angle and distance. You basically can't see very much at all. Furthermore, if there is an object in front of your character, the camera unnecessarily moves at an even more disorienting angle, so sometimes if an object passes in front of your character, the camera will freak out. Sometimes the camera will go *inside* the object that was occluding you, and you won't be able to see anything as the game doesn't backface cull these objects. This happens all the time in forest sections making navigating them nearly impossible.

The combat has no depth, you just circle-strafe and/or kite every enemy to death. You have no dodge/roll mechanics, nor any other interesting mechanics. You mash left click on everything. Your weapons will also degrade and break over time (there is no visual/audible indication of your melee weapon's status, nor any warning that it's about to break), and you can have only one ranged and one melee weapon equipped. The game will be over if you enter a room and your weapons break, as you can not leave a room without killing all enemies, and there is no way for you to damage enemies without weapons. When enemies attack you or you to them, there is not much indication, like there's no hit stun or i-frames or knockback, so  it just makes the game feel even more disjointed, floaty and disconnected.

There's so many bugs, for example pausing the game doesn't pause much of anything. Some enemies will still be able to move and attack, you can still die, and even the game over screen will render on top of your pause menu. It's like, instead of stopping the gameplay loop (or stopping the gameplay systems from running), there's instead just a bunch of random if statements sprinkled in the code. The 'targetting' reticle is literally just a pink sphere with wireframe, I would expect this as a debugging tool or prototype/mockup. It just looks completely out of place. Sometimes it just appears randomly on the floor.

I wouldn't be so harsh on this game if it were polished and/or there were some more interesting gameplay mechanics. Or if it was made in a weekend game-jam or something. But all these issues make the game unplayable as-is.

original review:

So I see potential here, but also some things that need work. Here are my thoughts after about a half-hour of gameplay:

1) Instead of text explaining the scenario, it would be good to start in the final release with a (skippable) cutscene that immerses us in the world and shows us what's happening. Maybe the radio call for help play, then we see our character jump, the thrusters fail, and the supplies lost. We then find ourselves on the ground and hear someone over the radio tell us we need to get our supplies before resuming the operation. Obviously, i expect this to be toward the end of the developmental roadmap.

2) Building on 1, maybe place simple explainers on the screen as we start moving around. Possibly triggered as we approach points on the map requiring us to crouch, jump, etc. The premise of the game reminds me of the start of Crysis, and I think that or The Outer Worlds serves as a good example of how to introduce the player to the controls while immediately dropping into gameplay

3) controls will need to be able to be remapped. I like to use Mouse4 for grenades and mswheelup to reload in games and was a bit disappointed to see controls cannot be remapped in the current build. Hopefully,  this is included in the roadmap. Mouse sensitivity also needs to be adjustable, as well as music and sfx volume

4) On the subject of SFX, footsteps and ambient sounds (like the occasional bird or insect) would make the game much more immersive. Similarly, sounds will need to be sourced for the hostiles (like roars for the zombie things and howls for the dogs?). It would also be nice to be able to listen for enemies in the distance to judge where potential threats might be and inform movement.

5) when using ADS the rear sight blocks too much of the picture and the crosshairs and the ADS sights are not aligned (the red crosshair is above the post), making it confusing as to which I should be using to aim and difficult to see much at all. Some adjustments to this model would be appreciated.

6)With no health bars for enemies or other form of feedback,it's sometimes unclear easier to understand whether I am hitting the target. It is not clear whether the rifle has limited range and/or bullet spread.

7) If I run out of ammo, I should be able to select fists (or a knife) for melee attack. Being able to buttstroke with the rifle would also be good. It was frustrating waiting for a dog to kill me because I had no way of attacking. This eventually led me to cease gameplay after dying multiple times with no recourse while searching for ammo. Melee combat might result in taking significant damage and make progressing difficult without ammo, but not having a melee option effectively made progress impossible and is quite discouraging. I never did find more ammo before running out, and once I was out of ammo, there was nothing I could really do since I can't reliably run past all enemies and I have no melee attack. This was my greatest source of frustration.

8) a map on the hud that starts obscured and is slowly revealed as I explore would be a nice way to make it easier to keep track of where I've been while not giving too much information. I'm not sure what direction I was expected to go (follow the gully, mabe?) but I quickly got lost. Being able to see on the hud where there is unexplored territory would help guide the player without giving too much information.

9) Invisible walls break the immersion, IMO. In places where the map ends, it might be nice to place rocks so it doesn't feel like I reached the end of the game map, but merely a diegetic obstacle. At one point I had an invisible wall in front of me and was looking forward at the skybox.

10) I understand the reasoning behind reloading a full clip at once. It is more realistic, to be sure. However, anyone who plays FPS games is used to reloading between engagements so as to not enter the next fight with a third of a magazine. The current reload mechanic punished this rather hard. I would like to see the next update switch to the 'one round clip' style of reloading that most other games have adopted for gameplay reasons.

As is, the game doesn't have me super eager to jump back in. The biggest issue for me is definitely the lack of a melee attack, for the reasons stated above. Changing that alone would make it possible to continue searching for ammo and press forward, even with significant difficulty, and greatly enhance the game, in my opinion. I personally feel this should be prioritized for the next update. Seeing release notes on the next update saying this has been added would get me back in the game and trying to progress further.

Again, I do see a lot of potential here. The plot could go a number of directions and the overall map design feels like it's been thought out and makes sense. The environmental graphics are very serviceable. My primary frustrations are the lack of melee attack, the issues with the weapon model when aiming down sights, and the current lack of an option to remap or adjust controls. These issues are detrimental to the core gameplay and are at present preventing me from exploring the story and seeing everything else the current build has to offer. I look forward to the next update and hopefully seeing these issues addressed so I can really see what this game has to offer.

[h1]Gameplay Summary[/h1]
I found TowerMancer randomly when its demo came out, and was pleasantly surprised when I saw it released not long after. TowerMancer is, quite literally, a Tower Defense. Just...not in the way you're thinking. You are tasked with building a tower, sourcing the materials for each room via your mindless imps, and defending said tower from destruction. The overall goal in each mission is to meet the unique objectives (usually amount of certain rooms, enemies defeated, etc).

[h1]Personal Review[/h1]
As of writing, all the negative reviews who's language I can read say that the game is either not fun or lame because you can't fight back against enemies. I can't say much about the reviewer who didn't enjoy it, since fun is subjective, but I can say that there are PLENTY of ways to fight back against enemies. Hell, the chaos of later levels in managing what defenses you have for what attacks might come your way paired with the need for momentum in building was surprisingly fun for me.
The first few levels serve as an intro, but they felt weak in comparison to the demo, and as such I feel that more people would find and enjoy the game if the devs put in the demo again because they would know what their getting into. For me, this is a goal-oriented game, both in skill and room unlocks, so being able to see at least a glimpse of what you can do at higher levels can be important at driving player engagement. Or at least, it is for me.

Regardless, if there's a demo: try it. If you can spare the $8: get it seriously its well worth $8. If there's a sale: why the hell are you reading this go play the game 4head.

Can't wait for "what comes next" ;)

So unlike several people mention, there is in fact a way to fight back when you get far enough in the game. You just have to progress to make traps. But they are single use and on a timer. The game is fun, but it's super tedious until you get there. It is still tedious later, and I think it could use a lot of work to make it better, but I enjoy it so far. It is not what I expect, but I got it on sale, which I think should be the games actual price based on how unfinished it feels. I do like the idea, and the story is kind of cool though. So that's my two cents, and I do enjoy it so I recommend it, just not for everyone because I can see the aspects people are complaining about and they do exist.

Pros:
- Challenging, fast paced gameplay
- Unique styled game play centered around tower defense, but includes management style systems as well
- A nice retro feel
- Engaging gameplay--some levels require a lot of concentration

Cons:
- Overall the game is kind of short once you get the hang of it. I completed all levels on hard difficulty with 3 stars in under 7 hours
- The benefits offered from powering up your various buildings lacks variation
- Once you get the hang of which building combinations are efficient, the challenge of the game goes down dramatically, and a majority of the buildings become useless or obsolete. I don't want to spoil what those combinations are, as I feel experimenting around with the various buildings and developing your own strategies is part of the fun for every game

Overall, I really enjoyed this game, and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys tower defense games, and doesn't mind a bit of a challenge! Feel free to ask me questions about the game if you're considering playing it!

Myth Bearer is probably what Hydlide would have been if Hydlide wasn’t terrible. You roam a top-down open world screen by screen, with paths blocked by (stationary) enemies. There’s a minor puzzle element involved in optimizing where you explore and which enemies you attack first because you’ll be relying on level-ups to refresh your hp most of the time.

Combat doesn’t occur until you go up to stab an enemy, at which point you’re shown a preview of the damage you will do to one another simultaneously before you press the button. This helps out immensely with optimizing your path as mentioned above.

Has equipment upgrades, magic, secrets, and a decent story for what it is. You’re expected to utilize levels, arrows and potions properly if you don’t want to die, and I will say one item and achievement will be blocked in the late game if you do die. Anywhere from 3-6 hours, if you’re thorough. I liked it enough to stick with it for everything.

I enjoyed this game a lot! It has some similarities to Desktop Dungeons or DRoD RPG, where you can choose who to fight when, and enemies are also 'resources' to be managed for their XP and other when-killed benefits.  This game ended up having a lot more depth and strategy and secrets than I was expecting after a first look.  I completed the main campaign, apparently there is a newgame+ mode, and also there were a few secrets I didn't uncover or challenges I didn't do in my first playthrough, which took on the order of seven hours.  The game seems designed for save scumming; items with unknown effects kind of demanded a "save, try it out, understand it, then reload" strategy in order to not waste finite resources, but I was fine with that.  The game content felt a little back-loaded - the game started kinda slow, but then a ton of stuff started happening and the story and abilities kinda spiral out of control towards the end, which was actually pretty fun.

My only minor complaints were UI-related.  The pixel font is somewhat hard to read.  The lack of an idle animation on your character can make it difficult to see where you are when you go to a new screen.  And there's not a ton of UI feedback when using/dropping items (left- versus right- click), so I sometimes accidentally dropped an item I intended to use, but did not notice until later.

But overall this was a very good time, and I look forward to other titles from this author.

Pick this one up for the really low price and help the dev out, he is likely to produce lots of great games as he develops his skill!

This has been really fun so far. There is zero hand holding even to the point of not being sure what different items do until you perhaps find some way to use them. The game doesn't really point you to any direction pretty much ever, so there's a lot of wandering around wondering what to do next and where to go, but there are some more or less cryptic hints on the walls that you can read.

At first the controls took a bit of time to get used to. This can be controlled solely with mouse or with keyboard and mouse. No controller support whatsoever, but you kinda need the mouse cursor to play the game a lot of the game is about hovering the cursor over the enemies to see their stats and sometimes the enemies are too far from the player character.

The combat is all about looking at the stats of the player and the enemies and deciding to make your move with that knowledge. The enemies don't move and only stand in one place, often blocking doors, entrances and items, and they don't attack before you attack them. You go next to them and click on them, and based on their stats and your stats they lose a certain amount of HP and you lose too. You can see how much HP the enemies have and how much HP one hit from you takes off them and how much HP gets taken from you with that click as well. If the power of your click exceeds the amount of HP the enemy has, it dies and doesn't take any HP from you during the final blow (that is very important to know when calculating how many times you can hit them).

If you go ahead and fight the enemies without thinking it any further, you will die very quickly. It's very important to think before you hit an enemy, because you have to be aware of how many health potions you have and when you should use them, and which enemies you should choose to fight and when.

You will gain experience points for defeating enemies and every time you level up you will get your HP meter filled up, so that's something you should be watching too and use that to your advantage. When you are strong enough, some enemies will become one-blow kills that don't take away your HP at all and instead basically will give you free HP.

The enemies don't seem to spawn back so the ones you have killed will stay dead.

Apparently there are intentional possibilities for sequence breaking too so there are multiple ways to go further.

Right now I'm contemplating on whether or not to buy health potion with the little money I still have and if I should use that to be able to get rid some tougher enemy blocking a path somewhere, or if with more exploration I could find another way to proceed. Maybe I will end up needing that money further in the game...
