So this game is obviously made by a small, low budget team just starting out and looking to gain experience and expand their resume. So this review will be written accepting that fact. It's like not like I'm critiquing a AAA studio here. With that outta the way, let's get into it. 

This is a 2D game purely built around platforming, weapons, and it's enemies. Meaning there is really no story. Just your run of the mill simple objective of beating the big bad guy at the end. Which is disappointing.  Because in games like this, a decent story would do alot to help lift it up above many others of it's kind. Some characters. Some backstory. Some speech bubbles. Some proper motivations as to why this quest is being embarked on. 

So you're just left with these levels and the gameplay that they bring. The platforming side of it was pretty good at times, but I was often reminded that I'm playing as a stiff and frigid character. There were some cool elements like fans and lava spits. Classic things like spikes. I got impressed when all those things started getting combined to make traps. I got hurt so much lol. It got really hard, especially that damned ice level, but as a result, it did feel accomplishing to beat it all. I particularly thought the worm level was creative and fresh. To navigate, you had to keep changing size, which I enjoyed. The void irritated me though. I hated having to traverse platforming just to get to the next level. And the ice slide series part made me super duper pissed me off. I was stuck at that part for like 10 minutes just trying to get to the next level. The ice level itself was also frustrating because of the character stiffness. A fluidly moving character would of made that level much more enjoyable.

The weapons side of things was a very cool concept. To overcome something in a level and then be able to use it from there on out as a weapon is beautiful way to provide progression to the character. Especially the shrink ray lol. However, I only ever really used the base gun, the banana gun (for health), and the bomb. I found all the others to be kinda useless since I could deal with any situation adequately with the 3 weapons I used during my playthrough. This may change in new game plus, idk, but I definitely didn't feel inclined to use any of the other guns in a first playthrough. Oh and my least favorite was the wind gun. Maybe I wasn't keen enough on how to use it well, but I thought it was absolutely useless. 

Now for the enemies. All very, very unique from eachother. But the best way to defeat most of em was from a distance with the base gun. The enemies had the most impact when combined with platforming sequences. That made them very dangerous and I thought that was smart design. The same way different platforming elements kept getting combined with eachother to create new obstacles. The bosses are a different story though. I think they all were pretty cool. Some left a more lasting impression on me than others. Some could you just kinda stand there and spam the base weapon on them. And if you got hurt too much, just banana gun yourself. Others required some strategy and patience. Like the ice boss, lava boss, and the Drakken of course. Drakken was the hardest as he should be! I died like 6 times to him. Thankfully I had farmed over 20 lives in the worm level lol. If I hadn't I would not have beaten this game today. Or tomorrow lol. Drakken was VERY well designed. It's clear alot of effort went into him. And the concept of him taking half your arsenal away was terrifying and cool at the same time. Especially when he was using those very weapons on you. I loved it. Just that boss fight redeemed alot of other shortcomings for me. 

Sadly though, there was nothing after that besides new game plus. No cutscene or text. Which adds to my lack of story point. In conclusion, I am very proud of this team sticking around for the long hull and finishing this. A finished and working product is a feat in itself and I commend you guys. Not even the AAA studios released finished products these days. Taking into account all circumstances previously mentioned, I give this a game a score of 7 out of 10. I may try out new game plus to experiment and see if I'm forced to use the other weapons more. If anything significant comes out of it, I'll update my review and also with anything I forgot. Thanks for reading!!

Edit: I forgot to address music and visuals of the game! The music was great! Each level had a unique track that fit very well with it's setting. So 2 thumbs ups for that. The visuals were better than I expected given that it's a 2D game. The character look doesn't leave me with any comments, but the background and look of the levels was not bad. I loved the scale of the last level. It felt large and epic like a castle should, also fitting to it's place as a last level. Sometimes the game was even kinda pleasing to look at.

As a "disclaimer", let me start by saying that I usually write silly and concise reviews for other steam users but since this is an early release, I prefer to write a more detailed review for the dev team to see. Hopefully, I don't come across as too rude or demanding. These are just my opinions, anyway. Do what you want with
them.
I would also like to point out that I haven't played the first game of this series nor I'm familiar with the company.
Oh, and I'm not a native speaker so you are going to notice some broken English and a limited capability to effectively illustrate my observations in my discourse. My bad.

The neutral:
# The premise is something I usually don't see in video games. An RPG, Town Building (I suppose?) hybrid. That's a niche to note. Not really anything bad or good about it but it does make the game stand out.
# The UI is quite reminiscent of gacha games. That can be jarring to people that dislike them or welcoming to those who do.
# The art style of the character models is a cutesy chibi style. It fits the fantastic "cartoonish" models of the overworld and buildings imo.
# The character portrait style has a similar vibe to Hades but turned anime. It's a in between of the two styles. I think given the chibi models for the characters and the general fantasy setting of the game, a "full" anime look would fit the game better. Imagine an isekai type of story were you are transported to this world and become the Principal of a school for heroes. The style is still good, though.
# No voice acting at the moment.
#The world map is fractioned in zones and those zones have blocked paths that progressively unblock.
# As far as I know, once you graduate your students, you never see them again. This mantains the game fresh but also prevents you from caring too much for the characters (even the champions).

The Good:
# Nice enviroments.
# Nice background music and effects. The music for the academy/town is relaxing and a bit mysterious. The special effects are a bit too loud in comparison but you can change them on the settings.
# Upcoming Main character option between a male mc and female one.
# Logo customization in the future.
# The characters are interesting. There's some "plot twists" moments with a lot of these characters. Also some averted trope moments. They feel like actual characters from a show even if they aren't the most complex of characters (which is understandable, obviously.)
# Story heavy. More often than not you'll encounter story content. Regardless of the literary value of the plot itself, the fact that you are constantly updated on the characters stories and relationships is a good decision. It prevents from making the gameplay repetitive.
# Clear tutorials.
# The gameplay is quite accesible. Perhaps different difficulties would be needed for different players. I think that due to the nature of the game and the temporary nature of the playable characters, it makes more sense to mantain this model instead.

The bad:
#Some lag in the initial cutscene where the graphics stopped appearing but you could still see the text. Also Rodno sword's animation is faster than the character model and you can see the sword floating in front of his hand. Probably just my laptop but I'm still sharing my experience. (I have the required specs, btw) 
# No manual or multiple saves. Also read my next point.
# Sometimes the game completely froze during battle (three times). Now, normally that wouldn't be a big deal to me if it wasn't for the fact that 1. there's no manual save and 2. There's no clear indication of when the game is saving other than the ocassional "Autosaving..." message that blends with the enviroment. I'm assuming it saves at the beginning of every cicle? Regardless, It'd be nice to have a logo in the corner indicating that the autosave is happening.
# Settings missing on the Title Screen. The settings do exist, for those who are wondering. They consist of screen resolutions and Vsync, different volume levels and sensitivity settings for the camera controls.
# There's no proper paragraphs in the dialogues sometimes. What I mean is that when a new paragraph should be shown in the dialogues boxes, there's a French spacing instead. There's also some minor punctuation issues where some full stops are missing. 
# This might be me being due for a visit to the ophthalmologist but some portraits have some slightly off proportions. Specifically the male characters. Examples: Rodno's neck. If you don't see it, focus on the neck from the clavicula to the jawline and then compare it to the shoulders. Rodno looks like he has an uncommonly long neck. Also Laivon torso seems strange. You cannot really tell where his hips are. And it makes him look like he has a set or two more of abs than he should. This is me nitpicking, though. I like the character design.
 # Conflicting story cutscenes. Spoilers [spoiler] Laivon betrays you but after that he introduces you to a leader(?). I'm assuming the character was supposed to be the new Arc teacher. There's also another instance, I think, where you are introduced to the Matriarch AFTER she asks for your assistance. [/spoiler]
# I was not able to finish Vilko's story. I promoted him but the task doesn't complete, even when I promote him to a different major and then chose the one that you are supposed to pick for him. I'm essentially stuck.
# There's a lack of variety in the students. I had two Zimmermans enrolled at the same time. I'm not sure how common that is, but I accepted students based on tuiton and I found it strange how I managed to have relatives so easily. The models are also quite repetitive, either because of their expressions, hair colours or skintone. Maybe different heights or makeup and scars could also be added? Since they all wear the same clothes, it'd be nice to add some flair to their faces.

To summarize:
I think the game shows promise. Not that I'm a creative director or anything, but I think there's still some work left to do in order to improve the gameplay and add variety to what you can do while you wait for the next story mission. I want to support the work and I hope the game comes closer to what you guys are envisioning.
Anyway, have a nice day :D

This game is a total mess. It cannot decide if it wants to be a JRPG, a VN or a stat sim. In the end you get an unholy mess of a game where none of the parts work well. Picture Master of Orion but with a ton of yakking every  2 turns between Xatyipu and Aarod and what they ate. You will find yourself asking for the game to just shut up after about year 1 as you got a TON of these scenes to go through before you can even do much. 

On top of that the battle system is REALLY bad. The enemies will spam ailments like mad. Prepare to be poisoned, drained, bleeding, etc every turn. Oh and if the skill misses the ailment STILL lands. On the other hand your ailments can miss. On top of that you get 2 actions per turn no matter the size of your party, then all of the enemies get to go. So it is not fair in how the turns work, and is set up to unfairly favor the enemy.

To top it off the boss battles are really bad. Bosses spam heal, regen, restore all shields and will do it so fast that you can easily find yourself losing all progress in the fight. The only strat that half works is to get Lightning Bolt, research Mage powers out the wazoo then zap zap them to death. At that point you can at least outdamage the regen. 

As it is I have no idea how this got out of early access in this state. It feels like either some RPG elitests told them how to make the game or something, as the game is so player unfriendly you feel like you are playing a game made by an 80s dev who hates their players and wants you to fail, and fail constantly. It ignores all we have learned about design. You will get quests to kill a monster, with no idea what it looks like. What is a Screamer? How do I know, you don’t tell me! Text pop ups will block story text. How did no one catch stuff like this before release?

In the end I hope the devs return to what they did in the first game if they decide to make a 3. The first game had some charm to it at least, and this game...has nothing. The entire game I found myself yelling at the game and the bad design decisions so often I feel like the game needs to add a warning to the front page that your blood pressure will be 175/140 playing this. 

Seriously. Learn from other games please. There is a reason game design exists. And do not listen to the RPG eliteists who want games to be like they were in the 80s. Those games we threw stuff at the wall and hope it stuck. We know better now what works, why not use it?

As a huge fan of Valthirian Arc 1, I really, really wanted to like this game. And to be fair VA2 definitely does a number of things right. It's got charm, the art style looks great, good music, and a chill atmosphere all give it a cozy game vibe. The whole problem with this game comes down to one catastrophic development mistake that I just cannot wrap my head around: The combat. 

In VA1 the combat was a very simple action combat style. Your whole squad would fight with you as you ran around in a little group and you could switch between characters at will and use their attacks and abilities. It was basic, it was fun, and it worked. In VA2 the combat is turn based, which works for some games, but not for this one. Add to that, they made it a system where you just attack with your strongest party member and the other members sit and do nothing. I don't think I have ever seen a more boring, dull, and restrictive system; it takes all the fun out of even having a team of multiple classes. Then the combat itself just does not balance out properly with enemies, which other reviewers go into in more detail, my main point is that this shouldn't have been a turn based combat system at all, to begin with. The whole combat system is just a mess, beyond just being turn based, this is turn based RPG mechanics done completely wrong.

So in closing, I think this is an amazing game concept with so much potential, and it's something that no one else is really doing. I love the idea of running a fantasy school for heroes and training all the different classes and building up an academy. I also think that a lot of dedicated and great people have worked on these games and I hope that they make a VA3 and go back to an action combat system, and actually save this franchise, but wow... I don't know how a team of developers could have sat around a table, looked at this combat system, and said "oh yeah, this combat is super fun, everyone's gonna love this." 

If you want to play a fun little RPG academy simulator, I highly recommend Valthirian Arc 1. Even with all it's flaws, it's way better then this. Sadly this combat system makes VA2 100% unplayable for me.

I was addicted to the original Valthirian Arc as a kid back when it was a Flash browser game. The combat was simple and repetitive - you just ran around the screen clicking on enemies - but it was really fun to develop your students, promote them to advanced classes, then get points when they graduate based on how powerful they are.

For Valthirian Arc 2 they decided to go with a turn-based JRPG-style combat system, which is risky because of how grindy this kind of game is by nature. Turn-based combat can be slow and clunky, so it has to be [i]really[/i] strategic and interesting to stay fun for a long time. Unfortunately Valthirian Arc 2's combat is neither strategic nor interesting so I was struggling to continue playing past my 5th quest to kill slimes. One strange design decision is that every time you take a turn, any of your 3 students may take that turn. So you naturally end up spamming the strongest move on your strongest student over and over and ignore the others.

The simplicity of the game is worstened by how forgiving it is. It might be relatively easy to kill slimes but if your quest wants you to defeat 10 of them your health and ability points might start running low. However... there are rest spots all over the map that will fully heal you and set your ability points to max, with no limit to how often you can use it, so situations where you might have to start thinking just don't happen. There are also minigames that pop up every so often like fishing, and if you beat the NPCs you can get a strong reward. However if you lose you can just keep retrying it until you win, so even when you do win it doesn't feel much like an achievement. 

The devs clearly did a decent job on the visuals - the character portraits are pretty and the 3D models are okay (but not my preference - low budget graphics might as well stick to 2D). However your academy looking kinda cute just highlights how little customisation is available to you. The academy is split up into fixed squares so all you really get to do is pick which of those squares your next building goes in. So the academy-building part of the game is mobile level. 

Lastly, the game generally just feels kinda clunky. I noticed a few sentences with weird-sounding grammar. Some hitbox for a few buttons were kinda off. Certain tasks like setting your student's schedules takes way more clicks than needed and several menus lack key information to make decisions meaning you have to scroll back and forth between screens.

The game is in Early Access, so it gets some leeway in that regard.  That said, Early Access doesn't mean I'm required to alter my opinions based on personal experience with the game.

Graphic wise, it's serviceable.  There's nothing ground-breaking or terrible about it, just pretty standard stuff.  I found the gameplay somewhat bland and not very engaging, but this may change with future developments and updates.  Moving around the exploration map and managing your Academy are just too bare bones at the moment.

You'll spend a bulk of your time managing the class schedules and rest time of your students, which is fun at first, but gets extremely monotonous when you have over 10+ students and no way to filter them for ease of access.  This needs to be streamlined.  The Devs could separate students by class year or some other grading system to remove some of the tedium of having to click on each one and navigating their information panels to see if they're full training or still require a few classes to finish out a stat tree.

The exploration missions and combat need a rework to make them more engaging.  I was bored to tears and found myself skipping all but the story missions and the shortest ones that gave the highest rewards.  Your character has an attack animation that's uses to interact with treasure chests, portals, and to break a few boxes that only seem to appear in the tutorial mission.  Past that, it appears to have no other function as you can't destroy the environment or strike enemies prior to battle for a pre-combat advantage.

The game has a fair amount of cutscenes, which are great for exposition and story dumps, but unfortunately they will sometimes play out of sequence and jumble the story around a bit.  The other problem, is that some quest lines are directly tied to cutscene triggers and you will fail to complete time-limited tasks long before the cutscene needed to unlock the mission chain is given.  I'm sure future updates will fix this.

The biggest issue I've encountered is that you can eventually run out of potential students and be unable to continue playing.  You can't begin a new year until all empty student slots are filled, and it's possible to run out around the 6th year if you've fully upgraded your maximum student amount.  This was the deal-breaker for me.  Until the devs address this issue, my only options are to wait or start over.

There is huge potential here, but not enough to keep me engaged or entertained past the first few hours.  The show-stopping design flaw mentioned above that completely halted my progress was the final nail in the coffin to my very mediocre and somewhat tedious experience with Hero Academy School Story 2.  I would like to revisit this game down the road after some serious progress has been made, but at this time I can't recommend it in its current state.

Then across three small worlds you have to destroy drones that all basically behave the same in every fashion. If you are far, they won't see you. If they see you or you shoot at them, they make a straight line over two you, sometimes even through walls or doors. To beat this game you must simply be far away and walk backward to not die.

I shouldn't even call them small worlds: they are reused assets from the first level repeating slightly differently in each of three small maps where you have to destroy a certain number of enemy drones. There is space flight and space combat, but it can fully be ignored and the objective reach without a single shot being fired from you or the space baddies flying around. You can shoot asteroids... but they serve absolutely no purpose whatsoever so it makes no difference if you do or don't.

I think I blew through this game in about seventeen minutes despite steam telling me it was a half hour, not that there was a lot of deep content or anything. I don't know why the game calls itself DEEP SPACE when really they might consider naming it "Shallow Hallways: Oh and space or Whatevs" The longest time I spent playing this was its only three agitating bosses. The first boss you meet in about seven seconds, after killing a single drone Klathion appears on the bridge and he charges a magic spell that instantly kills you no matter where on the floor you are, so you have to stand on a chair or console and shoot him. Second boss is a giant version of an annoying drone with two little drones. I found that if you ran around in circles like a maniac and shot the little drones first the big one is just too slow to catch you, but don't fall into a small groove or you'll get stuck and have to start over because he'll peck your health off. The third boss is Klathions ship, which you fight from inside a bridge and shoot five turrets through an open window. If you move slightly behind something, their direct shots can't hit you so you can down all the cannons with about seven mentally painful minutes of firing and waiting. 

For kicks I guess the end goal is to just shoot down the antagonist planet for whatever reason you felt like being evil, and then you find you have the games full list of achievements completed during that single playthrough.

The graphics are nice and blocky, so it seems sort of cute to look at, but I sincerely don't believe that this game is finished or even polished slightly enough to call it early access. I feel like this was the beta of some game that never was, from the early 2000's. That is not a compliment. You will literally be in the same exact hallway you were in a minute prior on a different planet, and then shooting one of three obscure, unexplained drones. You get a shot gun, which is a slower, less powerful machine gun you start with. I wound up using the shotgun only on the second boss to get rid of the two side drones really fast and found that I can switch between guns while the other gun is recharging to constantly load rounds onto an enemy. To be fair though, it IS a game. There are the normal game mechanics.

Anyway I will say yes to recommending this game, because I want the devs to feel supported enough to actually finish it. No, you can not press more than one command into your spaceship, so no rolling while boosting, but there IS a spaceship and space rocks to shoot at. I might have taken more time to write the review for this than I did playing the game.

Story rich deck builder battler with some pretty interesting mechanics and a bangin' soundtrack. There's awesome sound design to all of the strikes and power-ups as well. The story rich part is really the distinguishing feature from the countless other options out there.

That said, while there is a *lot* going on in the story, it's very difficult to dissect even from one ~25 hour playthrough. Everyone is lying to you all the time about everything. When you finally start to encounter trustworthy people who fill you in on what is really going on, you're still misinformed because everyone has been lying to THOSE people about everything always. It's really only at the very end of the 4th of 5 acts that you finally have a full picture of what is going on, why, and the stakes, by which point your meaningful choices have already been made. It is in many respects the HARD opposite of Mass Effect 3's ending. Rather than simply picking between 3 options at the end, you unknowingly narrow yourself down to a single option (of 3 to 4 endings) long before you have any comprehension of how the story could possibly conclude.

Full price, maybe not, but absolutely any discount at all makes this well worth it.

Difficulty: I would say increases quite steadily throughout the game, and it's very unlikely that your understanding of the mechanics, and character's power, will progress in step. I found I rolled through the early chapters effortlessly despite not really understanding all the mechanics until about the halfway point, and I continued to just barely scrape through the midgame without needing to take it seriously, and then in the endgame I would actually fail dungeons on each first attempt and have to deliberately re-spec characters to defeat certain encounters.

Picked it up to scratch a card-battler itch. The deck building and battling is satisfying, but I was pleasantly surprised by the art and world-building. If you like the usual suspects of the genre, you will likely enjoy this one.

The thing that surprised me most about Cookie Clicker (CC), despite the name, is that it's not actually an idle game, you are expected to be actively playing (to some extent) to make any sort of meaningful progress. I’ve played a ton of idle games and they all have idle elements, but I’ve never played one like CC where you were so punished for playing idle. My first prestige took me about ~25 hours. After that prestige, I unlocked a single currency to use within the prestige system. Some guides I looked up mentioned that I should prestige after I get around 365(!) of this currency. It would take me a month of playtime and hundreds of hours to achieve that by playing idle. Apparently the way you’re meant to play is by utilizing combos that enhance your cookies per second (CPS), basically stacking these buffs at the same time and then clicking is a huge boost to push to the higher levels. Unfortunately, this playstyle requires alert and active playing so to stack these boosts you need to first click the cookies when they randomly spawn. 

Some positive points are the minigames. Some, but not all, of the buildings have some neat minigames that add some flavor to the game other than just simply clicking. You have a garden, a literal stock exchange, and some passive/active buffs to decide on. I really loved the concept of these games, but unfortunately they either range from obnoxiously complex, like the garden and stock exchange, to a more set-and-forget gameplay with the grimoire and the temples. While I do love min/maxing, I ultimately play games for fun and learning these minigames in an optimal way required too much effort for what I felt was worth it. 

Overall, I felt CC was just average at best. Perhaps when it came out CC was better, but now there are idle games that actually bring some unique concepts to the genre. I would recommend NGU Idle and Melvor Idle if you are looking for a game with some deeper mechanics while also being idle.

In the world of video games, the term “action-packed” often evokes images of fast-paced shooters, complex strategy games, and high-octane gameplay that keep players on the edge of their seats. However, one game that defies conventional expectations is Cookie Clicker, a seemingly innocuous, idle clicker game that involves baking cookies. Despite its unassuming nature, Cookie Clicker has had a profound and transformative impact on my life, leading me to adopt new ways of thinking, improve my time management, and build habits that have shaped my personal growth. It’s not just a game about clicking cookies—it’s a powerful reflection of the value of incremental progress, strategic planning, and patience, all of which have translated into my everyday experiences.

While the concept of an idle game where you bake cookies may sound absurd, it has become clear to me that the game’s underlying principles mirror many aspects of real life.

In this essay, I will explore how Cookie Clicker has impacted my life in ways I never expected. From shaping my time management habits to fostering emotional resilience, this game has provided valuable insights that I carry with me into every day. By reflecting on the game’s psychological elements, the skills it has helped me develop, and the unexpected benefits it has brought, I aim to show how a simple idle clicker game has, in fact, changed my life for the better.

Section 1: The Psychology of Incremental Progress
One of the key aspects of Cookie Clicker that drew me in was its reliance on incremental progress. In the game, players click on a giant cookie to earn more cookies, which are then used to buy upgrades that further increase cookie production. This seemingly simple mechanic is underpinned by one of the most fundamental psychological principles in human behavior: the power of small wins.

The concept of incremental progress is powerful in that it taps into a deep-seated human desire for achievement. In Cookie Clicker, every click, every upgrade, and every milestone provides a reward, no matter how small. This constant feedback loop keeps players engaged, ensuring that they feel a sense of accomplishment even during short sessions. For me, this was a revelation. In the past, I often struggled to stay motivated on long-term projects because the results were not immediately visible. Cookie Clicker, with its quick and consistent rewards, helped me understand the importance of small, consistent steps in achieving a larger goal.

Psychologically, this is tied to the concept of “intermittent reinforcement,” a principle from behavioral psychology that explains how unpredictably timed rewards can lead to stronger, more persistent behavior. In Cookie Clicker, although there are constant rewards, some of the most significant milestones—like unlocking a new upgrade or reaching a high number of cookies—are spaced out over time. This unpredictability kept me coming back for more, and, over time, I began to apply the same principle to my real-life endeavors. Instead of waiting for big rewards to validate my efforts, I learned to appreciate the small wins along the way, whether they were minor accomplishments at work or simple improvements in my personal development.

Moreover, the game’s structure taught me that progress is not always linear. In Cookie Clicker, as you progress, you can experience periods where your production slows down, and it may feel like you’re not making as much progress as you’d hoped. This was particularly true when I hit certain milestones and realized that my next big upgrade would require exponentially more cookies. At first, this felt like a discouraging setback, but over time, I learned to appreciate the slower periods as opportunities to reflect and strategize. This mirrored experiences in my own life where progress was not always as fast as I wanted it to be, but instead of becoming frustrated, I learned to embrace the process.

As a result, the psychology of incremental progress in Cookie Clicker has become an invaluable lesson for me. It taught me that success is built on a foundation of consistent, small efforts, rather than waiting for a single, grand achievement. By breaking larger tasks into smaller, manageable chunks, I was able to stay motivated and build momentum in areas such as work, fitness, and even personal relationships.

I only "died" a handful of time, mostly due to forgetting the first step to just "move out of the way".

[spoiler] I did have one major game breaking bug in which I was unable to play the "Final Sever" card due to lack of EP (Energy Points). I really enjoyed this game and I haven't even completed all the bonus scenarios yet. I finished the Rome campaign and found it super challenging and fun. It's more of a resource production line manager like Anno than a city builder like CS. There's a balance you have to find especially early on between production and adding another building. You can't just spam buildings you really have to plan out your progress. Do you need to get housing leveled up or build a monument or have a certain amount of resources? You can easily fail by focusing on one aspect over another especially early on before you have a decent income. 

Your money comes mostly from taxes and it's easy to overspend initially. People don't pay taxes if they are unemployed so you'll start with placing a few fields and the buildings for bread and some houses for the worker, a well, a temple, this allows those level 1 workers to level up their houses and therefore pay more taxes and have room for more people. It's important to level up the housing so they hold more workers without using more required resources. The production chains get pretty complex and a bit micro-managey which I love. Some buildings need the level 2 and level 3 (medium and elite) workers with their houses and their particular needs. It's all a lot of planning and balancing for the main gameplay loop.

The campaigns - Rome, Africa, Gauls - are a bunch of scenarios strung together. There's no real story which is fine. I was impressed there was voice overs for the scenario intros. Each one is timed- I usually HATE this in game but it works here. In fact it's needed for the gameplay loop or there would be no challenge. For example getting a certain amount of resources, marble, meat, etc would have 0 challenge if you could just let it play forever.

One thing to note is there is no in game save function - and the reviews reflect this - your progress is saved between scenarios. This was a non-issue for me they take about 30 mins to an hour to complete and you can always just pause if you need to step away but a scenario is meant to be played in one sitting you can't save and come back to it. You'll definitely fail some scenarios and that's a good thing! The game is challenging and not casual and laid back like the graphics might imply. You'll learn from the fail and get better next time so passing the scenario is really satisfying.

Anyway it's an absolute steal for the price and I am looking forward to what the Dev does next.

This game caught my artistic eye with its aesthetics first, a clean and bold Memphis/mid-century/comic book art style, all wrapped up in a palette of my favorite complimentary colors: Warm, deep rusts and cool turquoise hues, perfectly capturing the essence of 1950's Los Angeles. Coupled with a game trailer and images consisting of postwar jazz-club nightlife, a moody, noir detective story, and, well, digital butts, it has all the makings for a fun, retro romp.

Having not read the book that it was adapted from, a 1948 novel by French author Boris Vian, I went in blindly. We will touch on this later. Rock Bailey, the game's handsome protagonist, is your typical self-absorbed 19-year-old trying to preserve his virginity who finds himself in the middle of a sci-fi-fueled plot to *ahem* acquire some of them high-quality eugenic genes by any means possible. (read into that what you will) Not the most endearing guy you wanna root for, but he's likable enough for a vain, flirty 19-year-old kid just trying to navigate the world.

All the elements that make up the gameplay (turn-based combat, clue-gathering, puzzle-solving) are fun and varied, but not very difficult. Little aspects, for instance, like how the cast of characters heal in battle, are cute and creative. I liked some more traditional elements of detective stories, like staking out a joint, infiltration without detection, and clue boards. Story has bizarre turns with fantasy elements that feel a bit dystopian, an unexpected contrast to the 1950's Los Angeles backdrop. The game is a bit short, clocking in around 5 hours (maybe more if you are the kind of Steamer serious about achievement hunts.) It's a fun time, and it looks good while doing so. No complaints there. That's why this next paragraph is so hard for me to write.

Towards the last chapter, this is where the story hits a major snag for me. The momentum and pacing become uneven, leaving a story that wraps up too abruptly and an epilogue that makes me feel like I deeply missed something along the way. Without divulging much, I think it lacked a bit of closure or more of something that makes you feel satisfied towards the end. It's like ordering the Spinach Steak at El Gato Diner and instead having your steak taken away before you are done and replaced with a bowl of Yesterday's soup. Both still fill you up, but leave you wanting something more substantial to finish the meal. After researching Vian's novel of the same name (and there's not a lot I could find), I took away that the game stayed true to the book, and I get why the game ends as it does. But still, I wanted to finish my last bites of steak.

Ultimately, To Hell with the Ugly excels in creativity, beautiful art, and fun gameplay. It's still definitely worth playing, has some stand-out features, and offers plenty for the player to enjoy.

From the charming art style to the heartwarming story, I had a great time playing Don't Stare. The animated cut-scenes were very well done and I found myself getting invested in the characters as the game progressed. The text dialog could be cut down in my opinion, since it did feel too much at times. Also, I think some of the levels need balancing as they are either too easy or too difficult. Hopefully these fixes are implemented in future updates. However, these points don't really detract from its overall story. The game really does capture the struggles of its introverted and socially awkward protagonist and the challenges they must face stemming from the relationships between their family and friends.

Overall I would recommend this game if you're looking for a wholesome platformer with a coming-of-age story.

Starting off, I want to say, I love the game, and I want to be able to recommend it. But I just can't for various reasons.

So, for longer feedback...

To start with the most important portion. The game used to be rock-solid for me during the pre-release days. I wasn't able to crash the game, even with trying silly things. At release I had major crashing problems (which turned out to be motherboard BIOS issues for the most part, so if you have similar problems... they upgraded the backend engine during the upgrade, and the new engine is VERY temperamental when it comes to hardware being "just so", so check for updates to BIOS, drivers, etc. And worse case make sure everything is seated and has appropriate cooling! It should solve 95% of the crashing issues)... but I still can have it crash on my unexpectedly.... Which brings me to the first reason I can't recommend it. The developer released the game with a "okay, we're done, no more updates, bbyyyyyyyyeeeeee" type post (it's in the dev log on steam, so go read them). Because of this, I don't expect to see any bug fixes or other fixes the game will invariably need. So, I can't recommend it. It WILL have bugs that they won't fix. Don't spend the money unless you are willing to accept that.

In terms of the game itself, during development this game had a lot of promise. It went some fun (and weird) directions at times, and it's story was looking really engaging. However, the jump from the previous version to the release was long, but seemed extremely rushed now that we know went into it. I don't know why that might have been (internal pressures, external pressures... who can say other than the devs?) but I do know we went from a single large map that pretty much REQUIRED you to figure out long-distance logistics and therefore use those mechanics, to multiple smaller maps that you don't need to think too much to get things from a to b. They also removed entirely the ability for alternate maps, so you get one map, that's it. Done. No other options. There are portions of the story that feel tacked-on, and plot threads that seem to be dropped. And the latter plot is VERY rushed compared to how the intro plot is pieced together, and I really dislike the way the ending works mechanically, because it feels like we slip into "cutscene mode" for the ending, and there was multiple ways they could have incorporated the ending into the game itself seemlessly... And, again, due to the developer saying "we're done, no more update", these issues will never be resolved. So, I can't recommend the game to anyone who likes following plot threads or trying to learn more about a world through gameplay, or to anyone who likes to have their character be DOING the thing, instead of watching the thing.
 
In terms of a factory-builder game... the early to late gameplay progression is streamlined, and works well. The late gameplay progression... is... I don't even know why most of it is there, to be honest. They introduce a new mechanic for end-game progression right at the end game, and it just feels like make-work. During the early-mid game some of the progression seems weirdly "gated", but there is lore behind why you can't easily access something in the tech tree. And speaking of the tech tree, especially the end-game tech tree, if you're playing for the story (and that's the only "mode" now in game, to be honest), you can skip pretty much all of the end-game tree but one thing. And that one thing is so easy to automate it seems almost like "oh yeah, oops, we're a factory-builder game, we should include that somehow in the ending" and not a pre-planned decision). I CAN recommend this game for the early to early-late gameplay. The factory design and automation stuff there will keep you amused for days, if not weeks (or more), if you like dealing with those sort of mechanics.

And, to address one of the biggest "gripes" I have heard about, the laser-tag thing. That looked like it would have been lots of fun with the right people( but I'm not a HARDCORE MULTIPLAYER PWNING N00BS type person). I thought it was integrated well into the lore of the game, while also enabling some fun extendable options to gameplay for later. Even though I loathe multiplayer in almost all cases, this seemed like an amusing and potentially interesting thing to include in the game. Honestly, I was looking forward to building out a stupid base, and messing around for a few hours in it with different friends... like real laser tag. It's just a spot of fun. I DO NOT consider this a reason to not recommend, nor do I see it as a reason to recommend.

So, long-story... Of the main categories of things about a game I like, all of them died immediately when the dev dropped the release and said "no further updates". That killed all potential for this game to be great. Even if they'd said "so, we're going to release a few minor patches to shore up bugs and stuff, on the side, over the next few months", I'd recommend this game with my full voice... but I can't. If you get it for free? It's a great game, but I don't recommend anyone spend money on it and reward the devs for dropping and running.

Review after beating the game.
I played roughly 40 hours prior to 1.0 in the old combined map, and then roughly 90 hours after 1.0.

I think the game deserves a solid 7/10.

Map Design
I had fun with this game, both before and after 1.0. A lot of the issues I have, are at least similar to other people's issues: it's a regret of what was vs. what is now. To sum it up for those who don't know, the game had 1 large map (Looks like it was ultimately going to be 2 large maps) but it got divided up into nearly 20. The seams between the cuts are extremely rough. I get Why the cuts were done the way they were, but it makes some individual maps have 0 purpose. If you don't know what you missed, and you're interested in the game... what's there wont hold you back. Just know everything before a pretty obvious texture shift in terrain, was all 1 map at one time.

Likewise, About 4/5 into the game is where I predict the funding and development stopped. Maps go from being genuinely impressive to behold, to having next to nothing on them. It's enough to undermine a couple maps entirely.

Mechanics
It's a standard factory game. There were some things missing, I found myself wanting. You can't top load containers or equipment pieces for example; but you could always add something to these kinds of games. The tech tree are useful to streamline your process and give you options. You have incentive to advance through the tech levels and get the new stuff, it drip feeds you utility up until pretty close to the end. There are some dead end techs and pieces of equipment... But by the time you get there, you're basically through the story. There should probably have been a few additional recycling options, to allow you to get a heap of raw materials back on a few of these... but it's not the biggest issue as resources are extremely plentiful.

The big problem comes with some resources later in the game, requiring a significant time sink to get to. This is unavoidable, and there's a hard skill wall built in here, where you suddenly go from dealing with X problem to a 3x problem to a 27x problem. It's a leap, and even Knowing how to deal with the problem I found it daunting and frustrating to wait through.

This problem kind of rears it's head at the end too, but it's an endless factory mode at the game's close. So I hardly think it counts.

Story
The story feels pretty decent, but has some odd shifts. There are a few tone shift points that feel hard, but ultimately it does all knit together. I was 50-50 on predicting and not expecting twists. Some things felt obvious, and some things genuinely surprised me; though, I think some of the timelines may not add up in the end.

The best way to sum it up? It's a neat idea, but kind of a messy execution. I still felt it pushed me to Finish the game, so I could get the big explanation of it all at the end.

Conclusion
The map design is a big - for me, and the story has some rough edges; but, the story's idea and the mechanics themselves did make me want to finish the story through. I would recommend it, but yeah: 7/10.

AN EXCELLENT FACTORY GAME

I don't understand why people ignored/hated this game, its one of the better factory games that makes you think 3 dimensionally for a change. The elevator that joins each level is what separates it from other games, not sure why so many people are annoyed by it. There's a decent story to give you a purpose, but at the same time you can build whatever you like on a massive scale. There's in built coop so you can build with friends and its incredibly stable and bug free. There is also the option to play laser tag capture the flag amongst your own factory that you build, just sad there's no one here. Get this if you have friends that would also buy it, or fine to play solo you'll get a lot of hours from it and the replay value to be neater or more efficient is always there. I can't fault it, it would be great to mod.

The tech tree is interesting in that it provides many ways to achieve products, and as your tech tree progresses, you can ramp up production or use up excess items or alternate recipes. You can even recycle over production. Its one of the few factory games that increases output through automation and tech progress, getting you out of making everything in your pocket, and reaping the rewards of building a large scale factory.

Having vast areas on many levels - each with there own distinct biomes and problems to solve, actually makes you think vertically, but means you can always utilise the lower levels for making an item and moving it to where you need it.

example:
after iron and copper and a few secrets, the first level area used to feel redundant, but now you can utilise the space to make other items like biobricks and ship them to each floor. I bring all floors with limestone down to the 1st floor and then ship biobricks on continuous loops back to each floor that needs it, this came in handy when I wanted to make biodesel later for sierra and shifting the sand. The sand byproduct can be made into a higher concentration of biobricks, adding to the loop and removing the sand. Each level if mined out with a 12x12 mole provides a ridiculous amount of factory volume.

I use admin level to make atlanteum, and loop any excess plant materials back to victor

I use the storage level for energy storage, and I use hydro for energy production. I also use the height of hydro waterfall to build research stacks, this means I can make research in one area from product brought thru the elevator/lift

You can use xray for blast mining and so on. Each level provides a logical area to process certain materials, and this leads away from the everything at victor issue the old game had.

Monorails are still useful to move products from the elevator to further distances and having dug out almost entire levels, I can say for certain that the overall volume when you consider the floors is close to half that per floor than the original max volume single level. To me this makes the space to build far superior to the original 1 level layout. 

The only flaws I can see are that the story aspect can pull you away from the progress aspect if you let it (too much sensory!), but this can be managed by turning off certain goal messages and concentrating on what you can accomplish in manageable chunks. If you leave all messages on, it can get a bit frustrating knowing what you are aiming for to progress up the tech tree.

I can only say that after many hours of challenge getting to sierra, I didn't find the power disconnection or the sand removal challenges any less engaging and in fact I welcomed the diversion and re-thinking that it forces on the player. Having all power removed makes you think vertically again, and makes you look back too, not only forwards, and you can re-optimise your production to meet the challenges with the easy upgrade tool. Every time I think I have a problem with excess materials, I learn a new tech recipe and realise I can improve production of something else I need to use them up - this shows how cleverly optimised the game is despite the complexity of the tech tree at first glance.

If you want a fair challenge and hours of replay and you love factory games, you should buy this and ignore a lot of the negative reviews. the game is not broken and I haven't come across game breaking mechanics that people talk about - and unreal tournament in your co-op built factory? good fun that's a welcome break from optimising that production line just one more time, because you found a better way!

This one was abandoned by the developer (see steam discussions) shortly after the 1.0 release, so it will never get any of the post-release bug fixes or balance updates that are sorely needed.

The game had so much going for it while in early access, active devs, great community and a few new and interesting features that would really have made Techtonica stand out in the factory automation crowd. The voxel terrain deformation and voice acted story line were particularly good, and do still exist in the final state of the game.

The biggest sore point though is the map. Gone is the open world that was a joy to explore, littered with story elements, secret areas and buried goodies. The one where you could build the sprawling factory of your dreams, weaving in and out of the terrain that you sculpted to fit just so.

The map now is divided into small chunks, separated by an elevator you can send resources up and down in. Sorry, did I say small, I mean minuscule, these map chunks feel about as big as a Quake 3 arena map I made 25 years ago. I put in a few hours worth and tried to get used to it, but after 3 levels I just can't imagine building a factory here. And you can't progress much further in the game without it, so I don't think I'll be coming back.

Even if you are interested in the very specific challenge of creating a series of small factories that link together to solve your automation problems, you'd be better off doing so in other, more feature complete and polished games.

Unlike other reviewers I have no issue with the developer abandoning the game after the early access release, everybody's got to eat and sometimes we have to make hard choices. I feel for them having poured so much into Techtonica only to have it fall. I'm glad I supported them trying to make something innovative and interesting. But as the game stands would I recommend it to others? That is a firm no, spend your money elsewhere.

This is by far one of the worst modern racing games I've played in a long time.

Lets talk about its 'PC port'. Firstly, this game was designed for the Switch first, then ported to PS4 and Xbox and then PC a year later, so the quality is already lowered just because its a Switch game. Secondly, this is quite literally the most barebones PC port ever. There is no graphical settings, (not even for resolution!), no rebinding of keys, and the best part is that there is [b]no 'Exit to Desktop' button.[/b] This is at a whole new level of laziness. Even in the worst of PC ports I played there is a button to quit the game. Nope, not in this game. I have to ALT+F4 it to close it. Oh and it also crashed on me as well. Literal insanity.

The visuals: This has that typical 'Unreal Engine 4 look' where the graphics are just smeared with the worst anti-aliasing and motion blur you can imagine. Not only that, but textures are just low quality and the game somehow looks good and bad at the same time. This will definitely give you eye cancer if you play it for too long.

The gameplay: Oh boy, so this game was pretty much made by a few people at Lion Castle using the Super Street: The Game source code, so even though Team 6 did not make this game, it still has their cancer ridden code all over it. Pretty much the underlying physics and vehicle handling are from Super Street. I mean, these don't even feel like F1 cars as their handling is so heavy and their acceleration/top speed is so slow. The handling is so heavy that you can't even make turns most of the time, and the e-brake is no help as it sends your car sliding like its on ice. Collisions also suck, as you can do takedowns in this game like Burnout. Yet when you fight with the opponents, you take damage yourself. Sometimes its not even worth it to engage in the car combat because you'll just die yourself.

The AI just sucks. Most of them will crash out before even getting around the first turn. They have a tendency to crash into each other constantly. They can't even drive on the track some of the time. Lastly, there was multiple times were an AI got stuck in a respawn loop where they would spawn back in, drive straight, crash into a wall, and repeat that same process over and over again.

The tracks: There is six in total, and they just aren't interesting at all. A lot of them are super flat, and don't have anything noteworthly other than straight lines and tight turns. One track does have a portion where the track crosses over so T-bone crashes can happen, but thats the only interesting one here. They didn't even bother to put people in the grand stands around the track. 

The audio design: I mean I can't even really comment on it because there is like hardly anything here. The music is just a boring stock soundtrack, and the F1 cars don't even sound like F1 cars. Other than that you just hear explosion sounds, some collision stuff and thats like it.

This is one of those games that they should pay you to play it. Terrible PC port, ugly visuals, terrible gameplay, brain dead AI, boring tracks and lackluster audio design. Save you money, and buy something else.

A Limbo-lookin' game themed around silent movies? Yup. I'll take one plz.

You've been trapped by a mad director [who mistakenly thinks you've wronged him] inside his latest film! and now you have to find a way to escape. 

I was wondering if this was going to be a horror game,but it isn't, it's just a puzzle platformer with darkish atmosphere.
Most levels have you dodging the occasional bad thing while solving puzzles to find three pieces of a film reel, which unlocks the portal to the next level [tho the last few levels don't need the reels] there's also a story scroll "hidden" in a chest somewhere in each level. [I say "hidden" but they're huge chests, and hard to miss] 
The game has 12 levels in all and took me a little under 2hrs to complete leisurely. 

Pros:
Really cool environment/aesthetic.
Surprisingly relaxing.
Some neat classic film references sprinkled throughout.
Those Steam-engine-camera-dog-things were awesome!
Story is corny,but cute.

Cons:
Puzzles are VERY easy,nothing is more complicated than memorizing small button sequences.
Levels are linear,and sometimes require heavy backtracking.
Bosses have too much health,they aren't hard at all,but take too long to defeat...becoming monotonous.
Story could have been more polished/The silent movie theme could've been leaned into more.
Fairly short.

Despite my gripes,I still quite enjoyed my time. 
If you like the look of it,and think 12 levels and less than 2hrs are worth $3,go ahead and grab it! if not,wait for a sale.

I saw a video on this game, and seeing how cheap this was, I thought "why not try it out for myself". For the most part, it seems like all the game breaking bugs are gone. But now for my thoughts. I love the gun play in this game. It's addicting to play, and a ton of fun. 

However, the zombies remind me more of demons or skin walkers (or the Rake). I feel like more variety and challenge is needed from these enemies. I feel like more enemy types as well as bosses that have some challenge to them can fix this. Another issue to bring up is how the zombies often randomly explode, and the explode sound effect is both loud and interrupts and puts an end to all and every sound that's playing at that moment. It's way too jarring. Not to mention, the levels. 

Of the 4 levels available to play on right now, I only actually enjoy one of these levels. It's Plaza Town Arena.  Let me explain what's wrong with the other levels. The woods level lacks any creativity in it, and once you walk out of the woods, you end up back at the middle. But what really bothers me is when you kill the zombies, the ammo drops end up in the grass, and you can't find them at all. This can be super frustrating. Not to mention, there's just not much to it at all. 

As for the Secret Lab. Same thing. It lacks any creativity or interesting twist with the level, but the most frustrating part of all. Even though you come with a flashlight on this level, it's just way too dark, and it's an easy level to get trapped by the zombies on. It's way too tight and narrow. 

As for the Simulation level, it's just simply too white, and I often times would get confused whether or not I was looking up or down. So I think some of the colors on that level should be changed to fix that. I however like the glitch effect the gun gives off on the level. 

To give an idea for why I love the Plaza level, here's why. It's an open and easy to navigate space, it's not too dark to see where I'm going, the zombies are easier to keep track of once they drop spawn in. However, I feel like they should spawn and come out of the blacked out entrances instead. And I love that blood fountain. I'd love to see it spurt blood, and maybe at different parts of the level, it'd be neat to see gargoyles with glowy eyes as decoration. Just an idea.

But in terms of levels I'd love to see, it'd be neat to see a Mansion level, a Castle, and perhaps a Graveyard at some point. It'd also be cool to get a game mode where players gotta fight from one part of a map to another. And secondary and melee weapons should be included in the future. And that number right next to the gun to show how many bullets are in the clip, it's unnecessary because the ammo is already displayed in the bottom right corner.

Overall, I choose to recommend this game because I see a lot of potential for this game, and I wanna see this game grow and get even better. $3 was too much of a good deal for me to turn down. I hope to see much more from this game.

1. When you hit a platform, there is a forward slide that makes the smaller platforms harder to manage.
2. The controls need more refinement. I haven't tried controller if that is even an option, but the wasd controls move the 'character' around too frantically, again making smaller platforms a hassle.
3. Obstacles are mostly jumpable without timing involved and sometimes you can avoid two or three obstacles altogether by just jumping over them once. 

General Nitpicking:
1. The countdown before every run gets to be irritating. Please make it a removable option.
2. For whatever reason, the level accomplishment populates at the beginning of the first level of the series. It would be more rewarding to make them unlock after the completion of the series.
3. You can press a button to start moving while the countdown is still going. Not even sure why crouch exists in this game.

Overall, I didn't find these issues were bad enough to break the game and I finished all of the levels so I would recommend the game if on sale unless the controls are fixed.

It's dark. You're low on gas. You've made a pretty good haul so far, but you're feeling worse for the journey. Just one more anchor and you can all it quits. And then you hear it; storm sirens. Only this is no ordinary storm - you are now in the shrinking eye of a radioactive storm of unmaking. You have to go. GO NOW.
Your car is a piece of shit. Truly. You've replaced every part a dozen times, the radio turns on whenever you close the trunk, and when you first found it, it couldn't do things like "turn left". And right now it's your only hope of survival.
The gateway opens up - a luminous pillar of yellow light in the distance that is your salvation. The eye is closing and if you stick to the road you won't make it in time. Reluctantly, you veer into the treeline. Your ride jerks uncomfortably as you mow down flora. Suddenly there's a loud THUNK as something hits your car - an anomalous, unthinking entity, affectionately named a Broken Bunny. Suddenly your headlights start blinking on and off. The doors all open at once. The radio turns on again for no reason and through distorted static you hear a preacher yelling at you about Jesus. The wheel jerks out of your grip and you veer into a ditch.
Shit shit shit! Crowbar in hand, you leap out of the car and smack the thing into a million pieces. You car is exorcised, but now you're facing the wrong way in a hole. You get back in and try to drive out, but the angle is too steep.
An angry yellow light covers the sky. You're now past the threshold and the storm is closing in on you. You're taking damage just being out here. This is bad. Getting out at this point is lethal.
You turn your wheel and manage to get some grip on the dirt sideways rather than upwards and after the longest 20 seconds of your life you're finally on level ground again. Through the trees you can see the gate way! You hit the gas with everything you've got. Anything you hit no longer matters as long as you keep moving.
The sky has now become red. The eye has totally collapsed and the radioactive storm is now in full effect. You can see the trees - the ground! - all disappearing. From somewhere there's a sound of screaming that you can't tell is from your car or the air itself.
You're yards away from the gateway now! The light almost filling your vision completely! Something cracks around you. Your radio, headlights, doors, all are going haywire. There's radiation everywhere and you feel yourself dying!
You're here! You're at the gateway! Light envelops you entirely! There's the sound of electricity and a blinding flash-

- And suddenly you're back. Back at the auto shop. Both you and your ride barely survived, but you did. Somehow. You breathe out. You pull in to the familiar comfort of your home in this strange land. The next little while is going to be spent repairing the damage, taking stock of your booty, and upgrading your ride so that you can go ever deeper, into more treacherous waters, and facing deadlier terrors. To find your only hope at escape.
Not for actual adults who have responsibilities- you can't save it and can only play when you have a long stretch of time. Premise is fun but in reality it's a literal grind.

I wanted to like this game but the save mechanics are utter garbage. If it was just "You died and have to start over at the last save" it'd honestly be fine, but no. If you happen not to make it to a gateway and the "emergency mechanics" kick in, you get sent back to the garage minus your inventory and all but the most basic tools. What's worse is it autosaves when this happens, meaning you can't go back to the last save. If it was a mission chain that took you over three hours to complete? Oh well. Not only is your progress set back, but you're actually in worse shape than you started.  It's actually possible to get softlocked due to this because the car is non-functional when it happens. Don't have enough materials still left at the garage to make it run again? Oh well, better grab a book or watch youtube or something while you wait hours for the 'friendly dumpster' to spit out enough materials for you to get it started again.. It's that or just start over from the beginning of the game.  IMHO the developers did not think the save system through at all. I could understand not being able to save mid zone, but at least let us save when changing zones, especially on long mission chains. or hell.. just let us die and just start again at at the last save... Even that would be less punishing and time wasting than the current system.

There's another factor to negative review as well.  Have an AMD GPU? Good luck.  Expect to not even be able to play this game at all until you use command line options to force dx11 mode and then it's playable, but the framerate is horrible. Without doing it, it just crashes when you load into the game.  From googling, it looks like this issue has been present since launch. And a year later, the developers still haven't cared enough to fix it.

[h2]The good:[/h2]
* [b]It's fun.[/b] Yeah.
* [b]It's unique[/b].
* [b]Grindiness is kept to a bare minimum[/b].
* [b]The story is shallow but effective[/b].
* The developers went above and beyond with [b]an excellent[/b] (but not perfect) [b]slew of accessibility options[/b].
* [b]Importing your own music to the game is dead simple[/b] and plenty of audio formats are supported.

[h2]The bad:[/h2]
* [b]You WANT to import your own music.[/b] Radio New Vegas has a better lineup. This game made me hate Bill Nye.
* [b]The game runs out of tricks a bit too quickly.[/b] It's a bad sign when a mission is called End of the Road and your first thought is "Good; it's ending."
* [b]The suggested difficulty is too easy.[/b] If you die anyway because you're bad at video games (like me!), you're punished with an obnoxiously long corpse run!
* [b]The save system is a glaring accessibility issue.[/b] The game saves after every junction, and junctions last about 10 minutes. Sounds reasonable, right? Nope! Quitting the game mid-run automatically counts the run as a loss and sends you back to the garage. The only purpose of these saves is minimizing lost progress from game crashes (I know this because my game crashed exactly one time during my playthrough). Runs can easily last 6 junctions during the endgame. That's [i]an hour[/i] without a (usable) save. Like, if you're worried about savescumming in your way-too-easy-anyway game, disallow loading mid-run saves on higher difficulties. The saves are there; let me use them!
* [b]The quirk system has SO MUCH unfulfilled potential.[/b] Out of over a dozen quirks I've only considered four to [i]barely[/i] be worth fixing and only one has been [i]very slightly[/i] helpful. Add to that the fact that the game keeps you flush with stable energy to bruteforce troubleshooting and quirk removal is cheaper than dirt and you've got an undercooked mechanic that would have otherwise justified the game's existence on its own. This could have been Ironwood's Shadows-of-Mordor-Nemesis-System moment! They just had emphasize it instead of treating it as one more curiosity! This is worse than the mechanic being bad! I'm frothing at the mouth here!

Pacific Drive is certainly a very unique game. What really drew me to it was the idea of having what is basically "S.T.A.L.K.E.R. The Racing Game." It does a great job at it! The story definitely has that kind of vibe, hell, they even call it "the zone" in Pacific Drive. I don't want to get too involved explaining the story but it was certainly really interesting all the way through.

Pacific Drive is a roguelite where you're gearing up your vehicle to become stronger and stronger. The game basically revolves around three key game mechanics.

1 - Exploring/Scavenging - You'll spend a good amount of time outside of your car on foot. During this time, you'll be scavenging for materials. There are some survival mechanics here but it's not too involved. 

2 - Maintaining/Repairing/Upgrading Your Car - Everything is a danger and you'll constantly have to repair and maintain your vehicle whether it's repairing your cracked windshield, repairing damaged body panels, or fixing flat tires. You'll also upgrade your car to be stronger as you progress.

3 - Driving - This is by far my favorite part of the game, there are several different anomalies blocking your path as well as just hazards in the road. Racing around, especially running from the storm, can be adrenaline pumping depending on the situation. It gets really exciting racing from the storm with it right behind you while you're low on health hoping you can hit that portal back to the garage before you run out of health.

There are a few different mechanics in this game and for the most part, not all of them will be for a lot of people. To be completely honest, about halfway through, the maintaining/repairing portion started to feel like a drag but fortunately there are some nice accessibility options that lets you basically skip that part and just focus on the driving and story. I ended up turning more and more features off just so I can focus on the part I enjoyed, the driving, because the rest felt like such a drag for me after a while. That's also because I'm not huge on these kinds of maintenance games, it's not to say it had poor mechanics, that part of the game just wasn't exactly for me.

The game also does not hold your hand at all. There were a lot of mechanics I didn't understand until I already put 5+ hours into the game. Part of it felt a little frustrating because I felt like I was behind where I should be not realizing what I should be collecting/doing. There is a "scan" function that puts things into your logbook but your logbook feels like an absolute waste without any relevant info. Furthermore, you can't really ignore it because you have to scan certain anomalies to unlock upgrades in the garage. 

That being said, the game is really interesting and there's nothing else quite like it. Driving around in The Zone was still an awesome feeling. If you like the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games and want to experience it in a different genre, this is definitely worth your time. I think it overstays its welcome a little bit and is a little too long but plenty of accessibility options will help you see it through to the end if you start to tail off in the latter half.

I've been looking for quite a while for a game that scratches the same itch as subnautica, and I finally found it with Pacific Drive. To me, some bullet points for things it nails:
- interesting environment, capturing a "vibe"
- a reason for doing things -- so many "survival craft" style games are just like "fuck it, you are naked and it's cold, bang some sticks together, good luck finding your own fun" --- there is a place for that kind of experience, but for me it's never enough. Like Subnautica, Pacific Drive has some narrative hooks to push you forward.
- fun progression systems -- the upgrades, the increased options, are all fun
- and of course, a REASON for those upgrades -- the further you explore, the more dangerous it gets, and those upgrades become more and more important.
- a safe upgradeable home base
- safe upgradeable mobile HQ - being able to "hide" in the car and be safe throughout the game, is great.
- This one is NOT the same as subnautica, but I really appreciated that they made the ENVIRONMENT scary, spooky, whatever, but at no time in this game is anything ever coming after you. The threats and dangers in the world are generally ignorant of your existence. The few cases where things might actively seek you, they are NOT scary or terrifying monsters. I appreciated that the game could "creep me out" but I could always tell myself it's just sounds, nothing is going to get me. I'm not a fan of scary games or whatever, so this allowed me to enjoy this experience a great deal.

All told, they knocked it out of the park with this one, and I'm absolutely smitten with this experience. An absolute favorite for me.

This game was fantastic from start to finish. First thing that should be mentioned is there is a degree of tedium to the game. Constantly opening and closing car doors, turning the key every time, putting the car in park or drive, turning on your lights, your wipers, and so forth. If that doesn't sound like your thing, then the game immediately wont be for you. The game does give you options to invest in as you progress that removes some of this, but if you're anything like me you these little tedious details a much more immersive and engaging part of the game. It creates little tense moments, like forgetting to put your car in park when you're on a hill, and having to make the decision between grabbing the materials you need and chasing down your car later, risking getting caught in an anomaly or a hurricane, or abandoning the materials and saving your car and any damage it will take rolling away. The games full of little decisions and tense moments like this, and the way the game engages you with them is great.

Next thing to address is that many of the reviews on here seem to criticize the save system of the game. This is somewhat baffling, since pretty much every detail in the game, down to the myriad of different difficulty and survival options, and yes even the save options, are editable in the settings. I've seen many different 20-30+ hour long reviews on here criticizing the default save option, yet you can easily toggle it to be whatever you want in the settings.  By default the game punishes you for abandoning a run and saving but you can change it to whatever you want with no penalties. Keep all your items, lose some items, lose everything, save on the go, pretty much everything is available in the settings. People playing a game for over 20-30 hours and not checking the settings is a recipe for frustration in any game. Check your settings people.

Lastly, the good. Really it comes down to the car. The story begins with you forming a 'connection' with this car that you need to investigate and diagnose, and oddly enough as you continue to play you'll find you the player getting more and more attached to it as well. The blossoms out into every other aspect of the game, looking for materials for upkeep and upgrades, exploring new maps and anomalies to research new parts, and a seriously great feeling of progression as you're subtly pushed deeper and deeper into the Zone chasing answers, lore, and upgrades. You get full customizability over your car and which parts and abilities it has, giving you a good diversity of builds to take advantage of, and the resource cost of trying new things never pushes the game too far into tedium. You never feel like you're doing the same thing over and over again solely to get upgrades, but keeping the balance between exploration, resource gathering, story and progression seamlessly balanced. The story is also quite good for this kind of survival/exploration game, and it gives you some freedom to tackle it at your own pace too. There are some surprisingly heartfelt moments in there that are worth experiencing.

All in all, the games great. If you've watched any videos or trailers and thought it looked somewhat interesting, then this will be your thing. There's no great surprises or hidden quirks about how the game plays, you largely get what you expect, but what will surprise you is how invested you get, and how engaging some of those little moments are. I knew I was hooked the first time I opened a gateway and had to drive like hell to reach it, barrelling through farmland, fences, blocked roads and forests before the instability reached me. This game will make you feel like an explorer, a detective, and one hell of a driver all at once.
