A top-down fantasy game with deck building elements. You play as Vahn who is betrayed by his fellow soldiers and falls in battle, Vahn is given another chance and finds himself in a small town having to start a new, he must build his strength and stop the darkness that plagues the kingdom. 

Now this is the abridged version of the beginning because the intro and the dialogue in the begging is over 5 mins long, way too long in my opinion I was starting to get bored after the min and a half. The intro is voiced and the quality is extremely bad, very quiet, the static is heavy and the voice actor speaks slower than the text is written, but this is not a real big sticking point for me, it's an indie game, developers may find difficulty to have a buget for voice actors and do this themselves, not an issue. The dialogue that follows though is a hard point for me, its drawn out, and lacks any real substance. I read the first dozen lines got bord and just fast peddled through a good bit. I understood what was going on in the story and the rest was genuinely just filler not needing to be there. If they can shorten the intro to be more modest this would be fantastic, realistically have your voiced intro and run a tutorial through the dialogue to keep players interested in the begging would be the best option. 

So, after the long-winded intro I finally got to the meat and potatoes of the game, I started off in a town called Green town and was told to go to the guild to find info on one of the culprits of my betrayal, Joined the guild and had my info, he was in a dungeon just south of the town, but I was far too weak to make it through the dungeon, so I look to the boards for the quest I needed to help me level up. The Boards are scattered throughout the zones and will let you know what the zones level requirements are going to be. This would be somewhat help full if it wasn't for reason’s that I will touch on later. Back to the quest simple enough, kill 20 goblins, ok there are plenty right outside of the town, walk up to the first 3 to kill and they charge me and almost kill me instantly. Sadly, I was shocked because this is supposed to be the first enemies you fight so I didn’t think the difficulty would be ramped up that hard, all I got in the beginning was a short 30 second tutorial and then thrown in to this world, but ok let's continue, then I saw it... something I couldn't believe, there was no save file, this game does not have an auto save and never told me that or if it did, I skipped it in the drowning dialogue in the begging 

After restarting and making sure I saved, I tried the goblins again and died quickly again, so I looked through the info screens and found that I had 15 points I could invest, didn’t know I had them. I like the leveling system I will say that its well Indepth for what you get. You can have more physical damage, more magic damage, more health and attack points, or how fast you recover your health and attack points. On top of that you also have your cards that you can use in battle. the cards as well can be leveled up to your level if you have enough points to do so increasing their damage and crits, and armor increasing in defense. I like how you can swap the cards around and choose your style of attack.  

Let's actually touch on how you fight in this game, A, S, D, AND F, are your attack buttons that can have up to 4 attacks assigned to them, It runs through them kind of like a combo attack, you can mix and match them how you see fit, Shift is your doge and C is your shield I like how this is set up and I feel like it could be extremely fun and fast passed, “could be” is the big thing though.  

After leveling up I repeated my death from the goblins and had to resort to keeping out of charging distance and kill them one at a time, starting my adventure off at a snail's pace. This did not change for most of the game. Most enemies hit hard and when they are grouped in 2s and 3s can easily overwhelm you and defeat you quickly. The reason for this is because for you to regenerate heath and attack points you must stand still and do nothing leaving you open for attack; you can block but this uses up one point each time you are hit negating the refill. So, with this being the way you need to fight the quest boards also make it tough. Most quest are to defeat a set number of specified creatures. That set number always seems to be 20.  

The boards also tell you the quest in the area are for levels x-y and this seems to be far from true. One area marked for levels 3-10, even at level seven, if it wasn't the goblins, I was very close to death if had to take them head on. You either need to be at the max level described or above if you want a fighting chance in the areas. And level seven is where I stopped playing from frustration and boredom, I had grinded to level seven after 4 and a half hours of playing and I made zero progress in the story. 

The fighting is slow and sluggish due to having to wait for recharges during and between fights. During fights its easy to get stuck in attacks, you can’t move and have no option but wait to die, which I feel like is a bug and can be fixed. Progression in the game is slowed to a crawl and needs to be picked up and possibly enemies need to be scaled down. And again with the intro scale back and make the tutorial most of the beginning to give the players more of an idea of what they are playing before throwing them to the wolfs. These are some of the big changes that need to happen to make this game open to a large audience. It's in early access and they can get criticism now to hopefully fix the issues, but I'm afraid this may sully the game in the beginning and people won’t look back to see how it is coming along. It may have been released prematurely and I am afraid it's going to flop even though I can see real potential in the game. I want to come back after some big updates to re-review this game hopefully to find the game I believe it can be, but for now I can’t recommend it to most if any at the stage it is now. If you love to game test this is a great game to get, you can be part of the helping force to get the game off the ground. If not then this is something to avoid for now.

The game is a unique hack-n-slash rpg with deckbuilding elements, where you make your way around Logra after being betrayed by your team and the prince and being sent back in time to turn the hands of fate.

First of all, besides the info dump at the beginning of the game, I love the story. I haven't seen anything quite like it, and it definitely helped to get me invested. The end of the first volume really reeled me in, as quite a bit of the information from the game's intro suddenly made sense in terms of what's happening.

Secondly, the flexibility with the abilities you can equip makes for a very in-depth combat system, even given the wait times to refill your stamina. I personally like the idea of taking evasive action after spending most of your stamina on a powerful combo.

Thirdly, it is challenging. Like, really challenging at points. After the fixes, most deaths seemed much less unfair and challenged me to sharpen my skills and reorganize my abilities and DP.

My only remaining problems are that the buildings are a little hard to distinguish at first so I had a hard time remembering where certain NPCs were.

Overall, the devs are really cool people, go support them by buying this game! It currently has a good lengthy main quest and a smattering of side quests to play through, and I felt it was worth it.

Moments a brilliance, but not without many small flaws.

This little indie game seems to want to emulate the games of old, and it really captures some aspects of those games.

Controls are similar to games like Mario, but it just doesn't feel quite as tight. I found myself struggling when I would try to jump immediately after landing, which only made the Battle Toads-esque section more frustrating. The game isn't very difficult, so it's easy to look past most of the control flaws. The characters hit box seems a tad "off" as well, which makes the protective bubble power up all the more frustrating, but I'll get to that.

The enemies, and bosses, are your standard side scroller fare. They're mostly brainless, and just waiting to have their head stomped on. Nothing groundbreaking, but they're fine.

There are a few small sections that mix the game up a bit. There's a boat section, which really made me think of Battle Toads or Bit Trip Runner, and a plane section. In my opinion, both had their flaws, but I still liked those little breaks from the main gameplay.

Graphics are fine, the game looks like what it's attempting to be. The enemy designs are nice, and I wish they had added more variations.

Sound is pretty incredible. This game has a solid soundtrack, sounding a lot like something Anamanaguchi would make.

There's only one real power up, which is a bubble. It protects you from damage, but only enemy damage. You're on your own with the spikes and buzz saws. It also will randomly pop if you get too close to an enemy, and sometimes even if you killed it.

There is a mode for speedrunning, but I can't help but think that it was an afterthought. The game just doesn't feel like it was meant for that. There are often long gaps of waiting for obstacles to get out of the way, even at the start of levels. I'm also not sure why they didn't omit the story aspects from the speedrun mode, they only slow everything down more.

While much of my review is criticism for this game, it's still not a bad time. It's only a few dollars, and I'd say it's worth a shot to play. You can tell that a lot of love went into making this game, and my review isn't meant to discourage the developer. I would be interested in future titles that the developer puts out, because they could make really good platformers. They just need to put some more time into it.

[b]Anime Artist 3: Harem[/b] is a lewd connect-the-dots/painting game-by-the-number game.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Connect dots and paint by the (proverbial) numbers. Each level begins with a round of "connect the dots", but there is no guide -- the idea is to memorize and follow the shape of the completed image, though a little trial and error will be necessary. Following the dots is the painting portion, where you must select the appropriate colors and shades to populate the image with. Again, the idea is to recall the original image and choose accordingly. In "Challenge Mode", your color palette is limited in uses, so it's important to make the most out of your colors. If you get stuck, there's a "Magic Brush" that does everything for you (but it's usage is extremely limited.) In "Hot Mode", you erase the clothes from the completed images (to uh, "relax"). You can use "Stars" earned by completing stages to unlock new outfits for the on-screen avatars (or nudity) -- [i]woot![/i]

[h1]Story[/h1]
There is no story (that I'm aware of). I [i]could[/i] snake around the Steam store page and try to learn about each character, but I don't think I should have to do that -- if it's not in the game, it [b]probably isn't important.[/b] A brief "bio" for each character would have sufficed.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The titlescreen is all [i]fancy-smancy,[/i] with a hexagonal user-interface -- I can dig it. From "Settings", you may adjust audio, display, gameplay and language preferences. However, the characters' voices cannot be toggled -- this should be an option in the "Settings" menu.  You can review CGs from the "Gallery", but only lewd ones (if the lewd-DLC is installed). Overall, the user-interface is a delight to see and click-through: I loved the way the interface is incorporated as art supplies, such as drawing sketchpads, tablets and tables. Though sometimes it appears to be somewhat blurry or cluttered, it's creativity is what I'd expect from a professional release. On a side note, the on-screen avatars interact with the mouse cursor and provide commentary and it's awesome.

[b]- The Goods-[/b]
There are twenty CGs to unlock, each with a nude variant (provided the lewd-DLC is installed). The artwork is high-quality, and the nudity is a welcome sight; however, don't expect anything saucier than bare chests. The four selectable characters can also be made nude, but again there's no lewdness to see ([b]but tiddies![/b]) Hey, if a woman is going to scold me for not connecting her dots, I'd rather she do so with butt-ass naked. . . [i]who's with me?[/i]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
I do recommend this game, but only if you're a fan of [i]connecting dots[/i] and [i]painting by numbers. [/i] [b]Anime Artist 3: Harem[/b] isn't an engaging game, but it's a relaxing game with plenty of waifus to go around! With the DLC installed, there are forty levels for you to enjoy, and there's nudity too (because everything's better with tits!) If you're on the prowl for sexy nakie ladies, [b]Anime Artist 3: Harem[/b] won't be a great fit your. . . [i]purposes.[/i] However, this game is a clear improvement from the previous entry in the series, with new characters and lots of new art to share with them!

[b]Anime Artist 3: Harem[/b] is an easy two-hour game of drawing and painting pictures of women in anime style. You get four artists to hire, and each allows you to access a different array of pictures.

If you've played either of the previous two games, [b]Anime Artist 3: Harem[/b] will be very familiar, as the mechanics are pretty much the same. Draw the sketch, paint the picture in, feel accomplished(?). This game, as it stands at time of this review, is not particularly new, but more a slight refinement of its predecessors. The outfits are cute enough and the additional voice work makes a nice touch. It's not a game that particularly needs a lot of brainpower to play or complete, but that's a good thing if what you need is a low-stress entertaining game with pretty pictures.

On the downside, this game suffers from the same issue as the earlier titles: replayability. Redrawing the same art is likely to bore most people quite quickly, leaving little option once you've finished the game the first time. Additional art packs would make a simple and quick solution, but such implementations would need to contain a fair amount of art to make them worth the purchase. I did feel that there could be more pieces of art to complete, even with all three DLCs installed.

The description of this game confuses me somewhat, as well. Hairstyles are not collectable, as far as I can tell; you get a selection of three hairstyles for each artist. The line 'don't forget to make them fall in love!' seems to imply an element to the game almost similar to a dating sim but if it has this functionality, I haven't seen it. Story-related content would certainly be a welcome addition if the developers were to add this in down the track, though.

Sadly the Gallery, like in its prior versions, lacks the ability to toggle between normal and 'lewd' versions.

All in all, this is a cute game you'll enjoy if you like cute games. You have the option of nudity if you care to use it, but don't need to if you'd rather not (spoiler: as of the time of this review, it's all quite soft-core). It's a proven framework that has a lot of potential for modular expansion. Hopefully the developers add consistently to this game, as I felt they moved on from the prior two a little too quickly.

I would love to recommend this game, as the mechanics and premise are interesting. Climb a mountain! Except this time in QWOP form. Well, it's clear after playing it for a while that some mechanics seem designed to pointlessly annoy you, and the rogue nature is honestly baffling for a game this cheaply designed. Not cheap as in the developer is trying to scam anyone or it's filled with bugs or anything, I mean it feels like the stamina and jumping system feel intentionally ridiculously punishing so as to make players fail more often. 

The mountain/cloud and water/rain levels are where the cheapness really feels blatant. The clouds blocking your view are truly nonsensical. How on earth would it be fun or interesting to wait literally 5-10 seconds for them to pass? If you don't wait, which you may opt not to since your stamina goes down still I believe, you're left doing circles with your character, trying to find a ledge completely blind. It was made so much worse when I had to JUMP while the clouds where blocking the view of either me or the ledge I wanted to grab. The jump mechanics are already really poor, as you need to charge it up and release it at the right time even though getting the arrow to highlight the ledge you want is a needless hassle. You may very well end up not even having enough stamina to do a necessary jump, and if that's the case, you literally can't do anything, may as well start over. Even worse, for some reason, your character can't grab onto anything on their way down, so if you mess up your jump, which is very likely, you lose or you're dead. This all gets taken to ridiculous lengths in the rain level. I'm already slipping, AND I need to aim this wonky arrow and time this unintuitive charge up? Once I died on the last (I would guess anyway) rain level that FOR SOME REASON EVEN HAS CLOUDS I was done. 

Super cool concept, fun in the beginning, but this would have been better without the rogue elements. That would at least make the cheap failures feel better, since you don't need to start the whole game over if you didn't grapple. The grapple points not bringing you back to the grapple point itself after you fail is also a strangely punishing design choice. If this was made in the spirit of Getting Over It or Jump King, with one giant mountain to climb, and you could lose massive progress fast, I think that would be a lot more enjoyable, and feel more akin to climbing a big mountain. 

Totally your vision for the game though, I don't want to sound like more of a dick than I already have so far. Happy others were able to enjoy it, but those were my gripes with the game and why I can't recommend it.

Just take your left is a very short mouse-driven game by Mehrdad Rezaei, who seems to be a solo Iranian developer.  Your character is an agent of some sort who is sent to steal a diamond from a castle, but is antagonized along the way by a small mouse who is determined to stop him.

Just Take Your Left is a short game that can be played from start to finish in about 15 minutes.  The game uses an autosave system and most of the puzzles in the game involve sierra-style player death; your first playthrough may take up to 30-45 minutes as you work through the puzzles as dying does tend to reset your progress a bit in some cases.  The game also has several QTEs with a short window that will kill you if you are not quick enough.

The star of the show here is the animations.  The game is packed full of hand-drawn antics that evoke the feel of some of the old Tex Avery or Tom and Jerry cartoons.  The Steam trailer showcases some of the best of these.  I only wish the rest of the game had risen to the quality of the animation.  

Since it is such a short game, my expectation is that the experience will be polished.  Unfortunately, the music doesn't quite fit in some scenes, and in other scenes, the backgrounds feel a tad unfinished.  The game's text feels as though it was run through a google translate a few times - it gets the point across, sort of, but the text is full of strange phrasing, odd translations and misplaced punctuation.  If I were making a game that I was planning to charge money for, and I were going to release it in a language I was not very familiar with, I would definitely run it by some native speakers for feedback - it feels like that was not done here.  It detracts from the game's charm.

There are also some bugs.  In some cases I managed to create artifact sprites of my player character, and I also accidently broke one puzzle trigger by hitting escape at the wrong time; I had to reload the save to continue.  I had a lever that hung around in my inventory even after I put it in the correct slot.  Also, oddly, there is no custom text for object interactions.  Using the incorrect inventory item on an object has the same effect as clicking that object.

If you are willing to overlook some flaws, and are looking for a short, hand-animated point-and-click, this is a decent candidate worth picking up.  If some of the issues are addressed in an update, I will likely change this review.  However, for the time being, if you are looking for a more polished hand-animated experience, I would point you instead towards TSIOQUE, Luna: The Shadow Dust, Feria D'Arles, or Theropods.

I picked this game up because I enjoy playing point and click adventure games, and the fact it had a really interesting art style, was an indie game, and had a few awards drew me to it. After playing and finishing the game (in just 25 minutes, and I had to look up the solution to only one puzzle), I can say the art style is pretty much the only thing this game has to recommend it.

I don't know if a lot (or at least some) of the issues are because the dev is Iranian, but in that case, it just really goes to show that trying to find people from other countries willing to help out (and there are a lot out there) for cheap, or even for free would help this case a lot.

Okay, the plot. You're Detective Morris, being forced by your boss to go get a diamond from a haunted castle. Is this how police work in Iran, they just... break into places and steal stuff? I mean, there's no mention of a warrant, or why you would go there for actual detective work. Maybe the person t hat stole it left it in an abandoned castle? It really could use some more set up. Also the mouse antagonist is a very odd choice. Why a mouse? Is this another joke that didn't translate well? I'm assuming because you can turn the tables on the mouse in a couple sections, and they didn't want to show you injuring another human... but they never really say why the mouse is there, besides hinting it also wants the diamond.

Speaking of which, the translation is bad. Not in a funny way, or even in a 'This doesn't make ANY sense' way but in a very obvious 'This is missing a lot' sort of way. I know humor is very subjective, but I'm not sure what could have been a joke in here, it was mostly just statements.  There's also very little text in general, which makes puzzles MUCH harder to solve. Morris going 'hmm' at things isn't helpful, a 'I don't want to break the glass with my gun, I only have one shot' would have been helpful. Of course, where you use the gun doesn't make any sense either.

Which brings me to my next problem; the puzzles are VERY nonsensical, and VERY heavy into 'guess what the dev was thinking' territory. Up until some at the end where it's just 'use what you last picked up, it's that linear'.And there's QTEs in the game. One of which made me stuck on a puzzle, because you need to notice a thing in the background for a hint of the puzzle, but you have a quarter second before death. And that' not even a QTE, that's a 'death until you solve it' area.

This also causes another issue; there's no saving. There's autosaves the game does, but that means you might get dumped several screens (and a few puzzles) behind where you died. And you can't save right before the QTE, so you need to do the puzzles over and over until you get the QTE right.

Lastly, the music REALLY doesn't fit. It's a very short loop that's way more cheerful sounding then I would expect, or want. It could be free music (which is fine) but it does not fit for a haunted castle, even for a comedy haunted castle. Either something slower in a minor key, or just in a minor key in general would have helped. I'm sure there's better free music that would have fit out there, this is just so out of place.

All in all, while I wouldn't recommend this game, I would be interested in seeing something by the dev if they made the game longer, and got some other people to help (mainly on translation and writing). I'm not angry, just disappointed.

Cyberpunk GTA 2. I could forgive the bugs and annoyances here and there, but I can't forgive one thing: the driving is bad. Like, really bad. Here's a list of everything that came to mind, I could be forgetting some things too:

Cars don't seem to accelerate and brake properly, it doesn't feel great to drive. They don't handle properly at all in cornering. Just in general, they feel like they "stick" to roads too much.
Their hitboxes are jank and frequently don't match the models.
Collisions feel dreadful, you bounce weird. You also get stuck on little corners of nothing, or hills/elevation changes you can't see, fairly frequently.
When you try to drive away from a wall while scraping against it, instead of steering you away from a wall, it almost always bounces and steers you INTO it so that your hood is against the wall and you can't drive (this is backwards, both for real-life physics and, you know, fun).
Cars will randomly and quite drastically slow down on completely flat straightaways for no discernible reason. I've tested going back over the same flat road after and had  no slowdown. No hills, nothing. Annoying.
While driving, there's seems to be some auto-straightening effect with orienting to east/west/north/south, which makes precise driving, and driving offroad on non-straight roads incredibly annoying as well. This might be what causes the random mystery braking, who knows.
When you exit a car, it massively accelerates, every single time, and if you are turning at the time, you're likely to run yourself over.
When you have to pick someone up, they can kill themselves on your car even when you're barely moving, or even dying from touching your bumper in the front, when you're reversing the opposite way.
Every time you get in a car, you fire your weapon and hit the car from inside the car, if you're pressing the gas to try and drive right away (on controller, anyway). A minor annoyance, but if they didn't even fix something THIS simple, it sort of speaks to their willingness to fix all of the glaring flaws with the driving.

So now that the game has received all 24 levels and i went and redid the old ones(since they were all reset showing 1h in-game records but i had also wanted to try them all again anyways...) as well as did the six new ones from the latest update, and have 100%'d the achievements like... is this my 3rd time now? At least second. Glad i won't have to do this ever again, enough Vietnam flashbacks gained by now. ;3 After all of this(and according to steam this new session of mine took about 3,7 hours, i know i most certainly haven't played twice during the past 2 weeks :P)... i think it's appropriate that i finally give this game a small review.

So what will you find inside this game... as i said in the beginning, 24 levels. Some of them will be fun and easy enough, some can be pretty challenging, and some will likely get on your nerves and make you want to call the game a "kusoge" even though it's clear the dev has put effort into making this game a good game. Certainly, the idea is really genius! As you  press keys on your keyboard, the same keys will raise like high blocks on the virtual keyboard on the screen. Using these blocks your task is to do stuff like push balls or cubes to paint other keys, come into contact with other keys, jump through hoops, in one of the last six levels even set the right combination into a combination lock(i thought that one was especially interesting to work with :D)! In another one you'll be setting new keys to missing spots on the keyboard... i hope you won't need to do this IRL too because of the game, though. D: I didn't but i know i did have to take breaks sometimes haha The idea is genius but... the controls... eh, some games just are meant to be difficult, i guess. Just keep in mind that you are likely to find some of these level frustrating because of how the objects respond to your key block manipulations but in the end... you can do it. I did it. All of them. Most more than once by now. Even the Make a Picture one which used to be impossibly annoying hard to do yet i did it. And now that the dev has tweaked that specific level after feedback(i guess i hadn't been the only one having difficulties with it? :P)... i actually somehow got the record time on the Steam leaderboards! <insert the JUST DO IT meme here> What a sweet revenge... Surely somebody will beat it eventually but i shall bask in the glory of being a record holder until then, with my record time of 4m 21s on Make a picture. :D (Also, a hint for that level: [spoiler]if an image tile is touching for example key J with its corner, if you keep tapping J key lightly, it will slowly drag the tile towards it little by little, though be careful not to flip the whole tile when doing this[/spoiler]. This technique helped me finish making the picture and bringing the two tiles close enough to each other, and it took me a long time to notice it back then, but this time after the tweak with all the other changes it yet again made things much easier on the third stage so i can thank remembering that old trick for letting me get a record time right on top. :) Good luck~ )

Pros:  
+ The interface is visually pleasing  
+ Licenses from some European leagues  
+ Automatic substitutions (can be enabled in settings)  
+ Fast simulation  
+ Junior teams of European clubs have simulated matches and their own leagues  
+ Good 2D match view  

Cons:  
- It’s impossible to view player statistics by season. Only current season stats and records are available  
- A lot of spam emails that quickly become annoying. You constantly get offers to sell players, even though they’re not on the transfer list. If they’re not listed, it means I don’t want to sell them, leave me alone already. After reaching the playoffs finals, I got an email from a fan saying the club is heading in the wrong direction and I should leave. Coaches from other clubs send villain-style emails like, "We’ll beat you, your team is useless, ha-ha-ha!" Why all this?  
- The transfer market doesn’t allow you to filter by skills or nationality, only by position  
- When offering a contract to a player, it’s impossible to understand what they don’t like. You just get an email saying, "Your offer didn’t satisfy the player." You have to blindly adjust the numbers in the offer. And if you’re negotiating with several players at once, you’ll quickly lose track of who you’ve offered what to since the offer history isn’t saved. You’ll need to grab a notepad and write everything down manually. Reminder: it’s year 2022.  
- When discussing a contract with a player, you only have two minutes. Why is this nonsense necessary? I’m playing offline, alone, why can’t I take my time to think about the offer? I have to frantically click buttons, hoping I can finalize the deal in two minutes.  
- On the Summary page during the match, you can’t see who is on the field or how many fouls each player has. You have to either go to the Stats page or switch to the game view mode to get this info.  
- A buggy team foul counter that updates whenever it feels like it  
- You can’t see the opponents’ schedule  
- The game felt quite easy. I started in the second division of Lithuania, and in two seasons, I won the championship and advanced to the EuroLeague.

Friends, I think we’ve all played some pinball “gimmick” games. Some are fun…..for a bit. Some are well thought out but aren’t quite “there”. Some really aren’t pinball at all.

Admittedly, I’ve only been playing jetPIN for a few minutes, but I wish to relate my first impressions. 

First, yes, jetPIN is indeed pinball, and I confess I’m challenged from the first seconds. The goal is to send the ball up through what is basically a flooding gully while evading the rising waters and collecting points from bumpers and targets. I'm speaking as a decent pinball player with four #1 (strictly) pinball scores in ZP. Yet in three tries, I’ve still not completed the first level of jetPIN. Aiming is such a critical aspect, I question if this is a game that beginners will have success with. Just whacking the ball is definitely a losing strategy (if, indeed, a strategy at all.)

Playing more, I can see that much of my difficulty has been in playing in portrait mode. Because of the nature of jetPIN, portrait mode appears to actually show LESS of the table at any moment than does landscape. I'd suggest trying both to determine your preference.

An issue that will stop many pinballers in their tracks is the lack of option to rebind keys. In fact, there are really no options at all for gameplay. As well, the physics aspect is acceptable, but nothing special. (About what one might expect at this price, and w/o other options.) Considering the "one size fits all" feel of jetPIN, I suppose it's not unexpected for difficulty levels to lack inclusion. (Even something as simple as a larger ball and longer flippers for beginners, for example.) But unfortunately, there is no provision for the vast range of skills displayed by Steam pinball players.

Obviously, I’ve not learned strategy or nuance yet, and knowing the table(?) seems perhaps even more critical in this game than most, as only a quite small section of the map is shown at any one moment. And all it takes is one mistake, and you can lose every bit of your progress (and more, since the water is rising as you play. The starting point is underwater very early on in the game.)

jetPIN can be played with a controller or a keyboard. Also, in either landscape or portrait mode. Obviously, no one should “sit” right out and buy jetPIN on my recommendation alone (and I’m not yet sure exactly what my recommendation will ultimately be.) Still, if you have $5 to spend, and are interested in a new-ish and challenging pinball experience, I’ve paid more for less more than once.

This game is very straight forward.  You drive the metro down several lines in the city as efficiently as possible (preferably before you run out of stamina) 
The controls are incredibly simple and it takes 2 minutes to learn how to play the game properly.  You can go forward, you can stop/ go back and you can open and close the doors.

Try not to blow stop signals at stations and don't bust the occasional speed limit or it's game over.  Run out of stamina before the end of the trip and you can't go to the last station. You get more or less money depending on how many passengers get on at each stop.  You control  how long the doors stay open.  When you have low stamina (before numerous upgrades, which cost in game money) it's a race against the clock to get to the last station before you run out of stamina.  
As the game description says you can also upgrade the train's speed, acceleration and braking which will help you complete routes more efficiently.  
Each route is between 6 and 10 stations long and last around (of course, depending on how well you run your train) 3-7 minutes.  
You start off with line 1 and you spend in game money to buy more lines as you go. Each new station you stop at successfully (don't blow through the stop ) you get a bonus 3000 coins.  Take this into account when buying new lines.  You can't upgrade your stamina or train until you stop at 10 different stations.  
There is a useful map of "Eco City" (very creative name I know) which helps you identify which lines you think you can complete with your train (use your brain and determine how much stamina you have and how far you get on shorter lines) 
As simple as this game is I can't say it is always easy.  It is an odd kind of frustrating when you are rushing your train and trying to strategies and save every second to complete a line (especially a new one) before you run out of Stamina and then fail because some passengers were a bit slow getting off your train.  

One thing I will caution people about is that I think many people may find the game very repetitive.  I personally don't mind, I play games like Airplane Mode (well I do really love planes) and enjoy them,  but I can definitely see how running trains through a tunnel over and over again (especially down the same line to make easy money for upgrades) can get old.  The scenery above ground or below ground or underwater doesn't change much (if you can say at all).  You are in a metro, going down tracks.  The most exciting that is going to happen is arriving at a new station.  You also have to stay alert because the speed limit on certain lines change regularly which means if you aren't careful it's back to the depot and you start from the first station.  It's repetitive but you have to stay alert you can't just put the train on autopilot while you... do whatever else you do. They could have added random events to spice things up, but that's not part of the game as far as I can tell. 

But the sound design is amazing, the graphics are simple but clean, the game is simple and the learning curve for the controls are non existent and overall it's a good game.
In my opinion, 8/10 when you consider everything and the price.
The game is worth it.

Fun, simple game with a light progression system with several routes to try and get through.  For $1 there's a pretty good challenge to be found here provided you like the idea of simple pick-up and drop-off as fast as you can.

In terms of controls, there's not much more than accelerate, brake, and control the doors.  At the same time, you'll be fighting a stamina system that slowly drains before you've ever started to move the train and signalling issues which may enforce speed limits or cause you to stop.

For the most part, you won't be able to make it to the end of even the first route and you'll need to move onto other routes before you do in order to unlock the upgrade system (the barrier of which is reach 10 new stations across as many routes as you like).  By the time you do, you should have plenty of cash to boost your stamina, acceleration, brakes, and top speed.  Even with your initial unlocks, you'll still probably struggle to complete the first route so inevitably the goal is to make enough money (based on how many passengers you pick up, so even your last station is worth money) to get even more upgrades so that you can complete the run by visiting every station on a route.

The graphics are functional and very simple.  I think this is a port of a mobile game, but it doesn't have much relevance here as you're only limited to three buttons anyway.  Curves and switches are assumed to be abstracted so it's really just a single shot of your train and the terrain blowing on by.  As a bonus, you can paint your train for each route by messing with some RGB values, but the novelty in that wears off real fast.

At each station, you'll have to open your doors and watch as people file out before people start to file in.  In typical passenger fashion, most of them will line up at the back car meaning you can make a choice of closing the doors early and taking off for a smaller payday or letting them all on at the cost of losing stamina.  You can also trigger the doors to hurry the stragglers up, but there isn't much penalty to leaving people behind other than an angry face emote and a hit to your delivery purse.

If you're looking for something simple with a straightforward challenge of "get to the end", you could do a lot worse with your dollar (on sale).  Despite its simplicty, the game is engaging for a time though there are no achievements to push you forward if you're one of those types of people.  It's a game you can easily pick up and play for a little bit in between responsibilities or even to just wind down your evening and scratch an itch before going to bed without having to worry about anything super intense.  While the more advanced routes will require you to pay attention and adjust your speed and the game is entirely a race against the stamina clock, it's still pretty chill.  It's obviously more suited to playing on your commute or while taking a dump, but if you've got a comfy chair and a tall cup of something warm, it's a cozy way to spend some time and let your brain unwind.

No doubt it can be said here that Hoppup! is a game that takes clear inspiration from Nexile's own titular indie game, that being the incredibly difficult and arduous precise platforming game 'Jump King', as this title takes a somewhat different direction in how it goes about achieving a fair but firm challenge and approaches it rather well in my honest opinion!

To get started though, one only has to look at the gameplay itself as this is where Hoppup! takes the most similar approach to Jump King, having a pixelized heroic character that you control to carefully navigate 2D platforms in a vertical manner as you gradually work your way from the bottom depths of a cavern network and make your way up throughout the six areas of the first level as they become progressively more challenging and demanding on the player's capabilities where precise platforming is concerned!

However, unlike Jump King where it only aids you with the gift of certain shortcuts once you have the confidence to try out more risky jumps and the skill to make it consistently happen, Hoppup! aims to make this more of a 'palatable' experience for casual gamers or even those completely new to the whole precise platformer genre as you are very quickly introduced to a pineapple fruit which, in my honest opinion, I thought was one of a good few 'collectables' that could allow you to change your characters skin as you progress higher and higher, however the only fruit that exists is this one, and for good reason considering how it allows you to respawn once when you miscalculate a jump and fall down more than an entire screen, with a small flag that indicates where your next respawn point is whenever you attempt a jump to another platform.

Now some pineapples are put out right in the clear open for you to see, however outside of the first one at the beginning of the game these are often tricky to reach and failing to get to them will often result in a lot of lost progress, however skilled players will be able to take advantage of these for extra second-chances, acting as a 'pseudo-checkpoint' of sorts for those with the skill to pull it off consistently. However, others are well-hidden in areas where there is a background covering it but has an 'opening' with no wall actually covering it on one side, although these are quite hard to notice on a first playthrough but are well-worth finding out as these are much easier to regain when you lose your pineapple power-up from a miscalculated jump by simply going back to the spot with much more ease than the open pineapples accessible only by tricky platforming!

Also to touch upon the exact 'physics' of this game as it were, this does differ from Jump King in that this game does not put as much horizontal momentum for shorter hops whilst bigger jumps get more vertical height movement, as instead Hoppup! will have the exact same projection for each jump, no matter how small or long the jump itself is, meaning one has to focus less on the 'angle' of the jump and more so reaching the distance from one jump to another, noting that hitting the ceilings too works differently as, on this game, you'll just stop all momentum and fall down like a rock which more often than not leads to lost progress.

Getting into the level or, rather the two 'levels' if you count the DLC as it's own level at that, you start off with the basic and fairly forgiving starting area down below the depths of the caverns as you slowly get accustomed to more difficult platforming, then there's the dungeon that introduces both curved platform sides to give the illusion of easier jumps alongside hidden areas, for better with Pineapples or for worse to trick you to fall down and lose progress) alongside the Temple area that cuts down on the size of platforms to get you accustomed to gradually harder platforming and the Outside area introducing clouds that act as 'fragile' platforms that break apart after stepping onto it for a few seconds requiring quick-thinking and reflexes to boot!

Such mechanics help to test the player's skills in precise platforming whilst also adding new challenges to overcome as you gradually become better at the game, helping to further push yourself in overcoming what lays ahead in the next area, no doubt making for quite the satisfying gameplay cycle here!

Although, to touch upon some issues of Hoppup! here, the DLC that the creator put out for free here (very much a plus in my eyes, even if the actual content itself is not quite so great!) is a MUCH harder challenge I truly feel should have had a third level inbetween to help even out the gap of difficulty as the starting area alone is a big step-up in difficulty and it doesn't help that even making ONE mistake will very likely send you all the way down to the very beginning, which is frustrating as this is likely an attempt to make up for it with the worst of Kaizo level design as there is a big shift from the final area of the first level that dabs a little into this but still is not NEARLY as consistent with big falls as the second level is, something that Jump King avoided by having the New Babe+ tower escalate the challenge more naturally via tighter platforming whilst Ghost of the Babe reels it back a little but ensures any falls made have a high chance of making you lose a great deal of progress, though not so bad that you can possibly fall from near the top right down to the bottom!

Other issues include a lack of music in general that gives each of the areas it's own distinct atmosphere, the graphics not being as well-polished as they could have been and also few characters to really have a conversation with to build some sort of lore behind the world of Hoppup! although, to my understanding, Jump King also has this problem but makes up for it by further expanding their dialogue outside of the one or two sentences giving them further personality and character as it were.

Overall though, I would still recommend Hoppup! to those looking to dip their toes into the precise platforming genre but also to hardcore veterans of the likes of Jump King, not so much for the first level but rather the second, although I will say that there isn't much in the ways of additional content outside of the DLC but, considering it is free alongside the general asking price being fairly cheap, it is only fair to view this game as a short but fun experience here, of which I mostly enjoyed for the first-half anyhow!

TLDR Version:

• A casual and more friendly entry to the infamously-difficult precise platforming genre (+)
• Hoppup! takes inspiration from revered Jump King by putting similar focus on one's jumps and how best to aim them as well as the consequences for undershooting/overshooting it (+)
• Gameplay is challenging and easy to lose progress but is also forgiving as Pineapples spread throughout help to give lesser experienced players a 'second chance' by respawning after a failed jump (+)
• Areas naturally become more difficult as wide platforms become increasingly shorter and harder to avoid obstacles whilst introducing new mechanics to further challenge the player (+)
• DLC offered by creator for free that introduces a whole new second, but much more challenging level (+)

• Game is relatively short and will not offer much in the way of content for those hoping to explore a product with more 'meat' to it (-)
• A lack of music hinders the atmosphere of the game as the ambiance of the areas have to do all the heavy work and could have added some much-needed charm (-)
• Graphics are lacking in detail and may not look appealing for long-term gameplay (-)
• The DLC 'The Frozen King' is a massive jump in challenge from the original level and can very easily put-off casuals alongside experienced precise platforming fans not expecting a sharp whiplash in Kaizo difficulty (-)

Nobody has reviewed this since launch, so I'll give it a go. This is my first review here at Steam, keep that in mind. Hopefully it can help someone decide if it's worth them laying down their hard earned money.

The core gameplay of BGB is fantastic. The deck building is balanced, there's a wide variety of opponents to duel, there's room for divergent strategies. A lot of care has been put into that part of the game, it really shows, and it makes it a blast to play. 

The dungeon/environmental part of the game is also done well. Basically, the deckbuilding is the main course, but to stop it from being potentially monotonous, the game gives you dungeons to walk through to contextualise the battling, but also to make the game deeper and not so uni-dimensional. So many games mess this idea up. Crappy side scrolling shooters in point-and-clicks, puzzles in visual novels...the basic idea is good, breaking up the essential part of the game with little diversions, but man, many games screw it up. People buy a puzzle game because they want puzzles, giving them a platformer for a part of it is purposefully giving them something they didn't sign up for. And that's assuming this intrusive piece is actually well done. Because they're not the main part, often these diversions don't get the attention they should require. The worst idea is too make these interlopers overly challenging. Don't under-engineer a part of your game, and then make it so hard that it's a chore to get through. I find this to be an endemic problem in games. BGB doesn't make that mistake, the dungeons are interesting enough that they pass the time between card battles, but not so long or difficult that they distract from the main gameplay. Definitely the card battles are the best part, the main part, but the dungeon parts do a good job at making that deckbuilding part better. It's more good judgement than anything, BGB doesn't shoot itself in the foot trying to be something it's not.

The game isn't entirely stable yet. The bugs aren't of the the re-boot the computer variety, it runs fine, but there's lots of times when you're left wondering, "hmmmm...I don't think that's the way that was supposed to work...". Personally, I'm an indie game fanboy, and I love the idea that one person, or one person and their friends, can go out and make a game, all by themselves, it's wonderful. I prefer to support creative people and turn a blind eye towards imperfections. But your mileage may vary. This is an indie game, still at launch, so by those standards, the game is actually not bad, but perfect it is not.

BGB is not huge. The craftsmanship of the deckbuilding is good enough that BGB is replayable despite it's small size. But there's only three dungeons, there's only so many NPC conversations, there's certainly deckbuilders with more cards and opponents, or with larger environments. What is here is good, but I wouldn't describe it as "epic". "Well crafted" would be better. BGB reminds me a lot of a well done mid-tier console game from ten years ago. The type of game that listed for ten bucks less than the most famous games of the time, and that nobody really paid attention to until it was discounted even more than that. But once it got cheap enough, people began to notice that it was a lot of fun. I think anybody going into BGB with a reasonable set of expectations should be glad they made their purchase.

I don't want to over hype BGB. It won't change your life or anything. But I'm glad I bought it, I've had fun with it so far. There's so many games available here at Steam, and some of them are complete garbage. Baby Goat Billy is miles above some of the dreck that you can get here. But it is modest in its goals and reach. If you can accept that, you'll probably like it. There's a level of polish in the gameplay that is actually pretty surprising. It gives some of that polish right back by having some bugs, so it's a mixed bag that way. 

That's it. I hope that was helpful to people. There's many choices to make when it comes to gaming, and it seems to me that it's often tough to know if something is any good or not. There's many talented and thoughtful contributors in the reviews at Steam, that really helps, but at the same time, there's also a sort of boosterism to it all. I would love this game to do well, because I think it's pretty good, and I know if I put too many discouraging words in, potential buyers will just move along. So there's a kind of drive to be overly positive. I'm hoping that this review was balanced enough to help you make an informed decision.

"Mixed feelings" is about the best way to describe my time with Final Fantasy VII Remake. Let's get the obvious out of the way first. No. This remake did not need three games. Are you insane, Square? The original was a pretty excellently paced RPG with a sweeping story with real scope. This is Bloat - The Game.

That aside, the original plot and cast still shine so brightly that this is worth it for seeing those moments replayed here in infinite more detail. And while I'm still more of a fan of turn-based combat in general, I'll freely admit the combat system in Remake is loads better than the original. It's also really cool to see Midgar fleshed out, though at times its scope seems bizarrely confined, especially when the game tries to shoehorn in small sections of an open-world feel.

But.

The parts of Final Fantasy VII Remake that deviate from the original script are pretty glaring. For the most part, this is largely irrelevant. Most of it is just added content and a mixed bag of character moments, and by itself, that would be fine. But then there are moments that actively hurt the plot structure. The most egregious of these is the point at which Jenova is introudced, which is, bizarrely, interrupted by an entirely too long new dungeon in Remake that adds nothing in terms of fun and kills the momentum of the Shinra tower section.

By and large too, what's new just doesn't feel written in the same vein as the original universe. Characters like Roche feel out of place. The "change your fate" plot points feel like someone's AO3 passion project without the fun sexy bits. Wedge, Biggs, and Jessie's new character moments are fun, but ultimately lack any emotional punch.

Then there's the music, which never entirely hits the mark. Some of the early orchestral music shows promise but then the game delves into weirder riffs on the classic score for the sake of... well, being weird. Nothing hits with the same depth and force of the original soundtrack or the many gorgeous takes that have come out since. It genuinely feels like they blew the entire budget on graphics and gameplay, then bought the dollar store composer for the music and the Dave's Discount Tacorium ad writer for the new content.

But, and this is the most important part of this review, there's a ton of heart to FF7 Remake, despite my complaints. The Aerith stuff in particular is very lovingly done, and Cloud's character progression is loads better than the original. Barret gets to play up his comedic role even more, and Hojo is delightfully sinister. The good far outweighs the bad here, but I am left wondering what might have been if they didn't try to Hobbit the everloving hell out of a classic game that didn't really need a lot of this extraneous content. I recommend it, but temper your expectations.

Before playing this I had only played the first part of Final Fantasy 7, and that was enough to make me fall in love with the worldbuilding and the characters.

This remake shows more of the story until the escape from Midgar, which is quite interesting.

Starting with the best points of the game, the combat is an interesting mix between turn-based from the original and real-time action, which works well and with different combat mechanics for each character. Leveling up weapons and choosing their advantages also allows greater flexibility in character development throughout the levels. And the part of inserting materials into the equipment is also another factor that helps in this aspect.

The game's story, with some differences from the original, is quite good. The entire conflict between Avalanche and Shinra is simple but creates interesting challenges for the main team, the villains have understandable objectives, and the Shinra leader has plausible arguments and justifications for his actions, all of this makes the story more interesting. As characters I will highlight Barret, for me the best developed character in this remake. The duality of leading a "terrorist" movement, of having to make the most difficult decisions while at the same time having to take into account the lives that are at stake, including that of his daughter. At the same time, he shows enormous motivation and dedication to his cause. The rest of the main characters aren't far behind either.

The least good points of this game are the fact because of the game being chapter-based and very linear, there are phases in which not all members will be available to be used in combat, this in itself is not the problem but rather the frequency with which it happens.

In combat, the members that are not being controlled not using spells or items also made me a little frustrated but nothing too worrying. And the biggest criticism I have of the game is the cutscenes, the game has very good and very beautiful cutscenes, but there are parts which they are VERY slow, they take a long time to show something simple or to highlight something that could have been quite quick, I even think that most of my playing time was in cutscenes. Despite being very beautiful, they took up a lot of game time in my opinion.

In conclusion I think its a wonderful game and experience for fans and newcomers to the Final Fantasy 7 story and despite its flaws it has some points that make it unique.

This is a pretty hard game to review, because, while I did have fun and I liked it, it was mostly because I knew how to manage my expectations. I can see how others could (and will) with a different perspective, easily dislike or even hate this game.

Disclaimer: I haven't played the original.

I'll start with what is 75% the reason I enjoyed this game: The combat.

Although it saddens me that modern games have been ditching turn-based combat in favor of more action oriented approaches, this game still manages to incorporate systems from older FF titles into it, and they feel great.

One of the best things about turn based combat is how it allows for more strategic gameplay, and one of the weaknesses of action based combat is that it can become little more than just button mashing. Combining aspects from these two led to a system that allows button mashing through the easier encounters of the game, but requires you to analyze and work around the strengths and weaknesses from tougher enemies. This keeps it from feeling repetitive, making it both enjoyable and occasionally challenging.

There are a lot of bosses, most of which I enjoyed, though I will say that more so than I'd have liked, some bosses failed to feel mechanically distinct, and their gimmicks could be boiled down to them alternating between states of physical invulnerability where you would have to exploit an elemental weakness with a spell and states of elemental invulnerability where you would have to physically attack it as much as you could before it went back to the former.

Nonetheless, that was rare enough to not become annoying or hamper the experience significantly. Combat is easily the most prominent highlight of the game and what I had the most fun with.

Now as for the other, perhaps even slightly controversial stuff. Let's start with the story, the characters, and pacing.

This story is not Shakespeare, it's not a deep dive into the intricacies of eco-terrorism, corporatism or anything, and it doesn't try to be. To any of these, it's what the Barbie movie was to feminism, a very surface level introduction. Overall, it's very lighthearted, and never shows you more than just enough to get the point it's trying to get across. This goes for everything, from the politics of the setting to the backstories of side characters.

If you head into it understanding that, you'll have a good time, but the moment you start to feel like it doesn't do enough or it's a little light on details, the "illusion" of cohesion will fall apart. This approach bites the game in the ass at times, and in my opinion, especially near the end it becomes a crutch used to justify what could be arguably seen as lazy storytelling on their end.

As for the characters, i feel that the game never gives enough attention to any of them for them to shine, and most of them feel like they're on the edge of being one dimensional. The biggest offender that comes to mind is Tifa. She rarely ever displays any personality apart from the typical nurturing, feminine yet strong character archetype. The only moment where she comes close to more is when [spoiler] she tells Cloud about feeling conflicted over the way Avalanche is handling the fight against Shinra, but that's it, she never really does anything about it. At most she shows a little hesitation, but she never protests and always goes along with whatever the rest of the group want to do. [/spoiler] The rest are a little better, but not by much, except maybe Cloud, who I'd still only consider decently written.

The pacing is the biggest issue with this game in my opinion, I didn't play the original but I can tell how padded it must feel in comparison. It drags out sections A LOT to justify the 35 hour runtime (and the price tag) and comes very close to going overboard at times. Especially in sections like the collapsed overpass or whenever it wants you to do side-quests (most of which are very bland, but thankfully optional). 
What bothers me is that the padding ranges from attempts at character development to filler, and it's sometimes hard to tell which is which because they struggle to prioritize who is worth spending that time on. For example, there are excessively long sections dedicated to very minor characters that feel like a waste of time that could've gone to more important characters, such as Barret or Tifa, who by the end of the game all we know is that he has a daughter, she is Cloud's childhood friend and both are members of Avalanche.
Other sections are dedicated entirely to traversal from point a to point b, such as the collapsed overpass as mentioned before, with little other than occasional combat encounters and some puzzles along the way. Once the game is over, I couldn't help but feel that those could've been shorter to give way to more important moments.

I could spend the entire day talking about this, especially about the ending and Sephiroth (who imo is the weakest link of the entire game), but this is review is getting too long, so I'm going to try to end it soon.

As a conclusion, I will say I do recommend this game. The combat alone justifies the price and even though I said all that about the story, it's told well enough to keep you interested in it, even with its many flaws. The characters are hot and have cute/emotional interactions too, so it's not like they're boring either. 
I'm interested in seeing where Rebirth takes things, as I feel there is still enough potential in this story to see what comes next.
 
Other minor gripes:

- The game stutters at times, specially in the DLC.
- There are some technical issues with the V-Sync settings.
- There is a disappointingly low amount of graphic settings.
- The game can sometimes have very unforgiving checkpoints where you can't save and if you quit you lose 40 minutes+ of progress.

Recommended.

[b]Recreating Midgar, its vibes and atmosphere in modern gaming era. That's "Final Fantasy VII Remake" all about. With gorgeous graphics it gives the players the opportunity to rediscover a much loved city from a new perspective. Indeed, Midgar is well designed and feels alive with familiar characters and the iconic music from the original game. Battles are pretty entertaining featuring fluid combat and cleverly mixing real time with turn based tactics. Yet, the game has some serious problems. Pacing is painfully bad with tons of small and big cut scenes between every ten steps you take. Moreover it's too linear restricting the player inside a narrow path, usually boringly following a companion. Filler content is bad with silly side missions that usually don't even have a plot, while puzzles are simply childish. Disappointingly characters cannot save the day as they have transformed into stereotypical caricatures. Nostalgia may do the trick for older players, but for a modern game it's impressively one dimensional and cannot offer an experience to remember. 


Manometer: 6/10[/b]


The good
- Gorgeous visually with awesome graphics and fantastically designed world. No matter what you had imagined while playing the original game, this recreation will certainly not disappoint you. Midgar feels dense and alive as you visit various sectors and Shinra's facilities. For the first time you have the opportunity to be really inside the slums, move freely, feel the dirtiness and the verticality of the pillars above you. A feeling that wasn't there in the original game due to the top down cameras and prerendered environments. It's a world that feels new, but also faithful to the original game keeping the same vibes.
- Good, fast paced battles. Although real time action, most of the time, at normal level ends up being a smashing button procedure in order to fill bars and activate the real abilities, battles are pretty entertaining. There are a lot of moves, materias, items to use and various elements to take into account. You can change between party members to take full advantage of each character's abilities. Enemies have special weaknesses and some of them need specific approach. Combining all these, the game allows you to try different strategies and manage your resources in an interesting way. Battles are a decent, pretty refreshing, mix of real time mechanics with classic turn based tactics.
- Decent RPG elements. There is a good amount of weapons that you have to master in order to learn their moves and you can update them with skill points to make your characters stronger. Materias also gain levels so it pushes you to use more those that you may want to upgrade. There are also armors and items to earn or buy from various merchants. It doesn't get too deep, but there are plenty of options to create your owns builds and roles inside you squad.
- Although most of the small enemies feel a bit generis and repetitive, bosses are awesome. They are well designed and impressive visually. They have special abilities and their weaknesses aren't always obvious. Boss battles have nice flow and they are probably the most interesting part of the game as you try to figure out how to defeat them
- Great animations that feel realistic and smooth especially during battles. Facial expressions are nice too revealing the personality and phycological state of each character.
- Good voice acting performances. Despite being a bit exaggerated they're pretty convincing and fit nicely to each character.
- Music is awesome. Maintaining and refreshing most of the original game's iconic tracks offers older players tons of nostalgia vibes. Music during battles is great and manages to enhance the flow even more. Sound design during battles is also good with convincing effects for attacks, impacts etc.
- Despite being too cheerful for my taste and the original game's darker vibes, It has good sense of humor overall. Some events are really hilarious. It can get a little bit tiring after a while though.
- There are some cool mini challenges and mini games that you can test your skills and go for the record.

The bad
- Unbelievably bad pacing. There are tons of cut scenes that kill the flow. Especially during the second half of the game there is a small cut scene literally after every ten steps that you take, only to have a small conversation with companions. Every single action you perform must be followed by a cut scene. There are chapters that you watch cut scenes for hours with only a few battles between them. For sure they had to explain a lot of things storywise, but let me play these events, not watch them. I felt so restricted and bored at times.
- Exploring this beautiful world should be more immersive and imaginative. It's too linear with only a few hidden places to discover and navigation is entirely going from spot A to spot B. Yet, even traversing linearly from a place to another is problematic. There is too much walking just following blindly someone else. Constantly, for no reason, without being in a places of particular interest, it restricts you from running. There are tons of narrow passages and ladders where you move really slowly, while your companions annoyingly tend to block your way in narrow spaces. 
- Filler content is bad. They wanted to add a few more hours of content, I get it, yet all these side missions are just shallow fetch quests without even a plot. Trying to find missing cats or giving vomit medicines to drunkards is as silly as it sounds. I'm sure that people of Midgar, such a unique place, had a lot more to say about past events, social structure, human relationships through their quests.
- One dimensional characters that look more like caricatures. Each character's traits from the original game are sort of cranked up to 11 here. Barret's even more boisterous than before, Aerith is always annoyingly happy and charming and Cloud is a taciturn tough guy that every cute girl loves. I mean when you consider the already existing love triangle of Cloud, Aerith, and Tifa, adding Jessie to the mix and making it a quadrangle just becomes silly. Also for some reason the overall cheerful vibes were too much for me. Don't get me wrong, there are many moments with good sense of humor, but these vibes of the super heros that make cool jokes during the most difficult situations or surrounded by dozens of enemies threw me off. It's just too difficult to love such stereotypical characters.
- Problematic story. I get it, it's part one of a trilogy, yet the events are not enough to tell a meaningful story. The main plot can be summarized in two reactor bombing missions and saving Aerith from Shinra. Essentially it's an intro to the characters with a cliffhanger ending and some things that don't make sense and will get explained in the next chapters. Moreover, I found a lot of things exaggerated. There was too much of explosions, slow motion action, epic scenes, gigantic enemies, acts of heroic self sacrifices. The original game had more calmness and mystery in it, it wasn't only about making a blockbuster.
- Battles are entertaining with nice mechanics, especially against bosses. Yet, facing smaller enemies can get repetitive. Mob's design feels a bit generic and battles against them are usually easy. Facing the same enemies again and again, especially after you have discovered their weaknesses feels boring and just slows you from reaching your destination. Also, some main missions, like the reactor five, lack serious level design. You navigate through identical. copy-paste rooms facing the same enemies for an hour.
- Puzzles are too simplistic, almost childish. Probably they added them just to make the game more interactive between the cut scenes without spending much time to design something really interesting or challenging.
- Bad optimization. There are too many stutters even for advanced gaming pcs.

Final Fantasy VII Remake is a stunning reimagining and retelling of the classic RPG from '97, blending nostalgia with modern flair. The game expands the original’s Midgar section into a sprawling, visually breathtaking adventure, with revamped combat that’s both dynamic and strategic—think real-time action meets tactical pauses for spell-slinging and ability combos. Our main protagonist in this adventure (Cloud, Barret, Tifa, and Aerith) shine with updated depth, witty banter, and voice acting that hits all the right notes. The story sticks close to the ‘97 blueprint but sprinkles in bold twists, keeping veterans guessing while welcoming newcomers. Sure, the pacing drags a bit with some filler quests, and the ending’s tease might polarize fans, but it’s a polished, emotional ride worth taking.
The Intermission DLC, starring Yuffie, is such a cherry on top. It’s a tight, 4-6 hour burst of ninja-fueled fun, with slick ninjutsu and throwing-star combat that feels fresh yet true to her roots. The new character Sonon adds a solid dynamic, and the glimpse into Midgar’s underbelly ties neatly into the larger narrative. It’s a standout addition that leaves you hyped for what’s next.

I "highly" recommend this game! I will elaborate why that is in quotation marks, and in turn why I am not recommending it outright. First I need to add a preface.

I like to unwind in the evening, and or at night before I go to bed. In the past I mainly used to read, watch movies & shows, or play video games. With the advent of VR I started to use that more, and more over everything else. Now I like to relax with several nature, and outdoors VR applications. So Nature Treks, Kayak VR: Mirage, Blue Planet VR, Google Earth, etc...  As well as watch 4K nature walk videos on Youtube.

Well a few months back, out of the blue, I suddenly have had no internet access in the evening, and at night, from time to time. Well normally that would be no problem, and I can just play these nature games/applications in VR. Well, for what ever reason, only a few locations are accessible in this application offline. I reached out to the developers, and they informed me that this is a bug that they are trying to fix.

That being said, when I do get internet access again, all of a sudden all of these different locations need to be updated. For the most part that is with a few exceptions. Oh yeah I should explain that. 

This application has a ton of locations, and these developers are adding more as time goes on for free! Which is a major upside for this application! Not only that some of these locations have additional areas you can visit, and the developers have even gone back and added new areas to previous locations! Anyways when you use the application you press a button, that opens up a menu, which has a bunch of photos going from left to right. You press these photos, with your controller, and it brings up info on the location, and an option to download it.

Since I have encountered this bug, when I go back online, I have to update most of these locations, again, and again. The developers have insisted that this is not a form of DRM, and I believe them. The reason why is because I noticed something after talking to these developers. Each time I have to update these locations, again, my game folder is suddenly getting larger, and larger in size...

Therefore if you are in a similar situation as me. Where you don't always have internet access, and or you are charged by how much you download, then you might want to hold off buying this game. Or if you do buy it then this is something to keep in mind. Right now, with my current internet provider, it is simply a monthly fee with unlimited use. In the past however, with my last provider, they charged for each Gigabyte downloaded... 

Updating most of these areas, each time, can add up to a lot overall. On the low end it is around 300 Megabytes for one location, and on the high end it is around a Gigabyte for a location... So yeah. That is the major problem this application is facing. Now if the things I mentioned are not applicable to you then by all means buy this game!!!! It is my favorite nature application!!!!

Just a very good rally sim all around, and what I've been looking for for a while. The driving feels properly realistic and if you play without assists you have to know what you're doing, but it doesn't feel like everything is a trap and the entire game hates you (*cough* Dirt Rally 2.0 *cough*). Feeling like I'm actually being challenged but without those "WTF ARE YOU KIDDING ME" moments that artifically difficult games tend to create is a massive plus.

Also, lots of rally locations and cars, nice choice of modes, graphics aren't amazing but are fine, works very well on an Xbox controller. Oh, and doesn't require you to install any spyware, I mean "anticheat" to play single player. (*cough* EA WRC Rally *cough*).

***** Some more thoughts after 10 more hours: *****

+ The cars feel like they have actual weight and react more or less how you would expect in real life (yes, I'm comparing to DR2.0 again and its bouncy toy cars)
+ Handling feels equally good and realistic on gravel, asphalt and snow
+ Default tunings actually make sense and are perfectly usable
+ AI doesn't seem to rubberband

- ...but it seems to get the same results regardless of conditions - it seems near-impossible to win on snow/ice while easily winning by 10 seconds on dry asphalt on the same difficulty
- Tuning options should have explanations, I've played hundreds of hours in rally sims and other racers, but I still got confused, and especially the gear ratio settings are completely counterintuitive
- Monte Carlo is as enjoyable as a root canal treatment, and the season mode seems set to torture you with it (at least the side barriers are not a death trap here)
- The anniversary mode should have a difficulty setting besides assists - it should be a great learning mode, instead with these required times already the third race is a sweaty grind
- Even on "realistic" level the damage seems very low

Overall a really good game though and definitely recommended.
