Quick early impression:

This game is really nicely done. While there are a few minor complaints about how some of the spells and combat work, overall this debut game form a new studio delivers a lovingly crafted and well thought out action adventure game that blends a number of familiar but fresh concepts into its own creation.

People are going to sleep on this game because it takes a little bit of time to open up and get into the meat of things and everyone is so used to instant gratification - but let me tell you - if you just put in a bit of time this game gets really difficult to put down.

There are bits of monster hunter in here with a really open and free form combat that allows you to combine some excellent physics based spells for some pretty neat results. It's the sort of game that just gets better and better the more you unlock and play. At first it feels a bit slow and you feel weak. The melee and ranged combat felt dull but once you start to build nicer gear things open up and get incredibly fun.

I had the most epic battle with a dragon that i think i've ever had in a video game. It was utterly thrilling the whole way through.
The battles with these giant creatures are so well done, from the freedom in how you approach them to the mechanics at play. It's honestly so much fun.

My first mistake was thinking i could rush into the action of the game and by doing so i missed out on alot of important story and guidance. This meant that i didn't really vibe with the demo as i was more interested in rushing and skipping dialogue.

While the full release does let you carry over your save i opted to start fresh and this time sit back and listen to the intro and to engage with the dialogue. The story is well told and wonderfully illustrated with gorgeous animated cut scenes. The dialogue scenes are again wonderfully illustrated and offer multiple paths for your answers as each fleshes out the game world and allows you to get to know each characters personality giving your companions a depth that you will miss when skipping. The voice work is very well done and each bit of information rounds out the lore or game world in a fairly natural way.

Visually the game is a real treat. The style is difficult to describe but i'm going to call it a photo-realistic cartoon look meaning the character and creature designs are stylised and more like something out of a comic book and the textures are not trying to be photo-real and yet the lighting and overall shading and rendering is very realistic and physically accurate. Its difficult to describe but the overall result is that you feel like you are inside a wonderful fantasy storybook where everything looks very tangible while still popping off your screen in a beautifully art directed style. I really like it and it really fits the overall theme and tone of the game.

Gameplay is really interesting. Without really spoiling the story, you are part of a small crew that have accessed a unique location and set out to investigate further. You go out on expeditions and gather resources while trying to progress further. You bring those resources back to your base to build up your gear and get stronger and more powerful. I have really only scratched the surface of this but so far that is what the main gameplay is based around. All the while you are pushing the story forwards and leaning more about this world.

Combat is where i feel the game could have been more fleshed out. The magic based stuff is really fun. You can use ice to stick enemies feet to the floor or block an archer from firing. You can pick them up and hurl them into walls or off cliffs or into environmental dangers. As the game progresses you can then combine a bunch of these into some pretty creative attacks. All this is great. I'm creating fire bombs by combining spells and taking out mobs with them. I'm freezing a dragons mouth shut so i can get in close to attack. Its amazing.

A short while in you can also upgrade or forge new weapons. I made a fire bow and instantly the ranged combat felt leagues better. 

I need to spend more time with the game so these are just early impressions from my time with the demo and this full release and mostly to say yeah its good. Its an AA game but punching well above its class and i can't wait to immerse myself more into this world and find out what else there is to do and see.

Will update when i've played more.

This game has a bright and vibrant environment with intriguing lore and world bulding. You get dropped into an existing band of weavers, essentially warrior mages, looking to explore a lost and isolated civilization that catastrophically shuttered itself off 50 years prior, instigating global instability. I think the characters have great character design and pretty good dynamics between them that you get to explore. They also exist outside of you with their own histories, which I think helps make them feel more real. I was a bit iffy at first on the switch from 3D to 2D for conversations, but the 2D sprites are detailed and change with various character reactions so I grew to like it. 

There's a crafting system in the game I really enjoy that changes your characters appearance and resistances. It's a bit like monster hunter, I wanted to hunt a big ice dragon so I crafted some cold resistant clothes, and then after the hunt I collected parts I could put towards crafting, enhancing, or reforging my weapons and clothes. For me, it's also a huge bonus there's no weapon durability to deal with. This game mechanically is a lot more than I expected.

So much of the environment is destructible or climeable and you can climb on any sufficiently large creature. A few hours in, I was clinging to a dragon in mid air. I ripped it's magical essence out of it's body, came crashing down into a building, destroyed it, and discovered some loot I missed. This game has a lot of cinematic moments like that that aren't scripted. A favorite thing of mine to do is to freeze a monsters foot or wing to the ground so I can hop on while they  scramble to get unstuck. Genuinely it's just really cool gameplay. 

What I appreciated about this game is that it has a lot of direction driving you forward without being hand holdy. It's open world, but the open world is segmented into zones, and even then you're explorable radius (the scrying distance) is expandable. I think this is a good approach. I think this is better than a game like Horizon Zero Dawn that has a fantastic and large open world that's too easy to get lost in and you never get back to the main story. But about 10-15 hours in I encountered a large cluttered city that was honestly pretty confusing to navigate. This was made worse by the fact that the quests I had to do didn't trigger correctly so I was just wondering what to do, before I googled it and learned I had to rollback to an earlier save. This game is not without it's bugs, quests not working correctly, items not appearing in the world, the physics being wonky. 

I think this game is doing some incredible things but it's not without its quirk. You have a fairly small (but expandable) inventory size so in the early game you spend a lot of time going back and forth to camp to drop off your inventory. But at least your inventory is immediately stored as soon as you step foot on camp so it's not as obnoxious as it could be. While I enjoyed the characters and dialogue a lot, sometimes it feels like people modeling healthy emotional communication which just feels a bit weird. And then, much later in the game, characters wont have conversation with each other and then use you as a mediator. It's pretty annoying to witness. I'd say the writing, especially the flavor text you find in the codex, is pretty good though. But there's so much of it it becomes tiring. 

All in all I'd recommend this game. It's got enjoyable gameplay and monsters to hunt with a really forgiving crafting system. But the bugs sapped my enthusiasm for the game about 27 hours in, and it also made it impossible for me to 100% the game. I might wait a few months for a more ironed out version of the game.

So far I'm really enjoying this mashup of dragons dogma/monster hunter gameplay with an actually interesting world/story/dialogue/characters, it wont be for everyone because the combat is physics based (some wonky stuff can happen like getting flung into the sky while holding onto a flapping wing) but if you dig that sort of thing you'll probably like this. There's also a free demo with easily 5+ hours of content in it which is awesome for a game like this with a moderately slow building intro.

Boss fights are really fun, there's a nonbinary cryptography nerd, and a Scottish woman told me I looked nice. 11/10.

Update, now that I've finished the game and gotten all the achievements; I have not had this much fun with a game in a long time. There are definitely some points of frustration from time to time, when climbing (especially climbing enemies) doesn't work exactly how I want it to or how I expect it to. But, these few moments of frustration are easily drowned out by the rest of the time when I am just having a blast. Really really good stuff.

I liked the worldbuilding and the characters the most in this. The story outside of those is fine. Without spoilers it can go like this - small band of adventurers find themselves trapped in an ancient city and slowly explore to unravel the secrets left behind. You've probably heard something similar before. Its the characters that make it special. The main characters can have disagreements and still treat each other with respect without sounding like they're fake. Some of the problems they deal with can hit home hard.

That said if you don't like world building or exploring characters... you can also skip it! The side quests add to the flavor of the world, but they don't make you do them and you you could click past all the dialogue and just read what your quest says to collect or do. The general gameplay loop is enjoyable and the further you get in the game the more options you have to focus on the parts that work best for you. Don't like grinding out the big monsters for resources? Collect a lot of small resources and trade up! You do like grinding just the big monsters? Good! The further you get in the game the more of them there are and the more of them you could possibly fight that day.

Only bad part for me is the controls for climbing can be a bit off at times, and you can't cancel an attack animation during or for what feel like extra time after. It would be nice if dodging just canceled whatever you were doing or was just a little more responsive. That said, i will be playing it through again despite that, and will be on the lookout for if they do anything else set in this world - even if with different characters.

While I found the story interesting, I skipped a lot of the dialogs to get straight to the point, the exploration and fighting. Above all else I enjoyed the game play and combat mechanics the most. The environment is very reactive to hot and cold and maxing out the strands really brings out the highest potential of your powers. While some powers felt underwhelming, I was actually surprised to find that I ended up using 80% of them and finding them useful during my play through. They all have a use. 

The boss battles can be tricky and challenging at times and it really helps to read the codex to figure out their weak points. 

The crafting system is especially interesting and even if you miss some schematics later in the game, you can adapt your gear, re-craft it to really fit your playing style. I played most of the game using light armor and bow whereas someone else can really build a heavy-armored character with 2-handed swords. I found some of the resource gathering a bit grinding, though I hadn't noticed that there was an actual market where I could trade resources. Had I noticed it earlier it would've helped. 

All in all I really enjoyed the game, the graphics are beautiful and the characters fully fleshed out. I would definitely recommend it.

The characters that you share the adventure with are a wonderful bunch and the voice acting is top notch, which is honestly really surprising. I'll update this review for a more detailed breakdown of all the game's elements when I finish the game... which might take a while since I'm savoring every moment I'm in the world of Eternal Strands.

Eternal Strands is a solid action-adventure game with a neat crafting and magic system.  You'll spend your time exploring the world, harvesting all kinds of crafting materials, and coming back to your camp to craft and upgrade your weapons, armors, and spells.

The combat is surprisingly tough.  Even small enemies can be a challenge.  You have to use both weapons and spells to survive.  Taking down the massive monsters is epic.  There's nothing quite like intercepting a giant rock they throw at you and hurling it right back at them!

Those first few hours into the game can be a bit rough as you are starting from scratch. Play carefully.  Dying means losing most of the crafting materials you've gathered on your current run.

Honestly, I've seen enough... The combat system is just awful.

There's plenty of good ideas here, but the general combat is a mix of clunky and floatiness, and the shadow of the colossus esque fights are terrible to navigate. You never feel like you have any control of clinging and jumping, and more often than not just find yourself falling off. They'd have been better off doing more grounded monster battles ala monster hunter. But that would obviously require a robust and worthwhile combat system. And it seems like the game realizes it doesn't have that.

I know that this game didn't sell exceptionally well, but honestly...it's beautiful. The graphics and effects are incredible, the monsters look amazing, and the gameplay is incredible fun. There are a few frustrating moments---sometimes the physics go a bit silly and launch the player a bit, or bits of the monster collide with you, forcing you to grab onto the new pieces instead of what you were on...but aside from those moments, I've absolutely fallen in love with this game.

The dialogue is deep and heartfelt, the character stories are intricate and well thought out, and the world building is *incredibly* well thought out. The bloody *items resetting in the world* is explained. I was like "okay, game mechanic" and then they popped lore in and I was luck... "well damn! Okay!"

Not to mention that I absolutely *LOVED* shadow of the colossus, so this game feels absolutely amazing.

Overall, devs, I just want you to know that this game touched my heart and made me feel *good.* There were character stories that drew tears from my eyes, and gameplay that simply made me feel elated. The spells are so fun to use, and the enchanted weapons are fantastic too.

This game may not be perfect, but nor is any piece of art. I love it.

Also, the voice acting...it's so amazing. Unlike most games, I just sat back in my chair and listened. I'll remember this experience for a long, long time.

Very fun game, and while there are a lot of things that could be done better seeing as it's the first game of the studio I'm very excited to see what they do next!

[h1]Great Debut Title - High Quality Indie Fantasy Action[/h1]

6h into the game, I'm having great fun with Eternal Strands. I like the artwork, the graphic style, the not too challenging combat, a mix of Zelda's Link and Shadow of the Colossus fights and the exploring the ruins of the Weavers' (magicians) lost city-state, the Enclave.

[b]Positive:[/b]
- stylish presentation from graphics, to cutscenes, to artwork and menu elements
  focus on a vivid style, lighting and special effects
- good performance, no hickups, crashes or stuttering (system and settings at the end)
- all-around fighting system: like Link from Zelda you wield magic, shoot a bow, work with Sword & Shield and 2H
- varied bosses from Colossus to Drake, beat em with skill or strategy or both
- reactive controls (maybe increase camera turn rate on controller a bit)
- professional and engaged voice actors
- flexible and simple crafting and upgrade system
- lotsa background lore for those who are interested in it

[b]Negative:[/b]
- nothing that stood out

[b]Settings and Performance: [/b]
All maxed, 4K (2k native with DLDSR 2.25x) and DLSS Quality, 70-80 FPS average (lowest was 52 in the introduction fight from the demo, heavy with volumetric fog and lighting and effects). 

[b]Full System:[/b]
i9 13900k, Gigabyte Aorus Z790 Master, 2x16 GB DDR5 GSkill Trident Z5 6Ghz, MSI RTX3080ti Gaming Trio X, Soundblaster Z, WD Black SN 850X 4TB M2, Corsair HX850 Platinum PSU (850W), 32" Samsung Odyssey G7 (curved, G-Sync), BIOS with microalgorithm fix, hyperthreading and E-Cores disabled, CPU multiplicator at INTEL default

[b]DLDSR & DLSS[/b]
Personally, I don't think a native 4K resolution on a 32" monitor is worth the price and the performance cost. DLDSR 2.25x together with DLSS on the other hand offer an objectively similar image quality to native 4K at lower performance cost. Same goes for those settings versus 2K with DLAA. You get better performance AND better image quality. I use it with nearly all of my games (e.g. FS 2024, FFVII Rebirth, Ghost of Tsushima, God of War Ragnarök, Sniper Elite Resistance to name just a few recent titles).

Caveat: some games (mainly UE5 titles, *spits*) aren't too happy with it and tend to crash, in those cases I disable DLDSR. 

[h3]UE5 and i9 processors (13900/14900):[/h3]
Having played the game for 6h without troubles, I was very surprised that Eternal Strands is using the UE5 engine. Usually, many UE5 titles are accompanied by stutters, traversal lag and crashes at release.

If you have an i9 processor and face crashes to desktop (at game start or randomly), check for the following:
- i9 micro algorithm bug
- BIOS updates (beware OEM windows versions and required reinstallation!)
- Intel Processor Diagnostic Tools to check your CPU health

Finished Eternal Strands after 50 hours, overall score 6/10.  I barely recommend Eternal Strands, with caveats.  This game is a good start for an original IP from a brand new studio.  But man, there's a lot of room for improvements for the potential sequel.

What I really enjoyed: story and campaign, character developments and Companion Quests, writing and voice acting, environments and artstyle, giant monster bosses.

Good enough but needs improvement/overhaul: physics system, magic system, inventory and crafting system, rank-and-file enemy variety and density, pacing.

Eternal Strands is an okay, cozy, watered-down mix between Immortals Fenyx Rising and Shadow of the Colossus, but not in the same tier as them.  Hopefully the (assumed) sequel will be massively better via building from the solid foundations this first game has established.

Having finally beat the game I can say with full confidence that this is a gem in a day and age of online-only, multiplayer slop games. The times where single player games like this were the standard, brimming with creativity and passion is where the industry peaked and I wouldn't have it any other way.

As a man who's not much of a story gamer and who prefers just to skip through cutscenes/dialogues, this kept my attention quite well in those aspects, so much so that I bothered to do all the side quests despite the fact they have no real rewards, other than getting to interact with the characters more. Oria's quest to find her father, Sola's quest to revive the smithing art of a decimated civilisation, helping Casmyn deal with her psychological struggles and a lack of annoying, long winded exposition all help this game's story shine.

The real fun, however I believe is the Shadow of the Colossus gameplay with the magic to help spice up the gameplay. Not only do you have your spells, but you have enchanted weaponry which act as another unique spell to use on bosses, my personal favourite being the Kinetic Two-Hander, which when fully upgraded lets you jump up to head-level with the great Arkons. I spent many hours farming up materials just to have strong weapons and gear, though it's (mostly) optional. I just grinded out the heaviest weapon to break through Archon Armor without freezing it first, but you don't truly need to do that, as every boss has a puzzle aspect that'll let you kill them without too much hassle.

Do give this game a try, so suits can see this and let devs make the singleplayer games of their dreams. :)

Much better than what my first impressions of it led me to believe it was.

Combat feels okay against adds, a bit "floaty" at times (low hit feedback and weapon swings feel a bit "light") but still enjoyable, big epic boss fights against massive enemies is where it's at, you can climb the bigger enemies and break armor of them to do more damage, you can even use ice magic on their joints to stop them from moving.

Very good debut title from Yellow Brick Games, looking forward for game improvements and future titles from these devs.

Overall, I think Eternal Strands does great at what it aims to do, which is provide a fun action-adventure set in a fantasy world. 

I'm not usually a fan of action-adventures (I much prefer RPGs for the deeper story with choice and consequence, as well as build variety), but I decided to give this one a try after playing a few minutes of the demo and enjoying the vibes. I think the price is absolutely reasonable for what you get, and I think it's worth buying it if you think you'll like it because it also supports an indie developer. 

Pros:
+ great visual style, especially the cutscenes and 2D character art
+ high quality writing 
+ great voice acting, music, and audio design
+ fun exploration and interesting interactions with the environment with fire/ice and kinetic magic

Cons:
- I personally found even the easy difficulty a bit too hard, so I'd love to see either a casual difficulty added, or at least some optional settings that would help me figure out when to block or dodge in combat. I haven't died yet, but it's been an extremely close thing in multiple fights, and that's not really the kind of experience I expect when I choose "Easy".
- the environment can feel a bit too same-y in a region, which can cause you to feel a bit lost. You don't have a full detailed map of the region you're exploring, and unless you come across a landmark (which there's too few of) you feel like you could be anywhere. Not a huge problem for me as I just tough it out and keep walking until I do figure out where I am and where I need to go, but it could be a source of frustration for other players so that's why I mention it.
- no way to manually turn on or off specific graphics settings, and here I particularly refer to Bloom and Motion Blur. There is only the option to turn up or down "post processing", which apparently includes these, but I have no idea which level I should set the post processing to in order to completely turn off Bloom and Motion Blur. I have it set to low just in case and the game has been alright for me, no nausea or headaches so far. (I get headaches and nausea from bloom and motion blur)
- not sure how satisfying the progression is. At the moment I've only played for 2 hours, but it's already felt a bit grindy to get enough resources to upgrade/craft new gear, and upgrade camp stations.
- limited inventory space. The previous issue is absolutely exacerbated by having way too few inventory slots for resources you gather when out on expeditions. Especially considering the fact that resources are really the main thing used for character progression (other than special "Strands" from big boss monsters). The inventory capacity feels like an arbitrary limitation imposed upon the player just so that they are forced to spend time juggling which resources to take and which ones to throw out or leave on the ground. For me, it meant that during my very first expedition I actually returned to camp without having finished any quest objectives because my inventory was full, and I wanted to be able to gather more types of materials. As I've mentioned, I only played for 2 hours at the time of writing this review, and the inventory thing already annoys me enough to rant about it on here.

Even with these negatives, I still recommend the game because it's quite fun to play. I think I would have enjoyed playing this even more back when I was a kid/teen and I had more of an appetite for action-adventures.
Especially with the more generous inventory this is a lot of fun. Sort of BOTW-y but with its own twists. I like how open ended and physics based the magic is.

This game was made with a lot of love and attention, and it clearly shows.

The visuals are gorgeous. The level design is really good, and the maps are very pleasing to explore and traverse. The story is nice: it's not a masterpiece, but its still pretty good to follow. The "adventurer group" mood is really done well, and you will get to know every member of the group and their relations to one another in nicely-written quests. The (english) voice acting is also very good.

The gameplay starts maybe a little slow, but you quickly get new powers and enchanted weapons that make it really good, with many emergent possibilities. The basic ice power is particularly well-done: you can immobilize parts of enemies, a flying ennemy will have trouble flying with a big chunk of ice attached to them, etc.

The games runs very smoothly, and I did not have a single bug playing it. I personally did not have any problem with resource management and inventory (stop hoarding those useless white materials!), but the devs already added some inventory space to make it more comfy anyway.

Overall, everything just clicks nicely together, with no unnecessary padding, for a really good experience. This is the kind of games with "modest" and realistic ambitions that I personally want to see more of.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game. One of the highlights for me was learning about each character and seeing how they evolve throughout the story. That said, there are a few minor issues I'd love to see tweaked/fixed in the future. The climbing mechanics could use some refinement. Sometimes, I found myself launching off walls due to jumping up at certain angles, and Brynn doesn't always climb where I intended (this was noticeable when scaling the great arks). Finally, my favorite aspect of the game is the story, which is presented through voice over text in the style of visual novels. I feel that it enhances the storytelling, making key moments even more memorable.

A beautiful story bogged down by untested gameplay. I wanted to recommend this game, I truly did. Physics based magic has been a dream of mine for many years in games and this game promised so much. I truly enjoyed the demo and the only thing I disliked was climbing was little funky but surely they fixed that for full released. The remainder of the game was 'god just slog through this boss so I can see the next part of the story' and there were times that I truly thought you know I can see past the issues and maybe still recommend this one to my friends. But the last few bosses kinda had me at nah, it's clear the developers had a singular vision of the 'right way' to fight these bosses and for a game trying to boast numerous spells and strategies, they're pigeonholing me. Then you get to the last boss, not the 1st you fight them, which is annoying, or the second which is okay, but the third. The third fight with the boss has only one way to win, it's clunky, it's awkward, there is no way around it and it ruins the fight. The fact that they've locked a quest for one of my favorite characters behind it is why I coming out here to say. NO, I do not recommend this game. I recommend watching someone else suffer through it or pull the cutscenes off youtube. To the devs, your writing staff is on point, you guys should write a book or a show or a series, I would love to see more of the world, truly I would. To your guys that designed the bosses, do better.

This game feels like it blends together Monster Hunter/Dauntless with Breath of the Wild. In a very light sense. 

The exploration feels great, I spent most of my time exploring every inch possible and am almost always rewarded by doing so with upgrade mats, rare monster spawns, or straight upgrades like new armor blueprints. Its a semi-open world / linear world but its wide enough and has so much verticality and hidden locations that I dont really notice that I am in a directed path of sorts.

The "boss" fights are pretty fun and intense. I love that you can use your magic to alter their behavior. For example you can use your frost ability on a dragons wings and it will prevent them from flying away. You can frost up their mouth and prevent them from spitting fire.

For a different encounter you can use gravity magic to weaken or rip off armor plates to expose weak spots. or you can throw things at the armor to break it over time. I am sure there are many more combinations but I am still at the entry point of the game.

It is not a "deep" game in terms of mechanics or requirements for gear like you would find in Monster hunter and it is not as open or "grand adventure" inducing as breath of the wild. But it takes the simple aspects from both these games and blends it together really well.

For $40 this so far has been worth it for me 100%

A solid puzzle experience whose core mechanic manages to be unique and unlike any other I've played, while drawing enough inspiration from indie classics such as VVVVVV or Undertale to bring a sense of familiarity to the whole thing. The mechanics of the map gameplay when introduced seem straightforward and intuitive, but as the game goes on the complexity of each level gets deeper and deeper with new elements thrown into the mix. There's a surprising amount of depth here that may not show at first glance. 

This game showcases a perfect mix, I think, of both levels that will test your wits and problem-solving and levels that require that perfect timing and fluid platforming movements. As someone who isn't normally a fan of puzzle games, I found the experience to be enjoyable and challenging, and for the price of admission I think you get your money's worth. 

Also the humour is goofy but it adds a charm to the journey I think would be missing otherwise.

If you're looking for a different perspective on culture and identity, this game is for you!

A very sweet game that authentically and compassionately captures the lives of a first generation Tamil family in Canada. The connection to family through food and recipes is the focus, and we see their struggle to integrate within a society that is often hostile towards them, while trying not to lose their culture and identity.
This is more of a novel than a game, but it is really quite beautiful, and gives a peek into the lives of people that deserve significantly more empathy than they receive.

There is a lot to love about this game, but it has its downsides too. The clicking can get tiresome, as can the need to restart a recipe. That being said, it was a sweet story with lovely art that made me hungry and seek out the recipes in real life. So that was nice! All in all, to want to play this game depends on what you're looking for. A sweet, mostly text-based story? Yes. An engaging cooking simulator? No. Something emotional? Sort of. Something different? Yes.
All that being said, I enjoyed it. And depending on what you're looking for, you might too.

The game beautifully shows the progression of age, emotion and identity through the various dishes (and heart-touching cutscenes) that the player cooks throughout the game. 

Venba has a lot of heart, and appeals to me not only because of the cultural values it presents, but also through a very universal story of family and immigration, relatable to thousands of people all over the world. Fans of the movie/book 'The Namesake' will find a lot of common elements between the two stories. Please give this game a try and excuse me as I cook some amazing recipes!

Yes, I may have teared up a bit.

I was born in the States, and my dad is an Indo-Caribbean born in Trinidad. We don't know where in India we come from; the books that have that kind of information, of our ancestors taken onto the boats, are likely in worse condition than Venba's recipe book. My dad was a Kavin - he and his parents moved here when he was 4 - he anglicized his name, was shamed for his foreign food, stopped cooking the recipes, and forgot the culture. My granmudda recently passed. I tried to learn from her what I could, but all too soon she was fighting dementia. Those blank, torn pages in that recipe book stabbed me thru the heart (positive). My dad's been missing home, so maybe us playing this game together will be the last little push we both need.

I've never cried over a game or any other form of media as much as I did while playing Venba. I can't speak for anyone else's experience but as an Indian who, like Kavin, grew up in a English speaking country and lost touch with my culture this game meant the world to me. From the beautiful art to the skilful use of sound and music and carefully thought out writing, Venba is a must play game!

The game's a visual treat... but that's the only positive thing I can say about it. And even that one positive isn't without its issues -- while the art style is visually compelling, it does not read well at all in terms of gameplay. It's not at all clear what is just foreground/background and what is actually an interactable part of the environment, especially in the first couple areas.

Controls are pretty much terrible, especially for a game with so few inputs. You press the joystick away from a ladder to jump off, but you press the jump button to jump off of a rope. Unless you're using keyboard; then you press jump to climb up a rope and you press the action button to jump off. There are very few tricky jumps, but the ones that do exist are frustrating, because the game doesn't seem to have coyote time and it's not clear when your character's hitbox leaves the platform. Do I have to jump before the midpoint of my character is past the edge? Before his trailing foot is past the edge? It didn't feel consistent, which maybe goes back to the art style being pretty to look at but getting in the way of gameplay. Maybe hitboxes of platforms just don't always line up with the art the same way.

There are many blind drops where if you just move a bit too far (with no way of knowing what's "too far" and very little air control while falling) then you miss the landing area and die from fall damage. There are also many traps and other types of insta-deaths that are not really telegraphed enough to anticipate them. I think the game is trying to use these as "jump scares" to increase feelings of tension, but it just makes things boring and annoying. Run to the right until a spike trap kills you and reset; jump before that part next time.

Way too many of the puzzles, especially early, are just things like "push an item to a ledge so you can make a jump" or "set an item on a pressure switch to disable a trap" -- if you've played a puzzle platformer in the past 25 years, you'll be bored to tears by these "puzzles".

The underwater controls are unbearable, especially because the game eats inputs if you press keys too early, so the underwater escape segment is incredibly frustrating. That's about where I finally just quit playing because the game isn't worth it. I skimmed through some let's play -type videos on youtube to see if I was missing out on anything by not finishing the game, and it really doesn't seem like there's any meaningful payoff to suffering through the gameplay.

I really enjoyed this game and the variety of levels, and the mechanics were pretty interesting.
Great retro 90's vibes. Controls felt pretty good for the most part. 
I completed all the levels and would definitely recommend.

That said I do have a few gripes (that will probably be fixed sooner or later).

GLITCHES
The most game breaking bug is the fish boss. 
If you die to him, he gets stuck and won't do anything, and the only way to start the match over is to exit the game and restart.
Which brings me to my second gripe. There's no way to exit the game. The pause menu contains some text to exit off to the side, but there's no way to access is, just music volume, resolution etc.
You'll have to close the game by other means.
One other bug to note is the hats. After putting on the hat, and dying a few times, I'd restart the level and be nothing but a hat. It seemed like I still had the same hit box, but basically was invisible. After a few more deaths it would sometimes fix itself.
I'd assume these bugs will be patched.

MECHANICS
The mechanics are mainly good, with the exception of the skateboard. You're not told how to double jump with the board and after I did figure it out, it was still hit or miss whether it would function correctly. Sometimes when jumping I'd stick to the board and sometimes I'd slide off.
Velocity transfer from the board to the character is very inconsistent.
This makes some of the last levels really frustrating, especially the Trick Ride level.
Sometimes after hitting a switch, speed would drastically slow down so I couldn't keep up with the board.
The other mechanic that seemed wonky was swimming. Inverted especially would jump in the opposite direction when the jump button was released, making for really jerky movement.

DIFFICULTY
The difficulty ratings mean nothing, really.
Some lower rated levels I found very difficult, while later levels were pretty easy.
Same goes for Bosses. The final boss was a joke. Maybe it was supposed to be, but 3 hits in quick success and it was over in like 20 sec. I played it again just to make sure it wasn't a glitch. It was very anticlimactic.


I think this game is definitely worth it, and with a few bug fixes, it'll be even better.

Before I say anything else, by default, the rotation on the character is very strange, but you can change it in the settings to a more traditional feel. I decided to play it on a keyboard with additional adjustments on the mapping, it was okay, you just need to improve the timing on the shield, dash, and maybe a melee as well.

Now, if I understood the credits correctly, the game is mostly made by one developer with some additional support, so in that sense, it's not a bad showing and something to be proud of, but in this condition, it's hard to justify $10 for it. It only has about 3 hours of story content, I am surprised you didn't go with early access, it's too short. You also credited a lot of tools/assets, and I understand the need for it, but from my perspective, the more you rely on those, the less genuine the experience is for the player. I hope you at least made all of the stages with the elevation, I actually think the game does not look all that bad, even though the world-building didn't feel all that interesting. 

It kinda has that 'cookie-cutter' gameplay and combat, it's not necessarily a bad thing, but I didn't find the delays on the actions all that friendly. A good example is your dash-based platforming, which is pretty horrible in this game. I often get a sense that normal dash distance is too short so I try to time it in the air, but you quickly realize it just does not work. An easy solution might be to just give the player more control over dash distance, maybe make it a bit longer too, but if you wanted to go a bit deeper, maybe some mid-air control so falling down a little was not always a fail - perhaps an auto hop near the edges.

Okay so the stage design was not terrible, maybe a bit too linear, you want to give the player more chances to explore, but I like that you tried to create some elevation, and occasionally jump down, actually could have used more of that. The aesthetic was okay, but the consistency suffered as it went on, the stages became pretty blurry toward the end, I kinda felt like you started to give up. Honestly, the story had no impact on me at all, feels too scripted, too much like following a path. Maybe you could have more recurring characters that come and go, try to build that attachment, and then you can turn them into friends or enemies at some point, give some special things for completing those arks. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I mean, I think you like 75% there on many things, combat is almost serviceable, the level design is almost serviceable, and the narrative is almost serviceable.  You should have worked more on the game before putting it out, it's not terrible, but it's not finished, feels just like a naked core of a game.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

[u] Timing [/u] - I think you can make the character a little faster, maybe 20%, see how it feels and go from there. I think the shield should pop a little faster too, I had a hard time doing reflection because of the slow delay on it. Dash platforming feels off, visually it feels like you should run into the abyss and then dash, instead of just making it pixel perfect, something needs to be done to combat it, maybe a longer dash with player control or edge hops, or maybe the character should not fall instantly, give like a 0.3-second mid-air movement so you can actually time it safely. Melee attacks feel kinda trashy, you don't want to give the character a little combo? Sometimes the game glitches out when you get power-ups, but you can fix it by dying. Perhaps the shield should also properly block melee enemies, if it does, I did not see it.

Almost forgot*, that slow mo effect that many games do, yea it works if the game is like super polished and it's cool when timed perfectly, but in this game it feels like lag, so I don't know, I would say be careful doing fancy effects like that, they don't feel as good as you might think, I often can't tell if the game is doing it or if I am getting an FPS drop.

[u] Stage Design [/u] - what you doing is okay, I think you need to give the player more freedom to explore, have more optional locations. The aesthetic quality felt uneven, toward the end you made it very blurry. Honestly, you could even color-swap it more, it would probably look more fun if you had more visual themes, even if you made them a bit more colorful. I like what you doing with elevation, probably could use more of that with the geometric structures and climbing them, also jumping down more.

[u] Narrative [/u] - I guess, try to approach your world as if the character were living in it, maybe have more characters that populate it and interact with you, maybe the hub locations more interesting, have some rewards associated with that, have more mystery and lore, you don't want it to feel like a story on the rails. 

[u] Content [/u] - too short, too many recycled enemies.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 5/10 [/b]

Not a bad effort honestly, you probably could work with this, take advantage of the player's desire to explore, try to make the world more interesting to navigate, and add more characters that "live" in the world. As far as the gameplay, it's not awful but you want to make it a bit more snappy, make it more fluid, it's better to make the game faster than slower, increase the movement speed, shorten delays on melee, and make dash platforming more reliable.

The content here is VERY generous. With multiple updates in 2024 and more planned in 2025, there's more than enough here to keep the playerbase happy. Some of the most notable updates are when new maps come out, all for free. They have regular big fixes and QOL patches dropping with lots of community engagement from the team. The DLC has thus far been cosmetic only. That DLC is also priced MUCH more fairly than the AAA wallet harvesting 20$ single skin bundles the industry has been getting so greedy with lately.

For the most part, you can ignore the story if you want and just go for high rounds. You can do the map's story if you want and have the plot of the game be your focus. If you want classic CoD Zombies eastereggs, they've got that available as a post story option. There was also an update late in 2024 that added camo grinding to the guns, plenty to work towards.

As a whole, for the asking price, Sker Ritual is really solid. There's more here than some AAA games offer and that's great. It doesn't look the greatest and there is definitely a little less polish than some more professionally made titles, but Wales Interactive is definitely doing a good job competing against the bigger shooters on the market. A very fun game I would hand an 8.5 out of 10 to in a heartbeat.

I love vehicular combat games, I constantly check Steam to see if there's any upcoming attempts to revive the genre. I was quite excited when I saw that Zaacar was a measly $2.39 during the Summer Sale.

Sadly, I don't think it's worth that right now. It's far too unfinished, even for an early access game. 

[b]TL;DR: Terrible vehicle handling, cars feel weightless. Barely any vehicle sounds. No one is playing. Can't unlock anything in bot matches and bots are braindead. Vehicle designs are just boring cars with Mad Max stuff thrown on them. Lastly, this game runs horribly (40-50 fps) on a 3080/i7 9700K.[/b]

The vehicle handling is some of the worst I've felt in a racing game. Every vehicle feels weightless, if you try to make the smallest of turns you'll be greeted by your car going sideways into a sharp drift. I tried both with and without the drift control option and it didn't help at all.

Additionally, sound in this game is [i]abysmal[/i]. There's barely any vehicle sounds. You can sort of hear each car's engine whining, but that's all there is for vehicle sounds. When enemies are firing weapons you won't hear anything unless you're within 20 feet of them. It makes the entire game feel lifeless. 

I also think each vehicle available is.. boring, aesthetically. They're just regular cars with some Mad Max stuff thrown on them, and you can't customize most of the appearance outside of specific upgrades. There's no trucks, no neat vehicle types you'd see in something like Twisted Metal or Vigilante 8, just a few muscle cars and a sedan.

There's no one playing, but you can do bot matches. Sounds okay, right? Well, I'm glad the developers added bot support, more games need to do this, but the bots are terribly braindead here. During the Arena mode the bots just get in massive piles at the center of the map while they try to push each other and go nowhere. During the Circuit mode they make perfect turns that you definitely can't do, and they act like you aren't there if you're in their path. They aren't fun to play against.

Worst off, it seems [b]you can't unlock anything if you do bot matches[/b], which means no upgrading your vehicle. Arena mode doesn't have any weapons spawn in the map, so if you want to bring a machinegun into a match you have to unlock the upgrade first, which you can't do since again, [b]no one is playing this game.[/b]

Final straw for me was that this game runs horribly on a 3080/i7 9700K. I'm getting 40-50 FPS no matter what graphic settings I use. There's nothing going on in the map other than 49 bots hitting each other, why is it running so terribly?

I see no reason to currently play this over something like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/243800/Gas_Guzzlers_Extreme/]Gas Guzzlers Extreme[/url], which came out 8 years ago yet offers many more modes (Full Auto/Death Race-style racing, weaponless racing, demolition derby, deathmatch, etc.), has more in-depth vehicle customization, runs very well, and it has far, [i]far[/i] better sounds and vehicle handling. 

I'll keep my eye on Zaacar to see if things get better in the future, but for now I'm refunding.

For the time being I can recommend this game with some reservation.

As for the concept: you start with a cube (the light green one), which you must connect with other cubes (the dark green ones) to create chains. These chains you need to build up and move around until you reach the yellow goal cube. In some levels you'll meet cubes of two other colors: purple and red. If one of your cubes touches the red cube, it goes 'poof' and vanishes and you lose. If one of your cubes touches a purple cube, it turns to 'stone' and becomes unmovable - useful if you have a chain that you want to break apart, but dangerous if you have only one cube (if this one cube becomes unmovable you lose, of course).

There's no real tutorial, only an introduction into the different cubes which is in parts difficult to understand - no full sentences and sometimes it seems that English isn't the mother tongue of the developer. So I had to play for a while until I understood how the game works and what it wants from me.

The concept is simple and even if you skip the introduction you can figure out the game quickly enough.
If the levels provided are not enough for you, you can download three additional areas with 10+ levels each.

Controls are ASWF or arrow keys.


This said, there are things that need improvement:
- the userface, especially the colors. In the top menu there are a handful different buttons ('get levels', 'settings', 'about', 'tutorial', and more) and all are some kind of greenish blue, except for the 'quit' button which is red. It'd be nice if the 'play' button would also stick out more.
- the controls. For each movement you need to press a key, even if you move a handful of surfaces in one direction. It would be nice if it would be enough to just keep an arrow key pressed for long movements.
- it would be nice if you could zoom in and out. And if you could use the mouse to spin around freely. At the moment you can't do any of this, it's just Q or E that turns the camera 90° degrees in one or the other direction. When you begin some levels, parts of them are out of the screen, which makes it hard to get an immediate grasp of the level.
- I have played four hours and there are still some unplayed levels, but I have already found two unsolvable levels (see my screenshots; no matter how I look at it, these two are simply unsolvable atm)
- I already received the achievements for completing two areas after only playing half of their levels.

These are my biggest criticms, but if you can overlook them (or are patient enough to wait for the dev to fix them) it's a nice enough and simple and fun game.

And hey: it's cheap.


Edit:
An earlier review mentions a missing soundtrack. Currently the game has background music and sound effects - very simple ones, but hey.

Second edit:
The dev was already so kind to fix the above mentioned unsolvable levels. Thank you!

It's not awful but it is bland and generic. It's impossible to recommend this game.
[hr][/hr]
Why not?

It promises to be FTL in 3d. With a 3d ship interior and 3d model crew moving from station to station. It looks fun but it isn't. It's much less than "FTL in 3d".

What it is is FTL's core game mechanics but without all the nice touches that elevated the experience of playing and suffering in FTL. The part that is fun is the weapons and combat/targeting, upgrading ship systems, traveling from point to point etc. The new 3d gimmick plays much worse unfortunately, and other additions are few and of mixed quality.

I don't mind FTL-like games existing. Doom-likes and rougelikes, or metroidvanias. I sometimes want more of the same. But this is considerably less of the same.
How?
Towards the end of development, subset games hired a professional writer to go over event text and dialogues, and it shows. Even though the story and writing is simple, it is GOOD!. In Zero Point, everything you read is boring and mundane. FTL mods put more effort into writing.

Then there's the music. It's not bad but it's generic. It does nothing.
FTL paid attention to color-blindness, Zero Point makes zero effort to do something similar.
And it's FTL hard.
But you just die and get dumped to the main menu. There are highscores but they are pointless. Just start a new game with some nobodies without any character or charm, die again and keep repeating until it's no longer fun.

[hr][/hr]
The biggest flaw of Zero Point is that it exists. Somebody had to make this. It's a shame they did an ok job technically but failed to put anything FUN into the game.
The design document must have been simple, as it basically copied the elements from FTL. Nothing wrong with that. Then a game was built according to spec, and... that was it. No effort anywere. nothing stands out. No clever writing, no fun hook.

There are a couple of innovations:
 - the 3d ships and some bizzare time dilation mechanic that replaces pausable realtime of the game that inspired Zero Point.
 - replacing the warp gate battle with an intercept chance. The exit is always unguarded but every node you visit raises this chance by 1-2%. If you get intercepted, you have to fight a very tough battle but if you win you reset the intercept chance.
 - characters are voiced. I wish they weren't. They say a few lines and it quickly gets dull.

If you want to play some FTL like combat in a 3d setting then you wont waste much money. But it is the time wasted playing this that is the problem. [b]Life is short and there are so many good games.[/b] This does not deserve more than a couple of hours, if that.

It might be fun on a tablet or portable device. It feels designed for such devices and it doesn't look so good on a desktop.

[hr][/hr]
I have a few nice things to say about it, but bottom line is [u]it's bad[/u]. Not worth playing.

If you've never played FTL, play that. It's superior.
If you have played FTL, just play FTL.

Race To Sanity is a beautifully crafted masterpiece, showing just how powerful Unity really is. This game is like a crazy combination of Day Off, Geometry Dash, and Turbo Dismount! Sporting the best vehicle known to man, the best driver known to me, and the most wiggly Squidward hair jiggle physics ever! It’s even got proper rag doll physics, and lots of unique death sounds! This game has 5 unique levels starting at the main character’s house and ending at my brain. You get to enjoy a surprisingly long credits list, the juiciest sound track, and all the laughter in the world as you realize just how well-spent your money really was. Best game on steam.

In Race To Sanity, your goal is to survive the craziest places as you travel from one part of the world to the next until you eventually end up in your mind!  In this physics-based ragdoll obstacle course, your goal is to travel a certain distance and fill up the progress bar at the top of the screen.  There are five levels for you to enjoy before your sanity explodes of impatience. Unfortunately, the game does not save, so make sure you do not close out or quit early.  Be warned; you will hate yourself every time you die without any reasonable cause because of bugs or glitches.  At any point, your wheelchair can randomly thrust itself into the air as it glides through the invisible air.  The physics in this game are clunky and cause spontaneous deaths at any point throughout the level.  Be prepared to accept defeat or conquer where those have failed!

One of my favorite things is to speed up the man's wheelchair by pressing forward until white rays of light begin to break the space-time continuum. But, of course, if you find this too fast, you can always slow down play like the big baby you are!  Real men love a challenge; take notes, ladies.  It's not about the destination when it was always about the journey.  This game is not for the weak so tread carefully, young warrior!  Only those of brave courage might see the wonders of this beauty.  That is if you succeed and beat all the levels.

SHORT STORY - FICTIONAL

First, the main character starts in an insane asylum where the goal is to escape the hospital horrors of toilets, beds, and filing cabinets that contain your paperwork!  Once you get out of the crazy house, you find yourself on a lonely desert road dodging maniacal drivers.  Here you will learn how powerful your arms are as you push the wheelchair to its most whole glory!  "Flying through the open skies, here I come," said the shirtless man as his legs flailed left and right!  Endlessly you find yourself pushing that wheelchair that binds you together because your legs have become noodles hoping to reach the other side before the inevitable strikes. Finally, as you grow tired and weary, you arrive at the local tavern, where you find piano tables, jukeboxes, and musical letters flying at incredible speeds towards your mortal body!  Be careful with those loose glass bottles; you might slip and hurt yourself, laddy!

After surviving the bar, you stumble across an arcade with bright colors and retro-themed game machines.  Here is where you shall learn about classic video games and their birthplace.  "Oh my! this reminds me of my local rave," said the man in the wheelchair as he narrowly avoided being crushed by the towering box of computational magnificence.  Lastly, we come to an extraordinary but unique level.  A place that does not exist in reality.  Only those of significant effort can face this challenge.  It was the last level of the game, but I had to complete it inside my mind this time!  Welcome to your brain as you ride the wheelchair past blood vessels, cells, and pills.  Here, you can use ramps to lift off the gravitational effects of this planet to hover over moving obstacles while jamming to some sick rock and roll!  These delusions will be no more once you complete the final level.  A sense of peace and gratitude overwhelms the player as he beats the race to sanity.

There were a few missions that tripped me up, but you'll be a lot more competent (both because of your experience and skill unlocks) at the end of your time with the game. Although the gameplay is fun, there's also typically only one, circuitous way to proceed in each level. I would welcome a bit more "immersive sim" into the experience.

A few other points:
[list]
[*] One particular tricky section involves timing how long it takes a guard to cross a room, so that you can emerge when his back is turned. Your screen turns black when you climb inside the cupboard to hide. Although this was definitely tricky, it also made me feel like a super spy.
[*] When you drop from one level to the one below, you will always fall in the center. This can make you accidentally set off infrared alarms that you thought you'd dodged.
[*] Lockpicking is tricky, even with the upgrade. This could probably stand to be a bit more intuitive and less random.
[*] When you retry a level, you (for some reason) keep the money that you acquired in your failed attempt and can collect it again. Therefore, you can (sort of) grind out enough cash to buy all the upgrades relatively early in the game. I did this unintentionally, just failing the same level over and over.
[*] I wish the game didn't have the pixelated breasts on the screens in the game. Not because I was offended, but because as far as I know, that's the only NSFW aspect of the game. Since Steam often censors NSFW games by default, fewer players are seeing this game than it deserves.
[*] Purchase the taser upgrade first. Although you don't need it much in the earlier levels, that extra charge will soon be a lifesaver.
[/list]

If you're a fan of this 2D style of stealth game (or you played Trilby: The Art of Theft and loved it), I'd recommend Moonshot. It's a little rough around the edges, but this sort of game isn't released very often.

For instance, out of the 100 cards from a category, if you choose to only use 10 of them, it will only cycle through the same 10 every time you play after finishing the first cycle. You also can't go back to a previous card. You also can't mark a card as learned or need help with in our to adjust priority of how often it appears. It seems the developers ran out of time and just released the game in an unfinished state. It's also disappointing that this game doesn't have much to do besides flash cards. I personally feel this application is more of a bank of words, rather than an effective study tool. If there are going to be more updates, these are things that should be considered to implement.

1. Key inputs during quizzes
I feel the lack of typing the answer kind of loses my motivation to answer more than 10 questions. I personally think it would be a more engaging experience if I am able to type these key inputs. It really gives off of a personal competitive vibe that brings the experience on a new level

2. Customization for flashcards.
Obviously if you are doing flashcards, it is almost essential to have a "custom" list depending on what you want to learn. Although there is a looping system, it doesn't really help since you don't choose what cards you want to study. The only method I found is by missing them on purpose and then practice the ones you missed.

When I was looking through the kanji section, I had a hard time how to "pronounce" the words since it has different ways to spell it. Let's take the word 本. It means book if it was pronounced as ほん aka hon. However there is another way to interpret the kanji, which is もと aka moto, and I wish there is a default audio file that tells me which is the more common pronunciation, which I learned from my Japanese Class was Hon.

Overall, it just feels this was made as a college project, I made a way worse version of a flashcard app before and I can definitely say it takes a lot of manual work when it comes to inputting a lot of information and files into an app. However, it doesn't really excuse the lack of polish this product holds and I do hope there are more updates so I can change my review.

This is a fun but short little adventure.

Pros:
+Some boss fights are challenging but fun to beat. 
+This game is more fast paced than most turn-based JRPG.
+Charming style.

Cons:
-Not a lot of dialogues, simple story and silent protagonists.
-Short
-Minor technical issues. Such as stuttering or mouse target selection overriding keyboard.

[h1]Story[/h1]

Selena and Shirley must journey to the fallen Kingdom of Askhar to defeat the source of the Darkness, or demons will eventually become too much for their village to handle. While Selena can receive blessings from the Goddess of Light, Shirley is a practitioner of dark magic and is disallowed from entering holy places. However, she can increase her powers by corrupting in soul in the Dark Sanctuary, a place that functions as a sort of shared spiritual world for all dark magic users.

The game is touted as having moral choices and soul corruption, but I found this to be very weak in comparison to games with similar plots. For one thing, the protagonists are silent, so it's very difficult to tell how the soul corruption affects Shirley's personality or her interactions with Selena. Additionally, there aren't that many opportunities to make moral choices, at least for mandatory events, though this may be due to the story's short length. The are two major moral choices concerning brainwashing and ironically enough, obtaining the final light power up.

The game has multiple endings depending on Shirley's corruption and a certain side path right before the final boss. Unsurprisingly, the ending is happier if Shirley isn't corrupted, but the no corruption and partial corruption paths only differ in small ways, which made the morality system feel underutilized. The full corruption route can branch in an interesting way that makes the player question if their choices were worth it and there is an interesting twist for the light power up.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The game features a standard turn-based system, but bosses are heavily evented so that there's a puzzle aspect to their fight. While their gimmicks are fair and victory is fairly reproduceable once the player figures them out, it can take a bit of trial-and-error to realize what is going on in the first place. My least favorite boss is the Corrupted Assassin, since his gimmick has more of a luck factor compared to most other bosses. That may explain why there's a secret way to skip his fight.

Selena has no MP or magic, but she can learn physical skills that have their own cooldowns. While this made resource management simpler with her, I feel that her accuracy isn't high enough to make up for the cooldowns, especially for life-saving skills like Shield Bash. It's entirely possible to see an enemy charge a strong attack, use Shield Bash in an attempt to stun them, miss, and eat a ton of damage.

Shirley seems like a standard mage at first and her kit covers all offensive and support needs, but she has no MP growth, which means the player will have to use her MP carefully. Soul corruption can increase her max MP and give her more perks, which means the party doesn't have to spend as many turns using MP items, giving them better turn economy for difficult bosses.

Most enemy attacks are survivable and fair, so it's entirely possible to cheese even the no corruption route with a big bag of consumables. However, the 2100 Darkness Affinity achievement can make the resource management aspect of the game much harder. DA is accumulated for every point of MP spent by Shirley, which means to get the achievement, the player must minimize their MP usage. This can also make it more tedious to grind for resources, though the middle section of the game does mercifully have physical-vulnerable mobs that drop Toka Grass and Soul Essence.

There are occasionally campsites that the player can visit to cook healing food items and rest. Cooking requires ingredients, and only Toka Salad is infinitely farmable if you're a hoarder. Resting requires one party member to stand guard while the other one sleeps. The guard has a chance of having to fight an enemy, though I have yet to get into a situation where the enemy can be immune to one of the party members' attacks, so it seems to be balanced. If Shirley is the one who sleeps, she can visit the Dark Sanctuary, and the closer the party is to the final boss, the more corruption Shirley can gain, though it does require DA thresholds.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

7/10

The gameplay is balanced enough that it's possible to beat the no corruption route even with sloppy gameplay, albeit with trial-and-error for some bosses. The story and morality system are lacking, but there are some interesting plot elements that could be made better if the protagonists had properly written dialogue, enough that it could have bumped the game to 7.5/10 or 8/10.

On paper, Subterene "checks a lot of my boxes." I liked the game's unique aesthetic and interface, it's advertised short run-time, and the idea of slowly piecing together this mystery that has occurred beneath the floor of the ocean.

Unfortunately, playing Subterene is a slog. The game gives you very little direction while you stumble upon probes and bumble from one mining depot to the next. For some this may make the game a true "exploration" game, but not for me when the act of exploring itself is so tedious. The speed at which your mining vehicle drills, turns, and accelerates is just PAINFUL. This is only exacerbated when your vehicle becomes caught on some small piece of a block, which happens ALL THE TIME.

When you do stumble upon one of the game's subnautical creatures, they can swim circles around you. They swim through blocks that you have to drill through, as turn your unwieldy vessel at a snail's pace to get your drill in position to attack. You can also use explosive charges in combat, but these are much more trouble than they are worth.

If stumbling on a probe after all this painstaking exploration was rewarding, that would've been one thing, but the messages that you find on the probes are wildly inconsistent and generally not helpful for elucidating the mystery. Some logs are dialogues between two former employees at the mining company, while others are a single line, such as "I thought that was a rock."

I feel like developer Possmonaut had a neat idea here, but just fumbled the execution. Suggestions for improvement might be:
[list]
[*]Either make the mining vehicle more nimble in terms of drill/turning/movement speed, or give the player some sense of where they should be going.
[*]Re-write each of the drone logs to be more interesting and/or informative. Obviously, some drones wouldn't have encountered anything interesting on their patrols before being put out of commission, but...you know, this is a video game.
[/list]

Although it's clear that the developer wants to make a survival horror game, remember that this can be done while still having a playable character (or mining vehicle) that feels good to use. Although obviously these are AAA examples, just look to games like Dead Space or the Resident Evil 2 remake to see this done well.

All in all, if you really, really like Into the Breach and have played it to absolute completion you might want to give this one a go, otherwise just do another run in that one.

Quick Description:
-Oakenfold is a turn based tactics game that takes inspiration from Into the Breach.  This is a really well designed, innovative, and challenging games that fans of this genre will likely really enjoy.  The main mechanic introduced is the ability to rewind time w/o any major penalty.  This allows for newbies to learn the game in a less forgiving way and gives more experienced players a powerful tool to exploit the enemy.  This tool may be powerful, but it isn't overpowered b/c there are a ton of insta-death traps that can immediately end even the strongest run.

Consensus:
-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  I had a blast w/ this game.  It took me about 9 hrs to have my first winning run w/ the fist class, and then I had a winning run w/ the 2nd class right after.  The 3rd class is the most difficult, as I haven't beaten the final boss w/ this class yet.  Into the Breach is one of the greatest turn based games ever made.  Oakenfold is not on that level, but it's still really fun.  I put Oakenfold into a similar category as games like Nitro Kid, Alina of the Arena, and Floppy Knights.  These are all great games, but none of them are generational games imo, and that's okay.  If you are a fan of the genre, Oakenfold is an easy game to recommend.

[b]bascatball jupiter[/b] is the almost identical follow-up to [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1451560]bascatball mars[/url], except with only [b]30 levels[/b] instead of 50 for the same price. my review will be largely identical as well, since it's still turn-based basketball where the ball is a cat and the court is a hex-based location somewhere on jupiter.

the goal once again is for the cat to end up inside the hoop by finding the correct path on every level, unlocked one after the other. the team consists of 4 players (and their numerous clones). the first can move as many tiles one by one as the movement counter on the scoreboard allows, plus pass or throw. the second guy is stationary and can only pass or throw. the third one always has 3 moves, then passes or throws. the last one is a loose cannon, moves around on its own after every turn and can only be controlled when he has the catball.

both passing and scoring have to happen with exactly one tile (or gap) between the player and the hoop and the two players respectively, and [b]all moves have to be used up before a pass and all passes dealt with before going for the money shot[/b]. the scoreboard shows available moves for the current player and all passes for the level. can't pass back and forth between the same guys, so if there are 6 passes and 7 players on the level, everybody has to be involved, and you normally can't step on a hex that's already been used.

the new mechanic of [b]disappearing and re-appearing tiles[/b] clears hexes, so they can be used again, but it also leads to a lot more trial and error because they all look the same, yet don't disappear at the same time and there is [b]still no undo[/b] to ease up on repeating the same moves. teleporters can be used over and over again and sometimes the basket has to be revealed first by pressing a button. and finally, there are new [b]cat players stealing balls[/b]. they don't move, so you only have to make sure they aren't standing between you and the other player before a pass.

[b]controls are very simple[/b], all you need is the left mouse button to move around, then click other players or the hoop to get rid of the ball. this is paired with [b]great graphics and music[/b], separate volume settings (though they still aren't saved between sessions), next/previous music track, [b]windowed mode (still an unresizable window, so it's still useless)[/b] and a level selection screen. no way to turn off the timer on the scoreboard, which doesn't do anything, but it's always my preference to get rid of it and I couldn't do it here.

this time [b]the dev went crazy with the achievements[/b]. one for unlocking a level, one for solving it, always a sign of cheapness, but it's still a fun little puzzler with less content than the original for the same price, and [b]without undo it can't be recommended[/b].

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio.  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores (but it's on the Playstation, you lucky console peasants, you).  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this asset flip might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Halloween Night Mahjong has the completely unrealistic cash grab price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  Because this is the kind of game you can just play for free on mobile phones, it's impossible to recommend anyone should pay money for the same experience on Steam.
