Lords of the Fallen (2023) refines Soulslike combat with dynamic attack chains, a forgiving shield system, and an interesting dual-realm mechanic. However, its camera issues, forgettable NPCs, and maze-like world design hold it back from true greatness.
---------------------------------------
Breakdown:
🔹 Story Quality: The world is dark, the gods are angry, and the characters are… there. Like many FromSoft-inspired titles, the story is cryptic and obtuse, but Lords of the Fallen doesn’t do enough to make it compelling. The NPCs and their quests feel like random encounters rather than meaningful narratives.

🔹 Story Depth: The Umbral world concept is a nice addition, but the lore itself is more “cool-sounding nonsense” than a well-thought-out narrative. No living cities, just a playground of monsters and ruins.

🎮 Controls: Combat is smooth and responsive, and the ability to mix light and heavy attacks dynamically is a clear improvement over Dark Souls. Shields are also more viable, with a Bloodborne-style health regain mechanic. Magic, however, feels a little stiff.

🌍 Immersiveness: The dual-realm mechanic adds a unique layer to exploration, but the world lacks believability. It’s more of a giant game level than a real place.

⚔️ Difficulty: Tough but fair. Boss fights are less about frustrating, drawn-out memorization and more about reaction and strategy. No ridiculous floating, slow-motion fakeouts before one-shot attacks—thankfully.

🗺 Level Design: Classic Soulslike interconnected areas, but some parts feel more like a confusing maze than an actual world.

🎨 Graphics: The game looks great! Environments are detailed, lighting is moody, and the Umbral world has a haunting aesthetic.

🎵 Sound & Soundtrack: Decent atmosphere, but nothing particularly standout. The sound design does its job, but the music isn’t as memorable as Elden Ring or Bloodborne.

🕹 Gameplay: The improved combat flow makes fighting fun, and the bosses don’t rely on cheap tricks. However, magic isn’t as fluid, and the camera can cause unnecessary deaths.

🐛 Bugs: No major issues post-patch. Runs great now, but it was likely a mess at launch.

⌛ Playtime: ~30-40 hours for a first playthrough, more if you explore everything.

🔁 Replayability: New builds could be fun, but the game doesn't push you to replay it like Elden Ring does.

💰 Price-to-Quality: If you grab it on sale or post-fix, it’s worth it. At full price? Maybe wait unless you're really craving a new Soulslike.

The Good:
✅ Dynamic combat that improves on FromSoft’s formula.

✅ Shields feel useful and rewarding, not just a crutch.

✅ No frustrating, overly telegraphed boss moves designed just to throw off your timing.

✅ Umbral world mechanic adds a cool twist.

The Bad:
❌ Camera can be your worst enemy.

❌ Story and quests are the usual Soulslike cryptic nonsense.

❌ World design feels more like a “game level” than a believable setting.

❌ Magic could be smoother.
---------------------------------------
Conclusion:
If you love Soulslike games but want something that actually refines combat rather than just copying Dark Souls, Lords of the Fallen is worth checking out. The ability to chain light and heavy attacks seamlessly makes the combat feel more fluid and engaging, and the shield system is genuinely interesting. However, the camera can be frustrating, the story is just another cryptic mess, and the world lacks true depth.

Glad I waited for patches—this is a much better experience now than at launch!

Holy crap what a turnaround. This game got the No Man's Sky treatment, and then some.

I purchased this game at launch and, had I written the review then, I would've not recommended it.

Today, though? This game is an easy "must-play" recommendation. One of the easiest in my many years of gaming, truth be told.

Let's start by getting the negatives out of the way. Does this game have a little bit of jank? Absolutely. There are times when attacks might whiff. There are even times when an ability you very obviously parried, or dodged, smacks you right in the face. Those times are few and far between. Negatives done. That's it. Yes, I'm being serious.

Now let's get to the positives, of which there are many. I'll go into bullet points and then in depth on each.

- The music is phenomenal
- The build variety is great
- The lore is deep and engaging
- The move-sets are unique and interesting for each weapon type
- The endings are better than most other Souls-likes
- The voice acting is competent and distinct
- You. Aren't. Handheld.
- The atmosphere, setting, and tone will haunt you long after you stop playing

Music: 8/10. It's not Elden Ring, so don't compare it to that. Let's be fair here. You're not going to get Godskin Apostle's theme from this game, but the music is always appropriate for the setting, being bombastic in both triumph and terror when needed, and ushering in eerie, dyadic waves straight into your brain as you traverse the darkest recesses of Mournstead, or when finding yourself relegated to the Umbral Realm.

Build Variety: 10/10. Whether you want to build to bleed and smite your enemies, castigate them with radiant light, or make your foes rethink their lack of obeisance with infernal fire, there is a build for you. There is a build for everything from bonking even the most stalwart over the head with a grand hammer, to deaths from a thousand cuts replete with poisons and frostbite. This may also be the first Souls-like game I've played where a ranged weapon build is not only viable, but absolutely busted and fun.

Lore: 10/10. The lore in this game is as deep as the ocean, and just about as wide. You will find yourself both enthralled and enamored as you uncover the mysteries that surround your journey through Mournstead. How did the most resolute in their faith turn to heresy? Why was a land once lush and full of life cursed with frozen death? Are you really forging your own path, or are you merely a pawn in a chess game of gods and monsters?

Weapon Variety: 9/10. There's not much to say here other than while not all weapon types are created equal, they're all fun, and you can mix-and-match when dual-wielding to your heart's content. Each weapon type has their own signature move (L1/B + R2/T) and they're all very satisfying (when they land).

Endings: 9/10. Each ending gives a satisfying conclusion, and answers questions that may linger about key aspects of the lore. Only reason for a lack of a 10 score is that I've played Lies of P, and have thus tasted perfection.

Voice Acting: 7.5/10. This is my lowest score and it's still a passing grade. Some lines are flat and delivered poorly or in a cheesy accent, but the majority of their cast plays their respective roles with aplomb.

Game Navigation: 8.5/10. There may be a time or two you really struggle to know where to go next, and what's appropriate for your level, but all things considered I find that aspect to be part of the fun.

Atmosphere: Is it possible to give an 11 out of 10? If so, that's what it gets. This game will haunt you, pulling you in to play more, and more, and more ever still to unlock all that you can, and spend more time in its lands.

Let me start off by saying that I think Lords of the Fallen  is overall a good game.
The Good:
- It has some interesting and rather unique game mechanics, such as the Umbral Realm and Umbral Lantern.

- The overall aesthetic is something I personally love, as it mixes Dark fantasy with heavy tones of Christianity. Beautiful churches and massive cathedrals. Some downright impressive tapestry. Even the small crown of thorns on certain enemies helmets were a nice touch. 

- I find the land of Mornstead also extremely interesting. As there are plenty of lore descriptions and Umbral lore snipits to find.

- The shortcuts. I love short cuts in these kinds of games as it allows you to better map out the map in your head. I would also argue that it feels just a little better to open a short cut to an old vestige or seedling. 

The Average
- The combat is rather safe. It’s your standard roguelike. I was playing a full Strength build, and was mainly just hyper armoring through enemy attacks and then bonking them with a hammer.

- I did mess around with some spells, and from the ones that I had and tested they seemed rather cool. All of them have pretty unique animations, and impressive designs.

The Bad
- The Story itself is rather weak. It boils down to “You see those 5 pillars of light, you gotta go to each one to keep the Evil God sealed away.”

- The game also doesn’t really explain in any detail where to go a fair amount of time, this goes for mainline progression and npc quests.
For example, After you kill a particular boss and cleanse one of the ritual sites it doesn’t explain at all where to go next. While indeed somewhere new has unlocked, their is nothing to guide you. No cutscene showing a far off gate opening, no item description, no way forward as the area itself is a dead end. The amount of times I had to double back through multiple areas in search of some single door I now had a key for was annoying.

This is the same for  npcs, one by one they’ll disappear from the hub area and you better hope you just run into them. 
For instance, one of the first npcs you meet is a member of the deacon of the Dark Crusaders. His questline boils down to him wanting heretical artifacts and tomes, to better understand and defeat them. Over the course of the game however he slowly goes insane until he just disappears completely. None of the other npcs tell you where he might be nor does he leave any clue.
Where does he go you might ask? To a side room deep within the mine area of the game, which is close to the beginning of the game. Then once you talk to him he disappears again without a trace. In order to complete most of the Npc quests (bar one) I needed to look up a guide.

- Nearly all the in-depth lore item descriptions are lock behind the Radiance Skill. Even though I was playing main with a strength build I had brought my radiance up to 20, but I was still unable to view the more in-depth more. Why lock what could be important hints behind a high skill requirement? It just doesn't make sense to me.

- The worst offender of all was Easy Anti-cheat and the game files itself.
It was a struggle to even get the game to run, as easy anti-cheat kept saying that there was some kind of Violation error. After hours of looking up help and guides I got it to work however, a few days later when I tried to start it up a new error popped up “Disk error fragment”. I spent hours trying to fix it but nothing worked.

All in all I think that the game is alright, however the fact that I have to fight the game to even play it just is too much.

LOTF is a well-made love letter to the Souls-like genre, which really doesn't deserve the hate. Combat is satisfying and weapon techniques are more than sufficiently diverse, with even more move variety than DS3. Definitely not the most original game ever, and don't expect every single shortsword to have a different moveset, but the iteration of familiar themes has enough originality to hook you into the world. As someone who's played a lot of souls-like and Fromsoft on PC and console, I wasn't crushed by the difficulty, but it's more than enough to force me to stay on my toes and definitely punishes my arrogance or distraction. Constantly surprised by enemy variety, and I'm not even halfway through.

I understand that this game had jank on release, and I played much later so I understand my experience is better. However, I can't help but feel that this game suffered the same review phenomenon as Forever Winter, where some gamers decided that because someone had dared to try and make the uncensored grimdark title that they had long wished for in the genre (souls-like, extraction shooter in these respective cases,) that their cynical brains refused to believe the game could be good, almost *wanted* it to be a letdown, and when both games had bugs early on they came out and gave it hell for even trying to give gamers what they so often said they wanted in a theoretical title.

That said, the game's not perfect by any means, I'm not trying to glaze here. I have a good graphics card and I run at about medium when optimized, still looks good but I'd like to see it in full glory. You can get stuck on terrain if you go looking for shenanigans, similar to DS3. And of course, there's the weird quirk of your character model always seeming just a little shorter than he/she should be? Like it might be that you're always in a combat stance and slightly crouched? There's no "sheathe weapons" button or more casual stance where you stand up straighter, which is a shame. I'd like to either see that added or just see the player character be like 8% taller than they are now.

This game is an interesting, but flawed take on the Souls formula.  It brings some unique ideas to the table but they feel 85% fleshed out at best.

An example of this would be the Umbral realm, a secondary layer of the world that you can freely traverse by using an item or get forced into by losing too much life.  The art style of this secondary realm is often really cool, and when you first get introduced to it the possibilities of hidden paths or secrets seem really cool.  In practice, most areas follow this flowchart:
Start in area -> find some progression blocker -> go to the Umbral to get past it -> open a shortcut so you never have to go to the Umbral again for that area.
In this flowchart, the shortcut is never very far either.

As far as secrets in this secondary world, they are almost always floating off in areas you could not reach normally.  It really seems like this is because they did not want to have to deal with placing new collision in an area that the player might already be standing.  So often, the whole puzzle is just noticing something that you cannot reach and then checking if there is a path in the Umbral.

While I enjoy that the development team is listening to player feedback and making changes, the game feels very different each time I launch it.  There are some things it is ok to stick to your vision on.
An example of this would be how you collect Vigor (souls equivalent).  Originally, killing an enemy would drop vigor on the ground and you had to run close to it to pick it up.  Later in a patch, they made it so you auto collect vigor no matter how close you are to it based on player feedback.  But then, other players complained that they liked the original way, and now it is a setting you can toggle.  Putting core mechanics like this behind a setting is not a good idea in my eyes, and weakens the vision of the game.

Overall I enjoyed my time with the game, but it has room for improvement in the sequel.

[h1]Disclaimer[/h1]
I finished the game once with the 'regular' ending, then played a bit more. It launched having lots of performance issues and a much higher difficulty. This review is for the current version as of writing.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Aggressively mediocre experience marred by a lot of a-hole design decisions and enemy placements. It has a good amount of content and some nice level design. It's worth playing if you have no other Soulslikes to dive into. The Surge was a clunkier but a more fun game.

[h1]Description[/h1]
Lords of The Fallen is for some reason another Lords of The Fallen game after Lords of The Fallen. Title makes no sense, the game is not a continuation or a remake or a reboot or anything, it's just nonsense.

It's a Soulslike with very familiar mechanics. It allows you to parry using any weapon, but parry doesn't put an enemy in vulnerable state, instead draining their stability. Stability is drained by hitting and parrying and will put an enemy in vulnerable state for a finisher if you drain it completely with a parry or if you perform a heavy attack after it's gone.

Basically it has some elements of Sekiro/Lies of P and Demon's Souls. Difficulty is rather on the low side after the nerfs, when the game first came out it was overflowing with enemy groups and a lot of enemies felt harder.

It has PvP invasions similar to Dark Souls 2, where you can be invaded at any point, but seems like after an invasion there's a very long cooldown before another. You can also play this in co-op, even transition areas alongside the host, unlike Dark Souls where you only play until the area boss. Co-op doesn't feel much rewarding though.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ Lots of content[/b]
Tons of armors, spells, weapons, areas and quests.

[b]+ Level design[/b]
Some levels are really well designed. I especially loved a big tower that you start exploring from the top down, it's a fun little spin on the 'ascend the tower' trope in gaming where you descend instead. Every level that doesn't rely on Umbral tends to be nicely designed, even when there are some questionable enemy placements sometimes.

[b]+ Generally functional[/b]
It's mediocre fun.

[b]+ They cared[/b]
This is not a low-budget cash-grab. There's enough in here to make me believe at least some people on the team wanted this to be comparable to Dark Souls or Demon's Souls. It's nowhere as good, but the attempt was there.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- Enemy variety[/b]
This game does a lot of what I hate - it has a few amount of enemies and overtime it just increases their HP when they appear in later levels. It's jarring that you will see same enemy you've been fighting all throughout the game and it suddenly has way more/less HP.

[b]- A-hole design[/b]
Both Demon's Souls and Dark Souls have had their moments of 'gotcha btch!'. Usually it happens like 2-3 times in the game. LoTF seems to revel in gotchas, there are so many ledges with a cheeky enemy programmed to throw you off of it it's insane. There are many other moments that feel like cheap gotchas designed by some a-hole on the dev team. For exampel there's a room with 2 dogs and a harmless slave in the middle, the game is designed in such way to always lock onto the slave if you use the lock-on mechanic, which will jerk your camera away from the threats. Even if you look square at the dog, the game will target the slave because of how it's designed, and the room is deliberately designed to do that. Of course you can just not use lock-on in that place, but that's not the point. Point is, this feels malicious.

My recommendation to devs - playtest your game. If you think it's cute that you die to a gotcha, now imagine that you have no dev tools or cheats and you actually have to replay a large portion of the game and potentially lose your resources along the way. This may be endearing once or twice, but when it happens so many times it's just fking anger-inducing.

[b]- Umbral gimmick[/b]
It's not fun first time through the game. You are taught to look out for butterflies for points where there's something in Umbral world, but that's often not true. Sometimes butterflies fly around and there's nothing. MANY times there is something and there are no butterflies. It's a tedious and boring mechanic that feels 'gamey' and artificial. There's maybe one place with a interesting usage of movable platforms and that's it.

[b]- Ugly characters[/b]
It doesn't matter if you change sex options to male/female when your females don't look good, mate.

[b]- Many other minor issues[/b]
- No counter on how many of specific item you have in your inventory when you are buying items. For example there is an achievement to acquire all armors in the game, but a lot of them are in shops and there's no way of telling if you have a specific piece or not without checking manually. It was one of the reasons I eventually dropped the game because getting all achievements would be much more busywork inventory management than I anticipated. If only you could view all armor items and sort them by set, but no...
- There's no ability to assign specific spells to specific catalyst.
- The quests are vague, hard to track and rely on obscure triggers, just like in most Souls games (basically play with a guide or you're not doing them).
- Slow-ass grind for donation items and you need hundreds of them for armors.
- Boss items require special resource that's annoying to farm.
- Abess enemy is just badly designed with a move that throws huge AoE around her, creating damage areas that linger for what feels like a couple minutes while having seemingly infinite poise, she also has strangely large HP pool and huge damage (thankfully there are only a few of them ingame).

And many more.

[h1]Lowdown[/h1]
It's very 'eh'. The original was a clunky game, but it had potential. The Surge was still clunky, but tried to do something more. These devs have decided to do their own thing after a split (I don't know the politics of it, and I didn't bother to check) and while the attempt was okay - The Surge 2 showed much more interesting changes than this. This just feels like something I played many times over with Lies of P, Dark/Demon's Souls and other games in the genre.

I'd give Same Name as The Original, but Reused a
[h1]6/10[/h1]
With next game I suggest being a bit more respectful to player's experience instead of relying on cheap gotchas and focus more on the purpose. For example - if you add an armor achievement, ask yourself how would a played complete it. If you had - you'd know that shop interface not showing if an item is in your possession is a problem and you could fix it. Same with a bunch of gotcha moments in the game - what's the purpose? Because if it's just to kill the player, maybe it's not a good idea?

(+)TECHNICALLY EXCELLENT: This is one of the technically best souls-like games,. The movement in this game is much quicker and sharper than its predecessor, it has excellent combat mechanics, with some truly excellent innovations, such as how range and magic and incorporated into combat.

(+)SOULSLIKE INNOVATIONS: While this game feels more like a fromsoft Souls game than any other soulslike I've played, it actually makes some positive changes to the formula, including using a secondary, overlaid world to find secrets, incorporating a better throwable ammo system, and having the option to place temporary save points. 

(+)RESPONSIVE DESIGNERS: It seems like the designers took every criticism of the first game seriously, and seem to have also responded to criticisms of this one as well by tweaking, updating, and fixing the game over time.

(-) UNCLEAR DIRECTIONS: I've played a few games in the souls genre at this point, and seldom have found a game where it is less clear where you are supposed to go next at various points. I do plenty of exploring, but the level design really should be pulling more weight in pointing you forward. You will get lost in this game at times without a walkthrough, unless you are excellent at the genre.

(-) MISSING FUN FACTOR: As one of the few people who enjoyed the first game, I do miss the slow, clunky aesthetic. Losing that aesthetic also meant that this game just wasn't as fun to me as I expected, and this game simply does not feel like its predecessor at all. Leveling up and beating the bosses didn't have the same fun factor as other games, and I don't know why. I have mixed feelings about this game. I was conflicted about whether or not to recommend it. Like many others here, I am a fan of FS games. While I enjoy this genre very much, I also acknowledge that each FS game has its flaws. After finishing my first playthrough of LOTF, I don’t think I can recommend the game in its current state.

The positives of the game:

+   Great art style: The environment is nicely done and is certainly one of the game's biggest strengths.

+    Two-worlds mechanic: This is a cool idea that sets the game apart from FromSoftware titles. It also functions as a second-life mechanic, similar to Sekiro, making the game more forgiving, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing.

+   Combat and gameplay: Overall, the combat is good and fun. The developers improved and innovated ranged combat in this genre.

+  Improved co-op: The co-op experience is better compared to FromSoftware games.

+   Ongoing updates: The game is still receiving updates and has seen some improvements. Hopefully, this will continue, as the game has the potential to be great. It’s good to see that the developers and publishers haven’t abandoned it.

Now the negatives:

 -   Lack of enemy variety: The game has very little enemy variation, to the point where you fight the same enemy types over and over again. This becomes tiresome and repetitive. The game desperately needs a 2.0 patch or DLC with more enemy types. Even adding just 3-4 new enemy types would be a significant improvement.

 -   Reusing bosses as standard enemies: The bosses in this game are okay in my opinion. It’s acceptable to have a few lackluster bosses if they have unique designs or are somewhat interesting lore-wise. However, the huge issue is that most bosses you encounter will later appear as standard enemies in later areas. I’m not talking about unique, one-time encounters—these are standard trash mobs with large health pools. This design choice is so tedious and frustrating that I eventually decided to run past these enemies, even though I usually enjoy exploring and fighting my way through new areas in FS games. I don’t understand how the developers thought this was okay. It would have been better to make the game shorter with a smaller world instead of resorting to this annoying enemy spam.

 -   Umbral realm: While the Umbral realm is a nice idea, it quickly becomes boring and tedious due to constantly respawning enemies. The "puzzles" in this realm are also repetitive—you essentially just pull a bridge toward you, jump across, and repeat. I don’t understand the developers’ intent here, as it adds little to the game.

 -   Frustrating area design: The level design can be very confusing and frustrating at times. I often found myself unsure of where to go or unable to locate important items. Many others have shared similar experiences. While this could be acceptable if done intentionally for a specific area to make it unique, the issue appears in many areas, and the feeling of being lost sucks here.

- Quests are just terrible! They imported the horrible quest design from ER in this game almost the same. If you dont look up Guides you WILL fail most quests. A blind playthrough WILL fail you most quests. This is an aspect they should have NOT copied from ER

 -   Limited weapon movesets: There are very few unique weapon movesets. Most weapons within the same category share the same moveset. I really enjoyed the variety of weapon movesets in games like ds2 and ER, so this was a letdown.

  -  Unnecessary political inclusion: Bringing current politics into a souls-like game feels out of place. After the Trump victory (would the CEO have made the poll if the other candidate had won?...), the CEO made a poll on X (I wonder who will vote in this poll and what the results will be...). No one noticed the body type A/B distinction in the first place. If male/female options were so important, they could have implemented them from the start without making a fuss, and no one would have noticed or cared. Or implement it without announcement in the next game. FS just did this silently and no one batted an eye. They never made a big announcement about it. Don’t get me wrong—I don’t have a problem with changing it to male/female, but I’m tired of seeing this culture war from the US inserted into games.

If the negative points don’t bother you , I could recommend the game if you’re a big fan of the genre and it’s on sale.

There's a good core to this game, but too many flaws that distract from the experience.  Combat is fine, although it does have a somewhat clunky feeling because you can't dodge after attacking for a very long time.  You get used to it, so I wouldn't say that's a huge problem.  Combat does have a serious flaw built into the control scheme: your dodge changes to a sidestep if you are locked onto a target.  You can still dodge by double tapping the button, but I shouldn't have to try hard to convince you that this is extremely unintuitive.  There are a lot of fights where side stepping is "good enough," but sometimes you really need to dodge, and it feels very bad that the button scheme changes based on whether you're locked on.

Combat isn't the main flaw of this game, though.  The level design has generally very long distances between checkpoints (vestiges).  You can use a consumable to create a temporary vestige at much more common flowerbeds, but they're expensive to buy and you don't get enough to use them on every flowerbed.  Flowerbeds are also inconsistent.  Sometimes they're right next to each other, sometimes there's a vestige right after a flowerbed that will make you feel stupid for planting a seed, and sometimes there's a surprising amount of distance between flowerbeds.  You get enough seeds that the checkpoints don't usually feel [i]too[/i] bad, but you sometimes might feel the need to risk a long runback to hold off on wasting a seed.  Because you can only have one seed at a time, you can't plant a seed, explore somewhere else, and come back later (unless you never use another seed).  So if you are exploring, just hypothetically, a very large snowy area with invisible archers and zero vestiges, decide you came here too early and want to go elsewhere, you might lose your progress.

I'll finally get to the main flaw of this game.  There's a lot of trash.  A lot.  Of trash.  The game has a nasty habit of having a "boss" end up becoming a common regular enemy.  This is common practice in these types of games, but this game takes it to another level.  It is common in this game for a boss to become a regular enemy [i]immediately[/i] after fighting the boss.  I don't think this game has the hardest combat in general, so these types of enemies aren't usually too hard, but it does make them an absolute slog to clear through.  You might have to fight 2 at a time.  With other mobs.  There are loads of ganks, archers or mages shooting at you from ledges, ambushes etc.  And there are very long stretches of the game with the same 2 or 3 enemies repeated over and over again.  All of this heavily incentivizes you to just skip the trash and run through, but you have to know where you're going to make that work, and that can sometimes be hard in this game for several reasons.  Exploration in this game is actually really cool and fun because of the umbral system, which is a neat idea, but I just wish the trash wasn't so boring to deal with.

Trash and checkpoints aside, the level design is pretty cool.  There is an umbral realm, which you can enter at will and when you die.  Some of the terrain changes in the umbral realm, so it is a big part of exploration, and there's plenty of hidden stuff to find.  The jump button is crap, though.

All in all, this is a mixed bag.  I think it has decent combat that isn't too hard, but it has endless hordes of trash mobs with high hp and plenty of BS, which makes the game somewhat unfun to play a lot of the time.  This isn't a game where you will spend most of your time dying to bosses.  You'll spend most of your time dying to trash and trying to figure out where to go.

This game feels like Dark Souls developed by a team of people who had only ever read exaggerated headlines about how totally hard and unfair it was. Every part of Lords of the Fallen is subpar or worse: 

* Very limited catalogue of player weapon animations 

* Very limited catalogue of enemies 

* Very limited catalogue of player weapons and armors

* Subpar sound design: The OST is fine, but combat sound design is lacking. It doesn't feel satisfying to hit enemies in this game, and I believe that is largely down to sound design in addition to subpar stagger animations.

* Bad enemy balancing: Mid-late game enemies, particularly minibosses feel significantly overtuned compared to earlier in the game, even in cases where they're the same enemies. Enemies seem to be arranged with little thought given as to why they're there or how many should be there, and when there is thought given, it's to set up ambushes that always seem to get you no matter how vigilant you're being, or multi-enemy encounters that can't be avoided due to entire groups of enemies being alerted on a single enemy's discovery of the player. The fire-hurling dogs alone would be worth this negative review.

* Bad Level planning: The distribution of enemies and checkpoints is very inconsistent. Sometimes you'll be rifling through your single-use healing items after ages of combat and wandering, eyes peeled, scouring the wastes for a checkpoint to finally replenish your healing, and other times there will be 2 checkpoint spots within a few seconds walk from each other, sometimes without even a single enemy between them. The checkpoint system itself is also a disaster, as the "mobile bonfire" system quickly becomes a compulsory system instead of an optional one, with nowhere near enough of the single-use checkpoint items being given to facilitate consistent use of the system. You can buy checkpoint items, but they're expensive early-mid game and there's no reason you should have to blow your cash on necessary level checkpoints. Instead, this system encourages the player to never use the checkpoint items, since the game can't be trusted to give reasonable checkpoints at reasonable times in the level. Some bosses don't even have checkpoints near them that you can use without a single-use checkpoint item, so there is massive FOMO every time you establish a checkpoint that isn't already setup for you when you arrive, and no way to know whether any checkpoint site you come across is worth using your limited resources on or not.

* Umbral system makes exploration feel like a chore driven by FOMO since you're never able to see everything, unless you want to stay in Umbral the entire time and end up getting spammed by Umbral fodder enemies, akimbo-blade grim reapers, and eventually pursued by nigh-unkillable enemies while you're looking around or engaged in some other fight already. 

* The environments are claustrophobic and have far too enemies crammed into them at times, especially if you explore in Umbral (there were points where I had to resort to kiting enemies backwards to the end of their leashes like I was playing World of Warcraft to avoid the extreme enemy spam.) The game, even outside of its spam sessions, also forces multi-enemy fights far too often, even though this game's combat system and cramped environments do not support multi-enemy encounters. This is further exacerbated by the faux magnetism present in combat animations which makes outpacing enemy attacks nearly impossible unless you're at Mexican standoff distance.

* The magic system is somehow worse than Souls, with far fewer spell options and even less imaginative integration. The multiple hotkeys idea is good, but it comes at the cost of severely limiting your spell options during combat. If Elden Ring had cut players down to 3 usable spells at any given time like this game does, then nobody ever would have complained about the lack of separate spell hotkeys.

* Animation design quality, along with enemy variety, is on par with a Ubisoft game; not even remotely up to Souls standards. Often, enemies have badly weighted animations that cause them to swing with timings that can't be anticipated, making it very difficult to discern when enemies are going to attack, essentially relegating it to a guess each time until you either memorize specific arbitrary queues or learn to vibe it out after getting piped for the 100th time, which defeats the entire point of the game by making skill progression feel like an obligatory war of attrition instead of legitimate improvement at the game and mastery of its systems.

* Simulated Magnetism in combat animations, as mentioned previously, causes enemies to slide into you constantly and makes it impossible to outpace or outdistance enemy attacks unless you're far outside of your own attacking distance. On the player's side, the magnetism just makes the animations feel unpolished and doesn't score well with the profusely cramped environments and ubiquitous death ledges.

* Mechanical oversaturation: There are too many active gameplay elements to consider at all times and it's all forced onto you at once. If it were introduced over the course of the game, it wouldn't be that bad, but even if it were, some of the mechanics are just unnecessary and bog down the experience, particularly the lamp mechanics: Umbral world switching, which quickly becomes a necessary compulsion rather than an interesting nicety or adventurous extra, as well as enemies requiring the use of the lamp to weaken them before normal combat can proceed.

Overall, Lords of the Fallen, even on current patch, is not a good game. Don't be fooled by the reviews saying it's good now. It may have improved since release, but not nearly enough, and its problems are too fundamental to ever be addressed at this point. The guess and check difficulty combined with the generally unengaging and imprecise combat renders an unfulfilling experience that is simultaneously frustrating and boring, and this is coming from someone with over 1300 hours in Elden Ring and many challenge runs, including RL1 all bosses and RL1 NG+7 all remembrances, under their belt at the time of writing. Souls games can be frustratingly difficult at times, but this experience truly has nothing to offer outside of being annoying.

For every flaw that this game has, the Dark Souls series has some you've probably overlooked through your nostalgia glasses. Their games are not the golden standard to be inspired by, and I'm glad developers like HEXWORKS are making something new and interesting with the genre. 

That being said, here are the things I don't like about this game. I think the Vestige seed system needs an overhaul in the sequel. I think making them a finite resource and temporary on top of that adds unnecessary backtracking and takes away from the game. You should be able to teleport to all of the ones you've placed in a submenu under the specific Vestige of a particular area. Now for the npcs. I don't really enjoy how they seemingly go places without a direction to follow, but that's a problem I have with FromSoftware too. For the weapons you get, the selection needs some work as well. I feel like half of the weapons look the same to me, and I wish there were more weapon types and movesets to have. It would be cool to have the ability to change the moveset of a weapon just for fun, but that's just something I would personally like to see.

As for what I like with this game, I'll name a few things that stuck out to me. I like the idea of the Umbral realm, as it gives the world another layer of exploration, but I feel like they should dive deeper into this concept in the sequel, as I don't feel like it's fully explored in this game. Another thing I really like is the armor/clothes selection. Almost every piece of armor in this game is very well designed, and I appreciate the art direction they went with. The armor tincts are a cool innovation as well, as it lets me have virtually unlimited customization. Unlike Elden Ring, I can actually mix armor pieces and it'll at least look decent with the right tinct. I think unlocking classes to play with after beating the game through one of its endings is a really cool idea, and they should do more with that. The option to add modifiers to a particular save file to switch up the game was an interesting idea. I'll probably have fun with that in another playthrough.

Overall, I think this game is really good, and its flaws don't particularly bother me that much. For the first entry in this rebooted series, I feel like it has a very bright future ahead of it. I can't wait to see what the developers do next!

The short answer: Not perfect, but very, very good. If you liked any of the Dark Souls games or Elden Ring, you'll probably like this. It takes a little something from just about all of Fromsoft's games, iterating on them while clearly respecting what they did.

The long answer: I have some problems with Lords of the Fallen, but even with them in mind, it's one of the best soulslikes I've ever played. I'll start with the bad:

The ease of access for certain things is a bit imbalanced. There are three types of magic, but one of them doesn't have a teacher at the main hub unless you find a secret - and said teacher leaves if you progress the game in a way you're very likely to shortly after finding them. It makes some sense in lore that this kind of magic is rarer, but I don't think it's balanced well - mostly because the other two kinds have permanent and easily accessible teachers in the hub area.

Enemy variety is a bit lacking, but the game does a good job of slowly introducing new enemy types so as to make the most of its limited roster throughout the whole game. Still, it does get a bit tiring to fight a miniboss only for the game to immediately begin using them as normal enemies.

The inventory system has a lot of great ideas but some frustrating ones. You can't swap weapons quickly - you have a right and left hand, and can one- or two-hand the right hand weapon easily, but anything else requires you go to your inventory to change. Ranged weapons are separate from this and go in their own slot, but you also cannot swap them with a button. Throwing items in this game are treated as ammo for a special ranged weapon, your throwing hand, but since you can only have one ranged weapon equipped, you effectively cannot use thrown items if you want to use a bow or magic. Spellcasting catalysts also only have around 3-5 slots to equip spells depending on the catalyst - and while this does allow the controls for spellcasting to be very clean and demands you think carefully about what spells you choose, there is enough variety in the spells in the game that I feel more options would've been good to have.

My final complaint is that co-op help isn't as seamless as it is in the souls games. Summon signs aren't a thing; rather, you must summon a random partner from a resting point. For NPC summons, they only appear for major bosses, which are very few and far between. I feel like given the way it works in Lords of the Fallen, they could've learned more from Dark Souls 2 for its multiplayer implementation.

Now for the good. With two worlds to consider, I would expect one of them to be a bit half-baked or boring, or at least be very similar to the other most of the time. Instead, both Axiom (the "main" world) and Umbral (the dead world) are very distinct and consistent in their mechanics, looks, and geography, and this leads to some really interesting decisions for the player. The Axiom, for example, is always safer to be in. You have the safety net of dying and being sent to the Umbral, there are less enemies, you're not on a timer. But the Umbral has many benefits of its own: most level obstacles like fire or water are removed, you have access to many more routes and shortcuts, and you earn more currency. Some boss fights go as far as to change significantly between Axiom and Umbral. They really did the most with the concept of having a second dimension to play with, and it's very satisfying to interact with the systems it creates.

Ranged weapons are also better than in most soulslikes. They use Ammo, a generic resource that comes back on a rest, in a similar way to Mana. So you don't need to spend money or time gathering arrows or throwables - you just pay a small amount of ammo per shot, generally spending more for stronger or more specialized ones. It's a simple, genius system that allows nonmagical ranged combat to feel good to use.

I also adore how it balances shields. Shields pose a balancing problem in many soulslikes. If they're too strong, they encourage turtling, but if shields are too weak it discourages most playstyles involving heavier weapons or armor. In Lords of the Fallen, shields are quite good, but blocked damage is dealt as withered health that can be recovered through attacking rather than negated completely. Thus, you are encouraged to watch for smaller openings to recover health instead of hiding behind a shield forever. It's the best of both worlds, encouraging more aggressive play but still rewarding those who choose be more defensive. Parrying is also accomplished via perfectly-timed blocks, like in Sekiro, so even weapons can be used to block if you have good timing, and you're rewarded highly for having the skill to be defensive with a weapon.

If you liked a single one of Fromsoft's action RPG library, you can be reasonably certain you'll enjoy this game. Some of the choices it makes are frustrating, but they are small issues in the grand scheme of an expertly crafted soulslike worthy of the name.

When Lords of the Fallen launched in 2023, it was met with a mix of excitement and frustration. The game had immense potential, but a rocky release held it back from greatness. Players encountered numerous technical issues, including performance drops, crashes, and inconsistent hitboxes that made combat feel unpredictable. Balancing was also a concern, with certain enemy encounters feeling more unfair than challenging. Despite these hurdles, the foundation was strong—an ambitious dark fantasy world, a unique dual-realm mechanic, and satisfying Soulslike combat that had the potential to shine.

Fast forward to 2025, and Lords of the Fallen has undergone a remarkable transformation. Thanks to dedicated post-launch support from the developers, nearly all of its early issues have been ironed out. Performance is now smooth across all platforms, enemy balancing has been refined, and quality-of-life updates have made exploration and combat more immersive than ever. The Umbral Realm, one of the game's most distinctive features, remains a thrilling risk-versus-reward system that sets it apart from other Soulslike titles.

Beyond its technical improvements, Lords of the Fallen stands out as a must-play for fans of dark fantasy and challenging RPGs. Its stunning gothic art direction, engaging boss fights, and deep lore make it a compelling experience that rivals some of the best in the genre. If you skipped it at launch due to its rough state, now is the perfect time to dive in. In 2025, Lords of the Fallen is not just a game that has been fixed—it's a game that has finally reached its full potential.

A warning, this is a Visual Novel, not an Action Game.

For players wishing to learn how to find the different branches, there seems to be, in general 4 Heroine Endings, each with Good and Bad, and after each ending, the start screen will display a silhouette of the "heroine"'s ending you unlocked. The first 2 times you play the game, you will unlock "extras" in the next playthrough, so Ending Meteora will be the first, after that, you will be capable of unlocking the second branch for Endings Noa and Anima, and after any of them, you unlock the ability to open the final branch, to the Coco Ending (Final).

In Ariadne, a visual representation of the story line and its branches, you can see the ramifications, and can also jump through past events from past branches at any time if you want to complete things. There is also a mini "encyclopedia" of terms in Ar, holding important terms of that event and what they meant at that time, so if you forgot something, check those to remember. However, you can only jump into major events, so sometimes, you may have to backtrack a lot if you want to just check the other option that you just went through because there were no major events in some time.

For how to play the game, you will go through 3 types of events:

- Novel mode is the most common, as the novel advances through it, and is the easiest to explain: People talk, you read, and so on. On a very strangely adopted method you have choices, which affects hidden parameters, like Obedience, Independence, being Open Minded and so on, but because there are no numeric parameters, my impression is that it changes the options you may face ahead, I would imagine that, if I'm too obedient, I may be unable to go against an order in the future, and if I'm too rebellious, the choices may not allow me to agree with certain characters. This is just a guess, as I have no real idea how it works, but for example, in my second playthrough where I was a little nicer to Noa, I got to see her concert, and I didn't even had such option in the first playthrough, but of course, maybe it's locked the first time, or maybe it was related to the parameters, but this uncertainty is awesome and just makes things more natural, because I don't need to think too much, and just go with what I think will be better, without worrying about missing much either.

The main problem is that, unlike other novels, there is no Log button, so careful when skipping text, as you can't read what you skipped, and will have to go back to the title menu and start the current part from the start to see it again.

- Search Mode are somewhat rare, but they are basically the moments when you have multiple options to either interact or talk with people. Sometimes it's just to interact with things or talk with the characters, but once interacted, unless they have an extra event, you can't do it anymore, and without Logs, be careful with button pressing again. The worse part of this is that there is no indication on what advances the story or not, so if you went to check on something and you left the place because you thought you would have to do something else to advance the story, well, you will move, and any other interactions will be lost until another play through. You don't lose anything technically, just... That feeling of 100% as soon as possible... Search mode may also be used in small puzzles, although those are linear, basically, find the item you have to interact to advance the story... Well, it's basically the same thing, really.

And here is the best part:
- Mecha Battles. They are essentially an **overloaded Novel Mode**: It's mostly linear and you don't have much control, but it's more interactive (press buttons), and sometimes you may have choices (attack, don't attack, if allowed, do something else), and is where you will find some branches in the story.
But... The experience... It can't be described. Check the official website for the artists doing the sound design to understand what I mean: https://altdeus.com/en/staffcast/artist.html

For the Sound Track, you have someone from MONACA, who is also known for OSTs like the Nier series, although if I were to compare the OST here, they remind me more of Gundam Unicorn, Aldnoah Zero, and Guilty Crown (the three by Hiroyuki Sawano). There is also kz (livetune), very famous for many great Hatsune Miku songs.

Please MyDearest, do sell the Soundtrack on Steam!

For the sequence of events, all mecha fans are guaranteed to love it: You have a full launch sequence, filled with the boot process, your Operator/AI/Partner Noa giving you her blessings, and mind you, she stays in the cockpit singing the battle theme, with a sound similar to Hiroyuki Sawano's more agitated insert songs.

I feel like I'm piloting the Macross, and I'm not talking about the Valkyries, instead, it's heavy and clunky, reminding me more of the the Battle 7, Battle Frontier or Macross Quarter in Battle mode, and everything you do and see is from the cockpit, so for example, up until now, I have not seen my own mecha properly (I could be vaguely or partially seen through monitors, or glasses, or even reflection when I'm inside, but never from a 3rd person view), the movements, although limited in view, feel a bit clunky, but not as in "bad clucky", but as in "I'm piloting a Goddamn Macross" type of clunkiness, so you know the weight of the movements, or when you get hit (although, of course, the VR can't make itself heavier).

You get all the dialogues and tension that you have to do to defend and attack, like pressing the floating buttons, or holding your hips guns, joining them into some Hyper Gun, and then aim, and as the sequence starts, and you have to press the button the the proper time to shoot, or you miss (The main mecha, the Alto Makhia, is a Cannon type mecha. The Ares Makhia, which uses a sword, is controlled by another character, which is soon to receive a DLC, so I'm expecting somehow being able to battle with the sword).

Keep in mind, this is not a fighting game, so if you are expecting Gundam Vs type of action, you may even feel bored by having the whole boot up sequence all over again, but if you understand the appeal of the Mecha genre, it's mechagasm: it's like you are in an anime, in first person, with an excellent OST, feeling the excitement of what is going to happen next, I just had to write this review now without even finishing the game yet! It's just that good of an experience, the feeling of inside the cockpit of your robot seeing the battle only through the visor, having your partner by your side talking to you and acting to help. It's a little sad that they are short, and there aren't thaat many of them compared to the rest of the game, but hell, that's why I'm going full playthrough, just to play all those parts again!

The plot... It's quite unique, I found small elements that remind me of Aldnoah Zero (OST), Macross (Divas and the "power of song"), Knights of Sidonia (Tsugumi's case) and Genesis of Aquarion (Much shorter than 12K years, if you catch the reference of what I mean), to name a few, only talking about the good parts, of course.

Now, do remember that you may wish to change the voices to Japanese for the anime feeling, I just want to play more and more, too bad I need to sleep, the experience is just that GREAT.

In regards to it's relationship with Tokyo Chronos being in the same universe, there are 2 names that come straight from there, and they are not that irrelevant. However if you have not played the previous game, at most you will be missing a reference, you won't lose anything else.
The mech battle is a gimmick (think of it as a dialog choice box alternative), but gawd, the plot... it's fixation ramped up to 1000.

TLDR: I liked this game - much more than Tokyo Chronos. It is bigger, better, and more polished in every way. It offers an experience that only VR can offer, and serves as an even better proof of concept that its predecessor. I feel like ALTDEUS just opened pandora's box, and it might just be the progenitor of a new wave of VR visual novels that will be even bigger and better than it is. Even with all its writing hiccups, I believe it is something special and worth trying if you own a VR headset. It is to VR visual novels what half life alyx is to VR adventure games: a huge breakthrough in the right direction for an entire genre. If you're interested in reading beyond this tldr, then here are my pros and cons:

Good:
+The visuals are wild. You'll be blown away within the first 30 minutes of playing this game. Sometimes, you'll have to crane your neck all the way up to see what is unfolding. Major events in this game happen on a very large scale. Combine this with the binocular vision of VR, and we have something truly special. This leads me into the next point:
+The mech sequences are brilliantly directed and choreographed. As I've hinted at before, VR is an amazing medium for making things look large and epic. I've watched and read a lot of mecha anime and visual novels that put you in the cockpit of a mech, but not a single one of them comes even close the capturing the orgasmic scale of ALTDEUS's mech sequences. There's just something about having your entire binocular field of vision being filled up by the cockpit, watching the action unfold in front of you on a giant scale that completely outclasses anything you may see on a simple computer screen. You just have to try this game to see what I mean.
+The music is great. Music plays quite a big role in this game, both plot-wise and atmosphere wise. The mech battles would not be half as awesome if it wasn't for the blaring pop music in the background that makes everything feels orgasmically grand and exciting. Imagine watching the last episode of an anime and the opening starts playing. That's how each mech sequence feels. In addition, even when the exciting stuff isn't happening, the music still manages to be very beautiful and fitting for whatever scene they are in. Overall, stellar in the music and sound department.
+Although the game is actually very limited in its graphical capabilities, it hides this fact very well through its clever use of lore and visual tricks to hide the parts of it that don't look good, and put the parts that do front and center. 

Bad:
- There's a dialogue tree system that tells you what stats you will gain or lose if you pick one choice or the other. I.e if you pick this dialogue option, you lose 60% obedience, but gain 50% teamwork. This would be fine and dandy if only these stats ACTUALLY DID ANYTHING. They are completely irrelevant and the game doesn't even keep track of them. They only serve as flair and nothing else, which is extremely misleading as the game makes it sound as if they matter when introducing this dialogue system to you.
- The story is overly reliant on flashbacks to make you care for a certain character, which in turn only made me hate her.
- The main character sucks; she's moody, grumpy, whiny, always going on about how miserable her life is and how everything sucks. Her arc is also very predictable and cliche. It's the same arc that every edgy, whiny protagonist goes through in every visual novel ever, and more often than not I find myself mashing the A button to get through her incessant monologues in which she constantly wallows in self-pity and regret.
- The way to progress in this game is still tedious just as it was in Tokyo Chronos. While the story is slightly tighter than Tokyo Chronos, it is still tedious to have to go through entire portions of the game again and again multiple times to finally get to the true ending.

Very highly recommend the game, 8.5/10 
+ Voice acting is superb. Honestly, I was blown away at times, you could really feel the emotions of the characters. 
+ Music. Holy cow, each song is memorable and there are moments where it syncs so perfectly to story beats.
+ The story
Although it can get a bit confusing, I found myself really caring for the characters especially when Anima is introduced.

It's like stepping into the shoes of a great anime story.  I've played some visual novels and enjoyed them immensely... But this one takes it to a new level of immersion.  Featuring impressive production values: the expert utilization of a memorable OST (41 tracks, but felt like there were even more variations with instruments showing up at the right time); distinctive voice actors that I recognize from anime; pretty designs and a compellingly executed story... But furthermore, the player is in a 3D VR space with everyone.  That adds a level of realism that no non-VR game can achieve.  

While there are only occasional points where actual VR actions affect gameplay, already just by being in VR with the characters, it furthers the illusion that you are there, experiencing the story.

I give this game high marks.  Room for improvement perhaps; with more interactions, more places to visit; but I really, really liked it.  You are getting your money's worth with this game if you like anime and/or visual novels.

On a tangent:
Games like this make me excited for the future...  Maybe one day this kind of genre will have a new term, no longer a visual novel, but a VR novel.  Its distinguishing feature being the human as the controller as a necessity for full realization.  Detecting body language, eye target, expression, and of course deliberate actions.  Shielding someone?  Choosing to touch a hand?  Pushing someone away?  Moved to tears?  Refusing to look in the eye?  Smiling?  Laughing out loud?

I can see a not-too-distant future where subtle character reactions to the player could further enhance a story as a major feature without distracting from the story.  Do you smile at Noa's concert?  Do you refuse to watch?  Give a character a quick nasty look?  Do you gaze at the stars or lock eyes?  Does Anima mimic your expression?  While decisions should still be deliberately displayed, there could be a lot of natural story branching based on the person acting out the story.

I don't know about others, but I found myself standing when Chole was standing, and sitting when she was sitting.  And trying to use hand gestures appropriately during the game to enhance the illusion that I was acting out the character.  The more I put into it, the more I got out of it...

[h1] It's a great and immersive Visual Novel. If you enjoy the genre and/or enjoyed Tokyo Chronos, it's a must buy!  [/h1]

ALTDEUS: Beyond Chronos takes on a whole new way to experience a Visual Novel, just like in it's predecessor, bringing the genre to VR. And oh boy did they get it right. Imagine your regular Visual Novel game, but now you are literally inside it, being part of the world and it's narrative. It's that awesome.

The developers also increased the immersion of the game when compared to it's predecessor. Now you got hands and you can interact with key objects to the story, which heavily contributes to the VR experience. Unfortunately, we still have the floating torso aspect. Having legs and actually moving in the game would surely be a neat feature, but I understand how limited this kind of animation would be inside a Visual Novel, even if it's a VR one. And after being in the game for a while you totally forget about it.

Anyway, let's get to the main points of the review:

[b] The Good: [/b]

[list]
    [*]High immersion and great narrative goes nicely together to make a great VR Visual Novel.
    [*]Story is awesome. Characters are well presented, distinct and likeable. Won't say much to not spoil anything.
    [*]Pacing is great. Pretty much no fillers or time-wasting flashbacks. You actually get to experience the story with little to no interruption.
[/list]

[b] The "Meh" (because it's not even that bad): [/b]

[list]
    [*]The choice system can be ambiguous sometimes. Some doesn't matter at all, some are game changing. It's initially hard to tell which are which at the beggining, but later you will get some indication like [spoiler] the flowers petals surrounding you during a decision [/spoiler].
    [*]Most like the item above, the Ariadne system, which shows you the path your choices are leading to, can be confusing. Although it shows the direction you are heading to, it doesn't really show you the why, which will probably make you replay some parts of the game to find the specific decision where you "split" in a different path. For example, for me to get to the [spoiler] True ending [/spoiler] was pretty much trial and error, back and forth, untill I finally found where I was making the wrong decision.
    [*]You don't really have a save feature, the game saves automatically. However, you do get the feature to "leap" to certain chapters of the game. I, personally, would rather have the first in a Visual Novel with multiple endings. Makes it easier for organizing exactly where key decisions are. Leaping to certain chapters help, but you will find yourself skipping a lot of dialogue to quickly get where you need to be.
[/list]

And that's it. The good certainly outweigh the "meh". 

If you enjoy Visual Novels, are a VR enthusiast, enjoyed Tokyo Chronos or really just want a good narrative experience where you feel like you are part of the story, this game is for you. You won't regret it.

I played Tokyo Chronos before this and, though unrelated in story, ALTDEUS is certainly the spiritual successor to the aforementioned game.  Comparing to Tokyo Chronos, MyDearest seems to be more comfortable working in the VR space.  The environments are generally more interactive, proportions are more realistic, and better use is made of the VR medium.

That being said, before purchasing this game you should know what you are getting.  This isn't a game in the traditional sense like Beat Saber or Half Life: Alyx.  If you have played any visual novels before then the formula will be familiar.  You are playing from the perspective of a single protagonist.  You can occasionally make choices that impact the course of the game, generally resulting in an early demise, a bad ending, or one of several possible good endings or a "true" ending.  Otherwise, you are mostly a spectator viewing the world from the protagonist's perspective.

ALTDEUS has a passable story.  There are plot holes, there are poorly explained revelations wrapped in technobabble, and there are one-dimensional characters making questionable choices.  That being said, if you can suspend disbelief and ignore the flaws then it's easy to get immersed in the story and the better-written characters.

In particular, the mech battles feel urgent and give a good sense of scale and danger.  Some of the more pivotal moments are choreographed with the excellent musical score, making such moments more impactful for it.

Graphics are passable.  Character models and art is generally quite good and well animated.  Background textures could use an improvement, and in particular some background elements were relatively low-resolution 2D sprites that stood out if you noticed them.

The Japanese voice acting (I did not play it in English), sound design, and music were great.  The music especially deserves a nod, because not only is it good in isolation but it is used to great effect throughout the game.

I can recommend this game to fans of anime and visual novels.  ALTDEUS will feel quite familiar to such players.  To others, imagine a choose-your-own-adventure style science fiction adventure movie.  If that sounds interesting to you, then give ALTDEUS a try.  If you are expecting a more traditional VR experience like SUPERHOT or GORN then this may not be for you, but you may still be presently surprised if you're open to something different.

Despite the overall idea, it's not especially titillating or "naughty" but I did largely enjoy going through the scenarios.  Most of the scenarios are presented in a largely positive way but there is at least one that is a bit disturbing, albeit accurate in its message.  For the record, I have no idea what level of female input went into making this game; the lead dev on their website is a male and there's various women with notagamestudio but I don't know anything else.

My main criticism came with the ending.  Throughout the game, there is a sort of phonetic-text cypher thing going on with letter replacement leading to statements like "YOO ARE CVMMINK" that are largely legible and understandable.  The dev says it has something to do a statement about censorship but it doesn't get in the way.  The final chapter though is a whole alphabet soup of illegible text.  This is a shame since I enjoyed the narratives in the previous nine chapters and this turned into an exercise in just brute-forcing cards until I reached an unsatisfactory ending.  A posting in the discussions has someone saying he completed all the achievements and still gets the same so it doesn't seem to be a matter of discovering some unlocking secret.  In any event, if there was a "message" to it, it missed the mark and had me leaving the game disappointed.  Overall though, I enjoyed it and found it worth playing so I still give it a thumbs up (though with an asterisk).

Lydie & Suelle is widely regarded as the best Mysterious game, and one of the best Atelier games period. And yet when I played it myself, it ended up being one of the most disappointing. So what went wrong? 

While the Atelier series isn't known for deep [b]characters[/b], this cast is a special kind of bad. So many characters are defined by a single (often annoying) gimmick. This is further exacerbated by the fact that every gimmick is repeated over and over again ad nauseum. No, I don't want to see Mathias hit on yet another girl. No, I don't want to see the twins' dad do another crazy irresponsible thing. No, I don't want to see Liane slobber over Firis for the umpteenth time. L&S has way more scenes than previous games, but these scenes quickly become a source of annoyance, rather than a source of excitement.

Atelier games usually have great [b]music[/b], but L&S is the exception. There's not a single song that's memorable or catchy, and in fact, if you ask me to think of L&S soundtrack, my mind draws a complete blank.

The Atelier series isn't known for its [b]combat[/b] system, the main problem being how easy it is to trivialize the game. But at least in most Atelier games, you'll need to reach around the halfway point before you can break the remaining half. In L&S, you can easily break the game 10% of the way in, and then the rest of the game becomes trivial and boring. (And I'm not even talking about using the DLC exp quest.) This is actually one of the most complex combat systems, introducing mechanics like follow-up attacks and battle mixes, but none of that matters when you can steamroll every fight with brute force.

The Mysterious series is famous for its tetris [b]alchemy[/b], which adds a ton of depth and strategy compared to "normal" alchemy. The previous two games were all about careful positioning and ordering of materials, to string together large bonuses. Unfortunately, L&S scrapped the system for something much more simple, and all the depth and combo potential disappeared. In fact, with the way alchemy works in this game, the tetris grid is pretty much a waste of time, because most of the time, I could predict what effects I get beforehand, so creating items isn't nearly as interesting anymore. Even adding mechanics like catalysts, astrological symbols, and enhancing agents didn't help- they felt more arbitrary than anything you could strategize around. Also, because every material can have up to four components, the tetris mechanic ends up being more tedious (especially because the crafting menu also has numerous quality-of-life issues), despite being less interesting.

The problems with alchemy don't even end here. For some reason, the devs decided that quality doesn't matter for most items, so you're not even rewarded for interacting with the mechanics. In fact, because of how easy it is to break the game, there's little point in making anything other than your overpowered equipment. As a result, this is the game where I did the least amount of item crafting, often choosing to buy from stores instead.

Don't be fooled by my playtime. It's not a measure of how fun the game is, it's a measure of how tedious it is. (And how strong the nostalgia is from seeing characters of the previous games.) Because I'm such a big Atelier fan, I was desperately clinging onto hope that L&S would turn around and become fun at some point. But at some point, I had to say, enough is enough.

This is a reminder that even when a game is highly praised, you still need to be careful. There's always a chance you'll end up like me, and end up with a game that rubs you the wrong way in every aspect.

The sequel to Atelier Sophie. Did you like Sophie? Don't worry, this game has taken away everything good about that game!

So, first and foremost, the specter hanging over the game: the time limit. You have 300 days to accomplish the main plot. Now, that isn't an inherent bad. The problem is that Atelier Firis loves wasting your time! Time passes ridiculously quickly by walking even inside a building - prepare for 6hrs to pass just entering a library. Do you want to lose half a day exiting a city? This is that game! Also, people's doors close at night. I hope you don't take too long walking, or exiting your atelier at noon might mean the person you're visiting shuts their door by the time you reach!

This is compounded by the shittiest movement system in the game. Fast travel is only available within, not between maps, and only to fixed landmarks. Several maps, for some reason, have no landmarks near some of their exits. Hope you enjoy spending 6hrs in game walking from the closest landmark in Flussheim to the harbour, because the game mandates you walk that path a dozen time.

Now, I can forgive some clunkiness for a good story, but this is the worst plot and characterisation in an Atelier game yet. The plot? Get to Reisenberg in 300 days, while dropping in on other alchemists to help them with their stuff to get your three recommendations along the way. Those subquests are very 'thirty bear asses', honestly. The closest to an actual plot worth a damn is Flussheim, which is immediately undercut by having the resident alchemist be kind of terrible. Like I said, be prepared to walk from the Flussheim Institute to the harbour a lot. She really wants you to do so.

And the characters, ho boy. See, you can pick up characters from anywhere, in any pattern. Unfortunately, since the game ahs no idea what characters are with you, they then drop off the story after you recruit them, and their recruitment is seldom interesting either. I've used Heinz and Drossel for the entire time. Who are they? What do they like? I have no idea, because you stop interacting with them! There's one compulsory recruit behind a bottleneck (Flussheim, again), and you think she's important, but... nope, vanishes after recruitment, again. So the only characters that exist are Firis and Lia, and Lia's characterisation is 'incestous pedophilic lesbian' which is completely something you enjoy seeing right? (it isn't, get a better hobby than trying to get into your kid sister's bed and infantilising her)

So yeah. Bad game, the only reason I stuck it out to the final exam (which once again hammers that no character matters besides Firis and Lia) is for Sophie, who is still The Best. Off to play something that respects my time.

Remember Geometry Wars? It's similar to that but with Music at its core instead of bright explosions. I kept my 360 solely for this game, thats how great it is. Years ago, I'd get home around twenty after four from work and fire this game up. It was easily one of my favorite ways to chill and wind down after a long day. The game isn't deep, but it has a lot of depth. 3 basic modes, the last 2 being locked until you beat the first mode. 

Gameplay

The game takes place in a 2d box. Your a little spaceship(that always reminded me of The Last Starfighter) and every enemy is a musical instrument. Some enemies only need 1 shot to kill(or trigger their instrument) while others, aka The Romulan looking ship (the rapper) requires numerous hits to kill. There's numerous waves which are all different. Each wave presents more difficulties than the last. There's changes in your weapons, rate of fire, enemy population and variety, and a lot more.  Later in the game, some pretty crazy things happen, which are pretty exciting to encounter and play through. You only get 3 lives. Theres no restart from checkpoint. So getting to the end is an amazing feeling. Its very reminiscent experience to playing old games at the arcade. Theres definitely a lot of strategy and you'll learn through your play though how to attack each wave. However, I always called them Shells(guitar), can and will ruin your day. They can go out of the play zone, and come back in. They only take one shot, but when youve been backed into a corner or running a wall and your trying to get out, having a shell sneak in behind you is frustrating. Especially when you seconds to the next wave.. It is very easy to get swarmed and overwhelmed so here's a couple of beginner's tips. 

Tips

Use the walls. It's important to use the walls, this will minimize how many sides you can be attacked from and you can concentrate your fire. 

Do not stay still for too long. Especially in a corner. It can cost you. 

After the first couple of waves avoid spending to much time in the middle. Very easy to get swarmed from all sides. However, use the middle to your advantage. It's a fantastic route to use for escape if and you can use it to get enemies to bunch up in a way you want. 

Run the wall. Run the wall shooting ahead or behind you will help a lot. Don't continually run the wall, take a couple of walls, turn around and go back or take middle and get them grouped up and fall back and take them out. There's a lot of trial and error. And do not stick to one thing. This game will punish you for it. Just relax and have fun. You will get there. 

Use your power ups when needed. They can pull you out of disaster. 

Conclusion

These games are not usually my cup of tea, but I fell in love with this one even though I'm not the best at it. For $1.99, I cannot recommend it enough. This game has endless replayability. Perfect for whether you've got 15 min or hours to play. I would easily consider this one of my all-time favorite games. It's 2 bucks.  I think you'll be surprised with how much you like it.

I generally have a huge soft spot for these kinds of indie storytelling experiences, so all of that would have been forgivable... except for one critical flaw:

YOU ARE ALWAYS MOVING.

You can't actually stop and appreciate the scenery, the nuances, the story being told by the environments themselves (which is where the bulk of the story actually is, since the narrated part is just meh). The bird should be able to stop and actually LOOK at all the many thoughtfully constructed dioramas, not just zoom past everything. There were so many cool places to explore, but I wasn't allowed to have that opportunity -- I was too busy trying not to run into walls and trees (which reset you to the beginning of the zone, for some reason, rather than just bouncing you off and allowing you to stay in the same area).

And don't be all "But that's not how flight works", because this is a god bird that flies through SPACE. It can hover. Don't give me that shit.

It could have been so fun. Instead, it was a waste of two hours and I finished it solely out of spite.
