You have been given a Z5 Powerlance computer that comes with an anthology of 8 puzzle games. Some games are better than others, but all of them are good. A few of them are fiendishly difficult. They are presented with a framing narrative which seems like a semi-autobiographical story about the developers themselves, as the story revolves around the lives of the fictional software developers who created the various games.

Some of the standout games:

-20th Century Food Court- This one is probably the most substantial game in the collection. Also one of the most challenging. You have to create assembly lines for food products within a limited space. The solution usually has to account for one or more potential variables, being able to produce any possible food order. You also have to place the modules which control your factory machines in a limited space on the screen. This one feels the most like other games by Zachtronics, although it can't really be compared to any particular one of them. Very challenging and satisfying to solve. 

-Dungeons and Diagrams- My personal favourite in this collection. This one makes for a good palate cleanser between levels of the more difficult games. A simple, well-designed fantasy puzzle game. You have to fill out an 8x8 grid by placing the walls of a dungeon, following certain rules such as enemies always appearing in a dead end, and treasure chests being in a 3x3 room with one entrance. Very stylish. Very satisfying to solve. Once you reach the end of the game you can generate new levels at random, which are usually just as good as the ones in the campaign. 

-Steed Force Hobby Studio- A simulator where you build little gundam model kits. First you cut the pieces out of a plastic frame, then you assemble the model. After that, you can paint and decorate the mech. This is by far the easiest game in the collection, and the one I spent the least time on. However, I could see how someone else might spend much more time on it if they enjoyed painting the mechs.

-XBPGH: The Forbidden Path- This one has a dark, creepy sci-fi aesthetic which I really enjoy. The presentation is very mysterious and atmospheric. I won't say much about the mechanics, because learning the rules of the game is part of the challenge. Later levels are fairly difficult. The most stylish game in the anthology.

Super pleasant visuals and music. I loved the two solitaires and the Dungeons & Diagrams game, but had no idea how to play any of the other games. I think there is something to like in this collection for almost anyone. Just be warned that half of the games are not casual puzzle games.

Last Call BBS is a fitting coda to the output of Zachtronics Games - a bundle of games iterating on the themes of their programming/hardware hacking puzzles, some wildcards (an airfix assembly and painting game with pseudo-gundams!), and of course solitaire! (and all this idea long before UFO50 did the same "frame story").
Fantastic Zachtronics game. The cell automata game was especially cool.
While many of the mini games are far too complex for me to really enjoy, I still thoroughly enjoyed this presentation, and I have played way too much Sawayama Solitaire!
Worth it just for 20th Century Food Court
A worthy sendoff.

After That Which Sleeps turned out to be That Which Wasn't (didn't put money on it, just annoyed) it wasn't looking good for the genre of game I never knew I wanted. A civilization-like game where you're not bound by a civilization's rules and borders yourself. Its a genre that doesn't even have many -unfinished- games to show for itself (Infiltration by Gornova, SBTT1,) but now Shadows Behind the Throne 2 is what I will point at to say 'More of this, please.'

I like it a lot, for more than just the unique experience***, but it took me a few hours in 3 separate play sessions to tutorialize myself enough to know what to do and start enjoying it consistently. I wanted this niche game to be to my liking even before I bought it.

It is a cryptic game with a UI that only a developer can love. Information you need is usually there, but you have to hunt for it. It took me a while to appreciate all the number keys in the world view.) For example the society view that lets you see all the nobles and their relations would be handy to see simultaneously with the election screen or when I've spent my magical power to the negative values, I cannot see the world's temperature because my powers won't display.

In SBTT2, you're a disembodied evil trying to take over a world with 200~ turns of pre-rolled history, wars and expansion, splits and civil wars. Your methods range from spawning monsters to affecting the world's weather to just driving societies from one war to another, all the while you try keeping mankind divided and ignorant to your growing threat. 

Your agents are your pieces moving across the map, weakening and infiltrating cities. All this leaves Evidence, which causes investigating agents to eventually start attacking your units. A country expelling all foreign agents turns the region into a hot stoveplate. No playstyle usually works without another backing its weaknesses, at least not as well, apart from a glaring balance issue with the Unholy Flesh**. 

I didn't see it in the beginning but every action the nations take from locking down to starting wars to investigating your doings by assigning titles is a two-turn vote taken by the simulated aristocracies of each nation in response to what you or the other nations are doing. Every nation has an average of 6-12 nobles who all have their greatest believed threats listed, their like and dislike for another, their personalities and some smaller things that affect their voting habits.

What I love about this game is that it feels like the world, while appearing rudimentary, has depth and a clear cycle to it. It can roll on without your interference, that's in fact its goal. Countries war and defend, conquering until they get too big with too many nobles leading to civil wars and splitting back to smaller rebellions unless there's a greater unifying threat.
 
Most of the time the name of the game is 'who's the biggest threat?' and that isn't meant to be you. The enemy agents try to find evidence, investigate it and deliver it to as many nobles as possible to get the nation to judge your agents. You can kill them, hold them off or enthrall up to a few but they're many, replaceable and you only get one spell each turn.

Your agents aren't fighters and the hordes of monsters you create can stomp through a nation or two until a big enough kingdom swoops in armies amassed. This is how its intended by the developer I think, even if it doesn't quite work that way at times**.  The player is recommended to play sneaky, scheming like a bastard. 

So you start by infiltrating a nation's politics, driving their voting to inaction while you spawn monsters. They notice and you create a plague to shift the fears from your monsters to internal issues. Then you manipulate the noble's liking to you through saving them from the plague you started, leveraging newfound political power to then dismiss a rival noble. Now they've survived the gray rot, beasts and outlawed your agents. You forgot to keep your vampire fed. You've now raised the world's awareness making nations paranoid towards all infiltration attempts. Your magic and enthrallments are spent.

But you can say it was all part of your plan, because you gained political standing in the largest nation. You can start your plans anew and that on-the-fly scheming is the heart of the game. Someone might not like the idea of the player having no true lose condition but I find it thematically appropriate for cosmic horror. The lightbringer ritual, which is supposed to seal you away for many turns and reset the board works for me as a concept, even if it is a little beta and buggy.

As for bugs: I've had a couple. Societies without borders or holds after being absorbed, a few times boosting a noble's fear must've caused the value to go to negatives or something because a noble earlier terrified of my dark agents suddenly considered +190 evidence found in his region to be a modest concern of "Total threat: 9" There's odd AI behavior, especially on merchant npcs...

Bugs, UI and all the rough edges aside, I consider it fun. As mentioned earlier**, even if it is a little unbalanced towards finding an uninhabited corner of the world and just making monster nests until you have enough to take on even the biggest empire. For contrast, whilst using politics, especially in large societies the game can feel like being subjected to endless prestige sandbagging and your noble burning out the other noble's liking while trying to get just one step of a war declaration to go the way you want them to. Using the monsters as a subtler tool while focusing on the harder politics is pretty fun, they can work together.

So that's the part of the game that I really like. The appearance is another beast entirely.

The store page shows the world without the filters, but to keep up with the moving borders and mixing nations between turns (the games are long if you're not using just brute force methods) you're going to keep juggling the nations, provinces, awareness, infiltration and liking masks. The nations mask will change the colors of the sand, snow and trees to bright cyan, neighboring the peppiest yellows and purples and with how dark the game is, this is jarring. When not flashing the disco button actively, you risk losing track of which countries have which cities when their borders fit together like saw's blade. Information is there, but you always have to hunt it.

Finally, the music. The guitar tracks didn't woo me at first, yet while a low thrum and a drum beating a heartbeat to some foreboding score would've let me get in the role of looming over a world with evil intentions, I think letting me think unbothered was a smarter choice from the developer. They really grew on me, especially the one with the echoing clock tick / bamboo stick.

I've looked at things like the 'mod credits' put under event windows and how the npc face generation seems to allow for players adding their own, additional, not replacing, bits for constructing 'the faces of the enemy.' Seeing what's looking like early integrated mod support and having seen the dev eagerly chat with their player base both on Itch.io as well as here on Steam, I'm not unhappy with my choice to support this game or the next one.

***So to draw this review to a conclusion, TL;DR, Shadows Behind the Throne 2 is a game I recommend to those who saw TWS' KS page and went 'oh, scam or not, that's a cool idea.' If you have interest for this type of a niche game, this is the most fleshed out version I've found of this genre (Ruinarch seems to be focusing on less global, more interpersonal level of interactivity with humanity) and if you can look past a lot of jagged edges, I can in turn recommend it.

Having nearly reached the end of dungeon 2: This is... okay. Graphics are decent for an indie, but overall the game feels awkward and simplistic.

Bug: If the map is up, you can't change items in the inventory.

Thoughts:
1: Escape should be a general exit from all menus/screens.

2: There should be sound/music volume controls.

3: I second the reviewer that noted the FOV was awkward. It does feel like moving in half steps, and if you watch the map, you [i]are[/i]. This isn't something that necessarily needs to be changed, but it is a departure from the genre norm.

4: Combat is rather simplistic in this iteration and could use a re-think. Perhaps a rock, paper, scissors arrangement of strengths/vulnerabilities for dealing damage and a similar set of dodge/damage reduction actions for the player? Random, untelegraphed behavior should generally be avoided as it means the player cannot learn/manage.

5: Some form of ranged attack/defense would also be welcome. It is a little odd to have a gun that only works at point blank range as well as creatures that have ranged attacks but won't use them until you have been to point-blank range.

6: Walk pace should be modestly faster.

7: Would be nice to either allow the fountains to overfill the flask, or re-filling the flask only drains the fountains of the replenished charges instead of completely consuming the fountain.

8: Do the mushrooms provide any benefit in the game? (the first one killed me, so I never tried another) If not, ditch them after the first. If so, some kind of explanation should be available, preferably in-game.

9: Eye interactions should both be repeatable and the player immobility instantly terminated with any key press.

10: Have some kind of indicator on the map for visited but unpressed switches.

11: Unvisited sections of the map revealed by the map item should look different than visited sections.

12: The player should get the gun after no more than a couple packs of bullets. I was getting concerned and thought I missed something when I had all these bullets (almost max capacity) and no gun to shoot them with.

13: Player should be able to skip the intro. Escape key is the recommended way.

14: Should be able to scroll around the map. This also means a re-center command for the map should also be available (though that might be as simple as closing then reopening the map).

My original review was harsh, and based more on frustration on controls rather than the overall design.
After playing the game a bit more, the UI still feels clunky, the non standard controls are disorienting, keybinding does help, but still feels awkward. The game itself is actually well designed: nice graphics, there's depth to the combat mechanics, world building overall feels original. Movement is a bit awkward, because of the FOV the dev chose, which makes it feel as if you are moving in half steps rather than full steps (like it looks as if you reached the end of the hall, but you are 1 step away); you get used to it, but doesn't feel as natural (this is probably because other dungeon crawlers use a wider FOV, it's not necessarily a problem, just not standard). A UI redesign is really all this game needs.
When I did the original review I did not see an "early access" label, and mistakenly thought the game was finished and out for some time, which led me to believe the game was older than it really is. Given my observations posted in this edit, the game does deserve a chance, since its really only the UI what concerns me. I will leave the post as it is for reference, my answer to the DEV still stands, however I will actually recommend it considering the overall design is good and the fact that the game is actually new.

The first thing you must know is that you do not "Shoot" in this game. All your weapons fire automatically. A lot of your targeting reticles stay at fixed distances, and most weapons operate based on a timed cooldown or require you to interact with indicators that appear randomly on the screen. All you focus on is your mobility and your dodging.

The game is fun at the beginning as you work on unlocking more pilots and more abilities known as "Augments", but as you finish those and move onto the late-game, the problems begin to show. Even by roguelike standards, the amount of luck required for you to survive in the late-game (Especially on Endless Mode) borders on ridiculous. Weapons and passive (Known as "Utilities") are either very good, or not good at all. Often times you will find yourself in situations where you could level up two or three times and not roll / reroll any helpful weapon or utility that compliments what you have to the point where it will literally end your run since synergies between abilities are very poor and experimenting often hurts you more than it helps.

Additionally, for a game that places so much emphasis on mobility, it such does like to punish the players for being mobile. More often than not, the screen is so covered in special effects that you'd be hard pressed to see where enemy shots and asteroids are. Trying to move across the stage to get a health pick-up often ends with you losing more health than actually gaining it because your enemies are many, and they can fire constantly with zero cooldowns.

Overall, Gunlocked is a decently fun game that starts strong, but ultimately falls flat due to gameplay mechanics that continually ramps up the difficulty but does nothing to empower the player in the late game

The soundtrack is super cool as well. I find myself just drifting off listening to the music collecting ice. After all, what's the rush? Well, you do eventually run out of Blimp power, but not if you've made a Salt Water (NaCl) Battery! 

The game doesn't really push you in any way. It's entirely up to you how you play this game. Are you a Capitalist, Smuggler, or Pirate? The real challenge this puzzle adventure game presents is how the heck do you "win" this game by escaping its world!?

Relaxing and beautiful. This game is exactly what it says it is, and if that sounds good to you then you should buy it. It's a simple game with a lot of care given to each of its parts. It's a visuals-focused experience which really does succeed in transporting you to serene, expressive locations that are a joy to explore and photograph.

The basic structure consists of visiting an islands, taking pictures, and then returning to your boat and choosing the coordinates for a new island. I really enjoyed the idea of using longitude and latitude coordinates for island seeds, and the nautical interface for it is a great touch. You can also save ("remember") islands, which you can then easily re-enter from the main menu.

By default, only the last photo you take on each island before leaving is saved, which forces you to be thoughtful and deliberate. However, there is an option to save as many pictures as you want, and I preferred this because often I would get that awesome picture but want to keep exploring and taking more pictures before leaving the island.

Speaking of options, there are quite a few, including a sprint button which is disabled by default but can be turned on if you find yourself getting impatient. I left it off because the default speed seems perfect for taking in the surroundings and noticing good pictures. But I think its great that the option is there.

The camera has a number of options and settings which allow you to accomplish a variety different looks and get creative with your photography. I think the aperture/ focus/ focus-lock system is implemented very smartly, and the filters actually look good (which is unusual for photo modes, lets be honest here). My only complaint wrt camera mode is that the buttons to skew the camera are mapped to J and L, and these are the only keys in the game which aren't re-mappable. I expect that this will be remedied in a future update tho, and it doesn't distract much from the enjoyability of lining shots up.

The exploration and atmosphere are really the star of the show, especially because of the excellent color palletes and shader work. There are a lot of really great atmospheric details which vary by island, from the phases of the moon to rivers which flow to the ocean, to variety of visually-striking weather effects. The islands really are the star of the show here, and are a joy to photograph. I've played several other open-ended first person photography games, and Shutter Stroll is by far the most visually striking and contemplative. You really just want to sit in these places, feel them on your skin, and take in the serenity.

Of course, as is always the case with procgen levels, there inevitably comes a point where its ability to show you new stuff slows down, and it becomes a little less exciting to explore. This is normal for a game like this, but there is always that feeling of "I wish there was more stuff". I will say that there are a fairly large amount of rare scenery to discover, some of which is really creative and beautiful; I thought I saw them all, but looking at screenshots I see several I never encountered. Still, I would have liked to see more varied foliage models and grass (since these are the most common type of scenery), and perhaps more occasions where the level generator went outside its typical patterns. Still, i think the game delivers on what it promises to wrt the amount of content, and Im still finding something to love about each island several hours in.

Regardless, Shutter Stroll is definitely worth your time and the very reasonable price of admission. Yes, its a relaxing time, but it's contemplative and affective too like the feeling of sitting by the ocean and just listening. There really is more to find than you might assume.

I'll probably fill this review out a bit more once I've spent a bit more time with the Steam version (because it looks like there's quite a bit to seek out and find), but I've played the Itch.io version for an hour and a bit.

I have a couple of touchstones for why it is that Shutter Stroll appeals to me. The first is actual nature photography; exploring a space, enjoying the sights and finding a way of re-framing them with a camera with the aim of capturing what being there feels like. Finding something that looks majestic, or solemn, or nostalgic, and trying to encapsulate that majesty, or solemnity or nostalgia in two dimensions. Shutter Stroll does this well; at every new island you'll find yourself looking for the perfect vantage point to frame the moon against the ocean, or find the right spot to capture the hills rolling off into the foggy distance.

The second touchstone is No Man's Sky 1.0, as it released in 2016. While I've enjoyed the game since then, it has never felt the same as it did when the bulk of what you were doing was being a tourist in a procedurally generated universe; even before it had a dedicated photo mode, I was using the PS4's built-in capture tools to document my travels. While it's obviously much smaller in scope, Shutter Stroll still recaptures a lot of those feelings for me; the wonder of discovering something unique, something that feels anomalous, and the transient nature of the islands. Explore, catalogue, move on.

If you're already familiar with Hiragana and Katakana and feel like you still mess up sometimes and want something to practice with. This is a good way to do it. I was feeling rusty on katakana so I grabbed this to do some drills and then went ahead and cleared out the hiragana sets as well. The one annoying thing was that everytime you beat a lesson/test it sends you back to the menu to select between school/home/whatever books you've bought instead of just bringing you back to the page you had been before.

I do like that you can navigate without having to use your mouse for the most part though, makes it pretty quick to get back in. That said, there were definitely surprises when I went to check out what else was in the game. I bought the "Farm" book not knowing what it was then was surprised to be tossed into a challenge mode that included Kanji, it took a little bit to realize that I had to open the book while in the challenge to play "match the kanji" to what was being shown to me. Neat, but unexpected. I found myself thinking "I wish there was a study mode" a few times, but I think that's what no-pressure mode is.

Scrapshoot is a unique mix of tower defense and real time tactics that allows you create unique and dynamic rounds and has great replayability. The unique mix of tower defense and real time tactics makes for some fast-paced and dynamic games where you're going to be scrambling to counter your enemy and events in the arena that changes how you play the game and tip the scales to one side or another. You can also modify your round to enable/disable certain game rules to create new ways to play the game and adds a layer of unpredictability. Its worth your time with it being easy to pick up for new players and incredibly fun with friends or by yourself.

So far I've played a fair number of matches, and can tell enough that it justifies its price and then some.

The core premise is easy to pick up, and I was able to understand what was happening less than a minute into the first match. You pick up scraps, and bring them to your side of the field to activate robots that travel across a lane. The bots then have to fight their way through the other team's bots and reach the other end of the lane to damage your opponent.

At a glance, it may seem pretty straightforward. Pick up scrap resources and items, then lay out which lanes to focus on. But the game quickly moves into unpredictability, which forces the player to stay engaged while making it difficult to completely control the battle. There may be a lot of scrambling just to keep up. Having only played against the AI, it's hard to judge how much *more* chaotic a multiplayer match would be, but it's a compelling experience. Strategies exist for how & when to collect/use your resources, and with enough experience you can plan out how to properly adjust to what the situation requires. You can't really hoard them, and it works out for the better because you always have to contribute to the next phase of battle.
Map-wide effects appear at random, and contribute really well to the game flow. My personal favorite is the lightning effect, where your bots on standby may suddenly be activated without having to spend any resources. It fundamentally changes the pace of the battle, and properly capitalizing on it can turn a match around.
Music is snappy, fun, and blends together with the visual presentation without coming off as "on the nose" or generic. It's been a few years since Persona 5 invented the genre of "jazz", and Scrapshoot's OST mixes it with several other styles that give each map a distinct flavor. You might not expect some of the songs, considering the art style, but it does fit cleanly into whatever vibes the matches end up having.
Similarly, the art of the game is retro and fun, with a good choice of color palettes and fun details in the background maps. Individual objects are easy to pick out from the crowd, and small touches boost the user experience without getting in the way. And as far as user experience goes, sound effects and subtle feedback tricks give an excellent feel to your actions.

I will leave a few potential improvements for the dev team to consider, for improving on an already great experience:
1. The only issue I have with the main menu is that it can be hard to tell which button is currently highlighted, since the outline blends into the background a bit. Similarly, the hat menu seems to have an issue where my input doesn't change the hat sometimes.
2. If possible for a smaller dev team, having multiple AI difficulties would be great. The existing AI is incredibly challenging, which is great for a trial-by-fire learning experience but also pretty tough. My victories really came within a hair's width.
3. Continuing on the AI, I did have one instance where the enemy AI seemed to stop for a while. Not sure what caused it, but I think it was a bug, and unfortunately not the Pyre kind. Hasn't reappeared in any matches since then.
4. Accessibility-wise, it already seems pretty well-designed for colorblindness. I'm not colorblind myself, but I have a tool that simulates the visuals to show whether an image works well with it. It's a good way to test visuals before recommending to friends who are colorblind. I'm happy to report that it looks great under most settings, except monochromatic colorblindness seems a bit tough to differentiate for some things. I couldn't say what the best solution is, but maybe some sort of option to add outlines for the robots, with a different grayscale tone for each team? idk really, but I do really like the accommodations that are already built into the art.
All in all, definitely recommend.

December 28, 2024 and I just completed Battle for Esturia which I purchased back in June of 2021.  I have a habit of beefing up my game collection during Steam sales and a large number of them either get tossed to the side after purchase because I have others I also want to look at or I completely forget about them. In this games case, it was a combination of the two.

Well, over three years later and I am on a retro-looking RPG kick and deciding to give this game another look.  Honestly the old style graphics don't bother me at all and hold a certain charm as they take me back to my C64 days.  Back then game play ruled because you could only do so much with the limited graphics.  For some reason I was thinking this was a rogue-like game - random maps, no saving, death is permanent, etc. I think it's because the developers other game The Sargosian Abyss IS a rogue-like game.   

The Battle for Esturia, however is a full fledged story based game on a static world. Perfect. A beginning, a middle and an ending which I have to admit sucked me into several prolonged gaming sessions to get through it.  While visually it looks simple and the game play seems to be simple as well, after leveling up a few times and selecting various skills I started to notice there was a bit more depth to this game than initially meets the eye.

The battles were a nice challenge and positioning your characters - you get 6 that you pick up along the way - becomes a bit of a chess game. For example, having your archers pick up piercing skills as they level up makes you try to get those characters to face monsters that were lined up so you could maximize their damage by having their arrows punch through the first enemy, then the one behind that, and the one behind that, etc.  It's rather satisfying seeing the arrows pass through 4 monsters!  

The game is also VERY forgiving despite you not being able to save. There is no scrolling world. Each screen is a section of the map. when you move off the edge of the screen, you are at the beginning of the next one.  From what I could tell, the game auto saves every time you leave a screen. So if a battle was too tough and your party died, you could select continue and you would be at the screen just prior to the one with the encounter that killed you. I REALLY liked this. I could either try a different tactic or leave and beef up some potions before heading back to try the encounter again. 

Story-wise there is nothing earth shattering or new. Pretty standard stuff - find an object someone lost, find a missing person, etc. The ultimate goal is to reclaim the throne that is rightfully yours from a lich king.   The maps and graphics are diverse enough to keep things from becoming redundant and stale.

Overall, I found this a be a solid and enjoyable gaming experience and well worth the time. I was actually sad when I finished it.  It was well worth the $10 price tag, even cheaper if you get it during a sale. I've paid a lot more for games that sucked, so I find this one easy to recommend if you are looking for an enjoyable 10-ish hours of gaming.

Overall, The Past Within is a game that exceeded my expectations in every way. It’s an eerie, thought-provoking journey that challenges you and your partner to think critically, communicate effectively, and explore the mysterious world it presents.

Let me preface this for anyone who doesn't own the game a "Token" is an inventory item you collect that can be used to upgrade units and their abilities, e.g "give +20 attack to this ability" "this unit can attack twice"



I wish i could give this a "Meh" but I did enjoy it more than I didn't.

It is a rather refreshing change from previous circle empire games but it still feels a bit janky, probably could have done with a little more testing. I do really enjoy what they are trying to do but it feels like some of the core mechanics are really limiting, i love the idea of having tokens to upgrade your units and customise them, however only 2 per ability and 3 per unit feels a bit frustrating and clamps down a little too much on the players freedom. 

Unit availability is a little bit of an issue as well, you sort of need to get lucky to be able to increase your army as they are part of random rewards for beating a circle or as part of the 3 choices you get when you level up. I do rather wish the token shop would let you buy units so you aren't stuck with whatever you are given (though i wouldn't mind this so much if it let you really stack tokens on a single troop, because then you could just deal with the hand you were dealt rather than be basically hampered by your luck that you didn't get many good troops given to you so you get screwed out of an entire play-through)

Another small gripe is how your troops melee attack, it very much lends itself to being unfriendly to large armies vs 1 strong dude which is a little silly seeing as the last boss is usually that!! By this i mean that you have to manually target each troop to melee attack a target, however if the boss decides to attack one of your troops it moves to that space and makes every unit surrounding the boss just not attack because it moved one space away, this leads to ridiculously long battles because your horde of goblins,spearmen etc cant hit a boss with thousands of health because it shuffled a measly 1 space!!!!

another small issue is at the start of a battle your troops are just placed in a blob round your commander which leads to some little annoying situations where your catapults and ranged units are on the front line, i would be very happy if we got a deplyment phase or something like that....

Overall though, i really like the concept. i just wish there were a few QoL changes like the above mentioned... mainly orientated around not hampering the players play-style when that is what i believe the shift from army composition to token management falls a little flat for me as you want to be able to really tune your units up for a fight but can't really do it in a meaningful way with the limited slots available. 

If you're thinking of buying the game because you like circle empires i would seriously look up some proper gameplay first though, it is very different from their previous titles. But still a fun time if you can get past some of the issues.

So keeping moving is extremely important. But. You need to keep in mind exactly what you are doing. And can't go too fast. Because stopping once at full speed will take around 2 full seconds. All reset you on contact to the last checkpoint. The lasers. Which is to be expected. The enemy marble/balls. Don't kill you on contact. I've never been a fan of the one hit kill style of difficultly and there is a lot of it in this game. But there are checkpoints.

I wish the movement was different. I don't mean marble skies or insanely different. Or even a jump. I get this is not, that type of game. And isn't trying to be. But less frustrating. This game really has a lot problems; some of which are probably unsolvable due to the game design. 

First, some pros: 
1. The command line design is actually the simplest I have ever seen; this makes controlling a lot easier. 
2. The game runs smoothly and has a clean interface. 

Now the cons: 
Let's start with something that can be fixed: 
1. [strike] Graphics error: I see a "discord" button on the airport selection page. [/strike] (Fixed)
2. [strike] Gameplay Bugs: I have experienced problems like collision, even with vertical separation. I have also experienced bugs that planes fail to intercept the localizer even I have guided the plane to the orange line. [/strike] (Fixed)
3. Lack of cues of aircraft entering your airspace: This makes it really hard to spot an incoming traffic if you are working on consecutive vectors. 
Some cons that may come from the game design: 
4. [strike] Insanely FAST traffic flow. The problem is fast, not just a huge amount of traffic. More specifically, traffics in this game flows a lot faster than what you would expect in real life. However, the traffic flow is still huge. I have tried 5-10 minutes sessions, and I really thought I was in a typing contest even with a very nicely designed command line! This speed and volume of traffic make it really hard to sequence and vector your planes. [/strike] (Speed changed) 
5. Lack of realism. About this, I am going to write a few paragraphs below. 

I can see the game tries to simplify the controlling process by having outbound traffic fly to a waypoint and inbound traffic on a heading waiting to be vectored to the final approach course. However, the outbound exit waypoint seems to be random (for example, for JFK, the exit waypoints are not the famous JFK exit gates but random waypoints on your scope), and inbound traffic comes in at 3500 feet. Using SID and STAR in real life usually helps build a departing and an arrival traffic flow pattern, which are related to airspace, terrain, noise abatement, and in-outbound traffic separations; without the procedures, the player has to build a pattern on one's own. However, it is not easy to build a complex pattern because the traffic flows FAST, so you cannot really send many commands to enforce a pattern. 
For a 5 dollar game, you prolly should not expect a high realism; however, I still want to talk about things that can enhance player experience. The game does include a number of airports. However, the airports are not really "designed"; I really feel the individual airports are not unique enough. Let me elaborate on this. For example, JFK (again) has VOR/Parkway visual approaches for Runway 13s; HND has very special runway operations. These specialties should be included as a part of the game because they are intriguing! I mean, we are all trying to find some realism in these simulation games, right?
So far its great! I wish you could choose difficulty (traffic wise) and maybe control tower in the future! For 5 bucks you cant go wrong.
It's just way too hard controlling the arrivals, I wish the controls would be improved.

This game is like if Breakout, Bejeweled, and Tetris multiplayer had an orgy and made the ultimate casual game. Each element is familiar but put together really well in a way that makes it fresh and exciting. The gameplay is top notch and super addicting. Games can get really close, and there are often nail-biting moments where you think you’re screwed but barely come out on top. In addition the game is super satisfying to play, which I chalk up to the excellent sound design. Breaking gems and hitting combos never fails to scratch an itch. The music is also really catchy and gets stuck in your head quite easily.

The default ruleset makes it so that gem patterns spawn asymmetrically. This can make games feel unfair sometimes as some patterns are better than others. I think a little unfairness makes for more interesting games but it’s really annoying when the AI gets a giant combo and you have no chance to cancel it out. Another unfair thing is the dice roll between rounds where you get a chance to win a power up. This is less of a problem as only one power up is a straight upgrade, but the rest are more nuanced which is nice as it adds depth. For example, Fast Ball lets you break gems faster but makes it harder to hit the ball, and Wave Ball/Curve Ball change your trajectory but don’t necessarily make it easier to hit what you want. Thankfully you can remove all unfairness in “Extras” if you dislike it. One other gripe with the gameplay I had is that it’s hard to predict when gems spawn in so getting a Perfect Clear, which gives you a huge advantage, seems to happen pretty randomly. Additionally I found some slowdown when you get Power Ball or Perfect Clear but it wasn’t a huge issue overall.


The plot isn't great and seems like a series of arbitrary events to make the 4 characters fight each other, but the dialogue is fun to read and I enjoyed the surreal character designs. Treasure Mode is where you’ll be spending most of your time and it’s a gauntlet type mode where you face ever tougher opponents. It’s pretty fun but the difficulty spikes massively between opponents so it’s hard to get past 4 or 5, and that’s with power ups. You get unlocks in this mode in the form of trophies and temporary power ups for the next round. I wish you'd unlock more characters (which are in the game but unplayable) or different color paddles or something to add to the feeling of progression but since it's made by two devs I'll cut some slack. I also wish you could play 2P mode against AI and customize their difficulty level. It seems like a huge oversight to not have this option as it wouldn’t be hard to add and I don’t always want to play story missions/gauntlet.

Overall this game is really great. The meat of these types of games is the gameplay and on that end it is fantastic. If you’re a casual game fan I’d recommend this game as you can’t get much better than this.

The simplest way to explain Sparkles & Gems is to take the games Breakout, Columns, and Puyo Pop - and then throw them all together into a cotton candy machine. An enchantingly weird offering from resnijars, the core gameplay loop involves hitting cascading gems with a ball and paddle, aiming to hit as many gems that have three or more of the same type grouped together to destroy them. Gems with sparkles cause multiple gems to explode. You play against an opponent trying to make your paddle hit against a gem or block to win, and just like in Puyo Pop, you can get multipliers on your score to cause the blocks on your opponent side to multiply. The gems respawn as though by magic and will take a quick wit to handle them all! There's a Story Mode in which you get to know the characters of the game, from OAT the ferret plushie to Sandway the business horse, and presents a fun tale similar to a fighting game storyline. Treasure Mode is a game mode where you play rounds of Sparkles & Gems against the PC to rack up stocks, battery power, and jam to help improve your future runs, and to gain treasure in the form of special items you can use to decorate your room in Treasure Mode. Naturally there's a two player mode as well. This game is CUTE, and really really fun! Try it out!

[b]cooking[/b] is very similar to [b]doodle god[/b], but with actual sense, not just combining random stuff to create more random stuff. at least that's what I thought at first, then blamed myself for being a big-time eater with zero idea about cooking, then realized that part of my being dumbfounded is because [b]everything consists of 2 or 3 ingredients[/b], which may sound easy, but it really isn't.

even I know preparing meals is more complicated than that, but I'm always happy to suspend my disbelief (especially when it comes to food, best not find out how the sausage is made), and of course certain ingredients still have to be created, then combined to make something else, so there are [b]recipes with multiple steps[/b]. and what sets this game aside from others is the [b]discovered recipes get replaced with real ones, so there's a culinary educational aspect[/b].

you'll go through [b]8 restaurants[/b] from all over the world with [b]about 10 local dishes each[/b]. double-click ingredients or drag them to the chopping boards, right click removes the last one, middle mouse clears all the slots. if you discover something, you usually get a pun, often served on a blinding background.

Listen. This game has some serious fundamental flaws.

There's a window where your attacks will just outright NOT come out if you press the attack button just after you stop moving forward. This happens a bunch as you use movement to position yourself (hopefully).

Jumping adjacent to walls will shorten your jump height. You always get the same height jump no matter whether you tap or hold the jump button. But if done next to a wall you'll only go up halfway and if you're holding into the wall you'll remain hovering there and not come back down until moving away. This is a valid issue as there's one tile wide vertical paths you need to jump through and spikes come out one side of the wall. But then your jump gets halved because you were too close to the wall and you've moved into spikes as a result.

Even though it's a square tile based environment you'll find the reality is the corners of the tiles are curved which results in your character unintentionally slipping off edges. It looks goofy, it feels terrible.

Bosses are trivial. Even though you're max HP is 3 you can pretty much just walk up to 5 of the 7 bosses and just mash until they're dead, because you've got incredibly generous i-frames on hit and bosses have so few they'll be hit by your follow-up even if you're mashing. It's a shame because doing Shadow Knight 'the right way' was incredibly satisfying, jumping over and scoring strikes while avoiding the slow moving projectiles raining down. Until I discovered (I ran the game a few times) that you can literally stand right in front of his feet and beat him without being hit as only the tip of his sword has a hitbox.
One boss drops a shield, which then gives you an extra hit to tank your way through bosses mindlessly.

Lingering hitboxes on retractable spikes. You've experienced it before. The spikes look like they're gone, but you still get hit. Combined with one particular room where these spikes are paired up, but their timing aren't synchronised, so you might get a nice time when both spikes retract at the same time or you could get a horrible time where they're the exact opposite, you see one pair retract and try to make it across but oh, you either moved too soon and got hit by spikes that aren't visible anymore or you got hit by spikes that aren't visible yet on the second pair coming out.

Auto saves: Sometimes the game autos saves when you pick up a gem, other times is won't do this until you've exited the current room. Even then you'll have to sit and wait for the save icon to take roughly 4 seconds to do it's thing to be CERTAIN it's actually saved before quitting out.

No alternate saves and easy to accidentally wipe your own progress: Typically a main menu would prioritise Continue over New Game but PF08's main menu doesn't have a cursor, you just press the corresponding button prompts. New Game is Start, X, Start. Quitting out to the Main Menu is Start, Back, X. Put it this way, I don't believe I've ever wiped my progress in a game until I played PF08.

Personal quibbles:
The map: Some rooms will be represented as 3 way junctions, but only 2 of the exists connect and the third is a dead end (with a gem of course) entered from a long detour. I hate this, it makes the map look more interconnnected than it actually is.

Interacting with boxes is too precise. Most are triggered by headbutting from underneath by jumping, but you'll need to be centralised, hitting the edges won't work. Why?

Identical enemies with wildly differing HP: The same enemies will have the same HP without the same room, but anywhere else it might change drastically. I believe the bigger example is the white parsnips. On one screen (0901) there's 3 of them with 5 HP each, then in other instance they'll have 1 or 2HP. When you play the game alot you'll get to know, but this threw me a lot during the casual playthrough.

Re-entering a room = Have to kill all enemies again: There's room with multiples exits, some will lead to cul de sacs, probably with a gem, then you'll immediately return and have to clear out the junction room again. The aforementioned room with the triple parsnips at 5HP each is an agonizing pace killer. I'm not asking for them to be empty, but could the exits stay open, we've already earned it.

Is it a Metroidvania? Not particularly. There's no room in the game you can't reach with the the starting abilities. Every enemy can be handled with the face-tank method. There's only 2 pickups than give extra movement abilities (double jump and hover) and in combination these allow you to reach 5/6 gems you couldn't get to other wise.

Despite all this I really like the game's aesthetic, the enemies fit well and there's a multitude of tiny objects that give it a detailed feel and foreground objects help with the atmosphere.

The rooms, individually, were very good though provoking combat scenarios. The occasional use of numbered box puzzles even had me racking my head for memories of what I've already seen elsewhere or what clue I could be missing in the current room.
I've played a few games where ultimately I had a lot of reservations about what I played, but I ended up looking forward to a better sequel. The Surge and Innocence: A Plague Tale are good examples. Pathfinder-08 is another. The potential is here.

With its deceptively pleasing music and graphics, Re:LieF draws you into its hypothetical "what if" scenario to unravel the mystery of the Tryment program on the island of Mikumojima. Whisked away from their daily lives to attend an experimental facility that aims to give people a second chance at entering society (for one reason or another), our cast of cute girls provide a lens to an overarching story.

If suspension of disbelief to accept a story's attempts to talk about contemporary technology with little explanation isn't your cup of tea then viewer discretion is advised. However, if you're okay with the depth remaining at a surface level, this moderately short sci-lite story may be worth your time.

Character art by kuronomitsuki is top notch, easily one of the main attractions on offer here. The girls are all cute, cool and detailed, with background art being allowed to speak for itself. To add onto this, music and soundtrack provide enough variety and memorable tracks to not want to mute while playing. Voice lines are voiced and delivery was consistent throughout the whole story.

Overall, I did not expect anything deep or groundbreaking, but Re:LieF was a short, cute adventure that more or less tidied up its loose ends with some creative liberties.

Nevermore is your usual hack and slash that does everything just right. Everything from the movement to the combat! More specifically, the usage of the hook allows you to throw projectiles back, pull enemies, and fly towards them. The game also offers booster packs and a level up system for stats that will boost your damage, health, or magic damage. The booster packs once equipped will grant you unique attacks associated with the mob from the card but once you have unlocked all of them, the game will be significantly easier (I suggest playing the game without booster packs after if you want a challenge). 

A couple of things that would be interesting to see would be some implementation of a passive or ability that allows you to pick up loot without having to walk over it (I found myself ignoring a lot of loot due to having to walk over each individual orb and bone), some cosmetic items or changes depending on the booster card active, and maybe even implementation of different classes with different abilities to add variation. Overall, the game is extremely enjoyable and I will most definitely find myself playing a lot more once they add more content. I highly recommend purchasing this game but suggest possibly holding out until more content is released.

I have a bit to spit at this game. I know its Early Access, but that is exactly my first problem. I don't think games should have "Early Access" stages. I think its ridiculous and a game should be released when its desired state is met, not before. Sure you want beta testers, but not people that are wanting to play the actual game to play it, when its not even finished. But anyway, I am just saying that I am critiquing a game that is not done, or not in its "playable state" in my opinion. 

First, I will start out with what I like about this game. The concept is what I love the most, and is what drew me into it. The idea of the game I think is marvelous. I am a big fan of the idea of a Roguelike based off of Edgar Allan Poe, especially the Nevermore poem which I find fascinating. Another thing I will add to what I like is the combat system. The mechanics of your fighting abilities feels great, and there are a wide array of moves. The game is easy to run, I wasn't really able to find any bugs either, and the game has a reasonable price (for when it's in its finished state). But that's about as far as my props go. 

Now for the critiques. There was quite a bit running through my head as I was playing. I know I only played an hour but there doesn't seem to be much content to play. Again, early access issues. But there is another thing related to my play time. It was way too easy. It was like the whole game was a tutorial mode. Maybe I am just used to extreme games, but some harder difficulty options would probably be appreciated. Especially because Roguelikes are usually notorious for difficulty, and Roguelike players will be expecting that. I don't normally write reviews. That said, the developer claims to want as much feedback as possible- so here I am. 

If the "recommendation" system were more flexible, I'd be sitting smack dab in the middle. 
I think this game has a good core concept, and I'm ignoring the lack of content because it's in early access. That said, I can't recommend this game as an avid roguelike fan, simply because it seems to flat-out ignore much of what attracts people to the roguelike genre. 

I need to make it clear how much I enjoy the roguelike genre (roguelites included). I've played every "big name" roguelike there is (possible exception in Inscryption), and I am always, ALWAYS looking for more. 

The good parts of this game are easier to explain than the bad. 

The good: 

-Combat is fun (fast but NOT fluid) 
-Environmental interactios seems interesting (needs expansion but this is an Early Access)
-Pixel art is pretty nice
-Runs on a toaster
-Costs barely anything (especially considering that it's on sale right now)
-From the store page, dev seems legitimately passionate. 

The Cons: 

This doesn't really feel like a roguelike, or a roguelite. Let me explain: Roguelikes are all about going in weak, and powering up throughout the run, trying to beat the scaling curve- whether it's through items, skill upgrades, etc. That is NOT the case here. The character you go in with is the character that you come out with. All of your power-ups are done in the hub world, before beginning a run. 

THIS IS NOT THE PROBLEM. I consider Hades to be the most well-designed roguelite of all time. It also features a similar hub world power-up system. There are two main differences: 

-Zagreus still starts off "weak" and powers up over the course of a run. You're forced to adapt to the boons you get, and as a result, every run is different. 

-The powerups you receive in Hades are, usually, "add-on" powers. They do not intrinsically change what Zagreus is capable of. In Nevermore, you receive different movesets, and very often, straight up stat buffs- which are huge. 

The player-controlled character also scales exponentially. After struggling to clear 2 rooms, I unlocked the magic bomb(?) skill (I think that's what it was called), and then had no issue beating the boss. The whole charm of roguelikes is that gradual feeling of progression. Learning the ropes bit by bit, and more importantly, that feeling of getting just a little bit further each time you queue up a run. The majority of that is not present here. 

Every other issue that I have with the game can be written off as Early Access jankiness. 

I DO NOT THINK THIS IS A BAD GAME. 
I think it has a lot of potential. I hope the dev is as open to feedback as he claims to be.

I picked this up a while ago to play with a friend using Steam's Remote Play Together feature. We found the concept of the game to be amusing and appreciated it's visual style. After we got started, we were treated to a narrator doing a half-decent Morgan Freeman and a drill sergeant doing his best R. Lee Ermey.

The way that [b]Kamikaze Veggies[/b] plays is as follows: you'll first pick a mission, and then you're given the opportunity to purchase a number of uses of each of the characters you have unlocked. More powerful characters cost more of your mission budget. For instance, at the beginning of the game you only have access to the carrot character. For one of the first missions, you have enough mission budget to perhaps purchase three uses of the carrot character. You'll deploy with your first carrot and do as many of the mission objectives as you can before it is killed. Upon death, you'll spawn in as the second carrot you purchased. If you haven't completed the mission by the time your third carrot perishes, you'll fail. The second character I recall unlocking was the pea character. You can then alternate with your selections if you wish. For instance, first spawning in as a carrot, then a pea, then a carrot again.

There are a few complicating factors here. First of all, you'll sometimes need to activate an ability that kills your character (usually creating an explosion) to progress in a level. This cuts down on how much leeway you have with your character lives in each level. However, in my experience, no matter what character you pick you're going to be relatively ineffective at dealing with the game's enemies. This means that you'll need to rely on stealth, and this system is not very good. Enemies seem to either be aware of you or not, without much in between. In addition, the physical layout of the levels makes it challenging to see if there is an enemy around the corner. You can find grenades from time to time to help you deal with enemies, but I didn't find these regularly enough to mitigate the aforementioned frustrations.

For myself and my co-op partner, the game involved a lot of running away from enemies to reset their awareness and exclaiming, "I wish I would've known that we would need to blow this up. I would've picked our characters (or the order of our characters) differently." The biggest thing that would improve the game, in my opinion, is perhaps giving the players a drone that they can use to scout out the map before picking their characters or spawning in. What enemies are present, and in what layout? Where are the objectives, and will they require my vegetables to sacrifice themselves in order to complete them?

Although I applaud developer Red Limb Studio for bringing something fresh into the gaming space, we only did a handful of missions before deciding to move on to something else.

I do appreciate that this is a straight homage to Duck Hunt. The mouse controls are as smooth as you'd expect from an FPS or aim trainer. Options are barebones; I wish there were an option to make the targeting reticule contrast better against the bright sky. (The sky looks a fair bit brighter than it does in the store pictures.) The way the ducks flop out of the sky but retain some/much of their prior momentum, makes for a great visual style. If you press E to skip ahead quickly, and aim well enough to shoot 2-3 ducks in one shot, it gives the impression of duck fireworks.

The game's biggest flaw is that the difficulty ramps up soo slooowly. For a halfway competent gamer, it takes forever for the game to get challenging. But some of the other reviewers are wrong: the ducks DO get faster, and it IS possible to get a game over. It just takes a LOOOONG time. And it's not clear to me exactly what the game over conditions are. It's a vibe; if you feel like aiming at ducks for an hour plus, this is a game for you. Unfortunately, I just don't think this is a good difficulty slope for this kind of game. It should get hard faster, or at least have an option to enable faster progress (with a different score tier, or something).

I've come across one other notable glitch. You reload your gun in between flights of ducks, which you can skip by pressing the E key (or use a controller mapped to E). Once, on round 45, when I was skipping pretty quickly between ducks, it skipped to the next flight of ducks before I had taken care of the previous one. It did a few flights in succession like this, so there were maybe as many as 8 ducks on the screen at one time, and I was running out of ammo while still missing the incredibly fast birds. I got a fly away, whereupon all the ducks left and it went to the next flight normally.

Plus two more non-notable glitches! When skipping fast into the end of a round, your dog can still be repeatedly jumping up in the background while another of your dog appears in the foreground to start the next round. And (maybe this is intentional, I don't know) sometimes your dog appears in mid-air to jump, making it a slight distraction next to the flying ducks.

A very common pattern for the ducks is for two or three to all fly toward the center of the screen and overlap in such a way that you can shoot them all in one shot. (In fact, they do it so often, one might be convinced at the beginning that this is the only pattern they fly in.) I'm sure this is a way to make it easier for the guns with less ammo, plus get through the ducks quicker. It feels cheap, even patronizing in the beginning, but in later, harder rounds, it is a lifeline. I'm not sure if shooting all at once gives a score bonus or anything, though it does play an overlapping sound so you can tell you shot multiple even if they're flying too fast to tell whether they're falling. I don't dislike this feature, exactly, but it could really be improved in conjunction with the difficulty to make it a more polished and widely-appealing game.

Ultimately, I don't exactly recommend the game, on account of the apparent memory leak and the tedious/unchangeable difficulty slope (not a difficulty curve, AFAIK). You may still enjoy it if you want to have a zen aiming experience for a long sitting. The price is right for that.

Allow me to preface this review by mentioning that I have done some studies of game development and game design and while I'm nowhere close to an expert on these subjects, my knowledge of them will be informing this review.

When checking the amount of hours I've spent in this game, you will notice that they're quite low, and there are a multitude of reasons for this, which I will try to point out in a coherent manner below.



====Voice acting====

While I haven't heard that many lines read by the voice actors in the game, the mixed quality of the voice acting has already been starting to show.

An example of less than optimal acting can be heard at the very beginning of the story when General Berwick talks to Ole.
When a mysterious portal suddenly appears in the room, Berwick asks casually (!) [i]"What's happening, Ole?"[/i], rather than asking the question in a confused or slightly frightened fashion, which would be more appropriate in this context.
It is likely that the developer didn't include how (in which emotion) he wants his lines read, leading to the emotions in the voice not matching the situation in the game.

This is just one example, and I have heard many other sub-optimal performances throughout my progression so far.

Another thing that's strange as well is that quite a few interactions in the game are partially voiced.
So a character might be heard saying his first three lines, but the rest of his speech will be exclusively in text.
To my knowledge, the common approach in this type of game is to have major story events be fully voiced, while general gameplay is purely text based, but I haven't seen this hybrid approach in other games, and I find it somewhat off-putting.

Some other voice acting, for example the one from opponents such as the zombies or the guards is pretty good though.



====Mechanics====

Overall, Rebellion Gaia is a normal turn-based RPG with a less than optimal implementation.

First, crew health and status effects are persistent, meaning that they do not reset after battle, and can only be reset by either finding a healer in a town and pay a fee OR returning to the very first area of the game, which has a spot where the crew can rest and heal without a fee.
The issue with this is that it incentivizes boring backtracking to the town/healing spot in order to heal the crew and not waste potions (which are quite expensive, especially when needing to heal multiple status effects at once).

Now you could argue that it is the player's fault to do the boring backtracking, but one of the important things to remember for a game designer is that:
[i]"Players can optimize the fun out of a game"[/i]
Therefore placing incentives correctly to avoid this behavior is important and very much within the responsibility of the designer.
Also, considering the high price of potions, I don't know whether it is even possible to play the game without using this strategy.

There would be multiple ways to fix these issues, such as adding resting places to every area to avoid the player having to leave it to heal, or removing the persistence of health and status effects entirely and healing the crew automatically after every battle.


Second, another area of concern is that the amount, strength, and health of enemies is apparently not randomized in many cases, leading to a scenario where when you encounter a group of ghouls for instance, they always appear in a group of 4, with the same abilities and same health.
In that case, as soon as you've worked out a strategy to defeat them, you will simply repeat that strategy every single time you encounter them as nothing has changed, making the battles tedious and boring.
Randomizing these values (within limits of course) would require the player to think about the strategy every time when entering a battle, even when it's against the same type of enemy.


Third, unskippable battle animations.
The animations in games like these are interesting for the first 5 minutes, after which the player would generally like to skip them to speed up the battle, especially when taking my second point above into consideration.
Making the player wait every single time the enemies are throwing their same attacks is unnecessarily tedious and will frustrate many players.


The combination of the above mechanics is really why I stopped playing the game.
I entered into an area with overpowered zombies, which can be defeated quite easily when at full health, but as your health is reduced significantly after only a few battles, it seems to be necessary to either return to a healing area constantly or bring a significant amount of expensive potions, some of which aren't even sold in the only town in the area.

At this point I really don't know what the game wants me to do.
Either I'm supposed to do what I'm doing now, which would be boring and tedious, or I'm not and the game failed to tell me how I'm supposed to walk through this area with random zombies regularly attacking me (more on lack of instruction below).



====Characters/Story====

I would argue that the story and characters are so far the weakest element of the game, which is quite a big deal considering that RPGs generally rely on their powerful storyline to keep the player hooked.

First up, I find that the characters in the game do not behave in a believable manner.
For instance, at the beginning of the game the protagonist is found after the airship he was in had crashed.
He claims that he cannot remember anything that had happened, only finding few clues at the crash site.
Yet a random stranger that found the protagonist is perfectly willing to invite him into his home accompany him on his adventures shortly after.

[i]"Random stranger in combat gear that crashed in a military airship and claims to have suffered significant trauma to his head, yeah come right into my home, what could possibly go wrong?"[/i]

Further members are added to the player's crew in a similar fashion.
Meet the person, exchange 5 sentences, you're part of my crew now.
No backstory (or minimal backstory), no emotional investment on either side, nothing.


This shallowness of the in-game characters also extends to another area that NPC's would often times be responsible for, which is instructing the player in how to play the game.
For example, when you're trying to kill some pig-dude, the name of which I've forgotten, to claim on a bounty, you require a rope in order to make it through to the part of a cave that he is located in.
Normally an NPC would inform the player about the requirement for the rope before his departure from the town to save him time, but in this instance no such instruction is given, leading the player to have to walk all the way back to the town just to buy said rope and go back to the cave afterwards if he didn't buy it as a precaution earlier.



====Bugs====

Finally, I've been able to locate a few bugs in the game.
One of which is particularly obvious and annoying, which is that when walking through an area, the screen will randomly flash red without any apparent reason.
If there is a reason for this, the player should be told and if not, this should be removed.

Such a bug really shouldn't exist in a release version, in fact it shouldn't even make it past the alpha stage.



====Addendum====

I hope this review has been helpful, as I tried to be specific about the areas that I take issue with, so that they could potentially be addressed.

After all this I want to add that I don't take issue with having spend the money I have spent on it, as a large part goes to support independent journalists and commentators, but if it wouldn't have been for that I would've requested a refund before the 2 hour mark as this game doesn't seem to me to be in a condition that it should've been released in.
It appears unfinished, bugged, and badly designed.

It should go without saying that this game is based. But being based does not necessarily make a game good. So, is this game any good then? I personally found it to be a very enjoyable experience but it is definitely an acquired taste. I have played many RPGs in my days and this one leans towards the more old-school mechanics of the genre. Healing items are expensive, so your best bet is to rest up at an inn which has the added bonus of removing your status effects. The early game is slow, and the enemies will give you a good pounding until you rack up a decent amount of experience and get better gear. I'd argue that the gear is more important since one of the unique things this game has going for it is the low value of levelling up. I beat the game and didn't even go past level 25. Keep in mind that I not only beat every dungeon and encounter in the game, but also spent a significant amount of time grinding. Grinding for gold that is.

The importance of your gear over your actual level is an interesting, if perhaps unintentional aspect of the game. Because items are expensive and you have to heal at inns, managing your gold becomes a game in and of itself. Every time you venture out to complete a dungeon or explore you have to carefully balance the amount of money you are expending in resources vs. the amount of money you are making from loot and mob drops. As I said, this makes the early part of the game a struggle and you will be carried by Dandix and his lightsaber. However, once you reach the city of Vanguard, the game finally opens up. More gear becomes available, a few side objectives are presented, and you get a boat not long after that. This gives you full access to the game's world except for a select few areas that remain locked until you progress far enough in the main quest line.

As for the dungeons and encounters themselves, they are nothing special. They are very much carried by the narrative. The game uses a lot of RPG Maker assets which goes to show just how limited the game's budget was, (probably nonexistent). However, the game built its narrative around this restriction so the clashing of the truther narrative doesn't conflict with the default fantasy elements presented. There is, surprisingly, an extensive amount of lore to cover all this in-game if you bother to read the books scattered around the game's world. 

The game is very much centred around topics covered by the truther community, so there are a lot of references and details that will go over the casual player's head. Many of these topics are presented in comedic and satirical ways. The writing itself very much leans into this aspect by contrasting the narrative's darker moments with its brighter ones. It feels like a normal, jolly adventure but the context really clashes which only adds to the humour. Honestly, if you aren't a fan of satire and know little to nothing about conspiracy theories, you may find your enjoyment in the game somewhat lacking since the plot is this game's carrying force.

For example, you can literally take down a Monsantocorp facility and infiltrate Epstein's island. There's also Jekyll Island which is a reference to the book "The Creature from Jekyll Island" by G. Edward Griffin, a book that's about shady deals that happened on that very island. On the other hand, most of the dungeons are pretty basic, featuring a limited assortment of enemy encounters themed around the location, a couple of puzzles, and a variety of loot, the best of which is guarded by a boss at the end. The variation in size can be a little much though. Some dungeons, like The Great Pacific Garbage Patch felt way too short while others like the irradiated ruins between Sweetwater and Vanguard feel almost too long given the status ailments you have to deal with. It's for this reason I'm glad the game allows surface encounters to be permanently eliminated once you beat them. It makes traversing previously trekked areas way easier when you only have to deal with extremely infrequent random encounters.

That being said, some of the levels like Mayflower, Dwarka, and Gobekli Tepe present introduce interesting elements that help spice up the experience, such as the constant presence of toxins, an underwater dungeon, and an increased focus on puzzles respectively. Many of the cities and towns also have an assortment of tasks to accomplish. Vanguard in particular has a lot of neat little story-driven missions you can participate in, as does Richford. These aren't without their problems though. Sometimes the puzzle elements are obtuse. The best example I can think of is having to move the basket of apples. It doesn't appear any different from any of the other props in the room and you have to literally drag it all the way across a super long hallway. The only hint you are given is that your bomb must be put in something to conceal it. The most egregious offender is the lever puzzle in the spike room of Gobekli Tepe. I had to look up a YouTube video to figure it out and even after watching it I still don't understand. While I appreciate the game's old-fashioned, hands-off approach, it's a bit much sometimes. 

This leads me to the game's biggest problem though, and that's its scope. The game feels too small for what it sets itself up to be and suffers for it. I feel like certain parts of the game were scrapped as development went on, leaving areas like Camp Kakuma, Haditha, Castle Rockefeller, and Castle Rothschild unfinished. I was hoping at some point that I would get the chance to explore, infiltrate, and take over Castle Rockefeller and Castle Rothschild, but I never got the chance. Instead, they are dealt with off-screen at the end of the game which left me extremely disappointed. 

Then we have Camp Kakuma and Haditha which are both settlements that have negligible impact on the experience. Had they not been there, the experience would have been no different. They fail to present you with interesting side-quests and have next to no interesting character encounters. They are extremely shallow when compared to the likes of Mayflower and Sweetwater. Those areas present lots of interesting encounters and even change depending on the actions you take in the game.

I also wish the whole rebellion part of the plot had been a slower burn. It felt far too quick and the [spoiler]literal city-destroying space laser that nukes Fawkes City[/spoiler] should have been held off until later in the plot. I would have loved to fight for the liberation of Richford, Vanguard, Sweetwater, etc, and taken the fight straight to Castle Rothschild and Castle Rockefeller, (maybe you can only choose to attack one of the two after liberating some of the smaller towns). Only after beating the lord of the castle does [spoiler]the giant space laser fire, annihilating one of the cities[/spoiler]. I would personally choose Vanguard, as it has a greater deal of emotional attachment to the player.

By rushing this major plot point, we lose a lot of precious time that could have been used to build tension and expand on the characters. We could have introduced Dandix's love interest far earlier in the narrative and given time to expand on their connection. It would have given the characters room to breathe in the narrative. They have very little agency and feel extremely one-dimensional. The only person who experiences any complex emotion is Dandix, which at least makes him a compelling main character, (Ole is my favourite though). Also, the love triangle was a bit too on the nose in my opinion.

While the characters are shallow and the game isn't without its problems, I very much appreciate the effort that was made by the developers. I still had tons of fun with this game and would encourage that them to take my feedback to heart so that their next project is all the better. For a dollar, it is well worth the money, especially if you're part of the truther community and want to help fight the good fight.

- Colors of the condiment bottles in the orders are different from the actual color of the condiment bottles. This makes it almost impossible to tell which condiment a customer has ordered, leading to many orders being thrown away. 

- Customers teleport in and out of nowhere. All the foot traffic walking down the street and none of it matters. Your customers don't walk up to a table and sit down. They just magically appear in the seat. And when they are done, they leave the same way they came. 

- The early game before you start selling coffee has you clean up trash, as if to say trash clean up is going to be something you get to do in the game. However customers are perfectly clean, never leaving even a single crumb of food. They are such immaculate eaters you don't even need to wipe down a table. Ever. This game has no tutorial except to teach you how to clean up trash, which doesn't exist as a game mechanic outside of the tutorial. This is one of those examples of things that just shouldn't be happening in a full release game that went through an entire early access release and development cycle. 

- Performance issues. With an RTX 2080 TI and an i9 i cant run the game maxed out. I have to turn several options down. You would think I had GTA V running with 25+ graphics enhancement mods with the 5FPS I was getting on first launch. 

- Food expires mere seconds after cooking it. While I was adding ketchup to a hot dog, the other hot dog on the grill went rotten in those 5 seconds. Believe me, i've eaten plenty of fast food hot dogs in my life, many of them were probably cooked hours before I came around. There is no need to be so strict about this mechanic. Also this game mechanic means it is impossible to prepare food ahead of time, which is something fast food restaurants in real life spend a considerable amount of time doing. Managers have to anticipate rushes and order their staff to get certain items prepared in advance. Since this game is literally named fast food manager, this should be a core element of the game.
