It has come to my attention that the dev has no interest in my thoughts on how to make this program user accessible. A few of the negative points I addressed were resolved, which is good, but Clip Studio can't hold a candle to the likes of Daz Studio. Sure Daz studio is daunting with DLC, but this is slowly becoming just as bad, with the minor exception that it's super difficult to get user content into Clip studio.
This will be my last review update. 
I cannot recommend Clip Studio, and will not be returning to it. 
I would love to be proven wrong in the future, but until I see software reviewers showering Clip Studio with praise, I'm out. 

TLDR version: 5/10*, Needs vast improvements
*: Only with nude/sex DLCs, otherwise 4/10 (It DOES function as a recording studio).
- Just wait for me to come back and change my review before you buy this. Get and learn Daz instead. 

The long read:
1. The UI is horrendous. It desperately needs a quality of life overhaul. It might look alright when you're not trying to make a scene with it, but as soon as you want to actually DO things with this program you very quickly realise just how un-intuitive things are.
2. The lag is gone! I can run scenes at the built in cap of 99fps and my PC only gives off a light whir. It has regained some functionality.
3. Building a scene is STILL pointless. If you take the time to go through all the steps to build your own good looking scene, it's going to take a very long time (Level designers, back me up). Then you save... and the only things that are saved are the positions and the timeline. NONE OF THE PROPS, CHARACTERS, ANIMATIONS, OR ANYTHING ELSE SAVES! You have to go through every single chunk of your timeline, search for what you used, and re-activate all of it piece by piece. What do the Devs expect? For us to power through a 40 hour long design session in one go, leave the program running while we nap, then start working on our actual scene recording... All while praying to the dark gods of computers that updates don't happen, or power doesn't go out.
The Dev has indicated she has no intention of fixing the issues. The current save system is fine in her books. Ergo as of this final review Clip Studio is asset flips and model posing. 
4. OMG the asset flips! So I bought a few DLCs, and I get it, they're not "expensive per-say" But the pre-made scenes in a lot of the things you can pick from are just ripped whole-hog from Humble Bundle packs, and possibly even Unreal Engine giveaways, with NO MODIFICATION to the sample scenes that come with them. The worst offenders are the Synty packs for sure. I'd almost go so far as to say the depths of "Just copy/paste that free asset we got" goes far enough to break the EULA of said packs.
5. Bad representation of the product. Every video shows the dev clicking effortlessly through all these options to change things, sometimes clicking buttons that don't even exist in the base product, all without mentioning that the buttons they're using are part of DLC packs. Asking the Dev where that button is gets "Watch this video" as a response, and give you a link to their entire library of videos (not the one that tells you that you have to buy the DLC to use those one or 2 buttons).
6. Clothing is fixed. Even though the models are basically all about the same general size and shape (give or take a breast slider) and the clothes seem to be weighted in a way that they LOOK like they could work on any character, THEY DON'T. You get ONE outfit option per character with a shader to change it's color... that's it. You can take the layers of clothes off, and put them back on, but you can't mix and match to at least TRY to make your scene a little different from every other person who uses this product. 
7. There is now a boob slider! However boobs only get bigger (No small tiddied girls for me :( )) The inflation looks a bit unnatural, and comedic. 
8. Character preview exists now, but the pictures used in the preview don't do the models any justice. They look far better than the previews indicate. 

The program is not worth your time or investment. Get Daz Studio instead, and spend a few bucks on a couple models, and hunt down the legitimate free Daz download sites.

This program is average at best. If you're a lazy Dev who doesn't care that their scenes look exactly the same as anyone else who uses Clip Maker, then this is for you. If you want to make projects that aren't asset flips, find something else.

This program went from "So bad I wrote what I spent on it off as a loss and learned Daz instead" to "Yeah, you can try it,at your own risk."

It's free now. Get it, try it out. It might work for what you want to do with it. It might not.

I still don't plan to use it the way I thought I would when I bought it. There are just better options out there. 

I will never update this review again.

This game is short and sweet. It definitely requires some thinking, and sometimes I found myself overthinking some of the simpler formulas. The characters are adorable, the design is fantastic, and overall - despite the super-cancer plot - it's very relaxing.

Unfortunately it's a very short game. If I weren't so scatterbrained, I could probably have finished it in half my initial playtime (16.4hrs) - if not less, because at least 2hrs were spent trying to put together a bigger lab post-story. Your long term goal is to find a cure for a plague before you die, but there's no real urgency to the task.

The game isn't particularly difficult, you only need to pay attention to what elements you have and what shape to fit them in. What I struggled with was how quickly I blazed through the story, only to find myself all alchemied out afterwards. I never needed a larger lab, I never needed a better resting spot - it would only distract me from the goal and artificially lengthen the game, much like the post-game. All that's left then is gathering achievements and base-building. Typically I love base-building, but what's the point? I had found the cure, I'd finished the story, I wasn't particularly concerned with achievements - it went so quickly from a deeply passionate labor of love to empty and soulless, which is very sad for such a wonderful overall experience.

I recommend it still because for the short time I did spend with it, I did enjoy it. It's a puzzle game with mandatory exploration aspects - two things I very much enjoy. The design of the world, the characters, the lore and worldbuilding - I can't overstate how absolutely delicious it all is. If that's up your alley, too, I recommend you give it a shot.

IMO- this game has flown UNDER the radar and deserves some accolades for its many strengths!
DDB V-9 is an outstanding value providing an open game engine that produces accurate season, team and player results. 

As-played lineups w/ player transactions and schedules are available if you're a stock replay person. Every season from the present back to 1959 have been created, and installing a season is a matter of just clicking on it. There are many other additional seasons as well. The stats package is quite good and the AI is VERY good! 

I like different game play options and there are many options to playing out a game: I can autoplay a complete game; I can manage one team and let the computer manager (CM) handle the opponent for a complete game; I can manage both teams for a complete game; I can let the CM play out the game inning by inning, or half inning by half inning, and pick up the game at a certain inning; I can let the CM play until a runner is in scoring position and pick up play; I can let the CM play until a run scores and pick up play, or I can simply sit back and watch the visiting and home CM's play a full game. 

These options really allow for someone like myself to keep an eye on every game, team and player and in so doing,  immersed in a league replay. The game engine factors in lefty/righty splits for both pitcher and batter, optional ballpark effects and accounts for great and not so great fielders, factoring in not only range but error probabilities. There are two available boxscores- an old fashioned basic (my preference) and the more modern day version. 

I've played many, many card & dice baseball games, to know statistical accuracy when I see it and DDV V-9 delivers accuracy, especially in the area of the "outliars" such as 1960s players like Bobby Richardson and Nellie Fox, who very, very rarely ever struck out. 

If you're a cards and dice guy, you have the option to roll your own dice. The program uses three 9 sided dice (0-9) providing play results from 0 to 999. League averages, lefty/righty pitcher/batter splits are all factored into providing an accurate assessment of each batter/ pitcher matchup.

Mark, the game designer, is the best regarding customer service, and ALWAYS replies to a gamers inquiries/ questions on the forum site. I play Strat, Replay, Inside Pitch, Diamond Mind, 4th St., OOTP and Action and DDB V-9 is SOLID! 
I have nothing but positive kudos for DDB V-9.

I have been playing baseball games for over 50 years, tabletop and PC. I have enjoyed most. 

SOM had been my longest played game, over 50 years as well. It does produce pretty accurate results but DDBB has been my go to baseball game since I discovered it while it was still in it's infancy.

I am a replay person and found that DDBB is the most statistically accurate game of all. One of the big things that this game has over SOMBB is the numerous options you can work with to create the type of game you want. There is a career mode as well as a mode that allows you to play along with the current season.

The #1 thing this game has that none other has is A++ customer support. Whether it's through the forum or through e-mail, Mark is very quick to respond as well as super fast to fix game issues. 

Most of the things that have been added are suggestions from players. 

Every season is available for FREE! What other game offers that?

Player pictures and team logos can be added. Team colors can be added to your season in the PBP box and on the player boxes that are on the field. Might seem like a small thing but it definitely makes the game more enjoyable for me.

You can import players from other seasons, you can create your players from scratch and you can edit the real life stats of players.

New additions are added between version updates.

Mark has shown his love of the game over the years and let's the customers know they are important. I hope the game continues to grow for many more years and I am proud to be a loyal customer. I definitely recommend it to any baseball lover.

The best in game baseball manager /total season game. There are no financial or any general manager aspects. No bells, whistles, or 3D graphics in a  single game. There are lineup  and strategy decisions that produce logical results. You feel like a true manager in game. My in game results so far are very similar to the actual MLB results in real life. Using baseball-reference.com you can download player pictures very easily. There there are also a gigantic number of free included and downloadable seasons and leagues. There is a developer who is very active in the Steam community  routinely interacts with the fan base. The upgrade from version 8 that I like best is that pitcher fatigue is now based on pitch count and not batters faced.

The Best Text Sim Baseball Game of its Kind!

1.  INCREDIBLE VALUE! All the seasons are FREE and custom draft leagues are very easy to set up. Want to see Ty Cobb face off against Gerrit Cole? Or how would Mike Trout do against Sandy Koufax? This can be easily done. The whole setup is fast and intuitive. And there are no extra charges unlike other baseball games which nickel and dime you for any extra season or player. 

2.  Statistical realism! Included in the game is a transparent mathematical formula of how batter/pitcher matchups are resolved and it makes sense! Certain games don't reveal their formulas and the cross era stats can be way out of wack . Or there are board game conversions which do reveal their formulas, but often times a statistical matchup in a game will be resolved just by reading the batters card and the pitcher is not even factored in. What fun is that?

Every matchup in digital diamond baseball involves the hitter, pitcher and fielder. It seems obvious that this should be done, but many other baseball text sims don't do this. When looking over the stats at the end of a cross-era season, the stats are believable.

3.  A worthy computer manager! So many other text sims get this wrong. Too many sacrifice bunts, or intentional walks that don't make sense or leaving a pitcher in to get shelled and then immediately pinch hitting for him the next inning. This doesn't happen in DIgital Diamond. The cpu manager is a worthy opponent and is customizable to play a more traditional type of baseball or a more analytical type of baseball.

4. Great customer service!! Mark, the creator of the game, is open to suggestions to the game and is very prompt with questions on email. I had a question on how to customize the play-by-play and he helped me by email and was just generally terrific.  (another fantastic feature that other games don't have. Some games allow you to kind of customize some of calls. This game allows people to FULLY customize ALL aspects of the play by play).

I highly recommend this game. If you are interested in cross-era play, dream matchups and becoming the next Connie Mack, then this is the game for you!

After playing the first Godbeast game, I was surprised to see a level based approach here, so no more getting lost!
There are some neat elements in MKII, like having to kill the enemies at the same time (you stun them and have to deal the finishing blow while the others are still stunned) and that made for some exciting prioritizing.

EDIT: played some more and really appreciate the combat, especially with a controller (I was struggling with Mouse + Keyboard)

Godbeast Mk.II is a very interesting game.

It's not very polished - in combat, the rigid camera can cause issues as enemies or props block the player from view, the UI navigation is very clunky, and there's no way to remap buttons which makes using a gamepad basically a no-go for me.

That said, there's a lot of really cool stuff here, and it's absolutely worth a try if you like stylish games and fast-paced combat.  The round-based combat system encourages clean, aggressive play - there's a mounting tension as you stun enemies one by one, trying to take them all down before the first one reawakens, and then sudden relief as the camera cuts to them one by one and they explode into health and energy pickups.

The game has a surprising amount of enemy variety, as well as a huge number of bosses for an indie game. I'm not finished with it yet, but there are at least four minibosses and at least four main bosses. Each of the main bosses has a weird and cool design, and their fights can get decently hard - I got stuck for a while at the Bishop, whose summon attacks and teleporting gave me a ton of grief.

I don't think this game is for everybody, but it's got enough cool stuff in it that I think it deserves much more attention than it currently has. Give it a try - you might like it!

Twilight Drive is a top-down driving game with a twist: grappling hooks for cars. Thankfully this proves to be a great mechanic rather than a gimmick and the system brings surprising depth with it. The different types of towers you can attach to give different effects which means the fastest line is not necessarily the traditional racing line - taking a longer route to hold on to an accelerator tower a little longer can be the difference between a silver and a gold medal. Discovering the best route is part of the joy of the game.

When you nail a section on a circuit and get the flow between towers just right it feels like an automotive version of web slinging through a city as Spider-man. And when you get it wrong, you’ll want to try again - the driving physics feel challenging but fair, and I always felt like any mistakes were due to me, not the game.

The tracks are short (around 30s -60s) so it’s great to pick up and play for short bursts, although that can easily turn into a longer session when you want just… one… more… go to try and shave off a few more hundredths of a second and beat your friend’s time. If you like the hunt for perfection in Trackmania, you’ll enjoy this part of the game.

New mechanics are introduced throughout and the tracks are varied. If you have friends with the game, the in-game leaderboards keeping track of the head to head scores are great for fuelling rivalries.

Highly recommended!

A quick but enjoyable turn-based tactics game. I would recommend anyone who is a fan of the Fire Emblem series, particularly the Gameboy Advance entries, to give this game a go. 

FE fans will already feel familiar with the grid-based tactical gameplay Kuro Tactics has to offer. You have your units on the map, move them next to an enemy unit, commence combat, and rinse and repeat until the map is cleared. Speaking of units, you control only three of them in this game from beginning to end: Kuro the knight, Arufa the wizard, and Shiro the healer. They each serve their respective purposes as the tank, damage dealer, and healer for the group. 

The game's campaign has ten maps to go through and if all of the maps are the same size and shape, each one is designed in a way that prevents them from feeling monotonous and samey. One element of the map design I enjoyed is the way parts of the maps are split into areas locked behind doors that need to be destroyed in order to progress. This makes it so that the enemy units don't all just rush you down from the first turn, meaning you control the pace and speed of your playthrough. 

The controls for the game are basic yet serviceable. WASD keys are for camera control while the mouse handles the rest such as selecting/moving units, attacking, equipping items, etc. One thing I will note is that because the mouse does everything, a common mistake I made was selecting Shiro and then clicking on another party member thinking I was just switching between them when that makes Shiro heal someone instead. Clicking anywhere on the map is enough of an easy workaround to prevent this. 

Now to really enjoy this game, the two most important things to keep in mind are experience point distribution and item management. EXP should be spread evenly between the three party members as just one of them dying is enough to cause a map defeat, so it's vital that all three level up so they can hold their own. 

Item management is equally if not more important. Every map objective is to open every treasure chests, so your inventory will fill up with new equipment as you progress. Each character has three slots for equipment (weapon/armor/accessory) and these items effect stats like health, attack, defense, action points, range, and movement. Items that give you more actions points are especially powerful as by the endgame, Kuro can hit enemies up for four times. 

TL;DR: If you like GBA tactics games, give this game a shot.

On the surface, this seems like another Banished clone, however it is far more simplistic and generic than Banished. This is both a plus and a minus.  
The plus is that it's more stable and much less taxing on system resources than Banished, which makes it easier to play on a lower spec system.  
The minus is that the supply chain system is almost comically simplified.  Consider the Gathering hut.  When placing the building, you can see how efficient the building will be based on where you place it, which is great.  Once you place the building, that value is locked in - even if you cut down the forest all around that gathering hut, it will still produce goods at the same rate and quantity because the worker magically produces the goods in the building - they don't actually need to gather anything.  This applies to every single resource building except the Forester hut, which actually has to cut down trees.  
Additionally, the fact that all the warehouse buildings are linked through some temporal rift makes things simpler but significantly less realistic.  There's much less management you need to do, which may seem like a good thing, but also makes the game less fun for people who actually want to manage their cities.  
As an aside, one of my pet peeves about this game is the fact that workers won't get their own resources from the supply depots.  They can be right next door to a depot, and just sit on their thumbs until a worker runs all the way across the map to get something from the depot for them.  
While this is a good game in that it works well, and has plenty of research and upgrades you can do, ultimately I'm disappointed by how simplistic it ended up being.

Just to add a bit though, Hera is portrayed a the villain in this game, forcing Hercules to conduct these labours if he wishes to enter Mt Olympus with the gods. In fact, according to legend, Zeus was a real cheater of a husband, leaving many illegitimate offspring to mortal woman, and Hercules was one such demi-god. So Hera was not doubt frustrated and wanted to get back at Zeus accordingly. Unfortunately, Hercules was just caught in the middle and ended up getting the rough end of the stick...

All of the characters were memorable and distinguished themselves well even in such a short time (playtime around 2h, give or take). The story also had some pleasantly unexpected turns and twists and I can much recommend going in for a second playthrough too, or just going back to change up some of the decisions, and see how that affects everything! I love puzzles, I'm a huge fan of puzzles, and most of my favorite games consist of puzzles. This game doesn't exactly have the same mind-bending puzzles as some other puzzle games, but they are puzzles that don't necessarily need too much thinking (except for the one with the wheels and matching symbols). 

Even if they aren't the thought-provoking puzzles I thought I was in for, the gameplay loop is extremely addicting. Seeing myself beat my own records and landing in 1st place is part of that addiction. It's definitely easy to pick up and learn, but there is a good enough difficulty curve that I improve in some area each run. I do hope to see more puzzle variants though (although having too many puzzle variants would overwhelm me, now that I think about it). 

There is a bit of jankiness in some mechanics. I notice that with the players' hands colliding with the walls has messed me up in some puzzles that require twisting of wheels. Sometimes I even feel as if there is friction with some wheels because my hand isn't grabbing it in the way the game expects. It's also hard for me to accurately twist the wheels in the matching symbols puzzle. I had to train myself to grab the star fragments/crystals because I often would smack it rather than grabbing it when I quickly go for them. It would also be nice if we can rebind the controls because I'd like to use my grip button rather than triggers to grip stuff (on Oculus Touch controllers).

Overall, I really enjoy this game because it's fresh and unlike anything I've played before. The gameplay loop is addicting and rising up on the leaderboards is satisfying. There may be a few bugs with the players' hands, but it's easy to retrain your movements to avoid that (bug fixes/patches are welcome too). I didn't pay attention to it beforehand because it fit so well, but the music really sets the mood of the game and each ritual that I do.

At first glance, this game seems like your standard, run-of-the-mill runner - dodge randomly generated obstacles and get the highest score that you can. Controls are simple: A and D to move, Q and E to strafe/blink, Left Shift to boost. I found it easier to use a controller, although Q wasn't automatically mapped for mine - I've published a controller configuration that works like a charm that you can use. You've got shields, which are replenished by defeating bosses; health, which is replenished by passing asteroids; and charges for both strafe and boost which replenish over time by themselves. You can adjust the difficulty.

What ultimately separates this game from other runners are the bosses that will appear randomly during your run. I think the boss mechanic is phenomenal. Defeating a boss is simple enough in theory (dodge the attacks until your boost is charged, then boost to hit, repeat until you hit the boss three times) but the bosses are surprisingly challenging and get more challenging each time you hit them. The boss variety in this game is stunning - each boss has a unique name, appearance, move set, and theme song (the music is phenomenally catchy, btw). The bosses do a fantastic job of breaking up the monotony typical of runners and are definitely the highlight of the game. There's even a dedicated boss-only mode called a boss-run, which has online co-op.

For each run you get a score (which can be published to the leaderboard) and omnifrags, which is the only in-game currency and is used to acquire new ships with different stats (strafe distance, shields, health, maneuverability, etc.) The DLC for the game gives you omnifrags per week for a one-time price, but you can honestly make more than the 500 it offers just by playing the game a few times a week, so the DLC is 100% optional - although considering this game is worth way more than $2 to begin with, throwing an extra $5 to the dev isn't the worst thing in the world.

Pros: badass music, fun score-seeking gameplay with challenging bosses to keep it interesting, easy-to-earn currency to spend on upgrading your ship, challenging
Cons: um, typo in the tutorial? Menus are a little janky, I guess.

All in all, the game is $2 and one of the best runners I've played, so pull the trigger.

Summary
Realms of Antiquity: The Shattered Crown, RoA in short, is a classically inspired role-playing experience with a top-down iconographic UI akin to the early Ultimas. RoA sports a diverse, extensive, and dynamic open game world populated by numerous concisely and well characterized NPCs, with excellent world building and writing, thrilling tactical combat, and countless quests to solve, places to explore and challenges to overcome. 
RoA is a technical marvel, given that this game was developed for, and runs in an emulator of, the TI99/4A home computer released in 1981. Every pixel in RoA oozes Adam Haase's, the single author's, love for classic RPGs like Ultima, Might & Magic, etc.
In short, RoA, Adam Haase's magnum opus, answers the question what would happen if you'd implement a classic RPG using modern day game design sensibilities on ancient hardware. The answer is everything an avid role-playing and retro gamer could have ever asked for.
Writing and World Building
The story of RoA is the story of a group of heroes plunged into a strange and fascinating world of high fantasy finding their way home. RoA is littered with smaller stories that unfold as you explore the world of Talanua. As in any good RPG, you can engage in those stories and steer them for better or for worse. The story is mainly driven forward through conversations with NPCs and title cards that are shown when, e.g., a building is entered.
RoA runs on a computer released in 1981. This imposes a tight limit on the amount of text or graphic that can be shown on screen and it requires a skilled writer to characterize NPCs and drive the story forward. Thankfully, Adam Haase is more than up to this task. His writing strikes a careful balance with descriptions that allow the mind to form a picture without overloading the player with text.
The world building of RoA is amazing. Adam Haase uses the limited tools available to him to create an engaging and believable world on the game’s level of abstraction. When the game can only show a metropolitan port city comprising two dozen houses and 10 people on the streets, it is up to the player’s mind to fill in the details. Yet, so much loving detail has gone in the game world, such as a bowyer shop that has an archery range out back or a hospice where you find a chest with padded armor. Its little details like these that make Talanua come alive. 
Talanua is huge and chock-full of settlements, dungeons, and encounters. Although most of Talanua is a high fantasy world, there are varying themes and cultural backdrops. While you start out near the classical rural fantasy village, you will explore regions inspired by Vikings and their mythology, humid tropical jungle isles, oriental wonderlands and much more.
The world is open and dynamic. You can go anywhere that you can survive right from the start. Note, if you try to take on a dragon with a single, level one hero, the outcome will be predictable. Even with this restriction, you have many viable options to go on from the starting area and with the right tactics you might negotiate areas that would otherwise be deadly. The world is dynamic in the sense that if you achieve a particular deed, then the NPCs and the world itself will react to it.
Combat and Magic
Combat is a central aspect of this in RoA and it is tactical, turn-based and plays out and on a square-tile grid. Skills and equipment allow for different approaches to combat. Nimble fighters with light armor that can dance across the battlefield and deal critical melee damage, strong, but slow protectors built to resist all but the most deadly attacks, as well as, archers sniping from the back of the ranks with deadly accuracy, all are viable options.
How much a character can do in combat depends on his or her stats and stamina. A fatigue meter serves to limit spells, but it is also used up, if you force your character to move/attack beyond his or her action points. Once stamina is drained, the character can no longer cast spells and any exhausting action will drain health.
The effective use of magic is crucial to combat tactics. Unless it is an ambush, enemies can be seen from far off which allows for effective use of buffing spells. You know the area is infested with enemies that charm? Better cast Mindguard. The place is crawling with difficult to hit fireflies? Buff the to hit chance. Don’t want to fight at all? Cast stealth and evade the confrontation.
In battle the party has access to a variety of offensive, buffing and utility spells. Those fireflies are a pest, so introduce them to the ice ball spell. Your paladin can hardly move, but is nigh impossible to hit? Teleport the character into the fray.
Available spells are determined by which spell book a character has equipped. Spell books contain 8 spells from the different schools of magic. You can’t switch spell books during combat, so choose wisely.
The many different monsters, you will encounter in different regions will force you to adapt your tactics and equipment to counter their strengths keeping combat challenging.
Equipment
Equipment is as varied and plentiful. There are numerous melee and ranged weapons, armor, trinkets, wands to equip and a cornucopia of potions, scrolls, touchstones with utilitarian effects. Equipment upgrades will be frequent and interesting until the very late game. RoA’s equipment is rounded off by adventuring equipment (light sources, lockpicks and trap disarm kits). Finally, there is also a hunger system, so you need to buy food from time to time.
One of my few gripes with the game is that you have a limited inventory and no long-term storage. So, you will need to make some hard decisions what to sell-off.
Characters and Character Development
The defining qualities of your characters are their class, attributes, and skills. Class controls usable equipment, thief skills and magic use. Attributes influence health, fatigue, movement speed and skills. Skills such as melee, lock-picking or lore determine the effectiveness of your character while performing certain actions. There is also magic affinity the one of the seven different schools of magic. Skills can be trained by specific NPCs.
Characters can rise 16 levels and they gain more health, stamina, and one skill point at level up. Development is somewhat flat which plays into the open world nature of the game while your characters still get notably more powerful each level-up. It is a difficult balance to strike and Adam Haase has done a good job at it. On rare occasions it is also possible to improve a character’s attributes.
Graphics and Interface
Your viewport into Talanua is a tile-based, top down view on your close environs. There are many diligently hand-crafted tiles for all kinds of objects and terrain to account for the varying locales in the game. The character and monster icons are delightfully drawn and will make the heart of every pixel aficionado beat faster.
The interface is keyboard based and works very well. Everything you need to do is streamlined and requires very few keypresses. In contrast to early RPGs very few keys are used thanks to context sensitivity. If you walk into an NPC, you strike up a conversation. If you walk into a boat, you board it.
Gameplay
The world is varied, the challenges diverse, and there is always something new and interesting to find for an enterprising player. The different enemies in the different regions require adaptation, so combat stays fresh. The dungeons themselves range from short excursions to long explorations and thus require adequate preparation. Finally, the game contains substantial optional content for those who like to explore.
So, is it fun? YES! This game has the addictive core gameplay loop of any open world RPG down pat. Explore, find new stuff, learn new lore, get better, repeat. It is pure unadulterated fun to any RPG enthusiast and/or addict.

If the likes of classic Ultima or its many spawn (The Magic Candle, Questron, etc) live in your heart, you owe it to yourself to play Realms of Antiquity. Yes there's a bit of a hump to get over in managing inventory menus but exploration and combat couldn't be simpler. At the same time the experience goes well beyond what many classic games achieved as the old design patterns have been updated with modern considerations to create rich tactical depth and variety.

The world is huge and full of things to find, and quests often have multiple solutions. You definitely need to take notes, although I managed to get through almost the entire game without mapping (there are two dungeons that practically require it). The setting is clearly crafted more for play than narrative but even so it's distinct and well-imagined, with a clear history to discover and plenty of easter eggs. It both takes itself seriously and allows itself to be fun at the same time (elephant-snakes!).

Of note, this game is running on TI-99 emulation and as such it's not completely seamless - there's a small pause on input that you quickly get used to. More of an issue is that the emulator hangs if left alone for too long so be sure to save before getting up to do something away from the computer.

These issues should be kept in mind but don't take away from a spectacular achievement in modern retro-gaming. It's early, but I'm pretty sure this is going to be my personal 2021 GOTY.

Despite being restricted to such archaic hardware, Realms of Antiquity The Shattered Crown is the next step on the evolutionary chain of Ultima inspired role playing games. The world of Realms of Antiquity is fun to explore, in fact the world design is this games single strongest aspect, and is full of things to discover. Either it be loot or entire dungeons! What truly makes the world design great is how diverse each area is while not becoming a theme park like so many other games. Logically telegraphed transition zones. you will start seeing cacti and brown dirt before entering the gulch. Areas placed in a manner that is environmentally logical. No scorching desert adjacent to icy plains. Towns themed around their environment. Stone buildings in the highlands and mud brick designs in the desert. While it seems odd to assign so much praise for what should be relatively minor aesthetic choices. It is important to remember that all of these things are all marks of passion from the single developer. That he made the game not solely for profit but because he wanted to make something outstanding, something ignored or even forgotten by some many people in the industry today.

Edit: I finally beat this, after having several months off it to cure my respawn induced burnout.  Here is my final review - 

A wonderful tribute to the ultra-old western RPG classics like Ultima 5 (closest comparison I think), that evokes a sense of adventure and exploration that is rarely encountered in today's games.  This game is very nearly one of the greats, and probably would be except...

It WAS deeply marred by a monster respawn system that bombards the player with trash monster encounters in Dungeon areas every minute or so, hampering exploration and causing, in me at least, great fatigue at the thought of having to engage in 'yet another fight'.  This has been toned back, and that was a good move by the Developer.  I'd tone it back even further but I'm happy to see it addressed in any form :).

The inventory system is also pretty clunky, but that is less of a problem.

All of that said, this is a very good game, and a rare gem if you like old-school world building and lots of atmosphere.  It is also a technical marvel given it was built for an ancient early 80s era TI-99 computer (!!!) and still plays better than some games built for modern powerhouses!

A tile driven CRPG designed to be run on a 80's era Texas Instruments personal computer (playable on steam via emulation) this game merges  nostalgia and innovation to create one of the most pleasurable gaming experiences I've had in years. 

In design and game play, it takes as inspiration the Ultima series (particularity Ultima 5) and then adds 30 years of design innovation in both quality of life (intuitive controls, inventory management) and in creating interesting choices.  The combat engine deserves special mention as it takes one of the least interesting things about it's source material (Combat in the original Ultima was a slog and was trivially easy once you equipped everybody with a magic axe) and creates a system that offers lots of interesting tactical crunch without being overwhelming. It's use of action points means a high strength, low dexterity fighter feels very different in combat than a high dexterity thief. Casting spells costs magicians fatigue and requires you to have the spell book containing the spell readied which provides hard choices (do I cast fireball or shield if I only have fatigue to cast one?) without being overly restrictive.  And equipment choice really matters-Do I arm my fighter with the best armor thereby restricting his movement? Do I arm my thief with a weapon that does more damage or do I arm him with a weapon that attacks five times a round? 

 The games setting and writing also blend nostalgia and innovation into a winning combination. The world you explore combines countless influences both from real world culture and mythology (there's a Viking land, and a desert kingdom out of 1001 Arabian nights) and popular culture (there's a vampire castle Bela Lugosi would be happy to inhabit, and a city on the sea with a distinctly lovecraftian vibe to it). This is a game where your party of fantasy heroes can fight a triceratops using a blaster rifle you found in a crashed space ship. Playing Realms of Antiquity I  often got the feeling that somebody had taken the whole toy box of my nerdy 80's childhood and turned it over for me to play with. 

Oftentimes, art based in reference and nostalgia can be weak and pandering- an attempt to make you love something simply because it's like something else you loved. But Realms of Antiquities avoids this pitfall through the strength of it's setting and it's writing. The game presents a lot of classic fantasy tropes but subverts your expectations about them (neither the missing princess, the quest giving prince, nor the evil overlord exactly what you'd expect them to be) and problems you cannot find an ideal solution to ( do you help the rebels or the king even of both of them are power tripping jerks who don't have the peoples well being at heart?).  Multiple times in the game your characters are the catalyst for people to see the errors of their ways and reform. You may be playing with the toys in your toy box, but the games story goes to surprisingly sophisticated places.

This is a wonderful game! A technical marvel, despite being a new, modern game made in 2020, it's written entirely in assembly language for a computer made way back in 1981. It's also incredibly well designed, cramming many modern tactical CRPG features you'd expect today into a retro-gaming wrapper you'd expect from the hardware this game was made for. 

The graphics are beautifully detailed for pixel art, and the game map has many surprising and delightful features to stumble across, and alongside the concise, well written dialogue, builds a living, breathing world in the mind of the player.

If this game had released on the TIS-99/4A back when it had it's heyday. I fully expect it'd have been heralded as a marvel of its time. Sure, we've had 40 years of games design experience to build on here, but nonetheless, Realms of Antiquity feels like a game from 1983, and a game from 2023, all at once.

My only misgivings are that I wish I'd found this sooner.

Extremely impressive old-school tile-based RPG.  It has colorful tiles that grow on you the more you play, a surprising amount of dialogue considering this was made for the TI99/4A, and a massive world with a lot of interesting maps (some of which are fiendishly designed) to explore and secrets to find. It sports a wide variety of spells, items, damage types, and armor types--it's a far deeper game than the ones originally released for 80s machines.  Some areas are much more challenging than others, and you have options in the order in which do finish quests and areas. It has simplified controls, so it's not one of those old school games that uses every key on your keyboard for something. 

If you grew up with Ultima, etc. I don't think you can fail to be amazed by RoA.  And if you didn't, this would be a great way to experience a perfected version of what some of the 80s RPGs were trying to achieve. There's no need to grind, but in the later part of the game, depending on how you have played, you may wish for fewer time-consuming combats once your party becomes too powerful for the vast majority of enemies. The game does provide a few means of reducing the incidence of these. For added difficulty you can play with a reduced party size and forgo allowing NPCs to join.
 
On a blind playthrough, at standard emulator speed, 100+ hours is a reasonable estimate for completion time. Most of this is spent in combat. Pay attention to the readme.txt to learn how to turn off the included emulator's Appmode so that you can speed up the emulator if desired. I would recommend against doing this until you've played enough to have a good feel for how the game works.

This is one of the most engaging RPGs I've played. The combat is interesting, the classes and characters feel different and the magic system is unique. It's a relatively new game that operates within the limits of an older system (The TI-99/4a and yes, it runs on original hardware if you choose). This does not, however, limit the game at all. In fact, in my opinion, it distils it into a well-crafted open world experience. There's a lot to discover here, quests, characters, plots, a world to explore; constrained only by your party's strength and preparedness.

There's a quick reference guide and a manual, which can be ignored, but I recommend you read it; it's a very useful guide to things like magic and also gives a good overview of all aspects in the game, there's also a hints section which gives some non-spoiler hints on areas you may be stuck on.

A puzzle-platformer made by a small Czech studio of four, with a greater emphasis on the platforming than the puzzles. Although it's not the prettiest game, I'd describe it as "competently made." A lot seems to have been done to make the platforming more forgiving, in a good, non-frustrating way. The game features the full suite of control customization options (which is sometimes too much to ask for smaller studios), as well the minimum of video options that you'd expect from this type of indie game. The one exception to this is FOV. The default FOV feels disorientingly narrow to me, even after having played the game to completion. An FOV slider would've been much appreciated. 

The game takes a minimalist approach when it comes to its visuals, especially when it comes to its user interface and set dressing. It feels like a lot of the same assets are reused throughout the game, and the environments tend to made up of a lot of these regular, geometric shapes, forming a visual style that's much more functional than attractive. A big thing that keeps the game from becoming visually stale is the diversity of its environments. The screenshots and trailer on the store page show just about every unique environment in the game, and as you can see, it's quite colorful. I should mention that the game you get is slightly less bright and colorful than what's shown in the screenshots, but it's not a super noticeable difference.

It's important to reiterate that the game is more of a platformer than a puzzle game, and even then, the platforming isn't the kind of platforming you'd see in a game like Ghostrunner or Mirror's Edge. Shy Eye Labyrinth is, above all else, a casual game. For me, the process of exploring the game and learning about the world it takes place in was its most interesting facet. The game has a dismally anticlimactic story in the grand scheme of things, but in moment to moment gameplay, it does a good job stringing you along with bits and pieces of lore. It creates the illusion of a deep story to uncover so that you constantly feel compelled to progress. Although I do wish the game had a more interesting story, here's what I'll say: A lot of video game writing is terrible. All a story needs to do is give the player a reason to continue playing, and Shy Eye Labyrinth's story does just that as inoffensively as possible. 

Overall, I liked the game. Some casual games can be extremely repetitive and take 20 hours of investment to start getting interesting. Shy Eye is short and sweet, with maybe around 4-6 hours of content. It's not a great game, but it's not terrible either. If you're looking for a thrilling game that'll keep you on the edge of your seat, you're better off looking for a Halo Infinite or Metro Exodus. But, if you're just looking for something casual to play over the weekend, Shy Eye is as good an option as anything.

This a truly a unique game that boggles the mind on terms of it's sheer scale. I feel like I've barely scratched the surface of a game that can scale with the actual observable universe.

The main gimmick of this game is the ability to shrink and grow yourself at set scales. However, I have not seen the end of this scaling. Each time you shrink you reveal new details in the world. A new maze to navigate. A new location with enemies to kill. Or another Ying forest inside of the Ying forest inside of the Ying Forest... etc.

The controls are simple but quite easy to grasp. The amount of customization you can do in this game as well is also quite huge. Though you first need to understand how to navigate through the menus or the know-how on mod the game to do so.

While this game at times can appear simple and act simple, there is something very complex happening behind the scenes as you shrink yourself further and further down exploring what seemed to be a simple cube.

In short, this is very simple game to pick up and play with seemingly endless exploration.

The graphics and sounds can definitely be a bit of a shock at first, but they get the job done, and you quickly become used to them. They add to the atmosphere, and can be quite charming. 

The combat is fairly basic. It mainly serves to guide the player away from certain paths, make them consider their space more deeply, and to encourage exploration by rewarding the player with upgrades.

But the main selling point is the exploration. It's a game with a lot of places to explore, and a lot of secrets to find. It's a game you can really get lost in, and spend hours exploring. I put off the main goal for quite a long time, as I simply pursued my own goals out of curiosity. This game has many such things, that may catch a players attention, and one's curiosity is often rewarded.

Even for a game that costs only 99 cents, it has a lot of issues. 

First off, why does the game look different on the Steam Store page? Aside from the first video, the game looks very different. Especially the first level. It looks a lot better on the Steam Store, but in-game it looks like a very badly made Gmod map. 

The story is pretty simple. Ortheo is looking for his friend, but while he's doing that, his flying ship breaks down. He will have to pick up gears from various levels to fix up his ship. The story is alright, I'll just skip to the gameplay and levels.

Ortheo controls pretty good. He's able to jump, double jump and dive. I don't think I've ever really struggled with the controls, aside from the camera.

The levels however are all very empty and ugly. Gears are way to easy to get and the enemies are pathetic. They can kill you in one hit, but it doesn't really matter cause you can just avoid them easily since you're gonna be platforming on high areas most of the time where the enemies can't reach you. There's also only one type of enemy in this entire game, they look slightly different in each level, but they still do the exact same thing. Imagine a Mario game, but the only enemy you fought were Goombas. That's what this game is.
You can also collect coins, but they're very worthless. They don't really do anything and for some reason they only spawn in the first level.

Lastly, we have the final and only boss in this game. His design looks neat, but the fight itself is lame. All you do is dive into him 3 times while he spawn those Goomba enemies. Once again, too easy. Dying also doesn't reset the boss' their health, so you can pretty much play without risk and still win.

This whole game, including the bonus levels took me 25 minutes to beat. I guess this is why the game costs 99 cents.

Other issues I didn't mention yet are the buggy menus, which can sometimes freeze on you to the point where you have to close and reopen the game just to get it fixed. The gears you collect are not centered when they're spinning around, which can be very annoying when you try to jump into them. All the achievements are also broken.

If there's one thing that I liked, then it's the soundtrack. The snow level and final boss theme sounds really great and the rest of the ost is good aswell.

Overall, even with the very cheap price and it being an indie game, this game really disappointed me and I honestly don't think it's even worth the 99 cents. I really hope the devs turn this around when the sequel releases.

I don't enjoy giving PunkWars a thumbs down but it just isn't quite enough to recommend. A fairly bare bones civ like 4x game. Some variations between factions make it interesting and I enjoyed the leveling ability for units but it doesn't add much to the combat which is a bit simple, the interface is a bit clunky, and giving right click commands fights with the camera controls to a point of annoyance. I tried to give this game a fair shake, but it's fundamentally broken. Most games end in a extremely slow war of attrition. There are too many ways for factions to bunker up and barely any to break through their defences. The idea is cool, but the execution is bad.

Its a nice little game, very Civ simplified. AI on harder difficulties are a little jacked but playable. The campaign is not a campaign however, its a skirmish vs 3 other AI and 2 cutscenes per faction playthrough. Replayability not convinced its existing as there is a lack of paths to victory.

---Gameplay---

The game is like a cross between civilization and jrpg - we have units that can level up, gain new skills and new special attacks. It definitely adds depth to the game and is not limited to empty clicking "attack this unit" - tactics are important here.

---Variety---

We have 4 factions to choose from - each of them has the same type of units - 2 infantry, flying, giant robot and 2 riding units. The differentiation at first glance is not very big, but the parameters and tactics of each faction are different - sure, you can win by flooding the enemy with units from the first tier, but if you get a moment of thought

---Level of difficulty---

The biggest challenge is to quickly develop your base - if we are late, we may have problems keeping up with the enemy and the savages. The game requires us to constantly develop - we have to acquire new resources, produce new units, because the moment of oblivion and the enemy may get dangerously close to us.

---AI---

Ai may not be very demanding, but I can see that she reacts to my movements. I like that it tries to hold on to the front lines and if it attacks it with a whole set of units, not one at a time. Thanks to this, we have typical waves - when it comes to combat it is addictive and requires a lot of reaction from us, but when it is calm, we can expand and regenerate. At some point, however, a climax occurs and we are able not only to repel the opponent's attacks, but also to approach his base. At this point, it all depends on how far away the buildings that produce units are - the best tactic is flooding the enemy with new waves, because you defend yourself quite sharply and your units die quickly. If we destroy one faction, we can defeat the next two quite quickly.

---Graphics---

Graphically, the game is at a high level - I recommend that you improve the contrast on the monitor a little, because the default settings can be a bit irritating. I like the details with which the game was created - I have not seen a 4x in which we could scrap the camera so. Moving elements of buildings, trains passing in steam, or cars driving on a diesel race track made a pleasant impression on me.

---Maps---

Probably the biggest problem with the game is the number of maps - we have 7 maps and 4 campaigns. It would be good if there were 10 of them, although taking into account the unequal starting positions of the factions and the variety between them, the available number should provide several hours of gameplay. Although I hope that the developers add new maps with the next patches, not paid dlc

---Sounds---

The music is okay, but the personalization of the individuals is average. Some of them have super-matched sounds, while others the sound does not match what we see on the screen. By far the biggest downside of the game.

---Pros:---
+ interesting game combination (4x meets jrpg)
+ tactical combat
+ possibility of choosing different strategies
+ next turn syndrome
+ great climate and interesting world


---Minuses:---
- a small number of maps
- average differentiation between fractions
- AI isn't too smart sometimes
- there is a critical moment, after which we are almost insurmountable

---Wanna have:---
* more projects could be used
* I'd love to see more than 4 factions
* you play until you ask for a multi or hot seat

After spending way too much time on this game of the trilogy, I have come to the conclusion that this is the best one out of them. When I first started, I set out on a journey to 100% the game's achievements, and after coming to a conclusion; I could not do it.
Unless I set my house on fire from the impending doom of leaving my Endless Furry Trilogy-Infested computer on every-night, sitting there clicking away at the furry icon on the middle of the screen, there was little to no chance. I had a good run, and I almost made it. The only achievement I have left is to achieve 1 Trillion Furr, but while I might return at a later date, for now I will be stuck on 99% achievement completion.
Now you might have seen me mention "The Trilogy". The Endless Furry trilogy started with Endless Furry Killer 2020, a 2D top-down shooter where your only two objectives are to kill the endless waves of furries, and to survive. The original is a very simple game, and I applaud the developer for being able to make it addicting, yet crashable within 45 or so minutes.
The second game in the trilogy, Endless Furry Killer 3D, is a 3D DOOM-like action-shooter that I find the most fast-paced and short-living fun. If you put on some songs from DOOM 2016 or DOOM Eternal, it could feel like a real DOOM game, lag included!
And now the final game in the trilogy, Endless Furry Clicker. A lot of the time this game was running in the background and the Furr Grinders did all of the work, but the mindless hours of clicking that this game let me do was the most intriguing part. As someone who doesn't enjoy any clicker-style games, this is the only one that has kept me attached and the only one that has constant-clicking fun, especially with the countless (4) songs you could unlock to listen to and the one clicking sound that was short but sweet.
In conclusion, if you ever have a weekend, the Endless Furry Trilogy is the best game set to buy to waste time.

When Tarsier created Little Nightmares 2, they stated in interviews and at press events that they'd learned some valuable "what not to do" lessons regarding depth perception when they'd developed the first game. Shoving my way through Daydream: Forgotten Sorrow this week, it was frustratingly clear that this dev team had no such trial balloon to look to, to iron out kinks. For every clever idea the game presents, it self-sabotages with sudden-death drops and critical items only interactive from EXACTLY one angle and no others, with no reliable way to discern what's upstage or downstage of your character. And oftentimes it occurs during speedy chase sequences where precision is required, which quickly rings the death knell for fun. The depth perception is almost wholly unreliable and based on guesswork; whoever designed the hang glider sequence, in particular, seems to have just guessed at every possible juncture, and then simply expected me to do the same when playing. "Die forty times, and then get inscrutably lucky on your forty-first attempt, with no idea what you did differently" is not competent nor trustworthy game design.

Also, not to sit here and lob cheap shots while it's down, but the game's Steam page wants me to believe I just played a game about "memories of a dying man" wherein I'm supposedly "assisting Griffin to shed the remains of his miserable life before his impending demise." All I can say to this is that if the developers earnestly believe they conveyed this plot through the actual game, their next at-bat needs a more talented writer, alongside the other shortcomings I've already mentioned needing shoring up.

While I often see Steam users complaining about the price to length ratio of games on the platform, I usually side with the developer. As an adult working full-time I have less time than ever to play games, and I don't love it when games feel artificially padded with repetitive or dull content. However, upon finishing [b]Forgotten Spirits[/b] I remarked to my co-op partner, "Wow, that was it?" We finished the game in 30 minutes. Luckily, I had bought the game on sale for 50% off ($5), which made the short length a little more palatable. However, the game still felt a little expensive for what it is.

We did enjoy what we played, though. I liked the "construction paper" art style that the game uses, and the asymmetric nature of the co-op (many tasks can only be performed by one of the two characters). Lastly, I liked the concept of switching characters from foreground to background and back again in order to solve puzzles and make progress. We found some of the secrets hidden within the levels, but I'm sure that there were more to find - we aren't typically completionists. 

If you think you'd enjoy a short, co-op puzzle game with an endearing art style, give [b]Forgotten Spirits[/b] a shot. However, I would absolutely wait for a sale.

gameplay is the usual find items, use them, figure out codes, and so on, except the girl can't reach a key slightly above her head, but has no problems installing a big-ass mirror on the ceiling of an underground military base without help. and [b]some of the puzzle mini-games are ridiculous[/b] as well. she can't take a dog on a leash, a cat in a box and a hot-dog over the river at the same time, for example. there's also the world's worst nonogram with no right-click action. [b]stuff like this can be skipped[/b] by clicking the fast-forward button twice, but gotta say, the one in the second room in the last chapter was pretty neat. the maze following it not so much but it was quick at least.

[b]the cursor and right click don't do anything[/b], no changes over hotspots, no hotspot indicator, exits aren't marked (though there are never more than 2 locations per chapter), can only zoom out/close puzzles by clicking a button, so [b]it's a tedious clickfest[/b]. Scrap Riders is a true hidden gem in the gaming world, offering a unique blend of point-and-click adventure and 2D side-scrolling brawler mechanics. Initially, the game faced some technical issues at launch, but in my recent playthrough, I encountered no crashes or bugs, indicating that the developers have since addressed these problems.

The gameplay of Scrap Riders is split into two engaging styles. The point-and-click adventure segments require players to find items or help characters to progress the story. This aspect is enriched by the humorous banter between the main character and his robot sidekick. The dialogue is witty, filled with clever references to retro titles and classic movies, and the game is peppered with small Easter eggs for players to discover as they explore.

The second gameplay style involves 2D side-scrolling brawling, reminiscent of classics like Double Dragon and Final Fight. The combat system, while basic, requires strategic gameplay rather than simple button-mashing. Boss battles are challenging but manageable if players take the time to learn the patterns and tactics of their opponents. This balance of difficulty ensures that the game remains engaging without becoming frustrating.

Graphically, Scrap Riders excels with its pixel art style, which is both nostalgic and visually appealing. The game environments, though small, are densely packed with interesting details and a distinct cyberpunk aesthetic. This is particularly evident when players transition from the badlands to the mega city, where the game truly comes to life with vibrant, atmospheric settings.

One of the game's strengths is its lack of grinding. Each objective moves the story forward, maintaining a brisk pace that keeps players engaged. The game is relatively short, taking around 5-8 hours to complete, depending on how much time players spend exploring and interacting with characters. This duration is perfect for the type of experience Scrap Riders offers, ensuring that the game remains fresh and enjoyable throughout.

The story is compelling, filled with twists and turns that keep players invested. The main character's quest to recover a stolen item from the head gang that has taken over the mega city is well-crafted and intriguing. The narrative is further enhanced by the engaging and often funny dialogue, which adds depth and personality to the characters and the world they inhabit.

In conclusion, Scrap Riders is a fantastic game that successfully combines elements of adventure and brawler genres. Its engaging story, witty dialogue, and beautiful pixel art make it a standout title that deserves more recognition. If you're a fan of 2D side-scrolling brawlers with a bit of adventure thrown in, Scrap Riders is highly recommended. This game offers a refreshing experience that will keep you entertained from start to finish.

Ahh .. the meme that never gets old; The [b]Gachimuchi Universe[/b], a.k.a "Professional Pants-Wrestling" (such as the films called [b]Workout Muscular Men 3[/b] or [b]Lords of the Locker room[/b]), starring the late [b]Billy Herrington[/b] (lovingly called "Aniki" which means "Big Brother") and friends, made famous by the japanese video-hosting site [b]Nico Nico Douga[/b] and the forum [b]2chan[/b] back in 2007. In addition to this, the game also features [b]Ricardo Miles[/b], a.k.a the "Red Bandana Guy", who is also considered canon to the Gachimuchi universe.

And that was just the background lore of the game setting, just so you don't think this is just any [i]random[/i] homosexual wrestling game.

So what is this game all about? Well, it is about asserting your dominance as an alpha male by wrestling other muscular men. But it is all in good fun, and should be considered more as a bonding experience than anything else. Simply having a good time with the boys (and an occasional lube).

When you start the game you get to chose between different modes, environments and characters, as well as preferred difficulty settings. You may also play with up to 4 friends but since I don't have any friends, I haven't tried this feature.

The gameplay is very simple. It is you against randomly spawning muscle dudes and once you engage in a match, you hit the space bar as fast as possible to wrestle them to the ground. This is all accompanied with suggestive animations and sound bytes from the actual movies which is very nice.

The game has some bugs; For example, sometimes the NPC's freezes, and it is very unclear when or how you knock someone out. Sometimes their life bars just don't seem to drop to the bottom even though you have defeated them. Even so, the majority of achievements are still easily taken within your first 20 minutes of playing. Hopefully the game will get some update that rectifies these issues, or a more comprehensive help guide. 

As the game is now, it isn't much more than a [i]gag[/i] gift (see what I did there?), so why do I still recommend it? 

Well, the answer is very simple; It is culturally important. In April 2022, A popular Russian TV-show actually discussed the GachiMuchi Universe on national TV, claiming it is the sort of media that people in Ukraine and the west is consuming on a regular basis, and the expert in the panel especially mentioned the movies with our beloved "Aniki", Billy Herrington. Even though I am [b][i]immensely flattered[/i][/b] that the people of this Russian TV-show thinks so highly of the cultural habits of Ukrainians and westerners, it just [b][i]isn't true[/i][/b]. Not enough people has experienced GachiMuchi Universe yet! But I really wish it was true!

That is why [b]everyone[/b] should play this game and enjoy a piece of GachiMuchi Universe. And considering the modest price tag of this game, you get a pretty decent chunk of valuable culture! 

I'll end by quoting Billy Herrington himself, may he rest in peace: "ASS WE CAN!"

Cyber Cult City is part action-roguelite and part mission-based imsim. Each of its procedurally generated areas represents a single cult-controlled city block, and it’s your job as the Mayor of Cyber Cult City to stomp out cultists and save the citizens.

Every level is a little sandbox that provides a basic objective and then sets you loose to approach it any way you see fit. You might be tracking down hostages in one map, or destroying cloning facilities in another. And this isn’t just a run-and-gun shooter - you can get some help and hints from loyal citizens, hack cars to send them careening towards your enemies, bat bullets away with your sword, or just spend some time fooling around and landing some sick jumps on your hoverboard. Completing the objective summons the handy Mayoral helicopter, and unlocks the next map on your path towards the final confrontation with Cyber Cult leadership.

In addition to your standard issue hoverboard, the basic Mayoral benefits package includes a pistol, a sword, a landmine and a grenade. In true roguelite fashion, there’s a number of stackable upgrades and mutators for each one of your weapons that dramatically change how they function, how much damage they do, and whether they can fire bouncing projectiles, heat-seeking missiles, vampiric landmines, and so forth. There’s dicey injectors full of street-juice that can boost or reduce your base stats, and even research trees to unlock MORE options down the road. 

Overall, this is a pretty fresh and original take on both rogue-lites and immersive shooters that provides way more player freedom than you'd expect. If you can get past the primitive visuals, you'll find a lot to like here.

TL;DR: GET THIS GAME! :)

Good indie games are hard to find—some of the lucky ones blow up and get famous but there are many great games made by small teams that don't get advertised enough or don't get found by that famous YouTuber and sadly remain obscure. I think Sunshine Heavy Industries is one such game.

The team behind this game has, in my opinion, done just about everything right: the graphics are elegant and consistent in style, the core gameplay loop is satisfying and fun, the writing is hilarious, and the relaxing electronic music is heart-meltingly beautiful and perfectly fitting for the game's overall vibes and style.

For the unfamiliar, this game is about building space ships according to certain specifications. The closest thing I can compare it to is Dragon Quest Builders where rooms have to meet certain criteria to correctly be classified as that room, but it leans more heavily into that idea with a currency system so that you have to both meet the requirements and make a profit on each ship. Doing that alone is usually fairly easy, but you can sort of choose your own level of challenge by considering what you want the ship to look like too. If you meet the requirements but think the ship is ugly, then you have the challenge of tidying it up before submitting it. Fixing one problem often creates another, leading to a satisfying loop of refining your ship until you're happy with it. As you progress, the requirements become more complex with many new types of ships and parts being added into the mix, so the gameplay doesn't get stale (or at least it hasn't so far). I'm only a few hours in but I can't wait to see what else it has to offer!

Sure the game looks nice, but this game is extremely BORING and slow. It's part Idle or Auto-clicker and part button smasher when you get to the bosses. "Idler" should be one of the top tags; this is not a fighting game at all.

It starts out well, and I really like the artistic design for everything, but quickly you'll see that every level and every monster all play out the same way. The difficulty for each monster doesn't mean anything, to the contrary, the game gets easier as you unlock the achievements. While the monster's attacks do behave differently, the strategy for each monster is identical. First, level up your monster to the point where it can heal itself, doesn't run out of attack juice, and has a decent attack; Then easily stomp through every level; Then repeat with next monster - do this for all 9 monsters. There's not enough variety in game-play to justify having 9 monsters. After maxing out the first monsters, dread set in when I accepted that I was going to have to go through that slog 8 more times.

You have to pay attention when starting out with a monster, but once you level it up, you can run it while doing other things. In order to get 100% on the achievements it is a massive grind of doing the same thing over and over and over and over and over and over.  There is no reason to max out your Giga other than the achievement. It has a terrible gameplay loop.  You can partially walk away for a lot of the grind, but you always have to interact with the boss fights, which are also extremely boring and easy.  So easy that you don't even want to bother with them because they are even slower than the rest of the boring game.

A few of the achievements are extremely annoying, and you have to pay attention to the boring grind when achievement hunting those especially annoying achievements. The frustrating thing is that it's not a full Idler, so you have to interact with it every 15-20 minutes or so. Most of my hours in this game was from the game waiting for me to click a button when I walked away to do laundry, cook dinner, or fell asleep. The only reason I stuck with it after the first 2 hours was to get 100% achievements; without achievements I would have quit after my initial session and never played it again.
I wouldn't be so negative if I could have run the game at 2x to 4x its normal speed.

Hack Grid is a fun little retro style puzzle game that's definitely entertaining. The DOS style is fun in both visuals and audio, with a very simple but thematically suited soundtrack.  I also like that you can toggle the CRT effect on and off to your preference.  The levels themselves are good in that the difficulty grows at a steady rate, so you're not suddenly stuck, and the instructions are clear when new elements of gameplay are introduced.

All in all, I'd recommend Hack Grid as a nice bit of fun to put your brain to the test!

Full disclosure: I was a playtester for this game.

In Hack Grid each level has a different setup of pieces and trails within a 4x4 grid (sometimes it's smaller).

In order to move a piece, it must have a straight line of trails or empty sockets leading to a differently colored piece. What makes the grids interesting is not only the different setups of pieces, but also the way the trails connect between them; It varies from level to level, and sometimes the lack of a direct trail between two pieces can trip you up, if you are not paying enough attention to the trails.

Aside from some special pieces, generally the pieces only come in 2 colors, which means that while removing pieces from the grid, if there are still more than 2 pieces left, you have to make sure not to eliminate the other color. Otherwise you'll find yourself stuck with two or more pieces of the same color that cannot remove one another. 

It gets a lot more tricky once you get to the levels with both pieces that change color each time they move, and pieces that change color each time another piece moves. When most pieces are changing their color each time you move a piece, it can get harder to wrap your head around multiple different color changing gameplay mechanics while predicting what the grid will look like multiple moves into the future. On the later levels I found myself playing more by trial & error, which is fine too, but perhaps doesn't have the same satisfaction as playing the level first inside your head, and then executing the perfect moves from the start.

Overall I found the levels to be sufficiently challenging, nothing too frustrating, though I did take a few breaks when I found my stupid brain repeating the same moves over and over again without success.

Personally not a fan of the CRT effect, but you can just disable it in the settings, so it's not a problem.

I'd recommend this game if you're looking for a simple but challenging puzzle game that can last a couple of sessions, but your mileage may vary.

One thing that I found a bit distracting was the music, although I can appreciate the DOS aesthetics with Soundblaster - but I like to do puzzle work with not much distractions. The great thing is that there are a lot of options to configure the game: colorblind mode, difficult languages etc. to make the puzzle solving a smooth ride. Also, keyboard control was something I missed, but the mouse control worked really fine.

If you like games like Baba is you, 2048, chess, klock!, lemmings and other type of puzzle games, or want to have a nice trip back to DOS gaming, I can warmly recommend the game. A great game - definitely worth the price.

This scrappy, spacefaring RPG very much seems like a labor of love (it was created by solo developer Sam Enright). The initial premise is certainly compelling - your protagonist, Doug, is abducted by aliens and told that a destructive cosmic force is soon to destroy Earth. Do you believe the aliens? Do you try and return home anyway? I loved flying around the game’s overworld, visiting planets and meeting new party members with interesting personalities. My favorite companion was easily Boom Boom, Doug’s guinea pig that was transformed by the aliens during the initial abduction to be larger, bipedal, and super-intelligent. The game’s core mechanic is the ability to capture almost any creature you fight, whose abilities you can then use in fights moving forward. With use, you can level up these summons to gain even more powerful abilities. There are some fairly difficult boss fights in the game, and Doug can capture these creatures as well (their abilities are some of the strongest in the game). Along with the ability to equip up to four summons, each character can equip four relics which further enhance combat abilities. The relics are quite diverse, and powerful synergies can be created. My main gripes with the game were getting lost on a few occasions, and the way that enemies respawn upon each screen transition.
