Had a good feeling about this one from the screenshots and trailer video, and sure enough it was just a wonderful little romp. Practically a love letter to 90s era handheld RPGs like Final Fantasy Legend or Pokemon, but with modern day sensibilities like faster movement & freedom to experiment. Being able to choose from a variety of palette choices was really nice, even if I never figured out how Custom was supposed to work.

The gameplay is smooth and simple. You have basic ammunition, which doubles as a sort of currency to obtain other kinds of bullets in exchange, and you have your war gear which is really just your healing items, bombs, and other stuff. Every time you finish a battle, the enemy drops a handful of different ammo along with some more basic bullets. Or sometimes it'll be scrap, which is great cause you use that stuff to craft more bombs, first aid kits, and other handy items.

The game is [i]very[/i] generous with scrap and bullets, which allows for you to play how you want. Many enemies have weaknesses like explode, ice, or shock that you can capitalize on via grenades or special ammo. Personally I found myself abusing the hell out of Molotov cocktails since they'll hit every enemy and can be a good opening move. Combat items like grenades will also damage enemies that are largely unaffected by your guns, too, so it's important to always have some on hand either way.

Both the upgrades for your guns and the skill parameters you can increase can be reset [i]for free[/i] at any time if you're not happy with how it turned out. I'd suggest putting plenty into Luck since it affects the drops after battle. The game's level cap is only 30, as well, which is fine cause this isn't the longest game to begin with. I found the length very agreeable, it never wore out its welcome. 

Don't want to spoil anything related to the story, but I enjoyed it a lot. Honestly a lot better written than anything that actually came [i]out[/i] in that contemporary 90s era. I sincerely doubt this will get a sequel, just from how it all plays out, but I would love to see another game [i]like it[/i] since the developers have clearly got the look, feel, and pacing down.

Fun little JRPG with some weak writing. Considering the constraints of the retro aesthetics, the visuals and audio are top notch, with fairly standard turn based JRPG gameplay built around item management rather than skills. Your party members don't have mana pools, or unique moves to use in combat. Instead, everyone shares a pool of different items and ammo types, and experience is used to increase stats which make your character hit harder, take less damage, or use items more effectively.

The game is, however, pretty easy. I'm not particularly good at JRPGs, and even I finished the game with only one game over at the very final boss, when I unwittingly used an item that stopped my designated support character from doing anything except attacking for as long as it took my party to get wiped. Collecting items and optimising their use was satisfying, but most of the challenge was from trying to optimise fights rather than simply beat them. You also have the option to re-allocate your stats and upgrades basically whenever you want at no cost, which may or may not be an upside depending on how you like your RPGs.

Now, the narrative. I didn't like it. It tried to tackle some lofty high concept stuff - war, geopolitics, nuclear armageddon, cultism, social stratification, artificial consciousness - but it's let down by flat characters and some rather uninventive writing, each of those aforementioned lofty concepts [i]referenced[/i] rather than analysed or developed in any meaningful way. The character writing is particularly weak - the characters are all archetypes, and dialogue is mostly just people taking turns to summarise their motivations and reactions to events in the narrative. Character development by cliffnotes.

I wouldn't recommend the game [i]for[/i] the narrative, but as something to give context to the battling and exploration gameplay, it's fine. Maybe it's just me, but I felt like the store page and the reviews alluded to a level of narrative depth that isn't actually there.
Sometimes a game is exactly what it advertises. For a Vast Future is a bite-sized RPG with Gameboy inspired graphics, interesting gameplay, and a decent story and characters.

I wish I could give a neutral score, but I'll optimistically give this game a hesitant thumbs up, in the interest of being constructive.

For a Vast Future does quite a decent number of things right. It's a game that is kept compact and doesn't overcomplicate itself in terms of story of mechanics. Stuff like armor upgrades and powerups are kept to weapon upgrades and stat bonuses of your choosing (which are freely customizable to fit situations) rather than through a vast array of weapons and armors typical of RPGs. The one thing is that "magic" and "skills" really don't exist in this game. Instead, you either have bullet types or item types. I don't especially mind the nature of managing resources in this game, but basically everything is finite, which does kinda fit the theme of the game but also isn't always fun to deal with, especially if you used most of your resources getting through a boss or dungeon. I never quite hit the point of not being able to progress, but there were a couple points I basically had no choice but to backtrack and kill worthless mobs just to have a stockpile of resources. This creates somewhat of a self-defeating gameplay loop, which is often poor design. A few more options that didn't take resources would have been nice.

The other thing is the narrative. Now, I think this game does a couple things pretty well. Its limited scope keeps what is ultimately a small game simple in terms of narrative, and a lot of the lore is wisely left to various logs of abandoned computers and bookshelves, which both give the world a bit of depth and also fit its post-apocalyptic setting. This also means that you can get as much or little out of it as you want at your own pace. Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the game's characters or main plot. They're simple and fine enough to get the game moving, but when it comes to moments of character actualization and development, things get really heavy-handed rather than showing any subtlety or intrigue. This would be fine, if not for there being some particular dialogue exchanges late in the game that just feel really clumsy. Which also ties into the main narrative. This game's final act narratively just feels really crappy, handwaving a kinda heavy subject a bit too quickly, and having just a pretty poor ending all around, like whatever was trying to be said with the narrative fell completely flat to the point it actually irks me, which is rare because I can often overlook this sort of thing if the rest of the game makes up for it.

To say nothing of at least a few bugs and oddities I encountered that periodically hindered the gameplay experience. As well, the 4-color Gameboy aesthetic honestly hurting the game visually more than helping. It's trying to go for a Final Fantasy Legend/SaGa 1-3 aesthetic but it can be a bit of an eyesore at times and the small sprites sometimes can make telling what is what frustrating. That's not to say they didn't try, and for the most part this isn't a problem, but occasional issues do end up occurring due to this stylistic choice. Music ain't bad though, at least.

I had a decent time with this game, the resource management aspect of its combat was interesting and it rarely felt like it was trying to be too ambitious, which worked for making an RPG that felt complete despite being only about 6-7 hours long on normal difficulty. But the game's final act was considerably heavy-handed and there are a couple parts of the combat system I didn't care for. If you want a short turn-based RPG with some interesting systems and that doesn't inundate you with text (instead leaving you to discover it and fill in the details of the world on your own time), it does pretty well, as long as you can overlook the rather...poor choices in writing (at least in my opinion) of the game's final act.

Short and sweet, For a Vast Future has a compelling plot, solid backstory, and especially scratches that aesthetic itch that I experienced with the SaGa (Final Fantasy Legend) games all those many years ago. I for one enjoyed it, and the average playthrough is about 8 hours, give or take an hour or two depending on the difficulty and whether or not you choose to grind for levels and scrap.

This game makes its own nostalgia!

I went into this game not knowing exactly what to expect, except that it'd be a short and sweet ride through a gameboy-styled lens. Despite a general apprehension when it came to expectations, and not really having fond memories of gameboy rpgs, it ended up hooking me right off the bat, and I ended up playing it daily until I completed it. 

Music:
So how did it create its own nostalgia? For starters, the music is incredible. I'd often play before bed, and I'd boot up the game in advance, just letting the title track play while working thru my before bed routine in anticipation of diving back in. The game is incredibly inviting once you're even mildly invested, and I believe the music is its strongest pillar in that regard. Each track is backed by catchy melodies that expertly utilize gameboy inspired chiptunes, and truly exemplify the moods the game is trying to convey. Quite often there is a theme of adventure and drive in the music that aims to move you forward, but there's an excellent contrast with some more moody tracks that aid in backing the game's exposition.

Story:
On the subject of exposition—the game's story is really quite light on the surface. Playing through the game does not ask much from the player in terms of time and investment unraveling the pieces. Each story moment is direct and bare bones, but that's not to say there is no depth. No, rather than beating the player over the head with long-winded soliloquy and narrative, the game chooses instead to let the player discover the story on their own terms. This is cleverly handled through various computer logs, diary entries, and other such things scattered throughout the game's buildings. All of which aim to provide the player with more context, while also serving a secondary purpose of world-building. 

Within these entries is an entirely different world to discover. Each parcel of information crafted to develop the world and story without needing a wall of text to do so. In a different game this might not work, but it felt so in-tune with the game world, that this self-driven narrative discovery almost felt like second-nature, and a part of your characters' own motivation. 

The Art:
The graphics in the game are generally well done. This is especially true for the maps and tilesets, which are both pleasantly constructed. Characters are a little too small to get a read on their personalities or dimension, so if there's one small gripe I have with the art, it's that the character design lacked enough distinction to distinguish one from another. Outside of that, there are a few inconsistencies with the level of visual quality, but nothing that would detract from the enjoyment of the game. Guy's Guns, a weapon upgrade shop, seems to have received a lot of attention in regards to polish, and sorta demonstrates how far the game's visuals could have been pushed had the developers had the time and resources to do so. 

The Gameplay:
Like other Retreaux Games titles, the gameplay is designed to be incredibly snappy and without friction. This is a big part of why the game's so inviting, and how it's so easy to come back to. It does not ask for your time beyond what it is trying to accomplish, and every design decision seems to suggest this is wholly intentional. 

From a motorcycle that you get early on that lets you travel each area in breakneck speed, to the sparse story exposition and clear direction given to the player, every gameplay element is designed to expedite progress and keep the player moving along. This is especially true with the combat.

Combat is turn-based and moves incredibly fast. Encouraging the player to utilize a bevy of bullet types and wargear (consumable items) to exploit enemy weaknesses and end the battles as soon as possible. While the depth to combat is not all there, there is just enough depth to where experimenting with strategies can pay off in dividends. By the end of the game I had some tried 'n true strategies that I stood by, but it took nearly half the game and a bit of experimenting to develop them. All in all combat felt rewarding, and rare was the occurrence where I wasn't in the mood for another battle. 

Biggest Surprise:
The ammo system was incredibly well done. There is no currency in the game, and instead it seems like bullets supplant the need for currency. It always felt good to get ammo drops from enemies or treasure chests. Better than one might feel if they got a standard currency reward instead. And that is largely in part, because ammo is required for each hero's basic attack, and basic ammo can be traded in for specialized ammo that helps craft more unique fighting styles for your heroes. I believe there's a lot more to discover in a game design space with this take on alternative currencies, so I hope other games take note and innovate on this concept in their own ways.

Conclusion:
For a Vast Future is an incredible game that I did not expect to like so much. I noticed I only have 19/24 achievements at the time of writing this, and the game was so enjoyable that I'll be starting another play through in order to get those 5 final achievements. Once those are wrapped, I will probably be anxiously waiting for a sequel!

This is a fairly good implementation of an old school style RPG, but one that largely avoids some of the things that made them tedious.  For the tl;dr of this explanation:  [i]expect about 8 hours of old school fun you're looking for minus a lot of drudgery you'd expect to suffer through, combat that's either brief or engaging, good character customization, and a mostly enjoyable experience.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
So, here's a quick list of what you'd expect from an old school game, and how this one handles them.  For A Vast Future is mostly linear but in a way that feels like the story is moving forward quickly.  No random battles; enemies are on the screen and can be avoided if you really, really want to.  Grinding is optional, but even if you do it the grind is over pretty quickly.  There's a small amount of exploration and side-exploration, but your characters' base move speed is quite high and the game gives you a motorcycle early-on that doubles your speed and gives you fast travel.  The fights, particularly boss fights had decent balance: I didn't feel especially challenged by any of them, but I also didn't breeze through them or feel cheated.

Aside from that, all of the story elements are good, as-is the music.  Where "For A Vast Future" departs from older games are combat and leveling.

All of the characters have the same Fight command; they shoot an enemy from the team's ammo pool.  However, aside from basic ammo, there is a huge variety of specialty ammo that any character can equip on their turn as long as another character isn't currently using it.  They will then use that ammo until they switch to something else.  (Changing ammo can also be done outside of combat from the Equip menu.)

The other primary combat command is Wargear; this is essentially the Items command in other games.  Anyone on the team can use any item the team has.  These include healing items, buffs, single target weapons (elemental and neutral), and all-enemy weapons (sometimes damage-all, sometimes damage-target and status-effect-all).  As to the Wargear itself, the vast majority of it can be crafted if you find the schematics.  There is no money in this game; you trade base ammo for specialty ammo, and craft wargear from various forms of scrap.  Ammo and scrap can be found but are also dropped by enemies.

Combat is turn-based, using the Speed stat to determine the combat order for all participants (this can be viewed during combat at any time).  As the fight progresses, either side may inflict status effects that alter the order of who fights next in combat.  Choosing ammo and using wargear winds up becoming much more organic than you might think from just reading the above description.  Different enemies have different strengths and weaknesses, and who is available to deliver what attack isn't guaranteed.

That keeps things interesting even before you factor in how the game handles leveling.  Gaining experience to go up in level only boosts your base stats.  Your characters also earn Skill Points (SP) every battle.  These are used to buy ranks in combat skills.  (These can be reset, for free, any time you're not in combat, so there's no risk in making a mistake.)  This allows you to heavily customize each character to play to their strengths, but the combat stats are the same.  There are also 6 weapon upgrades for each character that allow you to pick between one of two permanent improvements to combat.  These somewhat differ between characters and help you to specialize them.  Overall, the XP-SP system makes the game feel like you're constantly making progress (somewhere) with each character the entire game.

If you don't worry about being a completionist, your total playtime should be around 8 hours.  The Speedrun achievement for finishing FaVF in under 6 hours is definitely doable (though you may want to toggle Autosave off).

A surprisingly solid game.

The preview videos give you a pretty good idea of what the game is like, so check those out if you haven't already.

Is the game worth your time and money? If you like what the preview videos look like, and you like roguelikes, then yes.
If you want some more details, then continue reading.

So what is this game then. It's a roguelike where you explore stages with a few randomly set up hand-crafted rooms in each of them, and deal with the encounters in these rooms. These encounters are most often combat oriented, with some trap avoidance, bonus boss', and "other" types in there to break the monotony. There's also nice risk vs reward thing going on between trying to keep at least 50 coins on hand for the maximum room clear interest bonus vs using that money to buy cards or card slots to get stronger and actually survive the next encounter.

What kinds of rooms you encounter in any given run is determined at home when you make an exploration plan and set out. As far as I can tell, the game is set in and around a castle/manor, and different areas have different levels of pollution, those being light, moderate, heavy, and chaos twisted. On top of this you can select normal, hard, crazy, or nightmare for that exploration plans overall difficulty.

When you clear a room, most of the time you open up an altar. From that altar, you can get new cards, and equip and re-equip the cards you already have. With the exception of the level start shrine, all of them have a tendency towards one type and color of card, as shown by the light they emit, and the symbol hovering in said light. This doesn't guarantee that an orange shrine with a puppet on it will always spawn either type, but you can always spend 2 coins to re-roll the 5 cards offered.

So what are these cards you ask? They're your equipment. It's what makes you kill gud.
Every card has a different type, color, and its own active and passive abilities. Every color has a set bonus, as does every type, so you have to mix and match colors and types, since there are only a handful of cards that share a type and color. The set bonuses do all kinds of different things, like increasing how many bullets you fire per shot, making your bullets explosive/toxic/bouncy, or summoning autonomous stationary shadow turrets etc.

So besides having set bonuses, the cards also have levels, and you power them up by buying more of the same card. Buy 3 of the same card, and they combine into a level 2 variant. Get 3 level 2's and you get a level 3, which is where the upgrades stop.
You get up to 4 active slots, and 6 passive slots, for a total of 10. While equipped the cards type and color are always active, but as you might have guessed, the slot type determines if the cards active or passive ability is activated.
Thankfully the game has a card manual you can open whenever by pressing C, so you don't have to remember every card by heart, and can more easily plan around what shrines you should be rerolling. Now, seeing as the game is a roguelike, you lose all your cards when you die.

Now let's talk progress, as in the stuff you keep even after death. Beating bosses gets you loot to be used in the home base, and collecting lore pages gets you other bonuses like more starting money. The loot can be used to create and upgrade a different type of item. These items give larger straightforward bonuses like more damage or health, but you can only have one of these in use at a time, so that's another choice you need to make for yourself. Then there's the grand daddy of video game progress, beating stages to unlock more stages. It's a simple system. You beat castle floor 1, you unlock floor 2. Beat basement 1, unlock basement 2.

It's a challenging game, and I keep making it more challenging for myself by being too miserly, but I'd still recommend it to fans of the genre.

That should be everything that needs mentioning, but if you, the reader, have further questions, ask away.

This was a delightful hidden gem. For being made by one developer, the amount of content on display is inspiring. The experience overall is a bit unpolished, especially in regards to sound design and particle effects, but none of that holds it back in terms of gameplay and charm.

- Very few bugs. Kind of unexpected from a small indie game.
- charming world design. Great use of color throughout to give off a vaporwave dystopian aesthetic. Love the massive circuit board buildings.
- decent amount of puzzles and game mechanics to keep things feeling fresh. I was never bored.

Neutrals:
- The music is okay. It fits the vibe, but it's harder to listen to for long stretches.
- You have two characters to control, one that shoots and one that punches. The punching wasn't useful for the majority of the combat since most enemies are airborn, which is fine since the shooting makes up for it, but I think that could have used additional fleshing out.

Cons:
- The unpolished bits really held this one back. There were too many times that sound effects were either completely absent or very repetitive, and nearly every attack (player or enemy) is the exact same colored sphere.
- Honestly, sometimes there was too much content. It feels like a weird complaint, but the ending dragged on a bit long by throwing in one too many Hyrule field-sized expanses during parts that should have been a bit more climactic. The dev really showed his chops, but it's okay to hold back for the sake of pacing.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Caribbean Jigsaw has the farcical price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

The main draw and purpose of Inward is to foster a habit of meditation or mindfulness - which can be easy to learn and perhaps never fully mastered but which nevertheless can be of benefit even when not using Inward directly - that is, with the fullness of the practice, you can draw on the teachings regardless of your situation or your surroundings.
 
The guided meditation is very good, the soft sounds, accompanying music, and narration all blend together in a highly complimentary fashion.
 
Compared to its spiritual successor, PLAYNE, Inward is different in a few key areas.  PLAYNE placed a great deal of importance on consecutive days of meditation -- if you missed a day, then your streak was broken. 
Inward is more forgiving in terms of progressing your practice and discovering / unlocking more of your island - it mainly considers the number of days meditated - streaks, or days-meditated-in-a-row, are less central to discovery and progress.
 
Both PLAYNE and Inward have unique and satisfying visuals, music, and ambiance.  I enjoy them both very much.
 
Inward is free to play, so I highly encourage trying it out, especially if new to the concept of mindfulness or curious to learn more about the practice.

Make some noise! Incredibox is a simple music building game where the beatboxing is hot and you fit the beats into a box. Well... circle really. Each kit we'll call it has a little music video to unlock if you find the right peeps to perform. Once you've done that you can get cooking and make your own fire. I took some time to listen to what others came up with and man! You give peeps some tools and they can really put them to use! All in all, this is a great introduction to beat looping and layering. It would probably be a lot of fun to stream with audience participation as well!

The game is nice, but the drag-and-drop feature has its limits. I see that some people have managed to create rather 'advanced' mixes. I guess it's done using macros, but in the end, it's quite limited. Since we have a limited set of samples, it would be better to have more flexibility in placing, removing, and muting them.

We'll enjoy brute-forcing the set to see the animations, but the interface needs a redesign. It's not easy to find how to go back to the style selection. Don't hide the home menu like that.

Edit : My photophobia demands a dark mode.

A highly unique casual puzzle-platformer with cute, kid-friendly visuals, and a good number of engaging levels.
The puzzles are challenging enough to give the average person a fair cognitive workout, while not being so difficult or confusing that it becomes frustrating and not fun to play. 

Honestly, the biggest challenge is the initial learning curve to learn how the splitting mechanic works and what you can do with it. Once you get past that (probably within a few levels or so), the game becomes more intuitive and quite enjoyable. 

I will say, those who have issues with memory, visual persistence, or spatial perception may find this game much more challenging than others. It may seem like a simple mechanic, but it's not a simple cognitive task to store and compare spatial data for two separate and unfamiliar locations in our brains. This is something many of us take for granted, while for others it can be quite difficult, if not impossible to even do at all. 

I bring this up because very few games engage these cognitive tasks to such an extent. The closest thing I can think of are those "spot the difference" puzzles. This is in a very similar category in terms of cognition. 

That said, as a person with fairly average cognitive function, I enjoyed it quite a bit. Though, I still made several mistakes; forgetting the layout of the opposite dimension and getting hurt for it, struggling to comprehend the relationship between the spaces, etc. But that's the whole point, that's the challenge. 

I'd recommend giving it a try. It's well made, fun, and very unique.

[h1]Will you control the Chaos within you or embrace it to create a new future?[/h1]

Our new heroine is Erika – a young lady who is suddenly swept into a world of magic when one day, after her grandma’s recent disappearance, she discovers a secret portal to an alternate world. By travelling through this portal, she ends up in the Arcane Arts Academy – a college where the students learn to use all kinds of magic. There she encounters her grandma who is part of the teacher staff and learns that the reason for her disappearance from the real world was due to an alarming situation inside the academy.

After finding out that she has a witchy heritage and coming to the realization that she has the gift of chaos magic deemed to be very dangerous, Erika decides to enroll in the academy and learn how to control her powers. As she starts her new life as a student of magic, Erika makes new friends but also an enemy, finds love and attempts to help the teachers fight off the threat lingering upon the academy.

The gameplay is pretty much the same as in any other GameHouse game. As Erika, you will help your other college students by fulfilling their requests, combining various ingredients into potions or handing over the items they need for the class, while also billing them at the checkout. As you progress throughout the game, the complexity of available items and combinations increases substantially and the number of students you need to handle simultaneously also grows, while the amount of items you can carry at once also expands. By following GameHouse’s level patterns, each of them is preceded and succeeded by an animated cutscene that unravels a new story snippet.

The coins gathered from billing your fellow students exist only for the score. The stations cannot be upgraded or customized in any way, but there is one external scene – Erika’s room – that you can decorate with the diamonds earned from completing levels; though it is solely serve as a cosmetic value, it gives the player the motivation to retry the levels in order to get 3 stars and thus reaching the maximum diamonds.

What an interesting game!

The video trailer and game description give a decent overview of some of the main aspects of the gameplay, which involve using (some subset of) your available tools to solve a puzzle in the current room.  The large number of tools that each interact with a number of different room elements creates many puzzles that can be solved in multiple ways.  And after you get through the tutorial zone and perhaps a few short individual failed runs, you discover that the game is not merely about solving a series of individual room puzzles.  It's also a resource-management game, where you must realize when rooms have multiple solutions, and then carefully choose which solution--and thus which set of resources--you want to spend on the current room in order to preserve resources you know you will need in another room.  

Each floor of the prison contains about 4-10 rooms, with typically enough tool resources to solve those rooms plus a small surplus.  The surplus tools might let you continue even after making a mistake, or help you save up to purchase alternative/better tools in the occasional shops or bonus rooms you encounter.  Sometimes, to keep your options open, it makes sense to go on to the next floor without solving all the rooms or using all the shops on this floor, planning to return to the prior floor later when you have more (or just different) tool resources to use/spend.

The game is roguelike in that when you make a mistake and die, you restart at the beginning of a (new, random) prison.  But your unlocks are permanent, so once you unlock a new tool type or a new playable character, you will have that available for all future runs.  There is also 'scrap metal' which is a currency you can save across runs to eventually purchase other super-tool unlocks.

Anyway, with that said, here's some thoughts about what I liked or disliked in the game so far:

GOOD

There's a whole lot of content.  After 15 hours of play, I've only unlocked 3 of 4 playable characters and still have about a dozen super-tools I've yet to unlock.  Though I think I've seen most of the unique room layouts (see below), most individual rooms are still challenging to play as part of the overall run; rooms that are completely understood or trivial are still relatively rare.

There is a fun surprise the first time you make it to floor 6, which adds a new layer/twist to the puzzle solving.

A successful run typically takes me about 45 minutes, and is constantly challenging... but also I don't feel I need to play completely optimally to succeed (a mistake or two won't necessarily doom a run, though sometimes it will).

NEUTRAL

While the game is described as a roguelike, the puzzles rooms are not so much randomly generated as just selected from a large finite set of rooms created/curated by the developers, which will sometimes repeat, or appear with minor variations or rotations or reflections.  Early on (in the first few hours of gameplay), this may cause you to wonder if you've already seen most of the puzzle room content, but fear not.  First, many of the rooms won't appear until you've unlocked a tool (so you won't see any battering-ram rooms until you unlock the battering-ram), so some room layouts only first appear after you progress far enough.  Second, even when you find yourself in a familiar room in a subsequent run, you will usually reach it with a different set of resources, and realize e.g. that not only could you solve this room layout with two planks, but you could also solve it with a saw and a brick instead.  And then you may see the same room again, only this time you have a flame, or a bomb, which offers a completely different approach to solving the same room.  The point is, individual rooms are always puzzles in the context of the current run with the current resource set, and so even after room layouts become familiar, the rooms are still challenging to solve well for the current run.

Progress feels a little slow sometimes, but that makes new unlocks also feel very rewarding.  You might have a 25 minute run that dies without making any permanent-unlock progress, but then if you play well in the next run and unlock a new item or character it feels great.

As with many challenging roguelikes (think Spelunky?) sometimes the only way to discover new mechanics/interactions with newly unlocked elements is to try them out, which often may end in your death.  Many mechanics are reasonably intuitive, but you need to be willing to risk the run to learn what pouring a bucket of water across these live wires will do, as the knowledge from the outcome of that experiment (either way) will help you know how to solve puzzles with those elements in the future.  There is no undo.

There's not really any story/dialogue; this is a game about puzzle mechanics, resource management, planning, and recognition.

BAD

The game clearly feels 'indie' in a few ways: the art quality is low; there isn't much animation; the sounds are a little weird; the music is borrowed and kind of weird; there is plenty of room for more polish and usability features. (I know the devs are still working on more feature content as well as polish.)  If you want a game that looks/sounds/feels great this is maybe not the game for you.  This game delivers just enough in those areas to support the core puzzle mechanics.

OVERALL

I like this game because I don't know any other puzzle game quite like it, and because it is constantly challenging and I seem to keep unlocking new content which adds even more wrinkles/depth to the core gameplay.

[b]That other game.[/b]
There used to be a game called "The Castle Doctrine" (TCD), which this game takes much inspiration from, but by adapting the game to a new foundation, solves a lot of the problems of that game. In TCD, the goal was to both create a deadly maze in your home, while venturing out into other players' homes with a limited set of tools to find and exploit a weakness in their maze. Sometimes this meant sawing through a weak wall, or snipping a critical wire that powered their traps. 

The main problem with TCD though, was its own players. There was very little incentive to create fun puzzles in that game, so most ended up being boring to play, and the game killed itself when people started building impossible puzzles like combination locks.

The thing is... when you did find a fun maze, and you did find a weakness in a maze, it was really damn fun.

[b]Puzzle-Roguelike foundation[/b]
Herman Electro comes disposes of the entire multiplayer element, brings its own twists in the form of being a roguelike, but finds inspiration in the same type of puzzle. It works better. The puzzles are designed to make the player feel smart, and have fun.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
You play in a world that is very typical of modern roguelikes - you walk around a dungeon with a bunch of rooms, most of which contain a puzzle for you to solve, the world is divided into floors, and the deeper you go, the harder it gets. 

Most puzzles are designed around exploiting traps by using consumable items that you've gathered by completing other puzzles. The challenge comes managing your usage of those tools. You usually don't want to use too many on a single puzzle. The thing is, floors usually work as one huge puzzle - maybe you spot an exploit in one puzzle but don't have the tool for it, but that tool is a reward for another puzzle on the same floor. There's a lot to think about.

The roguelike nature generates different floors from a huge pool of puzzles so the game is different each time you play. The reason I mention this is to point out that the puzzles themselves are hand-crafted (which is a good thing).

[b]Presentation[/b]
The game's presentation isn't incredible, but if you can immerse yourself in the gameplay (and, in my personal opinion, turn off the music in favor of your own), it's serviceable, and I think the price now reflects that. Although the graphics aren't the most beautiful, they do what is important for a puzzle game and clearly show you what is happening, which is the important bit.

[b]Do I recommend?[/b]
Absolutely, if you enjoy the random "run based" nature of roguelike games, but want to solve puzzles rather than shooting tears at nightmarish creatures, I highly recommend this. The game used to be priced much higher which made it harder to recommend, but at the current price it is honestly a steal for the amount of content packed into here, if it's your thing.

The game is - well, for me - ruined by the screen that after finishing the puzzle instantly hides the griddler completely. Yes - you cannot see the result of your work. This bad decision seems to be a general problem of 8floor games. I have already played a mosaic jigsaw by 8floor: Once you have finished the jigsaw puzzle, you are not allowed to see the picture.
There are people who enjoy looking at the work they have done, and that can include jigsaw puzzles. So why aren't you allowed to see the finished picture? Admittedly, in the mosaic games, you can at least see the tiny preview icons. Obviously, such a preview would totally spoil the griddler, so a preview is not possible. And that's why the hiding screen on top of the solved griddler is so much more annoying: You simply cannot concentrate on the abstract dots of the griddler as a whole and then let your imagination unravel the meaning of those dots.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features extremely lazy, minimalist "art", of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with crappy "wings" to pad out the space).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

"Fill and Cross Pirate Riddles" has the gamer gouging price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

Outcasts of Orion is an autobattler roguelike combining a solid game loop and varied strategic potential to offer an engaging experience with much replayability. You draft from a variety of randomly presented abilities and units to craft your squad and discover unexpected synergies. The game does struggle a bit early on in conveying the appeal of its mechanic, but given some time, it reveals an underlying layer of depth that keeps you coming back. If you are a fan of either autobattlers or strategy roguelikes, this game is worth giving a shot.
------------------------------------------------------

At its core, Outcasts of Orion plays as an autobattler with positioning as the central focus. Each unit has a defined pattern of attack and behavior that can be predicted and taken advantage of. Similar to chess, it is key to know your own unit's compatibility with others and to think a few turns ahead to emerge victorious. Early parts of the game start with a basic rock, paper, scissors type of dynamic, with additional unit classes
making an appearance to add more variables for consideration.

However, the game shines brightest in its factions. Factions are a set of units that share unique traits and abilities where each faction offers a different take on existing unit classes. For example, an assassin can stealthily execute an enemy, blind and stun an enemy, or turn an enemy into an ally to swarm the field.
All are examples of how different faction can fulfill the same assassin role in differing ways. Beyond just careful positioning, there was much fun to be had in experimenting with different factions to discover unexpected synergies and exploits.

Though the game leads strong with a tight core game loop, the game does come with some areas that could be improved. Mainly, the game could benefit from a stronger tutorial as it leaves some areas unexplained. Even though I managed to pick up many aspects through trial and error, I imagine a gentle nudge in the right direction could go a long way in easing new players into the strategic potential of the game. Still, there were frequent updates by the developers that quickly addressed pain points. This gives me confidence that the developers are dedicated to continuously make the game better.

Overall, Outcasts of Orion is an engaging game with strategic depth and unexpected discoveries that has kept me coming back for more. I definitely recommend this game, and am looking forward to what more the developer has in store for the future.

Simple game mechanics can be an asset or a quick road to monotony depending on the context. Infinite Jump contains just that, very simple gameplay mechanics: perpetual movement to the right, frequent jumps over obstacles, and occasional shooting. I feel like I've got a bit of an obligation as the first reviewer to give more detail than I typically would otherwise.  I initially read Wizard's Choice (and other Delight Games content) on their mobile platform a while ago, so just know going in that the story content itself isn't new to me.  I've also been in touch with the dev team in the past and they've been very responsive, so I'm glad to have the opportunity to support the game here on Steam.  (Also note that my gameplay time doesn't reflect the time it takes to complete the game, which should take you about as long as it takes to read a fantasy novel cover to cover, each playthrough.)

If you aren't aware already, this game takes the form of a book with illustrations and branching choices.  Not a visual novel, but a book, with choices made to affect the outcomes of specific scenes.  It reads like a well-spun D&D campaign, with plenty of action, occasional silliness, and a dark atmosphere.

Delight Games stories are consistently solid, and they typically have a more tactical element to them than other interactive fiction games.  Wizard's Choice is no exception.  This is rooted in the stats that are tracked throughout each chapter, which function as both resources to enable specific choices as well as your final score for the chapter.  Sure, you can spam fireballs to get through things if you want, but ultimately you're going to run out of mana, and once that happens, you're going to have to get pretty crafty to stay alive.  However, the start of each chapter brings your stats back to default so you don't have to worry about whether you're going to mess up the whole book by being trigger-happy in the first few scenes.  

You will encounter situations where choices don't pan out the way you hoped or expected, and things sometimes happen to your character that you have no control over.  Personally, I think this is a point in the game's favor.  You make the best decision you can based on the information you have available and how badly you need to ration your stats.  This approach also ensures that the game doesn't force you to make every. single. choice. for your character.  

There are illustrations every few pages, and overall the UI is simple, but works.  The graphic effects may be distracting to some, but having come from the plain text version before, I find that I prefer the Steam copy.

Appears to be a CYOA with game-book mechanics (like Lone Wolf series), but it plays more like a Visual Novel style game. You are given three choices, with choice A giving a small benefit, choice B giving no benefit, and choice C resulting in a resource penalty, but they all advance the story to the next page. It's all trial and error to find the a path that will not end the progression because of resource depletion. Then, it's back to the beginning of the story again, to try different choices that successfully end of the chapter. How many times are you going to re-read the same first chapter story, recording your previous choice outcomes on some paper, so you can try to access the next chapter. For me, that number was two. The game designers should have added something to help with this boring task - like a save system or in-game record of choice outcomes.

This is a pretty good "choose-your-own-adventure" book, in computer form.  The story is well written, and the music and artwork are pretty good.  It has a bit less divergence in storylines than I might choose, but at least this way I'm not too worried about missing large pieces of plot.  The health/mana/gold resources are a clever idea, allowing various combinations of bad choices before the player loses.  The challenge is well constructed, and a player can avoid most of the bad decisions with critical thinking and reading carefully.

On Linux, there is a bug where the cursor renders at a massive size, but it doesn't detract much from the game and frankly I'm just happy to have another linux-compatible game.

The Good:

- The story is well-written even if it's not going to be everyone's cup of tea.
- The music suits the story.
- It is pleasing enough visually.

The Bad:

- You're stuck with only one good outcome so choice doesn't really matter since there aren't multiple ways, or paths, to success.  The main selling point for this game (choice) doesn't really exist or at least not in more than a superficial way.
- Except for the female priest cleric I hated all the characters including the one that you play.  This is personal preference but I felt an absence of any that were endearing in any way.

The Ugly:

- This game is very, very dark and could offend some.  Granted some D&D modules are like that but it's worth mentioning that this isn't for kids.  
- This game falsely advertises choice.  It is not the choice I expect from games like this.

It is a lot like the "John Wick" movie series: The first chapter you have a fighter buddy helping to keep the riff raff away so you can work your mojo. And an implied support system back in town. I liked the first "John Wick" movie because he was free to do his "thing" without fear. 

In Chapter 2, your Wizard is on the run, being hunted by everybody, like John Wick in Chapter 2 on. And one of the little "tips" that pops up on the loading screen says in the higher chapters your mental stat becomes as important as your health points; this leads me to think the Cult you ran across  causes eventual strain on your sanity that must be managed.  All this is NOT "breaking the game", it's just not something  I personally enjoy so it still gets a Yes vote from me and the game is reasonably priced so I am not upset. But I will end here.

If you have looked through the discussions, you will have noticed that the comments that this early access game has been abandoned.  This may or may not be the case, only time will tell.  Having played through the game for a while now, I personally hope that this will not turn out to be the case.  However, even if abandoned, there are aspects of this game that make it stand out, the primary one being the crafting.  Unlike most build/craft games that provide pre-made walls, furniture, or even whole buildings, this game provides a very unique and highly capable build system based on primatives.  

Through the use of these primatives, you can craft significantly more complex objects than can be found in most, if not all, other survival games currently on the market.  The only similar crafting system I have seen is found within Second Life.  Unlike Second life, however, there is no limit or cost to the number of prims that are used, so you can build really complex objects.  That being said, this game does lack a few of the nicer design elements found in second life:  you cannot upload your own textures, prims cannot be spliced into sub-shapes (i.e., a quarter sphere, holf a torus, etc.) and you cannot place different textures on different sides of an object.

You ability that this game has, though, is that the different material textures are linked to resources.  So, if you choose to make your object out of wood, you will need to chop trees.  Stone, you will need to mine (the voxel based world is also a great feature).  If your build uses multiple materials, you will need multiple materials to craft it and the requirement is dependent on the size object that you are creating.  This building system is what truly makes this game stand out from it peers.

Where it lacks, however, is actual game play.  The sun rises and sets, the shadows move, but unless you love building objects, there is not actually very much to do at this point in the development.  If there are creatures, villiages, NPC, or any other game elements, I have not found them yet.

So, if you simply love to build for the sake of making nice structures (you can build your house, plan your garden or otherwise use it as a CAD program, if you want), this game is for you.  If you are looking for a playable game, this is not one you should get yet.  Hopefully it is not abandoned and the game will continue to be developed.  If it is, it could become a outstanding game.  As it is, it essentially, a fun CAD system..  Only time will tell.  I hope this helps those who read it.  I will update the review if and when the game is further updated.

[u]In short:[/u] Yarne is a meditative, simplistic puzzle game about stretching and arranging strings. The levels are well designed and can get fairly difficult. The minimalist aesthetic does not excuse the lack of settings and several elements of jankiness. Even for roughly 5 hours of unique content I wouldn't recommend buying at full price, but on sale it's a decent pick-up if you're looking for a relaxing puzzle game.

[u]In long:[/u] The [b][u]mechanics[/u][/b] are fairly simple. Each level is comprised of hexagonal tiles. Some have polygons inside which represent curled-up strings. Grab them with the mouse and unravel them by crossing into different tiles. Since strings cannot cross, the challenge lies in finding configurations that allow all strings to be fully stretched out.
At first this is an easy task because of open boards and lots of surplus paths, but later [b][u]levels[/u][/b] can get fairly challenging. The game seems primitive at first, but over time certain patterns emerge and the aspect of iteration and problem solving becomes more prominent. It may not look like it, but the second half is certainly a full-blown puzzle game beyond just trial and error, and obvious solutions. Yarne has 100 hand-made levels across 4 sets. Usually there are multiple paths to the end of a set, allowing you to skip some levels if you get stuck. Later sets introduce longer or shorter strings, but walls are the only real new mechanic the game has to offer. I like how levels are thematically grouped and the difficulty curve is pretty well done. I had 95 of the 100 levels beaten in about 4.5 hours, but then got horribly stuck on a particular level for over 7 hours. If you are smarter than me (or willing to use the guide I published) you should expect roughly 5 hours of content from this game.

The [b][u]presentation[/u][/b] is generally well done and follows a minimalist aesthetic. Almost too minimalist as the menus are fairly indiscernable as well. The visuals are just pixellated lines on single-colour backgrounds. If yellow on blue is not your thing you gradually unlock 7 different themes/palettes. Finished levels tend to yield interesting and pretty patterns. The sound effects are simple but nice. The music is just a nice atmospheric loop that gives the game a fairly meditative feeling.
My only gripe with the presentation is the weird off-by-one counting system the game uses. Strings are wrapped up into polygons that gradually straighten out the more moves you make. These polygons stand for numbers and you can also toggle a straight-up nummeric display. So how many moves should a square denoted with 4 make? The answer is three. The first move counts it down to triangle/3, the second to line/2 and the third move marks it as solved. To me this makes absolutely no sense. Why would 1 be the target and not 0? Why does the shape not tell me the number of moves it can make?

The [b][u]technical side[/u][/b] is lacking. The game starts windowed in a fixed 1600x900 resolution and there is no ingame way of changing that (undocumented Alt+Enter works for full-screen though). In fact, there are no ingame settings at all, except for a mute button that for some reason affects sound effects but not the background music. I've never seen an odd arrangement like this.
Sometimes the game also wouldn't let me make legal moves and at the end, clicking around on the credits page I somehow managed to soft-lock the game into a level I could not exit again. It's stable (as expected from a Unity game), but there is definitely some jank with minor bugs going on.

Sadly you shouldn't expect any kind of support form the developers, as this game seems all but abandoned. Time to delve into the [b][u]background[/u][/b] of the game a bit. This game has all the hallmarks of a mobile port (no exit button, bad menus, virtually no settings, etc), but I could not find a mobile release anywhere. You have to scower the [url=https://rowanqueue.itch.io/yarne]game's itch.io page[/url] to find mention of an old iOS prototype "soon to be updated". This page is also where you can play the first 25 levels of the game in your browser as a demo, while the last post on the Steam forums is someone asking for a demo almost 1 year ago and never getting a reply. Yeah, it's pretty dead. One of the developers mentions on his [url=parkercrandell.com]personal website[/url], "Before I joined the team, Yarne only had an endless mode with randomly generated levels. [...] Many of the puzzles in Yarne are simply about teaching the players the fun and interesting patterns I found in development and then building out more interesting challenges from there." That is all fine and dandy, but where is this fabled endless mode now? It is available for free on [url=https://armorgames.com/yarne-game/19102]Armor Games[/url], but not included in the paid Steam version. Admittedly, it seems fairly primitive and would greatly benefit from user-controlled parameters (size, complexity, difficulty), but still... if you have a finished endless mode, why not put it into your product?

In [b][u]conclusion[/u][/b] I have some mixed feelings about Yarne. The game itself is fine, though quite simple and with a weird counting system. The levels are mostly well-made and often resolve into neat patterns, but an endless mode was seemingly cut from the game and could have greatly benefitted replayability. The settings are a joke and some minor bugs persist due to lack of developer support. It's janky, but if you know what you're getting yourself into, I can recommend buying this on sale.

Six Days in Fallujah is a controversial first-person tactical shooter that attempts to recreate the intense urban combat of the Second Battle of Fallujah during the Iraq War. Developed by Highwire Games and released in 2024, the game aims to blend documentary-style storytelling with realistic gameplay, but ultimately falls short of its lofty ambitions.

The game's core gameplay loop revolves around leading a fireteam of US Marines through procedurally generated urban environments. The combat is unforgiving, with just a few shots capable of taking you down. When critically wounded, you have a short window to be revived by teammates before bleeding out. Squad communication and teamwork are essential for survival. This creates a tense, high-stakes atmosphere that can be engaging when everything clicks.

As a squad-based tactical shooter, Six Days in Fallujah emphasizes careful planning and strategic decision-making over run-and-gun action. Players can issue commands to their AI squadmates, such as providing suppressing fire or breaching rooms. The procedurally generated missions ensure that no two playthroughs are identical, adding to the tension and unpredictability. This randomness can lead to some memorable moments, but it can also result in frustrating scenarios where luck plays too large a role.

One of the game's most touted features is its attempt to blend gameplay with documentary-style storytelling. The game includes interviews with US Marines, Iraqi soldiers, and civilians who were present during the actual battle. These segments aim to provide context and personal perspectives on the events being portrayed. While this approach is novel, the execution often feels disjointed, with the documentary elements failing to meaningfully integrate with the gameplay.

Visually, Six Days in Fallujah is competent but not outstanding. The game effectively conveys the claustrophobic nature of urban combat, with detailed interiors and atmospheric effects like dust clouds that limit visibility. The weight of your equipment is palpable in your movement, adding to the sense of realism. However, some animations can feel stiff, and the overall graphical fidelity doesn't push any boundaries.

The game's most significant issues lie in its handling of its sensitive subject matter. Critics argue that Six Days in Fallujah fails to adequately address the controversial aspects of the battle, including civilian casualties and alleged war crimes. The game's perspective is heavily skewed towards the US military viewpoint, with limited representation of Iraqi experiences. This one-sided approach undermines the game's claims of historical accuracy and documentary-like presentation.

Furthermore, the game's portrayal of the conflict has been criticized for glossing over the complexities of the situation. For example, it fails to address how US forces barred many Iraqi men from leaving the city before the battle, effectively trapping civilians in a war zone. The game also doesn't fully explore the long-term consequences of the battle on Fallujah and its people.

In conclusion, Six Days in Fallujah is a mechanically solid tactical shooter that offers tense, challenging gameplay. However, its attempts to tackle a recent, controversial historical event fall short, resulting in a game that feels both incomplete and potentially insensitive. While it may appeal to fans of hardcore military shooters, its handling of its subject matter is likely to leave many players uncomfortable.

Score: 6/10 - A competent tactical shooter marred by its problematic approach to sensitive historical events.

[h1] Silent Days in Fallujah[/h1]
(0.4.1.1)


You play as a US Marine during the battle for Fallujah. Each battle has a core objective based on a historical event, with landmarks being influenced as such, though optional objectives and the surrounding map are randomly generated. Objectives typically focus on clearing buildings or sabotaging enemy implements/fortifications. You have the choice of playing with either three other humans or a team of AI. This game does consult with veterans of the actual battle, and has recorded interviews with them. It should be noted: this is a later iteration of the game, not the original attempt shrouded in controversy. Any claims that the development has taken a decade are inaccurate.


[b]Pros[/b]
-Diegetic Mechanics
You have an armored personnel carrier (AAVP), on most missions, following you. To refill your ammunition, you pull it off your rucksack hanging off the side. To revive teammates, you have more marines dismount from inside the AAVP. To check your map and objectives, technically the game says you're checking a satphone but the overlay is just a menu so only half marks for that. Still, there is a concerted effort to keep the player in the game world.


-Claustrophobic Details
ADSing has two stages, point firing and actual sighting. The player's weapon barrel will be rebuffed by standing to close to a wall. You can get barrel stuffed by tight corners. Height over bore exists. All of these are great for realistic, quick-paced fighting expected in an urban environment.


-Innovative First Aid/Healing
I just want to throw this in here because I always appreciate when a game tries to do more than a 'get shot - hit hot key' mechanic. Granted, it doesn't go much further than that, but still it's a bit more. Each hit is actually a potential shot, with your character needing to take cover and pat himself down. There's a chance it turns out you're just being panicky, and nothing touched you. Other times, your gloves come up bloody and you have to self-aid. Now, self-aid is just a hot key and wait. But, still. Additionally, there's a deeper state of wounding where you have to limp out of the way and a squadmate has to work you over. So, there are a few layers to healing. It's not braindead; it's not full TCCC. But, I appreciate the thought that went into it. 


[b]Cons[/b]
-Low Playability
To be clear, this game has excellent replayability with how it handles RNG. That is fantastic. Unfortunately, there are two main problems with this game's core mechanics: Room clearing is a brutal and bloody drill that you typically will only perform with 3-to-1 odds. In SDF, however, you have a total of four fireteam members (plus the AI machinegun on the AAVP, should it actually be in a position to fire on the enemy). If you are playing online with randos, you are playing with three individuals you have not practiced this with. You do not know their skill levels or even if they have a microphone. In two hours, I had 1/3 lobbies where the host and other party members did not have a microphone or even use the ping function. This made the game unbearable. The 2/3 where we did have communication, it devolved into everyone trying to rush to beat the ridiculously short mission timer (a feature you can turn off in settings). There was constant miscommunication, people talking over each other, and repeated friendly fire. Both lobbies devolved into angry finger pointing. And that was with waiting around 5-10 minutes for a lobby at all, on a Friday. The AI singleplayer is even worse. It is unreal how bad the AI is in 2025. Your teammates walk in front of your muzzle. They stand around outside after you order them to kick-and-flood a room. And then, when you toss a frag through a window at the next house, two of them randomly decide it's their time and they follow the grenade on inside. They will get incapacitated by machine gun fire and then continue to limp towards the machinegunner instead of falling back. This essentially makes singleplayer impossible. 


-Developer Silence
There seems to be little official word from the developers between massive updates. There are great updates with plenty of stuff involved, but little to reassure folks that development is continuing between these long updates. Now, there is a developer politely replying to some Steam forum posts. That is positive. But in general, the studio seemingly goes into hibernation after each update. Should something happen to them between updates that cancels the game, it makes me wonder if they even would say anything about it. 


-Graphics
On a 4090RTX, there are many disappointing aspects to this. ADSing scopes reveals splotchy textures. Even with DLSS, there can be extremely pixelated edges. If there are more than 4-5 enemies on screen, their animations become choppy. Smoke grenade effects struggle depending on how far away you get from them. The differences between the levels of quality also don't seem to change that much either, so it leaves me wondering why there is so much struggle at higher levels when they all are similar to Valve source textures.


Overall, I hesitate to say this is a buy-and-wait. I believe the developers' strange approach to communication is harmful and negates their hard work. While current gameplay is hampered by bad AI and the small playerbase, there is absolutely potential for vast improvements to the game. However, whether there will be a community around to see them is another thing.

"Colossus Mission - adventure in space, arcade game" is a somewhat unimaginative Moonlander/SpaceWar!/Asteroids-in-a-maze game where you control the space shuttle in a cavern/complex and must move through each level using Moonlander/SpaceWar! style turn and thrust movement.  There's a number of obstacles to avoid as you need to keep your health up, and running into stuff hurts you, but there's "healing" blobs strewn about to help you keep going. 

On the upside this is story driven as you explore some alien ship but get teleported somewhere else.  While some effort went into game design, and there's over 70 bespoke levels (none of which are fun to play), the technical implementation was phoned in.  While the game works it's laughably bad in some parts... like the space shuttle you control is a 2D sprite that's been rendered from an angle, so you get this bizarre, frankly stupid view of your ship rotating around and the shadows etc looking just wrong... it's really terrible.  Did they flip the asset for the spaceship?  That might explain why it looks so misplaced.  The rest of the game isn't any better, either.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features somewhat lazy, simplistic 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.  

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

"Colossus Mission - adventure in space, arcade game" is relatively cheap at $3 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

This game is very similar to a game series called: "Emily is Here" wherein you're logging onto an old computer to chat with random people about nothing. the only difference is one game imitates AOL voice messaging software, while the other imitates a message service built from scratch on a floppy disk, called a BBC. 

Both have incredible potential to be interesting and/or exciting, but both games fail to be either, unless melodrama and insecure characters talking about mundane bullshit is your idea of entertainment. 

It is a well-built game(There were light glitches, but they were not a large hindrance on the game's mechanics) with great potential, squandered by Teenage Melodrama. Very Disappointing. 

The player choice aspect of the game was silly at best. The closest to a divergent answer with various endings was being asked if I preferred to "eat cereal with or without milk" or if I didn't want to answer. This game is more like a visual novel with certain binary choices, as opposed to a game that can have many endings depending on how you play. Personality Tests on Quotev are more interesting than this. There needs to be more branching paths for the story, and there needs to be an actual story, not just a flat conversation about random nonsense that anyone could make up. I'd play for the other endings, as I"m sure there are more, but listening to a bunch of characters written to be like adolescents just gathering on some discord server and engaging with small talk gets tedious very quickly. Who wants to listen to other people talk, if they have nothing of note to say?

The characters in this game all act like a bunch of insecure morons who just talk about boring day to day stuff, and then get upset if we don't answer them a certain way. This game reminded me of how insufferable and annoying teenagers are, and for this, and other reasons, I am only playing this game once.

Objectively speaking, The Graphics are Good, as well as the basic mechanics of the game, it runs fluidly for the most part, and the dad jokes were hilarious, but the story was lame, and the gameplay could be more expanded upon for this or future games, as this game ultimately is a cheap clone of Emily is Here(Since it's a dollar and all). without the customizing options and quirky humor and love triangle that made "Emily is Here" at least engaging.

If you read this game developers, I have a suggestion for the stories for your future games: This game was boring and lame, and if you want to fix that, give people a good reason for wanting to engage with your interesting idea. What if there was a glitch that was alive that possessed the email service, and messed up the email system to place you in a platformer game haphazardly put together by this "glitch" of interest with glitchy texts and stuff to unveil some deep secret, or what if this happened if you clicked on the admin option? i can see this game is going for a realistic tone with how much love was poured into the process of old computers being booted up(Which was a nice touch, definitely keep that), but there should be something going on. What if the creator of the service was working for government and they were part of some psyop test that was to test out the future for social media companies like Facebook to use now? Or What if all the characters were aliens attempting to understand teenage/adolescent behavior? Something needs to happen, the game was flat because nothing happened. You logged on, you talked, and then you logged off. This should not be marketed as strange and mysterious, with "internet  Strangers" when nothing happens, there's not even a lot of buildup! A Computer virus is as mediocre of a plot device as they come, especially since it happened at the end, and it barely impacted the story.

One of those story lines I mentioned could've been a cool underlying "secret," over the regular boring chat stuff, something like how "pony Island" was, or "Don't Chat with Strangers" which while were of a different genre, still carried a similar retro 90s style of gaming that was promoted in this game. It could also have More than 10 endings, like in "The Stanley Parable" too.

Lots of potential, met with a plateau, a rise to a flat.

But no, the dumb secret just leads you to this stupid ending where you're supposed to be "sad" that you failed a french class exam, and that your internet friends don't like you anymore, and that you spent time alone. This is a sad ending? It's more of a neutral ending if anything, because how can I connect with characters who are nothing but passive aggressive Lame-Os? I'm certainly not sad at the end, I'm not even engaged. Where' the interesting plot? Where's "THE CAKE?"(See what I did there?)

You can do waaaay better than this, I clearly can make a better story than you can, that's a sign you didn't try hard enough.  Hope to see your next game is way better than this one, because this was nothing short of disappointing.
