Castle Shikigami 2 aka Shikigami No Shiro 2 is another bullet hell SHMUP that adds a unique mechanic known throughout the franchise as Bullet Tension.  Basically, your character has a colored aura around them which turns red at maximum risk and your score multiplier and shot power are increased when grazing bullets with your character's hitbox.  This is the ultimate form of risk vs reward in a shmup, and most bullets are slow so that you can do special setups depending on the character you are using.  This is what I would personally consider the best in the franchise, and a really solid pickup overall if you never had access to previous ports of this game released back in the PS2/Xbox era.  It feels pretty accurate to arcade as well based on what I have seen so far for those that are concerned about arcade accuracy.

The one thing that isn't a con for me but will be a con for others is that there is no presence of the infamous meme English dub here as there was on the NA PS2 release.  This isn't a real issue for me personally, especially since I have uploaded ALL of the english dub to two Youtube videos.  If you really need that horrendous meme English dub you can always refer to those videos.  1/14/2022 Edit: NeoStrayCat has put up a guide on Steam to mod in all of that audio if you want it per a comment left by them.

Otherwise, this is a really solid port of a game that nobody should ignore and people should play it instead of remembering it only for it's meme English dub.

One of the best shootemups finally gets a widely available PC port. 

The new translation finally obsoletes the old, awful, meme translation that people only laughed at. Watch those cutscenes on youtube, laugh, and then come to appreciate the real work that went into meticulously localizing all the character dialog, weird and funny scenes, and the strange lore of the franchise that is strangely compelling the more you get into it.

The publishers and developers are keen on frequently patching the game and it has come a long way from launch. Bugs I have complained about on launch have since been fixed and more issues keep on being ironed out. This is a good sign that shows the devs are taking care of this release (unlike say, Cotton Reboot which was abandoned on steam with bugs). 

The gameplay is addictive. Each of the 6 characters (plus one "hidden" character, Chibi Fumiko) plays wildly different from one another, each necessitating their own strategies and play styles. The scoring makes the game as hard as you want it to be - want lots of coins? Risk it all by getting as close to bullets or enemies as possible and use your shikigami familiar to wipe them out. Want to play it safe? Hang back and let your normal shot take care of things... But you won't get as many lives and bombs that way. It's a great trade-off.

On top of that you have unique and interesting stages and lots, lots LOTS of memorable and interesting bosses and minibosses. Each boss outside of the first midboss (more of a tutorial really) has its own gimmick, and some of the human characters who face off with you rival and outshine what you would see in say, a touhou game (in fact, it's quite likely that ZUN homaged, or copied, several of their attack patterns for his own games, as he is wont to do). 


I love shmups with diverse rosters and excellent boss fights, so this game is tailor-made for me. The fact that its scoring system (the coin collectin' based on your proximity, aka the Tension System) is so fun is just another huge bonus. Don't wait on this, grab it, grab the first game, and even Sisters Royale (the unofficial Castle of Shikigami 4).

This is a great shmup that has stood the test of time. The "New Entry" mode is a great addition worthy of your time. The port quality it's a firm "OK" from me.  No problems with lag/slowdown, but the lack of certain features hold it back from being the definitive iteration of the arcade game, despite that being the mode with the most features. What's missing is:

1) Practice mode for all game types. This is the biggest problem. There is a stage select feature for the arcade mode only. The lack of this feature for New Entry or Dramatic Change modes is a real drag. 
2) Ability to select game rank (very easy, easy, normal, hard, very hard) and change score extends thresholds. The previous windows port and PS2 versions had these features. Odd that they are missing here as the steam version of Shiki 1 also has the equivalent options.  
3) Replays. I'm not sure if the PS2 version had this but the old windows version does.
4) Extra options (bullet size, hitbox displays etc). These were some goofy options in the PS2 port. I don't think the old windows version had them but could be mistaken. 
5) Graphical glitches - broken textures which can effect anything from text to enemy bullets and explosions.

This game gives you a one-pixel hitbox yet almost all the enemy bullets have a long tail and are slightly random in direction which makes it harder than it seems. Playable characters are plenty and their stats and abilities vary greatly which gives you a whole lotta time to challenge, though balanced poorly.

I'm rating Isonzo an 8.5/10 for now, potentially a 9/10 if they tweaked a few things but I'll rate it as a 9 officially on Steam. WW1 is my favorite war from a historical perspective and as such I play a lot of games from that period, but I don't like smelling my own farts so I'll get right into how I feel about this game and what I believe could be improved.

Isonzo is the best/most historically accurate WW1 FPS shooter on the market, so if that is important to you like it is to me then you're in luck. The game has incredible graphics, strong map design, solid player customization and a decent soundtrack but the lack of weapons/customization, balancing issues, lack of squad-comm dynamics and limited map choice hold it back. I honestly believe BTW (Beyond the Wire) was better than Isonzo as an overall WW1 FPS  in the early days of the two, especially if you got a full lobby because there was much more rich, funny and strategic team banter/communication integrated into every game or for whatever reason it has always felt that way to me. I think the map variety and the the gun-play felt a lot more clean and responsive (again, in the early days) as well. 

That said, Isonzo has done what BTW didn't or couldn't do and has done a great job with marketing, which, along with their commitment to creating new content is what has kept it alive up until this point. The game being well-made and fun certainly helps with that but unfortunately I don't believe its enough to sustain the player base long term. I personally believe Isonzo should be completely re-branded and expanded beyond just the Italian front of the war, they should make it into one all encompassing WW1 FPS title and I know I'm not the only person who feels that way. I would like them to remaster/remake Verdun and integrate it into the Isonzo package all together as one full game instead of having each of them as stand alone titles. I know why they are, but it just feels so unnecessarily inefficient to me. I don't like going from playing a modern, overall better game into something dated and clunky with the graphics of a toaster if I get bored with the current map rotation. 

I'm not sure how difficult something like that would be but I know it's not an impossible feat. Maybe the devs could buy the rights to BTW and rip/redesign their maps, adopt/adapt those squad mechanics, integrate gore and dismemberment etc. I'm not sure how possible any of this is from the technical perspective, I'm just spit-balling ideas for fun because I believe they would improve the game. Whatever the case and regardless of my opinion on any of it, Isonzo as it is right now is a great game and has without a doubt surpassed every other WW1 FPS I've personally played before including BTW and I held that game in high esteem for quite awhile, but in case this reads like I'm sucking off BTW that isn't my intent. I actually have far more hours on Isonzo than BTW (140+ on my other account) and BTW is a dead game now.

I just feel like it did a lot of things better and this title could be and do so much more if they would expand it to encompass the entirety of WW1 as a singular title, experimented with mechanics other games had or created some new concepts of their own. (not that they don't already, hopefully you know what I mean) I just want to see this game succeed and flourish for a long time because I wouldn't spend 30 minutes writing a review this long otherwise but it' should be clear that I care about it's future. Whatever the case, even if they do just stick with the current script PLEASE integrate more blood and create dismemberment because not only is it historically accurate but it adds an additional layer of entertainment and realism to the experience. Thanks for reading if you did!

From the single player/offline perspective: The short for playing on Steam Deck: be prepared to strain your eyes unless you choose sniper, in order to be playable (30-50fps) the quality is so low that using iron sights is painful.

Massive maps, you play either defence or offence and as offence, you have to make your way securing multiple points/sectors across this wide corridor style map, it's pretty great.
The maps have good veriaty and aren't all equal, some are easier to defend than others and I really enjoyed the difficulty navigating the terrain during combat.
Lots of bots running around that aren't too bad to play against, only real downsides are:
Friendly bots don't re-arm you or drop ammo crates, but they will heal you. Some classes just don't have enough ammunition so you need to kill yourself if you want more.
They won't use upgraded equipment, so you'll always be going against basic infantry and the occasional pistol equiped officer, no snipers, machine gunners (that aren't fixed emplacements) or grenadiers.

Graphics are beautiful and attention to detail on the weapons and how they function is impressive, even rarely getting a jam. My favourite is that the character will chamber the round while the stripper clip is still attached, pushing it out, which you often don't see in games. If you re-load your weapon while your magazine still has rounds in it, you'll either add rounds one by one, or have to remove them before adding a new clip, it entirely depends on the rifle which is very accurate to their real world usage. It makes each rifle feel unique as you'll have to take it into account whether or not you can re-load/add rounds in time, switch to a sidearm, or drop back to re-load. It adds a whole new dynamic I've not experienced in an FPS.

1, 2 BLAME! is a multiplayer only game in the style of Among Us, or the more traditional Werewolf/Town of Salem style games where 1 (or more) players are trying to sabotage/kill the rest of the team without being detected. 1, 2 BLAME manages to put some interesting spins on the Among Us formula by introducing the Accomplice role, changing how voting works with a timeout jail and more serious consequences for voting out an innocent player, powerful items scattered throughout the map that can help all roles, and by changing activities to require two steps: acquisition and submission (complete the task and then upload the results). There's also proximity chat and a comprehensive customisation menu for the in-game rules built in, making this a feature rich experience.
Sadly, the game is a ghost town, so unless you have at least 4 friends (total party of 5 required to start a game) I would recommend trying the free app version before purchasing on Steam. There are also some cosmetic micro-transactions in the game, and while it's disappointing to see somewhat predatory pricing points for the gem packs (always slightly less than what you need), there's nothing available that offers an in-game advantage, and a reasonable supply of premium currency can be earned in-game.

tl;dr
Good fun if you have enough friends, but try the free mobile version before buying on Steam.

Combat Chess is an ancient game from 1997.  It's a whopping 26 years old at the time of this review.  The game lacks support for any modern gaming display resolutions, hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on modern gaming PCs.  In fact it's so dated it seems to expect to run in a Windows 3.11/Windows 95 windowed session.  Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an ancient game.  This seems to have been put on Steam as a nostalgia gouge.

The game itself is just a lazy, unabashed ripoff of Battle Chess (copyright Electronic Arts, 1988).  We can hope that EA will sue these guys into the ground, but given the game itself is based on Chess and thus at least in part, public domain, and EA have had 26 years to enforce their copyright, it's sadly unlikely.  Anyway this is a garbage derivative ripoff of Battle Chess only inferior in all respects despite being almost 10 years newer.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The implementation here is of such poor quality, the developer couldn't work out how to make the game display in fullscreen, it only runs in a selection of Windows UI windows.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

You are in a post-pandemic world with a unique time travelling remote. That part was fun. Some items are available in the daytime, some in the dark. None of the puzzles are difficult. There is one at the end that you can easily overthink :-)), don’t.

The World After has been good fun so far! Although I am nowhere near finished with the game yet, I was compelled to write a mini-"review", seeing as (for some reason) there are no other reviews written yet. 
It's a beautifully-shot game, with cinematic videography. It looks great. Thus far, it's a seamless FMV/interactive game where your choices matter vis-a-vis progression of the storyline. It's a brilliant idea for a storyline, too (especially w/ the present-day wordlwide pandemic situation). I've just gotten into what is apparently some sort of a time-traveling situation.
I'm playing with English subtitles and voice-dubbing as the choice (there are other language choices). The dialogue is well-written, but my only quibble is, though the English voice over dubbing is very well done for the main character, the other characters' English language voice-dubbing are NOT well-acted. I'm not sure why. 
I've been producing,directing, and editing video for 40 years (recently retired), and have also done voice dubbing for just as many years, and I would have cringed as a producer to hear some of these voice-translations. Again, and thank goodness, the main character's English-dubbed voice is great, but NOT so the others. At least as far as I've gotten into the game, which admittedly is not much (Julie; the main character's friend, and the Alex Jones-type character: they're almost like bad Anime-stereotype examples of English-language voice acting). This being said, at least to me this is forvigable as the story itself and the game's appearance and environments are interesting and fun to navigate through.
Little in-game mechanics, such as holding spacebar to skip transitions from place to place you've already seen, are helpful.
Dialogue trees equally so. And, miracle of miracles: several save slots! An absolute rarity in today's adventure games (thanks, DEV teams!). 
When you combine the somewhat-rare FMV game that's beautifully shot, with a good storyline and interesting environments...with several save slots AND (ta-daaaa!!!!!) a VERY good price point? In my eyes, you've got a winner. I hope this team does more games like this. I just hope they use better voice actors for their English dubbing next time. Thank goodness the main character's English voice was really good. And,perhaps for those of you NOT playing in English, YOUR actors' voices are just fine. As I said, to me a MINOR quibble.
Definite thumbs-up for this game, especially for us adventure gamers.

While the backgrounds are great and the acting is fine, the actual game itself falls short of its potential. The point and click puzzles are entirely unrelated to the plot and often nonsensical. The sci-fi elements in the game COULD be used well in a point and click game to make puzzles more interesting and flesh out the world, but they're sorely underutilized. Using them is less of a logical step you realize you must take to solve a puzzle and more of something you just resort to. 

All of this would be halfway acceptable if the plot was entertaining, but there's hardly any plot at all. The collectible video logs are about the only thing to reference the plot and even then, they're more elements of a plot than an actual cohesive story. 

I regret having paid around $13 for this. For as little as the game offers, I wouldn't want to pay more than $3 for this.

C'est ce qui fait son charme et ses limites en même temps; son charme, car on peut vraiment dire que c'est un jeu inhabituel, qui nous fait naviguer au travers d'un petit village et de campagnes françaises dont je serais assez curieux de connaître les locations, avec un thème plus qu'actuel mélangé à du paranormal et une intrigue conspirationniste, sans pour autant faire l'apologie du conspirationnisme.

Ses limites, parce qu'ici on revient au bases du genre, dans un style très épuré voire un brin minimaliste.
Minimaliste, car le protagoniste ne montre d'animation réelle que lors des petites cinématiques de déplacement / intrigues, et j'avoue que j'aurais bien aimé pouvoir le déplacer à mon gré afin qu'il marche sous le contrôle de la souris - mais cela aurait peut-être nui au réalisme d'ensemble. Autre point: même sans avoir encore fini le jeu, je peux aisément dire que les énigmes sont un peu trop faciles et ne demandent pas beaucoup d'efforts de résolution, pas assez peut-être. La bande-son, sans être mauvaise du tout, est là avant tout pour poser une petite ambiance discrète, elle ne vous assourdit pas les cages à miel et semble être là pour compléter le tout, sans se poser en facteur plus remarquable que ça.

à part pour ces remarques, j'ai vraiment apprécié ma petite session de jeu jusque-là pour The World After, et compte bien le finir afin de découvrir ce qu'il se cache sous cette intrigue dont je devine peut-être - ou pas - le sens et message caché: celui de la liberté, de ne se laisser endoctriner ni enfermer, à tous les sens du terme, par qui ou quoi que ce soit; mais j'extrapole peut-être...^^"

Ce sera donc un bon 7/10 pour moi, avant tout pour le charme et l'originalité : )

A more open approach to the map would have been nice. 

The puzzles were simple but consistent with the world, and the day/night mechanic was a great idea. Except for the very last puzzle, the solutions are more or less apparent from the story or available items.
Unfortunately the audio only seems to work half the time. Technically you could still play with subtitles only as they still work, but that isn't good enough for me.

The World After is an FMV game with gameplay similar to Contradiction: Spot the Liar.

A writer has recurring dreams and the answer to their meaning lies somewhere in the French village where he resides.  It's an interesting set-up, and while there isn't a great deal to the plot, I liked what there is.

Unlike most modern FMV games, there is only one choice in this game to make.  It isn't the sort of game where you make many choices, and from those choices come many variations in the plot.  It's basically a point-and-click adventure game in FMV form, complete with inventory and a small number of characters to interact with.

I disagree with the reviewer who said it is a walking simulator.  It is not a walking sim at all.  Navigation is through point-and-click.  It's not the sort of game where you spend ages wondering around looking for things and not interacting with anyone.  Nor is it the sort of game where you have endless puzzles to solve in an environment where you are alone either.

There is a sense of adventure to the story of this game, so therefore it does warrant the adventure tag, in my opinion.  Don't expect a deep mystery that will take hours to fully explore and enjoy, like Gabriel Knight: The Beast Within, for example.  But you can expect an interesting, if perhaps confusing story.

The few puzzles that are here are easy to solve.  This is a game made to tell a story, not to provide a deep gameplay experience.  It is aimed at the casual gaming crowd.

The acting is quite good.  There isn't a lot demanded of the lead, but he acts out his part well.  And his character is not annoying either.

Overall, I like this game, even though it is very short and there isn't a great deal to it.  The sci-fi theme reminds me a little of a game I played yesterday - The Dark Side of the Moon.  If you have played and enjoyed that game, then I recommend this one too.

"...narrows your choices down to the best 2 possible moves per turn."

Lazy Chess adds a simple but interesting restriction to chess: what if you could only make the best moves available? It uses the Stockfish engine to suggest the top moves in each position, and you must choose one of them, while trying to figure out which one is the best, since that information is not available. So, with 2 possible moves, worst case scenario you’ll play a game where you always play the 2nd best move, which is still enough to win some games.
But it’s not so simple, because the AI will adjust the difficulty according to your performance. You have an ELO rating, that I think takes into consideration your wins and your best move ratio. But you can adjust the difficulty manually and add more possible moves (to a max of 4) to add extra challenge.
The game also has some extra modes, like suggesting the best move and a random one, and challenges, where you start from some famous positions. I think they’re novelties, but it’s nice to have extra content. There’s also multiplayer, but I couldn’t find anyone, and only managed to play against the AI during queues.
However, this concept has a big issue. If you check it against your own Stockfish, you’ll realize that some of the best moves suggested by your engine aren’t considered the best by the game. Sometimes, they aren’t even available at all! That can happen for a lot of reasons, including the depth of both engines (you can change the time limit to compute in-game), and the engine version. It’s very unreliable. I understand it’s a limitation outside the devs control, but it would be nice to have a disclaimer. It’s not necessarily the best moves possible, but the best moves considered by this version of Stockfish, within that depth. And even then, I think it can suggest different moves in the same position, because of the limited time, and especially in more complicated positions.
Other than that, I also have 2 more small gripes. The first one is that you can’t turn-off this mechanic. This means you can’t use this game to play chess normally, but also that you can’t use it to play against custom positions or openings. Especially the openings. For example, I wanted to play an Italian game, and couldn’t. And even then, I’m sure the game would say the best move was to play a Spanish game instead. Oh, and I didn’t find a way to play as the black pieces, which is huge. Even if it’s there, I couldn’t find it.
The second one is that this is an obvious mobile port. Some options open a white Android window, you can’t make the moves normally on the board (you cycle between them and choose one), there’re a few prompts opening other games from the devs, stuff like that. It works, don’t get me wrong, but there’s some lack of polish. Also, since there’s no Steam Cloud, it’s a mess to find where your progress is located, since it’s a weird format.
But despite all these issues, I really like this concept, allowing for a more casual chess experience, and it’s perfect for short sessions. Without explanations, it may be difficult to understand why those are the best moves, so it’s not a great learning tool on its own. But it is a cheap game, even at full price. Even if you just mess with the game for a few hours, I think it’s worth it. If you like chess, then I recommend you at least check this out. And if you don’t like it, then ask for a refund.

A mess, but an interesting one. You only really get something as bizarrely messy as this with indie games and I do think that’s kind of special. Starts off promising - very moody and unique, but pretty much as soon as a third main character gets introduced, it becomes increasingly clear that things in this story kind of just happen without rhyme or reason. I saw someone say “a slowburn needs the burn part” on a review recently and I like that, and I feel like it does apply here at times. It’s trying to be something artsy and deep - and far be it from me to say that something isn’t a piece of art just because it doesn’t fit with my or anyone’s preconceived notions of what art is - but it does generally lack an understanding of how to make itself feel as artistically rich as it clearly wants to. The last 20 or so minutes in particular very much lean heavily on exposition and creepypasta edginess, but I do hold respect for a game bizarre enough to go from a moody surreal horror story to an 80s action thriller to a meta techno thing, regardless of how rough it is. It’s certainly something that left me with more to chew on then a large portion of the soulless AA or AAA titles that strip away the voices of their individual creators in service of proven formulas and mass appeal.

Ripout has solid foundations, it has interesting concepts, but it executes on them poorly. Everything was functional, the progression seems unique, and I do like the concept of having to drop my primary weapon for utility or support options, but a lot of the stuff built around all of that just didn't lift it up high enough to stick around.

Regarding the horror tag, it's not quite descriptive. There are elements of body horror, I guess, but the game itself doesn't scare or horrify me. It hasn't left me feeling paranoid. A lot of bad horror doesn't leave quiet time to let you feel that paranoia or build tension. Ripout has it, but in the wrong spot. The quiet time is spent feeling safe, rather than on edge. When I walk into a room, I know there are enemies. I also know that once those enemies are dead, the room will be pretty much safe, until I complete an objective. Predictability nullifies the potential for scares. The game needs to break my trust more often, to let me think it's safe, and be tricking me into letting my guard down. That's what it needs to effectively be horror.

I found it particularly annoying when I would give up my primary weapon to disarm an enemy, only to have it immediately rearmed by what felt like RNG. It definitely seems like you can have your pet "rip out" (see? name) the enemy's armaments, but then they can just, with no cooldown or penalty, pick up a new weapon (or utility item) with no delay.

Perhaps I haven't given it long enough to get to that point, but I gave it an hour with a friend (which usually helps) and found it very uncompelling, but even on sale, I don't see the value here yet. I may come back and check on this game here and there, it might just be a diamond in the rough. Maybe it'll scratch itches for others that it missed for me.

Otherwise though, it doesn't have much else going for it. It's not really doing anything new or interesting, or a game play feel that I couldn't get somewhere else. The gun-play is unremarkable, the movement feels clunky, the upgrades are slow to progress and barely noticeable. It also tries to go for this Rogue-Like mission frame where you can get upgrades during a mission, but they only last for that ONE mission. Which, is fine. A little power bonus for a time, but they are almost not worth wasting time going out of your way searching for them. Oh, and the Rip-Out feature that you can do to enemies is, just, so subnominal I almost never noticed when it had actually happened.

And oh geez, the AI compnaion's voice acting is... I don't want to be mean about the VA, she's doing a fine job but not for this kind of game. It comes across too much like a Tik Tok tutorial or something, there's just something off about her tone for the setting, doesn't match up. Kind of annoying.

I generally found myself just sortof walking around from point to point, like I was looking through a museum, shooting enemies with little aplomb and moving on. Just couldn't get engaged. I can't imagine playing with friends would change that.

Oh god and the Web-Attack that some enemies can do is so annoying and can be run ending because the "melee to break free" didn't alway register, taking upwards of 5 or so hits if you're unlucky.

Anyways, it's put together well enough, but doesn't have enough to really stand on it's own, let alone stand out. At least not yet. The thing is, there is clearly a lot of integrity and care put into this, it's not slap dash or ramshackled together by anymeans. So I feel kind of bad giving it a thumbs down. But it just doesn't feel like it's "There" quite yet. I think that can change though. I'd like to see that

This is how I accidentally found one game breaking issue, which allowed me to earn practically unlimited money by taunting the opponents when I get on top of their heads or they get on mine, because then the AI gets confused and is trying to walk back and forth, trying to attack each other, so by telling your character to taunt in this situation, you can earn unlimited amounts of money from crowd bonuses. ---Pros:

-The artstyle is cute, the horse coats look beautiful, and the world is vibrant, if a little empty
-Almost no learning curve, and a neat difficulty curve(to me at least)
-At 10 hours, the gameplay loop still feels satisfying
-Game receives consistent updates to hopefully keep it satisfying
-Farming is fun and simple
-No annoyingly long wait times for breeding/foaling/growing up since the days progress at your own pace
-Nothing is so grindy that you can't put on a podcast in the background or read while doing it and get right back in when done, unlike some other horse games that're 90% "sit and wait for thing to happen" or literal "come back tomorrow"s, IRL
-Daily quests give you a good sense of purpose
-Looking for chests/capturing wild horses is fun
-Tack/character customization is pretty neat
-Horse traits are cute and make each one feel more unique
-I have not experienced any serious or actually annoying bugs!

---The Cons(since the game's in EA I'll focus most on what feels genuinely negative):

-Horse potential(which is finite) permanently goes into a specific stat every time you canter, do jumps, turn tightly, or gallop, ANYWHERE, discouraging riding your horses until they're fully trained so you don't waste potential, and **encouraging you to wear your horse's energy out** before riding them around for gathering/chores/fun! I like the thought of helping your horse improve just by spending time with them, but maybe stats like speed and flexibility should only improve when you're deliberately trying to improve them
-As others have said, being forced to keep horses in the stable seems wrong. Horses *would* lose energy running around in a pasture, but only one energy boost a day pressures me to keep my comp horses stabled, and the loss of potential(which is finite) each day they're in pasture pressures me to keep in-training horses stabled. Only fully-trained, two-treat-a-day (or non-competing/pregnant) horses get the privilege of being able to run around outside. Surely there's a better solution!
-No HUD compass. Not even a sun to navigate by! I get lost/go the wrong way constantly, and have to continuously turn on arrows guiding me to places, or reference the map to see where I am. There just aren't enough landmarks to justify not having one, and to me not having such a basic feature 8 months after release(that would presumably be pretty simple to add) is a bit of a priority red flag.

---Things I'd like to see adjusted, but aren't really cons:

-Tameness feels bare bones. Being able to click two buttons a couple times then AFK roundpen a wild horse to a perfectly tame horse in maybe 10 minutes is certainly convenient, but seems way too quick. I hope it can be turned into more of a process like trust!
-Speaking of the roundpen, it's just an AFK machine. You can train up to two stats(besides endurance) with no physical input, seemingly at the same pace as in-saddle training; and the roundpen is closer to the stable, so you're not having to trot slowly to any specific training ground. I won't complain too much since I just listen to YouTube vids while I do it but surely there's a balance issue here. I wrote this review roundpenning flexibility.
-Horse animations are very choppy. They're passable so I don't see this being looked at until the roadmap's done, but they're obviously kinda janky
-Some horses just aren't meant to last. Limited potential means you'll be selling/retiring your starter horses since you have limited space, with only a grindy statue blessing that needs to be repeated multiple times to make them comparable to late-game horses for comps or getting around. At that point you use the blessing on your better ones. I feel like I can't get attached!
-Townsfolk are also very bare bones, and have kind of uncanny movement/faces compared to their sprites.

Overall I'd recommend this game, but definitely looking forward to updates!

This is good old Frogger with a fresh coat of paint. You play a frog who needs to get from the bottom of the screen to the top by crossing streets and rivers, without being run over by cars or falling into the water. The gameplay is as engaging as ever. I've actually looked (unsuccessfully) for a Frogger clone on Steam for quite a while, and I always wondered why I couldn't seem to find one.

The game comes with three modes: one has nice looking, modern pixel graphics, one has an 8-bit look very similar to the Atari VCS version (and different levels), and the third one is a survival mode where your goal is collecting hearts that randomly pop up while going upward on a seemingly infinite lane.

The game also has achievements (which is nice) and online leaderboards (which are pointless in my opinion, because I doubt that a small one-man indie developer can keep the inevitable cheaters out).

One potential criticism is that the game is less forgiving than the original. In the original game, as long as you made contact with a log or turtle even just with your legs, you'd be safe. In this game, you drown. This means that this game requires much more precision when e.g. jumping onto fast-moving turtles. I've also run into a few situations where I died due to input lag. And I've seen criticism about the game only having a small number of levels, but I haven't yet progressed far enough to check that.

Unfortunately, the game is lacking any quality-of-life features whatsoever. Music can be turned on or off, but there's no volume slider, nor is there a separate option for the sound effects. Keyboard controls are limited to arrow keys or WASD and can't be rebound. This means that for players with AZERTY or Dvorak keyboards, the arrow keys are the only sensible option, which you can only access well with the right hand (which therefore cannot rest on the mouse). The game can be paused, but game states cannot be saved. All this is pretty disappointing and would probably have led to a downvote if I didn't like the Frogger gameplay so much. I hope that the developer will be more considerate about user-friendliness in future games (or perhaps with an update for this one).

I still recommend the game because it's a decently made  Frogger clone that captures the gameplay of the original while having a very low price. It's relaxing when played in short bursts, and the young ones can get a glimpse of a classic game that many of us old farts loved back in the 80s. ;)

Exorcised is a newly released Tower Defense game.
The game is set in a Japanese fantasy world, with many versions of Japanese females clothed in cultural Japanese style as the towers, and with demons as the enemies, no story or known plot in the game, so lets move on.

The game is pretty straight forward, like many other Tower Defense games, the enemy move on a fixed path from one side to the other and you, as the player, need to place those sexy female towers to eliminate them. 
There are several kinds of towers, each with somewhat different stats and characteristics which could be upgraded later on, and some different enemy types and bosses.
The game feature something new and fresh to the Tower Defense game genre in the form of a "Tetris" like formation, which called an Alliance. there are two types of Alliances, regular ones and advanced ones, with each type providing 5 formations with different bonuses. If used right, those formations could prove useful, but the longer you play, the less you feel the alliances impact in a level, for example I finished Level 300 of the last Map with only 3 alliences up (which is pretty low, and only 1 of them was an advanced one) and there are Towers that feels way stronger while maxed out than others, like the Exorcist or the Ninja (In most of my games I filled the map with Ninja as frontliners and Exorcists as backliners) which remove the excitement of choosing other towers instead or even building Alliances without those 2 types. 

The Maps in this game are pretty straight forward as well, you start playing in easy, and when you complete a certain number of waves in one of the maps, a new difficulty is unlocked, which provide you with new maps, although the maps do not add a new mechanic or a different approach by using the enemy demons differently or the level design itself, they do their part just about right. 

The feel of progression is almost non existent in the game, and many aspect are missing in the game for the player to feel this sensation, which is something that I, for once, must have in every game to feel entertained. 
But the game is pretty short, so I finished it before I noticed (about 3-5 hours of gameplay If you rush the x2-x4 regular time like I did). 

Overall the game is pretty decent for a Tower Defense game and I do recommend it even though there are many gameplay aspects to work on.

[b]piozila[/b] is a $2 mobile game that was initially sold in a really sorry state on pc for $8. happens all the time, unfortunately, but it's been $3 outside a sale since early 2022 and also received a bunch of post-release patches, making it look and work a lot better for a more reasonable price. it's still far from perfect though.

you're in charge of leon the chameleon, emerging from a toilet at the beginning. the goal on all [b]25 levels[/b] is to help him reach the exit by pushing things (and leon) around. it's essentially a reverse-[url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/950140/] hiding spot[/url]. the [b]move limit is optional[/b] (and only appears after the first move, not ideal), you get a trophy if it's not exceeded.

so yes, [b]it's another sokoban, big surprise[/b]. at least there's no cat in this one. what's there is [b]durability on everything[/b], which is quite novel. so you can't just push things around ad infinitum, even leon has a bar above his head, and [b]when the bar is exhausted, things turn into immovable cones[/b]. leon can be fed to recharge his bar, but moving food too much makes it disappear.

as we know, the only thing worse than cats is humans, and they raise their ugly heads here eventually too. they move around in a turn-based fashion and destroy stuff in one hit. what's more, they kill leon in the same turn as they step on an adjacent tile, very annoying. other hazards include spike traps (only affecting leon) and fire (can be fed or extinguished), plus there are keys and buttons, the usual stuff.

[b]controls are mouse-based.[/b] left click to select stuff, then click the appearing arrows to move them. luckily, a [b]'select auto' toggle got patched in[/b], otherwise it'd be a tedious select-move-reselect-move-reselect-move situation. it's still not fast enough and if you click again too soon, the item gets unselected instead of moved. right click or left anywhere that's not an item also does that.

can't move the camera, but mouse wheel zooms, x/v (why?) rotates slowly (I expected 45-degree steps but not against anything smoother), which can be done with the mouse on the edge of the screen as well, but if you turn that on, x/v stops working for no acceptable reason. 'r' is restart, took them 8 fucking months to implement and it's not even instant, just slowly reloads the level and resets the camera too ('reload', on the other hand, is full progress reset, very misleading).

[b]no undo[/b], which I somehow took for granted and now it's a dealbreaker, especially with [b]dying leading to a level reset[/b] and thanks to the perspective and how busy levels are, [b]misclicks can easily happen[/b]. I wouldn't mind a wall toggle either, to get rid of all of them. no matter how you rotate the level, some will always be in the way.

the graphics are nice (wasn't the case on release), you can customize leon and even click the sun to advance time and change time of day, though it's only cosmetic. the music is pretty good if very repetitive, but [b]there are annoying text display sounds[/b] (humans apparently communicate with morse code), and while display is fast enough, instant would be better. punctuation is also often missing and writing is pretty bad (in english anyway, there are other options), but can be turned off with the 'story mode' toggle. and it's nice that only tutorial messages repeat after a level reset, not the fluff (which still gets shown next time you launch the game and the last level loads, so it's not perfect).

despite some quality of life, [b]basic settings are lacking[/b]. no main menu, options come up on the side (esc doesn't bring them up, have to click). no volume sliders, only toggles for music and sound, no separate one for text display, no resolution options or windowed mode (alt+enter only makes a non-resizable window, gotta edit the registry to change anything). there's level select in the menu (also took them months to add), that's the only place to check level numbers after they pop up at the start of each stage. the 'dream' toggle makes another leon appear and you can move him with wasd/arrows outside the actual puzzle area. levels are small and there's nothing to explore or do, so it's completely pointless.

I appreciate the work they put in after release, but all those things and more should've been there from the start and there's still basic stuff missing. hiking up the price for an identical pc version is also not something to applaud, even if it's common mobile dev fuckery. if they ever patch in undo that also works from a fail state, make level reset instant and add more basic functionality, I'll flip the review to a recommendation. give it a miss until then.

I loved SUPERHOT's "time moves when you do" mechanic. You can obviously play levels as quickly as you'd like, but it could benefit you to play them methodically and carefully plan your attack. This mechanic allows the player to face down overwhelming odds, yet emerge victorious. It represented a merger between shooters and puzzle games that was almost seamless.

While I certainly didn't think this one dollar indie game would reach the heights of SUPERHOT, I did expect a bit more from it than this. If it didn't feel monotonous enough travelling to the white flag (the goal of each level) across these near-identical grassy forests, the game maintains a drab sepia palette that makes the entire experience feel lifeless. Additionally, the shooting itself was rather rote and unremarkable.

On the other hand, it could be that the game is a substantial piece of social commentary. The repetitiveness of the level design and the title, [b]Another Warfare[/b], referring to how mundane and commonplace war has become. The fact that you'll only see enemy bullets by moving forwards yourself encouraging the player (or country) to comprehend their role in perpetuating conflict. The goal of each level being a white flag, symbolizing surrender and finally, peace.

However, I can't help but feel like I'm reaching here. I'm not sure that [b]Another Warfare[/b] is going to be the 2D translation of SUPERHOT's mechanics that energizes me. It's a difficult mechanic to do correctly - I recently played [b]UltraGoodness 2[/b], another game that (in my view) misses the mark. The best translation of SUPERHOT's mechanics, for my money, can be found in [b]Iron Danger[/b]. Although in a different genre, the mechanic's implementation is well-done and allows for excellent decision-making opportunities on the part of the player.

I'll be honest: this game isn't for me. But I don't think I'm in its target audience. I chose to recommend it because, within its small scope, it's well made, and probably quite enjoyable for those who ARE in its target audience.

You have three game modes to choose from: challenge, random, and exploration. After playing challenge a few times, I definitely started to see the allure of fine-tuning your strategy to try and climb the leaderboard. You start to see more efficient ways to move through the level and maintain your score multiplier between clicks.

I honestly didn't see much difference in random mode, because this mode is all about random interactions, and I didn't really understand the interactions to begin with. Plenty of objects in the map can be "interacted" with, but usually the interactions don't involve much more than a few extra points and some sound effects (a dog in a dog house barking, a car revving, etc.). Every once in a while some fancy, magical visuals would appear, but I couldn't tell if this meant something good had happened, and, if so, what the good thing was. 

In exploration mode, you can play the map without a time limit, and objects you've already clicked on (and can't click on again) remain highlighted, so that you don't risk forgetting and wasting clicks. It takes the pressure off and lets you plan for challenge mode.

Suggestion for improvement: more interesting interactions. Maybe clicking on a car casts a spell on it, making it drive off and mow down people in its path. Or clicking the pool makes the water gush out, slowing down anyone caught in the current. This would make it more rewarding to be clever, in addition to fast and precise.

Overall, the game has some nice polish, with fitting music and impactful sound effects/visuals. If you like fast, simple games  with a focus on high scores, you should find your time with Urban Mage pretty satisfying.

It's a level-based isometric puzzle platformer.
The visuals & music are nice, the 360 camera helps alleviate SOME of the struggles with isometric platforming, and the puzzles are engaging enough.
However, I'm not recommending it because it is straight up broken.

So the goal of each level is to get to the end (of course), but there are multiple collectibles you are encouraged to collect along the way: 30-50 green light gems, 4-6 red crystals, & various health potions (not tracked on the pause menu but still accounted for at the end).

The levels can get fairly long for a level-based platformer, 15-25 minutes after the first world. And there are no checkpoints. And there is not an abundance of health; you only gain health from the pre-determined health potions set at defined points in the levels.
This leads to a lot of frustration, as early deaths could spell doom for your level later on. And just normal stuff that happens in isometric platformers, such as misjudging the depth of a jump, feels harsher.

But that alone wouldn't make me write this review. No, what's broken is that sometimes, damage dealt to you will kill you instantly, regardless of how much health you have. Damage only deals 1 heart normally. 

But twice in a row on level 3-3, a long level, I have been insta-killed when at 4-5 health. First halfway through the level when an exploding slime dropped me from 4 health, and the second at the VERY END. I needed to solve 1 more little puzzle to reach the goal, had found all collectibles, & a flying enemy dropping slime from above, hit me once, & insta-killed me.

What. The. Fuck.

That alone is worth a negative review. If developers decide to make a game hard, it better damn well be fair, and not have 1-shot bugs. Especially with these long levels.

That frustration is not worth your time or money, and it doesn't seem like the game will be fixed anytime soon. There are plenty of other platformers & puzzle games to look at without wasting your time on a Sisyphean game such as this that arbitrarily decides if you can beat a level or not.

Edit: Oh wow. Surprise. So in 4-2 I got close to the end of the level, and was on a section where you are on a moving platform and have to hit switches on fans to turn them off, or else you get blown off. I get through the section, reach land, then out of nowhere I get blown off stage with no fan present. When I respawn, my character again goes flying as if blown by a fan, but no fan is there. This repeats until I lose all health and die.

4-3 has a part where you put blocks on a pressure plate to activate some automatic platforms that appear then disappear periodically, except the timer must've gotten bugged because they appeared for 1-frame before retreating.

Terribly buggy game turns a difficult experience into an unbeatable, unfair one. Why waste 30 minutes on a level that will arbitrarily decide you lose when you could play a game that doesn't do that?

[b]rough kuts[/b] is a series of old horror movies now in the public domain, turned into interactive experiences. [b]night of the living dead[/b] serves as the 'base game' for the black & white stuff, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1734470/]the thirsty dead[/url] is the same for color movies, with a bunch more sold separately as dlc for both. living dead also has a demo if you want to give it a shot.

I've only seen remakes of some of these and haven't heard of the rest, but I'm sure such classics (or 'classics') deliver lovely cheese in spades. still, I was doubtful about the execution and expected something low-effort, especially seeing how quickly the 'developer' churns them out. and as usual, I was right, but [b]even I wasn't prepared for something this lazy[/b].

the game always starts in a resizable window and [b]the only setting is going full screen[/b], but only from the main menu, as alt+enter doesn't work, have to press esc to go back to windowed mode. [b]no volume settings, nor subtitles[/b], the steam overlay doesn't work either. and here's the real kicker: [b]you can't pause the fucking movie[/b], not even switching tasks works, it just keeps going until a choice comes up. there's a hidden button in the bottom right corner that lets you go back to the main menu, but it only works if a choice is on the screen. amazing...

but wait, there's more: [b]saving only happens when you die, so if you quit elsewhere, 'progress' is lost[/b]. loading a save will replay the last scene and let you do something else, which is nice, but can't skip straight to the choice, why could you? from what I've read, the other movies save every 10 minutes, which is still far from ideal. ever heard of scene selection?

the credits only include the writers, director and the main actors, and there's a characters section, but it's just pictures from the movie and their first name, and once started, it can't be interrupted. I had to go to windowed mode and close it because [b]alt+f4 doesn't work[/b] either.

as a bonus, the [b]librivox[/b] recording of the short story [i]the isle of the undead[/i] is available for listening, but of course [b]without a control panel[/b]. it's in 5 parts, each 15-20+ minutes long, and [b]all you can do is start or stop[/b], no pause or anything. I recommend going to the librivox website, downloading the same thing for free and listening to it however you want to have some actual control over it.

as good as the idea is, [b]it's a low-effort cash grab with barely any functionality[/b] even for something as simple as an interactive movie. since these titles are in the public domain, you're better off watching them for free where they're available and donating to the providers or librivox. anything's better than supporting this lazy-ass project. what an absolute joke...

I admire the idea behind it, and the fact that someone actually went ahead and tried to do something interesting, i.e. to try and turn something linear and static into something dynamic and playable. Unfortunately, how this particular implementation is presented, it's uninteresting, boring and not worth engaging in. While I do appreciate the effort, I do not appreciate the result.

So the concept is this: old classic films that went public domain are gamified by adding choices to them. You watch the movie, at some point the movie halts and asks you what to do, and you get to decide how the movie continues.

This sounds a lot like modern "choice videos" like e.g. the Netflix items Black Mirror: Bandersnatch and Minecraft: Story Mode. Possibly a throwback to the good old days, where a handful of DVDs allowed to do something simliar, e.g. switch camera angles in certain scenes, or just generally jump/pick scenes to create an alternate storyline.

What may sound like a neat idea to some, as myself, turns out to be utterly boring and frustrating, at least in this particular implementation.

First off, there is the immediately evident conceptual problem: the movie itself doesn't change. It's a linear experience, there's no different outcome, there are no alternate stories to be uncovered. 

Imagine a movie scene like this:
Moment 1 - A person is in a room, there is a noise outside.
Moment 2 - The person runs to the window to look and see what made the noise.
Moment 3 - The person can't see the source of the noise, so they run outside and look around there.

In this kind of game, you get to watch the movie up to Moment 1, then you get the choices to "look out of the window" or "rush outside".
- If you choose to "look out of the window", you get to watch Moment 2, automatically followed by Moment 3, because that's how the movie goes.
- If you choose to "rush outside", Moment 2 is skipped and the movie continues from Moment 3.

Imagine a dialog between two people:
Moment 1:
- Person A - Hi.
- Person B - Hi. 
Moment 2:
- Person A - How are you?
- Person B - I'm fine, but (follows a monologue about how that person is).
Moment 3
- Person A - Well, let's get going.

In this kind of game, after Moment 1 ends and both people have greeted each other, you get the choice to "engage in conversation" or "hurry them along", something along those lines.
- If you pick "engage in conversation", you get to see Moment 2, where Person A asks Person B and Person B gets to tell their story, followed by Moment 3, because that's how the movie goes.
- If you pick to "hurry them along", Moment 2 gets skipped and the movie continues from Moment 3.

Or to summarize, this kind of game is just "selective scene skipping".

This becomes tedious and boring after just a few minutes of gameplay already. (I probably spent more time writing this review than I spent actually "playing" the "game".)

After the conceptual problem, there are also technical issues:

- The movie is available in 720p only. I guess I don't have to explain how annoying it is to play something the size of a stamp on a 4K screen.

- The movie playback is jaggy and stutters. It's like the movie speeds up and slows down again every second or two. This is noticeable when I look directly at it, but also when I look of to the side, it's like someone's flicking through a thumb flicker book.
I have a pretty buffed out computer, it runs complex contemporary games like Red Dead Redemption 2 in 4K resolution at full details without even breaking a sweat. The simple playing back of a black-and-white 720p video will definitely not be enough to bring it down, so the jaggy playback must be due to poor encoding of the source video.

- There is no way to "save" the "game" or to skip ahead at least to the next choice. Imagine you're halfway through a 2 hour movie game, suddenly the dog needs to go for a walk, you need to hit the toilet yourself, and finally it's time to meet someone in real life.
The game, and of course the computer and Steam, would have to stay on and running all the time, until you return to finish the remainder of the game. If you close the game and just start it again later, you'd have to "play" the entire first half of the 2 hour movie game again, you can't just continue where you left off.
You also can't just pick random choices (remember: irrelevant, as they don't change the outcome of the movie) and skip through the first half of the movie, because there's no way to skip ahead.

So this kind of game implementation is not only conceptually tedious and boring, but also practically in the "game" flow.

The frustrating thing is - I love, I mean I LOVE, The Night of the Living Dead. The movie, that is. This game has robbed me of any interest in watching the masterpiece again anytime soon, and I've only played it for a quarter of an hour or something. If you love the movie like I do, just do yourself a favour and watch the movie again.

There are several of these games, and they're very affordable, so feel free to ignore my advice and see for yourself, just don't say I didn't try to warn you. ;)

[i] My Experience [/i]

From time to time, I'll jump into a game to try and recapture some of that [b]Hotline Miami[/b] magic. Sometimes I'm able to almost get there, with titles like [b]Intravenous[/b], [b]The Hong Kong Massacre[/b], [b]GARAGE: Bad Trip[/b], [b]Mr. Shifty[/b], or even in a freebie like [b]Red Hot Vengeance[/b]. Although the gunplay in Sefir is somewhat smooth, that's where my praise for this title ends.

From the jump, you're treated to this odd DOS menu that you'll need to start the game - it takes longer than it needs to in order to get into the action. Then when you're playing, you'll see quite a few cutscenes, putting even more time between you and the gameplay. As an American from the south, I could never quite wrap my mind around what this story was about. Perhaps there are certain words or cultural idiosyncrasies that I needed to be aware of to truly understand, since the story seems to take place in eastern Europe.

I seemed to do alright in the game, but some of the changes that Sefir made to the formula were not for the better. First off, it doesn't seem like you're able to lock-on to enemies. When enemies are so quick and the game requires such twitchy reflexes, the lack of this feature leaves a glaring hole. Secondly, you don't always die when you're shot - instead, you'll see a countdown on your screen until you bleed out. Although you might be able to quickly finish the level or find a medkit, bleeding out usually just means that each of your attempts on a level will end up taking longer to complete.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend Sefir. If you're looking for an experience similar to [b]Hotline Miami[/b], I'd recommend one of the titles I listed above.

Yield! is a game that stands out in the crowded world of turn-based strategy titles. What really sets Yield! apart, though, is the gameplay. It’s a turn-based strategy game, and each match is an intricate puzzle of decision-making, where every move counts. The balance between offense, defense, and resource management is incredibly well-crafted, and there are always multiple paths to victory. With its possibility to change the round times, the game modes can range from a near live-play experience to a true turn based game. Each match feels fresh thanks to a variety of units, technology, and map layouts that make every game unique. You’ll find yourself experimenting with new strategies, learning from your mistakes, and coming up with new tactics to outmaneuver your opponents.

Yield! is a standout title in the turn-based strategy genre. The combination of gorgeous visuals, clever gameplay mechanics, and multiplayer excitement make it a must-play for fans of the genre. Whether you’re strategizing against AI or facing off in a multiplayer match, Yield! delivers an experience that’s both challenging and rewarding. This is a game that will keep you coming back for more, and one you’ll be proud to recommend to friends. If you’re a fan of turn-based strategy, Yield! is an absolute must-have.

[h1]Experienced on the Meta Quest 2[/h1]

Is this a good MP game for VR? No, it isn't. However, might it be worth $2 for cheap MP fun going against bots or possibly friends? Sure, but more like a sideways yes. You can choose some different combat modes, including FFA, team MP, or zombies (spheres turn black and it's really a FFA). You can pick up any weapon on the ground: sniper rifle (scope doesn't work in VR), minigun, or rocket launcher.

There is only one map (a cargo dock). All player models are basically just colored spheres. You can choose to host or join a MP match if a server is active. Spoiler alert: there were no players online so I had to host a server. So I played against bots. I ran and I gunned and I died a lot. It was mindless, violent arcade fun. 

You do have full locomotion. I did not have any turning available and I didn't see any in the settings (unless I missed something). You can also jump. Game is running on the Unreal Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 90 fps. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs.

If you have low expectations, this might be the MP for you to play against bots. It's cheap. It works. You could do much worse in VR. I had fun, but at the same time, after about 30 minutes, I kind of didn't want to play any more (against bots). I probably would play longer against real players. Buy on deep sale only.

SANABI is a game whose reach sometimes exceeds its grasp, but is well worth playing anyway.

The good:
- Beautiful and expressive animation, in cutscene and out
- Some of the most satisfying grappling hook mechanics out of any game I've played
- A really great story with some satisfying reveals and a real tearjerker ending. I'll admit, I came into this game expecting another videogame dad story, and was more biased against it than I should have been. But it really, really delivered, and I was crying by the end despite myself. It's also the kind of story that's pretty different the second time around, once you know everything going on.

The bad:
- Some issues with translation mean the dialogue isn't always as natural as it could be (really a minor issue)
- It doesn't always feel like the developers are making full use of the movement system they've created. Longer levels with more room to build momentum would be appreciated.
- Similarly, combat and especially bosses in this game can be very frustrating. Interaction and reaction is the core of combat, but the grappling and momentum mechanics mean that there are very few ways to immediately react to an enemy. Overall, SANABI has a great story, great visuals, great movement, and only alright level design. I'm looking forward to a sequel, when the developers have figured out how to take full advantage of their movement system.

SANABI is a game of two natures -- levels full of smooth action with (mostly) tight controls alternated with dialog and cut scenes which, by the end of the game, can stretch over 15 minutes. If you enjoy both, like I did, it's an excellent game. If the flaws in either bother you, you may find that getting to "the good stuff" is too much of a hassle.

The interface of SANABI is mostly a joy. The controls (except for a couple weird decisions corner cases) are very smooth and enjoyable (on mouse -- controller is supported but terrible), the music is good, and the graphics are shockingly good -- I've never seen so much expressed through so few pixels. The video and sound are especially important, as they affect both of the game's core aspects.

The gameplay is what is advertised about Sanabi, and it's pretty straightforward. This is a grappling hook game. You will swing, yank, and otherwise manipulate yourself and your surroundings with a hook at the end of a chain. The graphics and audio are exactly what they need to be here -- there are never hard-to-see details, low framerates, obnoxious sounds, or anything else to stop you from enjoying the game. The game's different areas vary enough to not feel repetitive in gameplay or audio-visual, and all have a pleasing aesthetic. The gameplay itself is, again, what you'd hope -- smooth, flowy motion as you navigate dangers and engage in combat. The difficulty is a bit odd -- mostly pretty easy, with the exception of a couple memorable boss fights -- but even these spikes aren't overly brutal. Overall, the levels are a well put-together package.

The story of SANABI is mostly expressed through dialog and cutscenes. It's hard to discuss much without spoilers that would ruin the enjoyment of this aspect, because the game's mysteries are the core of its story, but discovering the answers to your questions is satisfying in both pace and resolution. The game's audiovisual design is, once again, a major asset here. The pixels available don't allow for gore-induced horror, and there's no overwrought music, but the aesthetic is used to its maximum. There are a couple dialog typos, and these are extra-painful in the middle of major story beats, but they don't garble the message or overly detract from the experience.

Not everyone is looking for a combination smooth platformer and mysterious story-driven game, but for those who are SANABI is a rare treat worth experiencing.

Dredge is like if [u]a fishing sim and a Lovecraftian horror game had a baby[/u], and it turned out to be both surprisingly relaxing and deeply unsettling. On the surface, you’re just a fisherman cruising around catching fish, upgrading your boat and living your best sea life. But beneath the waves something... [i]otherworldly[/i] is stirring and trust me, it’s not just the fish.

The fishing itself is straightforward. You cast your line by steering your boat to fishing spots marked on the map, and then you use a minigame mechanic to reel in your catch. Depending on the fish, the minigame changes in difficulty, with some requiring quicker reflexes and others just patience. It’s peaceful at first, but the deeper you go, the more you realize you're not just catching cod—you’re glimpsing ancient, eldritch horrors that should not be. The game lures you in with the chill vibes of upgrading your boat and collecting fish but before you know it, you're uncovering bizarre, unspeakable things beneath the waves. Imagine going from “Oh, this is fun!” to “What in the name of is [i]that thing[/i]?!” 

And you’re not just fishing for fun — there’s a whole eerie narrative unfolding as you explore strange islands and try to make sense of... well, whatever is going on. It’s as if the ocean is calling you like a siren song from the deep, pulling you toward madness. The deeper you venture, the more you realize that you might not be at the top of the food chain anymore—and the true horrors that lurk beneath the surface might not even be of this world.

- I would suggest getting the DLCs when they are on sale if you want more of the strange, unsettling world that Dredge creates.

[I] Mind Rite [/i] is a nice detective otome visual novel. That was a pleasant short relaxing read. Nothing exciting or mind-blowing but I really appreciate such stories. 

It's a classic otome with 3 very cute love options. It feels like the central part is solving a crime than making love relations and I admire that. All guys are truly attractive both visually and in character. I'm happy I left Reimo for last by the way when all the mysteries were totally revealed in his route. As usual I scanned through negative reviews (I always find them more impactful, it's fun to see what other players complain about XD) and I can kinda understand the feeling of displeasure that a bad guy wasn't fully punished but I wanted to argue so much that he is a victim here too. He deserves all the love and compassion, perhaps even more than other love interests. I really felt sad knowing [spoiler] he had to die in other routes [/spoiler].  
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2890789520  
As the story is rather short I can relate to the feeling that the development of love relationships seemed a bit rushed but I don't think it's a huge flaw in a lighthearted otome visual novels. No explicit content here btw. After the first playthrough there's not much unread text left, so the game is mainly skippable but I really enjoyed good endings with all 3 guys because MC had such different paths for her professional development. That felt amazing, it's not like what you can only choose is a man you can be with, you can be flexible, you can try out such different things, the world is vast with so many opportunities. That felt very inspiring! I don't remember many stories with this feature. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2892785293 
As for the detective part, I can't say it was too obvious but at the same time I wasn't too astonished when I learned the truth. There were enough hints throughout the investigation to make me feel really like a protagonist solving the crime herself. I think it was a nice balance. No wow effect but not too boring either. It's truly a decent game. Nice purchase, especially with a discount, for an evening read. 

English translation is quite decent. Not perfect as usual, the list of typos, literally translated our Russian idioms & some mistakes is still a bit long for me to be totally happy but anyway it's good enough to play and enjoy it in English. Some things even made me laugh, for example, shacks for tea)) 

To sum it up, praises:
+ 8 endings, 3 hot love interests;
+ pretty art in general, beautiful CGs in a neatly made gallery. Reimo's smile especially captured my heart (♥ω♥*) It was too charming! Oh my, I just opened my steam screenshots and realized I didn't make a single ss of his smile O_O What a loss T_T; 
+ overall enchanting atmosphere of the world full of magic, different races like elves, cat people, rites, magic creatures etc;
+ in a short story there were still some little cute details I appreciated so much, like different figurines symbolizing dif chars. It felt nice. I mean it's easier with a long text to make us sympathize with the characters, so in short games when I feel involved and immersed thanks to similar small things, it's great;  
+convenient steam guide to get all the achievements.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2892842207 
Some complaints:

--Sorry, wasn't a fan of music, soon turned it off, but I saw players really praising it in their reviews, so I guess it's just personal, I really rarely enjoy soundtrack in games;

I didn't really like or dislike Mind Rite, though I lament the inability to choose a neutral recommendation. It's an extremely short 2-3 hour otome with all routes and achievements easily completed in that time. As is the case with most of these VN's with such a short runtime, it really doesn't feel like much character development or story was able to make it through to the final cut. The romances feel rushed and barebones, with hardly any indication of chemistry at all. I do like the bits of lore we get about the whole world scattered throughout, and it seems like it would make for a pretty interesting setting if fully fleshed out. The protagonist is interesting enough, too, as a snarky half-elf - but even she suffers from the limited runtime. We never learn much about most of the characters' backstories.

Other than that, there's not much else to talk about. The music was very simple and a bit boring, mostly just looping through a small handful of piano tracks. The writing itself was okay, I can't speak for the Russian language but in English it seemed to have been translated decently well, no major errors other than a few sentences with awkward wording here and there. Sound effects are few and far between, so the world feels kind of empty with just piano music and silence otherwise. I personally liked the art, it was very consistent in both the sprites and the CG's and very cute. I've seen VN's that cost more than this one with less (and worse?) artwork so that alone sort of makes up for the price.

Despite it being only $7 USD regularly, though, I'd still say wait for a sale if you really want to get this game. I kind of came out of the whole experience just feeling nothing. The endings were short and finished off far too quickly, and even the happy endings were only bittersweet - which did sort of suit the situation, at least. Still, I'd rather give it a positive rec than a negative one because there was nothing really [i]bad[/i] about Mind Rite, and there were a few good things, even. Pick it up if you care to, but I think that it's an experience that can be made to wait.
