22 Hours, multiple playthroughs to 100%. Combat is optional until the near end, rather this is an exploration-focused RPG expertly showing there are still talented devs with experimental ideas & creating unique experiences. Compared to modern, homogenized video-games; the captivation of this game's otherworldly setting and vivid writing is compounded even more. Despite how it looks this is NOT Morrowind, but what they have in common is being a game that any serious RPG fan should try at least once.

An indie studio makes an RPG in a world where the genre has been co-opted by studios with legacy names and intentions to appeal to everyone through using analytics to optimize their game design. Most big name “RPGs” are only so in name these days.

It’s incredible how a small studio can create a proper RPG with a fraction of the resources of the big names, and still have it be an atmospheric and engaging experience that’s full of interesting and fun lore to explore.

This game feels like a lighter version of Morrowind (perhaps because it's the reference I've heard, but I can see the similarities), with simplified yet rewarding exploration, lore, skills and faction systems.

In the first two hours I learned about a world where the worship of gods has been banned, and the intrigue between those that want to resurrect worship and those that want to maintain their power through enforcing apostasy. The character that gives me the main quest is a former prisoner now forced to live inside an iron maiden and suffer incredible pain so as to focus them on their new mission and prevent them from speaking to their old gods.

The aesthetics and soundscapes create an oppressive, even hallucinogenic experience, and you often feel transported to this world. Weirdly enough, I've felt as if I want to be in it, which is a sign of a game I enjoy.

[strike]The only gripe I have with this is that it seems to loop the same music track, at least for the 4+ hours I’ve played it, and while that music is great, it gets old after a while.[/strike]

UPDATE: Happy to report that there are more music tracks as you reach other islands in the game. Still wish the music was more varied, but what's there is really nice.

[h3] More love for this game [/h3] 

Another update, because I want to say more about this game. I've been a fan of RPGs almost all my life, and this one has struck a chord. It feels like there's something in there that's deeper, despite the deceitful simplicity of its systems, the world feels meaningful, real.

This game emphasizes exploration, it encourages you through its design (it doesn't tell you, its designed for you to want to explore) to discover secrets in this world, but it feels like there are many more secrets out there that exist whether you find them or not. Exploration is so essential that there's no XP system, so progression hinges on finding items that can be used to upgrade stats and gear. The most important of these items are called delusions, which allow upgrading your stats. Delusions and upgrade items are limited, and since you find them through exploration, it makes you feel like what you do with those items really matters, and that each of them has its own story.

The lore is dark, but somehow also heartwarming and often as beautiful as the art in this game. Many characters find themselves in hopeless situations but still hope for something better, or at least for a release from their plight. You can make decisions that alter the fate of the world and its characters, which adds to the replay value.

This game has made me feel like I did back when I first found games like Oblivion, when the world was simpler and I only cared about enjoying the world set before me. I really hope more people support this because the developer deserves it, they put something special of themselves into this, I can feel it.

I hate to do this—I wish there were a "thumbs middle" option—but so far, I can't recommend this game.

The Good:

The graphics are well done, and the world is creatively and faithfully represented.
The level design and environments (five hours in) are impressive.
The lore is interesting and refreshing.
The writing is strong, with natural-sounding dialogue.

The Bad:

The Music: After five hours, I keep hearing the same melody looping over and over. Initially, I liked the track—it sets up a great atmosphere—but it quickly becomes incredibly distracting and intrusive. So far, the music doesn’t change during combat or important events. This, combined with the looping wind chimes when entering NPCs' houses, is maddening and takes away from the immersion.

The Combat: It’s just bad. While there’s some enemy variety, every fight feels the same: get close, bait an attack, stab, repeat. The combat feels repetitive and floaty. I started as a mage but have only found one spell that turns enemies against each other, and I’m still using the same broken sword from the beginning.

Exploration & Backtracking: While discovering new areas is enjoyable, there’s a lot of backtracking, which can be tedious. Also, toggling between running and sprinting feels clunky.

Stamina System: This is more of a personal preference, but I don’t enjoy how stamina drains from both attacking and running (which you do a lot). It’s not a dealbreaker, just a mechanic I’m not fond of.

I'm willing to keep giving this game a chance, as the plot is interesting and I'm curious to explore different biomes, but got so annoyed about the bad things about the game that I had to take a break from it.

Dread Delusion is a rather peculiar open world RPG brimming with personality.

Luckily the heavy dialogue of DD is rich and intriguing enough to do most of the work. If you can dig the retro graphics, its a visual treat the whole way through. There's three unique 'kingdoms' to explore, each with their own set of interesting characters and histories, all tying in to an effective overarching story.

Do NOT go into this game if you are looking for exciting combat, because the combat (if you can call it that) here is dogsh*te. For me, it kinda added to the charm. What is here, is some engrossing exploration and a multitude of zany side-quests, anchored by some deep and colourful worldbuilding.

The game can unfortunately get a little repetitive (what open world game doesn't), and you do a tonne of back-tracking, but the orchestral soundtrack and hyper colour pallet keep you engaged. It's not massively long for an open-world game either, doesn't outstay its welcome.

I'd be super interested in what Lovely Hellplace does next.

I love this game, but giving it a thumbs-up is hard. I would recommend it under certain circumstances. In general, I think it’s worth a shot. With that, let's get the deal breakers out of the way. 

This game has the most flat, uninteresting, boring combat I have played in any game ever. I am not joking, there is practically zero depth. It boils down to hitting the enemy and moving out of the enemy's way. That can work for some games like Dark Souls due to build diversity and enemy variety in move sets, but this game has neither. The sound design makes it even worse, there is zero weight behind anything. It feels like you are slashing air the whole game. Checks are literal dice rolls as well. The game takes the fun out of all of these interactions. Give me at least a half-assed mini-game, at least make me feel like I'm doing something.

Another thing to consider is that this is NOT an RPG. The game attempts to convince you it is, but it is not. Do not let the opening life choices deceive you, their only purpose is stats. You get no special dialog options, which is weird given the strengths of the game. Worse than cyberpunk in that regard. All of the roleplaying that can be done in this game is story and dialog-related. You can’t kill anyone special, etc. There is zero build diversity, there is only one good way to build your character objectively. Most of your character is going to be based on gear, which there is a decent variety but it still doesn't create many interesting unique play styles. Not going to be finding many build-defining items, just more cool helpful stuff. 

I’ll touch on the story later, but I only have one complaint with the story and that is the ending. There are two endings and there is an objectively correct one, which somehow manages to also go against one of the messages of the entire story. Baffling. Also, barely any voice acting. You have to use your eyes and read. 

The last thing I’ll say is that this game runs awfully. I have a 3090 with an i9-10900k and my game dropped frames heavily every time I went in between zones or went to a new area. Every time. No exceptions. When I am using a speed spell and practically flying around it is painful.

Well, with that out of the way, why would I give this terrible game any praise? Well, if the following sounds enticing despite the above then I would recommend the game. 

If you are itching for another game to give you that feeling that Skyrim and Elden Ring gave you on the first playthrough and want a good story to accompany that, then you are in luck. The world of Dread Delusion is utterly fascinating. It has been a long time since I have gotten so invested and consumed in a world. The characters have actual depth and feel like people. The world is unique. Truly unique, this game will show you shit you have not seen before. It feels alive, lived in. Exploration as a byproduct of this is amazing, and I would do it just to see the world even if there wasn’t anything to find.  Most of the time you won’t find anything special, but sometimes you will. Items in this game are all unique, and do things only they do. They are rare, and getting a cool one feels like taking a hit of crack. The leveling system was a stroke of genius in this regard as well. You don’t level by doing anything. Fighting, talking, nothing. What you do level from are skulls of delusion. These are items that can only be found looking around the world. This is brilliant and leans into the strengths of the game. 

The amount of effort and passion here is genuinely astounding in general. There are entire tombs in libraries in the game where you can read about random bits of lore. They nailed the world in Dread Delusion, one of my favorites in gaming. The writers did an insane job with this game, I have never seen this much text and dialog in an indie game ever. 

The story is simple on the surface. Hundreds of years ago, there was a cataclysm, forcing humanity to feel the surface and live on sky islands. There is a legendary pirate woman who found an incomprehensible power. The ruling government is not a fan of this and sends you out on your way to stop here with the promise of freedom if you succeed. You, a random unremarkable prisoner. A suicide mission to get rid of a mouth to feed in reality. You aren’t willing to give up so easily though, and end up setting off traveling the lands looking for the pirate lady’s OG crew to help track her down. I don’t want to spoil anything, but the story behind the cataclysm, why said lady wants this power, and why the original crew left is absolute kino. 

Each huge region has its own questline and story with at least two endings as well. Every quest in this game is amazing. Each has two endings usually, each having real ramifications on the area or world as a whole. Is it better to be fragile and beautiful, or strong and hideous? Is it better to inflict infinite pain on one person, or limited pain on many? Painful reality, or blissful illusions? These are vague implications to questions asked by optional side quests. The entire game has questions like these, and they don’t have wrong answers. The game has a bold mechanic. Only one save file. No takesies backsies. Many people hate this mechanic, but I’m glad it's in the game. It made me think about my choices much harder, and learn to live with them. The quest design is immaculate. Every single quest was engaging and satisfying, and holy mother of god there are many. 

A lovely part of the game that has nothing to do with it is the internet funny enough. This game doesn't have a comprehensive wiki on items and quest endings. There are tons of holes where you will just not be able to know something until you do it. This is quite special. You have to approach the game honestly, and it brings me back to the times before we all had wikis open playing games. 

This is exasperated by the insane amount of content in this game. The world is incredibly detailed and jam-packed with loot and lore while being huge at the same time. It does feel like it never ends. I was able to squeeze 40 hours out of one playthrough. Granted that was the autism beast taking hold of me but the game does hit the dollar-per-hour mark, which many indie do not. Last thing I will say is that this game is gorgeous, I am in love with the visuals. Just turn off the warbling. 

TL;DR: If you want a game with an amazing style, a decent amount of content, with a fascinating world, lore, and characters on top of exploration that will make you forget the time then this is for you. Just be prepared to get invested. 

However, do not go into this with the idea that it is an rpg. It is a story-based exploration game. An open-world dark fantasy visual novel you could say. You will not be fighting bosses, or learning a combat system. You will not be making your character build. You will be reading and running around the world and you will like it.

Dread Delusion is a fantastic game, but certainly not for everyone. Here are the most notable points:

[h3] Gorgeous World [/h3]
The game has an excellent aesthetic, with its PS1-esque artstyle, and vibrant colors. Its world is really interesting, and alien. Some compare it to Morrowind, but I feel it definitely has its own strengths, and is actually quite different. 

[h3] Exploration [/h3]
The most important part of the game has to be the incredibly rewarding exploration, and a lot of the mechanics play into this. It feels like every corner, nook and cranny is crammed with consumables, points of interests, and unique rewards that mostly require you to use one of your levelable skills. This means that especially in the early hours you'll find things that require a certain skill threshold you haven't achieved yet. This made me make a mental map of places to revisit at a later time, as well as creating specific goals to strive for. And best of all is that a lot of your "experience points" are the actual reward for the exploration, feeding into this loop of just going out there and seeing the world.

[h3] Lackluster Combat [/h3]
Combat is one of the least impressive parts of the game (light/heavy attacks, bows, and some spells), but it is not the focus at all, and serves more as simple filler (although the enemy designs are cool). A lot of the combat can also be avoided, and most of the enemies can be easily avoided, so it might not bother you, but it is good to take note of this if you prefer a rpg with more engaging combat mechanics.

[h3] Sometimes Tedious [/h3]
Keep in mind that the biggest aspect of Dread Delusion is wandering around. If you're not so sure anymore where you need to go for certain quests (there are no markers on your map or hud), this wandering can become a bit annoying, especially if you’ve already explored big parts of the map. The more you progress in the game, the more ways you can find to make traveling less tedious, and the atmospheric ambient music does help with your travels, but there were certainly stretches of time where I was aimlessly searching around for quest objectives.

[h1] Verdict [/h1]
In conclusion Dread Delusion is an incredible game, that doesn’t do anything groundbreaking gameplay wise, and can sometimes be a bit tedious, but definitely makes up for it with its great atmosphere and style, and above all keeps feeding into your wanderlust. I had a great time with this game and would highly recommend it if you prefer exploration, and sightseeing over bloodpumping action.

[h2]Art Direction - Demo vs Final Release [/h2]
I remember seeing the 15 minute video by Alpha Beta Gamer of the first demo for this game many years ago and being immediately captivated by the setting. I have checked in on the game a couple times since then to make sure I never forgot and that it was still alive and in development while eagerly waiting 1.0 launch, but I went into this essentially completely blind. So blind in fact that when I played the game, I couldn't help but feel that it seemed different from what I remembered. 

After finishing the game, I finally rewatched that demo video and - after digging a little deeper - realized that the game's direction took a big shift around a year after that. So in the end, I was a little sad that I never saw that massive walled city in its final form and full glory, but the game I played was no less impressive.

It was fascinating to recognize what was still preserved from that demo in the final game. I may slightly prefer the environmental art direction of that old demo but I would write that off to personal taste. The game's true and current art direction is equally as endearing and objectively more inventive and unique that the (mostly) standard dark fantasy style the demo had.

Enough about the demo vs final game though. The final game has its own space and I have plenty to say about that.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]
I can't claim to actually know anything about the development process or resources behind this game. I have the impression though that the scope of this game ended up being much larger than anticipated. Despite this, I honestly feel as if the open world exploration is the best of recent memory, if not of all time. Is this what Morrowind players felt like back in 2002-2004? The secrets are rewarding, the destinations are interesting, and the world's lore as well as local storytelling builds further intrigue and positive reinforcement.

By indie standards, the scope of this game is teetering on insanity (the only thing missing is a tacked-on fishing mini-game). However, I feel like Triple A devs could learn a lot about Dread Delusion's world as - by their standards - the game's scope is not so large (I'm talking to you Elden Ring - I love you but you should have been a little smaller). The relatively limited scope (by Triple A standards) works well, preventing the world from ever feeling empty/without purpose. There's something to investigate in nearly every corner, and the land feels grounded in the sense that it feels natural and makes sense that you would find a structure where it is.

[h2]Story & Lore[/h2]
The main narrative both serves as an effective vehicle to justify the player's motivations and actions as well as provides several compelling characters you meet along the way. With one or two exceptions, they're not immensely deep or complex, but they are very likable. The many side quests flesh out the world and never feel like they were added just to pad play time (whether or not they actually were added to pad playtime is a different story lol). There are several more multi-faceted characters to meet on these side-adventures and generally feel important enough to justify grabbing your character's attention over the main quest, depending on the role you wish to fill.

There are several lands that are vividly described which you will never be able to visit during your time playing Dread Delusion, and they do a damn good job making you wish you could. There are many short books to read on your travels if you wish to learn even more than I did.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Honestly this is probably the weakest portion of the game. I do appreciate that skill checks are very commonly used and that there are opportunities to use one over another in a given situation so you don't miss out on much loot. The crafting mechanic was welcome and just as simple as I like it to be. Combat is mediocre at best but personally I don't mind. I enjoy Oblivion and Skyrim's combat so I'm just not the kind of guy to wish for a deeper combat system. Specifically, melee is basic, the bow trivializes and already easy combat system, and magic in nigh pointless, BUT I do think the fundamentals of a good magic system is there so I hope they try again in whatever they do next.

[h2]In Conclusion[/h2]
Game is good. Great, even. Buy it now!~ and embrace your Delusions!

Dread Delusion is a game I've had my eye on for quite some time, since before release in fact, and I decided that now was the time to give it a go.  My expectations more or less were something in the same general sphere as Morrowind, a weird fantasy RPG with a lot of writing and a large focus on exploration.  In some ways, my expectations were vastly exceeded, and it only fell short in a few aspects.

First and foremost, I firmly believe that this game has the best dialogue writing I've seen in a video game, the characters are made relatable despite their outlandish circumstances and the fantastical problems they face, it strikes a very strong balance between otherworldly concepts and the unbending nature of the human condition.  The actual prose of the writing is distinct and flavorful, but without the overpowering sense that the writer trying too hard which is seen all too often in fantasy works.  The wider setting has a vast supply of lore to dig your claws into if that's something that motivates you, and even if that isn't your thing, each of the major factions are distinct enough in their core presentation that the surface-level enjoyment.  The player character is both nameless and faceless but despite this you are given ample opportunities to roleplay during quests and dialogue.

Next on the docket is the visual/audio aspects; I think it is not incorrect to say that Dread Delusion is known best by outside observers for its distinct visuals, the generous use of strong color makes it stand out among the many open-world RPGs that go for a more subdued color palette, this approach does a very good job of selling the varied alien landscapes, with the magenta neuron star always looming overhead.  A lot of care is put into relatively minor visual details, especially with the animations, the best examples of this are with the compass and spellbook, things which few games would put the extra effort into animating.  Visuals only falter in situations where some characters could maybe have models that better reflect their flavor.  The music tracks are good, with each fitting well into its assigned role in the experience, and the overall sound design is very satisfying, attacks are impactful and weird flora or fauna sound appropriately weird.  

The gameplay has its own high points, but it's also where low points start to appear.  The game feels good to play on a tactile level, movement is very smooth and the combat behaves mostly how you want it to apart from some very questionable collision with projectile spells.  I played my first playthrough on Normal, where the game is definitely too easy, as all of my 3 deaths occurred outside of combat.  I get the feeling, though, that the game would not be much more difficult on hard, as enemies have a very short attention span and are not good at giving the player chase, a problem which is exacerbated if the player is using tools that facilitate this even more.  The ease of escaping from enemies makes stealth mostly superfluous, as there is little to no threat in being caught outside of encounters in extremely tight spaces where you have restricted movement.

The RPG mechanics were done fairly well, the different statistics that make up the player character each have their own defined place in the game and everything sees regular usage, rings and trinkets make up a lot of your more granular character build aspects, and in the late-game you get access to specialized equipment upgrades that further solidify your chosen playstyle.  I found that combat-wise a lot of the mechanics just weren't needed, but this could just as easily be a side effect of playing on a relatively lower difficulty setting so I will not say anything definitive on that.  Spells are mostly good with some questionable choices, offensive spells tend to be different flavors of magic projectile, while utility stuff tends to have more going on.  I played what is essentially a pure caster for my playthrough, so i got a pretty thorough look at most of the magic in the game, and while the core mechanics made it enjoyable, more variety in the tactile caster experience would have been appreciated.

The most mixed bag is probably the exploration, on one hand, there are a lot of beautiful vistas and unique locations to visit, many of which are tied to quests which means they get to benefit from the writing element.  The puzzles, minor platforming, and minor obstacles which incorporate your character's skillset make exploration itself fun, and the possibilities that open up once you obtain your airship are honestly mindblowing.  Enemy variety manages to be good enough to not be a noticeable problem, as you are regularly encountering bizarre new threats to fight.  The problem which arises with the exploration is the incentives for exploring, mostly gear progression, which has very questionable pacing.  You only find new types of weapon to use in the 2nd or 3rd regions you visit despite the game having an upgrade system where you pick up different weapons at poor quality and upgrade them, if you want to preserve your resources for a more interesting weapon, you are going to be swinging around the rusty sword from the start of the game for a while.  You pick up ammunition from the start of the game despite there being no ranged weapon in sight for hours, and the amount of different weapons, armor, and spells in the game just does not match the amount of exploration there is to do overall.  This results in a lot of space between major pickups with a LOT of minor loot in-between and the occasional Delusion fragment (collectible exp) or ring/trinket.  This becomes less of a problem in the late-game where you almost feel showered with powerful goodies, but the first two-thirds of the game are rough in this regard.  Meanwhile, you also have to be careful using the minor loot you get, as player homes are very resource-intensive to fully upgrade (save up that goddamn jitterseed).

As a final note; I am very tired.  goodnight.

The Morrowind-esque visuals drew me to Dread Delusion, but once I got into it I found a tremendously imaginative game containing some of the most difficult role-playing choices I had to make in 2024. Just to give a taste of the game’s creativity - within the game’s lore, the language of the Gods of creation is called Cipher. One of the game’s islands is ruled by an AI programmed in this language, and it can therefore create out of thin air the goods that are needed by the island’s people. But as a collection of code, such an entity is vulnerable to malware. What happens when such an entity is hacked? Is this liability worth tolerating with such potential on the line? The AI’s ability to create only compounds the damage that it can do. What if it was coded to manufacture hemorrhagic viruses, or demons? If I’d gotten lost a fewer times or had a bit more fun with the combat, Dread Delusion would’ve ranked higher, but even as it stands the Oneiric Isles are a locale well worth visiting.

-You will die A LOT, but Converter rewards persistence. This is a game for platforming masochists.
-You will also explore a lot, solve a bunch of great puzzles, and will get hooked on collecting skill spheres and finding out what's next.
-Story is a bit vague but it makes sense in the end. Lots of 4th wall breaking done in a sensible way.
-Graphics are clean and the world is cleverly interconnected. 
-Progression is weird and there is a delayed gratification component in it. You will collect a skill and seemingly nothing will change. But once you actually get the chance to come back to previous map parts you will notice how superior you are to your former self. I think the developer has done this on purpose because the whole underlying idea of the game is incremental self improvement and patience while going through the hard times. 
-The game is not without issues though. Some animations are clunky and wooden, and the voice acting can be questionable at times. I personally found the line ridiculing vegans a bit too dowdy.

If you are a metroidvania lover and an avid completionist like me this may be the most satisfying game you will play in a long time.

I have played my fair share of the free demo already, and was looking forward to the games release. The game is great fun to be honest, it doesn't come at a very hefty price, which I think is a nice bonus. 

The gameplay is fun, the controls are very simple and it's easy to understand how to play. The artstyle and characters are beyond adorable and the levels start to get decently challenging rather quickly. 
Another thing I really like is that you do not have a single clue if you're beating the level the intended way (if there even is an intended way) or if you are just absolutely winging it but somehow still saving all the little potatoes.

The one in game thing that can sometimes be a little annoying is that whever you finish a level, the "level complete" screen is in a set position, meaning if you've been looking around while playing, you're gonna have to look around to find it. (This can also be difficult for people who are not used to being in VR).

Another thing I really hope the devs plan to add is custom levels. The game on release has 60 levels and I am not sure if there are plans to add more, but having a custom level creator would allow for the game to have near infinite content, which already sounds great.

Overall I would definetly recommend this game, its great fun.

Played on a Quest 2 over Air Link, with 22 levels completed at the time of this review.

A VR title that feels like "the full package" of what it tries to be.
Humble concept on the surface, but a delivery that sets it apart in the market. Near flawless polish, great attention to detail artistically, and a consistency that fellow VR players will know is lacking in most games, even today.

The challenges posed by these levels are very engaging, due to the unique combination of VR navigation and interaction, on top of the more traditional Lemmings-type game, but set in a 3D environment. With this, you will be juggling and multitasking, but with a limited range of vision, which really keeps you on your toes.

A round requires you to pre-plan, predict and quickly adapt to changing situations, and even sometimes inventing your own solutions on the fly. One example of this, that I found myself doing more than once, is quickly throwing down jumping pads to re-route spuds that I had lost control of, in tandem with controlling the main group. Pulling that off is intensely satisfying, because the game didn't outright intend for me to do that, but I had the agency to make it happen.

If there's anything to criticise, I would say that this game is too good to have any association with mobile game tropes like 3 collectible stars per level, and the level select screen's design. Though the game does very well with those things, it is clear to me that the developers are more than capable of annihilating those tropes with their own unique take on either.

Cute and challenging (especially if you're trying to get all the stars) puzzle game.

Some people complain about the platforming sections but if I don't know why this is an issue because the majority of puzzle games have some form of platforming these days and the platforming sections weren't bad at all.

I'll certainly be watching this devs future games.

If you're looking for a cozy yet spooky puzzler, Strange Horticulture is it. The graphics are fantastic, the story is intriguing, and the puzzles require you to really use your noggin without being too hard. I loved running my own gloomy little plant shop and helping to solve a murder mystery along the way. Absolutely recommend!

I loved this game far more than I anticipated. Its gloomy-yet-cozy aesthetic created an engaging but casual experience, and the art styles compliment each other perfectly. The game itself isn't very complicated and most of the puzzles aren't overly difficult, but I found plant identification to be the most satisfying part. The potion crafting seems to be a bit of an afterthought and I wish there were more to it than the handful of recipes that are made available throughout game-play. Another merit of this game is how it dispenses the lore of the world, and uncovering the whole story requires replaying the game to unlock every ending--which doesn't take too long at all.
I think that with the price point a lot of what you're paying for is atmospheric, so if you're not interested in that you might want to find a different mystery/crafting game. I really hope that we might get some DLC (maybe potion-centric?) in the future, but I highly doubt it since Bad Viking is already moving on to Strange Antiquites--which I eagerly await.

You can complete this game in one day if you commit to it. There's a little bit of confusion in the very beginning because there's not too much of a tutorial, or none at all, but it's simple and intuitive enough that you can pretty much guess your way to it. The answers to puzzles are pretty clear cut, there's no ambiguity about what plant is what when you really look at the details. Even then, it still makes you think for a second. The multiple endings are also fun. If you're a completionist, this game scratches all those itches. If you play right, you can gain all endings with maybe one or two playthroughs and then just jump back to some save points. At the end of every playthrough you're able to also complete your big book of plants to identify every single ingredient in the game. It's definitely fun and doesn't drag on at all. 
Short and sweet while still giving a good bit of dark lore.

It's a beautiful game, and much more so if you're into horror, Celtic culture and occultism. I am not even into that kind of thing and I can still recommend the game. It is quite satisfying to identify a plant and give it to the customer knowing that it will have the desired effect - or the complete opposite, if that is your inclination. The puzzles and mysteries are great fun and give a huge sense of accomplishment when completed.

The one caveat I have to give relating this is that there is much to learn and know, but this is countered by the fact that there is no hurry, and one can spend as much time exploring, identifying plants in the book, or organizing the shelves as one desires, and can progress to the next customer at any point they desire.
Perfect game for when you're sick (I am sick and it was perfect). Puzzles and gameplay are simple but still engaging, and cataloging all the plants is very satisfying.

In this Super cute, cozy, spooky puzzler, you get to run your very own gloomy plant shop and help out the locals which unravels a unique story! What more could you wish for!
It's an incredibly soothing game. If you're fond of this genre, you should absolutely get it and immerse yourself in its experience, especially during these cold and gloomy days!

Not a very long game, but one I enjoyed quite a bit. There is something calming about labelling all your plants, yet there is a spooky mystery story that draws you on. Enjoyed the atmosphere and the characters. And of course, there is Hellebore!

I would put this is kinda a similar bucket as Long Live the Queen (but not anime). You absolutely have to have more patience than I do since it can be kind of a slow burn. A few of the puzzles I eye rolled.

Friends played this in discord with all of them trying to figure it out. That'd definitely be a better experience since getting hard stuck eventually turns into, "I have run out of patience and am just looking it up."

I will have to come back for the rest of the achievement but I feel like I'll want to and a replay would be fun. Get it on sale, absolutely worth for $5. I will probably pick up their next game regardless of my reservations.
I absolutely recommend this mysterious puzzle/story game. The flavor text is great. The endings are all well made and interesting!

All-round is pretty fun. The story is the highlight, NPCs and choices are the best part, the gameplay is kinda rough. I wish there was a hard mode, as the game guides you through a lot of puzzles I'd have rather figured out myself. All the endings have a good satisfying pay-off, and were fun to aim for.

The game is kinda easy for most of it (you can use unlimited hints for free/ without downside, you have unlimited time, you can make a couple of mistakes, game tells you exactly what you need to give someone)

The only difficulty imo comes from map riddles to find more flowers, as you can't get any hints there. Which can just soft-lock you if you can't figure it out.
 Aside from that, difficulty is more a tediousness/ annoyance. If you click the wrong map square, you're now forced to wait for a minute to recharge and try again. You need to find 3 flowers by there latin names for no reason. The game only gives you a partial clue and doesn't explain that, etc.

My main issue with it is how there's no real way to fail. I feel like a timer would be nice, if you spend too long not doing anything they leave (or die cause you get 1 poisoned person you need to cure.)

I also ran into an issue a couple times where someone would ask for a flower I didn't yet have, and I couldn't solve the map-puzzle to find where it was. Which then forces you to water plants/ wait for a minute after each attempt. That's so tedious and annoying, I'd rather die and start over again. Or be awarded/ punished for not solving a map puzzle early, and being unable to do it when the person is standing there.

The death puzzles are really fun!! I wish they were used more.

The music was nice, the moment I realized what was going on, I started to aim for a specific ending and actually managed to get it, which was really satisfying.

(mild) SPOILERS BELOW

Being able to 'fail' by running out of time/ them storming off would also allow for more choices in what plants to give. Generally you're basically forced to give them the 1 plant they want, even if they tell you they're planning something bad with it, which kinda sucks. For some story events you're able to pick between 2 plants, but the game spells out which plants those are.

Really impressed by the variety of little riddles that never got boring, and there's something magical in the timing of clues-dropping: I regularly went from confounded to excited about an idea to thrilled that I figured out a delightful mechanic. Really scratches the itch for weird little occulty secrets hermitcore.
That alone was compelling and satisfying enough to make this a memorable & happily recommendable game to me.

What I did NOT expect, and was very excited to find out, was for the full game to ALSO go so intricate and deep with the storyline. I got really invested in the story and characters, to the point of exclaiming "NO, [name]!!" a couple times at least, and gasping at an endgame reveal I absolutely did not see coming but made me go "Oh right, that was a thing!!" (and made me really emotional and touched).

All in all, if you're looking for something relaxing with a just enough challenge to engage you, but not too much to stress over, this is a quaint little game, and I look forward to playing their spiritual successor title.

And I say this because the first time I played this game, it took me a while to get used to the controls. Other than that, this is a solid game.

Hashed out world, good map structure. It's just a bit more confusing than I think it was trying to be.

tl;dr This game is absolutely worth the less than $5 I got it for.
Would I pay $16 for it?
...
Ehhhhh? The problem with going for a strictly puzzle-game route is that once you solve them, you're unlikely to play them again, lovely as this entry into the genre is, even for other "endings"/achievements, when it doesn't seem like there's going to be much difference between aforementioned endings and your route through the story is pretty linear where you can basically get everything done in a single playthrough. 
Not to mention the fact that I beat SH in roughly 5 hours not particularly thinking I was doing anything in a hurry. Gameplay only covers, like, 16 or 17 days or something? And I have plant-based games I got on Big Fish Games back in the day for half their selling point for SH that I spent twice as much time in.
That being said, the sound design, artwork, and music are lovely, and the atmosphere of the shop is so calming. There were a couple of moments where I did wish that you could intentionally not give folks something they came to you for, and towards the end I wanted to be able to click on the label of a plant I had correctly identified as it was in the "hooray you got it" animation so the game would label it automatically and I didn't have to go find it to do it myself, ha!
All in all, I'm honestly excited that these devs are working on a follow-up and if I'm able to do so, will support the second installment full price simply because I ended up enjoying this one so much and I'd like to see them continue!
